topic.title: Classicism
topic.framework: The fixed base is Bacon and Dorr’s Classicism (C) in their relational type system. Types are generated from e and t by forming sigma→tau when tau is not e; every non-base type therefore ends in t. C is the smallest H-theory containing Logical Equivalence (Classicism, §1.3): lambda abstractions of H-equivalent formulas are identical. Preserve the theoremhood side condition; equivalence under optional assumptions does not satisfy it.

topic.notation: All type schemata use the fixed relational type system. Types and application associate to the right; curried application is parenthesized. Box applies after closing object variables. See Background for definitions and schema side conditions.

principles.name: Actuality
principles.statement: There is a true proposition that entails every true proposition.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.2, p. 25.

changes.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
changes.summary: At Cian Dorr’s request: Actual Profile, formerly its own principle, is now this principle’s form actual-profile, with the two results connecting them as its equivalence.

variants.name: Actual Profile
variants.statement: Every finite tuple has a true relational profile entailing every relation it instantiates; the tuple may be empty.
variants.formal: $\forall\bar x^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,\exists Y^{\bar\sigma t}\, .\,Y[\bar x]\land\forall Z^{\bar\sigma t}\, .\,Z[\bar x]\to Y\le Z$
variants.equivalence: Form to official: specialize Actual Profile to the empty tuple, so that its relation variables have type $t$; it then says that there is a true proposition entailing every truth. Official to form (Classicism, §2.2, n. 31): let $w$ witness Actuality. At a tuple $\bar x$, use the relation $\lambda\bar y\, .\,w\land\bar y=\bar x$. It holds at $\bar x$. If $Z[\bar x]$ is true, $w$ entails that truth, and NI preserves the tuple identities, so the relation entails $Z$. This gives the profile at every tuple of types.

principles.name: Analytic Necessitism
principles.statement: If there could be a real number structure, there is a rigid one that is necessarily a real number structure: a rigid property with necessarily distinct instances, with rigid order, addition, multiplication and natural numbers, which necessarily form a complete ordered field. One sentence for each type $\sigma$.
principles.definitions: See Background, Analysis, for real number structures and $\operatorname{RigidStr}$: $X$, $\le$, $+$, $\times$ and $N$ rigid in the map's sense (persistent and inextensible, each with its leading box) and the instances of $X$ necessarily distinct.
sources: Neil Barton and Zachary Goodsell, Continuum Contingency, draft of 14 October 2026, §5.8, eqs. (30)–(32), Theorems 4–5, and §5.9, Theorem 7.
Andrew Bacon, Could the truths of mathematics have been different?, draft of 9 October 2025, §5, p. 24, and Appendix C.2, the rigid and inflexible real number structures of Lemmas C.4–C.7.
Formulation without Rigid Comprehension by Zachary Goodsell, 23 October 2026, recorded by Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic).

references.note: Their First-Order Continuum Necessitism says that the reals, the rigid properties of natural numbers, are a rigid property with necessarily distinct instances; persistence and necessary distinctness being theorems there, its content is the Inextensibility of Reals, eq. (32). Rigid properties of numbers represent every set of numbers only under Rigid Comprehension, which their setting assumes.
Bacon's rigid and inflexible real number structures, with the rigidity of the canonical reals and of their power as the route to the Necessity of Analysis.

principles.about: The entity-level counterpart of the Necessity of Analysis: not only are the truths of analysis fixed, the continuum itself is a necessary existent with a fixed membership and structure. Asking for some rigid real number structure, rather than for the rigidity of the reals defined as rigid properties of numbers, keeps the principle a definite claim in every theory extending C: under Rigid Comprehension it says what Barton and Goodsell's principle says, and without Rigid Comprehension it is simply false wherever no rigid continuum exists. The antecedent makes it trivially true at types that cannot carry a continuum; where a continuum is merely possible it demands an actual rigid one. The relations must be rigid as well as the domain: a rigid domain alone could carry differently threaded field structures at different worlds, which code different sets of naturals and so differ on first-order analytical sentences.
principles.notes: Implies the Necessity of Analysis ([[analytic-necessitism-implies-necessity-of-analysis]]), by the induction of Barton and Goodsell's Theorem 7 run on the given structure; the two come apart over a ground model with enough large cardinals, where new reals can appear while projective truth is forcing-invariant. Under □Rigid Comprehension and necessary infinity at $\sigma$, the instance at the type of properties of numbers is Rigid Power at $\mathbb N_\sigma$: Rigid Power says that the rigid properties of numbers cannot acquire new members, and the field structure on them is definable and rigid. A record of that implication waits on a principle of necessary infinity, which the map does not yet have. Fails in [[stitched-cohen-extension]], where the ground model's reals are no longer complete at the extension.

principles.name: Arithmetic Necessitism
principles.statement: Given that necessarily zero is not a successor and successor is injective on numbers, the numbers at $\sigma$ form a rigid property with necessarily distinct instances. One sentence for each type $\sigma$.
principles.formal: $\Box I^*_\sigma\to\operatorname{Rigid}(\mathbb N_\sigma)\land \forall m\,n\in\mathbb N_\sigma\, .\,m\ne n\to\Box\,m\ne n$
principles.definitions: See Background for $I^*_\sigma$, $\mathbb N_\sigma$ and $\operatorname{Rigid}$. The numbers are the finite cardinalities of properties of type $\sigma$, so, unlike Analytic Necessitism, no existential quantifier over structures is needed: the principle is about the canonical numbers themselves. The antecedent is Barton and Goodsell's axiom of Infinity at $\sigma$, eq. (22); where it fails the instance is trivial.
sources: Neil Barton and Zachary Goodsell, Continuum Contingency, draft of 14 October 2026, §5.8, eq. (29), and Theorem 3, there attributed to Goodsell 2021.
Zachary Goodsell, Arithmetic is Necessary, draft of 5 June 2024, for the numbers as finite cardinalities.

references.note: Their First-Order Arithmetic Necessitism, with the naturals as the Fregean numerical relations on properties of individuals; the map's numbers at $\sigma=e$ are those cardinalities.
The numbers $\mathbb N_\sigma$, $\mathbf 0_\sigma$, $\operatorname{Suc}_\sigma$ and $I^*_\sigma$.

principles.notes: The entity-level counterpart of the Necessity of Arithmetic: not only are the truths of arithmetic fixed, the numbers are a necessary existent with fixed membership. Provable with □Rigid Comprehension ([[necessary-rigid-comprehension-implies-arithmetic-necessitism]], Barton and Goodsell's Theorem 3). It also holds in C5 ([[c5-implies-arithmetic-necessitism]]), where B and BF make the persistent property of being a number inextensible. Without such help what can fail is inextensibility: numbers are necessarily numbers in C, but at a world where no property has exactly the numerals as its extension, $\mathbb N_\sigma$, the least inductive property, gains members there.

changes.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
changes.summary: Notes updated: C5 gives Arithmetic Necessitism ([[c5-implies-arithmetic-necessitism]]).

principles.name: Atomicity
principles.statement: Every non-bottom entity of each relational type has an atom below it.
principles.formal: $\forall x^\tau\, .\,x\le_\tau\neg_\tau x\lor\exists y^\tau\, .\,\operatorname{Atom}_\tau(y)\land y\le_\tau x\qquad(\tau\ne e)$
principles.definitions:
where $\operatorname{Atom}_	au(y):= orall z^	au\, .\,(z\le_	au y\land z
e y)\leftrightarrow z\le_	au
eg_	au z$:
the entities strictly below $y$ are exactly the bottom elements of $	au$. In particular an atom is
not itself bottom. Here $x\le_	au
eg_	au x$ says that $x$ is bottom.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.2, p. 24.

references.note: Bacon states the same principle as the Weak Leibniz Biconditionals, with atoms in place of atoms, and notes that Classicism calls its substantive direction Atomicity.

changes.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
changes.summary: Added the alias Weak Leibniz Biconditionals and a reference to Bacon’s 2024 book; the statement is unchanged.

changes.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Zachary Goodsell
changes.summary: Added the alias Leibniz Biconditionals (Bacon 2025). In Could the truths of mathematics have been different? (§5, p. 23; Appendix A.3, Figure 2) the Leibniz Biconditionals quantify over world relations in the unboxed sense, so they are this principle; the statement is unchanged.

principles.about:
At type $t$, entailment orders the propositions, and an atom is a maximally specific possibility: a
proposition that is possible and settles every proposition one way or the other. Atomicity says that
every possible proposition is entailed by such a possibility. So the propositions behave as if they
were sets of possible worlds, with the atoms as the worlds. At a type $\sigma\to t$ the same holds for
properties, ordered by necessary inclusion.

Atomicity says nothing about how many atoms there are or which of them obtains. That some atom is true
is Actuality. That every property of propositions has a meet is Boolean Completeness. Together the two
make the propositions isomorphic to the powerset of the atoms.

variants.name: Dual form
variants.statement: Whatever is entailed by every atom of its type is the top element of that type.
variants.formal: $\forall x^\tau\, .\,(\forall y^\tau\, .\,\operatorname{Atom}_\tau(y)\to y\le_\tau x)\to\neg_\tau x\le_\tau x\qquad(\tau\ne e)$
variants.equivalence:
In C each relational type is a Boolean algebra under $\le_\tau$, with $\neg_\tau$ an order-reversing
involution; $x\le_\tau\neg_\tau x$ says that $x$ is the bottom element, and $\neg_\tau x\le_\tau x$
that it is the top. An atom $y$ is not bottom (take $z:=y$ in the definition). It also lies below
$z$ or below $\neg_\tau z$ for every $z$: the meet $y\land z$ lies below $y$, so it is either $y$
itself or bottom.

Official form to dual form. Suppose every atom lies below $x$. Apply Atomicity to $\neg_\tau x$. If
$\neg_\tau x$ is bottom, $x$ is top. Otherwise some atom lies below $\neg_\tau x$ and below $x$, hence
below bottom, which is impossible.

Dual form to official form. Suppose $x$ is not bottom but no atom lies below it. Then every atom lies
below $\neg_\tau x$, so by the dual form $\neg_\tau x$ is top and $x$ is bottom, a contradiction.

principles.name: Atomicity (type t)
principles.statement: Every non-bottom proposition has an atom below it.
principles.definitions:
where $\operatorname{Atom}_t(q):= orall r\, .\,(r\le q\land r
e q)\leftrightarrow r\le
eg r$: the propositions strictly below $q$ are exactly the bottom ones, so an atom is not itself bottom; $p\le
eg p$ says that $p$ is bottom.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.2, p. 24.
principles.notes: The type $t$ instance of [[atomicity-r]].

changes.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
changes.summary: At Cian Dorr’s request: the statement now says what the principle says; the notes link to the unrestricted form; definitions of its technical terms added.

variants.name: Dual form
variants.statement: Whatever is entailed by every atom is necessary.
variants.formal: $\forall p\, .\,(\forall q\, .\,\operatorname{Atom}_t(q)\to q\le p)\to\Box p$
variants.equivalence: The argument for the dual form of Atomicity, at type $t$, where $\neg p\le p$ says that $p$ is necessary.

principles.name: Atomlessness
principles.statement: Atomlessness in the displayed closed propositional formulation.
principles.formal: $\forall p\, .\,\Diamond p\to\exists q\, .\,\Diamond q\land q\le p\land q\ne p$
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, Appendix D, p. 76.

principles.name: Atoms are self-atoms
principles.statement: At each relational type, every atom is a self-atom: necessarily, if it is instantiated, it is an atom.
principles.definitions: where $\Diamond_\sigma X:=X\ne\bot_\sigma$ and $\operatorname{SelfAtom}_\sigma(X):=\Diamond_\sigma X\land\Box(\exists\bar x\, .\,X\bar x\to\operatorname{Atom}_\sigma(X))$: a self-atom is a possible entity that is necessarily an atom whenever it is instantiated; for a proposition, one that, wherever it is true, is the actual-world proposition there (Background, Self-atoms).
sources: Cian Dorr, the notion of a self-atom, Self-Atomicity (Self-Atomism) and the four bridge principles, 25 October 2026.
principles.notes: Bridge principle (Cian Dorr, 25 October 2026): atoms stay atoms wherever they hold. With Atomicity it gives Self-Atomicity, and it follows from [[atoms-are-strong-atoms-r]]. In a full action model it says that no non-identity arrow $m$ has $m\circ k=k$ for an arrow $k$ out of the evaluation object.

principles.name: Atoms are self-atoms (type t)
principles.statement: Every atom is a self-atom: necessarily, if it is true, it is an atom.
principles.definitions: where $\operatorname{SelfAtom}_t(p):=\Diamond p\land\Box(p\to\operatorname{Atom}_t(p))$: a self-atom is a possible proposition that necessarily, if true, is an atom; equivalently, in C, one that entails that it is the actual world, $\Box(p\to\forall q\, .\,q\to p\le q)$.
sources: Cian Dorr, the notion of a self-atom, Self-Atomicity (Self-Atomism) and the four bridge principles, 25 October 2026.
principles.notes: The type $t$ instance of [[atoms-are-self-atoms-r]]. Bridge principle (Cian Dorr, 25 October 2026): atoms stay atoms wherever they hold. With Atomicity it gives Self-Atomicity, and it follows from [[atoms-are-strong-atoms-r]]. In a full action model it says that no non-identity arrow $m$ has $m\circ k=k$ for an arrow $k$ out of the evaluation object.

principles.name: Atoms are strong atoms
principles.statement: At each relational type, every atom is a strong atom: it necessarily entails every entity of the type or its negation.
principles.definitions: where $\Diamond_\sigma X:=X\ne\bot_\sigma$ and $\operatorname{SAtom}_\sigma(W):=\Diamond_\sigma W\land\Box\forall Y^\sigma\, .\,W\le_\sigma Y\lor W\le_\sigma\neg_\sigma Y$ is a strong atom (Background, Strong atoms)
sources: Cian Dorr, the notion of a self-atom, Self-Atomicity (Self-Atomism) and the four bridge principles, 25 October 2026.
principles.notes: Bridge principle (Cian Dorr, 25 October 2026): exactly what Strong Atomicity adds to Atomicity, since the two together are equivalent to them, and what BF supplies in Bacon’s Exercise 8.12. It is the conjunction of [[atoms-are-self-atoms-r]] and [[self-atoms-are-strong-atoms-r]] only given [[self-atoms-are-atoms-r]]: the free-monoid model satisfies it while a non-atomic self-atom fails to be strong.

principles.name: Atoms are strong atoms (type t)
principles.statement: Every atom is a strong atom.
principles.definitions: where $\operatorname{SAtom}_t(W):=\Diamond_t W\land\Box\forall q\, .\,W\le_t q\lor W\le_t\neg_t q$ is a strong atom (Background, Strong atoms)
sources: Cian Dorr, the notion of a self-atom, Self-Atomicity (Self-Atomism) and the four bridge principles, 25 October 2026.
principles.notes: The type $t$ instance of [[atoms-are-strong-atoms-r]]. Bridge principle (Cian Dorr, 25 October 2026): exactly what Strong Atomicity adds to Atomicity, since the two together are equivalent to them, and what BF supplies in Bacon’s Exercise 8.12. It is the conjunction of [[atoms-are-self-atoms-r]] and [[self-atoms-are-strong-atoms-r]] only given [[self-atoms-are-atoms-r]]: the free-monoid model satisfies it while a non-atomic self-atom fails to be strong.

principles.name: Axiom of Infinity (type e)
principles.statement: There are not finitely many individuals. No finite cardinality holds of the universal property, so the domain of the type cannot be exhausted by finitely many steps from the empty property.
sources: Cian Dorr, suggestion of 19 September 2026.
Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.3, n. 47, p. 32.

references.note: The draft's informal infinity claim, which the map had recorded only in its schematic form.

principles.notes: See Background for $\mathbf{0}$, $\operatorname{Suc}$ and $\operatorname{FiniteCardinality}$. The quantified form is what is normally meant by an axiom of infinity. It implies the schema of the same name, and the converse fails by a compactness argument, so the two are kept as separate principles. Possible Infinity (type e), this axiom under a diamond, is recorded as a separate principle.

principles.name: Axiom of Infinity (type t)
principles.statement: There are not finitely many propositions. No finite cardinality holds of the universal property, so the domain of the type cannot be exhausted by finitely many steps from the empty property.
sources: Cian Dorr, suggestion of 19 September 2026.
Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.3, n. 47, p. 32.

references.note: The draft's informal infinity claim, which the map had recorded only in its schematic form.

principles.notes: See Background for $\mathbf{0}$, $\operatorname{Suc}$ and $\operatorname{FiniteCardinality}$. The quantified form is what is normally meant by an axiom of infinity. It implies the schema of the same name, and the converse fails by a compactness argument, so the two are kept as separate principles. Possible Infinity (type t), this axiom under a diamond, is recorded as a separate principle.

principles.name: BF
principles.statement: The Barcan Formula at every type. The predicate formulation closes the formula schema using lambda abstraction.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, Proposition 2.1, pp. 20–21.

variants.name: Polyadic form
variants.statement: BF for relations with any finite number of arguments.
variants.formal: $\forall X^{\bar\sigma t}\, .\,(\forall\bar x^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,\Box X[\bar x])\to\Box(\forall\bar x^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,X[\bar x])$
variants.equivalence: The original form is the case of a one-element tuple. Conversely, apply BF one variable at a time from the innermost. From $\forall x_1\ldots x_n\, .\,\Box X[\bar x]$, BF at $\sigma_n$, applied to $\lambda x_n\, .\,X[x_1\ldots x_n]$, gives $\forall x_1\ldots x_{n-1}\, .\,\Box\forall x_n\, .\,X[\bar x]$; repeat $n$ times. For the empty tuple both sides are $\Box X$.

variants.name: Dual form
variants.statement: If possibly something has a property, then something possibly has it.
variants.formal: $\forall X^{\sigma t}\, .\,\Diamond(\exists x^\sigma\, .\,Xx)\to\exists x^\sigma\, .\,\Diamond Xx$
variants.equivalence:
Instantiate either form at the negations of its propositional or relational variables, contrapose, and rewrite with $\Diamond=
eg\Box
eg$ and $q\le r\leftrightarrow
eg r\le
eg q$. This yields the other form, and the same steps lead back.

variants.name: Dual polyadic form
variants.statement: If possibly some tuple stands in a relation, then some tuple possibly stands in it.
variants.formal: $\forall X^{\bar\sigma t}\, .\,\Diamond(\exists\bar x^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,X[\bar x])\to\exists\bar x^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,\Diamond X[\bar x]$
variants.equivalence:
Instantiate either form at the negations of its propositional or relational variables, contrapose, and rewrite with $\Diamond=
eg\Box
eg$ and $q\le r\leftrightarrow
eg r\le
eg q$. This yields the other form, and the same steps lead back. Combined with the polyadic form, this gives the equivalence with the official form.

variants.name: Weak rigidity of the universal property
variants.statement: The universal property, of being something, is weakly rigid.
variants.formal: $\operatorname{WeaklyRigid}(\lambda z^\sigma\, .\,\top)$
variants.equivalence: $\lambda z\, .\,\top$ is weakly persistent in C, since $\Box\top$. Its weak inextensibility says that for every $Z$, if $\forall z\, .\,\top\to\Box Zz$ then $\lambda z\, .\,\top\le Z$, that is, $(\forall z\, .\,\Box Zz)\to\Box\forall z\, .\,Zz$: BF at $Z$. So the form is equivalent to BF at $\sigma$, instance by instance. See [[weak-rigidity-predicates]].

principles.name: BF (relational types)
principles.statement: The Barcan Formula at every relational type, that is, at every type other than e.
principles.formal: $\forall X^{\sigma t}\, .\,(\forall x^\sigma\, .\,\Box Xx)\to\Box(\forall x^\sigma\, .\,Xx)\qquad(\sigma\ne e)$
sources: Cian Dorr, suggestion of 11 October 2026.

references.note: Bacon's theorem concludes □BF at every relational type.

principles.notes: The restriction of [[barcan-r]] to the relational types, between BF and [[barcan-t]]. Bacon's Theorem 8.2 derives its necessitation from □Strong Atomicity and Rigid Comprehension. It does not imply BF: in full-two-object-chain-new-individual it holds, necessarily, while BF fails at type e. Nor does □BF (type t) imply it: stitched-cohen-extension and stitched-cohen-coalesced-middle have □BF (type t) and BF at type e, but not BF at type et.

principles.name: BF (type t)
principles.statement: If every proposition necessarily has a property, then necessarily every proposition has it.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §3.5, p. 59.
principles.notes: The type $t$ instance of [[barcan-r]].

variants.name: Dual form
variants.statement: If possibly some proposition has a property, then some proposition possibly has it.
variants.formal: $\forall X^{tt}\, .\,\Diamond(\exists p\, .\,Xp)\to\exists p\, .\,\Diamond Xp$
variants.equivalence:
Instantiate either form at the negations of its propositional or relational variables, contrapose, and rewrite with $\Diamond=
eg\Box
eg$ and $q\le r\leftrightarrow
eg r\le
eg q$. This yields the other form, and the same steps lead back.

principles.name: Boolean Completeness
principles.statement: Every property of entities of a relational type has a greatest lower bound in that type.
principles.definitions:
where $\operatorname{GLB}_\tau(y,X):=\forall z^\tau\, .\,(\forall w^\tau\, .\,Xw\to z\le_\tau w)\leftrightarrow
z\le_\tau y$: the lower bounds of $X$ are exactly the entities below $y$.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.2, pp. 23–24.
principles.about:
Classicism already makes each relational type a Boolean algebra under entailment, with finite meets
and joins: conjunction, disjunction and negation, pointwise at types $\sigma\to t$. Boolean
Completeness adds infinitary meets. However many entities a property collects, there is a strongest
entity entailed by all of them, the conjunction of the property's instances at type $t$. It is
needed whenever a construction conjoins an arbitrary collection of propositions, for instance in
building a world as the conjunction of all truths.

It fails in most of the finite-support action models, where the would-be meet of an infinite property need
not be pinned down by any finite set. Dorr's symmetric models show that it does not bring Rigid
Comprehension with it.

variants.name: Least-upper-bound form
variants.statement: Every property of entities of a relational type has a least upper bound in that type.
variants.formal: $\forall X^{\tau t}\, .\,\exists y^\tau\, .\,\operatorname{LUB}_\tau(y,X)\qquad(\tau\ne e)$
variants.definitions:
where $\operatorname{LUB}_\tau(y,X):=\forall z^\tau\, .\,(\forall w^\tau\, .\,Xw\to w\le_\tau z)\leftrightarrow
y\le_\tau z$: the upper bounds of $X$ are exactly the entities above $y$.
variants.equivalence:
Negation reverses the order and is an involution in C, so it exchanges least upper bounds and
greatest lower bounds. Given $X^{\tau t}$, let $X^\neg:=\lambda z\, .\,X(\neg_\tau z)$. For any $z$,
$z$ is an upper bound of $X$ iff $\neg_\tau z$ is a lower bound of $X^\neg$. So if $y$ is a greatest
lower bound of $X^\neg$, then for every $z$: $z$ is an upper bound of $X$ iff
$\neg_\tau z\le_\tau y$ iff $\neg_\tau y\le_\tau z$. That is, $\neg_\tau y$ is a least upper bound
of $X$. The converse direction is symmetric. Each instance at $\tau$ uses the other form only at
the same $\tau$.

Background records the same equivalence where it defines $\operatorname{LUB}$.

principles.name: Boolean Completeness (type t)
principles.statement: Every property of propositions has a greatest lower bound.
principles.definitions: where $\operatorname{GLB}_t(p,X):=\forall q\, .\,(\forall r\, .\,Xr\to q\le r)\leftrightarrow q\le p$: the lower bounds of $X$ are exactly the propositions entailing $p$.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.2, pp. 23–26; Appendix D, n. 92, p. 74.
principles.notes: The type $t$ instance of [[boolean-completeness-r]].

variants.name: Least-upper-bound form
variants.statement: Every property of propositions has a least upper bound.
variants.formal: $\forall X^{tt}\, .\,\exists p\, .\,\operatorname{LUB}_t(p,X)$
variants.equivalence: The argument for the least-upper-bound form of Boolean Completeness, at type $t$.
variants.definitions: where $\operatorname{LUB}_t(p,X):=\forall q\, .\,(\forall r\, .\,Xr\to r\le q)\leftrightarrow p\le q$: the upper bounds of $X$ are exactly the propositions entailed by $p$.

principles.name: Converse Witnessed Possibility
principles.statement: The converse of Witnessed Possibility, with precisely the same formula, type and constant side conditions.
principles.formal: $\Diamond P[\bar c/\bar x]\to(\exists\bar x\, .\,P)\quad(P\text{ pure, free variables among }\bar x;\ \bar c\text{ distinct constants of }\Sigma)$
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.5, n. 57, p. 38.

variants.name: Dual form
variants.statement: If a pure formula holds of everything, it is necessary of any distinct constants.
variants.formal: $(\forall\bar x\, .\,P)\to\Box P[\bar c/\bar x]\quad(P\text{ pure, free variables among }\bar x;\ \bar c\text{ distinct constants of }\Sigma)$
variants.equivalence:
Pure sentences (resp. sentences of $\mathcal L(\Sigma)$) are closed under negation, so the instance of either form at $
eg P$ is, after contraposition and $\Diamond=
eg\Box
eg$, the instance of the other at $P$.

principles.name: Countable Boolean Completeness
principles.statement: Every countable property of entities of a relational type has a least upper bound in that type, where a property is countable relative to a type $\sigma$ when it injects into the finite cardinalities of properties of type $\sigma$; one instance for each $\sigma$.
principles.definitions: where $\operatorname{LUB}_\tau(y,X):=\forall z^\tau\, .\,(\forall w^\tau\, .\,Xw\to w\le_\tau z)\leftrightarrow y\le_\tau z$: the upper bounds of $X$ are exactly the entities above $y$.
sources: Zachary Goodsell, Arithmetic is Necessary, draft of 5 June 2024, §3.1, eq. (10), p. 8; Definition 6, p. 13.

references.note: The source states the principle for property types $\sigma t$ with least upper bounds; the map ranges over every relational type, as its Boolean Completeness does. The source leaves the number type $\nu$, $0$ and successor as parameters; the map takes them to be $(\sigma t)t$, $\mathbf{0}_\sigma$ and $\operatorname{Suc}_\sigma$ for every type $\sigma$, a schema in $\sigma$.

principles.notes: See Background for $\operatorname{Ctbl}$ and $\operatorname{LUB}$. The restriction of Boolean Completeness to countable properties; the least-upper-bound form is used to match the source, and is equivalent in C to a greatest-lower-bound form, since the pointwise negation of a countable property is countable. The source's hypothesis that the properties form a countably complete Boolean algebra modulo necessary equivalence. Countability is measured at every type $\sigma$: where $\sigma$ has only finitely many members the instances are trivial, so the principle has content whenever some type is infinite, not only when there are infinitely many individuals. It suffices for the Necessity of Arithmetic at each $\sigma$ and is therefore incompatible with Maximalist Classicism.

changes.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
changes.summary: Made the type at which countability is measured schematic. The principle had fixed the source's number type at $(et)t$, so countable meant injectable into the finite cardinalities of individuals, and with finitely many individuals the principle held trivially. The old principle is the instance $\sigma=e$ of the new one, which is therefore stronger; verdicts that the old principle holds because there are few individuals are withdrawn.

variants.name: Greatest-lower-bound form
variants.statement: Every countable property of entities of a relational type has a greatest lower bound in that type.
variants.formal: $\forall X^{\tau t}\, .\,\operatorname{Ctbl}_{\sigma,\tau}(X)\to\exists y^\tau\, .\,\operatorname{GLB}_\tau(y,X)\qquad(\tau\ne e)$
variants.equivalence:
As for the least-upper-bound form of Boolean Completeness: negation exchanges least upper bounds of $X$ and greatest lower bounds of $X^
eg:=\lambda z\, .\,X(
eg_	au z)$. Negation is a bijection between the instances of $X$ and of $X^
eg$, so composing it with an injection into the natural numbers counted at $\sigma$ shows that $X^
eg$ is countable relative to $\sigma$ iff $X$ is.
variants.definitions: where $\operatorname{GLB}_\tau(y,X):=\forall z^\tau\, .\,(\forall w^\tau\, .\,Xw\to z\le_\tau w)\leftrightarrow z\le_\tau y$: the lower bounds of $X$ are exactly the entities below $y$.

principles.name: ND
principles.statement: Distinct things of any type are necessarily distinct.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.1, pp. 21–22.

variants.name: Polyadic form
variants.statement: Distinct tuples of entities are necessarily distinct.
variants.formal: $\forall\bar x\,\bar y^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,\bar x\ne\bar y\to\Box(\bar x\ne\bar y)$
variants.equivalence:
The original form is the case of a one-element tuple. Conversely, if $ ar x
e ar y$ then $x_i
e y_i$ for some $i$, and ND at $\sigma_i$ gives $\Box(x_i
e y_i)$, hence $\Box( ar x
e ar y)$. For the empty tuple, $ ar x
e ar y$ is false.

variants.name: Dual form
variants.statement: Things of any type that could be identical are identical.
variants.formal: $\forall x y^\sigma\, .\,\Diamond(x=y)\to x=y$
variants.equivalence: Each instance of one form is the contrapositive of the corresponding instance of the other.

variants.name: Dual polyadic form
variants.statement: Tuples that could be identical are identical.
variants.formal: $\forall\bar x\,\bar y^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,\Diamond(\bar x=\bar y)\to\bar x=\bar y$
variants.equivalence: Each instance of one form is the contrapositive of the corresponding instance of the other. Combined with the polyadic form, this gives the equivalence with the official form.

principles.name: ND (type t)
principles.statement: Distinct propositions are necessarily distinct.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, Proposition 2.2, p. 22.
principles.notes: The type $t$ instance of [[distinctness-necessary-r]].

variants.name: Dual form
variants.statement: Propositions that could be identical are identical.
variants.formal: $\forall p q\, .\,\Diamond(p=q)\to p=q$
variants.equivalence: Each instance of one form is the contrapositive of the corresponding instance of the other.

principles.name: Truths are ND-necessary
principles.statement: Every truth is ND-necessary, that is, necessary under the distinctness-preserving modality.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, Appendix E, p. 83.
principles.notes: Formerly named Distinctness-preserving collapse; renamed on 14 October 2026 when the Varieties of necessity category was added at the suggestion of Christopher Sun. The id is unchanged.

variants.name: Dual form
variants.statement: Whatever is possible under the distinctness-preserving modality is true.
variants.formal: $\forall p\, .\,\Diamond_{\ne}p\to p$

principles.name: Maximalism (pure)
principles.statement: Every closed pure identity not provable in C is false. The non-theorem condition is metalinguistic.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.4, pp. 35–36.
principles.notes: The reference theory in the side condition is the fixed background C. Until 8 October 2026 this was Distinctness Maximalism (pure), with Possibility Maximalism (pure) a separate principle, provably equivalent; they were unified at Cian Dorr's direction, the distinctness form official since it remains the interesting one over logics weaker than Classicism.

variants.name: Possibility form
variants.statement: Every closed pure sentence consistent with C is possible.
variants.formal: $\Diamond P\quad(P\text{ closed and pure; }C+P\text{ consistent})$
variants.equivalence:
Possibility to Distinctness: if a closed identity $A=B$ is not a theorem of C, its negation is consistent with C, so the possibility form gives $\Diamond(A
e B)$; by NI, $A=B$ would make this impossible, so $A
e B$. Distinctness to Possibility: if $P$ is consistent with C, the closed identity $
eg P=	op$ is not a theorem of C, so the distinctness form gives $
eg P
e	op$, equivalently $\Diamond P$.

principles.name: Maximalism (signature Σ)
principles.statement: The Maximalism schema for the fixed nonlogical signature Σ: every closed identity of its language not provable in C(Σ) is false.
principles.formal: $A\ne B\quad(A=B\text{ closed in }\mathcal L(\Sigma);\ C(\Sigma)\nvdash A=B)$
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.5, pp. 37–39.
principles.notes: Until 8 October 2026 this was Distinctness Maximalism (signature Σ), with Possibility Maximalism (signature Σ) a separate principle, provably equivalent; they were unified at Cian Dorr's direction.

variants.name: Possibility form
variants.statement: Every closed sentence of the language of Σ consistent with C(Σ) is possible.
variants.formal: $\Diamond P\quad(P\text{ closed in }\mathcal L(\Sigma);\ C(\Sigma)+P\text{ consistent})$
variants.equivalence:
Possibility to Distinctness: if a closed identity $A=B$ is not a theorem of C(Σ), its negation is consistent with C(Σ), so the possibility form gives $\Diamond(A
e B)$; by NI, $A=B$ would make this impossible, so $A
e B$. Distinctness to Possibility: if $P$ is consistent with C(Σ), the closed identity $
eg P=	op$ is not a theorem of C(Σ), so the distinctness form gives $
eg P
e	op$, equivalently $\Diamond P$.

principles.name: Extensionality
principles.statement: At each relational type, coextensive relations are identical; include the nullary propositional case.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §1.4, pp. 15–16.

principles.name: Finite-Type Analytic Necessitism
principles.statement: If a real number structure is possible at a type, there is a rigid, necessarily real structure at that same type. Its iterated rigid powers represent every admitted subset at each possibility, through any specified finite height. There is one sentence for each host type and finite height.
principles.formal: $\Diamond\exists\mathfrak R\, .\,\operatorname{Real}_\tau(\mathfrak R)\;\to\; \exists\mathfrak R\, .\,\operatorname{RigidStr}(\mathfrak R)\land \Box\operatorname{Real}_\tau(\mathfrak R)\land \operatorname{RepPower}_1(\mathsf P^{n+1}(X),\mathsf P^n(X))\qquad(n\ge0)$
principles.definitions: $X^{\tau t}$ is the carrier of the returned real number structure. Use the definitions of $\operatorname{Real}_\tau$, $\operatorname{RigidStr}$ and represented powers from Background, Analysis: the carrier, order, field operations and numberhood are rigid, and carrier members are necessarily distinct. Put $\mathsf P^0(X)=X$ and $\mathsf P(Y)=\lambda A\, .\,\operatorname{Rigid}(A)\land A\le Y$; $\operatorname{RepPower}_1(\mathsf P(Y),Y)$ includes rigidity of the power and necessary representation of every admitted predicate on $Y$. Types and finite heights are metalinguistic schema indices. The real carrier stays at the same host $\tau$ on both sides; successive powers have their native higher predicate types.
sources: GPT-6 Astra, prompted by Daniel Kodsi, Finite-Type Necessitism and Analytic Non-Contingency, source dated 30 October 2026, §4, Definition 2 and Theorem 8, pp. 6–8.

references.note: The existing analytic and second-order analytic principles extended by finite power iteration.

principles.about: Second-Order Analytic Necessitism represents relations of every finite arity on a real carrier. This principle also asks for successive powers: families of subsets, families of those families, and so on to any specified finite depth. The highest power clause supplies the preceding clauses for that same fixed witness. No infinite tuple of witnesses or cumulative code is asserted.
principles.notes: Finite-Type Necessitism together with Analytic Necessitism suffices ([[finite-type-necessitism-and-analytic-necessitism-imply-finite-type-analytic-necessitism]]). It implies Second-Order Analytic Necessitism ([[finite-type-analytic-necessitism-implies-second-order-analytic-necessitism]]) and its existing truth-non-contingency consequences. It may be vacuous where no real structure is possible; no implication back to guarded Finite-Type Necessitism without activation is asserted. The definition does not require higher powers to fit into the original real carrier's host type.

principles.name: Finite-Type Necessitism
principles.statement: If the canonical arithmetic at a type is necessarily genuine, its numbers have a rigid power containing representatives of every admitted subset, at every possibility. The same requirement applies after any specified finite number of iterations of this power construction. There is one sentence for each source type and finite height.
principles.definitions: Put $\nu_\sigma=(\sigma t)t$, $H_{\sigma,0}=\mathbb N_\sigma$ and $H_{\sigma,n+1}=\mathsf P(H_{\sigma,n})$, where $\mathsf P(X):=\lambda A\, .\,\operatorname{Rigid}(A)\land A\le X$. Inclusion is necessary inclusion. Rigidity and $I^*_\sigma$ have the definitions in Background; $\Box I^*_\sigma$ says that the canonical successor necessarily omits zero and is injective on the canonical numbers. For this canonical power, $\operatorname{RepPower}_1(\mathsf P(X),X)$ is $\operatorname{Rigid}(\mathsf P(X))\land \Box\forall F\exists G\in\mathsf P(X)\, .\,\forall x\in X\, .\,Fx\leftrightarrow Gx$. Fullness ranges over every admitted predicate. Types and finite heights are metalinguistic schema indices, not object-language quantifiers. If $X$ has type $\alpha t$, its power has type $(\alpha t)t$.
sources: GPT-6 Astra, prompted by Daniel Kodsi, Finite-Type Necessitism and Analytic Non-Contingency, dated 30 October 2026, §3, Definition 1 and Proposition 5, pp. 4–6; the accompanying Finite-type necessitism, companion proof notes, 29 October 2026, §§1,3–4 (unpaginated).

references.note: Arithmetic and continuum necessitism; the finite-type schema is the source's extension.

principles.about: The hierarchy starts with numbers, then subsets of numbers, then families of those subsets, and continues to any specified finite height. It fixes both the available mathematical objects and the fullness of their represented powers. Its first power already gives Arithmetic Necessitism.
principles.notes: Boxed Rigid Comprehension and current Rigid Power suffice ([[necessary-rigid-comprehension-and-rigid-power-imply-finite-type-necessitism]]). The necessary-arithmetic guard must be retained: the principle does not assert that a genuine arithmetic exists at any source. The guard alone supplies no unguarded implication to Non-contingency of CH. It does not put all levels into one host type or collect an infinite hierarchy. It implies [[arithmetic-necessitism]] by [[finite-type-necessitism-implies-arithmetic-necessitism]].

principles.name: 5-necessities are ND-necessary
principles.statement: Whatever is 5-necessary is ND-necessary.
principles.notes: Added at the suggestion of Christopher Sun, 14 October 2026. The converse implication is a theorem of C (Background, Hats, two-hat necessity and 5-necessity), so this principle says that the two operators are coextensive.

principles.name: Forcing Possibilism
principles.statement: Every complete Boolean algebra that is finite or has strictly fewer elements than there are propositions is isomorphic to the entailment algebra below some proposition other than top.
principles.formal: $\forall X^{\sigma t}\,\forall R^{\sigma\sigma t}\, .\, (\operatorname{CBA}(X,R)\land(\operatorname{Fin}(X)\lor X\prec\lambda p^t.\top)) \to\exists p^t\, .\,p\ne\top\land (X,R)\cong(\lambda q^t.\,q\le p,\le)$
principles.definitions: CBA says that R partially orders the Xs as a Boolean algebra and every property of Xs has a least upper bound. Fin means Dedekind finiteness, expressed with binary relations representing injections. X ≺ Y means that an injective relation from X to Y exists and none exists from Y to X; this is defined across the two carrier types. Isomorphism is witnessed by a binary relation giving an order-preserving and order-reflecting bijection. All these quantifiers are unboxed. Degenerate one-element Boolean algebras are allowed, represented by p = bottom. Type σ ranges over the map's admitted types, including e.
sources: Andrew Bacon, Arbitrarily Large Models of Classicism with BoxRigid Comprehension, Intensional Choice and Mathematical Possibilism, handout supplied 19 October 2026, §1 and §9.
principles.notes: Uses the handout's strict smallness convention (finite or strictly fewer propositions), attributed there to the body of Could the truths of mathematics have been different?. It does not use the appendix's non-strict reading, no bigger than the propositions. The two readings are not identified. No Lean verification is claimed.

references.note: Bacon's Mathematical Possibilism. The map's name records what the principle says, that every small complete Boolean algebra, hence every small forcing, is realised below some proposition.

changes.by: OpenAI Codex, prompted by Andrew Bacon
changes.summary: Linked the existing strict-smallness formulation to Modalized Domains §6.1; statement unchanged.

changes.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Zachary Goodsell
changes.summary: Renamed Forcing Possibilism, with Bacon's Mathematical Possibilism as an alias, and placed in the new category Mathematical contingency. Up to forcing equivalence, forcing notions are the complete Boolean algebras, so the principle says that every small forcing is broadly possible; the statement is unchanged.

principles.name: Fregean Axiom
principles.statement: Materially equivalent propositions are identical.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §1.4, pp. 15–16.

principles.name: Functional Choice
principles.statement: Every serial binary relation admits a selecting operation. Its output type is relational, as required by the type system.
principles.definitions: where $\operatorname{Serial}(U):=\forall x^\sigma\, .\,\exists y^\tau\, .\,(Ux)y$.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.3, pp. 31–33.

changes.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
changes.summary: At Cian Dorr’s request: definitions of its technical terms added.

variants.name: Polyadic form
variants.statement: Every serial relation from tuples admits a selecting operation of several arguments.
variants.formal: $\forall U^{\bar\sigma\tau t}\, .\,\operatorname{Serial}(U)\to\exists X^{\bar\sigma\tau}\, .\,\forall\bar y^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,(U[\bar y])(X[\bar y])\qquad(\tau\ne e)$
variants.equivalence: The original form is the case of a one-element tuple. Code tuples by their haecceities (Background, Polyadic forms). Given a serial $U$, put $U':=\lambda A\,y\, .\,(\exists\bar x\, .\,A=H_{\bar x}\land(U[\bar x])y)\lor\neg\exists\bar x\, .\,A=H_{\bar x}$, of type $(\bar\sigma t)\tau t$, which is serial. The original form gives $X'$ selecting from $U'$, and $X:=\lambda\bar y\, .\,X'(H_{\bar y})$ selects from $U$.

principles.name: Functionality
principles.statement: Operations with the same value on every argument are identical. The output type is relational.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §1.4, pp. 15–16, especially n. 18.

variants.name: Polyadic form
variants.statement: Operations of several arguments with the same value on every tuple of arguments are identical.
variants.formal: $\forall X Y^{\bar\sigma\tau}\, .\,(\forall\bar z^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,X[\bar z]=Y[\bar z])\to X=Y\qquad(\tau\ne e)$
variants.equivalence: The original form is the case of a one-element tuple. Conversely, by induction on the length of the tuple, one argument at a time. If $X[z_1\bar z']=Y[z_1\bar z']$ for all $z_1,\bar z'$, then for each $z_1$ the operations $Xz_1$ and $Yz_1$, of type $\sigma_2\cdots\sigma_n\tau$, agree on every tuple, so they are identical by the induction hypothesis. Functionality at $\sigma_1$ then gives $X=Y$. For the empty tuple the condition is $X=Y$ itself.

principles.name: Gallin Extensional Comprehension
principles.statement: Every relation is coextensive with one that is persistent and has a persistent pointwise negation. This is the source’s comparison with Gallin’s different rigidity convention.
principles.formal: $\forall X^{\bar\sigma t}\, .\,\exists Y^{\bar\sigma t}\, .\,\operatorname{Persistent}(Y)\land\operatorname{Persistent}(\neg Y)\land(X\equiv Y)$
principles.definitions: where $\operatorname{Persistent}(Y):=Y\le\lambda\bar x\, .\,\Box Y[\bar x]$, that is, $\Box\forall\bar x\, .\,Y[\bar x]\to\Box Y[\bar x]$.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.3, n. 37, p. 28.

references.locator: p. 77, as described in Classicism n. 37

principles.name: Independence (signature Σ)
principles.statement: No constant of Sigma is a pure operation applied to other constants: for a closed pure term A and distinct constants c, d_1,…,d_n with n ≥ 0, c differs from A applied to the d’s. With n = 0, no constant denotes a pure entity.
principles.formal: $c\ne A\,d_1\cdots d_n\quad(A\text{ closed and pure};\ c,d_1,\ldots,d_n\text{ distinct constants};\ n\ge0)$
sources: Andrew Bacon, Logical Combinatorialism, Philosophical Review 129 (2020), §4, p. 568 and n. 53.
principles.notes: Bacon’s independence of the fundamental, read for the constants of a fundamental language; his n. 53 derives it from Logical Necessity. The constant c has a relational type, since the applied term does.

principles.name: Inextensible Comprehension
principles.statement: Every relation, including a proposition, is coextensive with a inextensible one.
principles.definitions: where $\operatorname{Inextensible}(Y):=\Box\forall X\, .\,(\forall\bar x\, .\,Y[\bar x]\to\Box X[\bar x])\to Y\le X$.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.3, n. 38, p. 29.

principles.name: Infinity Schema (type e)
principles.statement: There are arbitrarily many pairwise distinct entities of this fixed type; one sentence for each positive integer n.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.3, n. 47, p. 32.
principles.notes: Schema-level reading of the source’s informal infinity claim; no choice-dependent equivalence with Dedekind infinity is assumed. One sentence for each n, so it is weaker than the quantified Axiom of Infinity (type e), which implies it. The converse fails by a compactness argument, which the map does not yet witness with a model.

principles.name: Intensional Choice
principles.statement: If a property is necessarily instantiated, then some property entailing it is necessarily uniquely instantiated.
principles.formal: $\forall F^{\sigma t}\, .\,\Box(\exists x^\sigma\, .\,Fx)\to\exists G^{\sigma t}\, .\,G\le F\land\Box\exists x^\sigma\, .\,(Gx\land\forall y^\sigma\, .\,Gy\to y=x)$
sources: Andrew Bacon, Could the truths of mathematics have been different?, draft of 9 October 2025, §6, p. 27.

references.note: Introduced as a modal version of choice, used with □Rigid Comprehension and Mathematical Possibilism for the contingency of CH (Theorem 6.1).

principles.notes: The source motivates it as a modalized generalization of interworld choice, which selects at each world one instance of a property instantiated at every world; the modal formulation needs no world propositions. The type $\sigma$ may be $e$. The selected property is unboxed: it exists at the evaluation point, but its unique instance may vary from world to world.

variants.name: Polyadic form
variants.statement: If a relation is necessarily instantiated, then some relation entailing it is necessarily uniquely instantiated.
variants.formal: $\forall F^{\bar\sigma t}\, .\,\Box(\exists\bar x^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,F[\bar x])\to\exists G^{\bar\sigma t}\, .\,G\le F\land\Box\exists\bar x^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,(G[\bar x]\land\forall\bar y^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,G[\bar y]\to\bar y=\bar x)$
variants.equivalence: The original form is the case of a one-element tuple. Code tuples by their haecceities (Background, Polyadic forms). Given $F$, the property $F':=\lambda A\, .\,\exists\bar x\, .\,A=H_{\bar x}\land F[\bar x]$ of type $(\bar\sigma t)t$ is necessarily instantiated. The original form at $\bar\sigma t$ gives $G'\le F'$ necessarily uniquely instantiated. Put $G:=\lambda\bar x\, .\,G'(H_{\bar x})$. Then $G\le F$. At each world the unique instance of $G'$ is a code $H_{\bar x}$, since $G'\le F'$, and by injectivity of coding $\bar x$ is then the unique instance of $G$.

principles.name: Logical Necessity
principles.statement: The Logical Necessity schema: necessity at distinct matching constants is equivalent to universal truth of the pure-formula. Preserve the side conditions of Witnessed Possibility.
principles.formal: $\Box P[\bar c/\bar x]\leftrightarrow(\forall\bar x\, .\,P)\quad(P\text{ pure, free variables among }\bar x;\ \bar c\text{ distinct constants of }\Sigma)$
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.5, n. 57, p. 38.

references.locator: Logical Necessity, cited in Classicism n. 57
references.note: Stated for a fundamental language; Bacon’s restatements with fundamentality and purity predicates (pp. 546–547) are not on the map.
Stated for a fundamental language; Bacon’s restatements with fundamentality and purity predicates (pp. 546–547) are not on the map.

principles.name: Modal Freedom (signature Σ)
principles.statement: For pure formulas P and Q with free variables among the disjoint tuples x and y, and distinct constants c and d of matching types, if P is possible at c and Q is possible at d then P and Q are jointly possible there.
principles.formal: $\Diamond P[\bar c/\bar x]\land\Diamond Q[\bar d/\bar y]\to\Diamond(P[\bar c/\bar x]\land Q[\bar d/\bar y])\quad(P,Q\text{ pure, free variables among }\bar x\text{ resp. }\bar y;\ \bar c\bar d\text{ distinct constants of }\Sigma)$
sources: Andrew Bacon, Logical Combinatorialism, Philosophical Review 129 (2020), §3, pp. 556–557, principle (5) and its generalization.
principles.notes: Bacon’s formalization of Schaffer’s Modal Freedom, stated for two distinct constants R and S of a fundamental language. The instance with no constants is equivalent to No Pure Contingency.

variants.statement: If a disjunction of pure formulas about disjoint constants is necessary, one of the disjuncts is necessary.
variants.formal: $\Box(P[\bar c/\bar x]\lor Q[\bar d/\bar y])\to\Box P[\bar c/\bar x]\lor\Box Q[\bar d/\bar y]\quad(P,Q\text{ pure, free variables among }\bar x\text{ resp. }\bar y;\ \bar c\bar d\text{ distinct constants of }\Sigma)$
variants.equivalence:
The instance of either form at $
eg P,
eg Q$ is, after contraposition and $\Diamond=
eg\Box
eg$, the instance of the other at $P,Q$.

principles.name: Modal Well-Ordering
principles.statement: Every type, including e, has a relation that is necessarily a well-order of it.
principles.definitions: where $\operatorname{WO}(R)$ says that $R$ well-orders the type: it is transitive, antisymmetric and total (so reflexive), and every instantiated property of type $\sigma t$ has an $R$-least instance.
sources: Cian Dorr, suggestion of 8 October 2026.
principles.notes: WO is defined in Background. The relation exists at the evaluation point, and at each world it well-orders what there is there; the order it induces may differ from world to world. A well-order need not be necessarily one, since distinct relata can be identical at other worlds, so this is stronger than Well-Ordering. It gives Intensional Choice at once (select the least instance), and it follows from Well-Ordering with Weak Rigid Comprehension and BF. It implies its own necessitation by 4, since $\Box\operatorname{WO}(R)$ gives $\Box\Box\operatorname{WO}(R)$, so no boxed form is recorded.

principles.name: Modalized Relational Choice
principles.statement: Every necessarily serial relation is entailed by a necessarily functional relation.
principles.formal: $\forall R^{\sigma\tau t}\, .\,\Box\operatorname{Serial}(R)\to\exists S^{\sigma\tau t}\, .\,\Box\operatorname{Functional}(S)\land S\le R$
principles.definitions: where $\operatorname{Serial}(U):=\forall x^\sigma\, .\,\exists y^\tau\, .\,(Ux)y$; and $\operatorname{Functional}(U):=\forall x^\sigma\, .\,\exists y^\tau\, .\,(Ux)y\land\forall z^\tau\, .\,(Ux)z\to y=z$.
sources: Cian Dorr, suggestion of 11 October 2026.
principles.notes: Due to Cian Dorr. It implies Intensional Choice (its polyadic form at the empty tuple is Intensional Choice) and Relational Choice; □Relational Choice with Intensional Choice implies it, the necessarily instantiated property of being a functional subrelation of a necessarily serial relation being necessarily uniquely instantiated below. Whether unboxed Relational Choice with Intensional Choice suffices is open: the argument needs the functional subrelations to exist at every world. Boxed, □Modalized Relational Choice is equivalent to □Relational Choice with □Intensional Choice. It implies its own necessitation ([[modalized-relational-choice-implies-necessary-modalized-relational-choice]]), so it is equivalent to □Relational Choice with Intensional Choice, and to its boxed form.

variants.name: Entailing form
variants.statement: Every relation is entailed by one that necessarily relates each thing bearing the first relation to something to exactly one thing.
variants.formal: $\forall R^{\sigma\tau t}\, \exists S^{\sigma\tau t}\, .\,S\le R\land\Box\forall x^\sigma\, .\,(\exists y^\tau\, .\,(Rx)y)\to\exists y^\tau\, .\,(Sx)y\land\forall z^\tau\, .\,(Sx)z\to y=z$
variants.equivalence: From the entailing form: if $R$ is necessarily serial, an $S$ as there is necessarily functional. To the entailing form: given $R$, $R':=\lambda xy\,.\,\neg\exists z\,(Rx)z\lor(Rx)y$ is necessarily serial, every type being inhabited in C; take a necessarily functional $S'\le R'$ and put $S:=\lambda xy\,.\,(S'x)y\land(Rx)y$. Then $S\le R$, and necessarily, if $x$ bears $R$ to something, the unique $S'$-value of $x$ is an $R$-value, so the unique $S$-value.

variants.name: Polyadic form
variants.statement: Every necessarily serial relation from tuples is entailed by a necessarily functional one.
variants.formal: $\forall R^{\bar\sigma\tau t}\, .\,\Box\operatorname{Serial}(R)\to\exists S^{\bar\sigma\tau t}\, .\,\Box\operatorname{Functional}(S)\land S\le R$
variants.equivalence: The original form is the case of a one-element tuple. Conversely, code tuples by their haecceities $H_{\bar x}$ (Background, Polyadic forms). Given a necessarily serial $R$, put $R':=\lambda A\,y\,.\,(\exists\bar x\,.\,A=H_{\bar x}\land(R[\bar x])y)\lor\neg\exists\bar x\,.\,A=H_{\bar x}$, of input type $\bar\sigma t$. It is necessarily serial: at each world a code is the haecceity of a tuple there, and $R$ is serial there. The original form gives a necessarily functional $S'\le R'$, and $S:=\lambda\bar x\,y\,.\,(S'H_{\bar x})y$ is necessarily functional and entails $R$, the coding being injective. At the empty tuple the polyadic form is Intensional Choice.

variants.name: Polyadic entailing form
variants.statement: The entailing form for relations from tuples.
variants.formal: $\forall R^{\bar\sigma\tau t}\, \exists S^{\bar\sigma\tau t}\, .\,S\le R\land\Box\forall\bar x^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,(\exists y^\tau\, .\,(R[\bar x])y)\to\exists y^\tau\, .\,(S[\bar x])y\land\forall z^\tau\, .\,(S[\bar x])z\to y=z$
variants.equivalence: The two equivalences above combined: the polyadic form and the polyadic entailing form are related as the original form and the entailing form, by the same construction with tuples in place of single arguments.

sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.1, pp. 21–23; §§2.2–2.3, pp. 25–34.

principles.formal: $\Box\forall x^\tau\, .\,x\le_\tau\neg_\tau x\lor\exists y^\tau\, .\,\operatorname{Atom}_\tau(y)\land y\le_\tau x\qquad(\tau\ne e)$

e y)\leftrightarrow z\le_	au
eg_	au z$: the entities strictly below $y$ are exactly the bottom elements of $	au$, so an atom is not itself bottom; $x\le_	au
eg_	au x$ says that $x$ is bottom.

principles.name: □Atomlessness

principles.name: □Atoms are self-atoms
principles.statement: Necessarily, at each relational type, every atom is a self-atom: necessarily, if it is instantiated, it is an atom.
principles.definitions: where $\Diamond_\sigma X:=X\ne\bot_\sigma$ and $\operatorname{SelfAtom}_\sigma(X):=\Diamond_\sigma X\land\Box(\exists\bar x\, .\,X\bar x\to\operatorname{Atom}_\sigma(X))$: a self-atom is a possible entity that is necessarily an atom whenever it is instantiated; for a proposition, one that, wherever it is true, is the actual-world proposition there (Background, Self-atoms).

principles.name: □Atoms are self-atoms (type t)

principles.name: □Atoms are strong atoms

references.note: □Functional Choice is the principle valid in the Gallin and Williamson models, from which Bacon and Dorr derive S5, Strong Atomicity, Rigid Comprehension and Boolean Completeness.

principles.name: □Plenitude
principles.statement: Necessarily, every total single-valued binary relation is represented by an operation. Its output type is relational, as required by the type system.
principles.definitions: where $\operatorname{Functional}(U):=\forall x^\sigma\, .\,\exists y^\tau\, .\,(Ux)y\land\forall z^\tau\, .\,(Ux)z\to y=z$.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.1, pp. 21–23; §§2.2–2.3, pp. 25–34.
OpenAI Codex, prompted by Daniel Kodsi, Adjunctions, atom projection, and persistent worlds, 28 October 2026, §§1–5; Pure uniformity and one necessary atom, §§3–4 (both unpaginated).
principles.notes: The necessitated form of [[plenitude-r]]. The additional atom forms use whole relational Boolean order. Necessary atomhood includes necessary nonzeroness; it is stronger than the strong-atom condition that allows the atom to become bottom.

variants.name: Polyadic form
variants.statement: Necessarily, every total single-valued relation from tuples is represented by an operation of several arguments.
variants.formal: $\Box\forall U^{\bar\sigma\tau t}\, .\,\operatorname{Functional}(U)\to\exists X^{\bar\sigma\tau}\, .\,\forall\bar y^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,(U[\bar y])(X[\bar y])\qquad(\tau\ne e)$
variants.equivalence: Each instance of the polyadic form of Plenitude is derivable in C from finitely many instances of the original form, and conversely; the derivations are on the page of the unboxed principle. Necessitating them and applying K carries the equivalence to the boxed forms.

variants.name: Necessarily atomic worlds
variants.statement: Necessarily, some true proposition necessarily remains an atom, including remaining nonzero.
variants.formal: $\Box\exists w^t\, .\,w\land\Box\operatorname{Atom}_t(w)$
variants.equivalence: The persistent-atoms proof on this page shows that this gives necessary ND at t and necessary Actuality, hence C5 and Atomicity, and therefore □Plenitude. Conversely, □Plenitude gives C5, Atomicity and necessary Actuality; atoms persist under C5 and the true atoms witness this form. The source is OpenAI Codex, prompted by Daniel Kodsi, 28 October 2026, §§1–5.

variants.name: Persistent atomic coverage at one relational type
variants.statement: Every nonzero relation contains a relation that necessarily remains an atom. Any one fixed relational type suffices.
variants.formal: $\forall R^\rho\, .\,R\ne\bot_\rho\to\exists a^\rho\, .\,\Box\operatorname{Atom}_\rho(a)\land a\le_\rho R\qquad(\rho\ne e)$
variants.equivalence: Existential projection takes necessarily atomic relations to necessarily atomic propositions. Coverage at t makes a true necessary atom necessarily available, giving the previous equivalent form. Conversely, □Plenitude gives Atomicity and C5; BF and necessary ND make each atom remain an atom. The proof is on this page. The type ρ is fixed externally, not quantified inside the formula.

principles.name: □Relational Choice
principles.statement: Necessarily, every serial binary relation has a functional subrelation.
principles.formal: $\Box\forall U^{\sigma\tau t}\, .\,\operatorname{Serial}(U)\to\exists S^{\sigma\tau t}\, .\,\operatorname{Functional}(S)\land(\forall x y\, .\,(Sx)y\to(Ux)y)$
principles.definitions: where $\operatorname{Serial}(U):=\forall x^\sigma\, .\,\exists y^\tau\, .\,(Ux)y$; and $\operatorname{Functional}(U):=\forall x^\sigma\, .\,\exists y^\tau\, .\,(Ux)y\land\forall z^\tau\, .\,(Ux)z\to y=z$.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.3, pp. 31–33.
Andrew Bacon, A Philosophical Introduction to Higher-Order Logics, Routledge, 2024, §8.4, pp. 175–176.

references.note: □Functional Choice is the principle valid in the Gallin and Williamson models, from which Bacon and Dorr derive S5, Strong Atomicity, Rigid Comprehension and Boolean Completeness.

principles.notes: The necessitated form of [[relational-choice-r]]. Added at Cian Dorr’s request on 22 September 2026, after the coalesced roots showed Relational Choice holding at a root while failing at accessible worlds.

principles.name: □Self-Atomicity
principles.statement: Necessarily, at each relational type, every possible entity (one distinct from bottom) is entailed by a self-atom: a possible entity that necessarily, if instantiated, is an atom.
principles.formal: $\Box\forall X^\sigma\, .\,\Diamond_\sigma X\to\exists Q^\sigma\, .\,\operatorname{SelfAtom}_\sigma(Q)\land Q\le_\sigma X\qquad(\sigma\ne e)$
principles.definitions: where $\Diamond_\sigma X:=X\ne\bot_\sigma$ and $\operatorname{SelfAtom}_\sigma(X):=\Diamond_\sigma X\land\Box(\exists\bar x\, .\,X\bar x\to\operatorname{Atom}_\sigma(X))$: a self-atom is a possible entity that is necessarily an atom whenever it is instantiated; for a proposition, one that, wherever it is true, is the actual-world proposition there (Background, Self-atoms).
sources: Cian Dorr, the notion of a self-atom, Self-Atomicity (Self-Atomism) and the four bridge principles, 25 October 2026.
principles.notes: The boxed form of [[self-atomicity-r]].

principles.name: □Self-Atomicity (type t)
principles.statement: Necessarily, every possible proposition is entailed by a self-atom: a possible proposition that necessarily, if true, is an atom, that is, one that entails that it is the actual world.
principles.definitions: where $\operatorname{SelfAtom}_t(p):=\Diamond p\land\Box(p\to\operatorname{Atom}_t(p))$: a self-atom is a possible proposition that necessarily, if true, is an atom; equivalently, in C, one that entails that it is the actual world, $\Box(p\to\forall q\, .\,q\to p\le q)$.
sources: Cian Dorr, the notion of a self-atom, Self-Atomicity (Self-Atomism) and the four bridge principles, 25 October 2026.
principles.notes: The boxed form of [[self-atomicity-t]], and the type $t$ instance of [[necessary-self-atomicity-r]].

principles.name: □Self-atoms are atoms
principles.statement: Necessarily, at each relational type, every self-atom is an atom.
principles.definitions: where $\Diamond_\sigma X:=X\ne\bot_\sigma$ and $\operatorname{SelfAtom}_\sigma(X):=\Diamond_\sigma X\land\Box(\exists\bar x\, .\,X\bar x\to\operatorname{Atom}_\sigma(X))$: a self-atom is a possible entity that is necessarily an atom whenever it is instantiated; for a proposition, one that, wherever it is true, is the actual-world proposition there (Background, Self-atoms).
sources: Cian Dorr, the notion of a self-atom, Self-Atomicity (Self-Atomism) and the four bridge principles, 25 October 2026.
principles.notes: The boxed form of [[self-atoms-are-atoms-r]].

principles.name: □Self-atoms are atoms (type t)

principles.name: □Self-atoms are strong atoms
principles.statement: Necessarily, at each relational type, every self-atom is a strong atom: it necessarily entails every entity of the type or its negation.
principles.definitions: where $\Diamond_\sigma X:=X\ne\bot_\sigma$ and $\operatorname{SelfAtom}_\sigma(X):=\Diamond_\sigma X\land\Box(\exists\bar x\, .\,X\bar x\to\operatorname{Atom}_\sigma(X))$: a self-atom is a possible entity that is necessarily an atom whenever it is instantiated; for a proposition, one that, wherever it is true, is the actual-world proposition there (Background, Self-atoms); and $\operatorname{SAtom}_\sigma(W):=\Diamond_\sigma W\land\Box\forall Y^\sigma\, .\,W\le_\sigma Y\lor W\le_\sigma\neg_\sigma Y$ is a strong atom (Background, Strong atoms)
sources: Cian Dorr, the notion of a self-atom, Self-Atomicity (Self-Atomism) and the four bridge principles, 25 October 2026.
principles.notes: The boxed form of [[self-atoms-are-strong-atoms-r]].

principles.name: □Self-atoms are strong atoms (type t)

principles.name: □Strong Actuality

principles.name: □Strong Atomicity
principles.statement: Necessarily, at each relational type, every possible entity (one distinct from bottom) is entailed by a strong atom: a possible entity that necessarily entails every entity of the type or its negation.
principles.formal: $\Box\forall X^\sigma\, .\,\Diamond_\sigma X\to\exists W^\sigma\, .\,\operatorname{SAtom}_\sigma(W)\land W\le_\sigma X\qquad(\sigma\ne e)$
principles.definitions: where $\Diamond_\sigma X:=X\ne\bot_\sigma$ and $\operatorname{SAtom}_\sigma(W):=\Diamond_\sigma W\land\Box\forall Y^\sigma\, .\,W\le_\sigma Y\lor W\le_\sigma\neg_\sigma Y$: a strong atom is a possible entity that necessarily entails every entity of its type or its negation.
sources: Andrew Bacon, A Philosophical Introduction to Higher-Order Logics, Routledge, 2024, §8.2, pp. 166, 169–170.
principles.notes: The necessitated form of [[strong-atomicity-r]]. The boxed form is the one Theorem 8.2 of the book connects with □BF and □Atomicity. Since strong atoms are only required to be possible, not necessarily possible, the unboxed form does not yield 5; Exercise 8.13 shows that requiring the atoms to be necessarily atoms does.

principles.name: □Transversal Choice
principles.statement: Necessarily, every equivalence relation, at any type including e, has a transversal, that is, a property with exactly one instance in each of its cells.

principles.name: Atomicity by necessarily-world propositions
principles.statement: Every possible proposition is entailed by a proposition that is necessarily a world.
principles.definitions: Here a world is a propositional atom: $\operatorname{Atom}_t(w):=w\ne\bot\land\forall q^t\, .\,w\le q\lor w\le\neg q$, equivalently the atom predicate in Background. The order is algebraic entailment, so $w\le p$ is $\Box(w\to p)$. Necessary atomhood includes necessary nonzeroness; it does not assert that $w$ is necessarily true.
sources: OpenAI Codex, prompted by Daniel Kodsi, Adjunctions, atom projection, and persistent worlds, 28 October 2026, §§2–5, unpaginated; Pure uniformity and one necessary atom, §§3–4, unpaginated.

references.note: Boolean atoms, Actuality, and the native C5 equivalences used in the proof.
Weak worlds are propositional atoms; the necessary-atom requirement here is stronger than the strong-world condition that permits becoming bottom.

principles.about: This strengthens propositional Atomicity by requiring the witnessing world to remain a nonzero atom at every accessible evaluation. It is equivalent in C to [[necessary-plenitude-r]] and [[necessary-gallin-extensional-comprehension-r]].
principles.notes: The witness order is $\exists w\,\Box\operatorname{Atom}_t(w)$, not merely necessary existence of some atom. It is stronger than [[strong-atomicity-t]]: a strong atom may become bottom.

principles.name: Necessity of Analysis
principles.statement: Every first-order analytical sentence is either true in every real number structure in every possible world or false in every real number structure in every possible world. One sentence for each type $\sigma$ and each first-order analytical sentence.
principles.formal: $\Box\forall\mathfrak R\, .\,\operatorname{Real}_\sigma(\mathfrak R)\to A(\mathfrak R)\;\lor\; \Box\forall\mathfrak R\, .\,\operatorname{Real}_\sigma(\mathfrak R)\to\neg A(\mathfrak R)\quad (A\text{ a first-order analytical sentence})$
principles.definitions: See Background, Analysis: a real number structure at $\sigma$ is a complete ordered field on a property of type $\sigma t$ together with its natural numbers $N$, and a first-order analytical sentence is built from the field relations, $N$ and identity, with quantifiers over the field's elements. Any two real number structures are isomorphic in the non-modal fragment, so within a world all of them agree on $A$; the schema says that the worlds with a continuum agree too. It quantifies over all real number structures rather than fixing the reals as rigid properties of numbers, so it assumes neither Rigid Comprehension nor choice, and its instances at a type with no real number structure in any world are trivially true.
sources: Andrew Bacon, Could the truths of mathematics have been different?, draft of 9 October 2025, §5, p. 20, the schema The Necessity of Analysis, and n. 49.
Neil Barton and Zachary Goodsell, Continuum Contingency, draft of 14 October 2026, §5.7 (analytical sentences) and §5.9, Theorem 7.

references.note: Bacon's schema, with his first-order real number structures, which carry the naturals predicate. Without $N$ the first-order language is that of real closed fields, and Tarski's elimination of quantifiers makes every instance a theorem (n. 49); with it the first-order analytical sentences have the strength of second-order arithmetic.
Their first-order analytical sentences quantify over the rigid properties of natural numbers, the reals of their setting with Rigid Comprehension; under Rigid Comprehension the two readings agree.

principles.notes: The sentence-level counterpart of Analytic Necessitism, which implies it ([[analytic-necessitism-implies-necessity-of-analysis]]); weaker than Necessity of Second-Order Analysis, which covers the continuum hypothesis. C5 does not prove it: it fails in [[full-boolean-valued-atom-and-atomless-universe-constructible]], Bacon's Boolean-valued model of C5 with BF and Functional Choice built inside $L$, where "every real is constructible" is true at the actual world and false in the atomless component; the proof of [[c5-implies-necessity-of-arithmetic]] uses BF at the type of numbers, and nothing comparable controls new extensions of properties of numbers. It fails likewise in the stitched models built over $L$ ([[stitched-cohen-extension-universe-constructible]], [[stitched-ch-reversing-universe-constructible]]), with □Rigid Comprehension and □Atomicity at type $t$. In the same models built over an arbitrary ground model it is left unknown: with a proper class of Woodin cardinals, projective truth is invariant under set forcing and it holds in them.

changes.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
changes.summary: Notes updated: the models built in $L$ that refute it.

principles.name: Necessity of Arithmetic
principles.statement: Every arithmetical sentence is either necessarily true or necessarily false, given that possibly zero is not a successor and successor is injective on numbers, where the numbers are the finite cardinalities of properties of a type $\sigma$. One sentence for each type $\sigma$ and each arithmetical sentence at $\sigma$.
principles.formal: $\Box(I_\sigma\to A)\lor\Box(I_\sigma\to\neg A)\quad(A\text{ an arithmetical sentence at }\sigma)$
sources: Zachary Goodsell, Arithmetic is Necessary, draft of 5 June 2024, eq. (1), p. 2; Definition 8 and Theorem 9, pp. 19–21.

references.locator: eq. (1), p. 2; Definition 8 and Theorem 9, pp. 19–21
references.note: The source's necessity schema, with its parameters $\nu$, $0$ and successor taken to be $(\sigma t)t$, $\mathbf{0}_\sigma$ and $\operatorname{Suc}_\sigma$ for every type $\sigma$, so that its natural numbers are the finite cardinalities of properties of type $\sigma$.

principles.notes: See Background for $I_\sigma$ and for arithmetical sentences. The antecedent $I_\sigma$ is needed because the axioms of arithmetic are not theorems of C: if there is only one entity of type $\sigma$, the second numeral is the empty cardinality, so successor is not injective. In C the first conjunct of $I^*_\sigma$ is a theorem, so $I_\sigma$ amounts to the possible injectivity of $\operatorname{Suc}_\sigma$ on finite cardinalities, which Possibility Maximalism (pure) grants. Where $\sigma$ necessarily has finitely many members, $I_\sigma$ is necessarily false and the instances at $\sigma$ are trivial. Each instance is a closed pure sentence, so the schema follows from No Pure Contingency; it follows in C from Countable Boolean Completeness, at each $\sigma$ from the instances counting at the same $\sigma$, and it is incompatible with Possibility Maximalism (pure) by Gödel's first incompleteness theorem.

changes.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
changes.summary: Made the type whose finite cardinalities are the numbers schematic, as for Countable Boolean Completeness; the principle had fixed it at $e$. The old principle is the instance $\sigma=e$ of the new one.

principles.name: Necessity of Second-Order Analysis
principles.statement: Every second-order analytical sentence is either true in every real number structure in every possible world or false in every real number structure in every possible world. One sentence for each type $\sigma$ and each second-order analytical sentence.
principles.formal: $\Box\forall\mathfrak R\, .\,\operatorname{Real}_\sigma(\mathfrak R)\to A(\mathfrak R)\;\lor\; \Box\forall\mathfrak R\, .\,\operatorname{Real}_\sigma(\mathfrak R)\to\neg A(\mathfrak R)\quad (A\text{ a second-order analytical sentence})$
principles.definitions: See Background, Analysis. A second-order analytical sentence may quantify over relations of any finite arity among the type's entities, applied to the structure's elements; the continuum hypothesis is one. Bacon restricts the second-order quantifiers to rigid properties, which makes no difference under Rigid Comprehension (his Proposition C.3, Analytic Extensionality); the unrestricted reading is used so that the schema assumes nothing about rigidity.
sources: Andrew Bacon, Could the truths of mathematics have been different?, draft of 9 October 2025, §5, pp. 20–22, and Appendix C.2, Theorem C.2 with Proposition C.3.
Neil Barton and Zachary Goodsell, Continuum Contingency, draft of 14 October 2026, §5.7 and §5.9.

references.locator: §5, pp. 20–22; Appendix C.2, Theorem C.2, Proposition C.3

references.note: Their second-order analytical sentences, with classes of reals as rigid properties of reals.

principles.notes: Contains the Necessity of Analysis and the Non-contingency of the Continuum Hypothesis ([[necessity-of-second-order-analysis-implies-non-contingency-of-ch]]). Bacon's Theorem 5.2 derives it from Atomicity at every type and □Rigid Comprehension ([[atomicity-and-necessary-rigid-comprehension-imply-necessity-of-second-order-analysis]]), and his Corollary 5.1 from C5 and □Rigid Comprehension, which the map derives through □Actuality and Atomicity. His Theorem 5.1 gives a model of C5 with Rigid Comprehension, not necessitated, in which the continuum hypothesis is structurally contingent, and the stitched forcing models of Barton and Goodsell with a forcing that changes the continuum hypothesis refute it under □Rigid Comprehension; neither verdict is recorded yet.

principles.statement: Each closed sentence of the language of the fixed signature Sigma, if true, is necessary. A sentence schema, standing to No Pure Contingency as Possibility Maximalism (signature Σ) stands to Possibility Maximalism (pure).
principles.formal: $P\to\Box P\quad(P\text{ a closed sentence of }\mathcal L(\Sigma))$
sources: Cian Dorr, suggestion of 22 September 2026.

principles.notes: Holds in every one-world model whatever the constants denote, so it is consistent; but it is incompatible with Witnessed Possibility and hence with Logical Necessity, Separated Structure and Maximalist Classicism for Σ: a constant of relational type is possibly top and possibly not top under Witnessed Possibility, while this schema makes whichever obtains necessary.
