principles.name: Non-contingency of the Continuum Hypothesis
principles.statement: Either necessarily every real number structure satisfies the continuum hypothesis, or necessarily every real number structure falsifies it: that every subproperty of the continuum either injects into the natural numbers or is in bijection with the continuum. One sentence for each type $\sigma$.
principles.formal: $\Box\forall\mathfrak R\, .\,\operatorname{Real}_\sigma(\mathfrak R)\to\operatorname{CH}(\mathfrak R) \;\lor\;\Box\forall\mathfrak R\, .\,\operatorname{Real}_\sigma(\mathfrak R)\to \neg\operatorname{CH}(\mathfrak R)$
principles.definitions: See Background, Analysis, for $\operatorname{CH}(\mathfrak R)$, with injections and bijections as relations. This is the instance of the Necessity of Second-Order Analysis at the continuum hypothesis, kept apart because the sources treat it on its own. Which way it fails, true but possibly false or false but possibly true, is a matter of models, not of the principle.
sources: Andrew Bacon, Could the truths of mathematics have been different?, draft of 9 October 2025, §5, pp. 21–22 (Conjecture 5.1, Theorem 5.1), and §6, Theorem 6.1.
Neil Barton and Zachary Goodsell, Continuum Contingency, draft of 14 October 2026, §5.6, eq. (27), §5.9, and Theorems 20–24.

references.note: Bacon's structural contingency of the continuum hypothesis is the failure of this principle.
Their formulation of CH for the reals as rigid properties of naturals; here it is read in any real number structure.

principles.notes: Follows from the Necessity of Second-Order Analysis ([[necessity-of-second-order-analysis-implies-non-contingency-of-ch]]) and so, by Bacon's Theorem 5.2, from Atomicity with □Rigid Comprehension. Bacon's Theorem 6.1, that □Rigid Comprehension, Intensional Choice and Forcing Possibilism refute it, is recorded as a conjecture until its proof appears ([[necessary-rigid-comprehension-intensional-choice-and-forcing-possibilism-incompatible-with-non-contingency-of-ch]]). Of Barton and Goodsell's stitched models, the one adding a single Cohen real ([[stitched-cohen-extension]]) leaves the truth value of the continuum hypothesis unchanged and satisfies it; the instance of their Theorem 20 that adds $\aleph_2$ Cohen reals or collapses the continuum, by cases on CH ([[stitched-ch-reversing]]), refutes it, with □Rigid Comprehension and □Atomicity at type $t$. Bacon's Theorem 5.1 model of C5 with Rigid Comprehension also refutes it and is not recorded. It fails in [[full-boolean-valued-atom-and-atomless]], Bacon's Boolean-valued model of §B.2 with the algebra chosen by cases on CH, and it is incompatible with Maximalism ([[maximalism-incompatible-with-non-contingency-of-ch]]).

principles.name: Plenitude
principles.statement: Every total single-valued binary relation is represented by an operation. Its output type is relational, as required by the type system.
principles.definitions: where $\operatorname{Functional}(U):=\forall x^\sigma\, .\,\exists y^\tau\, .\,(Ux)y\land\forall z^\tau\, .\,(Ux)z\to y=z$.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.3, pp. 31–33.

variants.name: Polyadic form
variants.statement: Every total single-valued relation from tuples is represented by an operation of several arguments.
variants.formal: $\forall U^{\bar\sigma\tau t}\, .\,\operatorname{Functional}(U)\to\exists X^{\bar\sigma\tau}\, .\,\forall\bar y^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,(U[\bar y])(X[\bar y])\qquad(\tau\ne e)$
variants.equivalence: The original form is the case of a one-element tuple. Code tuples by their haecceities (Background, Polyadic forms). Given a functional $U$, put $U':=\lambda A\,y\, .\,(\exists\bar x\, .\,A=H_{\bar x}\land(U[\bar x])y)\lor(\neg\exists\bar x\, .\,A=H_{\bar x}\land y=\bot_\tau)$, which is functional by injectivity of coding; $\tau$ is relational, so $\bot_\tau$ exists. The original form at $\bar\sigma t$ gives $X'$ representing $U'$, and $X:=\lambda\bar y\, .\,X'(H_{\bar y})$ represents $U$.

principles.name: Possibility+ (pure)

sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.6, p. 41 and n. 60; Appendix E, p. 83.

references.locator: §2.6, p. 41 and n. 60; Appendix E, p. 83

principles.notes: The consistency and purity restrictions are inherited from Possibility Maximalism, which the surrounding text says this strengthens; the shortened display on p. 41 must not be read as admitting contradictory P.

principles.name: Possibility+ (signature Σ)
principles.statement: The Possibility+ schema for the fixed nonlogical signature Sigma: for a formula P of L(Sigma) consistent with C(Sigma) whose free variables are the displayed individual variables, if those individuals are pairwise distinct and distinct from every individual denoted by a constant occurring in P, then P is possible. Include the empty tuple.
principles.formal: $\forall x_1^e\cdots x_n^e\, .\,\bigl(\bigwedge_{i<j}x_i\ne x_j\land\bigwedge_{i,\,c}x_i\ne c\bigr)\to\Diamond P\quad(P\in\mathcal L(\Sigma),\text{ free variables among }x_1\ldots x_n;\ c\text{ over the individual constants in }P;\ C(\Sigma)+P\text{ consistent};\ n\ge0)$

principles.notes: The clause requiring the individuals to differ from the constants named in P is forced: without it the C(Σ)-consistent formula x ≠ c would yield ◇(c ≠ c).

variants.name: Dual form
variants.statement: If a formula of the signature is necessary of some individuals and its negation is consistent with C(Σ), two of those individuals are identical or one of them is denoted by a constant of the formula.
variants.formal: $\forall x_1^e\cdots x_n^e\, .\,\Box P\to\bigl(\bigvee_{i<j}x_i=x_j\lor\bigvee_{i,\,c}x_i=c\bigr)\quad(P\in\mathcal L(\Sigma),\text{ free variables among }x_1\ldots x_n;\ c\text{ over the individual constants in }P;\ C(\Sigma)+\neg P\text{ consistent};\ n\ge0)$
variants.equivalence:
The instance of either form at $
eg P$ is, after contraposition and $\Diamond=
eg\Box
eg$, the instance of the other at $P$; $
eg P$ has the same free variables and constants as $P$.

principles.name: Possible Infinity (type e)
principles.statement: Possibly there are not finitely many individuals: the Axiom of Infinity at this type, under a diamond.
sources: Cian Dorr, suggestion of 20 September 2026.
principles.notes: Weaker than the Axiom of Infinity at this type by T. Since the Axiom of Infinity at type $e$ is consistent with C, Possibility Maximalism (pure) implies this principle. With No Pure Contingency, or with BF, it gives the Axiom back; whether it does so in C alone is recorded as an open question. See Background for $\mathbf{0}$, $\operatorname{Suc}$ and $\operatorname{FiniteCardinality}$.

principles.name: Possible Infinity (type t)
principles.statement: Possibly there are not finitely many propositions: the Axiom of Infinity at this type, under a diamond.
sources: Cian Dorr, suggestion of 20 September 2026.
principles.notes: Weaker than the Axiom of Infinity at this type by T. Since the Axiom of Infinity at type $t$ is consistent with C, Possibility Maximalism (pure) implies this principle, and indeed the Axiom itself by a longer route. With No Pure Contingency, or with BF (type $t$), this principle gives the Axiom back; whether it does so in C alone is recorded as an open question. See Background for $\mathbf{0}$, $\operatorname{Suc}$ and $\operatorname{FiniteCardinality}$.

principles.name: Possibly Witnessed Possibility
principles.statement: For pure formulas P with free variables among a finite tuple x and distinct matching constants c, a possible witness to P entails that P at those constants is possible. Equivalently, P necessary at the constants is necessary universally.
principles.formal: $\Diamond(\exists\bar x\, .\,P)\to\Diamond P[\bar c/\bar x]\quad(P\text{ pure, free variables among }\bar x;\ \bar c\text{ distinct constants of }\Sigma)$
sources: Cian Dorr, suggestion of 22 September 2026.
Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.5, pp. 38–39 and n. 57.

references.note: Separated Structure and Witnessed Possibility, between which this principle sits.
Separated Structure, to which this principle is equivalent in C.

principles.notes: Strengthens Witnessed Possibility by weakening its antecedent from an actual to a possible witness; its contrapositive is □P[c̄/x̄] → □∀x̄ P, the left-to-right direction of Logical Necessity with a box on the right. Equivalent in C to Separated Structure by the recorded results, so Logical Necessity is Separated Structure together with No Pure Contingency.

variants.name: Dual form
variants.statement: If a pure formula is necessary of distinct constants, it is necessary that it holds of everything.
variants.formal: $\Box P[\bar c/\bar x]\to\Box(\forall\bar x\, .\,P)\quad(P\text{ pure, free variables among }\bar x;\ \bar c\text{ distinct constants of }\Sigma)$
variants.equivalence:
Pure sentences (resp. sentences of $\mathcal L(\Sigma)$) are closed under negation, so the instance of either form at $
eg P$ is, after contraposition and $\Diamond=
eg\Box
eg$, the instance of the other at $P$.

principles.name: B for pure sentences
principles.statement: The B instance for every closed sentence in the pure language.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §3.5, n. 81, p. 59.

variants.name: Dual form
variants.statement: Each closed pure sentence that is possibly necessary is true.
variants.formal: $\Diamond\Box P\to P\quad(P\text{ a closed pure sentence})$
variants.equivalence:
Pure sentences (resp. sentences of $\mathcal L(\Sigma)$) are closed under negation, so the instance of either form at $
eg P$ is, after contraposition and $\Diamond=
eg\Box
eg$, the instance of the other at $P$.

principles.name: Relational Choice
principles.statement: Every serial binary relation has a functional subrelation.
principles.formal: $\forall U^{\sigma\tau t}\, .\,\operatorname{Serial}(U)\to\exists S^{\sigma\tau t}\, .\,\operatorname{Functional}(S)\land(\forall x y\, .\,(Sx)y\to(Ux)y)$
principles.definitions: where $\operatorname{Serial}(U):=\forall x^\sigma\, .\,\exists y^\tau\, .\,(Ux)y$; and $\operatorname{Functional}(U):=\forall x^\sigma\, .\,\exists y^\tau\, .\,(Ux)y\land\forall z^\tau\, .\,(Ux)z\to y=z$.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.3, pp. 31–33.

changes.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
changes.summary: At Cian Dorr’s request: definitions of its technical terms added.

variants.name: Polyadic form
variants.statement: Every serial relation from tuples has a functional subrelation.
variants.formal: $\forall U^{\bar\sigma\tau t}\, .\,\operatorname{Serial}(U)\to\exists S^{\bar\sigma\tau t}\, .\,\operatorname{Functional}(S)\land(\forall\bar x^{\bar\sigma}\,y^\tau\, .\,(S[\bar x])y\to(U[\bar x])y)$
variants.equivalence: The original form is the case of a one-element tuple. Code tuples by their haecceities (Background, Polyadic forms). Given a serial $U$, put $U':=\lambda A\,y\, .\,(\exists\bar x\, .\,A=H_{\bar x}\land(U[\bar x])y)\lor\neg\exists\bar x\, .\,A=H_{\bar x}$, which is serial. The original form at $\bar\sigma t$ and $\tau$ gives a functional $S'\subseteq U'$, and $S:=\lambda\bar x\,y\, .\,(S'H_{\bar x})y$ is a functional subrelation of $U$. The output type $\tau$ could be made a tuple as well, giving an equivalent doubly polyadic form; it is not listed.

principles.name: Rigid Comprehension
principles.statement: Every relation, including a proposition, is coextensive with a rigid one.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.3, pp. 28–30.

principles.name: Rigid Power
principles.statement: If a relation is rigid, so is the property of being a rigid relation that entails it.
principles.formal: $\forall F^{\bar\sigma t}\, .\,\operatorname{Rigid}(F)\to\operatorname{Rigid}(\lambda X^{\bar\sigma t}\, .\,\operatorname{Rigid}(X)\land X\le F)$
sources: Zachary Goodsell, 2019, as credited by Cian Dorr on 3 October 2026; full citation to be supplied.
principles.notes: Due to Zachary Goodsell. Gloss: sets cannot acquire new subsets, where rigid relations play the role of sets. It matters for the contingency of claims of analysis such as CH. Here $X$ ranges over relations of the same type as $F$, so the power property has type $(\bar\sigma\to t)\to t$. That property is persistent in C alone, since rigidity and entailment are both necessitated conditions and 4 holds; so the principle's content is the boxed weak inextensibility of the power property.

principles.name: Rigid Rigidity
principles.statement: Being rigid is a rigid property of relations, including propositions.
sources: Cian Dorr, suggestion of 10 October 2026.
principles.notes: Due to Cian Dorr. The property has type $(\bar\sigma t)t$. Its persistence is a theorem of C, so the content is that rigidity is inextensible. It is the instance of Rigid Power at $\lambda\bar x\, .\,\top$, whose power property is rigidity itself; so it follows from Rigid Power wherever $\lambda\bar x\, .\,\top$ is rigid, that is, given □BF (and at type $t$ outright). It implies □BF, and its own necessitation by 4. Whether it implies Rigid Power is open: the argument would need rigidity to be closed under conjunction, which fails in C when identity is contingent (the conjunction of the haecceities of distinct but possibly identical $x,y$ is persistent but not weakly inextensible).

principles.name: Second-Order Analytic Necessitism
principles.statement: If there could be a real number structure, there is a rigid one, necessarily a real number structure, together with represented powers of every arity up to $n$: rigid properties of rigid relations among the structure's elements that necessarily represent every relation on them. One sentence for each type $\sigma$ and each $n\ge1$.
principles.formal: $\Diamond\exists\mathfrak R\, .\,\operatorname{Real}_\sigma(\mathfrak R)\;\to\; \exists\mathfrak R\,\mathcal P_1\cdots\mathcal P_n\, .\,\operatorname{RigidStr}(\mathfrak R)\land \Box\operatorname{Real}_\sigma(\mathfrak R)\land\textstyle\bigwedge_{k\le n} \operatorname{RepPower}_k(\mathcal P_k,X)$
principles.definitions: See Background, Analysis, for $\operatorname{RigidStr}$ and $\operatorname{RepPower}_k$. A represented power of arity $k$ is a rigid property of rigid $k$-ary relations among the structure's elements such that, necessarily, every $k$-ary relation agrees on those elements with one of them. A rigid continuum does not fix which of its subproperties and relations exist; this adds that they too are fixed.
sources: Neil Barton and Zachary Goodsell, Continuum Contingency, draft of 14 October 2026, §5.8, eqs. (33)–(35), Theorem 6, and §5.9, Theorem 7.
Formulation without Rigid Comprehension by Zachary Goodsell and Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), 23 October 2026.

references.note: Their Second-Order Continuum Necessitism adds to the first-order principle that the property of rigid properties of reals is rigid with necessarily distinct instances; under Rigid Comprehension that property is a represented power of arity one, and relations reduce to properties by pairing.

principles.about: The entity-level counterpart of the Necessity of Second-Order Analysis. Representation is asked up to agreement on the structure's elements, which is all that analytical sentences can see (Bacon's Proposition C.3); the arities are bounded in each instance so that each instance is a single sentence, and a second-order analytical sentence uses only finitely many.
principles.notes: Implies Analytic Necessitism ([[second-order-analytic-necessitism-implies-analytic-necessitism]]) and the Necessity of Second-Order Analysis ([[second-order-analytic-necessitism-implies-necessity-of-second-order-analysis]]), hence the Non-contingency of the Continuum Hypothesis. Bacon's proof of his Theorem 5.2 shows, from Atomicity at every type and □Rigid Comprehension, that the canonical real number structure and the property of its rigid subproperties are rigid, which is this principle at the type of the canonical reals; whether those premises give it at every type is not settled by that argument. Fails in [[stitched-cohen-extension]], with Analytic Necessitism.

principles.name: Self-Atomicity
principles.statement: At each relational type, every possible entity (one distinct from bottom) is entailed by a self-atom: a possible entity that necessarily, if instantiated, is an atom.
principles.formal: $\forall X^\sigma\, .\,\Diamond_\sigma X\to\exists Q^\sigma\, .\,\operatorname{SelfAtom}_\sigma(Q)\land Q\le_\sigma X\qquad(\sigma\ne e)$
principles.definitions: where $\Diamond_\sigma X:=X\ne\bot_\sigma$ and $\operatorname{SelfAtom}_\sigma(X):=\Diamond_\sigma X\land\Box(\exists\bar x\, .\,X\bar x\to\operatorname{Atom}_\sigma(X))$: a self-atom is a possible entity that is necessarily an atom whenever it is instantiated; for a proposition, one that, wherever it is true, is the actual-world proposition there (Background, Self-atoms).
sources: Cian Dorr, the notion of a self-atom, Self-Atomicity (Self-Atomism) and the four bridge principles, 25 October 2026.
principles.notes: Cian Dorr’s weakening of Strong Atomicity (25 October 2026): a strong atom is an atom at every world, a self-atom an atom at every world where it holds. It lies strictly between Strong Atomicity and □Actuality, and is independent of Atomicity in both directions; the bridge principles [[atoms-are-self-atoms-r]], [[self-atoms-are-atoms-r]], [[self-atoms-are-strong-atoms-r]] and [[atoms-are-strong-atoms-r]] connect the three notions. The dual form, that whatever is entailed by every self-atom is necessary, is equivalent as for Atomicity.

principles.name: Self-Atomicity (type t)
principles.statement: Every possible proposition is entailed by a self-atom: a possible proposition that necessarily, if true, is an atom, that is, one that entails that it is the actual world.
principles.definitions: where $\operatorname{SelfAtom}_t(p):=\Diamond p\land\Box(p\to\operatorname{Atom}_t(p))$: a self-atom is a possible proposition that necessarily, if true, is an atom; equivalently, in C, one that entails that it is the actual world, $\Box(p\to\forall q\, .\,q\to p\le q)$.
sources: Cian Dorr, the notion of a self-atom, Self-Atomicity (Self-Atomism) and the four bridge principles, 25 October 2026.
principles.notes: The type $t$ instance of [[self-atomicity-r]]. Cian Dorr’s weakening of Strong Atomicity (25 October 2026): a strong atom is an atom at every world, a self-atom an atom at every world where it holds. It lies strictly between Strong Atomicity and □Actuality, and is independent of Atomicity in both directions; the bridge principles [[atoms-are-self-atoms-r]], [[self-atoms-are-atoms-r]], [[self-atoms-are-strong-atoms-r]] and [[atoms-are-strong-atoms-r]] connect the three notions. The dual form, that whatever is entailed by every self-atom is necessary, is equivalent as for Atomicity.

principles.name: Self-atoms are atoms
principles.statement: At each relational type, every self-atom is an atom.
principles.definitions: where $\Diamond_\sigma X:=X\ne\bot_\sigma$ and $\operatorname{SelfAtom}_\sigma(X):=\Diamond_\sigma X\land\Box(\exists\bar x\, .\,X\bar x\to\operatorname{Atom}_\sigma(X))$: a self-atom is a possible entity that is necessarily an atom whenever it is instantiated; for a proposition, one that, wherever it is true, is the actual-world proposition there (Background, Self-atoms).
sources: Cian Dorr, the notion of a self-atom, Self-Atomicity (Self-Atomism) and the four bridge principles, 25 October 2026.
principles.notes: Bridge principle (Cian Dorr, 25 October 2026). A self-atom need not be an atom: in the full model over the free monoid on $a,b$ the proposition $\{a,b\}$ becomes the actual-world proposition under either generator, but $\{a\}$ lies strictly below it. With Self-Atomicity it gives Atomicity; 5 implies it.

principles.name: Self-atoms are atoms (type t)
principles.statement: Every self-atom is an atom.
principles.definitions: where $\operatorname{SelfAtom}_t(p):=\Diamond p\land\Box(p\to\operatorname{Atom}_t(p))$: a self-atom is a possible proposition that necessarily, if true, is an atom; equivalently, in C, one that entails that it is the actual world, $\Box(p\to\forall q\, .\,q\to p\le q)$.
sources: Cian Dorr, the notion of a self-atom, Self-Atomicity (Self-Atomism) and the four bridge principles, 25 October 2026.
principles.notes: The type $t$ instance of [[self-atoms-are-atoms-r]]. Bridge principle (Cian Dorr, 25 October 2026). A self-atom need not be an atom: in the full model over the free monoid on $a,b$ the proposition $\{a,b\}$ becomes the actual-world proposition under either generator, but $\{a\}$ lies strictly below it. With Self-Atomicity it gives Atomicity; 5 implies it.

principles.name: Self-atoms are strong atoms
principles.statement: At each relational type, every self-atom is a strong atom: it necessarily entails every entity of the type or its negation.
principles.definitions: where $\Diamond_\sigma X:=X\ne\bot_\sigma$ and $\operatorname{SelfAtom}_\sigma(X):=\Diamond_\sigma X\land\Box(\exists\bar x\, .\,X\bar x\to\operatorname{Atom}_\sigma(X))$: a self-atom is a possible entity that is necessarily an atom whenever it is instantiated; for a proposition, one that, wherever it is true, is the actual-world proposition there (Background, Self-atoms); and $\operatorname{SAtom}_\sigma(W):=\Diamond_\sigma W\land\Box\forall Y^\sigma\, .\,W\le_\sigma Y\lor W\le_\sigma\neg_\sigma Y$ is a strong atom (Background, Strong atoms)
sources: Cian Dorr, the notion of a self-atom, Self-Atomicity (Self-Atomism) and the four bridge principles, 25 October 2026.
principles.notes: Bridge principle (Cian Dorr, 25 October 2026). With Self-Atomicity it gives Strong Atomicity Biconditionals; □5 implies it.

principles.name: Self-atoms are strong atoms (type t)
principles.statement: Every self-atom is a strong atom.
principles.definitions: where $\operatorname{SelfAtom}_t(p):=\Diamond p\land\Box(p\to\operatorname{Atom}_t(p))$: a self-atom is a possible proposition that necessarily, if true, is an atom; equivalently, in C, one that entails that it is the actual world, $\Box(p\to\forall q\, .\,q\to p\le q)$; and $\operatorname{SAtom}_t(W):=\Diamond_t W\land\Box\forall q\, .\,W\le_t q\lor W\le_t\neg_t q$ is a strong atom (Background, Strong atoms)
sources: Cian Dorr, the notion of a self-atom, Self-Atomicity (Self-Atomism) and the four bridge principles, 25 October 2026.
principles.notes: The type $t$ instance of [[self-atoms-are-strong-atoms-r]]. Bridge principle (Cian Dorr, 25 October 2026). With Self-Atomicity it gives Strong Atomicity; □5 implies it.

principles.name: Separated Structure
principles.statement: For each typed nonlogical constant c and closed same-typed terms F,G not containing c, equality after application to c implies equality of F and G.
principles.formal: $Fc=Gc\to F=G\quad(c\text{ a constant of }\Sigma;\ F,G\text{ closed, not containing }c)$
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.5, pp. 38–39.

references.note: Derived from Quantified Separated Structure and the assumptions Purity and Fundamentality; General Separated Structure on p. 565.

principles.notes: Until 8 October 2026 the general form below was a separate principle, General Separated Structure, equivalent in C by two recorded results; it became a form of this principle at Cian Dorr's direction. Bacon's instances of it: Rab = Sba implies R and S are converses; Rab = Fb implies R forgets its first argument; Raa = Fa implies F is the reflexivization of R.

changes.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
changes.summary: Added direct locators in Logical Combinatorialism; the statement is unchanged.

changes.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
changes.summary: Displayed the schema’s side conditions inside the math block, at Cian Dorr’s request; the statement is unchanged.

variants.name: General form
variants.statement: Let a_1…a_n and b_1…b_m be constants of Sigma, possibly with repetitions, none occurring in the closed terms F and G, and let pi be a bijection from variables x_1…x_k to the distinct constants among them. If F applied to the a’s equals G applied to the b’s, then abstracting the constants yields identical pure-position operations.
variants.formal: $F a_1\cdots a_n=G b_1\cdots b_m\to\lambda\bar x\, .\,F(\pi a_1)\cdots(\pi a_n)=\lambda\bar x\, .\,G(\pi b_1)\cdots(\pi b_m)\quad(a_i,b_j\text{ constants of }\Sigma,\text{ none in the closed }F,G;\ \pi\text{ a bijection from }\bar x\text{ to the distinct ones})$
variants.equivalence: General to official: take $n=m=1$ with $a_1=b_1=c$, so $k=1$; the instance reads $Fc=Gc\to\lambda x\, .\,Fx=\lambda x\, .\,Gx$, and $\eta$ turns the consequent into $F=G$. Official to general: let $c_1,\ldots,c_k$ be the distinct constants among $a_1\ldots a_n,b_1\ldots b_m$, with $\pi x_j=c_j$, and put $F^{\prime}:=\lambda x_1\ldots x_k\, .\,F(\pi a_1)\cdots(\pi a_n)$ and $G^{\prime}:=\lambda x_1\ldots x_k\, .\,G(\pi b_1)\cdots(\pi b_m)$. Neither contains any $c_j$, and by $\beta$, $F^{\prime}c_1\cdots c_k=Fa_1\cdots a_n$ and $G^{\prime}c_1\cdots c_k=Gb_1\cdots b_m$. Given the antecedent, $(F^{\prime}c_1\cdots c_{k-1})c_k=(G^{\prime}c_1\cdots c_{k-1})c_k$ with $c_k$ in neither applied term, so the official form gives $F^{\prime}c_1\cdots c_{k-1}=G^{\prime}c_1\cdots c_{k-1}$; after $k$ such steps $F^{\prime}=G^{\prime}$. Bacon derives the general form from Logical Necessity; the official form alone suffices (Claude Fable 5.1, 22 September 2026). If $k=0$ the schema is trivial.

principles.name: B for sentences of Σ
principles.statement: The B instance for every closed sentence of the language of the fixed signature Sigma.
principles.formal: $P\to\Box\Diamond P\quad(P\text{ a closed sentence of }\mathcal L(\Sigma))$
sources: Cian Dorr, suggestion of 22 September 2026.
Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §3.5, n. 81, p. 59 (B for pure sentences).
Andrew Bacon, Logical Combinatorialism, Philosophical Review 129 (2020), §3, n. 32, p. 556.

references.note: Bacon’s observation that B for sentences with a nonlogical predicate is undermined by Witnessed Possibility independently of contingent distinctness.

principles.notes: Sits between B and B for pure sentences. Incompatible with Witnessed Possibility, unlike its pure counterpart, which Witnessed Possibility tolerates.

variants.name: Dual form
variants.statement: Each closed sentence of the signature that is possibly necessary is true.
variants.formal: $\Diamond\Box P\to P\quad(P\text{ a closed sentence of }\mathcal L(\Sigma))$
variants.equivalence:
Pure sentences (resp. sentences of $\mathcal L(\Sigma)$) are closed under negation, so the instance of either form at $
eg P$ is, after contraposition and $\Diamond=
eg\Box
eg$, the instance of the other at $P$.

principles.name: Strong Actuality
principles.statement: There is a true strong atom: a true proposition that necessarily entails every proposition or its negation.
sources: Cian Dorr, formulation and name, 6 October 2026.

references.note: Strong atoms; the principle says that some strong atom at type $t$ is true, as Actuality says that some atom is.
Source of Actuality, which this strengthens.

principles.notes: Equivalently $\exists w\, .\,w\land\operatorname{SAtom}_t(w)$, since a true proposition is possible. It stands to Actuality as Strong Atomicity (type $t$) stands to Atomicity (type $t$): Actuality asks for a true proposition that settles every proposition, Strong Actuality for one that necessarily settles every proposition, including propositions that do not actually exist. In a full action model it holds at an object $W$ iff every arrow out of $W$ has at most one retraction.

changes.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
changes.summary: At Cian Dorr’s request: the form Strong Actual Profile, as Actual Profile is a form of Actuality.

variants.name: Strong Actual Profile
variants.statement: Every finite tuple has a true relational profile that necessarily entails every relation or its negation; the tuple may be empty.
variants.formal: $\forall\bar x^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,\exists Y^{\bar\sigma t}\, .\,Y[\bar x]\land\Box\forall Z^{\bar\sigma t}\, .\,Y\le Z\lor Y\le\neg Z$
variants.equivalence:
As for the form Actual Profile of Actuality. Form to official: specialize to the empty tuple, so that $Y$ and $Z$ have type $t$. Official to form: let $w$ be a true proposition with $\Box orall q\, .\,w\le q\lor w\le
eg q$. At a tuple $ ar x$, use $Y:=\lambda ar y\, .\,w\land ar y= ar x$, which holds at $ ar x$. It is a theorem of C, by Leibniz’s law, that $Y\le Z$ iff $w\le Z[ ar x]$ and $Y\le
eg Z$ iff $w\le
eg Z[ ar x]$; necessitating it and instantiating $q:=Z[ ar x]$ inside the box gives $\Box orall Z\, .\,Y\le Z\lor Y\le
eg Z$.

principles.name: Strong Atomicity
principles.statement: At each relational type, every possible entity (one distinct from bottom) is entailed by a strong atom: a possible entity that necessarily entails every entity of the type or its negation. The right-to-left direction is a theorem of C; the principle records the substantive direction.
principles.formal: $\forall X^\sigma\, .\,\Diamond_\sigma X\to\exists W^\sigma\, .\,\operatorname{SAtom}_\sigma(W)\land W\le_\sigma X\qquad(\sigma\ne e)$
principles.definitions: where $\Diamond_\sigma X:=X\ne\bot_\sigma$ and $\operatorname{SAtom}_\sigma(W):=\Diamond_\sigma W\land\Box\forall Y^\sigma\, .\,W\le_\sigma Y\lor W\le_\sigma\neg_\sigma Y$: a strong atom is a possible entity that necessarily entails every entity of its type or its negation.
sources: Andrew Bacon, A Philosophical Introduction to Higher-Order Logics, Routledge, 2024, §8.2, pp. 164–166.
principles.notes: Strong Atomicity is one direction of what Bacon calls the Strong Leibniz Biconditionals; the other direction is a theorem of C. His name for a strong atom is a strong world. It is his higher-order rendering of the possible-worlds thesis that a proposition is possible iff true at some world, with worlds required to settle merely possible propositions too. Definitions in Background ([[strong-atoms]]). The book presents the connection between Strong Atomicity and BF at relational types as new to it (§8.4, p. 177).

changes.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
changes.summary: At Cian Dorr’s request: definitions of its technical terms added.

changes.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
changes.summary: At Cian Dorr’s request: renamed from the Strong Leibniz Biconditionals to Strong Atomicity, and strong worlds to strong atoms; Bacon’s name kept as an alias.

variants.name: Dual form
variants.statement: Whatever is entailed by every strong atom of its type is the top element of that type.
variants.formal: $\forall X^\sigma\, .\,(\forall W^\sigma\, .\,\operatorname{SAtom}_\sigma(W)\to W\le_\sigma X)\to\neg_\sigma X\le_\sigma X\qquad(\sigma\ne e)$
variants.equivalence:
As for the dual form of Atomicity. A strong atom $W$ is non-bottom and, by T applied to its boxed clause, lies below $Y$ or below $
eg_\sigma Y$ for every $Y$. Official to dual: if every strong atom lies below $X$ but $
eg_\sigma X$ is non-bottom, a strong atom lies below $
eg_\sigma X$ and $X$, hence below bottom, which is impossible. Dual to official: if $X$ is non-bottom and no strong atom lies below it, every strong atom lies below $
eg_\sigma X$, so $X$ is bottom by the dual form.

principles.name: Strong Atomicity (type t)
principles.statement: Every possible proposition is entailed by a strong atom, one that is possible and necessarily entails every proposition or its negation.
principles.definitions: where $\operatorname{SAtom}_t(w):=\Diamond w\land\Box\forall q\, .\,w\le q\lor w\le\neg q$: a strong atom is a possible proposition that necessarily entails every proposition or its negation.
sources: Andrew Bacon, A Philosophical Introduction to Higher-Order Logics, Routledge, 2024, §8.2, pp. 164–165.

references.locator: Definition 3.19 and satisfaction clauses, pp. 55–57; idempotent model, p. 59
references.note: Semantics used to correct the supplementary singleton claim on 25 September 2026; the defining Strong Atomicity formula is unchanged.

principles.notes:
The type $t$ instance of [[strong-atomicity-r]]. Broken out as its own principle, like Atomicity (type t), at Cian Dorr’s request, because the type-t case can be settled in many models where the higher types have not been checked. A singleton need not be a strong atom in a one-object action model.
At an arrow h its shift is the precomposition fibre, but a proposition newly quantified
inside the box ranges over the entire target domain, not just shifted root propositions.
For the full monoid {1,k} with k²=k≠1, the singleton {k} shifts under k to {1,k},
which the target proposition {k} splits. Group actions do send singletons to singletons.

principles.name: Strong Possibility (pure)
principles.statement: Each closed pure sentence consistent with Maximalist Classicism is possible under the distinctness-preserving modality.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.6, p. 42.
principles.notes: The paper leaves consistency open. The definition of Box_ne and its dual is given in Background. Whatever is consistent with Max(C) is already possible by Possibility Maximalism (pure), which this principle implies; what it adds is possibility under the distinctness-preserving modality. So incompatibilities of the form Strong Possibility + □Y are recorded at Possibility Maximalism (pure) and inherited, and the collapse is the one recorded principle refuted by the stronger modality alone.

principles.name: Strong Possibility (signature Σ)

sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.5, pp. 37–39; §2.6, p. 42.
principles.notes: This keeps the signature-expanded reference theory throughout the consistency side condition. The separate pure-language variant uses Max(C). No conservativity between these two maximalizations is assumed. Consistency of Strong Possibility is left open in the source. Whatever is consistent with Max(C(Σ)) is already possible by Possibility Maximalism (signature Σ), which this principle implies; what it adds is possibility under the distinctness-preserving modality. Incompatibilities of the form Strong Possibility (signature Σ) + □Y are inherited through Possibility Maximalism (signature Σ) and Possibility Maximalism (pure); the collapse is refuted directly.

principles.name: Transversal Choice
principles.statement: Every equivalence relation, at any type including e, has a transversal, that is, a property with exactly one instance in each of its cells.
principles.formal: $\forall R^{\sigma\sigma t}\, .\,\operatorname{Equiv}(R)\to\exists F^{\sigma t}\, .\,\forall x^\sigma\, .\,\exists y^\sigma\, .\,(Rx)y\land Fy\land\forall z^\sigma\, .\,((Rx)z\land Fz)\to y=z$
principles.definitions: where $\operatorname{Equiv}(R):=\forall x^\sigma\, .\,(Rx)x\land\forall x^\sigma y^\sigma\, .\,(Rx)y\to(Ry)x\land\forall x^\sigma y^\sigma z^\sigma\, .\,(Rx)y\land(Ry)z\to(Rx)z$.
sources: Christopher Sun, observation communicated by Zachary Goodsell on 25 September 2026, that this formulation of choice for equivalence relations is used in the literature without a proof from Relational Choice; stated here in the map's relational type system.

references.note: The source's choice principles are Relational and Functional Choice. Transversal Choice is the selector form. It implies Relational Choice, and follows from it under Extensionality or Weak Rigid Comprehension, by the recorded results.

principles.notes: Equiv is defined in Background. The relation is required to be an equivalence relation only actually, and the transversal condition is unboxed, so both concern the evaluation point. The cell of $x$ is $\lambda z\, .\,(Rx)z$. Two members of one cell have coextensive cells, but in C properties are identical only when necessarily coextensive; this is what separates the principle from Relational Choice, which chooses from each property separately.

variants.name: Polyadic form
variants.statement: Every equivalence relation on tuples has a transversal.
variants.formal: $\forall R^{\bar\sigma\bar\sigma t}\, .\,\operatorname{Equiv}(R)\to\exists F^{\bar\sigma t}\, .\,\forall\bar x^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,\exists\bar y^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,(R[\bar x])[\bar y]\land F[\bar y]\land\forall\bar z^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,((R[\bar x])[\bar z]\land F[\bar z])\to\bar y=\bar z$
variants.equivalence: The original form is the case of a one-element tuple. Code tuples by their haecceities (Background, Polyadic forms). Given an equivalence $R$ on tuples, put $R':=\lambda A\,B\, .\,A=B\lor\exists\bar x\,\bar y\, .\,A=H_{\bar x}\land B=H_{\bar y}\land(R[\bar x])[\bar y]$, an equivalence on $\bar\sigma t$ whose cells are either the codes of one $R$-cell or singletons of non-codes. The original form gives a transversal $F'$ of $R'$, and $F:=\lambda\bar y\, .\,F'(H_{\bar y})$ is a transversal of $R$.

principles.name: Transversal
principles.statement: There is a property of properties that picks out exactly one property from each coextension class, that is, exactly one property coextensive with any given property.
principles.formal: $\exists F^{(\sigma t)t}\, .\,\forall X^{\sigma t}\, .\,\exists Y^{\sigma t}\, .\,FY\land(X\equiv Y)\land\forall Y'^{\sigma t}\, .\,(FY'\landX\equiv Y')\to Y'=Y$
sources: Christopher Sun, 26 September 2026, principle and its connections to Transversal Choice, Relational Choice and Actuality.

references.note: The source's choice principles are Relational and Functional Choice; Transversal Choice is recorded separately.

principles.notes: Due to Christopher Sun. It is the instance of Transversal Choice at type $\sigma\to t$ for the equivalence relation of coextensiveness, and Transversal Choice is equivalent to it together with Relational Choice. It isolates what Relational Choice lacks for the quotient argument: a canonical representative of each coextension class of properties, shared by coextensive properties even when they are distinct. The coextension and the choice are unboxed, so both concern the evaluation point. The type $\sigma$ may be $e$; the type $(\sigma\to t)\to t$ of $F$ is admitted since its output is $t$.

variants.name: Polyadic form
variants.statement: There is a property of relations that picks out exactly one relation from each coextension class.
variants.formal: $\exists F^{(\bar\sigma t)t}\, .\,\forall X^{\bar\sigma t}\, .\,\exists Y^{\bar\sigma t}\, .\,FY\land(X\equiv Y)\land\forall Y'^{\bar\sigma t}\, .\,(FY'\landX\equiv Y')\to Y'=Y$
variants.equivalence: The original form is the case of a one-element tuple. Code tuples by their haecceities (Background, Polyadic forms). Let $F''$ witness the original form at $\bar\sigma t$, and let $\operatorname{Code}:=\lambda A\, .\,\exists\bar x\, .\,A=H_{\bar x}$. Put $F:=\lambda Y\, .\,\exists Z\, .\,F''Z\land(\forall A\, .\,ZA\to\operatorname{Code}(A))\land Y=\lambda\bar x\, .\,Z(H_{\bar x})$. For each $X$, let $X'':=\lambda A\, .\,\exists\bar x\, .\,A=H_{\bar x}\land X[\bar x]$. A relation $Y$ with $FY$, built from $Z$, is coextensive with $X$ iff $Z$ is coextensive with $X''$, since both $Z$ and $X''$ hold only of codes. So exactly one such $Y$ is coextensive with $X$, namely the one built from the $Z$ that $F''$ picks in the coextension class of $X''$.

principles.name: Weak Rigid Comprehension
principles.statement: Every relation, including a proposition, is coextensive with a weakly rigid one, that is, with one that is weakly persistent and weakly inextensible.
sources: Cian Dorr, Boolean Completeness does not imply Rigid Comprehension, draft of 30 July 2026, Proposition 1, p. 2; p. 12.
Cian Dorr, suggestion of 19 September 2026.

references.note: The draft's unqualified "weakly rigid" is this map's, the whole matrix of Rigid shorn of its leading boxes.
Source of Rigid Comprehension, of which this is the un-necessitated weakening.

principles.notes: Weak rigidity drops the leading boxes from both conjuncts of Rigid. A weakly rigid relation is nevertheless persistent, so the principle is equivalent to its persistent form. See Background for the definitions. The draft that introduces the principle is a work in progress. Until 8 October 2026 the map's "weakly rigid" meant persistent and weakly inextensible, the persistent form below was this principle's official statement, and the present statement was a separate principle, Very Weak Rigid Comprehension, retired then at Cian Dorr's direction.

variants.name: Persistent form
variants.statement: Every relation, including a proposition, is coextensive with one that is persistent and weakly inextensible.
variants.formal: $\forall X^{\bar\sigma t}\, .\,\exists Y^{\bar\sigma t}\, .\,\operatorname{Persistent}(Y)\land \operatorname{WeaklyInextensible}(Y)\land(X\equiv Y)$
variants.equivalence: Persistence implies weak persistence by T, so the persistent form implies the official one. The interesting direction: a weakly rigid $Y$ is persistent. Apply its weak inextensibility to $X:=\lambda\bar x\, .\,\Box Y[\bar x]$. The hypothesis $\forall\bar x\, .\,Y[\bar x]\to\Box X[\bar x]$, that is $Y[\bar x]\to\Box\Box Y[\bar x]$, holds by weak persistence and 4; so $Y\le\lambda\bar x\, .\,\Box Y[\bar x]$, which is $\operatorname{Persistent}(Y)$. The same $Y$ therefore witnesses both forms.
variants.definitions: where $\operatorname{Persistent}(Y):=Y\le\lambda\bar x\, .\,\Box Y[\bar x]$, that is, $\Box\forall\bar x\, .\,Y[\bar x]\to\Box Y[\bar x]$; and $\operatorname{WeaklyInextensible}(Y):=\forall X\, .\,(\forall\bar x\, .\,Y[\bar x]\to\Box X[\bar x])\to Y\le X$.

principles.name: Weakly Inextensible Comprehension
principles.statement: Every relation, including a proposition, is coextensive with a weakly inextensible one.
principles.definitions: where $\operatorname{WeaklyInextensible}(Y):=\forall X\, .\,(\forall\bar x\, .\,Y[\bar x]\to\Box X[\bar x])\to Y\le X$.
sources: Cian Dorr, Boolean Completeness does not imply Rigid Comprehension, draft of 30 July 2026, Proposition 1, p. 2; p. 12.
Cian Dorr, suggestion of 25 September 2026.

references.note: Source of weak inextensibility, the inextensibility conjunct of Rigid shorn of its leading box.
Source of Inextensible Comprehension, of which this is the un-necessitated weakening.

principles.notes: Weak inextensibility drops the leading box from Inextensible; see Background for the definitions. A relation $Y$ is weakly inextensible exactly when $Y\le Z$ for every $Z$ that necessarily holds of each actual $Y$-instance, that is, when $Y$ lies below every upper bound of the haecceities $\lambda\bar z\, .\,\bigwedge_i z_i=y_i$ of its instances: $Y$ may lose instances at other worlds, but it cannot gain any beyond those its actual instances necessitate. Adding weak persistence, which says that $Y$ is itself such an upper bound, turns this into $Y$ being the least upper bound of those haecceities, which is weak rigidity. The type-$t$ instances are trivial, since $\top$ and $\bot$ witness them; haecceities and their finite joins are rigid; and the instance at $X=\top$ is a relativised Barcan Formula, $\top$ itself being weakly inextensible exactly when BF holds at the argument types. The principle follows from Actuality and separately from Boolean Completeness, which the recorded models show to be independent of one another, so it is strictly weaker than each. Whether it implies the boxed principle, Inextensible Comprehension, is open.

principles.name: Weakly Rigid Power
principles.statement: If a relation is weakly rigid, so is the property of being a weakly rigid relation that entails it.
principles.formal: $\forall F^{\bar\sigma t}\, .\,\operatorname{WeaklyRigid}(F)\to\operatorname{WeaklyRigid}(\lambda X^{\bar\sigma t}\, .\,\operatorname{WeaklyRigid}(X)\land X\le F)$
sources: Cian Dorr, suggestion of 10 October 2026.
principles.notes: Due to Cian Dorr. The variant of Rigid Power with "weakly rigid" in all three places (the $(W,W,W)$ variant in the candidate list). Here $X$ ranges over relations of the same type as $F$, so the power property has type $(\bar\sigma t)t$. It implies Tame Rigidity and Rigid Power, and □Tame Rigidity with Rigid Power implies it; with BF it implies □Tame Rigidity, so under BF it is equivalent to □Tame Rigidity and Rigid Power. Whether Tame Rigidity and Rigid Power imply it is open.

principles.name: Weakly Rigid Weak Rigidity
principles.statement: Being weakly rigid is a weakly rigid property of relations, including propositions.
sources: Cian Dorr, suggestion of 10 October 2026.
principles.notes: Due to Cian Dorr. The property has type $(\bar\sigma t)t$. Since a weakly rigid relation is persistent (Background), it implies □Tame Rigidity, so weak rigidity and rigidity are then identical; it is equivalent to the conjunction of Rigid Rigidity and □Tame Rigidity, and hence to its own necessitation. It follows from BF with Weakly Rigid Power.

principles.name: Well-Ordering
principles.statement: Every type, including e, is well-ordered by some relation.
principles.definitions: where $\operatorname{WO}(R)$ says that $R$ well-orders the type: it is transitive, antisymmetric and total (so reflexive), and every instantiated property of type $\sigma t$ has an $R$-least instance.
sources: Cian Dorr, suggestion of 8 October 2026.
principles.notes: WO is defined in Background: $R$ is transitive, antisymmetric and total, and every instantiated property has an $R$-minimal instance. The condition is unboxed, so it concerns the evaluation point only, and the well-order need not remain one at other worlds, since its field may contract there by contingent identities. Modal Well-Ordering asks for a relation that is necessarily a well-order. Well-Ordering is equivalent to Transversal Choice and to Zorn's Lemma, by the recorded results, as the well-ordering theorem is to the axiom of choice in set theory (Cian Dorr's conjecture of 7 October 2026). Relational Choice is enough only if it implies Transversal Choice, which is open.

principles.name: Zorn's Lemma
principles.statement: If a preorder is such that every chain, that is, every property it totally orders, has an upper bound, then something is maximal: everything above it is also below it.
principles.formal: $\forall R^{\sigma\sigma t}\, .\,\operatorname{Preorder}(R)\land(\forall X^{\sigma t}\, .\,\operatorname{TotalOrder}(R,X)\to\exists u^\sigma\, .\,\forall x^\sigma\, .\,Xx\to(Rx)u)\to\exists m^\sigma\, .\,\forall y^\sigma\, .\,(Rm)y\to(Ry)m$
principles.definitions: where $\operatorname{Preorder}(R)$ says that $R$ is reflexive and transitive; and $\operatorname{TotalOrder}(R,X)$ says that $R$ is transitive, antisymmetric and total on the instances of $X$.
sources: Cian Dorr, suggestion of 8 October 2026, to add Zorn's Lemma in preorder form with a proof from Transversal Choice.
Serge Lang, Algebra, Appendix 2.

references.note: Zorn's Lemma for partial orders on sets, derived from the axiom of choice through the Bourbaki–Witt fixed-point theorem applied to chains ordered by inclusion.

principles.notes: Preorder and TotalOrder are as in Background; everything is unboxed. The preorder form is used because the orders to which Zorn's Lemma is applied at higher types, such as extension of relations, are antisymmetric only up to coextension. Chains are required to be totally ordered, and so antisymmetric, so the hypothesis concerns fewer properties than comparability alone would; this makes the principle stronger. For a partial order the conclusion says that $m$ is maximal in the usual sense. Zorn's Lemma is equivalent to Transversal Choice and to Well-Ordering, by the recorded results; the proof from Transversal Choice follows Lang, through the Bourbaki–Witt lemma, and uses Transversal Choice beyond Relational Choice only to make the step from a chain invariant under coextension.

results.proof: Bacon's Theorem C.2. Its argument: the canonical real number structure, built from the finite numerical quantifiers (Theorem A.2), rigidified by Rigid Comprehension, is an inflexible real number structure, its elements being necessarily distinct relative to the necessity $\Box_N$ that assumes a possible natural number structure (Lemma C.4); with the Leibniz Biconditionals and Rigid Comprehension it is necessarily complete, hence necessarily a real number structure, and its rigid subproperties form a rigid property, by the pullback of possible rigid subproperties through world properties that the map records as atomicity-and-rigid-comprehension-imply-rigid-power (Lemmas C.5–C.7); the induction of Lemma C.1 extended to second-order sentences then makes every second-order analytical truth of it necessary; and any real number structure, at any type, agrees with it on second-order analytical sentences (Lemma C.3). results.proof: See the write-up. Let $F$ be rigid and $P:=\lambda X\, .\,\operatorname{Rigid}(X)\land X\le F$, of type $(\bar\sigma t)t$. $P$ is persistent in C. Suppose $\forall X\, .\,PX\to\Box\mathcal XX$ while $\lambda X\, .\,PX\land\neg\mathcal XX$ is possibly instantiated; Atomicity at the type of $P$ gives an atom $W$ below it. Bacon's Lemma C.6: Rigid Comprehension supplies a rigid $X$ coextensive with $\lambda\bar x\, .\,F\bar x\land\Box\forall Y\, .\,WY\to Y\bar x$; it lies below $F$, and the weak inextensibility of $X$ and of $F$, with $W$ deciding $\lambda Y\, .\,Y\bar x$ for each actual $\bar x$, make $W$ entail that $Y$ is coextensive with $X$, hence identical to it, coextensive weakly rigid relations being identical. Then $PX$ gives $\Box\mathcal XX$, while $W$ is possible and entails $\neg\mathcal XX$. So $P$ is weakly inextensible, hence weakly rigid, and Tame Rigidity at its type, which Rigid Comprehension gives, makes it rigid.

results.proof:
Call $q$ a floor of $X^{tt}$ when $Xq$, $\Diamond q$, and no possible instance of $X$ lies strictly below $q$. Let $W$ be the property of cardinalities holding of $Z$ when every instance of $Z$ that has a possible instance has a floor.

$W$ holds of $\mathbf{0}_t$, since its only instance has no instances at all, so the condition is vacuous.

$W$ is closed under $\operatorname{Suc}_t$. Let $WY$ and $(\operatorname{Suc}_t Y)X$, and take the witness $y$ with $Xy$ and $Y(\lambda u\, .\,Xu\land u\ne y)$; write $X^-$ for that abstract, whose instances are exactly the instances of $X$ other than $y$. Suppose $X$ has a possible instance. If $X^-$ has none then $y$ is the only one, and is a floor. Otherwise the hypothesis on $Y$, applied to $X^-$ as $\operatorname{Suc}_t$ presents it, gives a floor $q$ of $X^-$. If $y$ is not possible, or is not strictly below $q$, then $q$ is a floor of $X$, since a possible instance of $X$ strictly below $q$ is either an instance of $X^-$, against the choice of $q$, or is $y$, which this case excludes. If instead $y$ is possible and strictly below $q$, then $y$ is a floor of $X$. For a possible instance $r$ of $X$ strictly below $y$ is not $y$, hence is an instance of $X^-$, and $r\le y\le q$. If $r=q$ then $q\le y\le q$ makes $y=q$, against $y\ne q$; so $r$ is an instance of $X^-$ strictly below $q$, again against the choice of $q$.

So every finite cardinality has the property. Now suppose some finite $Z$ held of $\lambda p\, .\,\top$. That property has the possible instance $\top$, since $\top\ne\bot$ in C, so it would have a floor $q$. Atomlessness applied to $q$ supplies a possible $q'$ with $q'\le q$ and $q'\ne q$, and $q'$ is an instance of $\lambda p\, .\,\top$, contradicting the floor. Hence no finite cardinality holds of $\lambda p\, .\,\top$.

results.proof: Write $I(F)$ for $\exists x\, .\,Fx$ and $U(G)$ for $\exists x\, .\,Gx\land\forall y\, .\,Gy\to y=x$. First, Intensional Choice at $\sigma$ is equivalent in C to its entailing form $\forall F\,\exists G\, .\,G\le F\land\Box(I(F)\to U(G))$. From the entailing form: if $\Box I(F)$, a $G$ as there has $\Box U(G)$ by K. To it: given $F$, $F':=\lambda x\, .\,Fx\lor\neg I(F)$ is necessarily instantiated, since it is a theorem that it is instantiated; take $H\le F'$ with $\Box U(H)$, and put $G:=\lambda x\, .\,Hx\land Fx$. Then $G\le F$, and necessarily, if $I(F)$ then $F'$ and $F$ are coextensive, so $G$ is coextensive with $H$ and $U(G)$. Necessitating, the equivalence holds at every world. Now the matrix $G\le F\land\Box(I(F)\to U(G))$ of the entailing form is of the form $\Box A(F,G)$, $G\le F$ being itself a necessitated universal. And $\exists G\,\Box A(F,G)\to\Box\exists G\,\Box A(F,G)$ is a theorem of C: from $\Box A(F,G)$, 4 gives $\Box\Box A(F,G)$, and necessitated existential generalization gives $\Box\exists G\,\Box A(F,G)$. So the entailing form gives $\forall F\,\Box\exists G\,\Box A(F,G)$, and BF at type $\sigma t$ moves the box out: $\Box\forall F\,\exists G\,\Box A(F,G)$, which is the necessitation of the entailing form, hence □Intensional Choice at $\sigma$.

results.proof: Write $A(w):=w\land\forall q\, .\,q\to w\le q$, so that □Actuality is $\Box\exists w\, .\,A(w)$. Let $\Diamond p$. With □Actuality this gives $\Diamond(p\land\exists w\, .\,A(w))$, that is, $\Diamond\exists w\, .\,p\land A(w)$, and BF at type $t$, in its dual form, gives some $w$ with $\Diamond(p\land A(w))$. Put $s:=p\land A(w)$. Then $\Diamond s$ and $s\le p$. It remains to show $\Box(s\to\operatorname{Atom}_t(s))$, by an argument in C, which may therefore be necessitated. Suppose $s$. Then $A(w)$, so $w$ is true and entails every truth; in particular $w\le s$, while $s\le w$ since $A(w)$ entails $w$; so $s=w$. And $w$ is an atom: if $z\le w$, then either $z$ is true, so $w\le z$ and $z=w$, or $\neg z$ is true, so $z\le w\le\neg z$ and $z=\bot$. So $s$ is an atom, and $s$ is a self-atom below $p$.
results.notes: Under BF at every type, [[self-atomicity-t-and-bf-imply-self-atomicity-r]] lifts the conclusion to [[self-atomicity-r]], so BF and □Actuality give Self-Atomicity. The self-atom is the conjunction of $p$ with "$w$ is a true atom"; conjoining $p$ puts it below $p$ without appeal to B or ND, since $w\le p$ itself is only known to hold possibly.

results.proof: See the write-up. Choose, for each atom $w$, an $x$ with $w\le Fx$; restrict the choice to atoms and take a weakly rigid coextension $R$; put $G:=\lambda x\, .\,\exists w\, .\,w\land Rwx$. Weak inextensibility shows that every instance of $R$ that an atom makes true is, according to that atom, identical to an actual instance, and uniqueness follows by reasoning below atoms.

results.notes:
Cian Dorr proposed the construction with Rigid Comprehension. Only persistence and unboxed weak inextensibility of the coextension are used, so Weak Rigid Comprehension suffices. ND is not needed. Without ND, a weakly rigid functional relation need not stay functional, since distinct arguments can later be identified. That is why the chosen relation is restricted to atoms: two actual atoms cannot both be true together unless they are identical.

A stronger conclusion holds by another route (11 October 2026): BF, Weak Rigid Comprehension and Relational Choice give Modal Well-Ordering (through Transversal Choice, Zorn's Lemma and Well-Ordering), which gives Modalized Relational Choice (modal-well-ordering-implies-modalized-relational-choice); Atomicity is not needed. The atom argument here does not extend to Modalized Relational Choice: with inputs, the uniqueness step pulls two values back to actual instances whose inputs an atom may identify without ND, so the merged input could have two values. This record's Lean certificate is the composition through Modal Well-Ordering, not the atom argument.

By Boolean Completeness in its least-upper-bound form, let $S$ be a least upper bound of $H$ and put $Y:=\lambda\bar z\, .\,S[\bar z]\land X[\bar z]$. If $X[\bar y]$ then $\operatorname{Haec}_{\bar y}\le S$, so $S[\bar y]$ by T at $\bar y=\bar y$; hence $Y$ is coextensive with $X$. For weak inextensibility suppose $\forall\bar z\, .\,Y[\bar z]\to\Box Z[\bar z]$. For $\bar y$ with $X[\bar y]$ we get $\Box Z[\bar y]$, and $\forall\bar z\, .\,\bigwedge_i z_i=y_i\to Z[\bar z]$ is H-equivalent to $Z[\bar y]$, so $\operatorname{Haec}_{\bar y}\le Z$. Thus $Z$ is an upper bound of $H$, so $S\le Z$, and $Y\le S\le Z$.

results.proof: Fix two distinct atoms $w,w^{\prime}$ of type $t$ and let $F:=\lambda p\, .\,(\neg(w\lor w^{\prime})\land p)\lor(w\land(w^{\prime}\le p))\lor(w^{\prime}\land(w\le p))$, which exchanges the two atoms: $w\le Fp$ iff $w^{\prime}\le p$. Under $\Box$ND identity propositions are rigid, so $F$ is an involution commuting with the connectives, with $\forall$ (by BF) and with identity, as identities, not just materially: the hypothesis that $w,w^{\prime}$ are distinct atoms is rigid, so material equivalences proved under it lift to identities by the Modalized Fregean Axiom and pass under $\lambda$ by Modalized Functionality. Extend $F$ by conjugation to every type, $F^*_{\sigma\tau}X:=\lambda y\, .\,F^*_\tau(X(F^*_\sigma y))$; $F^*$ is an involution fixing every logical constant, so by induction on terms $F^*A=A[F^*\bar x/\bar x]$ for pure $A$, and $FP=P$ for closed pure $P$. Hence $w\le P$ iff $w^{\prime}\le P$. If $P$ is true and not $\top$, Atomicity at type $t$ gives atoms $w\le P$ and $w^{\prime}\le\neg P$, necessarily distinct, and the agreement puts $w^{\prime}$ below $\bot$. results.proof: See the write-up. C5 gives B, 5, ND and BF at every type. Suppose a real number structure at $\sigma$ is possible, at a world $w$. □Rigid Comprehension at $w$ gives rigid relations coextensive there with its domain, order, addition, multiplication and natural numbers; rigidity is necessary if true, so by B and 5 these relations are rigid at the actual world too, with necessarily distinct instances by ND. Every first-order fact about rigid relations with necessarily distinct instances is non-contingent (the induction of analytic-necessitism-implies-necessity-of-analysis), so the field axioms, true of the rigidified structure at $w$, hold at the actual world and necessarily. Completeness at any world $u$: a bounded subproperty of the domain has, by Rigid Comprehension at $u$, a rigid coextension; that it has a least upper bound in the domain is a first-order fact about rigid relations, true at $w$ by the completeness of the original structure, hence necessary, hence true at $u$ by B. So the rigidified structure is necessarily a real number structure. Its represented powers: the property of rigid relations holding only of tuples of its instances is persistent since rigidity is necessary if true, and inextensible by BF, rigidity being non-contingent under 5; Rigid Comprehension at each world represents every relation on the domain by one of them.
results.notes: Hence □Plenitude gives Second-Order Analytic Necessitism, Analytic Necessitism, the Necessity of Second-Order Analysis and the Non-contingency of the Continuum Hypothesis, since □Plenitude gives C5 and □Rigid Comprehension on the map; Extensionality reaches them through □Plenitude. Bacon's Corollary 5.1 is the sentence-level consequence. Atomicity is not used: with S5 the world of the given structure stays accessible, so completeness is read off there instead of being carried by Rigid Power.

sources: Cian Dorr, Boolean Completeness does not imply Rigid Comprehension, draft of 30 July 2026, Proposition 1, p. 2.
results.proof:
Fix a relational type $\tau=\bar\sigma t$ and $X^\tau$. Write $\operatorname{Haec}_{\bar u}:=\lambda\bar z\, .\,\bigwedge_i z_i=u_i$ and put $H:=\lambda Z^\tau\, .\,\exists\bar y\, .\,X[\bar y]\land Z=\operatorname{Haec}_{\bar y}$, the property of being the haecceity of some $X$ things. By Boolean Completeness in its least-upper-bound form, let $Y$ be a least upper bound of $H$. Two observations do the work. (i) If $X[\bar u]$ then $\operatorname{Haec}_{\bar u}\le_\tau Y$, and instantiating at $\bar u$ with $\bar u=\bar u$ gives $\Box Y[\bar u]$. (ii) If $\Box Z[\bar u]$ whenever $X[\bar u]$, then $\operatorname{Haec}_{\bar u}\le_\tau Z$ for each such $\bar u$, so $Z$ is an upper bound of $H$ and $Y\le_\tau Z$.

Coextensiveness. $X[\bar u]\to Y[\bar u]$ by (i). Conversely, let $w$ witness Actuality and put $P:=\lambda\bar z\, .\,(w\le X[\bar z])$. If $X[\bar u]$ then $X[\bar u]$ is true, so $w\le X[\bar u]$; a true entailment is necessary, so $\Box P[\bar u]$. By (ii), $Y\le_\tau P$, so $Y[\bar u]\to w\le X[\bar u]$; and $w$ is true, so $Y[\bar u]\to X[\bar u]$.

Persistence. Take $Z:=\lambda\bar z\, .\,\Box Y[\bar z]$ in (ii). If $X[\bar u]$ then $\Box Y[\bar u]$ by (i), hence $\Box Z[\bar u]$ by 4. So $Y\le_\tau\lambda\bar z\, .\,\Box Y[\bar z]$, which is $\operatorname{Persistent}(Y)$.

Weak inextensibility. Suppose $\forall\bar z\, .\,Y[\bar z]\to\Box Z[\bar z]$. If $X[\bar u]$ then $Y[\bar u]$ by coextensiveness, so $\Box Z[\bar u]$; hence $Y\le_\tau Z$ by (ii).

references.note: Boolean Completeness and Actuality; the least-upper-bound form of Boolean Completeness is equivalent to the stated greatest-lower-bound form in C.

results.notes: The argument stops short of Rigid Comprehension exactly at the leading box of Inextensible. It delivers a $Y$ that is inextensible at the actual world, while Rigid demands the biconditional at every world. The models recorded from the same draft show that the gap is real.

results.proof: Theorem 9 of the source, proved in HKC, which C extends. Natural numberhood is necessary (Lemma 3, an induction using the converse Barcan formula), distinct numbers are necessarily distinct given $I^*$ (Lemma 4, a double induction), $I$ implies $I^*$ (Lemma 5), so distinctness and, by tedious inductions, Sum and Prod are necessary or necessarily false given $I$ (Lemmas 6–7). sources: Andrew Bacon, Could the truths of mathematics have been different?, draft of 9 October 2025, §6, p. 27, "A straightforward consequence of Mathematical Possibilism is that it entails the axiom of infinity."
OpenAI Codex, prompted by Daniel Kodsi, Forcing Possibilism implies quantified Infinity: internal proof, 25 October 2026, §§1–4 (unpaginated); direct source misc for the supplementary proof.

references.note: Stated there for the axiom of infinity in the form that the finite numerical quantifiers over propositions form a natural number structure; the map's Axiom of Infinity (type t) says that no finite cardinality holds of the universal property of propositions.

results.proof: Suppose some finite cardinality holds of the universal property of propositions, say there are exactly $N$ propositions, $q_1,\dots,q_N$ (with $N\ge2$, as $\top\ne\bot$). At type $tt$ the properties $\lambda p\, .\,p=q_{i_1}\lor\dots\lor p=q_{i_k}$, one for each subset of $\{q_1,\dots,q_N\}$, are pairwise distinct, since two of them differ at some $q_i$, and under inclusion they form a complete Boolean algebra with $2^N$ elements: a finite Boolean algebra is complete, and its carrier, order, meets and joins are given by abstraction. It is finite, hence small. Forcing Possibilism gives a proposition $p\ne\top$ whose entailment algebra is isomorphic to it, so there are at least $2^N>N$ propositions, those entailing $p$. Contradiction. Hence no finite cardinality holds of the universal property of propositions.
results.notes: The one general consequence of Forcing Possibilism the map records: the principle is about the propositions there could be below some proposition, so any model with finitely many propositions refutes it, and through this result every such model on the map does, which settles the questions whether principles true in finite models, Atomicity, ND or BF for instance, imply it. Its other verdicts on the map come from Bacon's lottery model, which has it with □Rigid Comprehension and □Intensional Choice and without Atomicity. A separately credited internal-finiteness proof, valid without an external finite enumeration, is given in the proof supplement on this result’s page. The original proof and its certificate are retained.

results.proof: Gallin supplies a current truth evaluator E with necessarily endpoint-valued outputs and gives current ND. A current self-atom Q is therefore an ordinary atom. Its normalized order-character J(X)=E(Q<=X) is currently Boolean, necessarily endpoint-valued, and sends Q to top. A future counterexample to a finite Boolean law would be a disagreement between fixed endpoints and remain a counterexample thereafter. Current B applied to the whole universally quantified law rules this out, so the character is necessarily Boolean even on new future inputs. At a future point its endpoint value on Z persists. At any later instance of Q, self-atomhood makes Q an atom; the Boolean character forces its decision of Z to agree with that endpoint. Thus Q necessarily decides every future Z, making it strong. The accompanying write-up proves each step with full future-domain quantification.
results.notes: One current all-type implication, including type t. sources: Andrew Bacon, Logical Combinatorialism, Philosophical Review 129 (2020), §4, pp. 561–562.
results.proof: Let $c$ be a constant of type $\sigma$ and $F,G$ closed terms of type $\sigma\tau$ not containing $c$, with $Fc=Gc$. Enumerate the constants occurring in $F$ or $G$ as $\bar d$, all distinct from $c$, and abstract them: $F=F^\circ\bar d$, $G=G^\circ\bar d$ with $F^\circ,G^\circ$ closed and pure, by $\beta$. Let $P:=F^\circ\bar y\,x=G^\circ\bar y\,x$, pure with free variables $\bar y,x$. NI gives $\Box P[\bar d,c/\bar y,x]$, so Logical Necessity, left to right, gives $\forall\bar y x\, .\,P$. This closed pure truth is necessary by the empty-tuple instance of Logical Necessity, so $\Box\forall\bar y x\, .\,F^\circ\bar y x=G^\circ\bar y x$. CBF gives $\forall\bar y\, .\,\Box\forall x\, .\,F^\circ\bar yx=G^\circ\bar yx$ and Modalized Functionality, a theorem of C, gives $\forall\bar y\, .\,F^\circ\bar y=G^\circ\bar y$. Instantiating $\bar y:=\bar d$ yields $F=G$.
results.notes: Bacon derives the quantified form from Quantified Logical Necessity and Modalized Functionality and says the schematic form follows in the same way. Both directions of Logical Necessity are used: the witnessed direction to pass from the necessary identity at the constants to the universal claim, and No Pure Contingency to necessitate that claim before applying Modalized Functionality.

results.proof: Vacuously, at every type $\sigma$. In the full model with one world and one individual every type is finite. If the type $\sigma$ has $m$ entities there, the number $\operatorname{Suc}_\sigma^{m+1}\mathbf 0_\sigma$ holds of no property, so it is the empty property of type $\nu_\sigma$, and so is its successor. Thus $\operatorname{Suc}_\sigma(\operatorname{Suc}^m_\sigma\mathbf 0_\sigma)=\operatorname{Suc}_\sigma (\operatorname{Suc}^{m+1}_\sigma\mathbf 0_\sigma)$, while $\operatorname{Suc}^m_\sigma\mathbf 0_\sigma$, which holds of the universal property, differs from $\operatorname{Suc}^{m+1}_\sigma\mathbf 0_\sigma$. Both are numbers, so $I^*_\sigma$ fails there. So $I^*_\sigma=\top$ is a closed pure identity not provable in C, and Maximalism (pure) makes it false. Hence $\Box I^*_\sigma$ is false, and the instance of Arithmetic Necessitism at $\sigma$ holds.
results.notes: This is the coalesced-sums argument arithmetic-necessitism-complete-components, stated with its actual premise. The principle holds only vacuously here. Maximalism refutes the sentence-level [[necessity-of-arithmetic]] guard as well, and nothing about a necessitated form follows.

Let $\sigma$ be the type $((et)t)t$ of properties of the numbers at $e$, where Dedekind cuts live, and let $P$ be the closed pure sentence $\Diamond\exists\mathfrak R\,.\,(\operatorname{Real}_\sigma(\mathfrak R)\land A(\mathfrak R))\land\Diamond\exists\mathfrak R\,.\,(\operatorname{Real}_\sigma(\mathfrak R)\land\neg A(\mathfrak R))$, the negation of the instance of the Necessity of Analysis at $\sigma$ and $A$. $P$ is consistent with C: it is true at the root of coalesced-two-extensional-arithmetics-root, whose components $M_1\models\operatorname{Con}(T)$ and $M_2\models\neg\operatorname{Con}(T)$ each carry a real number structure of type $\sigma$, the Dedekind cuts over their numbers, in which $A$ is false and true respectively (the model's argument against the Necessity of Analysis). So Maximalism (pure), in its possibility form, gives $\Diamond P$, and by 4, $\Diamond\Diamond$ implying $\Diamond$, both conjuncts of $P$ hold: the instance of the Necessity of Analysis fails. So Maximalism (pure) and the Necessity of Analysis together give $\bot$.

sources: Cian Dorr, argument of 28 October 2026 that Maximalism (pure) and Self-atoms are atoms are incompatible (session transcript).
results.proof:
Let $p:=\operatorname{Atom}_t(	op)$, the closed pure sentence saying that $	op$ is an atom, that is, that every proposition is $	op$ or $ ot$. In C, $p$ is necessarily an atom if true: if $p$, then $p\le	op$ and $p
e ot$, so $p=	op$, which is then an atom. Let $E_1:=\exists x^e orall y^e\, .\,y=x$, saying that there is exactly one individual. The closed pure sentences $p\land E_1$ and $p\land
eg E_1$ are each consistent with C: they are true in the one-world full models [[full-henkin-singleton-base]] and [[full-henkin-infinite-base]] respectively, where $	op$ is an atom since $D_t=\{0,1\}$. By the possibility form of Maximalism (pure), both are possible; in particular $\Diamond p$, so $p$ is a self-atom, and by Self-atoms are atoms (type $t$) it is an atom. Now $p\land E_1$ and $p\land
eg E_1$ are possible, hence distinct from $ ot$, and lie below the atom $p$, so each is $p$. Then $p=(p\land E_1)\land(p\land
eg E_1)= ot$, contradicting $\Diamond p$.
results.notes: Cian Dorr's first version took $p$ to be "there is exactly one individual, and that proposition is an atom", split by $\Box$ and $\Diamond$ of claims about the number of individuals; the possibilities it needs call for models in which the number of individuals grows along an arrow. With $p:=\operatorname{Atom}_t(\top)$, $\Box$ is trivial wherever $p$ holds, and two one-world full models witness everything. Compare [[maximalist-distinctness-incompatible-with-atomicity-t]].

results.proof:
Suppose $\Sigma$ has a constant $c$ of type $t$. Let C5 be $\Box$ND and let $F:=\lambda p\, .\, (\Diamond p\land\Diamond
eg p)\land\mathrm{C5}\land\mathrm{Atomicity}\land orall x orall y\, .\, x=y$, a closed pure term of type $tt$: being contingent while $\Box$ND, Atomicity and "there is exactly one individual" hold. Let $\Psi:= orall p\, .\,
eg\Diamond F(p)$, closed and pure.
(1) $\Psi$ is consistent with Maximalist Classicism (pure): it holds at the evaluation point of coalesced-definable-root, which satisfies Maximalism (pure) (see its write-up). In brief: at that root $\Box$ND fails, so nothing is $F$ there; and at a world where the side conditions of $F$ hold there is necessarily exactly one individual, so the sentence defining a root proposition is there the same proposition as a pure sentence, which is not contingent by $\Box$ND + Atomicity (type $t$) ⇒ No Pure Contingency.
(2) Strong Possibility (pure) therefore gives $\Diamond_{
e}\Psi$, that is $ orall q\, .\,q	o\Diamond( \Diamond q\land\Psi)$. Suppose $\Diamond F(p_0)$ for some $p_0$. With $q:=\Diamond F(p_0)$ there is a world $w$ at which $\Psi$ and $\Diamond\Diamond F(p_0)$ hold, hence $\Diamond F(p_0)$ by 4; but $\Psi$ at $w$, instantiated at $p_0$, says $
eg\Diamond F(p_0)$. So $ orall p\, .\,
eg\Diamond F(p)$.
(3) $F(c)$ is a closed sentence of $\mathcal L(\Sigma)$ consistent with C($\Sigma$): the full S5 model over the two-element group with one individual, with $c$ true at one world and false at the other, satisfies it. Maximalism for $\Sigma$, in its possibility form, gives $\Diamond F(c)$, contradicting (2) at $p:=c$.
If the constant of $\Sigma$ has a relational type $ ar\sigma t$ instead, replace "contingent" in $F$ by "contingently universal", $(X
e	op\land\Diamond X=	op)\lor(X=	op\land\Diamond X
e	op)$: for a closed term $X=	op$ is the closed sentence $ orall ar x\, .\,X ar x$, non-contingent by the same route, and $F(c)$ is satisfied by the same two-world model with $c$ universal at one world only.

references.note: Maximalist Classicism, its possibility form, and the distinctness-preserving modality.

results.notes:
Uses Maximalism for $\Sigma$ at the one sentence $F(c)$, and Strong Possibility (pure) at the one sentence $\Psi$, whose consistency with Maximalist Classicism is witnessed by a model rather than by a principle of the map. The conjunct $\forall x\forall y\, .\,x=y$ in $F$ is an amendment: without it the consistency of $\Psi$ would need every closed sentence with the individual constant of the model's signature, not only the pure ones, to be non-contingent under $\Box$ND + Atomicity. The argument does not reach Strong Possibility for $\Sigma$, whose consistency premise is stronger; whether Maximalism for $\Sigma$ is compatible with it stays open.

A different proof was given later and independently by GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), prompted by Daniel Kodsi, 22–23 October 2026: Maximalism for $\Sigma$ splits the proposition that there is exactly one individual and the Fregean Axiom holds, refuting its atomhood, whose consistency with Maximalist Classicism (pure) Astra shows with a separate model; Strong Possibility (pure) then makes that atomhood true. With this incompatibility the conjecture that Strong Possibility for $\Sigma$ implies Strong Possibility (pure) became equivalent to the inconsistency of Strong Possibility for $\Sigma$; it was withdrawn on 29 October 2026 (see [[strong-possibility-signature-r]]).

results.proof:
See the write-up. For a closed $F^{tt}$ let $S_F:= orall p\, .\,p
e ot	o(p\land Fp
e ot\land p\land
eg Fp
e ot)$. Atomicity (type $t$) proves $S_F= ot$: an atom $w\le S_F$ gives $\Box(w	o(w\land Fw
e ot\land w\land
eg Fw
e ot))$, so by $\Diamond w$ and the necessity of identity both $w\land Fw
e ot$ and $w\land
eg Fw
e ot$, contradicting atomhood. In the full Boolean-valued model over the rigid complete algebra $\operatorname{RO}(\mathbb P)$ of Jech and Shelah, higher-order logic interprets third-order arithmetic, in which $\operatorname{RO}(\mathbb P)$ and its cylinders are definable; rigidity makes the definable isomorphism with this copy the identity, so a closed pure $F$ denotes the map sending $p$ to the first cylinder that splits it. Then $S_F$ has value $1$, so $C
vdash S_F= ot$, and Maximalism (pure) gives $S_F
e ot$.
results.notes: Settles the question whether Maximalism (pure) is consistent with Atomicity (type $t$); it makes [[maximalist-distinctness-incompatible-with-necessary-atomicity-t]] a consequence. Rigidity of the algebra is what makes a splitter pure-definable: an automorphism of the algebra extends to the full model and fixes every closed pure term. The model used also satisfies C5, so the same argument refutes Atomicity (type $t$) with Maximalism relative to C5.

results.proof: Distinctness Maximalism (pure) is equivalent to Possibility Maximalism (pure). Rigid Comprehension implies Boolean Completeness, which restricts to Countable Boolean Completeness, which gives the Necessity of Arithmetic (the source's Theorem 9). Possibility Maximalism (pure) is incompatible with the Necessity of Arithmetic (the source's Theorem 11): Gödel's first incompleteness theorem supplies an arithmetical sentence $A$ with $I\land A$ and $I\land\neg A$ both consistent with C, both are then possible, and the necessity schema forbids that. The source draws exactly this consequence for Rigid Comprehension in the remark after Theorem 11.

sources: Cian Dorr, the notion of a self-atom and the bridge principles, 25 October 2026; the proof by Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic) the same day, from the survey of Strong Atomicity results that Cian Dorr requested (session transcript of 25 October 2026).
results.proof:
Let $X$ be a self-atom of type $\sigma$ and suppose $Z\le X$, $Z
e X$ and $Z
e ot$. Since $Z\le X$ but not $X\le Z$, $\Diamond\exists ar x\, .\,X ar x\land
eg Z ar x$; and $Z
e ot$ is $\Diamond\exists ar x\, .\,Z ar x$, which 5 makes necessary. At a world where $X ar x\land
eg Z ar x$, $X$ is instantiated and so an atom; $Z\le X$ still holds; $Z
e X$ there, since $X ar x\land
eg Z ar x$; and $Z
e ot$ there by the boxed possibility. So $Z$ is a non-bottom strict part of an atom, which is impossible. Hence $X$ is an atom. 5 is applied to the proposition $\exists ar x\, .\,Z ar x$, so its type-$t$ form serves at every $\sigma$.
results.notes: Since 5 is equivalent to ND (type t) in C, Self-Atomicity with ND (type t) gives Atomicity. Without 5 the implication fails: see [[finite-support-cantor-fan]] and [[full-monoid-ac-equals-bc]].

results.proof: Let $\Box\operatorname{WO}(R)$, and let $F$ be necessarily instantiated. Put $G:=\lambda x\, .\,Fx\land\forall y\, .\,Fy\to(Rx)y$, so that $G\le F$. At any world, $F$ is instantiated and $R$ is a well-order, so $F$ has an $R$-minimal instance $x$. For any instance $y$ of $F$, Total gives $(Rx)y$ or $(Ry)x$, and in the second case minimality gives $y=x$, whence $(Rx)y$ by Total again; so $Gx$. If also $Gy$, then $(Rx)y$ and $(Ry)x$, and Antisymm gives $y=x$. Hence $\Box\exists x\, .\,Gx\land\forall y\, .\,Gy\to y=x$.
results.notes: The selected property is the least instance of $F$ in the necessary well-order, which may be a different individual at different worlds.

sources: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), prompted by Daniel Kodsi, Universal modal selectors and persistence of MRC, research note of 26 October 2026, §§2–4 (unpaginated), in Daniel Kodsi's pull request #18 of 26 October 2026 (branch classicism-integration-2026-10-26 of github.com/dkodsi/Logical-Maps).
results.proof: One necessarily functional relation chooses, at every world, an instance of every instantiated property; it can then be used to choose from the rows of any relation. Fix $\tau$ and let $U:=\lambda F^{\tau t}y^\tau\, .\,Fy\lor\neg\exists z\, .\,Fz$. It is a theorem of C that $U$ is serial (types are inhabited), so $U$ is necessarily serial, and Modalized Relational Choice at $(\tau t,\tau)$ gives $S\le U$ with $\Box\operatorname{Functional}(S)$. So necessarily, for every $F$, exactly one $y$ has $(SF)y$, and it is an instance of $F$ if $F$ has one. By 4 this holds at every accessible world as well. Now work at any accessible world $w$, fix $\sigma$, and let $R^{\sigma\tau t}$ be necessarily serial there. Put $T:=\lambda x^\sigma y^\tau\, .\,(Rx)y\land(S(\lambda z\, .\,(Rx)z))y$. Then $T\le R$, and necessarily, for every $x$, the row $\lambda z\, .\,(Rx)z$ is instantiated, so its unique $S$-choice is an $R$-value of $x$ and is the unique $T$-value of $x$. So $\Box\operatorname{Functional}(T)$, and $T$ witnesses Modalized Relational Choice for $R$ at $w$. As $w$ was arbitrary, this is □Modalized Relational Choice at $(\sigma,\tau)$; no Barcan Formula is used, since the box over the universal quantifiers comes from the boxed functionality of $S$.
results.notes: The instance at $(\sigma,\tau)$ of the conclusion uses the instance at $(\tau t,\tau)$ of the premise. With the recorded results, Modalized Relational Choice is therefore equivalent to □Relational Choice together with Intensional Choice, and to □Relational Choice together with □Intensional Choice. This makes [[no-pure-contingency-and-modalized-relational-choice-imply-necessary-modalized-relational-choice]] and [[modal-well-ordering-implies-necessary-modalized-relational-choice]] derivable. Astra's note also proves the type-specific variant BF at $\sigma\tau t$ + Modalized Relational Choice at $(\sigma,\tau)$ ⇒ its necessitation, by the argument of [[barcan-and-intensional-choice-imply-necessary-intensional-choice]]; at the level of principles that is subsumed here.
