Let $w$ witness Strong Actuality: $w$ is true and $\Box orall q\, .\,w\le q\lor w\le
eg q$. Given $X$, put $Y:=\lambda ar z\, .\,w\le X[ ar z]$. $Y$ is coextensive with $X$: $w$ is true and settles each $X[ ar z]$. $Y$ is persistent, $w\le X[ ar z]$ being boxed, by 4. For the persistence of $
eg Y$, that is $\Box orall ar z\, .\,\Diamond(w\land
eg X[ ar z])	o\Box\Diamond(w\land
eg X[ ar z])$: ND gives B (ND (type t) gives 5, and 5 gives B, both recorded), so $\Box\Diamond w$, and $\Box\Box\Diamond w$ by 4. At any world, if $\Diamond(w\land
eg X[ ar z])$ then $w
ot\le X[ ar z]$, so $w\le
eg X[ ar z]$ by the boxed condition on $w$, and by 4 this holds at every later world, where $\Diamond w$ also holds; so $\Box\Diamond(w\land
eg X[ ar z])$.
results.notes: With the recorded gallin-comprehension-implies-nd and gallin-comprehension-implies-strong-actuality, Gallin Extensional Comprehension is equivalent to ND together with Strong Actuality. results.proof: The argument of [[atomicity-and-rigid-comprehension-imply-rigid-power]] is a derivation in C from instances of Atomicity, at the type of the power property, and of Rigid Comprehension, at the type of the relation and at that of its power property. sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, Proposition 2.11, p. 30 and n. 42.
results.notes:
Downgraded from proved to conjectured on 28 September 2026, at Cian Dorr's request. The source's proof (Proposition 2.11, note 42) has two gaps, found that day by an agent working in the Lean-Classicism formalization project; the write-up sets out the paper's argument with the gaps marked. (a) Part (iv) of note 42 boxes a claim that holds pointwise in the object variables by BF, where □BF would be needed. Cian Dorr agreed. (b) The same part's "without loss of generality" step replaces the atom $w'$ by $w''$, the greatest lower bound of the propositions $p$ with $w\le(p=w')$. The proof then needs $w\le(w''=w')$, so that $w''$ is still possible and below $X^*z\land\neg Yz$ where $w$ holds; nothing in the premises gives this, and □BF does not help. A propositional structure in which that step fails is sketched in the project's VERIFICATION.md; it has not been extended to a model of C with all the premises, so it shows that the step needs an argument, not that the proposition is false. What is proved there: Actuality, Boolean Completeness and BF (at the relevant types), together with a restriction principle, give Rigid Comprehension with the paper's witness $X^*$. The restriction principle says that for all $p,q$ there is an $r$ with $p\le(r=q)$ such that $r\le s$ whenever $p\le(q\le s)$. It holds in C5, with $r:=q\land\Diamond p$. Restructured this way, gap (a) disappears, and gap (b) becomes the question whether the premises here give the restriction principle. What would settle the conjecture: a derivation of the restriction principle, or another argument, from boxed Atomicity, Boolean Completeness and BF; or a model of C with those three principles that fails Rigid Comprehension. The source's first cross-reference to Proposition 2.6 was replaced in the earlier transcription by Proposition 2.7; the statement and premises are unchanged.

Refuted, 1 October 2026: the model ultralimit-fork, from Branden Fitelson (with Claude and GPT-6 Astra), satisfies Classicism, □Atomicity, □Boolean Completeness, □BF and □Actuality, and fails Rigid Comprehension at type $t\to t$. It extends the propositional structure mentioned above to a model of C with all the premises, so gap (b) is a genuine gap. The record stays conjectured, as the map's convention requires; the model is the refuting evidence. Gap-free in the end is part (ii), which gets Actuality: Atomicity (type $t$) and Weak Inextensible Comprehension imply Actuality (atomicity-t-and-weakly-inextensible-comprehension-imply-actuality), and Boolean Completeness implies Weak Inextensible Comprehension.

sources: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, argument no-atoms-no-self-atoms, 25 October 2026, turned into a result at Cian Dorr's suggestion of 29 October 2026.
results.proof: By 4, $\Box$Atomlessness gives $\Box\Box$Atomlessness, so at every world, and every world it sees, there is no atom of type $t$. Nor is there one of a relational type: an atom $X$ of type $\bar\sigma t$ would give the atom $\exists\bar x\, .\,X\bar x$ of type $t$, since for $q$ below it, $\lambda\bar x\, .\,X\bar x\land q$ is below $X$, so it is $X$ or $\bot$, and $q$ is then $\exists\bar x\, .\,X\bar x$ or $\bot$. So, necessarily, nothing is a self-atom: a self-atom is possible, so instantiated at some world it sees, where it is an atom. Necessarily, then, every self-atom is a strong atom (and so an atom), vacuously.
results.notes: With [[necessary-atomlessness-implies-necessary-atoms-are-strong-atoms-r]], every boxed bridge principle follows: these are the verdicts of the argument no-atoms-no-self-atoms, stated as consequences of □Atomlessness.

results.proof: Fix the type tuple $\bar\sigma$ and put $T:=\lambda\bar x\, .\,\top$. $T$ is persistent trivially, and inextensible: necessarily, if $\forall\bar x\, .\,\Box Z\bar x$ then $\Box\forall\bar x\, .\,Z\bar x$, by BF at each type in the tuple, which □BF gives at every accessible world. For the empty tuple $T=\top$ is rigid in C. Rigid Power makes $\lambda Y\, .\,\operatorname{Rigid}(Y)\land Y\le T$ rigid. Since $Y\le T$ is a theorem of C, that property is necessarily coextensive with $\lambda Y\, .\,\operatorname{Rigid}(Y)$, hence identical to it. Unboxed BF does not suffice for this argument: it makes $T$ only weakly rigid.

sources: Christopher Sun, argument reported by Cian Dorr on 26 September 2026; see the write-up.
Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.3, pp. 28–30 (inextensibility); Proposition 2.1, pp. 20–21 (BF).
results.proof:
Let $w$ witness Actuality and fix $F$ of type $ ar\sigma t$. Put $C:=\lambda ar z\, .\,\Diamond(w\land F[ ar z])$. $C$ is coextensive with $F$: if $F[ ar z]$ then $w\land F[ ar z]$ is true, hence possible; if $
eg F[ ar z]$ then $w\le
eg F[ ar z]$ by Actuality, so $
eg\Diamond(w\land F[ ar z])$. For inextensibility, two theorems of C: (i) $
eg C[ ar z]$ is $\Box(w	o
eg F[ ar z])$, so by 4 $
eg C[ ar z]	o\Box
eg C[ ar z]$, and hence $(C[ ar z]	o\Box X[ ar z])	o\Box(C[ ar z]	o X[ ar z])$; (ii) therefore $( orall ar z\, .\,C[ ar z]	o\Box X[ ar z])	o orall ar z\, .\,\Box(C[ ar z]	o X[ ar z])$. The closed instance of BF for the property $\lambda ar z\, .\,C[ ar z]	o X[ ar z]$, universally closed in $X$, turns the consequent of (ii) into $\Box orall ar z\, .\,C[ ar z]	o X[ ar z]$, which is $C\le X$. So BF (this instance) implies $ orall X\, .\,( orall ar z\, .\,C[ ar z]	o\Box X[ ar z])	o C\le X$ in C; necessitating and using the necessity of that instance gives $\Box orall X\, .\,( orall ar z\, .\,C[ ar z]	o\Box X[ ar z])	o C\le X$, which is $\operatorname{Inextensible}(C)$. The box on BF is used exactly once, to discharge the instance under the leading box of inextensibility.

references.note: Definitions of inextensibility and the BF principle. The witness is not one the paper uses.

results.notes: Actuality alone gives the coextensive witness and its weak inextensibility at the actual world; □BF is what makes the same witness inextensible at every world by this argument. Sun's later argument with the same witness needs only unboxed BF, recorded as actuality-and-bf-imply-inextensible-comprehension, from which this result follows. Together with the recorded routes, Inextensible Comprehension now follows from Actuality with any of □BF, Distinctness-preserving collapse, or C5 (through Rigid Comprehension); the □BF route explains the verdict in the full permutation-group, involution-group and surjection-monoid models, which have Actuality and □BF but not Distinctness-preserving collapse.

sources: Original argument of 3 October 2026, in response to Cian Dorr's question about Rigid Power.
results.proof: See the write-up. At any world, a counterexample to the weak inextensibility of the power property yields an atom $a$ entailing that some rigid $X\le F$ lacks a property $\mathcal X$. Rigid Comprehension pulls $X$ back to a rigid $X'$ coextensive with $\lambda z\, .\,Fz\land\Diamond(a\land Xz)$. Using the rigidity of $F$ and $X'$ below the atom, $a$ entails that $X$ and $X'$ are coextensive, and coextensive weakly rigid relations are identical; so $a$ entails $\mathcal XX$.

references.note: Rigidity and Rigid Comprehension.

results.notes: No B is used, so this covers settings that the C5 route does not reach. The argument uses BF, Atomicity and Rigid Comprehension at every world where weak inextensibility is checked, hence the boxed premises; it is a C-proof from those boxed premises, so the conclusion is boxed too.

sources: Zachary Goodsell, Arithmetic is Necessary, draft of 5 June 2024, Lemmas 3–4 and 8; the map write-up countable-boolean-completeness-implies-necessity-of-arithmetic records their proofs.

results.proof: Fix $\sigma$, $\nu=(\sigma t)t$ and $\rho=\nu t$. Goodsell’s numerical-haecceity argument (Lemma 8) proves the discharged C theorem $\mathrm{CBC}_{\sigma,\rho}\to\operatorname{WeaklyInextensible}(\mathbb N_\sigma)$. Necessitate that theorem and apply K to obtain $\Box\mathrm{CBC}_{\sigma,\rho}\to\Box\operatorname{WeaklyInextensible}(\mathbb N_\sigma)$, exactly the native inextensibility clause including its leading box. The unconditional number-persistence theorem (Lemma 3), itself necessitated, supplies native persistence. Under the Arithmetic Necessitism guard $\Box I^*_\sigma$, Lemma 4 gives necessary distinctness of current numbers. Discharging that guard proves the instance at every $\sigma$.
results.notes: A recovered composition of existing arithmetic lemmas. The extra box on CBC licenses all-future weak inextensibility. Current CBC alone cannot be necessitated while it remains an undischarged assumption; this proof does not establish current CBC implies Arithmetic Necessitism.

results.proof: In C, $\Box p$ is $p=\top$, so ND at type $t$ instantiated at $y:=\neg p$, $z:=\top$ reads $\Diamond p\to\Box\Diamond p$, the 5 axiom; with T this gives B, $p\to\Box\Diamond p$. Under the boxed premise $\Box$ is therefore necessarily N, K and B, an S5 operator, so $\Box_5p\to\Box p$ by the definition of $\Box_5$. With the chain $\Box\le\Box_{\ne}\le\hat{\hat\Box}\le\Box_5$ all four operators are identical, necessarily.
results.notes: Boxed ND at type $t$ makes $\Box$ itself S5, so every operator in the tower collapses to $\Box$ (collapse at level 0); the other boxed principles of the category follow by the composition results. Proposition D2 of The Bounds of Possibility gives the same step for identity-based operators.

sources: Neil Barton and Zachary Goodsell, Continuum Contingency, draft of 14 October 2026, §5.8, Theorem 3, in CR∞, C with □Rigid Comprehension and the axiom of Infinity (eq. (22)); the paper attributes the result to Goodsell 2021.
Zachary Goodsell, Arithmetic is Necessary, draft of 5 June 2024, for the numbers as finite cardinalities and the properties of successor used.

references.note: Stated for the naturals as the Fregean numerical relations on properties of individuals, with Infinity as an axiom of the logic; the map's numbers at $\sigma=e$ are those cardinalities, and the axiom is the principle's antecedent $\Box I^*_\sigma$. The map's rigidity convention is theirs.

results.proof:
Assume $\Box$Rigid Comprehension and $\Box I^*_\sigma$. Persistence of $\mathbb N_\sigma$ is a theorem of C: numbers are necessarily numbers, by induction with the property $\lambda n\, .\,\Box\mathbb N_\sigma n$, which holds of $\mathbf 0_\sigma$ and passes to successors by K (the step arith_N_box of the Lean proof of c5-implies-necessity-of-arithmetic), necessitated. Necessary distinctness: distinct numbers $m
e n$ are comparable, say $\operatorname{Sum}_\sigma(m,k,n)$ with $k
e\mathbf 0_\sigma$, by the trichotomy of the order on numbers, which induction gives; sums of numbers are necessary when true (arith_Sum_box), $k$ is necessarily a nonzero number, and at every world $I^*_\sigma$ makes $\operatorname{Sum}_\sigma(m,k,n)$ with $k
e\mathbf 0_\sigma$ imply $m
e n$, by induction on $k$ from the injectivity of successor; so $\Box\,m
e n$. Inextensibility, at any world: Rigid Comprehension there gives a rigid $Z$ coextensive with $\mathbb N_\sigma$; $Z$ holds of $\mathbf 0_\sigma$ and is closed under $\operatorname{Suc}_\sigma$, and, $Z$ being rigid and $\mathbf 0_\sigma$ and the successors of its instances the same entities at every world, it is necessarily so; hence necessarily $\mathbb N_\sigma\le Z$, the numbers being the instances of every inductive property, while $Z\le\mathbb N_\sigma$ necessarily by persistence of its instances, which are numbers. So $\mathbb N_\sigma$ is necessarily coextensive with a rigid property, and inherits its inextensibility: for any $X$ with $ orall n\in\mathbb N_\sigma\, .\,\Box Xn$, inextensibility of $Z$ gives $Z\le X$ and so $\mathbb N_\sigma\le X$. This is the argument of Theorem 3 of Barton and Goodsell, run at every type.
results.notes: Rigid Comprehension is used at every world, for the rigid coextension of $\mathbb N_\sigma$ there, so the premise is its necessitation; the antecedent $\Box I^*_\sigma$ of the principle is their axiom of Infinity. Without Rigid Comprehension the conclusion holds in C5 ([[c5-implies-arithmetic-necessitism]]).

references.note: □Rigid Comprehension, Intensional Choice and Mathematical Possibilism (the map's Forcing Possibilism) entail structural contingency about the continuum hypothesis, $\Diamond\exists X(\operatorname{Real}X\land\operatorname{CH}(X))\land\Diamond\exists X(\operatorname{Real}X\land\neg\operatorname{CH}(X))$, which contradicts both disjuncts of the Non-contingency of the Continuum Hypothesis at that type.

results.notes:
Stated by Bacon as a theorem, with the proof deferred to another venue; his handout of 19 October 2026 on the lottery-algebra model and the draft Modalized Domains on Possibility Frames do not reproduce it (the lottery record notes a transfer argument not given there). The expected proof: Forcing Possibilism supplies a proposition whose entailment algebra is a complete Boolean algebra forcing CH, and one forcing its negation; under □Rigid Comprehension and Intensional Choice the real number structures at the worlds below each are those of the corresponding generic extensions. Recorded as conjectured until a proof is supplied; a written proof, or a model of the three premises deciding CH one way necessarily, would settle it.

As encoded, with the map's strict reading of smallness (finite, or with strictly fewer elements than there are propositions), the conjecture is refuted: [[full-free-monoid-glued-constants]], [[full-free-monoid-glued-constants-singleton]], [[full-free-product-glued-constants]], [[full-double-retraction-glued-constants]] and [[ultraproduct-countable-full-s5-finite-individuals]] satisfy □Rigid Comprehension, Intensional Choice, Forcing Possibilism and Non-contingency of CH. Each has exactly $2^{\aleph_0}$ propositions, and an infinite complete Boolean algebra has at least $2^{\aleph_0}$ elements, so only finite algebras are small there, and Forcing Possibilism never asks for an algebra that changes CH. (For the ultraproduct, this holds in every factor.) The expected proof needs a CH-changing algebra to be small: an algebra forcing $\neg$CH has at least $\aleph_2$ elements, and one forcing CH over a model of $\neg$CH may have $2^{2^{\aleph_0}}$, so a premise saying that there are more than $2^{2^{\aleph_0}}$ propositions would suffice for that step, while one saying only that there are more than $2^{\aleph_0}$ might not. In the lottery cloud of Modalized Domains (Bacon and Claude Opus 5.5, Remark 6.12), which the source cites, every complete Boolean algebra of size below a strong limit $\mu$ is small and realized; Bacon's Theorem 6.1 is cited there as showing that CH is contingent in it.

Suggested repair (Cian Dorr, 25 October 2026): add the premise that there are more than $2^{2^{\aleph_0}}$ propositions, i.e. that no injective relation runs from the properties of the reals of some real number structure into the propositions. All five models above falsify it. It is not recorded as a principle until the repaired implication is proved, since by itself it would only call for large variants of many models.

results.notes: Downgraded from proved to conjectured on 11 October 2026, at Cian Dorr's request. The proof of Theorem 8.2 in the book has a gap, found while formalizing it in Lean and confirmed by Cian Dorr; the write-up sets out the book's argument with the gap marked. The argument proves $\forall p\,.\,Wp\to p=r$ at the evaluation point and then boxes it as following "from necessary assumptions". But step (i), that a $W$-proposition $p$ falls under some member of $H$ at every world, uses the claim that the world property $U=\lambda q\,.\,v\land q=p$ is $H$ because it is a world property accessible to $W$; that holds at the evaluation point, where $H$ is coextensive with the accessible world properties, but at another world $H$ is known only to be rigid, and need not contain the world properties built there from that world's $v$ and $p$. The step is needed exactly at such worlds, since $W$ may have no actual instance. Boxing Rigid Comprehension does not obviously help, since $r$ must be defined from a single actual $H$. What would settle the conjecture: a repair of step (i), or a model of C with □Strong Atomicity and Rigid Comprehension in which BF fails at some relational type. No recorded model refutes it, and without this record the map does not derive it. With □Rigid Comprehension and Rigid Power in place of Rigid Comprehension the conclusion holds (strong-atomicity-necessary-rigid-comprehension-and-rigid-power-imply-bf-relational, Cian Dorr), so a countermodel must fail one of those. The converse half of Theorem 8.2, atomicity-and-bf-relational-imply-strong-atomicity and its boxed form, is unaffected.

results.proof:
First the unboxed statement, for a relational type $	au= ar\sigma t$. Let $X^	au
e ot$. Intensionality’s contrapositive gives $\Diamond\exists ar y\, .\,X ar y$, and BF at the argument types gives $ ar x$ with $\Diamond X ar x$. The type-t Strong Atomicity gives a strong atom $w\le X ar x$: $w
e ot$ and $\Box orall q\, .\,(w\le q\lor w\le
eg q)$. Put $W:=\lambda ar y\, .\,w\land ar y= ar x$. Then $W
e ot$, since $W ar x=w$, and $W\le X$, since $\Box(w	o X ar x)$ and Leibniz’s law give $\Box orall ar y\, .\,W ar y	o X ar y$ by K. $W$ is a strong atom at $	au$: under the box, for any $Y^	au$, instantiate the strong-world clause of $w$ at $q:=Y ar x$; if $w\le Y ar x$ then $\Box orall ar y\, .\,W ar y	o Y ar y$, that is $W\le Y$, by the same K step, and if $w\le
eg Y ar x$ then $W\le
eg Y$ likewise; so $\Box orall Y\, .\,(W\le Y\lor W\le
eg Y)$, the passage under the outer box being by necessitation and K since each step is a theorem of C. For each $	au$ this derives the closed instance $\mathrm{SAt}_	au$ from $\mathrm{SAt}_t$ and finitely many BF instances in C; necessitating that conditional and applying K gives $\Box\mathrm{SAt}_	au$ from $\Box\mathrm{SAt}_t$ and $\Box$BF.

references.note: Strong atoms and Strong Atomicity.

results.notes: The unboxed form, Strong Atomicity (type t) + BF ⇒ Strong Atomicity, is already derivable on the map through Atomicity: Strong Atomicity (type t) gives Atomicity (t), Atomicity (t) + BF gives Atomicity, and Atomicity + BF gives Strong Atomicity. The direct construction above proves it in one step and is what is necessitated here; the boxed form was not derivable, since no record boxes the type-t instance of Atomicity. Only BF at the argument types of the target type is used, as in atomicity-t-and-bf-imply-atomicity.

results.proof: Fix the type tuple, with $P_F$ and $R_F$ as in weakly-rigid-power-implies-rigid-power. □Tame Rigidity at this type gives, necessarily, that every weakly rigid relation is rigid; with T the converse holds at every world. So $\operatorname{WeaklyRigid}$ and $\operatorname{Rigid}$ are necessarily coextensive at this type, $P_F$ and $R_F$ are necessarily coextensive, and they are identical in C. Now suppose $\operatorname{WeaklyRigid}(F)$. Tame Rigidity (by T) makes $F$ rigid; Rigid Power makes $R_F$ rigid, so by T weakly rigid; so $P_F=R_F$ is weakly rigid. Without the box the argument fails at weak inextensibility: $Z:=R_F$ satisfies $\forall X\, .\,P_FX\to\Box ZX$ at the evaluation point, so the weak inextensibility of $P_F$ requires $P_F\le R_F$, which is Tame Rigidity below $F$ at every accessible world.

references.note: T for the fixed background modality.

results.proof: Apply Intensional Choice at the type $\sigma\sigma t$ to $F:=\lambda R\, .\,\operatorname{WO}(R)$, which is necessarily instantiated by $\Box$Well-Ordering. This gives $G\le F$ that is necessarily uniquely instantiated. Put $R':=\lambda x\,y\, .\,\exists R\, .\,GR\land(Rx)y$. At any world the unique instance $R_0$ of $G$ there is a well-order, since $G\le F$, and $R'$ is coextensive with $R_0$ there. WO depends only on the extension of its argument at the evaluation point (Background), so $\operatorname{WO}(R')$ holds there. Hence $\Box\operatorname{WO}(R')$.
results.notes: Intensional Choice is used at the type $\sigma\sigma t$ to obtain Modal Well-Ordering at $\sigma$.

results.proof:
Let $c$ be a constant of $\Sigma$ of some relational type $	au$. The pure formulas $x=	op_	au$ and $x
e	op_	au$ have witnesses, so Witnessed Possibility gives $\Diamond(c=	op_	au)$ and $\Diamond(c
e	op_	au)$. By excluded middle one of the closed $\Sigma$-sentences $c=	op_	au$, $c
e	op_	au$ is true, and No Contingency (signature Σ) makes it necessary, contradicting the possibility of the other.
results.notes: Hence No Contingency (signature Σ) excludes Logical Necessity, Separated Structure, Possibly Witnessed Possibility and Maximalist Classicism for Σ, while it is consistent with No Pure Contingency and holds in every one-world model.

results.proof: Every closed instance of Actuality is a closed sentence of the pure language, since the principle is stated with object-language quantifiers and contains no nonlogical constant. Given Actuality, each of those instances is true, and No Pure Contingency makes a true closed pure sentence necessary. So every closed instance is necessary, which is what the boxed principle asserts. Any type range and side conditions stay outside the box, as the Modal scope convention requires.

references.note: Formulation of No Pure Contingency. The draft does not draw this consequence.

results.notes: One of a uniform family. No Pure Contingency carries any pure principle of the map to its boxed form, because a boxed principle here says exactly that each closed instance of the base is necessary. The argument turns on the base being stated with quantifiers rather than as a schema over arbitrary formulas, since an instance carrying a nonlogical constant would fall outside No Pure Contingency.

results.proof:
The type-$e$ instance of Intensional Choice fails in symmetric-all-surjections, a model of C. Let $a$ be an individual and $F:=\lambda x\, .\,x
e a$, which is necessarily instantiated since every world has infinitely many individuals. Suppose $G\le F$ is necessarily uniquely instantiated, pinned down by a finite $N
i a$. Let $h$ be a surjection sending all of $N$ to one individual $p$; at $h$, $G$ has a single instance $y
eq p$, since $G\le F$ and $h(a)=p$. A permutation $\sigma$ fixing $p$ and moving $y$ gives an arrow $\sigma\circ h$ agreeing with $h$ on $N$, so by pinning $G$ has the same extension at both arrows, while by symmetry its extension at $\sigma\circ h$ is $\{\sigma(y)\}$. Contradiction. So the negation of that closed pure instance is consistent with C, Possibility Maximalism (pure) makes it possible, and □Intensional Choice says the instance is necessary.

references.note: The symmetric ideally full action models.

sources: Zachary Goodsell, Arithmetic is Necessary, draft of 5 June 2024, §6, Theorem 11 and n. 14, pp. 24–26.
Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, 20 September 2026, for the consistency of C with $I$ (full-henkin-infinite-base).
results.proof:
Theorem 11 of the source, applied to C. The theorems of C are recursively enumerable, and C is consistent with $I$, since $I^*$ and hence $I$ hold in the full Henkin model with a countably infinite individual domain. So the arithmetical sentences $A$ with $C\vdash I	o A$ form a consistent, recursively enumerable extension of Peano arithmetic (the source's Lemma 1 supplies the axioms). By Gödel's first incompleteness theorem there is an arithmetical sentence $A$ for which neither $I	o A$ nor $I	o
eg A$ is a theorem of C, so $I\land A$ and $I\land
eg A$ are both consistent with C. Both are closed pure sentences, so Possibility Maximalism (pure) gives $\Diamond(I\land A)$ and $\Diamond(I\land
eg A)$. But the instance of the Necessity of Arithmetic at $A$ says $\Box(I	o A)$ or $\Box(I	o
eg A)$, and by K each disjunct contradicts one of the two possibilities.
results.notes: The source's theorem is general: the maximalization of any recursively enumerable extension of HK consistent with $I$ refutes some instance of the necessity schema. The record uses Possibility Maximalism (pure) directly; the equivalent Distinctness Maximalism form gives the same through the recorded equivalence. The argument is metatheoretic in two places, the recursive enumerability of C and Gödel's theorem, like the consistency side condition of Possibility Maximalism itself.

sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.4, pp. 35–37 (Distinctness); §3.2, Definition 3.6 and Proposition 3.7, pp. 47–48 (full Henkin models); §2.3, n. 47, p. 32 (Infinity).
results.proof:
For $k\ge1$ let $E_k$ be the closed pure sentence saying that there are exactly $k$ individuals, $\exists x_1^e\cdots x_k^e\, .\,( igwedge_{i<j}x_i
e x_j)\land orall y^e\, .\, igvee_i y=x_i$. Fix $n$ and take $E_1,\ldots,E_n$. For $i
e j$ the identity $E_i=E_j$ is closed and pure, and C does not prove it. A full Henkin model whose individual domain has exactly $i$ members is a model of C in which $E_i$ is true and $E_j$ is false, and at type $t$ that model's propositions are its two truth values, so the two sentences denote different things there. Distinctness Maximalism therefore gives $E_i
e E_j$. So $E_1,\ldots,E_n$ are $n$ pairwise distinct propositions, which is the $n$-th instance of Infinity at type $t$.

references.note: Formulations of Distinctness and Infinity, and the full Henkin models that supply the non-theoremhood side condition. The draft does not draw the connection between them.

results.notes:
Recorded from Distinctness Maximalism because the proof uses its non-theoremhood side condition directly. The equivalent Possibility Maximalism form gives the same result through the recorded equivalence. The witnesses need not be possible propositions, and at most one of them is true. What Distinctness Maximalism supplies is that C proves no identity among them. Only the type-$t$ instance follows, since the witnesses are propositions about how many individuals there are, not individuals.

The argument does not lift to the Axiom of Infinity at type $t$, and it is worth recording how far it does reach. For each fixed $k$ it refutes the claim that there are exactly $k$ propositions. If there were, then among the $k+1$ sentences $E_1,\ldots,E_{k+1}$ two would have to coincide, so C proves the finite disjunction of those identities, and Distinctness Maximalism refutes every disjunct. That is the schema over again, one sentence at a time. The axiom asks for the same of every cardinality falling under $\operatorname{FiniteCardinality}$, including ones that no closed term names, and Distinctness Maximalism bears only on identities between closed pure terms, so it says nothing about the domain over which $\operatorname{FiniteCardinality}$ quantifies. Any one derivation uses finitely many of its instances, and those are satisfiable while the universal property still carries a cardinality that the induction clause admits. The route through Atomlessness is closed too, since the map carries a model of the signature Distinctness Maximalism schema that satisfies Actuality, and Actuality excludes Atomlessness.

Added 20 September 2026: a different argument does reach the axiom. Applying the consistency side condition once, to the single sentence that every finite cardinality has a possibly instantiated successor, gives that sentence outright by persistence, and from it the Axiom of Infinity at type $t$ follows in C; see pure-possibility-implies-axiom-of-infinity-t. The limits described above concern the numeral-by-numeral argument recorded here.

sources: Cian Dorr, argument sketch of 20 September 2026.

Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.4, pp. 35–36 (Possibility); §2.3, n. 47, p. 32 (Infinity); §1.5, p. 17 (S4 for the defined necessity); §3.2, Definition 3.6 and Proposition 3.7, pp. 47–48 (full Henkin models); Appendix E, pp. 80–83 (coalesced sums).
results.proof: Write $g(Z)$ for $(\operatorname{Suc}_e Z)(\lambda x^e\, .\,\top)$ and let $\Pi$ be the closed pure sentence $\forall Z^{(et)t}\, .\,\operatorname{FiniteCardinality}_e(Z)\to\Diamond g(Z)$: there could be any positive number of individuals. Zero must be left out, since Existence makes $\mathbf{0}_e(\lambda x\, .\,\top)$ identical to $\bot$. $\Pi$ is true at the root of the model coalesced-all-finite-individual-domains, so it is consistent with C and Possibility Maximalism gives $\Diamond\Pi$. Being a finite cardinality is persistent, and the defined necessity satisfies 4, so $\Diamond\Pi$ yields $\Pi$ itself. Under $\Pi$ the map $g$ is injective on finite cardinalities: two finite cardinalities are either identical or necessarily share no instance, by an induction that stays inside the presentation $\operatorname{Suc}_e$ supplies, and the second disjunct is excluded when the two values of $g$ coincide and are possible. Hence the propositions $g(Z)$, $Z$ finite, carry a copy of the successor structure: the relation taking $g(Z)$ to $g(\operatorname{Suc}_e Z)$, and every other proposition to itself, is total and injective on $\lambda p\, .\,\top$ and misses $g(\mathbf{0}_e)$. A property with such a relation has no finite cardinality, by induction on the cardinality. So no finite cardinality of type $(tt)t$ holds of $\lambda p\, .\,\top$. The full proof, with the six lemmas, is in the write-up.

references.note: Formulations of Possibility and Infinity, the S4 laws of the defined necessity, the full Henkin models, and the coalesced-sum construction that the consistency model follows. The draft does not draw the connection between Possibility and the Axiom of Infinity.

results.notes: Recorded from Possibility Maximalism because the proof applies its consistency side condition to one sentence, $\Pi$, which quantifies over every finite cardinality at once. That is what reaches the domain over which $\operatorname{FiniteCardinality}$ quantifies, where the numeral-by-numeral argument recorded for the Infinity schema could not. The equivalent Distinctness Maximalism form gives the same result through the recorded equivalence, so Pure Maximalist Classicism implies the Axiom of Infinity at type $t$. ND is never used. The sentence $\Pi$ is not implied by the Axiom of Infinity at type $e$, by the model full-henkin-infinite-base. The argument can also be run entirely at type $t$, using the powers of two as the possible numbers of propositions; the write-up sketches this variant without carrying it out.

sources: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), prompted by Daniel Kodsi, Relational Choice and Boolean Completeness imply Actuality, research note of 22 October 2026, §§1–2 and 7 (unpaginated), in Daniel Kodsi's submission of 24 October 2026 (branch classicism-results-2026-10-24 of github.com/dkodsi/Logical-Maps).
results.proof: See the write-up. Boolean Completeness at $tt$ gives: a pairwise disjoint property of propositions whose join is true has a true member (join the haecceities $\lambda z\, .\,z=a$ of the members at $tt$; if $J$ is that join, $Jx\land Jy$ entails that $x=y$ or $x\land y=\bot$, and a true $q$ with $Jq$ exists by the truth of the join). If Actuality fails, the false propositions have join $\top$. Relational Choice from $t$ to $t$ chooses, for each $b$ below the join, a false proposition not below $b$; the Bourbaki–Witt tower of $b\mapsto b\lor s(b)$ yields pairwise disjoint false increments with join $\top$, a contradiction.
results.notes: The instances used are Relational Choice from $t$ to $t$ and Boolean Completeness at $tt$, which implies it at $t$; all unboxed. With [[actuality-implies-transversal]] and [[transversal-and-relational-choice-imply-transversal-choice]] this settles the conjecture [[relational-choice-and-boolean-completeness-imply-transversal-choice]]. The Bourbaki–Witt lemma is in Background, *General lemmas*.

sources: Zachary Goodsell, question of 25 September 2026, after Christopher Sun's observation; the quotient argument as recorded.
results.proof: Let $R^{\sigma\sigma t}$ be an equivalence relation and write $[x]$ for the cell $\lambda z\, .\,(Rx)z$. The relation $U^{(\sigma t)\sigma t}$ with $(UC)y:=Cy\lor\neg\exists z\, .\,Cz$ is serial, so Relational Choice gives a functional $S$ with $(SC)y\to(UC)y$. Put $Fy:=\exists x\, .\,(S[x])y$. Existence: given $x$, functionality gives $y$ with $(S[x])y$; the cell $[x]$ has the instance $x$, so $(U[x])y$ gives $(Rx)y$, and $Fy$ holds. Uniqueness: suppose $(Rx)y$, $Fy$, $(Rx)y'$ and $Fy'$, with witnesses $x_1$ and $x_2$, so that $(S[x_1])y$ and $(S[x_2])y'$. As before $(Rx_1)y$ and $(Rx_2)y'$, so $x_1$, $y$, $x$, $y'$ and $x_2$ lie in one cell and $(Rx_1)\equiv (Rx_2)$. Extensionality at type $\sigma t$ gives $[x_1]=[x_2]$, and functionality of $S$ gives $y=y'$.
results.notes: The only use of Extensionality is to identify the coextensive cells $[x_1]$ and $[x_2]$. In C alone properties are identical only when necessarily coextensive, which the hypothesis does not supply; see the recorded question relational-choice-r-implies-transversal-choice-r. The arrow is also derivable through Extensionality implies Rigid Comprehension and the arrow from Relational Choice with Weak Rigid Comprehension; it is recorded directly because it is the argument usually given.

sources: Zachary Goodsell, question of 25 September 2026, after Christopher Sun's observation; proof as recorded.
results.proof: First, two weakly rigid properties $C$ and $C'$ of type $\sigma t$ that are coextensive are identical. If $Cz$ then $C'z$, and weak persistence of $C'$ gives $\Box C'z$; so $\forall z\, .\,Cz\to\Box C'z$, and weak inextensibility of $C$ with $X:=C'$ gives $C\le C'$, that is $\Box\forall z\, .\,Cz\to C'z$. By symmetry $C'\le C$, so $\Box(C\equiv C')$, and Intensionality (necessarily coextensive relations are identical, a theorem of C, Classicism §1.5) gives $C=C'$. Now let $R^{\sigma\sigma t}$ be an equivalence relation. Relational Choice at types $(\sigma t,\sigma)$ gives a functional subrelation $S$ of the serial $(UC)y:=Cy\lor\neg\exists z\, .\,Cz$. Put $Fy:=\exists C\, .\,\operatorname{WeaklyRigid}(C)\land(C\equiv (Ry))\land(SC)y$. Existence: given $x$, Weak Rigid Comprehension gives a weakly rigid $C$ coextensive with $\lambda z\, .\,(Rx)z$; $C$ has the instance $x$, so the $y$ with $(SC)y$ satisfies $Cy$, hence $(Rx)y$; then $\lambda z\, .\,(Ry)z$ is coextensive with $\lambda z\, .\,(Rx)z$ and so with $C$, which gives $Fy$. Uniqueness: if $(Rx)y$, $(Rx)y'$, $Fy$ through $C$ and $Fy'$ through $C'$, then $C$ and $C'$ are both coextensive with the cell of $x$, hence with each other, so $C=C'$ by the first paragraph, and $(SC)y\land(SC)y'$ gives $y=y'$ by functionality.
results.notes: Weak rigidity is the weakest rigidity condition on the map, so the same proof runs from full Rigid Comprehension, and through the recorded arrows from Extensionality, Gallin comprehension with BF, C5 with Actuality, and boxed Functional Choice, which gives boxed Plenitude and so C5 and Actuality. Only the type-$\sigma t$ instance of the comprehension principle is used.

results.notes:
Does Relational Choice alone give a transversal for every equivalence relation? Christopher Sun observed that the literature claims this without proof. The converse is recorded. The quotient argument chooses from each cell $\lambda z\, .\,(Rx)z$ and needs the cells of two members of one class to be the same property; in C that is necessary coextension, and the hypothesis gives actual coextension only. No definable substitute for the cell helps, since an operation definable from $R$ identifies $x$ with $x'$ only when they are necessarily indiscernible with respect to $R$. A Zermelo-style well-ordering argument breaks at the same point: coextensive but distinct stages receive different chosen elements. The expectation is that the implication fails. What would settle it: a proof that uses the chosen relation to break the symmetry between coextensive cells, or a model of C with Relational Choice that is not extensionally full at its evaluation point. Every recorded model of Relational Choice is extensionally full there, in that every set of tuples from the domains is the extension of a rigid element, and that fullness verifies Transversal Choice by the same metatheoretic choice, so none separates the two. Symmetric Henkin models in the Fraenkel–Mostowski style cannot separate them either; see the write-up.
Update of 28 September 2026: Christopher Sun showed on 26 September that Transversal Choice is equivalent to Relational Choice together with Transversal (transversal-and-relational-choice-imply-transversal-choice), so this question is equivalent to whether Relational Choice implies Transversal. Anything that implies Transversal, such as Actuality, closes the gap.
Update of 28 October 2026: Vicinity also closes the gap ([[vicinity-and-relational-choice-imply-transversal-choice]], from GPT-6 Astra, prompted by Daniel Kodsi). So a model separating Relational Choice from Transversal Choice must falsify Vicinity, and hence ND at type $t$ and Actuality.

sources: Christopher Sun, Possible Worlds Without Atomicity, draft of September 2026.
results.proof: Lemma: coextensive weakly rigid relations are identical. Let $F$ and $G$ be weakly rigid with $F\equiv G$. If $F[\bar x]$ then $G[\bar x]$, and the weak persistence of $G$ gives $\Box G[\bar x]$. So $\forall\bar x\, .\,F[\bar x]\to\Box G[\bar x]$, and the weak inextensibility of $F$, instantiated at $G$, gives $F\le G$. Symmetrically $G\le F$. Together these say $\Box(F\equiv G)$, and necessarily coextensive relations are identical in C (Intensionality), so $F=G$. Now let $F$ be weakly rigid. Rigid Comprehension at the same type supplies a rigid $G$ coextensive with $F$. A rigid relation is weakly rigid, since T strips the leading boxes from both its conjuncts. By the lemma $F=G$, so $F$ is rigid.

references.note: Intensionality and T.

results.notes: The lemma uses only the unboxed persistence of $F$ and $G$, so Rigid Comprehension makes every very weakly rigid relation rigid as well. With Rigid Comprehension ⇒ Weak Rigid Comprehension, this gives Sun's equivalence of Rigid Comprehension with Tame Rigidity plus Weak Rigid Comprehension.

results.proof: For a property X of relations, choose a rigid coextension $X^*$. Define $U=\lambda\bar z\, .\,\forall Y\, .\,X^*Y\to Y[\bar z]$. results.proof: Let $R:=\lambda X\, .\,\operatorname{Rigid}(X)$ and $Z:=\lambda F\, .\,\operatorname{Rigid}(\lambda X\, .\,\operatorname{Rigid}(X)\land X\le F)$. By Rigid Power, every $F$ with $RF$ has $ZF$, and so $\Box ZF$, since rigidity, if true, is necessary ([[rigid-necessary]]). Rigid Rigidity makes $R$ rigid, so in particular inextensible; at the actual world, by T, this says that if every $F$ with $RF$ has $\Box ZF$ then $R\le Z$. So $R\le Z$, that is, $\Box\forall F\, .\,\operatorname{Rigid}(F)\to \operatorname{Rigid}(\lambda X\, .\,\operatorname{Rigid}(X)\land X\le F)$, which is □Rigid Power.
results.notes: The instance of Rigid Rigidity used is the one at the type of $F$, together with Rigid Power at the same type. Since □BF and Rigid Power imply Rigid Rigidity ([[necessary-barcan-and-rigid-power-imply-rigid-rigidity]]), □BF and Rigid Power imply □Rigid Power.

results.proof: Fix $\sigma$ and let $R:=\lambda Z^{\sigma t}\, .\,\operatorname{Rigid}(Z)$. Rigid Rigidity at $\sigma t$ makes $R$ weakly inextensible at every accessible world. Work at any such world, and suppose $\forall y\, .\,\Box Xy$. For each rigid $Z$, weak inextensibility of $Z$ applied to $X$ gives $Z\le X$, that is $\Box\forall y\, .\,Zy\to Xy$. So $\forall Z\, .\,RZ\to\Box QZ$ for $Q:=\lambda Z\, .\,\forall y\, .\,Zy\to Xy$, and the weak inextensibility of $R$ gives $\Box\forall Z\, .\,\operatorname{Rigid}(Z)\to\forall y\, .\,Zy\to Xy$. Necessarily every $y$ has a rigid haecceity $\lambda z\, .\,z=y$: it is persistent by the necessity of identity (a theorem of C), and inextensible, since $\Box Zy$ gives $\Box\forall z\, .\,z=y\to Zz$. So $\Box\forall y\, .\,Xy$. This is BF at $\sigma$ at an arbitrary accessible world, so □BF.

sources: Cian Dorr, conjecture of 10 October 2026.
results.notes: Cian Dorr proposed it on 10 October 2026, with an argument that assumed rigidity is closed under conjunction. It is not, in C: if $x\ne y$ but possibly $x=y$, the conjunction of their haecceities is persistent but not weakly inextensible, since weak inextensibility would require $\Box\,x\ne y$. Under □ND conjunctions of rigid relations are rigid and the argument goes through, but C5 already gives □Rigid Power. A countermodel must therefore have contingent identity at some accessible world: a rigid $Y$ not below a rigid $X$ that comes below it at an accessible world by identifications, without becoming identical there to any rigid subrelation of $X$ at the evaluation point. With the recorded results, the conjecture would make Rigid Rigidity equivalent to □BF + Rigid Power, and Weakly Rigid Weak Rigidity equivalent to BF + Weakly Rigid Power. Since Rigid Rigidity implies its necessitation, the conjecture is equivalent to Rigid Rigidity ⇒ □Rigid Power. It is refuted: coalesced-two-extensional-arithmetics-root (20 October 2026) satisfies Rigid Rigidity but not Rigid Power, as do the two supported-product models.

references.note: Analytical formulas do not distinguish relations that agree on the structure's elements, which lets the represented powers stand in for all relations; and categoricity across structures.

results.proof: See the write-up. Take the rigid structure $\mathfrak R$ and represented powers $\mathcal P_1,\dots,\mathcal P_n$ given by the premise for the arities occurring in the sentence $A$. Extend the induction of analytic-necessitism-implies-necessity-of-analysis to second-order formulas whose relation parameters are instances of the $\mathcal P_k$: such a parameter is rigid and holds only of tuples from $X$, so its atomic facts are necessary if true and impossible if false as before; a relation quantifier $\forall R\,\psi(R)$ is necessarily equivalent to $\forall R\in\mathcal P_k\,\psi(R)$, because necessarily every relation agrees on $X$-tuples with an instance of $\mathcal P_k$ and $\psi$ cannot distinguish relations so agreeing (Analytic Extensionality), and the restricted quantifier is handled by the rigidity of $\mathcal P_k$ as the quantifier over $X$ was. Categoricity for second-order analytical sentences finishes as in the first-order case.
results.notes: Every second-order analytical sentence uses finitely many arities, so the instance of the premise with $n$ the largest of them suffices. With [[necessity-of-second-order-analysis-implies-non-contingency-of-ch]] this gives the Non-contingency of the Continuum Hypothesis from Second-Order Analytic Necessitism.

results.proof: Let $X^{\bar\sigma t}\ne\bot$. results.proof: Let $P:=\exists q\, .\,\operatorname{SelfAtom}_t(q)\land q$. Every self-atom $q$ entails $P$: $\Box(q\to\Diamond q)$ is a theorem, and 4 turns $\Box(q\to\operatorname{Atom}(q))$ into $\Box\Box(q\to\operatorname{Atom}(q))$, so $\Box(q\to\operatorname{SelfAtom}_t(q))$ and $q\le P$. A true self-atom is a true atom by T, and a true atom entails every truth, so $P\to$ Actuality is a theorem of C; necessitate it and apply K.
results.notes: Strengthens [[strong-atomicity-t-implies-necessary-actuality]], since Strong Atomicity (type t) implies Self-Atomicity (type t). Fix a relational type $\sigma=\bar\sigma\to t$, write $W\bar x$ for application to a tuple, and let $J(R):=\lambda\bar x\,.\,\exists W\,.\,RW\land W\bar x$, the join of the members of $R$. Let $A$ be rigid and coextensive with being an atom of type $\sigma$. (a) $\Box\forall\bar x\,\exists W\,.\,AW\land W\bar x$: $J(A)$ is entailed by every atom, so by the dual of Atomicity at $\sigma$ (which Strong Atomicity at $\sigma$ gives) it is necessarily universal. (b) Necessarily every $A$-instance decides every entity of type $\sigma$, since the actual atoms are strong atoms by Strong Atomicity.
(ii) At every world $v$, each $Y$ of type $\sigma$ is $J(R_Y)$ for a rigid $R_Y\le A$ coextensive at $v$ with $\lambda W\,.\,AW\land W\le Y$, by Rigid Comprehension at $v$: $J(R_Y)\le Y$ by weak inextensibility of $R_Y$, and $Y\le J(R_Y)$ by weak inextensibility of $A$ at $v$ applied to $\lambda W\,.\,(\exists\bar x\,.\,W\bar x)\to W\le Y\to R_YW$, with (a) and (b) at later worlds; antisymmetry gives identity.
(iii) Rigid Power makes $\lambda R\,.\,\operatorname{Rigid}(R)\land R\le A$ rigid; if $\forall Y\,.\,\Box XY$, its weak inextensibility gives $\Box\forall R\,.\,(\operatorname{Rigid}(R)\land R\le A)\to X(J(R))$, and with (ii) under the box, $\Box\forall Y\,.\,XY$. This is BF at $\sigma$.

results.proof:
The argument of [[strong-atomicity-t-implies-necessary-actuality]], with Strong Actuality in place of Actuality. Write $D(w)$ for $\Box orall q\, .\,w\le q\lor w\le
eg q$ and $A$ for Strong Actuality, $\exists w\, .\,w\land D(w)$. Every strong atom $w$ entails $A$: by 4, $D(w)	o\Box D(w)$, and $\Box D(w)$ gives $\Box(w	o w\land D(w))$, hence $\Box(w	o A)$, which is $w\le A$. Now suppose $\Diamond
eg A$. Strong Atomicity (type $t$) supplies a strong atom $w\le
eg A$. With $w\le A$ this gives $w= ot$, contradicting $\Diamond w$. Hence $\Box A$.
results.notes: Stronger than [[strong-atomicity-t-implies-necessary-actuality]] and [[strong-atomicity-t-implies-strong-actuality]], which now follow, Strong Actuality implying Actuality. results.proof:
A strong atom is a self-atom. From $\Box orall Y\, .\,W\le Y\lor W\le
eg Y$, reason under the box: if $W$ is true it is not bottom, and an entity that is not bottom and lies below every entity of its type or its negation is an atom, since a strict part $Z$ of $W$ has $W\le
eg Z$ (else $W\le Z$ and $Z=W$), so $Z\le W\le
eg Z$ is bottom. Hence $\Box(W	o\operatorname{Atom}(W))$, and with $W
e ot$, $\operatorname{SelfAtom}(W)$. The strong atom below a possible entity is therefore a self-atom below it.
results.notes: Self-Atomicity is a weakening of Strong Atomicity: the fork model [[full-three-object-fork]] and the monoid model [[full-monoid-ac-equals-bc]] satisfy it, with Atomicity and Strong Actuality, and fail them.

sources: Cian Dorr, suggestion of 11 October 2026, after the gap in Bacon's Theorem 8.2.
results.proof:
Let $A$ be rigid and coextensive with being an atom, by Rigid Comprehension at $t\to t$. (a) $\Box\exists w\,.\,Aw\land w$: each atom $a$ has $\Box Aa$, so entails $\exists w\,.\,Aw\land w$, and Strong Atomicity (type t) gives Atomicity (type t), whose dual makes a proposition entailed by every atom necessary. (b) $\Box\forall w\,.\,Aw\to\forall q\,.\,w\le q\lor w\le\neg q$: Strong Atomicity puts a strong atom below each atom, which by atomicity is the atom itself, so each actual instance of $A$ necessarily decides every proposition, and weak inextensibility of $A$ boxes the claim.
(ii) At every world $v$, each proposition $p$ is $\exists w\,.\,R_pw\land w$ for a rigid $R_p\le A$: by Rigid Comprehension at $v$ (the premise is boxed) let $R_p$ be rigid and coextensive with $\lambda a\,.\,Aa\land a\le p$; $R_p\le A$ by its weak inextensibility. Necessarily, from $v$, $R_pw\land w$ gives $p$, by weak inextensibility of $R_p$ applied to $\lambda w\,.\,w\le p$. Conversely apply weak inextensibility of $A$ at $v$ to $Z:=\lambda w\,.\,w\to w\le p\to R_pw$: for a $v$-instance $a$ of $A$, either $a\le p$, so $R_pa$ and $\Box R_pa$, or $a\le\neg p$ by (b), and then necessarily $a$ and $a\le p$ are not both true; so $\Box Za$. At a later world where $p$ is true, (a) gives a true $A$-instance $w$, which by (b) entails $p$, so $R_pw$ by $Z$. So $p$ and $\exists w\,.\,R_pw\land w$ are necessarily equivalent from $v$, hence identical.
(iii) Rigid Power makes the power property $P_A:=\lambda R\,.\,\operatorname{Rigid}(R)\land R\le A$ rigid. Suppose $\forall p\,.\,\Box Xp$. Then $\Box X(\exists w\,.\,Rw\land w)$ for every $R$ with $P_AR$, so weak inextensibility of $P_A$ gives $\Box\forall R\,.\,P_AR\to X(\exists w\,.\,Rw\land w)$; with (ii) under the box, $\Box\forall p\,.\,Xp$. This is BF (type t).

references.note: A salvage of the theorem's idea, with □Rigid Comprehension and Rigid Power.

results.notes: Cian Dorr's salvage of Bacon's Theorem 8.2 (now conjectured). Strong Atomicity is used only at type $t$ and at the evaluation point, Rigid Comprehension at $t\to t$ at every world, and Rigid Power at $t\to t$. With the Tame Rigidity that Rigid Comprehension gives and the recorded TR + BF (relational types) ⇒ □BF (relational types), the map derives □BF (type t). So a model of □Strong Atomicity and Rigid Comprehension refuting BF (type t) must fail □Rigid Comprehension or Rigid Power at $t\to t$. The relational form is strong-atomicity-necessary-rigid-comprehension-and-rigid-power-imply-bf-relational.

results.proof:
Write $D(w):= orall q\, .\,w\le q\lor w\le
eg q$, so that $\operatorname{SAtom}_t(w)$ is $\Diamond w\land\Box D(w)$. (1) By Rigid Comprehension let $A$ be a rigid property of propositions coextensive with $\operatorname{SAtom}_t$. Each current instance $w$ has $\Box D(w)$, so weak inextensibility of $A$ gives $\Box orall w\, .\,Aw	o D(w)$. And $J:=\exists w\, .\,Aw\land w$ is $	op$: otherwise $\Diamond
eg J$, and Strong Atomicity (type $t$) gives a strong atom $w\le
eg J$; but $w$ is an instance of $A$, so $w\le J$, and $w= ot$, contradicting $\Diamond w$. So $\Box\exists w\, .\,Aw\land w$. (2) Let $\sigma$ be a relational type and $X$ of type $\sigma t$. Fix a current instance $w$ of $A$. By $D(w)$, every current $z$ has $w\le Xz$ or $w\le
eg Xz$; by Rigid Comprehension let $P$ and $Q$ be rigid and coextensive with $\lambda z\, .\,w\le Xz$ and $\lambda z\, .\,w\le
eg Xz$. Identities being necessary, weak inextensibility of $P$ applied to $\lambda z\, .\,w	o Xz$ gives $\Box orall z\, .\,Pz	o(w	o Xz)$, and likewise $\Box orall z\, .\,Qz	o(w	o
eg Xz)$. Every current $z$ is in $P$ or $Q$, so, by persistence, $ orall z\, .\,\Box(Pz\lor Qz)$, and BF at the relational type $\sigma$ gives $\Box orall z\, .\,Pz\lor Qz$. So necessarily, if $w$, then $X$ is coextensive with $P$, which is rigid ([[rigid-necessary]]): $\Box(w	o E_X)$, with $E_X:=\exists Y\, .\,\operatorname{Rigid}(Y)\land X\equiv Y$. Weak inextensibility of $A$ applied to $\lambda w\, .\,w	o E_X$ gives $\Box orall w\, .\,Aw	o(w	o E_X)$, and with (1), $\Box E_X$. This holds for every current $X$, so BF at the relational type $\sigma t$ gives $\Box orall X\, .\,E_X$: Rigid Comprehension at relational argument types is necessary. (3) Individual and mixed argument tuples reduce to relational ones by a theorem of C, which is therefore necessary. For a tuple type $ ar\sigma$ let $H_{ ar x}:=\lambda ar z\, .\, ar z= ar x$, of the relational type $\delta:= ar\sigma t$, and $\operatorname{Code}(H):=\exists ar x\, .\,H=H_{ ar x}$. Given $X$ of type $ ar\sigma t$, let $P$ be rigid and coextensive with $\lambda H\, .\,\exists ar x\, .\,H=H_{ ar x}\land X ar x$, and $Y:=\lambda ar x\, .\,P(H_{ ar x})$, which is coextensive with $X$ since $H_{ ar x}=H_{ ar y}$ iff $ ar x= ar y$. Each current instance of $P$ is a code, necessarily, so weak inextensibility gives $\Box orall H\, .\,PH	o\operatorname{Code}(H)$. $Y$ is persistent since $P$ is. At any point, if $Y ar x	o\Box Z ar x$ for all $ ar x$, then each instance $H_{ ar a}$ of $P$ there has $\Box orall ar x\, .\,H=H_{ ar x}	o Z ar x$, and weak inextensibility of $P$ gives $Y\le Z$. So $Y$ is rigid.
results.notes: With [[necessary-rigid-comprehension-implies-necessary-weak-rigid-comprehension]] and [[necessary-weak-rigid-comprehension-implies-necessary-boolean-completeness]], □Boolean Completeness follows. BF is used only at the evaluation point and only at relational types; BF at type $e$ is not needed, and fails in full-two-object-chain-new-individual, where Strong Atomicity and Rigid Comprehension hold. Astra also proposed a countermodel showing that BF at relational types cannot be weakened to □BF (type $t$); it is not recorded yet.

results.proof: See the write-up. For each type-$t$ atom $w$, choose a strong atom $X_w$ of type $\sigma t$ below $\lambda y\, .\,w\land Fy$; take a weakly rigid $R$ coextensive with the property of being some $X_w$, and put $G:=\lambda y\, .\,\exists X\, .\,RX\land Xy$. Weak inextensibility carries to every world the facts that each instance of $R$ is a strong atom below $F$, and that any two instances are identical or not both instantiated. A strong atom has at most one instance.

results.notes:
Strengthens [[bf-weak-rigid-comprehension-atomicity-and-relational-choice-imply-intensional-choice]], since BF and Atomicity imply Strong Atomicity; BF is not used, and the modal reasoning needs only T and 4. Strong Atomicity is used at type $\sigma t$, where atoms would not do: an atom of type $\sigma t$ settles only actual properties, while the uniqueness step needs the chosen property to settle the haecceity of an instance at another world.

The argument does not extend to Modalized Relational Choice. With inputs, values would be chosen for pairs of an atom and an actual input. Distinct actual inputs may be identified, without ND, at a world where the atom is true, and the merged input then has two values, so the pair-lemma step fails. And without BF an input that is not actual has no chosen value at all.

Strengthened by [[self-atomicity-atomicity-t-weak-rigid-comprehension-and-relational-choice-imply-intensional-choice]]: self-atoms of type $\sigma t$ serve for strong atoms, with Atomicity (type t) kept for the indices.

sources: OpenAI Codex (GPT-6), prompted by Daniel Kodsi, research notes finite-c5-profile-cells and signature-sp-barcan of 22 October 2026, and Strong Possibility: explicit Barcan failures and the signature boundary, 28 October 2026, §§2–3 (unpaginated), in Daniel Kodsi's pull request #21.
results.proof:
(1) Let $B$ be the closed pure sentence "$\Box\mathrm{ND}_t$, there is exactly one individual and there are exactly four propositions". It is consistent with C, being true in the full model with two worlds and one individual. Over C, $\Box\mathrm{ND}_t$ gives C5 ([[necessary-distinctness-necessary-t-implies-necessary-distinctness-necessary-r]]) and so BF at every type ([[necessary-nd-implies-bf]]). Under C5, a closed formula built from identities by connectives and quantifiers denotes $	op$ or $ ot$: identities do by ND and NI, connectives preserve this, and if every instance of $ orall x\,\varphi$ is $	op$ then BF makes $ orall x\,\varphi$ necessary. The last two conjuncts of $B$ are such formulas, and $\Box\mathrm{ND}_t	o\Box\Box\mathrm{ND}_t$. So $B	o\Box B$ is a theorem of C. (2) $\operatorname{Atom}(B):= orall p\, .\,B
e ot\land(B\land p=B\lor B\land p= ot)$ is a universal Boolean combination of identities, true at the root of [[coalesced-definable-root]], where Maximalism (pure) holds. The argument is the one for the atoms $A_n$ in that model's write-up. Let $V$ be a component object where $B$ is true. By C5, BF and [[modalized-functionality-r]], an entity of type $\sigma t$ at $V$ is fixed by its values, propositions, at the finitely many entities of type $\sigma$; and every function is realised, by $\lambda x\, .\, igvee_i(x=a_i\land q_i)$. Quantifiers are finite meets and joins. So the domains at $V$ are the full finite function spaces over one individual and the four-element Boolean algebra, with crisp identity, and the truth at $V$ of a formula depends only on this structure and the ultrafilter of truths at $V$. Any two such pointed structures are isomorphic, the swap of the algebra's two atoms exchanging its two ultrafilters. So a root proposition $p$, with witness $t$, has the same value at every arrow $\langle V,aangle$ with $B$ true at $V$. At the identity $B$ is false, as there are infinitely many root propositions. So $B\land p$ is $B$ or $ ot$, and $B
e ot$ since the components are complete for C. (3) By the reflection lemma of [[strong-possibility-and-strong-actuality-incompatible]], Strong Possibility (pure) gives $\operatorname{Atom}(B)$. It also gives Maximalism (pure) ([[strong-possibility-r-implies-possibility-schema-r]]), so $B
e ot$, that is $\Diamond B$, since $B= ot$ is not a theorem of C. (4) Let $\Phi:=\lambda p\, .\,B	o(p=	op\lor p= ot)$. For each $p$, $\operatorname{Atom}(B)$ gives $B\land p=B$ or $B\land p= ot$, which is necessary by NI; and necessarily, if $B$ then $B=	op$ by (1), so $p=	op$ or $p= ot$. So $ orall p\, .\,\Box\Phi p$. But at a possible point where $B$ is true there are four propositions, two of them neither $	op$ nor $ ot$, so $\Diamond
eg orall p\, .\,\Phi p$. This contradicts BF at type $t$.
results.notes: Full BF and Functionality are excluded too, by recorded implications. Codex's write-up also gives a counterinstance at every input type, and at type $e$, through $\lambda\bar x\, .\,p$ and the sentence "there is exactly one individual". It also proves the same incompatibility for Strong Possibility over a fixed finite signature, which is not recorded, since signature principles on the map range over arbitrary signatures. Step (2) rests on the construction of coalesced-definable-root, which has not had a second reader.

results.proof: Let $R^{\sigma\sigma t}$ be an equivalence relation, and write $[x]$ for its cell $\lambda z\, .\,(Rx)z$. Transversal at $\sigma$ gives $F^{(\sigma t)t}$ such that each property is coextensive with exactly one $F$-property. Relational Choice at types $(\sigma t,\sigma)$, applied to the serial relation $(UC)y:=Cy\lor\neg\exists z\, .\,Cz$, gives a functional $S$ with $(SC)y\to(UC)y$. Put $Gy:=\exists Y\, .\,FY\land(Y\equiv (Ry))\land(SY)y$. Existence: given $x$, let $Y_x$ be the $F$-property coextensive with $[x]$. It has the instance $x$, so the $y$ with $(SY_x)y$ satisfies $Y_xy$, hence $(Rx)y$. Then $[y]$ is coextensive with $[x]$ and so with $Y_x$, and $Gy$ holds through $Y_x$. Uniqueness: suppose $(Rx)y$ and $(Rx)y'$, with $Gy$ through $Y$ and $Gy'$ through $Y'$. Then $Y$ is coextensive with $[y]$, $[y]$ with $[x]$, $[x]$ with $[y']$, and $[y']$ with $Y'$; so $Y$ and $Y'$ are $F$-properties coextensive with $[x]$, and $Y=Y'$ by the uniqueness clause of Transversal. Now $(SY)y$ and $(SY)y'$, so $y=y'$ by functionality of $S$. Thus $G$ is a transversal of $R$.
results.notes: With the converse arrows from Transversal Choice to Transversal and to Relational Choice, Transversal Choice is equivalent to Transversal together with Relational Choice. The argument is the quotient argument of relational-choice-and-extensionality-imply-transversal-choice, with the $F$-representative of each cell in place of the cell itself; this is the step Relational Choice alone does not supply. Consequently Relational Choice implies Transversal Choice if and only if it implies Transversal.

results.proof: Let $U^{\sigma\tau t}$ be serial. For $x^\sigma$ and $y^\tau$ write $\langle x,y\rangle$ for the rigid pair $\lambda u^\sigma v^\tau\, .\,u=x\land v=y$, of the admitted type $\sigma\tau t$; the case $\tau=e$ is included. Pairing is injective: if $\langle x,y\rangle=\langle x',y'\rangle$, apply both sides to $x$ and $y$. The left side is $x=x\land y=y$, a theorem of H, so by Logical Equivalence it is $\top$; hence $x=x'\land y=y'$ is $\top$ and so true. Call $P$ a $U$-pair if $\exists x y\, .\,(Ux)y\land P=\langle x,y\rangle$. Let $E$ relate two $U$-pairs when some $x$ is the first coordinate of both, and relate any two non-$U$-pairs. By injectivity $E$ is an equivalence relation on type $\sigma\tau t$, and the cell of a $U$-pair $\langle x,y_0\rangle$ consists exactly of the pairs $\langle x,y\rangle$ with $(Ux)y$. Transversal Choice gives $F^{(\sigma\tau t)t}$ with exactly one instance in each cell. Put $(Sx)y:=(Ux)y\land F\langle x,y\rangle$; this is a subrelation of $U$. Given $x$, seriality gives $y_0$ with $(Ux)y_0$, so the cell of $\langle x,y_0\rangle$ has a unique $F$-instance $\langle x,y_x\rangle$, and $(Sx)y$ holds iff $\langle x,y\rangle$ is that instance iff $y=y_x$. So $S$ is functional.
results.notes: Transversal Choice is therefore at least as strong as Relational Choice over C. Whether it is strictly stronger is the recorded question relational-choice-r-implies-transversal-choice-r.

sources: Serge Lang, Algebra, Appendix 2.
Cian Dorr, suggestion of 8 October 2026, to prove Zorn's Lemma from Transversal Choice and to ask whether it needs Transversal Choice rather than Relational Choice.
Cian Dorr, suggestion of 27 October 2026, to prove it through the Bourbaki–Witt lemma.
results.proof: See the write-up. Apply the [[bourbaki-witt|Bourbaki–Witt lemma]] at type $\sigma t$ to the $R$-chains, preordered by inclusion, so that $\approx$ is coextension. The supremum of a family of $R$-chains that inclusion totally preorders is their union, which is again an $R$-chain. Relational Choice, which follows from Transversal Choice, chooses for each chain a point that extends it if anything does. The step relation $F$ adds that point. To make $F$ invariant, as the lemma requires, the point is chosen at the representative of the chain's coextension class given by Transversal, the instance of Transversal Choice at $\sigma t$ for coextension. The lemma gives a chain that nothing extends, and any upper bound of it is maximal.

references.note: Lang derives Zorn's Lemma for partial orders on sets from the Bourbaki–Witt fixed-point theorem, applied to the chains ordered by inclusion. The translation replaces sets by properties and the choice function by a functional relation. It adapts the argument to preorders, and uses Transversal to make the step invariant under coextension, which for sets is automatic.

results.notes: Only the invariance of the step goes beyond Relational Choice. Since Zorn's Lemma implies Well-Ordering and so Transversal Choice, proving it from Relational Choice alone would settle whether Relational Choice implies Transversal Choice, which is open. The Lean certificate formalizes an earlier proof of the record, which followed Lewin's proof by conforming subsets.

results.proof: See the write-up. Let $s$ be the true proposition of [[vicinity-and-relational-choice-imply-transversal-choice]], below which every identity is settled and material quantification over a settled family of propositions computes its actual meet or join. If no atom is true, some true $h\le s$ has nothing but atomless elements below it. [[relational-choice-r|Relational Choice]] partitions each nonzero $p\le h$ into proper parts, settledly, and the [[bourbaki-witt|Bourbaki–Witt lemma]], with [[boolean-completeness-t|Boolean Completeness]] at $t$ for the glbs of chains, gives a descending chain $M$ following the true parts, all of whose members are true except the last, $m$, which is their glb. A second use of Relational Choice codes the discarded parts in one proposition $b$, which yields a term $g$ agreeing with the step of $M$ at its true members. The [[bourbaki-witt-admissible|admissible Bourbaki–Witt lemma]] for $g$, with the settled properties admissible, gives a settled chain $N$ containing $M$, whose members above $m$ form a settled family of truths with glb $m$. So $m$ is true, a contradiction.

sources: Cian Dorr, Boolean Completeness does not imply Rigid Comprehension, draft of 30 July 2026, footnote on p. 12.
results.proof: Take the propositional case first. Given $F^{tt}$, let $C^{tt}$ be weakly rigid and coextensive with $F$, and put $q:=\exists p\, .\,Cp\land p$. Every $F$ proposition $p$ is $C$, hence necessarily $C$ by persistence, so $p$ entails $Cp\land p$ and thereby $q$; so $q$ is an upper bound of the $F$ propositions. Now suppose every $F$ proposition entails $r$. The $C$ propositions are the $F$ propositions, so every $C$ proposition entails $r$; entailments are necessary if true, so $\forall p\, .\,Cp\to\Box(p\le r)$. Weak inextensibility with $X:=\lambda p\, .\,(p\le r)$ gives $C\le X$, so at every world $Cp$ implies $p\le r$; hence $Cp\land p$ entails $r$ whatever $p$ may be, and $q\le r$. So $q$ is a least upper bound of the $F$ propositions. The same reasoning with extra parameters gives the least-upper-bound form at every relational type, and that form is equivalent in C to the greatest-lower-bound form in which the principle is stated.

references.note: Boolean Completeness and the equivalence of its two forms.

results.proof: See the write-up. Given a well-order $R$, take weakly rigid properties coextensive with the initial segments of $R$, and a weakly rigid property $R^*$ coextensive with being one of them. Weak inextensibility of $R^*$ carries facts that hold necessarily of each actual segment to every instance of $R^*$ at every world. In this way $R^*$ is necessarily a chain under $\le$ that is well-ordered by $\le$; BF at $\sigma$ makes its instances necessarily cover $\sigma$; and an induction using weak inextensibility of the strict segments shows that its instances necessarily separate any two distinct individuals. Then $\lambda x\,y\, .\,\forall M\, .\,R^*M\land My\to Mx$ is necessarily a well-order.
results.notes: Well-Ordering is used only at the evaluation point, Weak Rigid Comprehension only at the types $\sigma t$ and $(\sigma t)t$, and BF only at $\sigma$, once. Modal Well-Ordering implies its own necessitation and Intensional Choice, so the premises give boxed Intensional Choice; this improves on bf-weak-rigid-comprehension-atomicity-and-relational-choice-imply-intensional-choice by trading Atomicity and Relational Choice for Well-Ordering. Cian Dorr's sketch used Rigid Comprehension and asked whether the family of rigid initial segments is necessarily well-ordered; the step needing a new idea turned out to be separation, handled by applying weak inextensibility to the strict segments.

sources: Cian Dorr, suggestion of 8 October 2026, to connect Transversal Choice, Zorn's Lemma and Well-Ordering; proof as recorded.
results.proof: Fix $\sigma$ and apply Zorn's Lemma at $\sigma\sigma t$. For $S^{\sigma\sigma t}$ let $\operatorname{Fld}(S):=\lambda x\, .\,(Sx)x$, and call $S$ good if $\forall x\,y\, .\,(Sx)y\to(Sx)x\land(Sy)y$ and $\operatorname{WO}(S,\operatorname{Fld}(S))$. Say $S\sqsubseteq S'$ ($S'$ end-extends $S$) if $\forall x\,y\, .\,(Sx)y\to(S'x)y$ and $\forall x\,y\, .\,(Sx)x\land(S'y)x\to(Sy)x$; this is reflexive and transitive, and if $S\sqsubseteq S'$ then $S'$ agrees with $S$ on $\operatorname{Fld}(S)$. Put $(\mathsf RS)S':=\neg\operatorname{Good}(S)\lor(\operatorname{Good}(S')\land S\sqsubseteq S')$, a preorder on $\sigma\sigma t$ in which everything not good lies below everything. Chains have upper bounds: if $\mathsf R$ totally orders $\mathcal X$, its good members are $\sqsubseteq$-comparable, and $T:=\lambda x\,y\, .\,\exists S\, .\,\mathcal XS\land\operatorname{Good}(S)\land(Sx)y$ end-extends each of them. $T$ is good: any finitely many points of $\operatorname{Fld}(T)$ lie in the field of one good member $S$, on which $T$ agrees with $S$; and if $Y\subseteq\operatorname{Fld}(T)$ has an instance in $\operatorname{Fld}(S)$, the $S$-minimal instance of $\lambda w\, .\,Yw\land(Sw)w$ is $T$-minimal in $Y$, since $(Tw)m$ with $(Sm)m$ gives $(Sw)m$. So $T$ is an $\mathsf R$-upper bound of $\mathcal X$. Zorn's Lemma gives a maximal $m$. It is good, since otherwise $(\mathsf Rm)(\lambda x\,y\, .\,\bot)$ holds and the converse fails, the empty relation being good. If some $z$ had $\neg(mz)z$, then $m':=\lambda x\,y\, .\,(mx)y\lor((mx)x\land y=z)\lor(x=z\land y=z)$, which puts $z$ on top, would be good with $m\sqsubseteq m'$; maximality gives $m'\sqsubseteq m$, so $(mz)z$, a contradiction. So $\operatorname{Fld}(m)$ is coextensive with $\lambda x\, .\,\top$, and $\operatorname{WO}(m)$, since WO depends only on extensions.
results.notes: The standard argument. End-extension of relations is only a preorder, since coextensive but distinct relations end-extend each other, which is why Zorn's Lemma is recorded for preorders. The non-good relations are placed at the bottom so that the preorder is defined on the whole type.

sources: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), prompted by Daniel Kodsi, Absorbing entrance with finitely supported pair intensions, research note of 26 October 2026, §§1–5 (unpaginated), in Daniel Kodsi's pull request #18 of 26 October 2026 (branch classicism-integration-2026-10-26 of github.com/dkodsi/Logical-Maps).

references.note: Action models; the domains here are the finitely supported part of a full action model.

meets.sigma-top: Every constant of Σ is relational and denotes the top element of its type, which is fixed by every swap.
meets.infinitely-many-individuals: The individuals are the countably many $A_n^i$.

models.definition: Two objects $r$ and $s$, with one arrow $a:r\to s$, the integers as the arrows $s\to s$ (composed by addition), none from $s$ to $r$, and $k\circ a=a$ for every integer $k$; so only $1_r$ and $a$ leave $r$. The individuals at both objects are $A_n^0,A_n^1$ ($n\in\mathbb N$), fixed by every arrow. The group $\Gamma=\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}$ acts on them by swapping the $n$th pair when $\gamma(n)=1$, and on everything else through them; it is not part of the category. A relational domain at an object holds the intensions of the full action model (sets of tuples tagged by the arrows out of the object) that have finite support, being fixed by every $\gamma$ vanishing on some finite set. Evaluation point: $1_r$. Interpretation of Σ: every constant of Σ is relational, and each denotes the top element of its type.

arguments.text:
Intensional Choice holds at $r$ at every type: if $F$ is necessarily instantiated, pick $x$ in its row at $1_r$ and $y$ in its row at $a$; the intension holding of $x$ at $1_r$ and of $y$ at $a$ is finitely supported, entails $F$, and has exactly one instance at both arrows out of $r$. It fails at $s$ at type $e$, for the intension $F$ holding at the arrow $
u(n)$, for a bijection $
u:\mathbb N	o\mathbb Z$, of the $n$th pair: $F$ is fixed by every swap and necessarily instantiated, but if $G\le F$ is necessarily uniquely instantiated with support $N$ and $n
otin N$, the swap of the $n$th pair fixes $G$ and the arrow $
u(n)$ and exchanges the two candidates for $G$'s instance there.

At each object and relational type the order is inclusion of tagged sets. The actual instances of a property with support $N$ form a family invariant under the swaps vanishing on $N$, so its union is supported by $N$, admitted, and the least upper bound.
A singleton tagged tuple is supported by the union of its entries' finite supports, so it is admitted, and it is an atom below every relation containing it.

Since $k\circ a=a$, every proposition at $r$ transports along $a$ to $\varnothing$ or $\mathbb Z$. Let $Q$ hold at $1_r$ of every proposition and at $a$ of these two. Then every proposition necessarily has $Q$, but $\{0\}$ lacks it at $a$.
$\{1_r\}$ and $\bot$ are distinct at $r$, and both transport to $\bot$ along $a$.

A weakly rigid $Y$ has rows containing $k\cdot Y_1$, by weak persistence, and contained in it, by weak inextensibility tested against that haecceity disjunction; so it is rigid.

models.definition:
Take the full Henkin models $M_n$ with individual domain $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ for every $n\ge1$, and add a root world. Individuals are threads $(a_n)_n$ with $a_n\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$. Application is componentwise, identity at world $n$ is the identity of $M_n$ and at the root is identity of elements. Every theorem of C holds at every world. Evaluation point: the root.

The root has one distinguished arrow to the root of each component, and every arrow from the root into a component factors through it.

Propositions are sets of worlds; an entity of a function type is a family of $M_n$-entities together with an arbitrary root component defined on whole threads.

arguments.text: At the root the finite cardinalities are the numerals, the $k$-th numeral's successor holds of the universal property at world $k+1$, and $\Diamond$ at the root is truth at some world, so the sentence that there could be any positive number of individuals, used in pure-possibility-implies-axiom-of-infinity-t, holds there. The root has uncountably many individuals and infinitely many propositions, so both Axioms of Infinity hold there.
Two threads that agree at some world are distinct but possibly identical, so ND fails at type $e$.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: At a type $\sigma\to t$ a root entity is a pair $(G_0,(G_n)_n)$ with $G_0$ any function on the root domain and $G_n$ in the full domain of $M_n$; entailment is componentwise. Atomicity: below a nonzero $G$ lies the atom that is true at the root of one argument $a$ with $G_0(a)=1$ and bottom in every component, or, if $G_0=0$, the atom that is bottom at the root and in all but one component $M_n$, where it is an atom of that full model below $G_n$. Both kinds of atom are strong atoms: at the root they entail every entity or its negation, being singletons in one coordinate and bottom elsewhere, and their shifts to the components are bottom or atoms of a one-world full model. So Strong Atomicity Biconditionals hold at every type. Boolean Completeness: the componentwise meet of any set of root entities is a root entity and is the greatest lower bound. Rigid Comprehension: given $X$ with root extension $E$, let $Y$ have root component $X_0$ and, in $M_n$, the projection of $E$ to the $n$-th coordinates; $Y$ is persistent, since a root instance has its projection in every component, and inextensible, since a relation necessary of every root instance contains those projections, while in the one-world components persistence and inextensibility are automatic. Each component is a full Henkin model, in which all of these hold, so the boxed forms hold at the root; Countable Boolean Completeness, the weak rigid comprehension principles and Necessity of Arithmetic follow by the recorded results.

arguments.text: Intensional Choice holds at the root, as the map derives from this record's other verdicts. Every other world is a world of one of the full Henkin components, where a necessarily instantiated $F$ has an instance $a$ and $G:=\lambda x\, .\,x=a$ is in the domain, entails $F$ and is necessarily uniquely instantiated. So Intensional Choice holds at every world.

At the root every truth is ND-necessary (recorded), so every truth is 5-necessary there. Every other world is a one-world Henkin model $M_n$, in which $\Box$ is the identity operator, hence so is every operator in the tower from $\Box$ to $\Box_5$, and every truth is 5-necessary. So the principle holds at every world.

arguments.by: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), prompted by Daniel Kodsi, 23 October 2026; checked and recorded by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: At every type. Every set of tuples of root entities is the root component of a root relation, so internal completeness, injections and isomorphisms at the root agree with the external ones. A root proposition is a truth value with a proposition of $A$ (of which there are $32$) and one of $B$ (a set of worlds), so there are continuum many, and among them infinitely many atoms, those false at the root, bottom in $A$, and a singleton in $B$. An infinite complete Boolean algebra has at least continuum many elements (it has infinitely many pairwise disjoint nonzero elements, whose subfamilies have distinct joins), so a complete Boolean algebra that is Dedekind finite, or has fewer elements than there are root propositions, is finite. A finite one with $k$ atoms is isomorphic to the propositions below the join of $k$ of those atoms, which is not $\top$.

Let $F$ be the root property with universal root component, $F_A$ as its component in $A$ and the universal property as its component in $B$: it is necessarily instantiated. A property entailing $F$ and necessarily uniquely instantiated would have as its component in $A$ a property entailing $F_A$ and necessarily uniquely instantiated there.

arguments.text: The worlds of the root are its identity and the worlds of $A$ and $B$, and a closed sentence holds at a component world iff it holds there in the component; so a boxed principle holds at the root iff the principle holds at the root and the boxed one in $A$ and $B$. Atomicity: the singletons of root tuples, with zero components, are admitted, and a nonzero component lies above an atom of $A$ or of $B$, both of which satisfy □Atomicity. Rigid Comprehension: give a root entity's root extension $S$ the transports into $A$ and $B$ of the haecceity disjunction of $S$, rigid there ($A$'s domains contain the finite disjunctions of haecceities, $B$ is full); the result is rigid and coextensive with it, and $A$ and $B$ satisfy □Rigid Comprehension. 5-necessities are ND-necessary: at the root the proposition true at the root alone is in the domain and seen from no component world, so every truth is ND-necessary there; $A$ and $B$ satisfy the boxed principle. In $B$, an S5 model with more than one world, $\Box_5$ is $\Box$, so not every truth is 5-necessary.
