references.note: The coalesced sum, here of two components.

settings.construction: Let $T$ be C with Extensionality, Well-Ordering at every type and $I^*$ (zero is not a successor and successor is injective on the finite cardinalities of individuals). $T$ holds in the full standard model on $\mathbb N$, by choice in the metatheory, so $T+\operatorname{Con}(T)$ is consistent, and by Gödel's second incompleteness theorem so is $T+\neg\operatorname{Con}(T)$. Take one-world Henkin models $M_1$ of $T+\operatorname{Con}(T)$ and $M_2$ of $T+\neg\operatorname{Con}(T)$, as action models with one object and only its identity arrow, and coalesce them at a new root as in Definition E.2. The root's individuals are the pairs of an individual of $M_1$ and one of $M_2$. Evaluation point: the root. Interpretation of Σ, fixed for this record: every constant of Σ is relational, and each denotes the top element of its type.

meets.two-actual-components: Both components are one-world Henkin models, where the top proposition is the true atom; the root domains are the fullest.
meets.free-root-component: The root domains are as full as compatibility allows.
meets.sigma-top: This is the interpretation the construction fixes.

arguments.by: Cian Dorr, recorded by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic)
arguments.text: At type $e$. The root sees three worlds: itself and the two component worlds, each of which sees only itself. $I^*$ holds in both components, so $I$ holds at both component worlds and at the root. The arithmetical sentence $A:=\operatorname{Con}(T)$ holds at the world of $M_1$ and fails at that of $M_2$, so neither $\Box(I\to A)$ nor $\Box(I\to\neg A)$ holds at the root.

arguments.by: Cian Dorr, recorded by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic)
arguments.text: At every relational type the root domain contains, for each world and each tuple there, the entity true of that tuple at that world and of nothing else: the root component is free, and each component contains the singleton of each of its tuples, definable from them. Such an entity lies below every entity or below its negation, and necessarily so, since its transport to a component world is that singleton or $\bot$; so it is a strong atom, and every nonzero entity has one below it. In the one-world components the same holds trivially. For BF, the root individuals are pairs, so each component individual is the image of a root individual, and likewise at every type, root entities being families of component entities; the components, with one world each, satisfy BF.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
arguments.text: The closed pure sentence $\exists p\, .\,p\land\Diamond\neg p$ is true at the root, where the proposition true only at the root is contingent, and false at each component world, which sees only itself; so it is not possible there, and B for it fails at the root.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
arguments.text: Each component is one-world and extensional, so it has exactly two propositions, and the root, whose propositions are a truth value at the root with one of each component's, has eight; so there are finitely many propositions at every world. The root individuals are the pairs from two infinite domains, with literal identity, so any number of them are distinct. $T$ proves the Axiom of Infinity at type $e$: if a finite cardinality $n$ held of the universal property, $\operatorname{Suc}n$ and $\operatorname{Suc}\operatorname{Suc}n$ would both be the empty cardinality, by Extensionality, while $n\ne\operatorname{Suc}n$, against $I^*$; so it holds at the component worlds and is possible at the root.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
arguments.text: The propositions form a finite Boolean algebra at every world, so every family has a greatest lower bound.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
arguments.text: At a one-world component $\Box$ is idle. Every truth is ND-necessary there, with $\top$ as witness; every relation is weakly persistent and weakly inextensible, so Tame Rigidity holds there trivially; and Intensional Choice holds, the singleton of a chosen instance being definable. At the root, a weakly rigid relation is rigid, since Rigid is weak rigidity at every world and the other worlds are the components; and Truths are ND-necessary holds there already.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
arguments.text: Each component satisfies Well-Ordering, being a model of $T$. For a type $\sigma$, let $R$ have as root part a well-ordering of the root's entities of type $\sigma$, chosen in the metatheory, and as component parts well-orderings in the components; the root domains being fullest, $R$ is in the domain, and it well-orders the type at every world, every root property of type $\sigma t$ having a root part that is a subset of the root's entities.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's request
arguments.text:
Throughout, $M_1$ and $M_2$ are the two one-world extensional Henkin components, with $M_1\models\operatorname{Con}(T)$ and $M_2\models
eg\operatorname{Con}(T)$, and $D^\sigma_r$, $D^\sigma_1$, $D^\sigma_2$ are the domains of type $\sigma$ at the root and at the components. From the root three worlds are accessible, the root itself and the two components; from a component only itself. Since $M_i$ is extensional and one-world, an entity of $M_i$ of type $ ar\sigma t$ is identified with its extension, a set of $ ar\sigma$-tuples of $M_i$, and a set $S$ of $ ar\sigma$-tuples of $M_i$ is called internal in $M_i$ when $S\in D^{ ar\sigma t}_i$, that is, when it is the extension of an entity of $M_i$; every set definable in $M_i$ with parameters is internal in $M_i$, by comprehension. The word always refers to one of the two components, named each time; at the root one speaks only of root entities and their root extensions. A root individual is a pair $(a_1,a_2)$ with $a_i\in D^e_i$, transported to $a_i$ along the distinguished arrow $d_i$. A root entity of a relational type $ ar\sigma t$ is a triple $Y=(Y_o,Y_1,Y_2)$: $Y_o$, its root extension, is an arbitrary set of root $ ar\sigma$-tuples, and $Y_i\in D^{ ar\sigma t}_i$, its $M_i$-component, is its transport along $d_i$; the root domains being fullest, every such triple is in $D^{ ar\sigma t}_r$. For a root tuple $ ar x$ let $\pi_i ar x$ be the tuple of $M_i$-components of its entries, and for a set $S$ of root tuples let $\pi_i[S]:=\{\pi_i ar x: ar x\in S\}$, a set of $ ar\sigma$-tuples of $M_i$ that need not be internal in $M_i$. For any $n\in D^\sigma_1$ and $m\in D^\sigma_2$ some root entity $x$ of type $\sigma$ has $\pi_1x=n$ and $\pi_2x=m$: the pair $(n,m)$ when $\sigma=e$, the triple $(\emptyset,n,m)$ otherwise.
Six facts about the semantics are used. (a) At the root, $\Box\varphi$ holds iff $\varphi$ holds at the root, at $M_1$ and at $M_2$, root parameters replaced by their components. (b) Quantifiers at the root range over the root domains, at $M_i$ over those of $M_i$. (c) At the root $Y ar x$ holds iff $ ar x\in Y_o$; at $M_i$, after transport, iff $\pi_i ar x\in Y_i$. (d) So $Y\le Z$, that is $\Box orall ar x\, .\,Y ar x	o Z ar x$, holds at the root iff $Y_o\subseteq Z_o$, $Y_1\subseteq Z_1$ and $Y_2\subseteq Z_2$. (e) Transport commutes with denotation: the $M_i$-component of the root entity denoted by $\lambda X\, .\,\varphi(X, ar F)$ with root parameters $ ar F$ is the entity of $M_i$ denoted by $\lambda X\, .\,\varphi(X, ar F_i)$. (f) In the one-world model $M_i$ the box is idle, so every entity $Y$ of $M_i$ is weakly persistent ($Y ar x	o\Box Y ar x$ reduces to $Y ar x	o Y ar x$) and weakly inextensible ($ orall X\, .\,( orall ar x\, .\,Y ar x	o\Box X ar x)	o Y\le X$ reduces to $ orall X\, .\,Y\subseteq X	o Y\subseteq X$); hence every entity of $M_i$ is weakly rigid and, the box being idle, rigid.
Rigidity at the root. $\operatorname{Rigid}(Y)$ is $\Box\operatorname{WeaklyRigid}(Y)$; at the root, by (a), it says that $Y$ is weakly rigid at the root and that $Y_i$ is weakly rigid in $M_i$ for each $i$, and the latter holds by (f). So $Y$ is rigid at the root iff it is weakly persistent and weakly inextensible there. Weak persistence at the root, $ orall ar x\, .\,Y ar x	o\Box Y ar x$, asks of each root tuple $ ar x\in Y_o$ that $Y ar x$ hold at the root (trivial), at $M_1$ ($\pi_1 ar x\in Y_1$) and at $M_2$ ($\pi_2 ar x\in Y_2$); so it holds iff $\pi_1[Y_o]\subseteq Y_1$ and $\pi_2[Y_o]\subseteq Y_2$. Weak inextensibility at the root, $ orall X\, .\,( orall ar x\, .\,Y ar x	o\Box X ar x)	o Y\le X$ with $X=(X_o,X_1,X_2)$ ranging over root entities, has the hypothesis $Y_o\subseteq X_o$, $\pi_1[Y_o]\subseteq X_1$, $\pi_2[Y_o]\subseteq X_2$ and, by (d), the conclusion $Y_o\subseteq X_o$, $Y_1\subseteq X_1$, $Y_2\subseteq X_2$. The three parts of $X$ being independent, this is a separate condition on each component: given $X_1\in D^{ ar\sigma t}_1$ containing $\pi_1[Y_o]$, the root entity $(Y_o,X_1,	op_2)$ satisfies the hypothesis, so $Y_1\subseteq X_1$ is required, and likewise for $M_2$; conversely the two component conditions give the conclusion for every $X$ satisfying the hypothesis. So weak inextensibility at the root holds iff for $i=1,2$, $Y_i\subseteq X_i$ for every $X_i$ internal in $M_i$ with $X_i\supseteq\pi_i[Y_o]$. Together: $Y$ is rigid at the root iff for each $i$, $Y_i$ is a set internal in $M_i$ that contains $\pi_i[Y_o]$ and is contained in every set internal in $M_i$ that contains $\pi_i[Y_o]$; that is, $Y_i$ is the least internal superset of $\pi_i[Y_o]$ in $M_i$.
Lemma. Let $M$ be a one-world extensional model and $S$ any set of $ ar\sigma$-tuples of $M$, internal or not; call an $X$ internal in $M$ a least internal superset of $S$ if $S\subseteq X$ and $X\subseteq X'$ for every $X'$ internal in $M$ with $S\subseteq X'$. If $S$ has a least internal superset $X$, then $X=S$; so $S$ has a least internal superset iff $S$ is itself internal in $M$, and then that superset is $S$. Proof: suppose $X$ is a least internal superset of $S$ but $X
ot\subseteq S$, and pick $ ar a\in X\setminus S$. The haecceity $\lambda ar y\, .\, ar y= ar a$ is internal in $M$ by comprehension with the parameter $ ar a$, hence so is $X':=X\land
eg(\lambda ar y\, .\, ar y= ar a)$, which as a set is $X\setminus\{ ar a\}$. As $ ar a
otin S$, still $S\subseteq X'$; by leastness $X\subseteq X'$, so $ ar a\in X'$, which is absurd. So $X=S$, and $S$ is internal. Conversely an internal $S$ is its own least internal superset. The point is that an internal set strictly above $S$ is never the least one above $S$: it can be shrunk by a point while staying above $S$. Applying the lemma with $S=\pi_i[Y_o]$ gives the criterion (Rig): a root entity $Y=(Y_o,Y_1,Y_2)$ of type $ ar\sigma t$ is rigid at the root iff for each $i=1,2$, (1) $\pi_i[Y_o]$ is internal in $M_i$ and (2) $Y_i=\pi_i[Y_o]$. A rigid root entity is thus determined by its root extension, and a set $S$ of root tuples is the root extension of a rigid root entity iff $\pi_1[S]$ is internal in $M_1$ and $\pi_2[S]$ is internal in $M_2$, the rigid entity then being $(S,\pi_1[S],\pi_2[S])$.
The power property. Rigid Power at type $ ar\sigma t$ is $ orall F\, .\,\operatorname{Rigid}(F)	o\operatorname{Rigid}(P_F)$ with $P_F:=\lambda X^{ ar\sigma t}\, .\,\operatorname{Rigid}(X)\land X\le F$, a root entity of type $( ar\sigma t)t$; at the root, by (b), it says that $P_F$ is rigid at the root for every root entity $F$ that is rigid at the root. For such an $F$, the root extension $(P_F)_o$ is the set of root entities $X$ that are rigid at the root with $X\le F$ at the root; by (Rig) such an $X$ is $(E,\pi_1[E],\pi_2[E])$ for a set $E$ of root tuples with both projections internal, and by (d) $X\le F$ says $E\subseteq F_o$ together with $\pi_i[E]\subseteq F_i$, which is automatic since $F_i=\pi_i[F_o]$; so $(P_F)_o$ consists of the $(E,\pi_1[E],\pi_2[E])$ with $E\subseteq F_o$, $\pi_1[E]$ internal in $M_1$ and $\pi_2[E]$ internal in $M_2$. The $M_i$-component $(P_F)_i$ is, by (e), the entity of $M_i$ denoted by $\lambda X\, .\,\operatorname{Rigid}(X)\land X\le F_i$, and by (f) every entity of $M_i$ is rigid, so $(P_F)_i=\mathcal P_i(F_i):=\{X_i\in D^{ ar\sigma t}_i: X_i\subseteq F_i\}$, the internal power set of $F_i$, itself internal in $M_i$ as the extension of $\lambda X\, .\,X\le F_i$. Now apply (Rig) to $P_F$ at type $( ar\sigma t)t$. The projection $\pi_i[(P_F)_o]$ is the set of the $\pi_i[E]$ for $E\subseteq F_o$ with both projections internal, the set of $M_i$-components of rigid subrelations of $F$; each member is an internal subset of $\pi_i[F_o]=F_i$, so $\pi_i[(P_F)_o]\subseteq\mathcal P_i(F_i)=(P_F)_i$ always. Hence the criterion (RP): for a root entity $F$ rigid at the root, $P_F$ is rigid at the root iff for each $i=1,2$, (1) $\pi_i[(P_F)_o]$ is internal in $M_i$ and (2) $(P_F)_i=\pi_i[(P_F)_o]$, which by the inclusion just noted says that every $A\subseteq F_i$ internal in $M_i$ is $\pi_i[E]$ for some $E\subseteq F_o$ whose other projection $\pi_j[E]$ is internal in $M_j$. Clause (2) implies clause (1), $(P_F)_i$ being internal, so (RP) comes down to clause (2): Rigid Power holds at the root iff for every rigid $F$ and each component, every internal subrelation of $F$'s component there is the component of a rigid subrelation of $F$. To refute it one exhibits a rigid $F$, an $i$ and an $A\subseteq F_i$ internal in $M_i$ that is $\pi_i[E]$ for no $E\subseteq F_o$ with $\pi_j[E]$ internal in $M_j$.
The witness, at type $
u t$ with $
u:=(et)t$, the type of finite cardinalities of individuals. Let $N_i\subseteq D^
u_i$ be the set of finite cardinalities of $M_i$, the extension in $M_i$ of $\lambda n\, .\, orall\mathcal C\, .\,\mathcal C0\land orall m\,(\mathcal Cm	o\mathcal C(\operatorname{Suc}m))	o\mathcal Cn$ with $\mathcal C$ ranging over $D^{
u t}_i$; it is internal in $M_i$. Write $ ar k^{M_i}\in D^
u_i$ for the denotation of $\operatorname{Suc}^k0$ in $M_i$ and $\operatorname{Std}_i:=\{ ar k^{M_i}:k\in\mathbb N\}$ for the standard numbers of $M_i$; $\operatorname{Std}_i\subseteq N_i$, each $ ar k^{M_i}$ lying in every inductive class, and the $ ar k^{M_i}$ are pairwise distinct by $I^*$. Claim 1: $\operatorname{Std}_2$ is not internal in $M_2$. Since $M_2\models
eg\operatorname{Con}(T)$ there is $n_0\in N_2$ that $M_2$ takes to code a $T$-proof of $ ot$; $n_0$ is not standard, since $T$ decides every bounded arithmetical statement about standard numerals, so that if $n_0$ were $ ar k^{M_2}$ then $k$ would really code a $T$-proof of $ ot$, and there is none, $T$ having a model. If $\operatorname{Std}_2$ were internal in $M_2$ it would be an inductive class in the sense of $M_2$, containing $ ar 0^{M_2}$ and closed under $\operatorname{Suc}$, and so would contain $n_0$ by the definition of $N_2$; it does not.
Define $\psi:N_1	o\operatorname{Std}_2$ by $\psi( ar k^{M_1}):= ar k^{M_2}$ for $k\in\mathbb N$ and $\psi(n):= ar 0^{M_2}$ for $n\in N_1\setminus\operatorname{Std}_1$ (the second clause matters only if $M_1$ has nonstandard numbers; $M_1$ might have been taken to be the full standard model on $\mathbb N$, which satisfies $T+\operatorname{Con}(T)$, and then $N_1=\operatorname{Std}_1$); $\psi$ is onto $\operatorname{Std}_2$ and uses no choice. Let $F:=(F_o,	op_1,	op_2)$ be the root entity of type $
u t$ whose $M_i$-components are the universal properties of $M_i$, with extensions $D^
u_i$, and whose root extension $F_o$ is the set of $x\in D^
u_r$ such that either $x_1\in N_1$ and $x_2=\psi(x_1)$, or $x_1
otin N_1$, where $x_1$ and $x_2$ are the $M_1$- and $M_2$-components of $x$: either the $M_1$-component is a finite cardinality of $M_1$ and the $M_2$-component is the standard number of $M_2$ that $\psi$ assigns to it, or the $M_1$-component is not a finite cardinality and the $M_2$-component is anything. Claim 2: $F$ is rigid at the root. By (Rig) it suffices that $\pi_1[F_o]=D^
u_1$ and $\pi_2[F_o]=D^
u_2$, these being internal as the extensions of $	op_1$ and $	op_2$. For the first, let $n\in D^
u_1$: if $n\in N_1$, the root entity $x:=(\emptyset,n,\psi(n))$, with empty root extension, is in $D^
u_r$ (fullest domains) and in the first part of $F_o$, with $x_1=n$; if $n
otin N_1$, $x:=(\emptyset,n,m)$ for any $m\in D^
u_2$ is in the second part. For the second, let $m\in D^
u_2$: the second part of $F_o$ supplies $x:=(\emptyset,n,m)$ provided $M_1$ has some $n
otin N_1$, an entity of type $
u$ that is not a finite cardinality. It does: $	op_
u$, the property holding of every property of individuals. For $0$ holds only of the empty property, while $\operatorname{Suc}m$ holds only of nonempty properties, holding of $A$ iff some $x$ with $Ax$ has $m(\lambda y\, .\,Ay\land y
e x)$; so the class of those $n$ that do not hold both of the empty property and of some nonempty property contains $0$, is closed under $\operatorname{Suc}$ and is internal in $M_1$, hence contains every member of $N_1$; and $	op_
u$ holds of the empty property and of any singleton.
Claim 3: $P_F$ is not rigid at the root. Take $i=1$ and $A:=N_1$, internal in $M_1$ and a subset of $F_1=D^
u_1$, so that $A\in\mathcal P_1(F_1)=(P_F)_1$. By clause (2) of (RP), $P_F$ is rigid at the root only if $N_1=\pi_1[E]$ for some $E\subseteq F_o$ with $\pi_2[E]$ internal in $M_2$. But if $E\subseteq F_o$ has $\pi_1[E]=N_1$, every $x\in E$ has $x_1\in N_1$, so lies in the first part of $F_o$ with $x_2=\psi(x_1)$; hence $\pi_2[E]=\psi[N_1]=\operatorname{Std}_2$, not internal in $M_2$ by Claim 1. So $N_1$ lies in $(P_F)_1$ but not in $\pi_1[(P_F)_o]$, clause (2) of (RP) fails for $F$ at $i=1$, and $P_F$ is not rigid at the root. Unwound, the failing instance of inextensibility is this: let $H:=(	op,H_1,	op_2)$ be the root entity of type $(
u t)t$ with $H_1:=\lambda X\, .\,
eg(X=N_1)$, internal in $M_1$. Then $ orall X\, .\,P_FX	o\Box HX$ holds at the root, since for $X$ rigid with $X\le F$, $HX$ holds trivially at the root and at $M_2$, and at $M_1$ it says $X_1
e N_1$, which holds because $X_1=\pi_1[X_o]$ with $X_o\subseteq F_o$ and $\pi_2[X_o]=X_2$ internal in $M_2$, which Claim 3 shows incompatible with $\pi_1[X_o]=N_1$; but $P_F\le H$ fails at $M_1$, where $(P_F)_1=\mathcal P_1(	op_1)$ holds of $N_1$ and $H_1$ does not. So Rigid Power fails at the root at type $((et)t)t$. The boxed form fails with it, $\Box$ at the root reaching only the root and the components, where Rigid Power holds trivially by (f). And since at the root weak rigidity is rigidity and in the components both are trivial, $F$ is weakly rigid and $\lambda X\, .\,\operatorname{WeaklyRigid}(X)\land X\le F$ is the same root entity as $P_F$, so Weakly Rigid Power and its boxed form fail too.
The obstacle in one line. The set $S$ of root entities $x$ of type $
u$ with $x_1= ar k^{M_1}$ and $x_2= ar k^{M_2}$ for some $k\in\mathbb N$, the entities that are the same standard number in both components, is the root extension of plenty of root entities of type $
u t$, namely of $(S,Y_1,Y_2)$ for any $Y_1\in D^{
u t}_1$ and $Y_2\in D^{
u t}_2$, the root domains being fullest; but by (Rig) none of them is rigid, since $\pi_2[S]=\operatorname{Std}_2$ is not internal in $M_2$. There is no rigid root relation whose root extension is "same standard number in both components". The witness $F$ is this non-rigid relation padded until it is rigid, on the number side so that $\pi_1$ sees every finite cardinality of $M_1$ and on the non-number side so that $\pi_2$ sees all of $D^
u_2$, and $N_1$ is the internal subset of $F_1$ that could only come from the unpadded part. A rigid relation can be thin enough, a graph, that the rigid subrelations below it are forced to have non-internal projections.
Which types, and how the filling in of the construction matters. The same bookkeeping gives the criterion (Crit): Rigid Power at type $ ar\sigma t$ fails at the root iff for some $j
e i$ there is a set $B$ of $ ar\sigma$-tuples of $M_j$, not internal in $M_j$, with $|B|\le|D^{ ar\sigma}_i|$. For the one direction, fix a tuple $ ar x_0$ of $M_i$ and a surjection $\psi:D^{ ar\sigma}_i\setminus\{ ar x_0\}	o B$, let $F_o$ be the set of root tuples $ ar x$ with either $\pi_i ar x
e ar x_0$ and $\pi_j ar x=\psi(\pi_i ar x)$, or $\pi_i ar x= ar x_0$, and let $F:=(F_o,	op,	op)$; then $\pi_i[F_o]=D^{ ar\sigma}_i$ and $\pi_j[F_o]=D^{ ar\sigma}_j$, the tuples with $\pi_i ar x= ar x_0$ pairing $ ar x_0$ with every tuple of $M_j$, so $F$ is rigid by (Rig); and $A:=D^{ ar\sigma}_i\setminus\{ ar x_0\}$, internal in $M_i$ as $	op$ minus a haecceity, is $\pi_i[E]$ only for $E\subseteq F_o$ avoiding $ ar x_0$, whose $\pi_j[E]=\psi[A]=B$ is not internal in $M_j$. For the other direction, which uses choice, suppose clause (2) of (RP) fails for some rigid $F$, $i$ and $A\subseteq F_i$; choose for each $a\in A$ one $ ar x^a\in F_o$ with $\pi_i ar x^a=a$, possible as $A\subseteq\pi_i[F_o]$, and let $E$ be the set of these; then $\pi_i[E]=A$, so $B:=\pi_j[E]$ is not internal in $M_j$, and $|B|\le|A|\le|D^{ ar\sigma}_i|$. Consequences: with countable Henkin components, which is what the Henkin construction gives, $D^{et}_2$ is countable while $\mathcal P(D^e_2)$ is not, so some set $B$ of individuals of $M_2$ is not internal in $M_2$ and $|B|\le\aleph_0=|D^e_1|$; Rigid Power fails already at type $e	o t$, and in general at every type at which either component is not full. With $M_1$ the full standard model on $\mathbb N$, Rigid Power at $e	o t$ fails iff $M_2$ has a countable set of individuals not internal in $M_2$, as it does if $M_2$ is countable. Rigid Power could hold at $e	o t$ only if every non-internal set of individuals of either component outnumbered the individuals of the other. Both components cannot be full at type $et$: if $M_2$ were full at $et$ and at $eet$, an internal bijection between $A$ and $B$ would be true equinumerosity and the absence of an internal injection of $A$ into a proper subset of itself true finiteness, so the class of those $n$ that hold of something, hold only of finite properties and are closed under equinumerosity would be internal and inductive, every finite cardinality of $M_2$ would be the property of having exactly $k$ members for a true $k$, and $M_2$ would satisfy $\operatorname{Con}(T)$. A filling in with Rigid Power at $e	o t$ would thus need $M_2$ full at $et$ but not at $eet$, with uncountably many individuals and every countable set of them internal; whether $T$ has such a model has not been checked. Whatever the filling in, the failure at $((et)t)t$ remains, using only the countable non-internal set $\operatorname{Std}_2$ and the infinitude of $D^
u_1$.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's request
arguments.text: In the notation of the argument rigid-power. Rigid Rigidity at type $\bar\sigma t$ is $\operatorname{Rigid}(\lambda X\, .\,\operatorname{Rigid}(X))$, which is $\operatorname{Rigid}(P_\top)$ for the root entity $\top$ whose root extension is the set of all root $\bar\sigma$-tuples and whose components are $\top_1$ and $\top_2$; it is rigid by (Rig), since $\pi_i[\top_o]=D^{\bar\sigma}_i$ is internal in $M_i$. Check clause (2) of (RP) for $\top$: given $A\subseteq D^{\bar\sigma}_i$ internal in $M_i$, let $E$ be the set of root tuples $\bar x$ with $\pi_i\bar x\in A$; then $\pi_i[E]=A$, and $\pi_j[E]$ is $D^{\bar\sigma}_j$ if $A\ne\emptyset$, every tuple of $M_j$ pairing with some member of $A$, and $\emptyset$ if $A=\emptyset$, either way internal in $M_j$. So $P_\top$ is rigid at the root, at every type. In each component every entity is rigid by (f), so $\lambda X\, .\,\operatorname{Rigid}(X)$ is rigid there trivially, and the boxed form holds at the root by (a). At the root, $\lambda X\, .\,\operatorname{WeaklyRigid}(X)$ has the same root extension as $\lambda X\, .\,\operatorname{Rigid}(X)$, weak rigidity and rigidity coinciding there, and the same components, everything, by (f); so it is the same root entity, and it is weakly rigid, being rigid. In the components it is weakly rigid trivially. So Weakly Rigid Weak Rigidity and its boxed form hold.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Zachary Goodsell
arguments.text: At type $e$: inextensibility of $\mathbb N_e$ fails at the root. The antecedent $\Box I^*_e$ holds, $I^*$ being an axiom of $T$, true in both components, and true at the root, where the numbers are the standard numerals, the root parts of entities being free, and the individuals are infinitely many. In $M_2$, which satisfies $\neg\operatorname{Con}(T)$, the numbers at $e$, the instances of the least inductive property in the Henkin domain, include a nonstandard number $c$, one coding a proof of a contradiction from $T$, since no standard numeral does; so no property of $M_2$ has exactly the standard numerals as its extension, such a property being inductive. The property $\lambda x\,.\,x<c$ of $M_2$, definable from $c$ by the order on numbers, holds of every standard numeral and not of $c$. Let $X$ be the root entity whose root part is the set of root numerals, whose $M_1$-part is the numbers of $M_1$ and whose $M_2$-part is $\lambda x\,.\,x<c$. Every number at the root necessarily has $X$: at the root it is a root numeral, and along the distinguished arrows it becomes the corresponding numeral of $M_1$ or of $M_2$, numerals being closed terms. But $\mathbb N_e\le X$ fails, since at $M_2$ the number $c$ lacks $X$. So $\mathbb N_e$ is not inextensible and Arithmetic Necessitism fails, although the persistence of $\mathbb N_e$ and the necessary distinctness of the numbers hold, as in every model of C with $\Box I^*_e$. This is the failure the principle's notes anticipate: at $M_2$ no property has exactly the numerals as its extension, so the least inductive property gains members there.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Zachary Goodsell
arguments.text: At the type $\sigma:=((et)t)t$ of properties of the numbers at $e$. In each component, a model of $T$ and so of C with $I^*_e$, there is a real number structure of type $\sigma$: the Dedekind cuts over the numbers at $e$, with the rationals coded as numbers, form a complete ordered field, completeness holding by comprehension since the union of a bounded family of cuts is a cut, and its least inductive subproperty is the image of the numbers, so its arithmetic is the component's. Let $A$ be the first-order analytical sentence $\exists n\in N\,.\,\operatorname{Proof}_T(n,\bot)$, written with $N$, $+$ and $\times$. In $M_2$, which satisfies $\neg\operatorname{Con}(T)$, every real number structure makes $A$ true, and in $M_1$, which satisfies $\operatorname{Con}(T)$, every one makes it false, the real number structures at a world all being isomorphic there. The root reaches both components, so neither $\Box\forall\mathfrak R\,.\,\operatorname{Real}_\sigma(\mathfrak R)\to A(\mathfrak R)$ nor $\Box\forall\mathfrak R\,.\,\operatorname{Real}_\sigma(\mathfrak R)\to\neg A(\mathfrak R)$ holds at the root: the Necessity of Analysis fails, and with it the Necessity of Second-Order Analysis and Analytic Necessitism, which imply it.

models.notes: Suggested by Cian Dorr on 19 October 2026 as a small model of the boxed Strong Atomicity and □BF without the Necessity of Arithmetic. The root has three atoms, the singletons of its three worlds, all strong atoms. The components are one-world extensional Henkin models, and they satisfy Well-Ordering at every type, so that the choice principles hold at every world. No Lean verification is claimed.

models.definition:
Let $T$ be C with Extensionality, Well-Ordering at every type and $I^*$ (zero is not a successor and successor is injective on the finite cardinalities of individuals). $T$ holds in the full standard model on $\mathbb N$, by choice in the metatheory, so $T+\operatorname{Con}(T)$ is consistent, and by Gödel's second incompleteness theorem so is $T+\neg\operatorname{Con}(T)$. Take one-world Henkin models $M_1$ of $T+\operatorname{Con}(T)$ and $M_2$ of $T+\neg\operatorname{Con}(T)$, as action models with one object and only its identity arrow, and coalesce them at a new root as in Definition E.2. The root's individuals are the pairs of an individual of $M_1$ and one of $M_2$. Evaluation point: the root. Interpretation of Σ, fixed for this record: every constant of Σ is relational, and each denotes the top element of its type.

The root has one distinguished arrow to the root of each component, and every arrow from the root into a component factors through it.

Root domains are as full as compatibility allows: a root proposition is a choice, for each component, of a proposition of that component’s root domain, together with a truth value at the root’s identity arrow, and a root entity of a relational type is likewise a family of component entities with a root component that is an arbitrary function of the root arguments.

met.actual-world-isolated: The singleton root proposition, true at the root's identity arrow and nowhere in a component, is in the domain and entails every truth; the components have no arrows back to the root (Classicism, Appendix E, p. 83, on the distinctness-preserving collapse).
met.two-actual-components: Both components are one-world Henkin models, where the top proposition is the true atom; the root domains are the fullest.
met.free-root-component: The root domains are as full as compatibility allows.
met.sigma-top: This is the interpretation the construction fixes.

references.note: Full action models, here the target, with a restricted domain at the entrance.

meets.infinitely-many-propositions: The propositions true at a single $h_n$ are pairwise distinct.
meets.codomain-intensions: An intension at $r$ with the same value $V$ at every $h_n$ and at $b$ is admitted, with $d_n=d_\infty=(V,V)$, which $k$ fixes; $s$ is full.

settings.construction: The arrows $s\to s$ are $1$ and an idempotent $k\ne1$, with the full action-model domains over one individual. Besides its identity, $r$ has arrows $h_n:r\to s$ ($n\in\mathbb N$) and $b:r\to s$, where $k\circ h_n=b$ and $k\circ b=b$. An entity of relational type at $r$ is an arbitrary current extension together with target entities $d_n$ (its transports along the $h_n$) and $d_\infty$ (along $b$) such that $k\cdot d_n=k\cdot d_\infty=d_\infty$ and $d_n=d_\infty$ for all but finitely many $n$.

arguments.text: At $r$, at every relational type, the singletons of one current tuple and of one tuple $\bar a$ at an arrow $h_n$ (with $d_n$ the target singleton at the coordinate $1$ and everything else $0$) are admitted, and every nonzero entity contains one: a nonempty extension at $b$ is the extension at all but finitely many $h_n$. Their transports are $0$ or target singletons at the coordinate $1$, which are atoms that $k$ sends to $0$. So they are strong atoms. The full target is atomic at every type.
At $s$ the proposition $\{k\}$ is an atom with $k\cdot\{k\}=\top$, which $\{1\}$ splits at $k$; so no strong atom entails it, and Strong Atomicity at $t$ fails at $s$.

At every type. Transport along each $h_n$ is onto: any target entity $d$ is the transport of an entity with $d_n=d$ and every other component $k\cdot d$. So if every entity at $r$ necessarily has $F$, the extension of $F$ at each $h_n$ is everything; and at $b$ it is the extension at an $h_n$ outside $F$'s finitely many exceptions.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, in a trawl for cheaply settled verdicts; checked by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: Every type has finitely many entities at $s$, so $I_\sigma$ fails at every world of $s$, and at $e$ everywhere. At $r$ every relational type is infinite and, by extensional fullness, the numbers are the numerals with standard sum and product. So $I_\sigma\to A$ is necessary or necessarily false according as $A$ is true.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, in a trawl for cheaply settled verdicts; checked by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: BF at $t$ holds at $r$ (recorded) and fails at $s$ (recorded), and a closed pure sentence has the same value at the two worlds $h_0$ and $b$ of $s$; so $\mathrm{BF}_t$ is true at $r$ and not possible at $h_0$.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, in a trawl for cheaply settled verdicts; checked by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: Let $p$ be true at $h_0$ and $h_1$ and nowhere else. At each of them its transport is $\{1\}$, an atom of $s$, so $p$ is a self-atom; it is the join of two propositions each true at one $h_n$, so not an atom, nor a strong atom. At $s$, $\{k\}$ is an atom whose transport along $k$ is $\top$, so it is not a self-atom and nothing possible below it is: Self-Atomicity at $t$ fails at $s$.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, in a trawl for cheaply settled verdicts; checked by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: At $s$, full, a rigid relation is $H_D:=(D,k\cdot D)$, and a rigid $Y\le H_D$ at $1$ or at $k$ is $H_E$, $E\subseteq D$ or $E\subseteq k\cdot D$, the transport of $H_{E'}$ with $E'$ the members of $D$ sent into $E$; so power properties are exact images and Rigid Power holds at $s$. At $r$, a rigid $F$ with current extension $A$ has rows $h_n\cdot A$ at the $h_n$, by weak inextensibility, and row $V$ at $b$ with $(V,V)$ rigid, so $V=k\cdot V$ consists of points fixed by $k$; since $V=h_n\cdot A$ for all large $n$, $h_n\cdot\bar a=k\cdot h_n\cdot\bar a=b\cdot\bar a$ for those $n$ uniformly, and $V=b\cdot A$. So for $A'\subseteq A$ the exact image of $A'$ is admitted and rigid, and every rigid relation below a transport of $F$ is the transport of one of them. Hence the power property of $F$ is weakly rigid, and rigid, by Rigid Power at $s$.

arguments.text: At type $tt$. At $r$ there are continuum many entities of type $tt$, current extensions being arbitrary, and they carry a real number structure. A rigid structure necessarily one would carry one at $s$, along $h_0$; but every type has finitely many entities at $s$.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
arguments.text: As for individuals (the argument infinitely-many-individuals), at type $t$: the Infinity schema holds, and by extensional fullness the property of cardinalities that hold only of properties with finite extensions is in the domain, has every finite cardinality, and excludes those holding of the universal property of propositions, whose extension is infinite.

conditions.text: The model is extensionally full at every object: every set of tuples from the domains at an object is the extension, at the identity arrow, of an element of the domain of the matching relational type there.
conditions.reason: At $r$ the current extension of an entity is arbitrary, and $s$ is a full action model.

conditions.text: There are infinitely many propositions at the evaluation world.
conditions.reason: The propositions true at a single $h_n$ are pairwise distinct.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, at Cian Dorr's suggestion
arguments.text: For each object $U$ and type $\sigma$ fix a well-ordering $<_U$ of the domain $D^\sigma_U$, and let $W$ be the intension of type $\sigma\to\sigma\to t$ with $W(h):={<_{\operatorname{cod}h}}$. Its value depends only on the arrow's codomain, so by the condition it is in the domain, and at every world its extension well-orders that world's type-$\sigma$ domain. Given $F$ with $\Box\exists x\, .\,Fx$, put $G:=\lambda x\, .\,Fx\land\forall y\, .\,(Fy\to\neg Wyx)$, the $W$-least $F$. It is definable from $F$ and $W$, so in the domain; $G\le F$, and its extension at every arrow is the singleton of the least element of $F$'s. So Intensional Choice holds, and the same at every reachable object gives $\Box$Intensional Choice. Cian Dorr's observation that such models are qualitatively full, made precise.

conditions.text: At every object reachable from the evaluation point, the domain contains every intension whose value at an arrow depends only on the arrow's codomain.
conditions.reason: An intension at $r$ with the same value $V$ at every $h_n$ and at $b$ is admitted, with $d_n=d_\infty=(V,V)$, which $k$ fixes; $s$ is full.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
arguments.text: At any reachable object $W$, let $U$ be a serial relation in the domain there. Using the axiom of choice, pick for each $x$ a $y$ with $(x,y)$ in the extension of $U$ at the identity, and let $S$ be the intension whose value at every arrow $W\to W$ is the graph of this choice and whose value at arrows with any other codomain is empty; it depends only on the codomain, so the condition puts it in the domain, and at the identity it is a functional subrelation of $U$. Likewise a set of representatives of an equivalence relation at $W$, made into such an intension, is a transversal. Since $W$ was any reachable object, both principles hold at every world.

conditions.text: At every object reachable from the evaluation point, the domain contains every intension whose value at an arrow depends only on the arrow's codomain.
conditions.reason: An intension at $r$ with the same value $V$ at every $h_n$ and at $b$ is admitted, with $d_n=d_\infty=(V,V)$, which $k$ fixes; $s$ is full.

The arrow $b$ is not onto, but no admitted predicate at $r$ can detect it, since each agrees with its transport along $b$ along all but finitely many of the onto arrows $h_n$.
models.definition: Two objects, the target $s$ and the entrance $r$. The arrows $s\to s$ are $1$ and an idempotent $k\ne1$, with the full action-model domains over one individual. Besides its identity, $r$ has arrows $h_n:r\to s$ ($n\in\mathbb N$) and $b:r\to s$, where $k\circ h_n=b$ and $k\circ b=b$. An entity of relational type at $r$ is an arbitrary current extension together with target entities $d_n$ (its transports along the $h_n$) and $d_\infty$ (along $b$) such that $k\cdot d_n=k\cdot d_\infty=d_\infty$ and $d_n=d_\infty$ for all but finitely many $n$. There is a single individual at both objects, and no arrow returns to $r$. Evaluation point: $1_r$. Interpretation of Σ: every constant of Σ is relational, and each denotes the top element of its type.

models.definition: Start with the unsymmetric ideally-full [[paired-individuals-two-object]] category: W=N with its two-element blocks and V=N union {star}, with every block-respecting map. Add a singleton object A, only its identity endomorphism, every constant map from A to W or V, and no map from either old object to A. Compose as ordinary maps. Use finite pins, trivial symmetry groups, and the original individual action. Evaluate at A; relational signature constants may be interpreted as top. The old outgoing categories, typed domains and truth values are unchanged.

references.note: Ideally full action models with the ideal of finite sets are models of C.

models.definition:
An ideally full action model in the sense of Classicism, Appendix D, over a category with two objects, each carrying the ideal of finite sets: a model of C by Proposition D.4. The member's construction and evaluation point follow.

The category has two objects $W_0$ and $V$; its non-identity arrows are $k_u:W_0\to V$, one for each $u\in2^{\mathbb N}$, so $V$ is terminal and every composite is an identity or some $k_u$. The individuals are $\mathbb N$ at $W_0$ and $\{0,1\}$ at $V$, and $k_u$ acts on them as $u$. The domain of propositions at $W_0$ therefore consists of the sets of arrows pinned down by a finite $N\subseteq\mathbb N$: the sets $p$ such that $k_u\in p$ and $u^{\prime}|_N=u|_N$ imply $k_{u^{\prime}}\in p$, that is, $\{1\}$ or not together with a clopen subset of Cantor space; at $V$ the domain is $\{\varnothing,\{1_V\}\}$. Evaluation point: $1_{W_0}$. Interpretation of Σ, fixed for this record: every constant of Σ is relational, and each denotes the top element of its type.

meets.extensionally-full: At $W_0$ the identity is the only arrow into $W_0$, so an intension with any value at the identity and $\varnothing$ at the $k_u$ is pinned down by $\varnothing$; at $V$ the domain is full.
meets.infinitely-many-individuals: The individuals at $W_0$ are the natural numbers.
meets.codomain-intensions: An intension depending only on the codomain is pinned down by $\varnothing$, and the model is ideally full.
meets.sigma-top: This is the interpretation the definition fixes.
meets.infinitely-many-propositions: The clopen subsets of Cantor space.
meets.actual-world-isolated: $\{1_{W_0}\}$ is pinned down by $\varnothing$, since its transport along every $k_u$ is empty, and it entails every truth; no arrow leads back to $W_0$.
meets.identity-singletons: $\{1_{W_0}\}$ is pinned down by $\varnothing$, and at $V$ the domain is full.
meets.unique-retractions-everywhere: No arrow leads into $W_0$, and $V$ has only its identity.
meets.irreversible-arrow: Any $k_u$: no arrow leads back to $W_0$.
meets.retracted-arrows-invertible-everywhere: Only identities are retracted.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, 25 October 2026
arguments.text: At $W_0$ an entity of a relational type is a pinned intension $I$, a set of pairs $\langle k,\bar a\rangle$. Its pairs at $1_{W_0}$ form singletons $\{\langle1,\bar a\rangle\}$, each pinned down by $\varnothing$ (its transport along every $k_u$ is empty), which are atoms, self-atoms and strong atoms, the transport being empty. Its pairs at arrows $k_u$ form sets $\{\langle k_u,b_u\rangle : u\in C\}$ with $C$ clopen and $b_u$ depending on finitely many coordinates of $u$; such a set is pinned, and it is a self-atom, since at each $k_u$ it becomes $\{\langle1_V,b_u\rangle\}$, an atom of the full domain at $V$. So every possible entity at $W_0$ has a self-atom below it. No atom lies over the $k_u$: a nonempty pinned set over a cylinder splits by a further coordinate. So at $W_0$ the atoms are the singletons at $1_{W_0}$, which are self-atoms and strong atoms. At $V$ the domain is full with one arrow, so all three principles hold there; hence all three are necessary.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, 25 October 2026
arguments.text: The proposition $\neg\{1_{W_0}\}$, the set of all $k_u$, is possible and pinned down by $\varnothing$, and no atom lies below it: a nonempty pinned subset contains a cylinder, which splits into two nonempty cylinders. So Atomicity (type t) fails. The same set is a self-atom that is not an atom, so Self-atoms are atoms (type t) fails.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, 25 October 2026
arguments.text: Each $k_u$ acts surjectively at type $t$, the two propositions at $V$ being the transports of $\varnothing$ and of the set of all arrows; so BF (type t) holds at $W_0$ (Classicism, Proposition 3.24(ii)).

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, 25 October 2026
arguments.text: $k_u$ sends both $\varnothing$ and $\{1_{W_0}\}$ to $\varnothing$, so it is not injective at type $t$ and ND (type t) fails (Proposition 3.24(i)). And $\Diamond\{1_{W_0}\}$ is true while $\Box\Diamond\{1_{W_0}\}$ is false, every $k_u$ transporting $\{1_{W_0}\}$ to $\varnothing$; so 5 fails.

And there are at least three individuals at $W_0$ and not at $V$, which every $k_u$ sees alone.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Zachary Goodsell
arguments.text: The numbers at a type $\sigma$ are the instances of $\mathbb N_\sigma$, the least property containing $\mathbf 0_\sigma$ and closed under $\operatorname{Suc}_\sigma$ (Background); the numerals $\mathbf 0_\sigma$, $\operatorname{Suc}_\sigma\mathbf 0_\sigma,\ldots$ are closed terms, so each denotes at every object, and transport along an arrow carries its denotation at the source to its denotation at the target. At any object $v$ reachable from the evaluation point, extensional fullness gives a property whose extension at $v$ is exactly the numerals there; it contains $\mathbf 0_\sigma$ and is closed under successor, so the numbers at $v$ are exactly the numerals, every numeral being an instance of every inductive property. Persistence of $\mathbb N_\sigma$ and, given $\Box I^*_\sigma$, the necessary distinctness of the numbers are theorems of C (the proof of necessary-rigid-comprehension-implies-arithmetic-necessitism). Inextensibility, $\Box\forall X\,.\,(\forall n\,.\,\mathbb N_\sigma n\to\Box Xn)\to\mathbb N_\sigma\le X$: at a reachable $v$ and for an arrow $j$ from $v$ to $u$, the numbers at $u$ are the numerals there, which are the transports along $j$ of the numbers at $v$, so any $X$ that necessarily holds of the numbers at $v$ holds at $u$ of the numbers there. So $\mathbb N_\sigma$ is rigid, and Arithmetic Necessitism holds at every type. No choice is used.

arguments.text: The Infinity schema holds, there being $n$ distinct individuals for every $n$. For the Axiom: by extensional fullness the domain has a property of cardinalities true of $Z$ exactly when every property $Z$ holds of has a finite extension. It holds of $\mathbf{0}_e$, which holds only of empty properties, and passes from $Y$ to $\operatorname{Suc}_e Y$, which holds of $F$ only if $Y$ holds of $F$ less one of its instances. So every finite cardinality has it, and none holds of the universal property, whose extension is infinite.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, at Cian Dorr's suggestion
arguments.text: For each object $U$ and type $\sigma$ fix a well-ordering $<_U$ of the domain $D^\sigma_U$, and let $W$ be the intension of type $\sigma\to\sigma\to t$ with $W(h):={<_{\operatorname{cod}h}}$. Its value depends only on the arrow's codomain, so by the condition it is in the domain, and at every world its extension well-orders that world's type-$\sigma$ domain. Given $F$ with $\Box\exists x\, .\,Fx$, put $G:=\lambda x\, .\,Fx\land\forall y\, .\,(Fy\to\neg Wyx)$, the $W$-least $F$. It is definable from $F$ and $W$, so in the domain; $G\le F$, and its extension at every arrow is the singleton of the least element of $F$'s. So Intensional Choice holds, and the same at every reachable object gives $\Box$Intensional Choice. Cian Dorr's observation that such models are qualitatively full, made precise.

conditions.reason: An intension depending only on the codomain is pinned down by $\varnothing$, and the model is ideally full.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
arguments.text: At any reachable object $W$, let $U$ be a serial relation in the domain there. Using the axiom of choice, pick for each $x$ a $y$ with $(x,y)$ in the extension of $U$ at the identity, and let $S$ be the intension whose value at every arrow $W\to W$ is the graph of this choice and whose value at arrows with any other codomain is empty; it depends only on the codomain, so the condition puts it in the domain, and at the identity it is a functional subrelation of $U$. Likewise a set of representatives of an equivalence relation at $W$, made into such an intension, is a transversal. Since $W$ was any reachable object, both principles hold at every world.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Zachary Goodsell
arguments.text: Let $v$ be any object reachable from the evaluation point and $\mathfrak R$ a real number structure at $v$ (Background, Analysis). Its completeness is tested against the subproperties of its carrier present at $v$, and by extensional fullness every subset of the carrier's extension there is the extension at the identity of one of them; so the carrier, with the extensions of $\le$, $+$ and $\times$, is a complete ordered field in the sense of the metatheory and, by Huntington's theorem, a theorem of ZF, is isomorphic to the real numbers. For the same reason the extension of $N$, the least subproperty containing $0$ and closed under adding $1$, is its set of natural numbers, that set being the extension of a subproperty. A second-order analytical sentence $A(\mathfrak R)$ quantifies over the relations among entities of the structure's type at $v$, applied to the structure's elements, and their extensions at the identity are all the relations on the carrier, again by extensional fullness. So $A(\mathfrak R)$ holds at $v$ exactly when $A$ holds in the real numbers under full second-order semantics, which depends neither on $v$ nor on $\mathfrak R$. Hence $\Box\forall\mathfrak R\,.\,\operatorname{Real}_\sigma(\mathfrak R)\to A(\mathfrak R)$ holds when $A$ is true of the reals and $\Box\forall\mathfrak R\,.\,\operatorname{Real}_\sigma(\mathfrak R)\to\neg A(\mathfrak R)$ when it is false: every instance of the Necessity of Second-Order Analysis holds, and with it the Necessity of Analysis and the Non-contingency of the Continuum Hypothesis, as recorded. No choice is used.

arguments.text: Let $V$ be the evaluation object or the target of an arrow out of it, and $w:=\{1_V\}$, in the domain at $V$. It is true at $1_V$. Under an arrow $f$ out of $V$ it becomes $\{k : k\circ f=1_V\}$, the set of retractions of $f$, which has at most one member and so lies below $q$ or below $\neg q$ for every proposition $q$ at $f$'s target. So Strong Actuality holds at $1_V$. A closed sentence holds at an arrow iff it holds at the identity of the arrow's target, so Strong Actuality holds at every world after the evaluation point, and □Strong Actuality holds there.

models.definition:
Proposition D.5, part 7 (p. 78): the arrows are the maps $f_n$, for $n$ a power of $2$, sending $m$ to the greatest multiple of $n$ not exceeding $m$; $f_1$ is the identity. In every part, $W_0^\ddagger$ is the set of finite subsets of $\mathbb N$ and the model is ideally full: a proposition is a set of arrows whose membership depends only on the arrows’ values on some finite set of numbers (it is pinned down by that set), and an entity of a higher type is an applicative behaviour profile pinned down by a finite set in the same sense. The individuals are the natural numbers, acted on by the arrows themselves. Propositions and properties are thus about finitely many numbers and indifferent to how the arrows treat the rest. Evaluation point: the sole object, at the identity arrow.

Interpretation of Σ, fixed for this record: every constant of Σ is relational, and each denotes the top element of its type.

met.finitely-pinned-domains: The model is ideally full: every entity is pinned down by a finite set of numbers, and every intension pinned down by one is in the domain (Definitions D.1–D.3).
met.infinitely-many-propositions: The propositions that a given number is fixed by the arrow, one for each number, are pairwise distinct, each pinned down by that number (the shared argument axiom-of-infinity-t).
met.codomain-intensions: With one object such an intension is constant, so it is pinned down by $\emptyset$, and the domain holds every finitely pinned intension.
met.one-object-action-model: Each part of Proposition D.5 is a one-object category acting on $\mathbb N$ (Appendix D, Definitions D.1–D.3).
met.extensionally-full: The model is ideally full, hence extensionally full at every object (Appendix D, the remark after Definition D.3): for any set $R$ of tuples from the domains at an object $V$, the intension that assigns to every arrow out of $V$ into an object $U$ a fixed set $R_U$ of tuples from $U$’s domains, with $R_V=R$, is pinned down by $\emptyset$, so it is the intension of an element of $V^{\bar\sigma\to t}$ with extension $R$ at $1_V$.
met.infinitely-many-individuals: The individuals are the natural numbers.
met.non-injective-arrow: The rounding $f_2$ sends $0$ and $1$ to $0$.
met.arrows-finitely-determined: Each $\{f_n\}$ is pinned down by a finite set: $f_n$ is the only arrow sending $n$ to $n$ and $n-1$ to $0$.
met.actual-world-pinned: $\{f_1\}$, $f_1$ being the identity, is pinned down by $\{0,1\}$.
met.pinned-atoms: Each $\{f_n\}$ is pinned down by a finite set ($\{n-2,n-1,n\}$ for $n>1$, $\{0,1\}$ for the identity).
met.unbounded-haecceities: With $A:=\mathbb N$: the strongest persistent property with extension $\mathbb N$ pinned down by $\{0,\ldots,n\}$ has, at $f_m$, the multiples of $\min\{m,n\}$ as extension.
met.no-least-pinned-cover: An arrow $f_n$ is determined by its value at any $m\ge n$ and all $f_n$ with $n>N$ agree on $\{0,\ldots,N\}$, so the finitely pinned propositions are exactly the finite and cofinite sets of arrows. Let $F$ be the family of singletons $\{f_n\}$ for $n$ an even power of $2$: a finitely pinned superset of $\bigcup F$ is a cofinite set, and removing from it an odd-power member gives a strictly smaller one.
met.actual-world-isolated: The actual-world proposition, whose only member is the identity, is pinned down by a finite set, so it is in the domain and entails every truth; every other arrow is non-injective, so no composite with it is the identity.
met.actuality-contingent: The actual-world proposition is in the domain, being pinned down by a finite set; at every arrow some composite is not the identity, since every other arrow is non-injective, so it is necessary at no arrow, and a non-identity arrow carries it to the empty set.
met.irreversible-arrow: A non-identity arrow is non-injective, so no arrow composes it back to the identity.

models.definition:
Proposition D.5, part 7 (p. 78): the arrows are the maps $f_n$, for $n$ a power of $2$, sending $m$ to the greatest multiple of $n$ not exceeding $m$; $f_1$ is the identity. In every part, $W_0^\ddagger$ is the set of finite subsets of $\mathbb N$ and the model is ideally full: a proposition is a set of arrows whose membership depends only on the arrows’ values on some finite set of numbers (it is pinned down by that set), and an entity of a higher type is an applicative behaviour profile pinned down by a finite set in the same sense. The individuals are the natural numbers, acted on by the arrows themselves. Propositions and properties are thus about finitely many numbers and indifferent to how the arrows treat the rest. Evaluation point: the sole object, at the identity arrow.

Interpretation of Σ, fixed for this record: one designated relational constant $c$ of type $\tau=\bar\sigma t$ denotes $\lambda\bar x\, .\,a$, where $a$ is the unique true atom of the model, the actual-world proposition, whose only member is the identity arrow; every other constant of Σ, of which there is at least one, is relational and denotes the top element of its type.

met.finitely-pinned-domains: The model is ideally full: every entity is pinned down by a finite set of numbers, and every intension pinned down by one is in the domain (Definitions D.1–D.3).
met.infinitely-many-propositions: The propositions that a given number is fixed by the arrow, one for each number, are pairwise distinct, each pinned down by that number (the shared argument axiom-of-infinity-t).
met.codomain-intensions: With one object such an intension is constant, so it is pinned down by $\emptyset$, and the domain holds every finitely pinned intension.
met.one-object-action-model: Each part of Proposition D.5 is a one-object category acting on $\mathbb N$ (Appendix D, Definitions D.1–D.3).
met.extensionally-full: The model is ideally full, hence extensionally full at every object (Appendix D, the remark after Definition D.3): for any set $R$ of tuples from the domains at an object $V$, the intension that assigns to every arrow out of $V$ into an object $U$ a fixed set $R_U$ of tuples from $U$’s domains, with $R_V=R$, is pinned down by $\emptyset$, so it is the intension of an element of $V^{\bar\sigma\to t}$ with extension $R$ at $1_V$.
met.infinitely-many-individuals: The individuals are the natural numbers.
met.non-injective-arrow: The rounding $f_2$ sends $0$ and $1$ to $0$.
met.arrows-finitely-determined: Each $\{f_n\}$ is pinned down by a finite set: $f_n$ is the only arrow sending $n$ to $n$ and $n-1$ to $0$.
met.actual-world-pinned: $\{f_1\}$, $f_1$ being the identity, is pinned down by $\{0,1\}$.
met.pinned-atoms: Each $\{f_n\}$ is pinned down by a finite set ($\{n-2,n-1,n\}$ for $n>1$, $\{0,1\}$ for the identity).
met.unbounded-haecceities: With $A:=\mathbb N$: the strongest persistent property with extension $\mathbb N$ pinned down by $\{0,\ldots,n\}$ has, at $f_m$, the multiples of $\min\{m,n\}$ as extension.
met.no-least-pinned-cover: An arrow $f_n$ is determined by its value at any $m\ge n$ and all $f_n$ with $n>N$ agree on $\{0,\ldots,N\}$, so the finitely pinned propositions are exactly the finite and cofinite sets of arrows. Let $F$ be the family of singletons $\{f_n\}$ for $n$ an even power of $2$: a finitely pinned superset of $\bigcup F$ is a cofinite set, and removing from it an odd-power member gives a strictly smaller one.
met.actual-world-isolated: The actual-world proposition, whose only member is the identity, is pinned down by a finite set, so it is in the domain and entails every truth; every other arrow is non-injective, so no composite with it is the identity.
met.actuality-contingent: The actual-world proposition is in the domain, being pinned down by a finite set; at every arrow some composite is not the identity, since every other arrow is non-injective, so it is necessary at no arrow, and a non-identity arrow carries it to the empty set.
met.irreversible-arrow: A non-identity arrow is non-injective, so no arrow composes it back to the identity.

models.definition:
Proposition D.5, part 5 (p. 78): the arrows are the monotone surjections $h$ of $\mathbb N$ with $h0=h1$, together with the identity. In every part, $W_0^\ddagger$ is the set of finite subsets of $\mathbb N$ and the model is ideally full: a proposition is a set of arrows whose membership depends only on the arrows’ values on some finite set of numbers (it is pinned down by that set), and an entity of a higher type is an applicative behaviour profile pinned down by a finite set in the same sense. There is a single individual, which every arrow fixes; the arrows still act on $\mathbb N$, which supplies the pinning sets. Propositions and properties are thus about finitely many numbers and indifferent to how the arrows treat the rest. Evaluation point: the sole object, at the identity arrow.

Interpretation of Σ, fixed for this record: every constant of Σ is relational, and each denotes the top element of its type.

met.finitely-pinned-domains: The model is ideally full: every entity is pinned down by a finite set of numbers, and every intension pinned down by one is in the domain (Definitions D.1–D.3).
met.infinitely-many-propositions: The propositions that a given number is fixed by the arrow, one for each number, are pairwise distinct, each pinned down by that number (the shared argument axiom-of-infinity-t).
met.codomain-intensions: With one object such an intension is constant, so it is pinned down by $\emptyset$, and the domain holds every finitely pinned intension.
met.one-object-action-model: Each part of Proposition D.5 is a one-object category acting on $\mathbb N$ (Appendix D, Definitions D.1–D.3).
met.extensionally-full: The model is ideally full, hence extensionally full at every object (Appendix D, the remark after Definition D.3): for any set $R$ of tuples from the domains at an object $V$, the intension that assigns to every arrow out of $V$ into an object $U$ a fixed set $R_U$ of tuples from $U$’s domains, with $R_V=R$, is pinned down by $\emptyset$, so it is the intension of an element of $V^{\bar\sigma\to t}$ with extension $R$ at $1_V$.
met.one-individual: The only individual is fixed by every arrow, at the sole object.
met.non-injective-arrow: Every arrow other than the identity sends $0$ and $1$ to one number.
met.factorizable-arrows: If $h$ is the identity, take $N^{\prime\prime}:=N\cup S$, $k^{\prime\prime}:=1$ and $j:=k^{\prime}$. Otherwise $h$ collapses $0$ and $1$; take $N^{\prime\prime}$ as for the monotone surjections, with $0,1\in N$. If $k$ is the identity, $k^{\prime}$ agrees with $h$ on $\{0,1\}$, so it is a collapse; take $k^{\prime\prime}:=k^{\prime}$ and $j:=1$. If $k$ is a collapse, the construction for the monotone surjections gives $k^{\prime\prime}$ and $j$ that collapse $0$ and $1$, as $h$ and $k$ do.
met.actual-world-pinned: As in part 4: the identity is the only arrow that does not collapse $0$ and $1$, so $\{1_{\mathbb N}\}$ is pinned down by $\{0,1\}$.
met.collapse-unpinned: The other arrows are those that collapse $0$ and $1$, pinned down by $\{0,1\}$, and a collapsing monotone surjection is not determined by its values on a finite set.
met.d6-surjective: Restricting part 4 to surjections, every arrow is a surjection of $\mathbb N$. So each arrow acts surjectively on the pinning sets, the finite subsets of $\mathbb N$, and on the individuals, whether these are the natural numbers or a single one that every arrow fixes.
met.unbounded-haecceities: As in parts 2–4, with $A$ the even numbers.
met.no-least-pinned-cover: Let $F$ be the family of propositions $A_m$ ($m\ge1$), each pinned down by $\{2m,2m+1\}$, that the arrow sends $2m$ to $0$ and $2m+1$ to $1$, so that its first step is at the odd position $2m+1$; the identity belongs to no $A_m$. met.actual-world-isolated: The actual-world proposition, whose only member is the identity, is pinned down by a finite set, so it is in the domain and entails every truth; every other arrow is non-injective, so no composite with it is the identity.
met.actuality-contingent: The actual-world proposition is in the domain, being pinned down by a finite set; at every arrow some composite is not the identity, since every other arrow is non-injective, so it is necessary at no arrow, and a non-identity arrow carries it to the empty set.
met.irreversible-arrow: A non-identity arrow is non-injective, so no arrow composes it back to the identity.

meets.uniformly-pinned-rigidity: Let $Y$ be weakly rigid, pinned down by $S=[0,s]$, with extension $E$ at the identity. Pinning and weak persistence give $Y(k)\supseteq k_2\cdot E$ for every $k_2$ agreeing with $k$ on $S$, and weak inextensibility, tested on the intension $k\mapsto\bigcup\{k_2\cdot E:k_2\text{ agrees with }k\text{ on }N\}$, pinned down by $N$, gives the reverse inclusion; so $\bigcup\{k_2\cdot E:k_2\text{ agrees with }k\text{ on }N\}=Y(k)$ for every finite $N\supseteq S$. meets.collapse-unpinned: The other arrows are those that collapse $0$ and $1$, pinned down by $\{0,1\}$, and a collapsing monotone map is not determined by its values on a finite set.
meets.positive-preserving: Every arrow is monotone, and the arrows with $h0=h1=1$ send $0$ to a positive number.
meets.transport-gap: Take $N=\{0\}$, $i$ any arrow with $i0=2$ (hence $i1=2$ and range within $[2,\infty)$), and $q:=\{k : k1=1\}$, pinned down by $\{1\}$: the arrows $k$ with $k0=k1=1\le k2$ and $k^{\prime}$ with $k^{\prime}0=k^{\prime}1=0$, agreeing beyond $1$, are separated by $q$. settings.monoid: Proposition D.5, part 4 (p. 78): the arrows are the monotone maps $h$ of $\mathbb N$ with $h0=h1$, together with the identity.

meets.non-injective-arrow: Every arrow other than the identity sends $0$ and $1$ to one number.
meets.uniformly-pinned-rigidity: Let $Y$ be weakly rigid, pinned down by $S=[0,s]$, with extension $E$ at the identity. Pinning and weak persistence give $Y(k)\supseteq k_2\cdot E$ for every $k_2$ agreeing with $k$ on $S$, and weak inextensibility, tested on the intension $k\mapsto\bigcup\{k_2\cdot E:k_2\text{ agrees with }k\text{ on }N\}$, pinned down by $N$, gives the reverse inclusion; so $\bigcup\{k_2\cdot E:k_2\text{ agrees with }k\text{ on }N\}=Y(k)$ for every finite $N\supseteq S$. If some $p\in E$ were pinned minimally at $T$ with $t:=\max T>s$, take $s'\ge t$ and the jump map $k$, sending $0$ and $1$ to $0$, the identity on $[2,s']$ and adding $100$ beyond: an arrow agreeing with $k$ on $S$ and sending $t$ to $s'+1$ puts into the $S$-union an element pinned at $s'+1$, while every element of the $[0,s'+1]$-union is pinned inside $k([0,s'])\cup[s'+100,\infty)$. So $E\subseteq\operatorname{Pin}(S)$, and then $k_2\cdot p=k\cdot p$ whenever $k_2$ agrees with $k$ on $S$, so $Y(k)=k\cdot E$.
meets.actual-world-pinned: The identity is the only arrow that does not collapse $0$ and $1$, so $\{1_{\mathbb N}\}$ is pinned down by $\{0,1\}$.
meets.collapse-unpinned: The other arrows are those that collapse $0$ and $1$, pinned down by $\{0,1\}$, and a collapsing monotone map is not determined by its values on a finite set.
meets.positive-preserving: Every arrow is monotone, and the arrows with $h0=h1=1$ send $0$ to a positive number.
meets.transport-gap: Take $N=\{0\}$, $i$ any arrow with $i0=2$ (hence $i1=2$ and range within $[2,\infty)$), and $q:=\{k : k1=1\}$, pinned down by $\{1\}$: the arrows $k$ with $k0=k1=1\le k2$ and $k^{\prime}$ with $k^{\prime}0=k^{\prime}1=0$, agreeing beyond $1$, are separated by $q$. The model is a one-object finite-support model, and the intension the argument uses is pinned down by $N$.
meets.unbounded-haecceities: As in parts 2 and 3, with $A$ the even numbers.
meets.no-least-pinned-cover: Let $F$ be the family of propositions $A_m$ ($m\ge1$), each pinned down by $\{1,2m,2m+1\}$, that the arrow is constant on $\{1,\ldots,2m\}$ and increases at $2m+1$; the identity belongs to no $A_m$. The least superset of $\bigcup F$ pinned down by $\{0,\ldots,N\}$ consists of the non-identity arrows whose first increase after $1$ is at an odd position or beyond $N$, and it strictly shrinks as $N$ grows.

models.definition:
Proposition D.5, part 4 (p. 78): the arrows are the monotone maps $h$ of $\mathbb N$ with $h0=h1$, together with the identity. In every part, $W_0^\ddagger$ is the set of finite subsets of $\mathbb N$ and the model is ideally full: a proposition is a set of arrows whose membership depends only on the arrows’ values on some finite set of numbers (it is pinned down by that set), and an entity of a higher type is an applicative behaviour profile pinned down by a finite set in the same sense. There is a single individual, which every arrow fixes; the arrows still act on $\mathbb N$, which supplies the pinning sets. Propositions and properties are thus about finitely many numbers and indifferent to how the arrows treat the rest. Evaluation point: the sole object, at the identity arrow.

Interpretation of Σ, fixed for this record: one designated relational constant $c$ of type $\tau=\bar\sigma t$ denotes $\lambda\bar x\, .\,a$, where $a$ is the unique true atom of the model, the actual-world proposition, whose only member is the identity arrow; every other constant of Σ, of which there is at least one, is relational and denotes the top element of its type.

met.finitely-pinned-domains: The model is ideally full: every entity is pinned down by a finite set of numbers, and every intension pinned down by one is in the domain (Definitions D.1–D.3).
met.infinitely-many-propositions: The propositions that a given number is fixed by the arrow, one for each number, are pairwise distinct, each pinned down by that number (the shared argument axiom-of-infinity-t).
met.codomain-intensions: With one object such an intension is constant, so it is pinned down by $\emptyset$, and the domain holds every finitely pinned intension.
met.one-object-action-model: Each part of Proposition D.5 is a one-object category acting on $\mathbb N$ (Appendix D, Definitions D.1–D.3).
met.extensionally-full: The model is ideally full, hence extensionally full at every object (Appendix D, the remark after Definition D.3): for any set $R$ of tuples from the domains at an object $V$, the intension that assigns to every arrow out of $V$ into an object $U$ a fixed set $R_U$ of tuples from $U$’s domains, with $R_V=R$, is pinned down by $\emptyset$, so it is the intension of an element of $V^{\bar\sigma\to t}$ with extension $R$ at $1_V$.
met.one-individual: The only individual is fixed by every arrow, at the sole object.
met.non-injective-arrow: Every arrow other than the identity sends $0$ and $1$ to one number.
met.uniformly-pinned-rigidity: Let $Y$ be weakly rigid, pinned down by $S=[0,s]$, with extension $E$ at the identity. met.collapse-unpinned: The other arrows are those that collapse $0$ and $1$, pinned down by $\{0,1\}$, and a collapsing monotone map is not determined by its values on a finite set.
met.positive-preserving: Every arrow is monotone, and the arrows with $h0=h1=1$ send $0$ to a positive number.
met.transport-gap: Take $N=\{0\}$, $i$ any arrow with $i0=2$ (hence $i1=2$ and range within $[2,\infty)$), and $q:=\{k : k1=1\}$, pinned down by $\{1\}$: the arrows $k$ with $k0=k1=1\le k2$ and $k^{\prime}$ with $k^{\prime}0=k^{\prime}1=0$, agreeing beyond $1$, are separated by $q$. met.unbounded-haecceities: As in parts 2 and 3, with $A$ the even numbers.
met.no-least-pinned-cover: Let $F$ be the family of propositions $A_m$ ($m\ge1$), each pinned down by $\{1,2m,2m+1\}$, that the arrow is constant on $\{1,\ldots,2m\}$ and increases at $2m+1$; the identity belongs to no $A_m$. The least superset of $\bigcup F$ pinned down by $\{0,\ldots,N\}$ consists of the non-identity arrows whose first increase after $1$ is at an odd position or beyond $N$, and it strictly shrinks as $N$ grows.
met.actual-world-isolated: The actual-world proposition, whose only member is the identity, is pinned down by a finite set, so it is in the domain and entails every truth; every other arrow is non-injective, so no composite with it is the identity.
met.actuality-contingent: The actual-world proposition is in the domain, being pinned down by a finite set; at every arrow some composite is not the identity, since every other arrow is non-injective, so it is necessary at no arrow, and a non-identity arrow carries it to the empty set.
met.irreversible-arrow: A non-identity arrow is non-injective, so no arrow composes it back to the identity.

models.definition:
Proposition D.5, part 3 (p. 77): the one-object category whose arrows are all the monotone maps of $\mathbb N$. In every part, $W_0^\ddagger$ is the set of finite subsets of $\mathbb N$ and the model is ideally full: a proposition is a set of arrows whose membership depends only on the arrows’ values on some finite set of numbers (it is pinned down by that set), and an entity of a higher type is an applicative behaviour profile pinned down by a finite set in the same sense. There is a single individual, which every arrow fixes; the arrows still act on $\mathbb N$, which supplies the pinning sets. Propositions and properties are thus about finitely many numbers and indifferent to how the arrows treat the rest. Evaluation point: the sole object, at the identity arrow.

Interpretation of Σ, fixed for this record: every constant of Σ is relational, and each denotes the top element of its type.

met.finitely-pinned-domains: The model is ideally full: every entity is pinned down by a finite set of numbers, and every intension pinned down by one is in the domain (Definitions D.1–D.3).
met.infinitely-many-propositions: The propositions that a given number is fixed by the arrow, one for each number, are pairwise distinct, each pinned down by that number (the shared argument axiom-of-infinity-t).
met.codomain-intensions: With one object such an intension is constant, so it is pinned down by $\emptyset$, and the domain holds every finitely pinned intension.
met.one-object-action-model: Each part of Proposition D.5 is a one-object category acting on $\mathbb N$ (Appendix D, Definitions D.1–D.3).
met.extensionally-full: The model is ideally full, hence extensionally full at every object (Appendix D, the remark after Definition D.3): for any set $R$ of tuples from the domains at an object $V$, the intension that assigns to every arrow out of $V$ into an object $U$ a fixed set $R_U$ of tuples from $U$’s domains, with $R_V=R$, is pinned down by $\emptyset$, so it is the intension of an element of $V^{\bar\sigma\to t}$ with extension $R$ at $1_V$.
met.one-individual: The only individual is fixed by every arrow, at the sole object.
met.no-atoms-anywhere: One object. A proposition pinned down by a finite $N$ and containing a monotone map $k$ contains every monotone map agreeing with $k$ on $N$; two of these, one constant beyond $\max N$ and one strictly increasing there, lie in disjoint nonempty propositions pinned down by a larger finite set. So no proposition is an atom.
met.no-actuality-anywhere: One object, so Actuality, a closed pure sentence, holds at every world iff at the identity, where it fails (recorded in this model’s verdicts).
met.non-injective-arrow: The constant map with value $0$ is monotone.
met.uniformly-pinned-rigidity: Let $Y$ be weakly rigid, pinned down by $S=[0,s]$, with extension $E$ at the identity. Pinning and weak persistence give $Y(k)\supseteq k_2\cdot E$ for every $k_2$ agreeing with $k$ on $S$, and weak inextensibility, tested on the intension $k\mapsto\bigcup\{k_2\cdot E:k_2\text{ agrees with }k\text{ on }N\}$, pinned down by $N$, gives the reverse inclusion; so $\bigcup\{k_2\cdot E:k_2\text{ agrees with }k\text{ on }N\}=Y(k)$ for every finite $N\supseteq S$. If some $p\in E$ were pinned minimally at $T$ with $t:=\max T>s$, take $s'\ge t$ and the jump map $k$, the identity on $[0,s']$ and adding $100$ beyond: an arrow agreeing with $k$ on $S$ and sending $t$ to $s'+1$ puts into the $S$-union an element pinned at $s'+1$, while every element of the $[0,s'+1]$-union is pinned inside $k([0,s'])\cup[s'+100,\infty)$. So $E\subseteq\operatorname{Pin}(S)$, and then $k_2\cdot p=k\cdot p$ whenever $k_2$ agrees with $k$ on $S$, so $Y(k)=k\cdot E$.
met.evens-avoidable: With $N_0\subseteq[0,M_0]$: $i$ the monotone map that is the identity on $[0,M_0]$ and adds one beyond it; an even $b>M_0+1$, whose only preimage under $i$ is the odd $b-1$; and $N^{\prime}:=[0,b]$: a monotone map agreeing with $i$ there has the same preimages of $b$ within $[0,b]$ and takes values at least $i(b)=b+1$ beyond it.
met.positive-preserving: Every arrow is monotone, and the constant map to $1$ sends $0$ to a positive number.
met.transport-gap: Take $N=\{0\}$, $i$ any monotone map with $i0=2$, so that every $i^{\prime}$ agreeing with it on $N$ has range within $[2,\infty)$, and $q:=\{k : k1=1\}$, pinned down by $\{1\}$: two monotone maps agreeing on $[2,\infty)$ with $k2\ge1$ may take the values $1$ and $0$ at $1$. The model is a one-object finite-support model, and the intension the argument uses is pinned down by $N$.
met.unbounded-haecceities: As in part 2, with $A$ the even numbers.
met.no-least-pinned-cover: Let $F$ be the family of propositions $A_m$ ($m\ge1$), each pinned down by $\{0,2m-1,2m\}$, that the arrow is constant on $\{0,\ldots,2m-1\}$ and first changes value at $2m$. The least superset of $\bigcup F$ pinned down by $\{0,\ldots,N\}$ consists of the arrows whose first change of value is at an even position or beyond $N$, and it strictly shrinks as $N$ grows.

arguments.text: At type $e\to t$. In the source's terms an upper bound of the haecceities of the members of $A$ is a persistent property whose extension contains $A$. arguments.text: At type $e\to t$, for the property of being even, which is in the domain as the constant intension $\{\langle b,h\rangle : b\text{ even}\}$, pinned down by $\emptyset$. Unpacking $\operatorname{Inextensible}$ as in the left-to-right half of Dorr’s rigidity criterion (draft, Lemma 14, p. 7, with Lemma 13): even the unboxed matrix, evaluated at the identity, says that $Y$ is contained in every persistent (transport-closed) $B$ in the domain whose extension includes $Y$’s. For a finite $N^{\prime}$, the smallest such $B$ pinned down by $N^{\prime}$ is $B_{N^{\prime}}:=\{\langle b^{\prime\prime},i^{\prime}\rangle : i^{\prime\prime}(b)=b^{\prime\prime}\text{ for some even }b\text{ and some arrow }i^{\prime\prime}\text{ agreeing with }i^{\prime}\text{ on }N^{\prime}\}$, which is transport-closed and pinned down by $N^{\prime}$. Now let $Y$ be coextensive with evenness and pinned down by a finite $N_0$; then $\langle b,i\rangle\in Y$ for every even $b$ and every arrow $i$ fixing $N_0$ pointwise. Take the arrow $i$, the even $b$ and the finite $N^{\prime}$ that the condition provides for $N_0$: no arrow agreeing with $i$ on $N^{\prime}$ sends an even number to $b$. So $\langle b,i\rangle\in Y\setminus B_{N^{\prime}}$, and $Y$ is not even weakly inextensible.

models.definition:
Proposition D.5, part 2 (pp. 76–77): the one-object category whose arrows are the monotone surjections of $\mathbb N$ (the source first considers all surjections, which gives the same package, and restricts to the monotone ones to make the failure of Boolean Completeness easier to exhibit). In every part, $W_0^\ddagger$ is the set of finite subsets of $\mathbb N$ and the model is ideally full: a proposition is a set of arrows whose membership depends only on the arrows’ values on some finite set of numbers (it is pinned down by that set), and an entity of a higher type is an applicative behaviour profile pinned down by a finite set in the same sense. There is a single individual, which every arrow fixes; the arrows still act on $\mathbb N$, which supplies the pinning sets. Propositions and properties are thus about finitely many numbers and indifferent to how the arrows treat the rest. Evaluation point: the sole object, at the identity arrow.

Interpretation of Σ, fixed for this record: every constant of Σ is relational, and each denotes the top element of its type.

sources: Cian Dorr, suggestion of 7 October 2026, in conversation with Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic): the monoid of the functions on $\mathbb N$ that are injective or identify $0$ with $1$, for a model with Vicinity but not Actuality outside C5.
