arguments.text: At $V$ let $p:=\mathrm{fix}^{VV}_{\{\star\}}$, the true proposition that $\star$ is fixed. For any true $q$ at $V$, pinned by $N_q$, the surjection $u\colon V\to W_0$ that is the identity on $\mathbb N$ and sends $\star$ into a block $B$ disjoint from $N_q$ lies in $\Diamond q$ (a surjection fixing $N_q$ and collapsing $B$ onto $\star$ brings it back into $\mathrm{fix}^{VV}_{N_q}$) but not in $\hat\Diamond p$, since every $v$ with $vu\in p$ collapses $B$ onto $\star$ and so cannot return to $\mathrm{fix}^{00}_B$. So B fails for $\Box_{\ne}$ at $p$. By Proposition D11 of The Bounds of Possibility, $p\to\hat{\hat\Box}\hat\Diamond p$, so $\hat\Diamond p$ is two-hat necessary; it is not ND-necessary, which is what the failure of B says. Actuality fails: the true propositions $\mathrm{fix}^{VV}_N$ descend strictly.

arguments.text: Let $k$ be an arrow out of the evaluation object $w$ with $ka=kb$ for two distinct points $a$ and $b$ of the set the arrows act on, and let $q$ be the set of arrows $j$ out of $w$ with $ja\ne jb$. It contains the identity, is pinned down by $\{a,b\}$, is symmetric (an arrow separates $a$ from $b$ iff its composite with a permutation of the points does), and contains no arrow $j\circ k$. Let $\tau$ be $tt$, or $tttt$ in the case noted below. No entity $x$ of type $\tau$ at $w$ is determined by its transport along $k$: let $y$ agree with $x$ except at the arrows in $q$, where the top entity of the argument type of $\tau$ is added to its value or removed from it. Then $y$ is pinned down by a finite set along with $x$, is symmetric if $x$ is, so is in the domain; it differs from $x$ and has $k\cdot y=k\cdot x$, transport along $k$ reading only the values at the arrows after $k$. If $\mathfrak R$ were a rigid real number structure at $w$ of type $\tau$, necessarily a real number structure, with carrier $X$ (Background, Analysis), an instance $x$ of $X$ and $y$ as above would give $k\cdot y=k\cdot x\in X_k$ by persistence, $Xy$ by inextensibility, and $k\cdot y\ne k\cdot x$ by the necessary distinctness of the instances: so $X$ has no instance. The antecedent of Analytic Necessitism holds, however, at type $\tau$. The propositions are infinitely many and, in the recorded instances, include a copy of the natural numbers, so by extensional fullness the entities of type $tt$, which include one with any set of propositions as extension at the identity, include a copy of the sets of natural numbers and so of the reals, whose order, sum, product and natural numbers are the extensions at the identity of relations in the domain; the structure is complete, every subset of its carrier being the extension of a subproperty, so $\exists\mathfrak R\,.\,\operatorname{Real}_{tt}(\mathfrak R)$ holds at $w$. (Should the propositions be infinite without including a copy of the natural numbers, the same holds at type $tttt$, the sets of sets of propositions being Dedekind-infinite in ZF.) So Analytic Necessitism fails. No choice is used.

arguments.text: Every arrow is surjective on individuals, hence on finite sets of individuals, so Proposition D.6 of Classicism gives BF at every type with any object as the evaluation point.

Let $p_0$ be the proposition that the world is $W_0$, the set of arrows $W_0\to W_0$, true and pinned by $\emptyset$. It is not two-hat necessary: every $C_1(\mathrm{fix}^{00}_N)$ contains a surjective arrow $\iota\colon W_0\to V$ injective on $N$, collapsing a block outside $N$ onto $\star$ (given $r$ true at $V$ pinned by $N_1$, let $v\colon V\to W_0$ be the identity on $\mathbb N$ with $\star$ sent to a block $\{e,\pi e\}$ disjoint from $N_1$; then $v\iota$ agrees with $1_{W_0}$ on $N$, $\iota$ being the identity on $N$, and a surjection fixing $N_1$ and collapsing that block onto $\star$ brings $v$ back into $\mathrm{fix}^{VV}_{N_1}$). It is 5-necessary: let $Y_k$, for an arrow $k$ out of $W_0$, be the set of propositions at $\mathrm{trg}(k)$ pinned by a finite set of individuals in the range of some arrow from $W_0$ (at $W_0$ all propositions, at $V$ those pinned by old individuals); $Y$ is pinned by $\emptyset$. For $z$ pinned by $S$ put $N_z:=S\cup\pi S$; an arrow injective on $N_z$ cannot collapse a block of $S$ onto $\star$, so $k^tz\in Y_k$ for every $k\in C_1(\mathrm{fix}^{00}_{N_z})$ and $\hat{\hat\Box}(Yz)$ holds for every $z$. Since $\hat{\hat\Box}\le\Box_5$ and $\Box_5$ satisfies BF at type $t$ (Theorem D16 and Corollary D6 of The Bounds of Possibility), $\Box_5\forall z\,Yz$ holds, and $\forall z\,Yz=p_0$ because at $V$ the proposition that $\star$ is fixed is pinned by no set of old individuals (the identity and a surjection sending $\star$ into $\mathbb N$ and collapsing a block away from that set onto $\star$ agree on it).

revisions.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, from an audit of GPT-6 Astra's note (prompted by Cian Dorr)
revisions.note: The text said $v\iota=1_{W_0}$, which cannot hold for the non-injective $\iota$, and used a map that is not surjective. Now $\iota$ is the identity on $N$, so $v\iota$ agrees with $1_{W_0}$ on $N$, and the return map is a surjection fixing $N_1$ that collapses $\{e,\pi e\}$ onto $\star$. The verdict is unchanged.

arguments.text: The three-hat operator $\hat{(3)}\Box$ is necessarily B here: at $W_0$, $C_2(\mathrm{fix}^{00}_N)=C_3(\mathrm{fix}^{00}_N)$ is the set of arrows $W_0\to W_0$ injective and block-injective on $N$ (arrows into $V$ drop out at $C_2$ by the argument for $p_0$, and block-bijections, which are surjective, are in every $C_n$), and at $V$ likewise $C_1=C_2$ on $\mathrm{fix}^{VV}_{N}$. So it is an S5 operator, and $\Box_5\le\hat{(3)}\Box$. But $\mathrm{fix}^{00}_N$ is true and not $\hat{(3)}\Box$-necessary, since a block-bijection moving a point of $N$ lies in every $C_2(\mathrm{fix}^{00}_{N^\prime})$. The argument for the non-surjective model carries over, every arrow used in it being surjective or replaceable by a surjective one that agrees with it on the finite set in question.

models.name: Paired-individuals two-object model: block-respecting maps

certificate.produced_by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), 14 October 2026, at Cian Dorr's direction

sources: Cian Dorr and Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), conversation of 14 October 2026 (transcript in the private notes).
Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, Appendix D, Definitions D.1–D.3 and Proposition D.4, pp. 73–74 (ideally full action models).
models.definition:
An ideally full action model in the sense of Classicism, Appendix D, over a category with two objects, each carrying the ideal of finite sets: a model of C by Proposition D.4. The member's construction and evaluation point follow.

A two-object ideally full action model. Fix a fixed-point-free involution $\pi$ on $\mathbb N$ (say $2k\leftrightarrow 2k+1$), which partitions $\mathbb N$ into two-element blocks. The objects are $W_0$, with individuals $\mathbb N$, and $V$, with individuals $\mathbb N\sqcup\{\star\}$ where $\star$ forms a block by itself. The arrows are all block-respecting maps between these sets: $g(\pi c)\in\{g(c),\pi g(c)\}$ for every $c$, so a block maps into a block, either injectively or collapsed to a point, and the new individual $\star$ can be hit only by collapsing a block onto it. The pinning action is the identity on individuals, the ideal is the finite sets, and the individuals are the type-$e$ domains, so the model is ideally full in the sense of Classicism, Appendix D, and a model of C by its Proposition D.4. The evaluation point is the identity on $W_0$.


Interpretation of Σ, fixed for this record: every constant of Σ is relational, and each denotes the top element of its type.

meets.infinitely-many-individuals: The individuals are infinite at both objects.
meets.no-atoms-anywhere: At either object let $p\ne\bot$ be pinned down by a finite $N$ and contain $h$. Take a block $B$ disjoint from $N$ and its $\pi$-image and $b\in B$: some arrow agreeing with $h$ on $N$ sends $b$ to $h(b)$ and some sends it elsewhere, both in $p$ (in the surjective model the infinitely many other blocks keep it surjective), so the arrows in $p$ sending $b$ to $h(b)$ lie strictly between $\bot$ and $p$.
meets.infinitely-many-propositions-everywhere: At both objects the propositions that an arrow sends $0$ to $n$, one for each $n$, are pinned down by $\{0\}$ and pairwise distinct.

arguments.text: Let $p_0$ be the proposition that the world is $W_0$, the set of arrows $W_0\to W_0$, true and pinned by $\emptyset$. It is not two-hat necessary: every $C_1(\mathrm{fix}^{00}_N)$ contains the inclusion $\iota\colon W_0\to V$ (given $r$ true at $V$ pinned by $N_1$, let $v\colon V\to W_0$ be the identity on $\mathbb N$ with $\star$ sent to a block $\{e,\pi e\}$ disjoint from $N_1$; then $v\iota=1_{W_0}$, and the map collapsing that block onto $\star$ and fixing everything else brings $v$ back into $\mathrm{fix}^{VV}_{N_1}$). It is 5-necessary: let $Y_k$, for an arrow $k$ out of $W_0$, be the set of propositions at $\mathrm{trg}(k)$ pinned by a finite set of individuals in the range of some arrow from $W_0$ (at $W_0$ all propositions, at $V$ those pinned by old individuals); $Y$ is pinned by $\emptyset$. For $z$ pinned by $S$ put $N_z:=S\cup\pi S$; an arrow injective on $N_z$ cannot collapse a block of $S$ onto $\star$, so $k^tz\in Y_k$ for every $k\in C_1(\mathrm{fix}^{00}_{N_z})$ and $\hat{\hat\Box}(Yz)$ holds for every $z$. Since $\hat{\hat\Box}\le\Box_5$ and $\Box_5$ satisfies BF at type $t$ (Theorem D16 and Corollary D6 of The Bounds of Possibility), $\Box_5\forall z\,Yz$ holds, and $\forall z\,Yz=p_0$ because at $V$ the proposition that $\star$ is fixed is pinned by no set of old individuals (the identity and the map sending $\star$ to $0$ agree on every such set).

The three-hat operator $\hat{(3)}\Box$ is necessarily B here: at $W_0$, $C_2(\mathrm{fix}^{00}_N)=C_3(\mathrm{fix}^{00}_N)$ is the set of arrows $W_0\to W_0$ injective and block-injective on $N$ (arrows into $V$ drop out at $C_2$ by the argument for $p_0$, and block-bijections are in every $C_n$), and at $V$ likewise $C_1=C_2$ on $\mathrm{fix}^{VV}_{N}$. So it is an S5 operator, and $\Box_5\le\hat{(3)}\Box$. But $\mathrm{fix}^{00}_N$ is true and not $\hat{(3)}\Box$-necessary, since a block-bijection moving a point of $N$ lies in every $C_2(\mathrm{fix}^{00}_{N^\prime})$.

withdrawn.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, after GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), prompted by Cian Dorr
withdrawn.reason: The premise fails: $k^tz$ is pinned down by $k(S)$, but an arrow $k\colon W_0\to V$ can collapse a block of $S$ onto $\star$, so $k(S)$ need not consist of old individuals. For $z$ the proposition that an arrow sends $a$ to $\star$, pinned down by $\{a\}$, and $k$ collapsing the block of $a$ onto $\star$, $k^tz$ is the proposition that $\star$ is fixed, which no set of old individuals pins down; so $\Box(Yz)$ fails. Read literally (individuals in the range of some arrow from $W_0$), $Y$ holds of every proposition at $V$ and $\forall z\,Yz$ is $\top$. BF holds at every type (argument barcan-local-sections). The argument for 5-necessity uses $Y$ only along arrows injective on $S\cup\pi S$ and is unaffected.

arguments.text: With $Y$ as in the argument for 5-necessity, $k^tz$ is pinned by $k(S)$, a set of individuals in the range of $k$, so $\Box(Yz)$ holds for every $z$, while $\Box\forall z\,Yz$ fails at the inclusion $\iota$, whose target has the proposition that $\star$ is fixed.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
arguments.text: At $\sigma=\tau=t$, at the evaluation point. Let $A_m$ ($m\ge1$) be the set of arrows $h$ into the evaluation object that are constant on $\{0,\ldots,2m-1\}$ (blocks $0$ to $m-1$ collapsed to one point $c$) with $h(2m)\ne c$, pinned down by $\{0,\ldots,2m\}$. For $S=\{0,\ldots,2K+1\}$, a union of blocks, an arrow lies in the least $S$-pinned superset of $\bigcup_m A_m$ iff it is constant on $S$ or its first change of value is at an even position in $S$: an arrow constant on $S$ agrees on $S$ with a block-respecting arrow that stays constant through block $m-1$ and changes at $2m$, for any $m>K$. The arrow constant on blocks $0$ to $K$ that maps block $K+1$ injectively onto $\{c,\pi c\}$, with $2K+3\mapsto\pi c$, lies in that superset for $S$ but not for $\{0,\ldots,2K+3\}$, so the supersets strictly shrink and the family has no least upper bound, as in the shared argument boolean-completeness-t of the one-object finite-support models. Extensional fullness puts the family in the domain, and with it the relation pairing $A_m$ with the $m$-th numeral at type $t$; the numerals at $t$ are standard by the same fullness, and pairwise distinct since the $A_m$ are infinitely many propositions. So the family is countable relative to $t$.

arguments.by: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), prompted by Cian Dorr; checked and recorded by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: For arrows $h\colon A\to B$ and finite $N\subseteq A$, $T\subseteq B$ there are arrows $j\colon A\to B$ agreeing with $h$ on $N$ and $\sigma\colon B\to A$ with $j\sigma$ the identity on $T$: keep $h$ on the blocks meeting $N$, send fresh pairs of $A$ bijectively onto the pairs meeting $T$ with $\sigma$ inverting them, and if $\star\in T$ collapse a further fresh pair onto $\star$ and let $\sigma$ send $\star$ into it. If $R$ at $A$, pinned down by $N$, is necessarily true of every entity, and $b$ at $B$ is pinned down by $T$, then $b=(j\sigma)\cdot b=j\cdot(\sigma\cdot b)$ is in the extension of $R$ at $j$, which is its extension at $h$. So BF holds at every type with either object as evaluation point, and □BF holds.

arguments.by: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), prompted by Cian Dorr; checked and recorded by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: Write $F_h$ for the extension of $F$ at $h$ and $B_N(E)_h$ for the transports $f\cdot a$ of members of $E$ along arrows $f$ into the codomain of $h$ agreeing with $h$ on $N$; as in tame-rigidity-factorizable, a relation pinned down by $S$ with extension $E$ is weakly rigid iff it is $B_N(E)$ for every finite $N\supseteq S$. Block-respecting maps factor finitely: given $h\colon A\to B$, $k\colon B\to C$, a finite union $S$ of blocks (containing $\star$ at $V$), a finite $N\subseteq B$ and $f$ agreeing with $kh$ on $S$, for every finite $M$ there are $r$ agreeing with $h$ on $S$ and $j$ agreeing with $k$ on $N$ with $jr=f$ on $M$ (send the pairs of $M\setminus S$ bijectively to fresh pairs of $B$ and let $j$ copy $f$ there). Then for $F$ weakly rigid with that pin $S$, and $Z$ at $B$ pinned down by $N$ necessarily holding of each member of $F_h$, each $b=f\cdot a\in F_{kh}$ is $j\cdot(r\cdot a)$ with $r\cdot a\in F_r=F_h$, so $b\in Z_j=Z_k$. So $h\cdot F$ is weakly inextensible for every $h$, and $F$, persistent by C, is rigid. This holds at both objects and with all arrows or only surjective ones.

arguments.by: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), prompted by Cian Dorr; checked and recorded by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: At type $(t)t$. At the evaluation object $A$ let $p_n$, for even $n$, be the endomorphisms fixing $n$, pinned down by $\{n\}$; for an endomorphism $f$, $f\cdot p_m=p_n$ iff $m=n$ and $f(n)=n$ (otherwise an endomorphism sending $n$ and $f(m)$ to $n$, or fixing $n$ and moving $f(n)$, separates them). The property holding of every $p_n$ at arrows into $A$ and of nothing at arrows into the other object is pinned down by $\varnothing$. Suppose $Y$, pinned down by $S$, is weakly inextensible with that extension. Take $n$ with its block outside $S$ and a block permutation $g$ fixing $S$ with $g(n)$ in another block; then $p_n$ is in $Y$'s extension at $g$. Each $p_m$ necessarily has the property $Z$ of being $f\cdot p_{m'}$ for some even $m'$ and some arrow $f$ agreeing with the current arrow at $n$, so $Y\le Z$, and $p_n=f\cdot p_{m'}$ with $f(n)=g(n)\ne n$, which is impossible.

arguments.by: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), prompted by Cian Dorr; checked and recorded by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: The lifting of rigid-power-surjections, with blocks. Given $h\colon A\to B$ and a finite union $N$ of blocks, some surjective arrow $j$ agrees with $h$ on $N$, maps some pair bijectively onto each pair of $B$, and has finite fibres, only finitely many with more than one point. For such $j$ and weakly rigid $F$ with extension $E$, the extension of $F$ at $j$ is $j\cdot E$ (lift through the bijective preimage pairs). Given a rigid $X\le h\cdot F$ with extension $D$ and pin $T$, let $P$ be a finite union of blocks containing $N$, the fibres of $j$ with more than one point and $j^{-1}[T]$, and $D_0$ the members of $E$ that $j$ sends into $D$. Every endomorphism $u$ fixing $P$ satisfies $ju=vj$ for a block-respecting $v$ fixing $T$, so $D_0$ is closed under such $u$, and $Y:=B_P(D_0)$ is weakly rigid (move the rest of a pin of $a$ outside any larger $Q$ by a block permutation fixing $P$), so rigid, below $F$, with $j\cdot Y$ coextensive with $X$, so equal to it. So the power property of $F$ is weakly inextensible, hence rigid by Tame Rigidity, at both objects.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Zachary Goodsell
arguments.text: Let $k$ be an arrow out of the evaluation object $w$ with $ka=kb$ for two distinct points $a$ and $b$ of the set the arrows act on, and let $q$ be the set of arrows $j$ out of $w$ with $ja\ne jb$. It contains the identity, is pinned down by $\{a,b\}$, is symmetric (an arrow separates $a$ from $b$ iff its composite with a permutation of the points does), and contains no arrow $j\circ k$. Let $\tau$ be $tt$, or $tttt$ in the case noted below. No entity $x$ of type $\tau$ at $w$ is determined by its transport along $k$: let $y$ agree with $x$ except at the arrows in $q$, where the top entity of the argument type of $\tau$ is added to its value or removed from it. Then $y$ is pinned down by a finite set along with $x$, is symmetric if $x$ is, so is in the domain; it differs from $x$ and has $k\cdot y=k\cdot x$, transport along $k$ reading only the values at the arrows after $k$. If $\mathfrak R$ were a rigid real number structure at $w$ of type $\tau$, necessarily a real number structure, with carrier $X$ (Background, Analysis), an instance $x$ of $X$ and $y$ as above would give $k\cdot y=k\cdot x\in X_k$ by persistence, $Xy$ by inextensibility, and $k\cdot y\ne k\cdot x$ by the necessary distinctness of the instances: so $X$ has no instance. The antecedent of Analytic Necessitism holds, however, at type $\tau$. The propositions are infinitely many and, in the recorded instances, include a copy of the natural numbers, so by extensional fullness the entities of type $tt$, which include one with any set of propositions as extension at the identity, include a copy of the sets of natural numbers and so of the reals, whose order, sum, product and natural numbers are the extensions at the identity of relations in the domain; the structure is complete, every subset of its carrier being the extension of a subproperty, so $\exists\mathfrak R\,.\,\operatorname{Real}_{tt}(\mathfrak R)$ holds at $w$. (Should the propositions be infinite without including a copy of the natural numbers, the same holds at type $tttt$, the sets of sets of propositions being Dedekind-infinite in ZF.) So Analytic Necessitism fails. No choice is used.

withdrawn.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, after a trawl subagent's report
withdrawn.reason: The step from $k\cdot y=k\cdot x\in X_k$ to $Xy$ (or $y\in X_h$) by inextensibility does not follow: inextensibility bounds a rigid carrier from above, by the transports of its actual instances, and puts nothing new into its actual extension. The conclusion is false in many of the models the argument was applied to: entities fixed by every arrow, or transported injectively, can carry a rigid real number structure that is necessarily one (see analytic-necessitism-codomain-fixed and analytic-necessitism-full-continuum).

conditions.text: Write an entity of relational type at the evaluation object as its intension $k\mapsto Y_k$ over the arrows $k$ out of it, so that $Y\bar a$ holds at $k$ iff $k\cdot\bar a\in Y_k$; $Y$ is pinned down by a finite set $N$ of the points the arrows act on when $Y_k=Y_{k^{\prime}}$ for any arrows $k,k^{\prime}$ agreeing on $N$. Every entity in a domain is pinned down by a finite set, in the sense that $k\cdot x=k^{\prime}\cdot x$ for arrows agreeing on it, and the domain of each relational type at the evaluation object holds every intension pinned down by a finite set (in a symmetric model, every symmetric one).

references.note: Full action models, here the target, with a restricted domain at the entrance.

meets.infinitely-many-propositions: The propositions $(\varnothing,\{n\})$, true at $h_n$ alone, are pairwise distinct.
meets.codomain-intensions: An intension at $r$ whose value at every $h_n$ is the same is a pair $(A,b)$ with $b$ a constant profile, which the successor fixes; $s$ is full.

settings.construction: The arrows $s\to s$ are the natural numbers under addition, with the full action-model domains over one individual. Besides its identity, $r$ has arrows $h_n:r\to s$ for $n\in\mathbb N$, with $m\circ h_n=h_{m+n}$. An entity of relational type at $r$ is a pair $(A,b)$ of an arbitrary current extension $A$ and a target entity $b$ that is eventually stationary under the successor $S$ (some $S^{N+1}b=S^Nb$); its transport along $h_n$ is $S^nb$.

arguments.text: At every relational type. At $r$ the singletons of one current tuple (with target part $0$) and of one target coordinate $(n,\bar a)$ (with empty current extension; the successor carries it to the coordinate $n-1$ and then to $0$, so it is eventually stationary) are admitted, and every nonzero entity contains one. Their transports are $0$ or singletons, which are atoms of the full target domain and decide every target relation. So they are strong atoms; the full target is likewise strongly atomic, at every arrow.

At $t$: the target parts of the propositions at $r$ are the finite and cofinite sets of numbers, so every proposition at $r$ necessarily has the pure property $\Diamond\Box p\lor\Diamond\Box\neg p$; but the set of even numbers, at $s$, lacks it. At a relational type $\tau$: with $E_\tau$ an operation whose target part is the shift, every entity at $r$ necessarily has $\Diamond(E_\tau Y=Y)$, while an entity at $s$ alternating between even and odd coordinates never does.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, in a trawl for cheaply settled verdicts; checked by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: At every relational type. At $s$ the atoms are the singletons $\delta_{m,\bar a}$ of one tuple at one coordinate. A self-atom $Y$ at $s$ with least nonempty coordinate $m$ is instantiated at the arrow $m$, so its transport there is an atom, $\delta_{0,\bar a}$, and $Y=\delta_{m,\bar a}$. At $r$, a self-atom with nonempty current extension is an atom; with empty current extension, the same shift makes it $(\varnothing,\delta_{m,\bar a})$. These singletons are strong atoms at both objects.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, in a trawl for cheaply settled verdicts; checked by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: At $e$ there is one individual at both objects, so $I_e$ fails at every world. Every relational type is infinite at both objects, and by extensional fullness the numbers there are the distinct numerals with the standard sum and product, so an arithmetical sentence holds at a world iff it is true.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, in a trawl for cheaply settled verdicts; checked by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: BF at $t$ fails at $r$ (recorded) and holds at every world of $s$, a full action model whose arrows are cancellable and act onto the one individual. So the pure sentence $\neg\mathrm{BF}_t$ is true at $r$ and not possible at $h_0$.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, in a trawl for cheaply settled verdicts; checked by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: At $r$, a weakly rigid $(A,b)$ has $b_n=h_n\cdot A$ at every coordinate $n$: weak persistence gives $\supseteq$, and weak inextensibility, tested against the entity with current extension $A$ and target part $h_n\cdot A$ at coordinates below $N$ and everything from $N$ on, gives $\subseteq$ below every $N$. At $s$, full, a weakly rigid $Y$ has $Y_m=m\cdot Y_0$, by the test of the haecceity disjunction. Such exact images are rigid, and the transports $S^nb$ of the former are again of that form, so weak rigidity is rigidity at both objects.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, in a trawl for cheaply settled verdicts; checked by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: At type $tt$. Let $A$ be the propositions $(\varnothing,\{j\})$, $j\in\mathbb N$, with $(\varnothing,\varnothing)$; then $h_n\cdot A$ is the set of singletons with $\varnothing$, for every $n$, so $F:=(A,b)$ with $b$ that constant profile is rigid. At $h_0$, the property $P$ of being rigid and below $F$ holds of the exact image $X_D:=m\mapsto m\cdot D$, $D$ the singletons of even numbers, which alternates and so is no transport of an entity at $r$. The entity with $P$'s current extension and target part $h_0\cdot P$ at coordinate $0$ and everything after necessarily holds of $P$'s instances but omits $X_D$ at $h_0$, so $P$ is not weakly inextensible.

A rigid structure necessarily a real number structure would be one at $r$, on countably many propositions, with completeness the external notion since current extensions are arbitrary.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, at Cian Dorr's suggestion
arguments.text: For each object $U$ and type $\sigma$ fix a well-ordering $<_U$ of the domain $D^\sigma_U$, and let $W$ be the intension of type $\sigma\to\sigma\to t$ with $W(h):={<_{\operatorname{cod}h}}$. Its value depends only on the arrow's codomain, so by the condition it is in the domain, and at every world its extension well-orders that world's type-$\sigma$ domain. Given $F$ with $\Box\exists x\, .\,Fx$, put $G:=\lambda x\, .\,Fx\land\forall y\, .\,(Fy\to\neg Wyx)$, the $W$-least $F$. It is definable from $F$ and $W$, so in the domain; $G\le F$, and its extension at every arrow is the singleton of the least element of $F$'s. So Intensional Choice holds, and the same at every reachable object gives $\Box$Intensional Choice. Cian Dorr's observation that such models are qualitatively full, made precise.

conditions.text: At every object reachable from the evaluation point, the domain contains every intension whose value at an arrow depends only on the arrow's codomain.

arguments.text: At any reachable object $W$, let $U$ be a serial relation in the domain there. Using the axiom of choice, pick for each $x$ a $y$ with $(x,y)$ in the extension of $U$ at the identity, and let $S$ be the intension whose value at every arrow $W\to W$ is the graph of this choice and whose value at arrows with any other codomain is empty; it depends only on the codomain, so the condition puts it in the domain, and at the identity it is a functional subrelation of $U$. Likewise a set of representatives of an equivalence relation at $W$, made into such an intension, is a transversal. Since $W$ was any reachable object, both principles hold at every world.

conditions.text: At every object reachable from the evaluation point, the domain contains every intension whose value at an arrow depends only on the arrow's codomain.
conditions.reason: An intension at $r$ whose value at every $h_n$ is the same is a pair $(A,b)$ with $b$ a constant profile, which the successor fixes; $s$ is full.

models.notes: Separates □Strong Atomicity (hence □Strong Actuality) from the Barcan Formula at every relational type; the Barcan Formula at $e$ holds trivially, with one individual. The entrance's domains are the eventually stationary part of the full action model; closure under the terms of C needs only that the finitely many parameters of a term have a common stage after which the successor fixes them.
models.definition: Two objects, the target $s$ and the entrance $r$. The arrows $s\to s$ are the natural numbers under addition, with the full action-model domains over one individual. Besides its identity, $r$ has arrows $h_n:r\to s$ for $n\in\mathbb N$, with $m\circ h_n=h_{m+n}$. An entity of relational type at $r$ is a pair $(A,b)$ of an arbitrary current extension $A$ and a target entity $b$ that is eventually stationary under the successor $S$ (some $S^{N+1}b=S^Nb$); its transport along $h_n$ is $S^nb$. There is a single individual at both objects, and no arrow returns to $r$. Evaluation point: $1_r$. Interpretation of Σ: every constant of Σ is relational, and each denotes the top element of its type.

models.definition:
The stitching construction of Barton and Goodsell (Continuum Contingency, §8). Work in a generic extension $V[G]$ of a ground model $V$ of ZFC by a weakly homogeneous, hence $V$-decisive, forcing $P$ (§7.1): a set of ordinals definable in $V[G]$ from parameters in $V$ lies in $V$.

The forcing $P$ is chosen by cases on the continuum hypothesis in $V$. If $V\models\mathrm{CH}$, $P:=\operatorname{Add}(\omega,\omega_2)$, which adds $\aleph_2$ Cohen reals, so that $V[G]\models\neg\mathrm{CH}$. Otherwise $P:=\operatorname{Col}(\omega_1,2^{\aleph_0})\times \operatorname{Add}(\omega,1)$: the collapse, with countable conditions, adds no reals and makes the continuum of $V$ have size $\aleph_1$, and the Cohen real then adds a real and preserves CH, so that $V[G]\models\mathrm{CH}$. Both forcings are weakly homogeneous (a product of weakly homogeneous forcings is weakly homogeneous), hence $V$-decisive.

Ground model, fixed for this record: $V$ is an arbitrary model of ZFC.

Let $C_0$ be the canonical extensional model of $V[G]$ (§7.2.5): one object with its identity arrow, the natural numbers as individuals, two propositions, and at each relational type every function of $V[G]$ between the lower domains, so that its relations of a type are, up to extension, all the subsets in $V[G]$ of the tuples of that type. Call an element of $C_0$ definable when it is definable in $V[G]$ from parameters in $V$. The root $\hat M$ is built in $V$ (§8.3, Definition 1, with the group $W$ trivial): its individuals are the natural numbers; its propositions are the pairs $\langle a,b\rangle$ of a truth value $a$ at the root and a truth value $b$ at $C_0$; and an element of a relational type at the root is a pair of a function in $V$ on the root domains, which gives its extension at the root, and a definable element of $C_0$ of the same type, which gives its extension at $C_0$, the two compatible in that the $C_0$-coordinate of the function's value at an argument is the definable element applied to the argument's $C_0$-component. Every such pair is in the domain, so a root relation may be any set in $V$ of root tuples together with any definable relation of $C_0$. The action model $M$ (§8.4) has the two objects $\hat M$ and $C_0$, their identities, and one arrow $h\colon\hat M\to C_0$, the identity on the individuals, which sends every other element to its $C_0$-component. Truth at the root is the first coordinate, so at the root $\Box p$ holds iff $p$ is true at both objects, and $C_0$ sees only itself. The source works in the full simple type hierarchy; the restriction of its model to the map's relational types is an action model of the same kind. Evaluation point: $\hat M$, at its identity arrow.

Interpretation of Σ, fixed for these records: every constant of Σ is relational, and each denotes the top element of its type.

arguments.text: At type $et$, for the analytical sentence $\Phi$ saying that every real is constructible: membership of a real in $L$ is $\Sigma^1_2$ (Shoenfield), so $\Phi$ is $\Pi^1_3$, a first-order analytical sentence in any real number structure, whose natural numbers code sets of naturals by its reals. Real number structures exist at type $et$ at both objects (see the argument for the failure of Analytic Necessitism). At $C_0$, the full extensional model of $L[G]$, every real number structure has the reals of $L[G]$, among them a real not in $L$, and Shoenfield absoluteness makes the $\Sigma^1_2$ definition of constructibility mean the same in $L[G]$; so $\Phi$ fails in every real number structure there. At the root every set in $L$ of root tuples is the root extension of a root relation, whatever its $C_0$-extension, so the root read at the root is the full hierarchy of $L$ over its domains, and $\Phi$ holds in every real number structure there, as it does in $L$. The root sees both objects, so neither disjunct of the instance holds there.

Neil Barton and Zachary Goodsell, Continuum Contingency, draft of 14 October 2026, §7.1 and §8, Definition 1.

references.note: The stitching construction, here applied over a coalesced sum and with invariantly named rather than ground-definable elements.

models.definition: An action model in a Cohen extension $V[G]$ of a model $V$ of ZFC, with Cohen real $c$. Four objects: $A$, the full extensional one-world hierarchy over $\mathbb N$ built in $V$; $B$, the same built in $V[G]$; $s$, their coalesced sum with the fullest domains, with individuals $\mathbb N\times\mathbb N$, arrows $a\colon s\to A$ and $b\colon s\to B$ acting as the two projections, and $D_{s,\bar\sigma t}=\mathcal P^{V[G]}(D_{s,\bar\sigma})\times D_{A,\bar\sigma t}\times D_{B,\bar\sigma t}$; and the root $r$, with the individuals of $s$ and an arrow $h\colon r\to s$ that is the identity on them. The only other arrows are the identities and the composites $ah$ and $bh$, and every set of arrows out of an object is a proposition. A root entity of type $\bar\sigma t$ is a pair of a set in $V$ of root tuples, its extension at $r$, and a $\mathbb P$-name for an element of $D_{s,\bar\sigma t}$, its transport along $h$, that $1$ forces to be fixed by every finite bit-flip of the Cohen real, taken up to equality forced by $1$; every such pair is admitted. Every constant of Σ is relational and denotes the top element of its type. Evaluation point: $r$.

meets.sigma-top: This is the interpretation the definition fixes.

arguments.text: At every relational type, with any argument types. A root relation $(E,[u])$ is coextensive with $Y_E:=(E,[R_E])$, where $R_E:=(hE,a(hE),b(hE))$ consists of the images of the tuples of $E$. $a(hE)$ is a ground set, since the $A$-projection of an invariantly named entity is forced into a ground set and so is a value computed in $V$; and $R_E$ has an invariant name. $Y_E$ is an exact-image relation, persistent and inextensible at $r$ and at $s$, since every member of its extensions there and at $A$ and $B$ is the image of a member of $E$; so it is rigid.

At every object every set of arrows out of it is a proposition, so its propositions form a finite power set. The singletons are possible and decide every proposition, and their transports are singletons or $\bot$ (or $\top$ at $A$ and $B$), so they are strong atoms and every nonzero proposition contains one. Transport of propositions along each arrow is onto, so BF holds at type $t$ everywhere; and every family of propositions has a meet.

At $r$, a serial root relation has a serial extension in $V$, and choice in $V$ gives a functional subrelation of it, admitted with transport $\bot$. At $s$, choice in $V[G]$ on the fullest domains does the same, and $A$ and $B$ are full in $V$ and $V[G]$.

revisions.note: Added a type clarification to the write-up: the family of haecceities has type (et)t, while its members and hypothetical join have type et. The Boolean Completeness witness is at et, as this argument already states; the original proof text and all verdicts are preserved.

arguments.text: At $s$, at type $et$. If $Y=(c\times\{0\},C,C^{\prime})$ were weakly rigid, weak persistence would give $c\subseteq C$, and for $n\notin c$ weak inextensibility applied to $Z_n:=(\mathbb N\times\mathbb N,\mathbb N\setminus\{n\},\mathbb N)$, necessary of every $(k,0)$ with $k\in c$, would give $C\subseteq\mathbb N\setminus\{n\}$; so $C=c$, which is not in $V$. Likewise a least upper bound $J$ of the haecceities of the $(k,0)$, $k\in c$, would have $J_A=c$. So Weak Rigid Comprehension and Boolean Completeness fail at $s$, which $r$ sees.

At type $et$. Every root entity of type $et$ has, as transport, an invariantly named element of $D_{s,et}$, whose three components are ground sets. So $Y_{D_{r,et}}$, the exact-image relation of all of them, holds necessarily of every root entity of type $et$, but at $s$ it does not hold of $(c\times\{0\},\varnothing,\varnothing)$. BF fails at $et$; at type $e$ it holds, $h$ being the identity on individuals and $a,b$ onto.

At type $(et)t$. The root entity with empty root extension whose transport is the set of $s$-entities of type $et$ that are not transports of root entities, with empty terminal components, is nonzero. A nonzero entity below it with a single instance at $s$ would have that instance invariantly named, hence a transport of a root entity. So every nonzero entity below it has two instances there, which a ground coordinate test separates.
$\{1_r\}$ and $\bot$ are distinct propositions at $r$, and both have transport $\bot$ along $h$.

models.notes: With strong-atomicity-t-rigid-comprehension-and-barcan-relational-imply-necessary-rigid-comprehension, this shows that BF at relational types cannot be weakened to □BF (type $t$), even with □Strong Atomicity (type $t$), □Relational Choice, □Actuality and BF at type $e$. The invariantly named class of the construction is strictly larger than Barton and Goodsell's ground-definable one (the set of finite modifications of the Cohen real is invariantly named but not ground-definable); the arguments work for either. Claude Fable 5.1's audit confirmed every verdict and supplied the absoluteness argument for closure of $A$'s domains in $V[G]$.

models.notes:
Verdicts the engine derives, checked directly. □Well-Ordering: a well-ordering in $V$ of a root domain is the root extension of a root relation with any definable $C_0$-extension, the well-ordering conditions being unboxed, and at $C_0$ the full domain contains a well-ordering of each type. Functionality fails at type $(et)t$: the property of properties of individuals in the argument for the failure of BF and the one with $C_0$-extension $\mathcal P(\mathbb N)^{V[G]}$ take the same value, the necessary proposition, at every root property of individuals and differ at $C_0$ on the Cohen real. ND fails at type $t$: the proposition true at the root alone and the one true nowhere are distinct at the root and both become the false proposition at $C_0$; and the pure sentence that ND fails at type $t$ is true at the root and false at $C_0$, so No Pure Contingency fails. Atomicity fails at type $(et)t$, as atomicity-and-rigid-comprehension-imply-rigid-power requires: the root property $Z$ of properties of individuals with empty root extension and $C_0$-extension the reals of $V[G]$ not in $V$ is not bottom, and a root property $A$ below it has a definable $C_0$-extension $g$ of new reals; were $A$ an atom with $c\in g$, then for each $n$ the root property with $C_0$-extension $\{x\in g : x(n)=c(n)\}$, definable from $g$ and the bit $c(n)$, would lie below $A$ and not be bottom, hence be $A$, so that $g=\{c\}$ and $c$ would be definable from parameters in $V$, hence in $V$. At type $et$, by contrast, every nonbottom property has an atom below it, since a nonempty definable set of natural numbers has a definable singleton below it.

The source's Theorem 20 (first- and second-order continuum contingency with □Rigid Comprehension and □Relational Choice, though not the contingency of CH) and Theorem 21 (the same with □Atomicity at type $t$), in the simplest instance of the construction. In the source's terms the reals, the rigid properties of natural numbers, are persistent but not inextensible: new reals appear at $C_0$. The construction presupposes a generic filter, so, as always with forcing, what it establishes is consistency relative to ZFC; a countable transitive ground model, or Boolean-valued names, turns it into a construction in ZFC. The source varies the construction: any $V$-decisive forcing in place of Cohen forcing (Theorem 20 varies the continuum hypothesis either way), a finite group $W$ of automorphisms of the root (Theorem 21), the canonical coin-toss model in place of the extensional one with $W$ the reals of $V$ (Theorem 22, which gives Recombination, not a principle of the map, and refutes Atomicity at type $t$, Corollary 23, answering a conjecture of Christopher Sun; on the map □Rigid Comprehension without Atomicity at type $t$ is already witnessed by symmetric-collapse-pair), and iterated stitching (§10). This record is the simplest instance; a single Cohen real leaves CH as it was, so Non-contingency of CH holds here, and the instance of Theorem 20 that changes CH is stitched-ch-reversing. It is the first model on the map with Atomicity at type $t$ and □Rigid Comprehension in which Rigid Power fails; it separates □Strong Atomicity (type $t$) with □Rigid Comprehension from BF at the relational types and from Atomicity at the higher types; and it shows that the Atomicity in atomicity-and-rigid-comprehension-imply-rigid-power cannot be weakened to type $t$.

arguments.text: At type $et$, for the analytical sentence $\Phi$ saying that every real is constructible: membership of a real in $L$ is $\Sigma^1_2$ (Shoenfield), so $\Phi$ is $\Pi^1_3$, a first-order analytical sentence in any real number structure, whose natural numbers code sets of naturals by its reals. Real number structures exist at type $et$ at both objects (see the argument for the failure of Analytic Necessitism). At $C_0$, the full extensional model of $L[G]$, every real number structure has the reals of $L[G]$, among them a real not in $L$, and Shoenfield absoluteness makes the $\Sigma^1_2$ definition of constructibility mean the same in $L[G]$; so $\Phi$ fails in every real number structure there. At the root every set in $L$ of root tuples is the root extension of a root relation, whatever its $C_0$-extension, so the root read at the root is the full hierarchy of $L$ over its domains, and $\Phi$ holds in every real number structure there, as it does in $L$. The root sees both objects, so neither disjunct of the instance holds there.

models.notes:
Verdicts the engine derives, checked directly. □Well-Ordering: a well-ordering in $V$ of a root domain is the root extension of a root relation with any definable $C_0$-extension, the well-ordering conditions being unboxed, and at $C_0$ the full domain contains a well-ordering of each type. Functionality fails at type $(et)t$: the property of properties of individuals in the argument for the failure of BF and the one with $C_0$-extension $\mathcal P(\mathbb N)^{V[G]}$ take the same value, the necessary proposition, at every root property of individuals and differ at $C_0$ on the Cohen real. ND fails at type $t$: the proposition true at the root alone and the one true nowhere are distinct at the root and both become the false proposition at $C_0$; and the pure sentence that ND fails at type $t$ is true at the root and false at $C_0$, so No Pure Contingency fails. Atomicity fails at type $(et)t$, as atomicity-and-rigid-comprehension-imply-rigid-power requires: the root property $Z$ of properties of individuals with empty root extension and $C_0$-extension the reals of $V[G]$ not in $V$ is not bottom, and a root property $A$ below it has a definable $C_0$-extension $g$ of new reals; were $A$ an atom with $c\in g$, then for each $n$ the root property with $C_0$-extension $\{x\in g : x(n)=c(n)\}$, definable from $g$ and the bit $c(n)$, would lie below $A$ and not be bottom, hence be $A$, so that $g=\{c\}$ and $c$ would be definable from parameters in $V$, hence in $V$. At type $et$, by contrast, every nonbottom property has an atom below it, since a nonempty definable set of natural numbers has a definable singleton below it.

The source's Theorem 20 (first- and second-order continuum contingency with □Rigid Comprehension and □Relational Choice, though not the contingency of CH) and Theorem 21 (the same with □Atomicity at type $t$), in the simplest instance of the construction. In the source's terms the reals, the rigid properties of natural numbers, are persistent but not inextensible: new reals appear at $C_0$. The construction presupposes a generic filter, so, as always with forcing, what it establishes is consistency relative to ZFC; a countable transitive ground model, or Boolean-valued names, turns it into a construction in ZFC. The source varies the construction: any $V$-decisive forcing in place of Cohen forcing (Theorem 20 varies the continuum hypothesis either way), a finite group $W$ of automorphisms of the root (Theorem 21), the canonical coin-toss model in place of the extensional one with $W$ the reals of $V$ (Theorem 22, which gives Recombination, not a principle of the map, and refutes Atomicity at type $t$, Corollary 23, answering a conjecture of Christopher Sun; on the map □Rigid Comprehension without Atomicity at type $t$ is already witnessed by symmetric-collapse-pair), and iterated stitching (§10). This record is the simplest instance; a single Cohen real leaves CH as it was, so Non-contingency of CH holds here, and the instance of Theorem 20 that changes CH is stitched-ch-reversing. It is the first model on the map with Atomicity at type $t$ and □Rigid Comprehension in which Rigid Power fails; it separates □Strong Atomicity (type $t$) with □Rigid Comprehension from BF at the relational types and from Atomicity at the higher types; and it shows that the Atomicity in atomicity-and-rigid-comprehension-imply-rigid-power cannot be weakened to type $t$.
models.definition:
The stitching construction of Barton and Goodsell (Continuum Contingency, §8). Work in a generic extension $V[G]$ of a ground model $V$ of ZFC by a weakly homogeneous, hence $V$-decisive, forcing $P$ (§7.1): a set of ordinals definable in $V[G]$ from parameters in $V$ lies in $V$.

Here $P$ is Cohen forcing, which adds one real.

Ground model, fixed for this record: $V$ is Gödel's constructible universe, so that $V[G]=L[G]$; that is, the construction is carried out over $L$, which ZFC proves to be a model of ZFC + $V=L$, so this adds nothing to what the construction presupposes. In particular $V\models\mathrm{CH}$.

Let $C_0$ be the canonical extensional model of $V[G]$ (§7.2.5): one object with its identity arrow, the natural numbers as individuals, two propositions, and at each relational type every function of $V[G]$ between the lower domains, so that its relations of a type are, up to extension, all the subsets in $V[G]$ of the tuples of that type. Call an element of $C_0$ definable when it is definable in $V[G]$ from parameters in $V$. The root $\hat M$ is built in $V$ (§8.3, Definition 1, with the group $W$ trivial): its individuals are the natural numbers; its propositions are the pairs $\langle a,b\rangle$ of a truth value $a$ at the root and a truth value $b$ at $C_0$; and an element of a relational type at the root is a pair of a function in $V$ on the root domains, which gives its extension at the root, and a definable element of $C_0$ of the same type, which gives its extension at $C_0$, the two compatible in that the $C_0$-coordinate of the function's value at an argument is the definable element applied to the argument's $C_0$-component. Every such pair is in the domain, so a root relation may be any set in $V$ of root tuples together with any definable relation of $C_0$. The action model $M$ (§8.4) has the two objects $\hat M$ and $C_0$, their identities, and one arrow $h\colon\hat M\to C_0$, the identity on the individuals, which sends every other element to its $C_0$-component. Truth at the root is the first coordinate, so at the root $\Box p$ holds iff $p$ is true at both objects, and $C_0$ sees only itself. The source works in the full simple type hierarchy; the restriction of its model to the map's relational types is an action model of the same kind. Evaluation point: $\hat M$, at its identity arrow.

Interpretation of Σ, fixed for these records: every constant of Σ is relational, and each denotes the top element of its type.

models.name: Supported model over the ultrafilters of a complete homogeneous algebra, with a free root

references.locator: §3.5, pp. 58–61; Appendix E, Definition E.2, pp. 80–83
references.note: Action models, and the unrestricted root of the coalesced sums.

settings.component: Here $B$ is the regular open algebra of Cantor space, complete, atomless and homogeneous (every nonzero interval is isomorphic to $B$). The worlds $W$ are the ultrafilters of $B$, $D$ is a single individual, $G=\operatorname{Aut}(B)$ acting on the ultrafilters, and the support points are the elements of $B$. A relation is admitted only if, for each tuple $\bar x$, the set of worlds at which it holds of $\bar x$ is $\hat b:=\{U:b\in U\}$ for some $b\in B$; so the component's propositions are the sets $\hat b$, a copy of $B$.

meets.one-individual: There is a single individual.
meets.actual-world-isolated: The root proposition $(1,\varnothing)$, true at $r$ alone, is in the domain and entails every truth at $r$ (argument actuality), and no world of the component sees $r$.

arguments.by: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), prompted by Daniel Kodsi; checked and recorded by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: For finite $P\subseteq B$, the elements of $B$ fixed by the automorphisms fixing $P$ pointwise are the joins of the cells of $\langle P\rangle$, and the join of a set invariant under those automorphisms is attained by at most two members per cell, by homogeneity (write-up, Lemmas 1–2). So at a world of the component a family of propositions in the domain, being supported, has as union a finite union, which is a proposition and its least upper bound. At $r$ the least upper bound of root propositions $(\varepsilon_i,\hat b_i)$ is $(\bigvee\varepsilon_i,\widehat{\bigvee b_i})$, the join taken in the complete algebra $B$.

arguments.by: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), prompted by Daniel Kodsi; checked and recorded by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: At every type. In the component the same entities are available at every world, transport being trivial. At $r$, every component entity is the transport of a root entity, the one with empty current extension; so what holds necessarily of every root entity holds at every world of every entity there.

arguments.by: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), prompted by Daniel Kodsi; checked and recorded by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: For a serial $U$ at $r$, choose in the metatheory a functional subrelation of its current extension, and pair it with the empty component entity: the result is admitted, functional, and below $U$ at $r$.

arguments.by: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), prompted by Daniel Kodsi; checked and recorded by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: At $r$ the proposition $(1,\varnothing)$, true at $r$ alone, is true and below every truth. No atom lies below a nonzero $(0,\hat b)$, since $B$ is atomless.

arguments.by: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), prompted by Daniel Kodsi; checked and recorded by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: At a world $U$ of the component, an actual-world proposition would be some $\hat b$ with $b\in U$ and $\hat b\subseteq\hat c$ for every $c\in U$, so $b$ would be an atom of $B$. $B$ is atomless, so Actuality fails at every world of the component, which $r$ sees.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, in a trawl for cheaply settled verdicts; checked by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: At $r$ every set of tuples of root entities is the current extension of a root entity, its pair with any component entity, and the propositions at $r$, the pairs $(\varepsilon,\hat b)$, are infinitely many and genuinely distinct. So the argument infinitely-many-propositions applies at $r$, where all the quantifiers involved are evaluated: the root property of cardinalities whose current extension is the cardinalities holding at $r$ only of properties with finite current extension holds of $\mathbf 0_t$ and is closed under $\operatorname{Suc}_t$, the current extension of $\lambda u\,.\,Xu\land u\ne y$ being that of $X$ less $y$. So every finite cardinality holds at $r$ only of properties with finite current extension, and none holds of $\lambda u^t\,.\,\top$.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, in a trawl for cheaply settled verdicts; checked by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: At type $tt$, relative to $t$. An element $y\notin\langle Q\rangle$ has continuum many images under $H_Q$: it meets some cell $e$ of $\langle Q\rangle$ with $0<y\wedge e<e$, and for each $0<z<e$ homogeneity gives isomorphisms $[0,y\wedge e]\cong[0,z]$ and $[0,e-y]\cong[0,e-z]$, which with the identity off $e$ make a member of $H_Q$ carrying $y$ to $(y-e)\vee z$. So a countably infinite $S\subseteq B$ is invariant under no $H_Q$. For $b\in B$ let $F_b$ be the component property true everywhere of $\hat b$ and of nothing else, supported by $\{b\}$. At $r$ let $X$ have as current extension the root properties $(\varnothing,F_b)$, $b\in S$; it is countable relative to $t$, a root relation pairing them injectively with the numerals $\operatorname{Suc}^n_t\mathbf 0_t$, which differ at $r$ in their current extensions. Suppose $(R,L)$ were a least upper bound of $X$, with $L$ supported by $P$. Entailment between root entities is inclusion at $r$ together with entailment between component parts, so $L$ is true everywhere of $\hat b$ for $b\in S$, and so, by invariance, of $\hat x$ for every $x$ in the set $S_P$ of $H_P$-images of members of $S$; and some $x\in S_P\setminus S$. The component property true everywhere of $\hat z$ for $z\in S_{P\cup\{x\}}$, and nowhere else, is admitted, and paired with $\varnothing$ it is an upper bound of $X$. But $x\notin S_{P\cup\{x\}}$, since $H_{P\cup\{x\}}$ fixes $x$, so $(R,L)$ is not below it.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, in a trawl for cheaply settled verdicts; checked by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: At every type, at $r$ and at every world of the component. In the component, let $F$ be supported by $P$ and instantiated at every world, with fibre $\hat c_x$ at $x$. The $c_x$ form an $H_P$-invariant set with join $1$, so by finite attainment (write-up, Lemma 2) $1=c_{x_1}\vee\dots\vee c_{x_k}$ for some $x_1,\dots,x_k$. Let $G$ hold of $x_i$ exactly at the worlds in $\hat e_i$, where $e_i:=c_{x_i}-\bigvee_{j<i}c_{x_j}$, and of nothing else. Its fibres are finite joins of the $e_i$, and it is supported by $P$ together with finite supports of the $x_i$, whose automorphisms fix each $x_i$ and so each $c_{x_i}$; so $G$ is admitted, $G\le F$, and at each world exactly one $x_i$ has $G$, the $e_i$ partitioning $1$. At $r$, a root $F=(R,a)$ with $\Box\exists x\,Fx$ has a nonempty current extension and a component part $a$ as above; pair a singleton $\{x_0\}\subseteq R$ with the $G$ built for $a$. Only finitely many choices are made.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, in a trawl for cheaply settled verdicts; checked by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: At every type. The component has no atoms: if $X$ has a nonempty fibre $\hat b$ at a tuple, meeting it pointwise with $\hat d$, where $0<d\wedge b<b$, gives an admitted $Y$ with $\bot<Y<X$. So at a world of the component nothing is a self-atom, a possible entity being instantiated somewhere and an atom nowhere. At $r$ a self-atom $(R,a)$ has $a=\bot$, since wherever it is instantiated it is an atom and the component has none; being possible it has $R\ne\varnothing$, and $(R,\bot)$ is an atom at $r$, that is, $R$ is a singleton. Such a $(R,\bot)$ is a strong atom: at $r$ it entails each root entity or its negation, according as the tuple in $R$ is in the current extension, and at a world of the component its transport is bottom. So self-atoms are atoms, and strong atoms, at $r$ and at every world it sees.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, in a trawl for cheaply settled verdicts; checked by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: At $r$, by Actuality: the actual-world proposition entails each truth $q$, which entails $\Diamond q$. At a world of the component a true $\hat b$ has $b\ne0$, and every world of the component sees every other, so $\Diamond\hat b$ is true throughout the component, which is all that world sees; so $\top$ entails it, and witnesses Vicinity.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, in a trawl for cheaply settled verdicts; checked by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: Actuality is a closed pure sentence, true at $r$ and false at every world of the component (arguments actuality and no-actuality-in-component). Those worlds see only worlds of the component, so $\Diamond$Actuality is false at each of them, and $\Box\Diamond$Actuality is false at $r$.

arguments.text: Write $\chi_T$ for the component relation true everywhere of the tuples in $T$ and nowhere else; it is admitted just when $T$ is invariant under some $H_Q$. For any $T$ and finite $Q$, the set $T_Q$ of $H_Q$-images of members of $T$ is so invariant, and a tuple fixed by $H_Q$ lies in $T_Q$ only if it lies in $T$. (a) In the component, a relation $Y$ weakly rigid at a world $U$ has every fibre empty or $W$: weak persistence makes a fibre containing $U$ all of $W$; and if $T$ is the set of tuples $Y$ holds of at $U$, weak inextensibility applied to $\chi_{T_Q}$, for $Q$ a support of a tuple outside $T$, empties the fibre there. Such relations are rigid. (b) At $r$, with $\operatorname{tr}R$ the transports of the members of $R$, a root $(R,a)$ is weakly rigid iff $a=\chi_{\operatorname{tr}R}$: weak persistence gives $a$ the fibre $W$ on $\operatorname{tr}R$, and weak inextensibility applied to $(R,\chi_{(\operatorname{tr}R)_Q})$ empties it elsewhere; conversely, if every $\bar x\in R$ is necessarily in $(S,s)$, then $R\subseteq S$ and $s$ has fibre $W$ on $\operatorname{tr}R$, so $(R,a)\le(S,s)$. By (a) such an $(R,a)$ is rigid. Now let $F=(R,\chi_T)$, $T=\operatorname{tr}R$, and $\Phi:=\lambda X\,.\,\operatorname{WeaklyRigid}(X)\land X\le F$. By (b) the current extension of $\Phi$ is the $(R',\chi_{\operatorname{tr}R'})$ with $R'\subseteq R$ and $\operatorname{tr}R'$ invariant under some $H_Q$; by (a), $\le$ being boxed, its component part is $\chi$ of the set of $\chi_{T'}$ with $T'\subseteq T$ invariant under some $H_Q$. These are exactly the transports of the former, taking for $R'$ the members of $R$ with transports in $T'$. So $\Phi$ is weakly rigid, by (b).

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, in a trawl for cheaply settled verdicts; checked by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: At every type $\sigma$. The numerals $\operatorname{Suc}^n_\sigma\mathbf 0_\sigma$ denote, in the component, entities fixed by every automorphism, so the relation $\chi_N$ true everywhere of them and of nothing else is admitted; taken as $W$ in the definition of $\operatorname{FiniteCardinality}_\sigma$ it shows that at each world of the component the numbers at $\sigma$ are exactly the numerals. At $r$ the root entity whose current extension is the root numerals, paired with $\chi_N$, does the same. So $\mathbb N_\sigma$ denotes at $r$ the pair of the set of root numerals and $\chi_N$, the transports of the root numerals being the component numerals, and it is rigid by (b) of the argument weakly-rigid-power. Given $\Box I^*_\sigma$, distinct numbers at $r$ are numerals $\operatorname{Suc}^i_\sigma\mathbf 0_\sigma$ and $\operatorname{Suc}^j_\sigma\mathbf 0_\sigma$ with $i\ne j$, and their transports are distinct at every world of the component by $I^*_\sigma$ there.

arguments.text: At $\sigma=e$ there is one individual, so $\operatorname{Suc}^2_e\mathbf 0_e$ and $\operatorname{Suc}^3_e\mathbf 0_e$ are the same necessarily empty property, $I^*_e$ fails at every world and $I_e$ fails throughout. At a relational type $\sigma$ there are infinitely many entities at $r$ and at each world of the component, and every finite set of them is the extension there of a property in the domain, so the numerals are distinct and $I^*_\sigma$ holds everywhere. As in the argument arithmetic-necessitism, at $r$ and at each world the numbers at $\sigma$ are exactly the numerals; and $\operatorname{Sum}_\sigma$ and $\operatorname{Prod}_\sigma$ hold exactly of the true sums and products, taking for $R$ the relation, true everywhere or with that current extension, of the pairs of numerals $(\mathbf i,\mathbf{i+m})$, resp. $(\mathbf i,\mathbf{i\cdot m})$, which automorphisms fix. So wherever $I_\sigma$ holds an arithmetical sentence at $\sigma$ has its standard truth value.

models.definition: Fix a set $W$ of worlds, a set $D$ of individuals, a group $G$ acting on $W$ and on $D$, and a set $X$ of support points on which $G$ acts. Here $B$ is the regular open algebra of Cantor space, complete, atomless and homogeneous (every nonzero interval is isomorphic to $B$). The worlds $W$ are the ultrafilters of $B$, $D$ is a single individual, $G=\operatorname{Aut}(B)$ acting on the ultrafilters, and the support points are the elements of $B$. A relation is admitted only if, for each tuple $\bar x$, the set of worlds at which it holds of $\bar x$ is $\hat b:=\{U:b\in U\}$ for some $b\in B$; so the component's propositions are the sets $\hat b$, a copy of $B$. The component is the action model on the category with object set $W$ and exactly one arrow between any two objects, every arrow acting on $D$ as the identity. Transport between its objects is then trivial, so an entity of relational type $\bar\sigma t$ there is a relation $F\subseteq D_{\bar\sigma}\times W$, giving its extension at each world, and the same entities are available at every world. $G$ acts on these relations by $g\cdot F:=\{(g\bar x,gw):(\bar x,w)\in F\}$, its action on the argument entities being defined in the same way by recursion on their types. $F$ is supported by a finite $P\subseteq X$ if $g\cdot F=F$ for every $g$ fixing $P$ pointwise. The component's domains hold the supported relations satisfying the member's further restriction, if any. Identity is genuine identity, transports being bijective. A root object $r$ is added, with one arrow to each world of the component and none back. A root entity of relational type is a pair $(R,a)$ of an arbitrary set $R$ of tuples of root entities, its extension at $r$, and a component entity $a$, its transport along every arrow out of $r$; the root's individuals are those of $D$, each arrow acting on them as the identity. So the propositions at $r$ are the pairs of a truth value at $r$ and a component proposition. The evaluation point is $r$. Every constant of Σ is relational and denotes the top element of its type.

So a $\Sigma$-sentence is possible iff it is true under some interpretation, which gives Logical Necessity.

The finite cardinalities are the standard numerals, and each holds exactly of the properties with that many actual instances. The universal property of individuals has $\kappa^+$ of them, so it has no finite cardinality. The axiom is closed and pure, so it holds necessarily.

None is rigid: two distinct instances $a,b$ of its carrier are identified at the arrow $(\varepsilon,s)$ for a surjection $s$ with $s(a)=s(b)$, so they are not necessarily distinct. arguments.text: At the types $(e\to t)$ and $e$. Let $U:=\lambda Xy\, .\,Xy\lor\neg\exists z\, .\,Xz$, a closed term, hence in the domain, and serial. A functional subrelation $S$ of $U$ would lie in the domain at the evaluation object, so it is symmetric and pinned down by a finite set $N$. Two facts about such an $S$ (Dorr, draft, Lemma 19(iv)): every $g\in G$ fixing $N$ pointwise satisfies $g^{[\sigma]}S=S$, and symmetry gives $\langle gA,gy,g\rangle\in S$ whenever $\langle A,y,1\rangle\in S$; together, $\langle gA,gy,1\rangle\in S$. Now let $A$ be the property the condition gives for $N$. Its extension is nonempty, so $S$ relates $A$ at the identity to some $y$ in its extension. The condition gives a member $g$ of the symmetry group that fixes $N$ pointwise, fixes $A$ and moves $y$ to some $gy\ne y$, so $S$ relates $A$ to $gy$ as well, and $S$ is not functional at the identity arrow. The well-ordering of the individuals that Cian Dorr had in mind is refuted by the same two facts, but the direct route needs no derivation of a well-ordering from Relational Choice in C.

conditions.reason: $M=\emptyset$, and for $N$ the property of not belonging to $N$: the transposition of $y$ with another individual outside $N$ is a permutation, so lies in the symmetry group.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: At type $e$. Let $F$ and $a$ be as the condition gives them, and suppose $G\le F$ is necessarily uniquely instantiated. $G$ is in the domain, so it is symmetric and pinned down by a finite set, which we may take to contain $a$; call it $N$. Let $h$ be the arrow the condition gives for $N$. Then $G_h=\{y\}$ for some $y$ in $F_h$. If $\sigma$ in the symmetry group fixes $p$, then $\sigma\circ h$ agrees with $h$ on $N$, so $G_{\sigma\circ h}=G_h$ by pinning, while symmetry gives $G_{\sigma\circ h}=\{\sigma y\}$. So no symmetry fixing $p$ moves $y$, and by the condition $y=p$. Each model's witness takes $F$ with $p$ outside its extension at $h$, a contradiction. $\Box$Intensional Choice fails with it, by T.

models.definition:
A symmetric ideally-full intensional action model over one object, the set of natural numbers. Its arrows are all the surjections of that set, and its symmetry group is all the permutations. A relational domain holds exactly the intensions that are symmetric, meaning indifferent to relabelling the individuals of a world, and pinned down by some finite set. The evaluation point is the identity arrow.

Individuals, fixed for this record: the individuals at each object are the base the construction describes, and the arrows act on them as on the base.

Interpretation of Σ, fixed for this record: every constant of Σ is relational, and each denotes the top element of its type.

met.surjective-arrows: The arrows are all the surjections of $\mathbb N$.
met.homogeneous-individuals: Every permutation of $\mathbb N$ is in the symmetry group, and relabelling by it is an automorphism of the model, carrying each individual to its image.
met.hull-conditions: With $M_0=\emptyset$ (the draft's argument for this model): every finite set is amalgamable, since an arrow is prescribed only on a finite set and extends freely to a surjection, and points can always be moved off a given finite set by a permutation fixing another.
met.finite-pinning: Every object carries the ideal of finite sets.
met.retractable-means-actual-pattern: With $N^\prime=N$: if $x\circ u$ is the identity on $N$ then $u$ is injective on $N$, so it agrees on $N$ with a permutation.
met.infinitely-many-orbits-everywhere: For a finite set $N$ of individuals, the property of being one of them, $h\mapsto h(N)$, is symmetric and pinned down by $N$; symmetries preserve the size of $N$, so these properties lie in infinitely many orbits at the one object.

The $Y_A$ are continuum many and pairwise distinct at $v$. For a set $T$ of $k$-tuples of them, the intension whose value at an arrow $h$ is the set of transports along $h$ of the tuples in $T$ depends only on $h$'s codomain, is symmetric, each such transport being fixed by the target's symmetries, and is pinned down by $\emptyset$; its extension at $v$ is $T$.

settings.construction: A symmetric ideally-full model with a prefix object $A$, whose base is the countable atomless Boolean algebra $B$, and tail objects $V_m$ ($m\ge0$) and $V_\infty$, whose bases are countable atomless Boolean algebras with colour subalgebras: at $V_m$, free on $c_0,\dots,c_{m-1},d_0,d_1,\dots$, the colours are $C_m:=\langle c_0,\dots,c_{m-1}\rangle$; at $V_\infty$, free on $c_0,c_1,\dots,d_0,d_1,\dots$, they are $C_\infty:=\langle c_0,c_1,\dots\rangle$. The arrows $A\to A$ are the automorphisms of $B$; the arrows from $A$ to a tail object are the surjective homomorphisms with dense kernel (every nonzero element has a nonzero element of the kernel below it); the arrows between tail objects are the surjective homomorphisms $f$ with $f[C_V]\subseteq C_W$; no arrows go from the tail to $A$. arguments.text: At every relational type. If a set $D$ of tuples is invariant under the automorphisms fixing a finite subalgebra $P$ pointwise, then $h\mapsto h[D]$ is in the domain, pinned down by $P$, and rigid, as an exact-image relation. For arrows $h,h^{\prime}$ into the tail that agree on $P$, and $a\in D$ pinned down by $M\supseteq P$, an automorphism $u$ fixing $P$ with $hu=h^{\prime}$ on $M$ exists because $\ker h$ is dense: within each atom of $P$, the atoms of $M$ are matched with a partition having the right images, nonzero pieces with zero image being carved out of a kernel element. So $h^{\prime}\cdot a=h\cdot(u\cdot a)$. The extension of a relation pinned down by $P$ is such a $D$.

At every type. Let $F$ be rigid at $A$, so $F_h=h[F_1]$, and $Y\le h\cdot F$ rigid at the target of $h$. At $A$, invert $h$. At $V_m$, pin $F$, $Y$ and the finite colour algebra by a finite $P$, and fix one kernel element $z$ meeting every live atom of $P$ and covering the dead ones. Every tuple of $F_1$ is then conjugate, by an automorphism fixing $P$ and not changing its image, to one whose pinning algebra has its kernel below $z$. The orbit, under the automorphisms fixing $P$ and $z$, of the normalised tuples with image in $Y$ gives a rigid $X\le F$ with $h\cdot X=Y$: the image of a conjugate is moved back into $Y$ by an endomorphism of $V_m$ fixing the colours and the pin of $Y$. At $V_\infty$, pass through a finite-colour object by tail arrows $c$ and $k$ with $kc$ fixing the pins of $Y$ and of the test. So the property of being rigid and below $F$ is weakly inextensible, hence rigid by Tame Rigidity. With □BF, Rigid Power at the universal relation is Rigid Rigidity, so Rigid Power is necessary (rigid-rigidity-and-rigid-power-imply-necessary-rigid-power).

At type $et$. At $V_\infty$ let $U$ have extension $C_W$ at every arrow into $W$: symmetric, pinned down by $\varnothing$, persistent because arrows preserve colour, and weakly inextensible, since a test pinned down by $P$ and necessary of every colour is met at any $h$ by each $y\in C_W$, as some arrow agreeing with $h$ on $P$ sends a fresh colour generator to $y$. It is not rigid: along the arrow $l$ to $V_0$ sending every colour generator to $0$ its extension is $\{0,1\}$, and it does not entail the disjunction of their haecceities, which along an isomorphism back to $V_\infty$ has two instances while $l\cdot U$ has infinitely many. An entrance $A\to V_\infty$ exists, so □Tame Rigidity fails. And the weakly rigid subproperties of the universal property at $A$ are rigid, by Tame Rigidity, but $U$ is a weakly rigid one at $V_\infty$ that is not, so Weakly Rigid Power fails.

arguments.text: At the types $(e\to t)$ and $e$. Let $U:=\lambda Xy\, .\,Xy\lor\neg\exists z\, .\,Xz$, a closed term, hence in the domain, and serial. A functional subrelation $S$ of $U$ would lie in the domain at the evaluation object, so it is symmetric and pinned down by a finite set $N$. Two facts about such an $S$ (Dorr, draft, Lemma 19(iv)): every $g\in G$ fixing $N$ pointwise satisfies $g^{[\sigma]}S=S$, and symmetry gives $\langle gA,gy,g\rangle\in S$ whenever $\langle A,y,1\rangle\in S$; together, $\langle gA,gy,1\rangle\in S$. Now let $A$ be the property the condition gives for $N$. Its extension is nonempty, so $S$ relates $A$ at the identity to some $y$ in its extension. The condition gives a member $g$ of the symmetry group that fixes $N$ pointwise, fixes $A$ and moves $y$ to some $gy\ne y$, so $S$ relates $A$ to $gy$ as well, and $S$ is not functional at the identity arrow. The well-ordering of the individuals that Cian Dorr had in mind is refuted by the same two facts, but the direct route needs no derivation of a well-ordering from Relational Choice in C.

settings.construction: A symmetric ideally-full intensional action model over one object, the set of natural numbers, equipped with an equivalence relation $E$ that has infinitely many classes, each infinite. Its arrows are the surjections $h$ of that set that reflect $E$ ($hx\mathrel Ehy$ only if $x\mathrel Ey$), so that an arrow identifies two points only if they are in the same class; these are closed under composition. Its symmetry group is the automorphism group of $E$, the permutations that map classes onto classes. The evaluation point is the identity arrow.

meets.moving-proposition-stabilizers: Choose distinct pinning points $a,b,c$ outside a given finite $N$ in one infinite qualitative class. The symmetry $g=(a\ c)$ fixes $N$. The proposition $p_{ab}$ holds at an outgoing arrow $w$ exactly when $w(a)=w(b)$; it is symmetric and pinned by $\{a,b\}$. A surjection mapping each class onto itself can identify $a,b$ while keeping $c$ distinct. It reflects the qualitative equivalence, hence is an allowed arrow, and distinguishes $p_{ab}$ from $g\cdot p_{ab}=p_{cb}$. The points here are pinning-carrier points, also when the individual domain is a singleton. Source: OpenAI Codex, prompted by Daniel Kodsi, 22 October 2026, singleton applications §2; recorded 30 October 2026.
meets.no-actuality-anywhere: One object, so Actuality, a closed pure sentence, holds at every world iff at the identity, where it fails (recorded in this model’s verdicts).
meets.exact-collapses-of-every-size: Take $n\ge2$ points of one class: the surjection sending them to one of them, the rest of the class bijectively onto its other points, and fixing the other classes reflects $E$.
meets.one-object-action-model: It has one object (Dorr, draft, §3.1: closed pure terms denote entities fixed by every arrow).
meets.finitely-pinned-domains: A relational domain holds exactly the symmetric intensions pinned down by a finite set, and every individual $n$ is pinned down by $\{n\}$.
meets.transposable: $M=\emptyset$, and for $N$ the property of not belonging to $N$: the transposition of $y$ with another individual of its class outside $N$, which exists since the classes are infinite, maps classes onto classes, so lies in the symmetry group.
meets.surjective-arrows: The arrows are surjections by definition.
meets.finite-pinning: Every object carries the ideal of finite sets.

arguments.text: At type $e$, as in symmetric-infinite-classes, whose argument uses only the symmetry group, which is the same here. The class of a fixed individual is the extension of a property pinned down by that individual. A classifier pinned down by a finite set cannot choose a representative for the class of an individual in a class disjoint from that set: the representative is fixed by every automorphism fixing the classifier's pinning set and preserving the class, so its least pinning set lies inside the classifier's, and then its extension would be preserved by an automorphism swapping the class with another.

e n_0\land y\mathrel E n_0$ is, and it is necessarily instantiated, the classes being infinite at every arrow. Suppose $G\le F$ is necessarily uniquely instantiated, pinned down by a finite $N
i n_0$. Let $h$ map the class of $n_0$ onto itself, sending $N\cap[n_0]$ to $n_0$, and be the identity on the other classes: an arrow. Then $G_h=\{y\}$ with $y\in[n_0]\setminus\{n_0\}$, so $y

The transposition $\sigma$ of $y$ with another member of $[n_0]$ outside $h(N)$ is a symmetry fixing $h(N)$ pointwise, so $\sigma\circ h$ agrees with $h$ on $N$ and $G_{\sigma\circ h}=G_h=\{y\}$, while symmetry gives $G_{\sigma\circ h}=\{\sigma y\}$. $\Box$Intensional Choice fails with it, by T.

eg\, x\mathrel E n_0\land

e[n_0]$ disjoint from $N$ and $m\in[n_0]\setminus N$. Some arrow $k$ agrees with the identity on $N$ and maps $[n_0]$ onto $[n_0]\cup D$ with $km\in D$, fixing the other classes that meet $N$ and mapping the remaining classes onto the remaining classes.
