models.definition:
A symmetric ideally-full intensional action model over one object, the set of natural numbers, equipped with an equivalence relation $E$ that has infinitely many classes, each infinite. Its arrows are the surjections $h$ of that set that reflect $E$ ($hx\mathrel Ehy$ only if $x\mathrel Ey$), so that an arrow identifies two points only if they are in the same class; these are closed under composition. Its symmetry group is the automorphism group of $E$, the permutations that map classes onto classes. The evaluation point is the identity arrow.

Individuals, fixed for this record: the individuals at each object are the base the construction describes, and the arrows act on them as on the base.

Interpretation of Σ, fixed for this record: every constant of Σ is relational, and each denotes the top element of its type.

met.symmetric-domains: The relational domains hold exactly the symmetric intensions pinned down by a finite set (Dorr, draft, Definitions 15–18).
met.construction-individuals: The individuals are the base, acted on as the construction says.
met.moving-proposition-stabilizers: Choose distinct pinning points $a,b,c$ outside a given finite $N$ in one infinite qualitative class. The symmetry $g=(a\ c)$ fixes $N$. The proposition $p_{ab}$ holds at an outgoing arrow $w$ exactly when $w(a)=w(b)$; it is symmetric and pinned by $\{a,b\}$. A surjection mapping each class onto itself can identify $a,b$ while keeping $c$ distinct. It reflects the qualitative equivalence, hence is an allowed arrow, and distinguishes $p_{ab}$ from $g\cdot p_{ab}=p_{cb}$. The points here are pinning-carrier points, also when the individual domain is a singleton. Source: OpenAI Codex, prompted by Daniel Kodsi, 22 October 2026, singleton applications §2; recorded 30 October 2026.
met.no-actuality-anywhere: One object, so Actuality, a closed pure sentence, holds at every world iff at the identity, where it fails (recorded in this model’s verdicts).
met.exact-collapses-of-every-size: Take $n\ge2$ points of one class: the surjection sending them to one of them, the rest of the class bijectively onto its other points, and fixing the other classes reflects $E$.
met.one-object-action-model: It has one object (Dorr, draft, §3.1: closed pure terms denote entities fixed by every arrow).
met.finitely-pinned-domains: A relational domain holds exactly the symmetric intensions pinned down by a finite set, and every individual $n$ is pinned down by $\{n\}$.
met.transposable: $M=\emptyset$, and for $N$ the property of not belonging to $N$: the transposition of $y$ with another individual of its class outside $N$, which exists since the classes are infinite, maps classes onto classes, so lies in the symmetry group.
met.surjective-arrows: The arrows are surjections by definition.
met.finite-pinning: Every object carries the ideal of finite sets.
met.infinitely-many-orbits-everywhere: For a finite set $N$ of individuals, the property of being one of them, $h\mapsto h(N)$, is symmetric and pinned down by $N$; symmetries preserve the size of $N$, so these properties lie in infinitely many orbits at the one object.
met.full-continuum-everywhere: At a reachable object $v$, let $\tau$ be a type with infinitely many orbits there, and for a set $A$ of them let $Y_A$ be the intension of type $\tau t$ whose value at an arrow into $v$ is the union of the orbits in $A$ and at other arrows is empty: symmetric, the values being invariant, and pinned down by $\emptyset$, so in the domain; its transport along any arrow depends only on the arrow's codomain. The $Y_A$ are continuum many and pairwise distinct at $v$. For a set $T$ of $k$-tuples of them, the intension whose value at an arrow $h$ is the set of transports along $h$ of the tuples in $T$ depends only on $h$'s codomain, is symmetric, each such transport being fixed by the target's symmetries, and is pinned down by $\emptyset$; its extension at $v$ is $T$.

arguments.text: At input type $tt$ and output type $t$. The full symmetric profile construction admits the property $A$ whose profile at $w:V\to W$ is the propositions moved by some symmetry of W fixing $w[N]$ pointwise. It is N-pinned, and conjugation of stabilizers proves symmetry. If a selector S for the serial membership relation were pinned by finite N, every symmetry fixing N would fix both S and A as whole intensions. The condition makes A nonempty at V. A selected member would therefore be fixed by every such symmetry, contradicting its membership in A. This uses finite supports only at the evaluation object, full admission of symmetric pinned profiles, and no external choice. The construction-specific condition witnesses and complete proof are in the writeup. conditions.text: Write an entity of relational type at the evaluation object as its intension $k\mapsto Y_k$ over the arrows $k$ out of it, so that $Y\bar a$ holds at $k$ iff $k\cdot\bar a\in Y_k$; $Y$ is pinned down by a finite set $N$ of the points the arrows act on when $Y_k=Y_{k^{\prime}}$ for any arrows $k,k^{\prime}$ agreeing on $N$. models.definition:
Over ZFC let B=RO((2^omega)^omega), let B_fs be the union of the subalgebras depending on finitely many rows, and let G act by finitely many finite-prefix permutations. Build the typed finite-support Boolean hierarchy with individuals omega, propositions B_fs and all finitely supported functions at admitted relational types; crisp identity and ambient Boolean meets interpret equality and quantifiers. A Boolean-Henkin reduction gives a countable C5 model with standard canonical numbers and necessarily no real structure at any type. In the ground universe take a countable elementary extension A with a number c necessarily above every standard numeral. Give A the trivial G-action.
The hybrid has root individuals omega×D_e^A, root propositions B_fs×B_A and root relations pairs of a finitely supported Boolean current profile and an admitted A-component. Projection to A is surjective and commutes with application and lambda; equality is (literal current identity, component equality), and quantifiers use current Boolean meets and the original A-quantifiers. Apply the Boolean-Henkin reduction to the current Boolean valuation, retaining the component data and witnesses. Every signature constant is relational and denotes top. The full construction, soundness, generic-symmetry lemma and truth reduction are in writeups/symmetric-cohen-arithmetic-growth.md.

arguments.text: For a putative field supported on J, a generic-truth-filter-fixing prefix-transposition involution is an actual order automorphism. The dense-open moving-object lemma therefore forces every field element to be fixed by the whole J-stabilizer. The field lies in the intermediate universe V[U_J], where all of its subsets have admitted J-supported representatives. A fresh Cohen row gives a new bounded rational cut, represented by an admitted predicate at the same evaluation point, with no supremum in that field. Thus the current existential Real value is 0 at every type. Its A-component is also bottom, so the entire proposition object is bottom: necessarily no real structure exists. Every SANA guard is false.

settings.construction: A symmetric ideally-full model on two objects. $W_0$ has base $\mathbb N$ with a fixed pair $\{0,1\}$, and $W_1$ has base $\{0\}$. The arrows $W_0\to W_0$ are the permutations preserving $\{0,1\}$ setwise, the surjections $h$ with $h0=h1$ (the collapsers), and the constant maps $k_n$; there is one arrow $!:W_0\to W_1$, an arrow $c_n:W_1\to W_0$ with value $n$ for each $n$, and the identity of $W_1$. These are closed under composition: $c_n\circ!=k_n$, $!\circ c_n=1_{W_1}$, $h\circ c_n=c_{hn}$, and a composite with a collapser or a constant collapses $\{0,1\}$ and is a surjection or a constant. The symmetry group is the permutations preserving $\{0,1\}$ at $W_0$ and trivial at $W_1$. Both objects carry the ideal of finite sets. Evaluation point: $1_{W_0}$.

meets.finitely-pinned-domains: The domains hold every symmetric intension pinned down by a finite set, and every entity in them is one.
meets.finite-pinning: Both objects carry the ideal of finite sets.
meets.transposable: For finite $N$, the property of not belonging to $N\cup\{0,1\}$ (at an arrow $h$, the points outside $h[N\cup\{0,1\}]$; empty at arrows into $W_1$) is symmetric and pinned down by $N\cup\{0,1\}$; the transposition of a member $y$ with another point outside $N\cup\{0,1\}$ fixes $N\cup\{0,1\}$ pointwise, so is in the symmetry group and fixes the property.
meets.separable-collapses: The pairs $\{n,m\}$ with $n,m\ge2$: a surjection that collapses $0$ with $1$ and $n$ with $m$, and nothing else, is an arrow.
meets.symmetry-group-pinned: Pinned down by $\{0,1\}$: an arrow into $W_0$ that does not collapse $0$ and $1$ is in the symmetry group, and every composite with an arrow that does collapses them; there is one arrow into $W_1$.
meets.actual-world-isolated: The actual-world proposition is the symmetry group, pinned down by $\{0,1\}$; every world outside it is a collapser, a constant or $!$, and every composite with one of these collapses $\{0,1\}$ or lands in $W_1$.
meets.actuality-contingent: The symmetry group is in the domain; from every world a collapser leads outside it, and a collapser carries it to the empty proposition.
meets.irreversible-arrow: A collapser, or $!$; no composite with either is in the symmetry group.
meets.exact-collapses-of-every-size: Take $\{0,1\}$ and $n-2$ further points: the surjection sending them all to one point and the remaining points bijectively onto the others is a collapser.
meets.collapse-onto-point: As in symmetric-collapse-pair: $a:=0$ and $F:=\lambda x\, .\,x\ne 0$; for finite $N$, $h$ a surjection sending $N\cup\{0,1\}$ to one point $p\ge2$ and injective elsewhere. A member $y\ne p$ of $F_h=\mathbb N\setminus\{p\}$ is moved, fixing $p$, by swapping $0$ and $1$ (if $y\in\{0,1\}$) or by transposing $y$ with another point outside $\{0,1,p\}$; composites of $h$ with symmetries are collapsers.
meets.hull-conditions: With $M_0=\{0,1\}$. (B1) For $M\supseteq\{0,1\}$, an arrow into $W_0$ agreeing with a symmetry on $M$ does not collapse the pair, so is a symmetry: the symmetries are separated, and an arrow $h$ that is not collapses the pair, as does any $h^{\prime}$ agreeing with it on $M$. For $P\cap Q\subseteq M$, prescribe $h^{\prime}$ on $P$, $h$ on $Q$ and $h0=h1$ on the pair (consistent, the pair lying in $M$), and extend to a surjection: it is a collapser. There is one arrow into $W_1$. (B2) As for symmetric-collapse-pair: a permutation fixing $N\supseteq\{0,1\}$ pointwise preserves the pair and moves the finitely many points of $P\setminus N$ off $Q$.

models.notes: Cian Dorr's suggestion of 29 October 2026: the one-object model symmetric-collapse-pair as $W_0$, with a point $W_1$ added as in symmetric-two-object-all-maps. The constant maps forced by composition do not spoil BF at $W_0$, since each agrees on any finite set with a surjective collapser. BF, Boolean Completeness, and necessarily Strong Actuality and Boolean Completeness at type $t$, hold at $W_0$; BF at type $t$ fails at $W_1$.

meets.collapse-onto-point: Take $F:=\lambda x\, .\,x\ne a$, so $p\notin F_h$. $h$ is a surjection sending $N\cup\{a\}$ and both members of the pair to one $p$ outside the pair. Swapping the pair, or transposing $y$ with a point outside the pair, fixes $p$.

meets.actual-world-isolated: The actual-world proposition is the symmetry group, the set of arrows that are permutations, pinned down by the fixed pair; no composite with a non-bijective arrow is a permutation.

references.note: Symmetric ideally-full models, of which this is one.

settings.construction: A symmetric ideally-full model on two objects. The tail $B$ has the pinning base, arrows and symmetry group of symmetric-qualitative-links, together with one further point $d$, fixed by every arrow and every symmetry and in the image of no other point. The entrance $A$ has pinning base $\{*\}$, trivial symmetry group and the ideal of finite sets, and one arrow $i:A\to B$, sending $*$ to $d$, so that $m\circ i=i$ for every arrow $m$ out of $B$; there are no arrows from $B$ to $A$. Evaluation point: $1_A$.

meets.finitely-pinned-domains: Both objects carry the ideal of finite sets, and the domains hold every symmetric intension pinned down by a finite set.
meets.actual-world-isolated: $\{1_A\}$ is in the domain and entails every truth, and the only other world, $i$, sees only itself.
meets.finite-pinning: Both objects carry the ideal of finite sets.
meets.symmetry-group-pinned: The symmetry group at $A$ is its identity alone, pinned down by $\varnothing$.
meets.actuality-contingent: The proposition true at $A$ only is the strongest truth; its transport along $i$ is $\bot$, so it is necessary at no world and $i$ does not fix it.

models.notes: Rigid Comprehension, Weakly Rigid Power, Atomicity, Relational Choice and □Strong Actuality do not make Tame Rigidity necessary. Recorded with one individual, as built; the base at $A$ being the single point $*$, the group's variant with the base as individuals is not generated. The construction works for any one-object symmetric ideally-full tail with one individual: the entrance has these principles and fails the necessitation of whatever fails in the tail. Lean certificates of Relational Choice and of the failures of BF at $t$ and at the relational types are Astra's (Classicism.Meta.Intensional.FixedPointEntrance.Qualitative), ported from the submission; the rigidity verdicts are not formalized there.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr’s request
arguments.text: No Contingency (signature Σ) fails, since the Σ-sentence $\forall\bar x\, .\,c\bar x$ denotes $a$, true and contingent; Witnessed Possibility fails for the pure formula $x=\top_\tau$, witnessed by $\top_\tau$, since $\Diamond(c=\top_\tau)$ is $\Diamond\Box a$ and $a$ is necessary at no world; Separated Structure fails with it, being equivalent to Possibly Witnessed Possibility; Independence (signature Σ) and Distinctness Maximalism (signature Σ) fail through the other relational constants: such a constant $c'$ of type $\tau'$ denotes what the closed pure term $\top_{\tau'}$ denotes, and $c'=\top_{\tau'}$ is a true identity that C(Σ) does not prove. The designated constant refutes neither: closed pure terms denote entities fixed by every arrow (Classicism, §3.5, p. 58), whereas some arrow does not fix $a$, so no closed pure term denotes $\lambda\bar x\, .\,a$.

arguments.text: A set $D$ of root tuples closed under the surjections fixing a finite $S\subseteq N$ pointwise has an admitted exact-image relation $h\mapsto h[D]$, pinned by $S$, which is rigid. A weakly rigid root relation pinned by $S$ has such an extension by weak persistence, so it is identical to that exact image: every weakly rigid root relation $F$ has $F_h=h[F_{1_A}]$, and is rigid, at every type.

A rigid relation at $B$ entailing the transport of a root rigid relation is itself an exact image, pinned by a finite subset of $N$: compress its pinned block labels to finite ones, apply the exact-image criterion for relations whose pinned labels have finite fibres, and return. Then every rigid $Y\le h\cdot F$ is $j\cdot X$ for a root rigid $X\le F$ and an arrow $j$ agreeing with $h$ on any prescribed finite set, which makes the rigid power property of $F$ weakly inextensible; Tame Rigidity makes it rigid.

At type $et$. At $B$ the fibre relation $U_{q_i}$, with extension $R(g(q_i))$ at $(f,g)$, is weakly rigid but not rigid: an arrow sends $q_i$ to $q_{\{a,b\}}$, after which a further arrow fixing that label and collapsing $a,b$ separates it from $\delta_a\lor\delta_b$. So □Tame Rigidity fails. Its extensions lie in $N$, so it entails $i\cdot F$ for the rigid root property $F$ with extension $h[N]$ at every $h$. Every current instance of the weak power property of $F$ is rigid, by Tame Rigidity, while $U_{q_i}$ is an instance at the entrance $i$ that is not: the weak power property is not weakly inextensible.
At type $e$. Every individual at $A$ necessarily falls under the rigid property $F$ with extension $h[N]$ at every arrow $h$, but after an entrance the labels are individuals outside it.

arguments.text: At the types $(e\to t)$ and $e$. Let $U:=\lambda Xy\, .\,Xy\lor\neg\exists z\, .\,Xz$, a closed term, hence in the domain, and serial. A functional subrelation $S$ of $U$ would lie in the domain at the evaluation object, so it is symmetric and pinned down by a finite set $N$. Two facts about such an $S$ (Dorr, draft, Lemma 19(iv)): every $g\in G$ fixing $N$ pointwise satisfies $g^{[\sigma]}S=S$, and symmetry gives $\langle gA,gy,g\rangle\in S$ whenever $\langle A,y,1\rangle\in S$; together, $\langle gA,gy,1\rangle\in S$. Now let $A$ be the property the condition gives for $N$. Its extension is nonempty, so $S$ relates $A$ at the identity to some $y$ in its extension. The condition gives a member $g$ of the symmetry group that fixes $N$ pointwise, fixes $A$ and moves $y$ to some $gy\ne y$, so $S$ relates $A$ to $gy$ as well, and $S$ is not functional at the identity arrow. The well-ordering of the individuals that Cian Dorr had in mind is refuted by the same two facts, but the direct route needs no derivation of a well-ordering from Relational Choice in C.

arguments.text: At type $e$. settings.construction: A symmetric ideally-full intensional action model over one object, the set of natural numbers, equipped with an equivalence relation that has infinitely many classes, each infinite. Its arrows are all the surjections of that set, as in Base 1 of the draft, and its symmetry group is the automorphism group of the equivalence relation: the permutations that map classes onto classes. The evaluation point is the identity arrow.

meets.no-actuality-anywhere: One object, so Actuality, a closed pure sentence, holds at every world iff at the identity, where it fails (recorded in this model’s verdicts).
meets.exact-collapses-of-every-size: The arrows are all the surjections: for any $n\ge2$ points, the one sending them to one of them and the remaining points bijectively onto the others.
meets.all-surjection-arrows: The arrows are all the surjections of $\mathbb N$, as in Base 1.
meets.section-arrows: As in symmetric-all-surjections, the arrows being all the surjections: let $k^{\prime}$ agree with $k$ on $N$ and send distinct fresh points $x_t\notin N$ to $t\in T$, and let $\sigma$ be a surjection with $\sigma t=x_t$.
meets.factorizable-arrows: Take $N^{\prime\prime}:=S$ and, enlarging $N$, assume $h(N^{\prime\prime})\subseteq N$. Let $k^{\prime\prime}$ agree with $h$ on $N^{\prime\prime}$; for $m\in M\setminus N^{\prime\prime}$ let $k^{\prime\prime}m$ be some $n\in N$ with $kn=k^{\prime}m$ if there is one, and otherwise a fresh point outside $N$, one for each value of $k^{\prime}$. Let $j$ agree with $k$ on $N$ and send each fresh point to its value. Both extend to surjections, infinitely many points being left free, and $jk^{\prime\prime}$ agrees with $k^{\prime}$ on $M$.
meets.finitely-pinned-domains: A relational domain holds exactly the symmetric intensions pinned down by a finite set, and every individual $n$ is pinned down by $\{n\}$.
meets.collapse-onto-point: Take $F:=\lambda x\, .\,x\ne a$, so $p\notin F_h$. $h$ is any surjection constant on $N\cup\{a\}$; a transposition inside $y$'s class that fixes $p$ is an automorphism of the equivalence relation, and moves $y$.
meets.one-object-action-model: It has one object (Dorr, draft, §3.1: closed pure terms denote entities fixed by every arrow).
meets.transposable: $M=\emptyset$, and for $N$ the property of not belonging to $N$: the transposition of $y$ with another individual of its class outside $N$, which exists since the classes are infinite, maps classes onto classes, so lies in the symmetry group.
meets.surjective-arrows: The arrows are all the surjections of $\mathbb N$, as in Base 1.
meets.hull-conditions: With $M_0=\emptyset$, as in Base 1: an arrow is prescribed only on a finite set and extends freely to a surjection; and a point outside $N$ can be transposed with a member of its own class outside $N\cup Q$, the classes being infinite, by a class-preserving permutation fixing $N$ pointwise.
meets.finite-pinning: Every object carries the ideal of finite sets.

arguments.text: At type e. The class of a fixed individual is the extension of a property pinned down by that individual. A classifier F pinned down by a finite set cannot choose a representative for the class of an individual in a class disjoint from that set: by symmetry and uniqueness the representative is fixed by every automorphism that fixes the pinning set of F and preserves the class, so its least pinning set lies inside the pinning set of F, and then its extension would be preserved by an automorphism that swaps the class with another.

Let $F$ and $a$ be as the condition gives them, and suppose $G\le F$ is necessarily uniquely instantiated. $G$ is in the domain, so it is symmetric and pinned down by a finite set, which we may take to contain $a$; call it $N$. Let $h$ be the arrow the condition gives for $N$. Then $G_h=\{y\}$ for some $y$ in $F_h$. If $\sigma$ in the symmetry group fixes $p$, then $\sigma\circ h$ agrees with $h$ on $N$, so $G_{\sigma\circ h}=G_h$ by pinning, while symmetry gives $G_{\sigma\circ h}=\{\sigma y\}$. So no symmetry fixing $p$ moves $y$, and by the condition $y=p$. Each model's witness takes $F$ with $p$ outside its extension at $h$, a contradiction. $\Box$Intensional Choice fails with it, by T.

models.definition:
A symmetric ideally-full intensional action model over one object, the set of natural numbers, equipped with an equivalence relation that has infinitely many classes, each infinite. Its arrows are all the surjections of that set, as in Base 1 of the draft, and its symmetry group is the automorphism group of the equivalence relation: the permutations that map classes onto classes. The evaluation point is the identity arrow.

Individuals, fixed for this record: the individuals at each object are the base the construction describes, and the arrows act on them as on the base.

Interpretation of Σ, fixed for this record: every constant of Σ is relational, and each denotes the top element of its type.

met.symmetric-domains: The relational domains hold exactly the symmetric intensions pinned down by a finite set (Dorr, draft, Definitions 15–18).
met.construction-individuals: The individuals are the base, acted on as the construction says.
met.no-actuality-anywhere: One object, so Actuality, a closed pure sentence, holds at every world iff at the identity, where it fails (recorded in this model’s verdicts).
met.exact-collapses-of-every-size: The arrows are all the surjections: for any $n\ge2$ points, the one sending them to one of them and the remaining points bijectively onto the others.
met.all-surjection-arrows: The arrows are all the surjections of $\mathbb N$, as in Base 1.
met.section-arrows: As in symmetric-all-surjections, the arrows being all the surjections: let $k^{\prime}$ agree with $k$ on $N$ and send distinct fresh points $x_t\notin N$ to $t\in T$, and let $\sigma$ be a surjection with $\sigma t=x_t$.
met.factorizable-arrows: Take $N^{\prime\prime}:=S$ and, enlarging $N$, assume $h(N^{\prime\prime})\subseteq N$. Let $k^{\prime\prime}$ agree with $h$ on $N^{\prime\prime}$; for $m\in M\setminus N^{\prime\prime}$ let $k^{\prime\prime}m$ be some $n\in N$ with $kn=k^{\prime}m$ if there is one, and otherwise a fresh point outside $N$, one for each value of $k^{\prime}$. Let $j$ agree with $k$ on $N$ and send each fresh point to its value. Both extend to surjections, infinitely many points being left free, and $jk^{\prime\prime}$ agrees with $k^{\prime}$ on $M$.
met.finitely-pinned-domains: A relational domain holds exactly the symmetric intensions pinned down by a finite set, and every individual $n$ is pinned down by $\{n\}$.
met.collapse-onto-point: Take $F:=\lambda x\, .\,x\ne a$, so $p\notin F_h$. $h$ is any surjection constant on $N\cup\{a\}$; a transposition inside $y$'s class that fixes $p$ is an automorphism of the equivalence relation, and moves $y$.
met.one-object-action-model: It has one object (Dorr, draft, §3.1: closed pure terms denote entities fixed by every arrow).
met.transposable: $M=\emptyset$, and for $N$ the property of not belonging to $N$: the transposition of $y$ with another individual of its class outside $N$, which exists since the classes are infinite, maps classes onto classes, so lies in the symmetry group.
met.surjective-arrows: The arrows are all the surjections of $\mathbb N$, as in Base 1.
met.hull-conditions: With $M_0=\emptyset$, as in Base 1: an arrow is prescribed only on a finite set and extends freely to a surjection; and a point outside $N$ can be transposed with a member of its own class outside $N\cup Q$, the classes being infinite, by a class-preserving permutation fixing $N$ pointwise.
met.finite-pinning: Every object carries the ideal of finite sets.
met.infinitely-many-orbits-everywhere: For a finite set $N$ of individuals, the property of being one of them, $h\mapsto h(N)$, is symmetric and pinned down by $N$; symmetries preserve the size of $N$, so these properties lie in infinitely many orbits at the one object.
met.full-continuum-everywhere: At a reachable object $v$, let $\tau$ be a type with infinitely many orbits there, and for a set $A$ of them let $Y_A$ be the intension of type $\tau t$ whose value at an arrow into $v$ is the union of the orbits in $A$ and at other arrows is empty: symmetric, the values being invariant, and pinned down by $\emptyset$, so in the domain; its transport along any arrow depends only on the arrow's codomain. The $Y_A$ are continuum many and pairwise distinct at $v$. For a set $T$ of $k$-tuples of them, the intension whose value at an arrow $h$ is the set of transports along $h$ of the tuples in $T$ depends only on $h$'s codomain, is symmetric, each such transport being fixed by the target's symmetries, and is pinned down by $\emptyset$; its extension at $v$ is $T$.

settings.construction: A symmetric ideally-full intensional action model over two objects, $E$ and $O$, with individuals $\mathbb N$ at $E$ and $\mathbb N\sqcup\mathbb N'$ at $O$, $\mathbb N'$ a disjoint copy of $\mathbb N$; members of $\mathbb N$ at $O$ are old, members of $\mathbb N'$ new. The arrows are injections: from $E$ to $E$ all injections of $\mathbb N$; from $E$ to $O$ the injections with range among the old individuals; from $O$ to $E$ all injections into $\mathbb N$; from $O$ to $O$ the permutations preserving old and new ($G_O$) and the injections with range among the old ($K$). The symmetry groups are all permutations of $\mathbb N$ at $E$ and $G_O$ at $O$, and both objects carry the ideal of finite sets. The evaluation point is the identity arrow on $E$.

infinitely-many-orbits-everywhere.text: At $E$ and at $O$, the only objects, the properties of being one of a finite set of individuals lie in infinitely many orbits under the symmetry group, which preserves the size of the set.

meets.finitely-pinned-domains: Both objects carry the ideal of finite sets: the domains hold every symmetric intension pinned down by a finite set, and every entity in them is one.
meets.transposable: $M=\emptyset$, and for $N$ the property of not belonging to $N$, at $E$, where the domain is symmetric and finitely pinned: the transposition of $y$ with another individual of $E$ outside $N$ lies in its symmetry group.
meets.finitely-many-propositions: $E$ has four propositions: each set of arrows from $E$ to one object is a single class under symmetry and finite pinning, a finite partial injection extending to a symmetry.
meets.finitely-many-propositions-everywhere: $E$ has four propositions and $O$ eight, generated by the arrows into $E$, $G_O$ and $K$, the last two separated by whether the arrow sends a given new individual to a new one.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction, correcting the argument given by Claude Fable 5.1
arguments.text: For the universal property of individuals at $E$. A coextensive $Y$ holds of everything at every arrow to $E$, by symmetry and pinning; inextensibility at $E$, with the property of being old, keeps the new individuals out of $Y$ at the inclusion $\iota:E\to O$. At $\iota$ every $Y$-thing is necessarily distinct from $0'$, yet after any arrow $m:O\to E$, $Y$ holds of $m(0')$; so $Y$ is not weakly inextensible at $\iota$.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
arguments.text: The haecceities of the even numbers have no least upper bound: one pinned down by $N$ would, by a symmetry fixing $N$, hold at the identity of an odd $m\notin N$, while the property of differing from the image of $m$ is an upper bound that does not.

arguments.text: Let $U$ hold of every individual at arrows into $E$ and of exactly the old individuals at arrows into $O$. It is symmetric, pinned down by $\emptyset$, and equal to $B_N$ of its extension for every finite $N$, so weakly rigid. At the inclusion $i:E\to O$ its extension is the old individuals, each necessarily distinct from a new individual $b$, all arrows being injective; but after any arrow $m:O\to E$ the transported relation holds of $mb$. So $i\cdot U$ is not weakly inextensible, $U$ is not rigid, and Tame Rigidity fails at type $e$.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, after Cian Dorr’s observation that a choice over the individuals cannot be finitely pinned down
arguments.text: At the types $(e\to t)$ and $e$. Let $U:=\lambda Xy\, .\,Xy\lor\neg\exists z\, .\,Xz$, a closed term, hence in the domain, and serial. A functional subrelation $S$ of $U$ would lie in the domain at the evaluation object, so it is symmetric and pinned down by a finite set $N$. Two facts about such an $S$ (Dorr, draft, Lemma 19(iv)): every $g\in G$ fixing $N$ pointwise satisfies $g^{[\sigma]}S=S$, and symmetry gives $\langle gA,gy,g\rangle\in S$ whenever $\langle A,y,1\rangle\in S$; together, $\langle gA,gy,1\rangle\in S$. Now let $A$ be the property the condition gives for $N$. Its extension is nonempty, so $S$ relates $A$ at the identity to some $y$ in its extension. The condition gives a member $g$ of the symmetry group that fixes $N$ pointwise, fixes $A$ and moves $y$ to some $gy\ne y$, so $S$ relates $A$ to $gy$ as well, and $S$ is not functional at the identity arrow. The well-ordering of the individuals that Cian Dorr had in mind is refuted by the same two facts, but the direct route needs no derivation of a well-ordering from Relational Choice in C.

arguments.by: OpenAI Codex, prompted by Daniel Kodsi
arguments.text: At both objects every type domain is finite and every designated symmetry acts trivially. Inductively, finitely pinned intensions are constant on each arrow kind: a target symmetry matches any two arrows of that kind on their finite pinning set. At E there are two outgoing kinds; at O there are three, and composition preserves kinds. Each intension is therefore a finite list of subsets of finite tuple domains, and source symmetries fix that list. For an actual equivalence relation choose one element from each of its finitely many cells and represent the transversal by a finite disjunction of equalities. This works at every admitted type at both E and O, proving boxed Transversal Choice. Boxed Relational Choice is derived from the existing boxed TC-to-RC theorem and is not duplicated here. Original proof: OpenAI Codex, prompted by Daniel Kodsi, singleton applications §3, 22 October 2026, unpaginated; direct source misc. Only finite choice is used.

arguments.text: With one individual every entity is fixed by every symmetry, and is a union of finitely many classes, one for each kind of arrow (to $E$, from $E$ to $O$, in $G_O$, in $K$) and tuple of arguments; by induction on types, so every domain is finite and complete. Transport along an arrow then depends only on its kind, and the kind of a composite on the kinds of its factors, so the intension whose extension at $h$ is $X$'s extension at the identity transported along $h$ is a union of classes, in the domain; it is persistent and inextensible, at both objects.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: At type $e$. Write $G$ for the symmetry group and $\sim$ for the equivalence relation; the constant intension with value $\sim$ is symmetric and pinned down by $\varnothing$, so for an individual $a$ the property $\lambda x\, .\,x\sim a$, pinned down by $\{a\}$, has as extension the class of $a$. Suppose $F$, pinned down by a finite $S$, picked exactly one property from each coextension class, and let $Y$ be the one it picks with extension a class $C$ disjoint from $S$. A $g\in G$ fixing $S$ pointwise fixes $F$ (by pinning and symmetry), so $g\cdot Y$ is picked too; if $g$ also maps $C$ onto itself, $g\cdot Y$ has extension $g[C]=C$, so $g\cdot Y=Y$ by uniqueness, that is, $Y_{k\circ g}=Y_k$ for every arrow $k$. Let $Y$ be pinned down by a finite $T$. The permutations of each class fixing $S$ pointwise are such $g$; with the permutations fixing $T$ pointwise, which include transpositions across classes outside $T$, they generate every finitary permutation of $\mathbb N\setminus S$, and with the permutations fixing $T$ these generate all those fixing $S$ pointwise. So $Y$ is pinned down by $S$. Now take $g^{\prime}\in G$ fixing $S$ pointwise and exchanging $C$ with another class disjoint from $S$: $Y_{g^{\prime}}=Y_1$ by pinning, and $Y_{g^{\prime}}=g^{\prime}[Y_1]$ by symmetry, so $C=g^{\prime}[C]$, which is false. So there is no such $F$.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, after Cian Dorr’s observation that a choice over the individuals cannot be finitely pinned down
arguments.text: At the types $(e\to t)$ and $e$. Let $U:=\lambda Xy\, .\,Xy\lor\neg\exists z\, .\,Xz$, a closed term, hence in the domain, and serial. A functional subrelation $S$ of $U$ would lie in the domain at the evaluation object, so it is symmetric and pinned down by a finite set $N$. Two facts about such an $S$ (Dorr, draft, Lemma 19(iv)): every $g\in G$ fixing $N$ pointwise satisfies $g^{[\sigma]}S=S$, and symmetry gives $\langle gA,gy,g\rangle\in S$ whenever $\langle A,y,1\rangle\in S$; together, $\langle gA,gy,1\rangle\in S$. Now let $A$ be the property the condition gives for $N$. Its extension is nonempty, so $S$ relates $A$ at the identity to some $y$ in its extension. The condition gives a member $g$ of the symmetry group that fixes $N$ pointwise, fixes $A$ and moves $y$ to some $gy\ne y$, so $S$ relates $A$ to $gy$ as well, and $S$ is not functional at the identity arrow. The well-ordering of the individuals that Cian Dorr had in mind is refuted by the same two facts, but the direct route needs no derivation of a well-ordering from Relational Choice in C.

settings.construction: Appendix D, p. 79, the final construction, the paper’s precursor of the symmetric ideally-full models of Dorr’s draft (Definitions 15–18, p. 8): the base has two objects $W_0$ and $W_1$, both copies of $\mathbb N$, all permutations of $\mathbb N$ as the arrows between any pair of objects, the ideal of finite sets at each, and the symmetry groups $G_{W_0}$ = all permutations and $G_{W_1}$ trivial. The paper states the symmetry condition on propositions only, as the constraint that a set of arrows in $W_i^t$ containing an arrow $h$ into $W_0$ contains $g\circ h$ for every permutation $g$ of $W_0$, and takes the finitely pinned entities at higher types; since every arrow is invertible, that is the draft’s symmetry condition at every type, applied to the entities’ values. Intuitively $W_0$ is a state in which all individuals are qualitatively indiscernible and $W_1$ one in which each plays a unique role. Evaluation point: $W_0$, at its identity arrow.

meets.moving-proposition-stabilizers: Fix a pinning-carrier point $k$ at $W_1$, whose designated symmetry group is trivial. For $a$ at $W_0$, let $p_a(w)$ mean that $w$ has target $W_1$ and $w(a)=k$. This proposition is symmetric and pinned by $\{a\}$; it is false on arrows ending at $W_0$. Given finite $N$, choose distinct $a,c$ outside it and $g=(a\ c)\in G_{W_0}$. Then $g\cdot p_a=p_c$. A permutation $w:W_0\to W_1$ with $w(a)=k$ has $w(c)\ne k$, so these propositions differ. No collapsing arrow is used. The points here are pinning-carrier points, also when the individual domain is a singleton. Source: OpenAI Codex, prompted by Daniel Kodsi, 22 October 2026, singleton applications §2; recorded 30 October 2026.
meets.infinitely-many-orbits-everywhere: With the base as individuals, at $W_0$ and $W_1$ the properties of being one of a finite set of individuals lie in infinitely many orbits, symmetries preserving the size of the set. With one individual: at $W_1$, whose symmetry group is trivial, there are infinitely many propositions, each its own orbit; at $W_0$, the propositions $\{h:h(N)\subseteq M\}$ about arrows into $W_1$, for finite $N$ and $M$, lie in infinitely many orbits, the symmetries of $W_0$ moving $N$ but not $M$.
meets.finitely-pinned-domains: Each object carries the ideal of finite sets, and the domains hold the finitely pinned symmetric entities of every type.
meets.transposable: $M=\emptyset$, and for $N$ the property of not belonging to $N$, at $W_0$: the transposition of $y$ with another individual outside $N$ is a permutation of $W_0$, so lies in $G_{W_0}$.
meets.actuality-contingent: The actual-world proposition is the set of all arrows $W_0\to W_0$, in the domain by the source argument; at every world an arrow into $W_1$ leads outside it, and such an arrow carries it to the empty set.

models.notes: The cited construction is a model of the map’s relational-type framework. The description identifies its evaluation point; construction and verification are given at the PDF locations in References. Everything that implies these fails with them. Plenitude still holds by C5 plus Actuality and Propositions 2.5 and 2.14, so this model separates it from Functional Choice even under C5, Rigid Comprehension and Boolean Completeness. settings.construction: A symmetric ideally-full intensional action model over one object whose individuals carry qualitative structure. The domain is the disjoint union of points, of two companions for each point, and of infinitely many links for each ordered pair of distinct points. A ternary relation holds of two points and a third individual when that individual is a link over the two if they differ, and a companion of them if they coincide, so the relation's fibres are infinite over distinct points and of size two over a repeated point. The arrows are required to preserve that relation. The symmetry group is the relation-preserving permutations that fix a distinguished pair of points setwise, and the remaining arrows are the surjective relation-preserving maps that collapse that pair. The evaluation point is the identity arrow.

meets.moving-proposition-stabilizers: Choose distinct point endpoints $u,v$ away from the distinguished point-pair, and three links $a,b,c$ over $(u,v)$ outside a given finite $N$. Transposing $a,c$ while fixing everything else is a symmetry fixing $N$. The proposition $p_{ab}(w)\leftrightarrow w(a)=w(b)$ is symmetric and pinned by $\{a,b\}$. A surjection on points collapsing the distinguished pair and fixing $u,v$ extends to a surjective relation-preserving arrow: map each companion pair onto the corresponding companion pair, and each link fibre onto its target link fibre or companion pair. On the unchanged fibre over $(u,v)$ identify $a,b$ but keep $c$ distinct. Every target fibre has a source fibre, so the whole map is onto. It distinguishes $p_{ab}$ from $g\cdot p_{ab}=p_{cb}$. The common writeup checks this extension explicitly. The points here are pinning-carrier points, also when the individual domain is a singleton. Source: OpenAI Codex, prompted by Daniel Kodsi, 22 October 2026, singleton applications §2; recorded 30 October 2026.
meets.finitely-pinned-domains: The domains hold every symmetric intension pinned down by a finite set (finite-pinning), and every entity in them is one.
meets.one-object-action-model: It has one object (Dorr, draft, §3.1: closed pure terms denote entities fixed by every arrow).
meets.transposable: $M=\emptyset$, and for $N$ the property of being a link not in $N$ (links are carried to links by every member of the symmetry group, whose inverse is again $R$-preserving): a chosen $y$ is a link $\langle m,n,k\rangle$, and its transposition with a link $\langle m,n,k'\rangle\notin N$, which exists since the fibre is infinite, preserves $R$ and fixes every point, so lies in the symmetry group.
meets.separable-collapses: The pairs $\{0,m\}$ for points $m$ other than the distinguished pair $0,1$: by the draft's extension step (proof of its Proposition 50), an $R$-coherent prescription on a closed finite set containing $0$, $1$, $m$ and $m'$ that merges $0$, $1$ and $m$ but not $m'$ extends to a collapsing arrow, as in the record's argument for the failure of Atomicity (type t).
meets.surjective-arrows: The arrows are relation-preserving permutations and surjective relation-preserving maps.
meets.symmetry-group-pinned: Membership in the symmetry group is the condition that the distinguished pair is not collapsed, so the group is pinned down by that pair.
meets.actual-world-isolated: The actual-world proposition is the symmetry group, pinned down by the distinguished pair; under a collapsing arrow $i$, a composite $k\circ i$ would have to be a permutation, and no composite with a map that collapses the distinguished pair is injective.
meets.actuality-contingent: The actual-world proposition, the symmetry group, is in the domain; at every world a collapsing arrow leads outside it, and a collapsing arrow carries it to the empty set.
meets.irreversible-arrow: A collapsing arrow: no composite with it is injective.
meets.finite-pinning: Every object carries the ideal of finite sets.

models.notes:
This is the draft's answer to the question its two-object model leaves open. Boxed Boolean Completeness, boxed Actuality and the boxed type-e instance of BF all hold, and Rigid Comprehension still fails, so the obstruction need not live at a world where BF fails; it can live inside a qualitative fibre that BF at type e cannot see.
The type-e instance of BF holds, and necessarily, since every arrow is surjective, so a property necessarily had by everything is the top property.
With these verdicts the model is the map's witness that Boolean Completeness, □BF and □Actuality, together with Weak Rigid Comprehension, do not imply Rigid Comprehension. That was the draft's aim for this section.
The source is a work in progress, and its own status note describes this section as exploratory though complete for the claims recorded here. Everything that implies these fails with them.

The set of numerals at each type is invariant under every arrow, hence symmetric and pinned by the empty set, so finite cardinality is standard and no finite cardinality holds of the universal property at either type.

history.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
history.summary: Recorded the failure of Relational Choice, at types (e→t) and e: a functional subrelation of the serial relation pairing each property with its members would be symmetric and finitely pinned, and a symmetry fixing its pinning set would carry its choice for the property of lying outside that set to a second choice. Cian Dorr’s observation that a choice cannot be finitely pinned; argument in the notes.

history.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
history.summary: Recorded the Distinctness-preserving collapse by the argument used for the other symmetric models. Let $a$ be the symmetry group, the model’s Actuality witness, so $a\le p$ for every true $p$. Take $q:=a$: under an arrow $i$ in the group, $p$ holds since $i\in a\subseteq p$; under a collapsing arrow $i$, $\Diamond a$ would need $k\circ i$ to be a permutation, and no composite with a map that collapses the distinguished pair is injective. So every truth is $\Box_{\ne}$-necessary.

models.definition:
A symmetric ideally-full intensional action model over one object whose individuals carry qualitative structure. The domain is the disjoint union of points, of two companions for each point, and of infinitely many links for each ordered pair of distinct points. A ternary relation holds of two points and a third individual when that individual is a link over the two if they differ, and a companion of them if they coincide, so the relation's fibres are infinite over distinct points and of size two over a repeated point. The arrows are required to preserve that relation. The symmetry group is the relation-preserving permutations that fix a distinguished pair of points setwise, and the remaining arrows are the surjective relation-preserving maps that collapse that pair. The evaluation point is the identity arrow.

Individuals, fixed for this record: the individuals at each object are the base the construction describes, and the arrows act on them as on the base.

Interpretation of Σ, fixed for this record: every constant of Σ is relational, and each denotes the top element of its type.

met.symmetric-domains: The relational domains hold exactly the symmetric intensions pinned down by a finite set (Dorr, draft, Definitions 15–18).
met.construction-individuals: The individuals are the base, acted on as the construction says.
met.moving-proposition-stabilizers: Choose distinct point endpoints $u,v$ away from the distinguished point-pair, and three links $a,b,c$ over $(u,v)$ outside a given finite $N$. Transposing $a,c$ while fixing everything else is a symmetry fixing $N$. The proposition $p_{ab}(w)\leftrightarrow w(a)=w(b)$ is symmetric and pinned by $\{a,b\}$. A surjection on points collapsing the distinguished pair and fixing $u,v$ extends to a surjective relation-preserving arrow: map each companion pair onto the corresponding companion pair, and each link fibre onto its target link fibre or companion pair. On the unchanged fibre over $(u,v)$ identify $a,b$ but keep $c$ distinct. Every target fibre has a source fibre, so the whole map is onto. It distinguishes $p_{ab}$ from $g\cdot p_{ab}=p_{cb}$. The common writeup checks this extension explicitly. The points here are pinning-carrier points, also when the individual domain is a singleton. Source: OpenAI Codex, prompted by Daniel Kodsi, 22 October 2026, singleton applications §2; recorded 30 October 2026.
met.finitely-pinned-domains: The domains hold every symmetric intension pinned down by a finite set (finite-pinning), and every entity in them is one.
met.one-object-action-model: It has one object (Dorr, draft, §3.1: closed pure terms denote entities fixed by every arrow).
met.transposable: $M=\emptyset$, and for $N$ the property of being a link not in $N$ (links are carried to links by every member of the symmetry group, whose inverse is again $R$-preserving): a chosen $y$ is a link $\langle m,n,k\rangle$, and its transposition with a link $\langle m,n,k'\rangle\notin N$, which exists since the fibre is infinite, preserves $R$ and fixes every point, so lies in the symmetry group.
met.separable-collapses: The pairs $\{0,m\}$ for points $m$ other than the distinguished pair $0,1$: by the draft's extension step (proof of its Proposition 50), an $R$-coherent prescription on a closed finite set containing $0$, $1$, $m$ and $m'$ that merges $0$, $1$ and $m$ but not $m'$ extends to a collapsing arrow, as in the record's argument for the failure of Atomicity (type t).
met.surjective-arrows: The arrows are relation-preserving permutations and surjective relation-preserving maps.
met.symmetry-group-pinned: Membership in the symmetry group is the condition that the distinguished pair is not collapsed, so the group is pinned down by that pair.
met.actual-world-isolated: The actual-world proposition is the symmetry group, pinned down by the distinguished pair; under a collapsing arrow $i$, a composite $k\circ i$ would have to be a permutation, and no composite with a map that collapses the distinguished pair is injective.
met.actuality-contingent: The actual-world proposition, the symmetry group, is in the domain; at every world a collapsing arrow leads outside it, and a collapsing arrow carries it to the empty set.
met.irreversible-arrow: A collapsing arrow: no composite with it is injective.
met.finite-pinning: Every object carries the ideal of finite sets.
met.infinitely-many-orbits-everywhere: For a finite set $N$ of individuals, the property of being one of them, $h\mapsto h(N)$, is symmetric and pinned down by $N$; symmetries preserve the size of $N$, so these properties lie in infinitely many orbits at the one object.
met.full-continuum-everywhere: At a reachable object $v$, let $\tau$ be a type with infinitely many orbits there, and for a set $A$ of them let $Y_A$ be the intension of type $\tau t$ whose value at an arrow into $v$ is the union of the orbits in $A$ and at other arrows is empty: symmetric, the values being invariant, and pinned down by $\emptyset$, so in the domain; its transport along any arrow depends only on the arrow's codomain. The $Y_A$ are continuum many and pairwise distinct at $v$. For a set $T$ of $k$-tuples of them, the intension whose value at an arrow $h$ is the set of transports along $h$ of the tuples in $T$ depends only on $h$'s codomain, is symmetric, each such transport being fixed by the target's symmetries, and is pinned down by $\emptyset$; its extension at $v$ is $T$.

models.notes:
This is the draft's answer to the question its two-object model leaves open. Boxed Boolean Completeness, boxed Actuality and the boxed type-e instance of BF all hold, and Rigid Comprehension still fails, so the obstruction need not live at a world where BF fails; it can live inside a qualitative fibre that BF at type e cannot see.
The type-e instance of BF holds, and necessarily, since every arrow is surjective, so a property necessarily had by everything is the top property.
With these verdicts the model is the map's witness that Boolean Completeness, □BF and □Actuality, together with Weak Rigid Comprehension, do not imply Rigid Comprehension. That was the draft's aim for this section.
The source is a work in progress, and its own status note describes this section as exploratory though complete for the claims recorded here. Everything that implies these fails with them.

models.notes:
This is the draft's answer to the question its two-object model leaves open. Boxed Boolean Completeness, boxed Actuality and the boxed type-e instance of BF all hold, and Rigid Comprehension still fails, so the obstruction need not live at a world where BF fails; it can live inside a qualitative fibre that BF at type e cannot see.
The type-e instance of BF holds, and necessarily, since every arrow is surjective, so a property necessarily had by everything is the top property.
With these verdicts the model is the map's witness that Boolean Completeness, □BF and □Actuality, together with Weak Rigid Comprehension, do not imply Rigid Comprehension. That was the draft's aim for this section.
The source is a work in progress, and its own status note describes this section as exploratory though complete for the claims recorded here. Everything that implies these fails with them.

settings.construction: A symmetric ideally-full intensional action model over one object, the set of natural numbers. Its arrows are of two disjoint kinds: the surjections for which the distinguished individual is its own only preimage, and the functions that omit the distinguished individual from their range. Its symmetry group is the permutations fixing that individual, which is now a proper subset of the first kind. An arrow's value at the distinguished individual still tells the two kinds apart, but no finite set separates any arrow. The evaluation point is the identity arrow.

meets.no-atoms-anywhere: One object. A symmetric proposition pinned down by a finite $N$ and containing an arrow $k$ contains every arrow of the same kind agreeing with $k$ on $N$ up to symmetry; two of these, one identifying two fresh points outside $N$ and one separating them, have different kernels, which symmetry (post-composition with permutations) preserves, so they lie in disjoint nonempty symmetric propositions pinned down by a larger finite set. So no proposition is an atom.
meets.no-actuality-anywhere: One object, so Actuality, a closed pure sentence, holds at every world iff at the identity, where it fails (recorded in this model’s verdicts).
meets.exact-collapses-of-every-size: Take $n\ge2$ points other than the distinguished individual $d$: the map constant on them with a value other than $d$, and injective off them with values avoiding $d$ and that value, omits $d$ from its range, so is an arrow of the second kind.
meets.factorizable-arrows: As in symmetric-range-gap, with $d$ in $S$ and $N$ and the kinds told apart by the value at $d$, the first kind now being the surjections for which $d$ is its own only preimage. For $m\in M\setminus N^{\prime\prime}$ let $k^{\prime\prime}m$ be some $n\in N$ with $kn=k^{\prime}m$ when $k$ is of the first kind and there is one (then $n\ne d$, as $k^{\prime}m\ne d$), and otherwise a fresh point outside $N\cup\{d\}$, one for each value of $k^{\prime}$; let $j$ agree with $k$ on $N$ and send each fresh point to its value, never $d$. Arrows of the first kind need only be surjective with $d$ the only preimage of $d$, so $k^{\prime\prime}$ and $j$ extend to arrows of the kinds of $h$ and $k$, and $jk^{\prime\prime}$ agrees with $k^{\prime}$ on $M$.
meets.finitely-pinned-domains: A relational domain holds exactly the symmetric intensions pinned down by a finite set, and every individual $n$ is pinned down by $\{n\}$.
meets.collapse-onto-point:
As for the range-gap model: $F:=\lambda x\, .\,x
e a\land
eg Ex$ with $E$ the constant intension $\{d\}$ of the distinguished individual, and $h$ a range-deficient function constant with value $p
e d$ on $N\cup\{a\}$; $F_h$ omits $p$ and $d$, and permutations fixing $p$ and $d$ move every other point.
meets.one-object-action-model: It has one object (Dorr, draft, §3.1: closed pure terms denote entities fixed by every arrow).
meets.transposable: $M=\{0\}$, the distinguished individual, and for $N$ the property of not belonging to $N\cup\{0\}$: the transposition of $y$ with another individual outside $N\cup\{0\}$ fixes $0$, so lies in the symmetry group.
meets.fixes-or-omits: The arrows are the surjections for which $0$ is its own only preimage, which fix it, and the functions omitting $0$ from their range.
meets.transport-gap: Take $N=\{0\}$, $i$ any arrow with $i0\ne0$, so that every arrow agreeing with it on $N$ omits $0$ from its range, and $q:=\{k : k0=0\}$, the first class of arrows, pinned down by $\{0\}$ and symmetric: an arrow $k$ of the first class and the arrow $k^{\prime}$ agreeing with it off $0$ but sending $0$ elsewhere, which omits $0$ from its range since $0$ is $k$’s only preimage of $0$, are separated by $q$. The intension the argument uses is pinned down by $N$, and symmetric, since $g\cdot q=q$ for $g$ fixing $0$ and $(g\circ j)0=0$ iff $j0=0$, so it lies in the domain.
meets.hull-conditions: With $M_0=\{0\}$, the distinguished individual (the draft's argument for this model). Two arrows agreeing there lie in the same one of the two classes, and a prescription taken from the two of them extends within that class, by nonzero values in the second case and by surjective nonzero values in the first; points are moved off a finite set by a permutation fixing $0$.
meets.retractable-means-actual-pattern: With $N^\prime=N\cup\{0\}$: if $x\circ u$ is the identity on $N^\prime$ then $u$ fixes $0$, so is of the first kind, and is injective on $N^\prime$; it therefore agrees on $N$ with a permutation fixing $0$, a member of the symmetry group.

arguments.by: Cian Dorr
arguments.text: At type e. Take the property of being positive unless things are as they actually are, which is pinned down by the distinguished individual and is symmetric. Every individual necessarily has it, since an arrow either fixes the distinguished individual or omits it from its range and so sends everything to something positive; but it is not necessary that everything has it, since any arrow moving the distinguished individual leaves it out.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: At type $e$. Let $F$ and $a$ be as the condition gives them, and suppose $G\le F$ is necessarily uniquely instantiated. $G$ is in the domain, so it is symmetric and pinned down by a finite set, which we may take to contain $a$; call it $N$. Let $h$ be the arrow the condition gives for $N$. Then $G_h=\{y\}$ for some $y$ in $F_h$. If $\sigma$ in the symmetry group fixes $p$, then $\sigma\circ h$ agrees with $h$ on $N$, so $G_{\sigma\circ h}=G_h$ by pinning, while symmetry gives $G_{\sigma\circ h}=\{\sigma y\}$. So no symmetry fixing $p$ moves $y$, and by the condition $y=p$. Each model's witness takes $F$ with $p$ outside its extension at $h$, a contradiction. $\Box$Intensional Choice fails with it, by T.

Its symmetry group is the permutations fixing a distinguished individual, and its arrows are those permutations together with all the functions that omit the distinguished individual from their range. The evaluation point is the identity arrow.

Individuals, fixed for this record: there is a single individual at every object. The arrows still act on the base as the construction says, and the base still supplies the pinning sets and the symmetry groups.

Interpretation of Σ, fixed for this record: every constant of Σ is relational, and each denotes the top element of its type.

met.symmetric-domains: The relational domains hold exactly the symmetric intensions pinned down by a finite set (Dorr, draft, Definitions 15–18).
met.one-individual: There is a single individual at every object.
met.moving-proposition-stabilizers: Choose distinct pinning points $a,b,c$ outside a given finite $N$ and the distinguished point $d$. Then $g=(a\ c)$ is a symmetry fixing $N$. The symmetric proposition $p_{ab}(w)\leftrightarrow w(a)=w(b)$ is pinned by $\{a,b\}$. A function omitting $d$ from its range can identify $a,b$ while keeping $c$ distinct; it is an allowed arrow and distinguishes $p_{ab}$ from $g\cdot p_{ab}=p_{cb}$. The points here are pinning-carrier points, also when the individual domain is a singleton. Source: OpenAI Codex, prompted by Daniel Kodsi, 22 October 2026, singleton applications §2; recorded 30 October 2026.
met.exact-collapses-of-every-size: Take $n\ge2$ points other than the distinguished individual $d$: the map constant on them with a value other than $d$, and injective off them with values avoiding $d$ and that value, omits $d$ from its range.
met.factorizable-arrows:
Put the distinguished individual $d$ in $S$ and $N$, take $N^{\prime\prime}:=S$ and, enlarging $N$, assume $h(N^{\prime\prime})\subseteq N$. An arrow's value at $d$ tells its kind: a permutation fixing $d$, or a map omitting $d$; so $k^{\prime}$ has the kind of $kh$, and $k^{\prime\prime}$ and $j$ will have the kinds of $h$ and $k$. Let $k^{\prime\prime}$ agree with $h$ on $N^{\prime\prime}$; for $m\in M\setminus N^{\prime\prime}$ let $k^{\prime\prime}m:=k^{-1}(k^{\prime}m)$ if $k$ is a permutation and $k^{\prime}m\in k(N)$, and otherwise a fresh point outside $N\cup\{d\}$, one for each $m$ if $h$ is a permutation and one for each value of $k^{\prime}$ if not. Let $j$ agree with $k$ on $N$ and send each fresh point to its value. Since $k^{\prime}m
e d$ for $m
e d$, $k^{\prime\prime}m
e d$; where $h$ is a permutation so is $k^{\prime}$ or $k$ omits $d$, and $k^{\prime\prime}$ is injective on $M$; where $k$ is a permutation the new values of $j$ lie outside $k(N)$ and are distinct. So both extend to arrows of their kinds, and $jk^{\prime\prime}$ agrees with $k^{\prime}$ on $M$.
met.finitely-pinned-domains: A relational domain holds exactly the symmetric intensions pinned down by a finite set, and every individual $n$ is pinned down by $\{n\}$.
met.collapse-onto-point:
The distinguished individual $d$ is fixed by every symmetry, so take $F:=\lambda x\, .\,x
e a\land
eg Ex$, where $E$ is the constant intension $\{d\}$, pinned down by $\varnothing$. Let $h$ be a range-deficient function constant with value $p
e d$ on $N\cup\{a\}$. Then $F_h$ omits $p$ and $d$, and permutations fixing $p$ and $d$ move every other point.
met.one-object-action-model: It has one object (Dorr, draft, §3.1: closed pure terms denote entities fixed by every arrow).
met.transposable: $M=\{0\}$, the distinguished individual, and for $N$ the property of not belonging to $N\cup\{0\}$: the transposition of $y$ with another individual outside $N\cup\{0\}$ fixes $0$, so lies in the symmetry group.
met.separable-collapses: The pairs $\{n,m\}$ of positive numbers: a function omitting $0$ from its range that collapses $n$ with $m$ and nothing else is an arrow.
met.symmetry-group-pinned: The two classes of arrows are told apart by an arrow's value at the distinguished individual.
met.fixes-or-omits: The arrows are the permutations fixing $0$ and the functions omitting $0$ from their range.
met.transport-gap: Take $N=\{0\}$, $i$ any arrow with $i0\ne0$, so that every arrow agreeing with it on $N$ omits $0$ from its range, and $q:=\{k : k0=0\}$, the symmetry group, pinned down by $\{0\}$ and symmetric: a permutation $k$ fixing $0$ and the arrow $k^{\prime}$ agreeing with it off $0$ but sending $0$ elsewhere, which omits $0$ from its range, are separated by $q$. The intension the argument uses is pinned down by $N$, and symmetric, since $g\cdot q=q$ for $g$ fixing $0$ and $(g\circ j)0=0$ iff $j0=0$, so it lies in the domain.
met.actual-world-isolated: The actual-world proposition is the set of arrows that are permutations, pinned down by $\{0\}$; no composite with an arrow omitting $0$ from its range is a permutation, since the other arrows fix $0$ and so cannot restore it to the range.
met.actuality-contingent: The actual-world proposition, the symmetry group, is in the domain; at every world an arrow omitting $0$ leads outside it, and such an arrow carries it to the empty set.
met.irreversible-arrow: An arrow omitting $0$ from its range: no composite with it restores $0$ to the range.
met.hull-conditions: With $M_0=\{0\}$, the distinguished individual (the draft's argument for this model). Moving points off a finite set can be done by a permutation fixing that individual; an arrow that $M_0$ does not separate omits $0$ from its range, as does any arrow agreeing with it at $0$, so a prescription taken from the two of them extends by nonzero values to an arrow of that kind.

models.notes: The first of the draft's two variants in which BF is made to fail. Actuality and the range deficiency come from the same finite test here, which is what the next variant prises apart. Atomicity and Rigid Comprehension are not settled in the draft and are left unknown. The source is a work in progress. Everything that implies these fails with them.

history.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
history.summary: Added both Axioms of Infinity at Cian Dorr's direction. The individuals are the natural numbers and identity at the identity arrow is literal, so no numeral counts them. The propositions that a given individual is fixed by the arrow, one for each individual, are pairwise distinct, symmetric and pinned by that individual, so there are infinitely many propositions. The set of numerals at each type is invariant under every arrow, hence symmetric and pinned by the empty set, so finite cardinality is standard and no finite cardinality holds of the universal property at either type.

models.name: Symmetric ideally-full model: recurrent finite colour approximations

certificate.produced_by: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), prompted by Daniel Kodsi, 26 October 2026
certificate.recorded_by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, 28 October 2026

sources: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), prompted by Daniel Kodsi, Symmetric ideally-full model: recurrent finite colour approximations, research note of 26 October 2026, §§2–12 (unpaginated), in Daniel Kodsi's pull request #18 of 26 October 2026 (branch classicism-integration-2026-10-26 of github.com/dkodsi/Logical-Maps).
Cian Dorr, Boolean Completeness does not imply Rigid Comprehension, draft of 30 July 2026, Definitions 15–18, p. 8; Theorem 36, p. 18.

references.locator: Definitions 15–18, p. 8; Theorem 36 and Corollary 37, pp. 18–19
references.note: Symmetric ideally-full models, of which this is one, and the hull theorem for Boolean Completeness.

settings.construction: A symmetric ideally-full model with an object $W_m$ for each positive integer $m$ and an object $W_\infty$, each with base a copy of $\mathbb N$ in which a set $E_V$ of coloured points is fixed: $m$ of them at $W_m$, an infinite coinfinite set at $W_\infty$. The arrows $V\to W$, for every pair of objects, are the surjections $f$ of the bases with $f[E_V]\subseteq E_W$. The symmetry group at $V$ consists of the permutations preserving $E_V$ setwise. Every object carries the ideal of finite sets. Evaluation point: $1_{W_1}$.

meets.finitely-pinned-domains: The domains hold every symmetric intension pinned down by a finite set, and every entity in them is one.
meets.no-atoms-anywhere: At every object a nonzero proposition pinned down by $S$ and containing $h$ contains arrows agreeing with $h$ on $S$ that collapse and that separate two uncoloured points outside $S$.
meets.finite-pinning: Every object carries the ideal of finite sets.
meets.surjective-arrows: Every arrow is a surjection of the bases.
meets.transposable: For finite $N$, the property of being uncoloured and outside $N$ (at an arrow $h$, the points outside $h[N]$ and the target's colour set) is pinned down by $N$ and symmetric, its extension is infinite, and the transposition of any member with another fixes $N$ pointwise, preserves the colour set and fixes the property.
meets.separable-collapses: Pairs of uncoloured points; for any two disjoint such pairs some surjection fixing the colour set collapses the one and not the other.
meets.hull-conditions: With $M_0=E_{W_1}$: (B1) prescriptions agreeing with $h^{\prime}$ on $P$ and with $h$ on $Q$ agree on $P\cap Q\subseteq M$ and send coloured points to coloured ones, so they extend to an arrow, the uncoloured complement being infinite; (B2) a permutation fixing $N\supseteq E_{W_1}$ pointwise can move the finitely many uncoloured points of $P$ outside $N$ off $Q$.

arguments.text: At $W_1$ (indeed at every $W_m$), at every type. If a set $D$ of tuples is closed under the endomorphisms fixing a finite $S\supseteq E_{W_1}$ pointwise, then $h\mapsto h[D]$ is pinned down by $S$ and symmetric, so it is in the domain and rigid: for $h,h^{\prime}$ agreeing on $S$ and $a\in D$ pinned down by $M$, an endomorphism $u$ fixing $S$ with $hu=h^{\prime}$ on $M$ exists, since every coloured point is in $S$, and $h^{\prime}\cdot a=h\cdot(u\cdot a)$. A weakly rigid $F$ pinned down by $S$ has such an extension by weak persistence, so it is that exact image.

At type $et$. At $W_\infty$ let $U$ have extension $E_V$ at every arrow into $V$: pinned down by $\varnothing$, symmetric, weakly persistent by colour preservation, and weakly inextensible, since a test necessary of each coloured point and pinned down by $N$ is met, at any $h$, by each $y\in E_V$, as some arrow agreeing with $h$ on $N$ sends a coloured point outside $N$ to $y$. It is not rigid: along an arrow $c$ to $W_1$ it has extension $\{a\}$, $E_{W_1}=\{a\}$, but it does not entail the haecceity of $a$, which along any arrow back to $W_\infty$ has a single instance while $c\cdot U$ has infinitely many. So □Tame Rigidity fails. And at $W_1$ the property of being a weakly rigid relation of type $et$ entailing the universal one, whose actual instances are rigid by Tame Rigidity, does not entail the property of being rigid, $U$ being a counterexample along an arrow to $W_\infty$: Weakly Rigid Power fails.

At every type. At $W_1$, let $F$ be rigid and $Y\le h\cdot F$ rigid at the target of $h$. If the target is some $W_m$, an arrow $j$ agreeing with $h$ on a finite $N$ and bijective off it, and a set of instances of $F$ closed under the endomorphisms fixing a finite set, give a rigid $X\le F$ with $j\cdot X=Y$. If it is $W_\infty$, pass through a $W_r$ whose colours map bijectively onto finitely many colours of $W_\infty$ containing the relevant ones, and return. So the property of being rigid and below $F$ is weakly inextensible, hence rigid by Tame Rigidity. With □BF every universal relation is rigid, and Rigid Power at it is Rigid Rigidity; so Rigid Power is necessary (rigid-rigidity-and-rigid-power-imply-necessary-rigid-power).

At type $et$, for $\lambda x\, .\,x
e a$ with $a$ the coloured point of $W_1$. A weakly rigid coextensive $G$, pinned down by a finite $S
i a$, holds of an uncoloured $x
otin S$; an endomorphism fixing $S$ and sending $x$ to $a$ fixes $G$, so weak persistence puts $a$ in $G$'s extension.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, after Cian Dorr’s observation that a choice over the individuals cannot be finitely pinned down
arguments.text: At the types $(e\to t)$ and $e$. Let $U:=\lambda Xy\, .\,Xy\lor\neg\exists z\, .\,Xz$, a closed term, hence in the domain, and serial. A functional subrelation $S$ of $U$ would lie in the domain at the evaluation object, so it is symmetric and pinned down by a finite set $N$. Two facts about such an $S$ (Dorr, draft, Lemma 19(iv)): every $g\in G$ fixing $N$ pointwise satisfies $g^{[\sigma]}S=S$, and symmetry gives $\langle gA,gy,g\rangle\in S$ whenever $\langle A,y,1\rangle\in S$; together, $\langle gA,gy,1\rangle\in S$. Now let $A$ be the property the condition gives for $N$. Its extension is nonempty, so $S$ relates $A$ at the identity to some $y$ in its extension. The condition gives a member $g$ of the symmetry group that fixes $N$ pointwise, fixes $A$ and moves $y$ to some $gy\ne y$, so $S$ relates $A$ to $gy$ as well, and $S$ is not functional at the identity arrow. The well-ordering of the individuals that Cian Dorr had in mind is refuted by the same two facts, but the direct route needs no derivation of a well-ordering from Relational Choice in C.

revisions.note: The members' seven copies, which differed in the property $A$ and the transposition, stated once; each member's $A$ and transposition moved to the condition transposable. The qualitative-contrast model's second argument (OpenAI Codex, 24 September) was dropped.

revisions.note: The condition transposable no longer mentions the finite set $M$ or the pinning of $A$ by $N\cup M$: the argument uses only that $g$ fixes $N$, the set pinning down $S$, and that $A$ is in the domain. So $g$ is now said to fix $N$ pointwise. Proved in Lean.

conditions.text: For each finite set $N$ of individuals at the evaluation object, some property $A$ in the domain has a nonempty extension there, and each individual $y$ in that extension is moved by a member of the symmetry group that fixes $N$ pointwise and fixes $A$.
conditions.reason: For finite $N$, the property of being uncoloured and outside $N$ (at an arrow $h$, the points outside $h[N]$ and the target's colour set) is pinned down by $N$ and symmetric, its extension is infinite, and the transposition of any member with another fixes $N$ pointwise, preserves the colour set and fixes the property.

settings.monoid: free-words

models.notes: The symmetric all-surjections model of Dorr's draft with pinning sets of size at most $\kappa$ in a base of size $\kappa^+$, a free-word factor on the arrows, and Σ glued along the words. It adds Logical Necessity to that model's package: Logical Necessity holds with □Boolean Completeness, □BF and □Weakly Rigid Power, while Actuality, Vicinity and Relational Choice fail. Finite pinning would not do, since the gluing absorbs the pinning sets of infinitely many witnesses, and nor would the surjections alone, since a later collapse merges any gluing sites among the points. The variant with an idempotent in the monoid factor keeps all of this but BF; the variant with the members of $U$ as individuals adds the Axioms of Infinity.
models.definition: Fix an infinite cardinal $\kappa\ge|\Sigma|$, a set $U$ of size $\kappa^+$, the monoid $S$ of surjections $U\to U$, and a monoid $K$: $K$ is the free monoid $W$ of finite words on an alphabet of size $\kappa$, with empty word $\varepsilon$. The arrows of the one object are the pairs $(k,s)$ with $k\in K$ and $s\in S$, composed by $(k,s)(k',s'):=(kk',s\circ s')$; the evaluation point is $1:=(1_K,\mathrm{id})$, and the symmetry group is $\{1_K\}\times\operatorname{Sym}(U)$. There is a single individual, fixed by every arrow; $U$ only supplies the pinning sets and the symmetries. A relational domain consists of the profiles $F$, assigning to each arrow a set of argument tuples, that are pinned down by a set $N\subseteq U$ of size at most $\kappa$ ($F_{(k,s)}$ depends only on $k$ and $s|_N$) and symmetric ($F_{(k,\pi s)}=\pi\cdot F_{(k,s)}$ for every permutation $\pi$ of $U$). Transport is $(h\cdot F)_j:=F_{jh}$. Σ is interpreted by gluing: individual constants denote distinct individuals (or the only one), and each relational constant glues, along fresh final letters of the word coordinate, chosen interpretations witnessing every satisfiable $\mathcal L(\Sigma)$-sentence (see the write-up).

met.one-object-action-model: One object, with the semantics of Dorr's intensional action models: a formula holds at an arrow iff it holds at $1$ with its parameters transported.
met.no-actuality-anywhere: One object, so Actuality, a closed pure sentence, holds at every world iff at the identity, where it fails (recorded in this group's verdicts).
met.infinitely-many-propositions: The propositions $q_{a,b}$ of the argument atomlessness are pairwise distinct for distinct pairs.
met.right-cancellative-factor: The free monoid is right cancellative.
met.one-individual: There is a single individual at every world.

settings.construction: A symmetric ideally-full model on two objects, $W_0$ with base $\mathbb N$ and $W_1$ with base $\{0\}$, the arrows being all maps between the bases; write $!$ for the arrow $W_0\to W_1$ and $c_n$ for the arrow $W_1\to W_0$ with value $n$. The symmetry group is $\operatorname{Sym}(\mathbb N)$ at $W_0$ and trivial at $W_1$. Both objects carry the ideal of finite sets. Evaluation point: $1_{W_0}$.

meets.finitely-pinned-domains: The domains hold every symmetric intension pinned down by a finite set, and every entity in them is one.
meets.finite-pinning: Both objects carry the ideal of finite sets.
meets.transposable: For finite $N$, the property of not belonging to $N$ (at an arrow $h$ into $W_0$, the points outside $h[N]$) is symmetric and pinned down by $N$, with an infinite extension; the transposition of any member with another point outside $N$ fixes $N$ pointwise and the property.
meets.separable-collapses: The pairs $\{2k,2k+1\}$; for any two of them some map of $\mathbb N$ collapses the one and is injective elsewhere.
meets.hull-conditions: With $M_0=\varnothing$: (B1) every map of $\mathbb N$ is an arrow, so prescriptions agreeing with $h^{\prime}$ on $P$ and with $h$ on $Q$, which agree on $P\cap Q\subseteq M$, extend to an arrow, and there is only one arrow into $W_1$; (B2) a permutation fixing $N$ pointwise moves the finitely many points of $P$ outside $N$ off $Q$.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, after Cian Dorr’s observation that a choice over the individuals cannot be finitely pinned down
arguments.text: At the types $(e\to t)$ and $e$. Let $U:=\lambda Xy\, .\,Xy\lor\neg\exists z\, .\,Xz$, a closed term, hence in the domain, and serial. A functional subrelation $S$ of $U$ would lie in the domain at the evaluation object, so it is symmetric and pinned down by a finite set $N$. Two facts about such an $S$ (Dorr, draft, Lemma 19(iv)): every $g\in G$ fixing $N$ pointwise satisfies $g^{[\sigma]}S=S$, and symmetry gives $\langle gA,gy,g\rangle\in S$ whenever $\langle A,y,1\rangle\in S$; together, $\langle gA,gy,1\rangle\in S$. Now let $A$ be the property the condition gives for $N$. Its extension is nonempty, so $S$ relates $A$ at the identity to some $y$ in its extension. The condition gives a member $g$ of the symmetry group that fixes $N$ pointwise, fixes $A$ and moves $y$ to some $gy\ne y$, so $S$ relates $A$ to $gy$ as well, and $S$ is not functional at the identity arrow. The well-ordering of the individuals that Cian Dorr had in mind is refuted by the same two facts, but the direct route needs no derivation of a well-ordering from Relational Choice in C.
