settings.construction: A symmetric ideally-full intensional action model over two objects, each a copy of the natural numbers. The arrows from the first object to itself are the permutations; the arrows from the first to the second and from the second to itself are all the functions; there are none back. Both symmetry groups are all the permutations. The first object carries the ideal of finite sets, the second the improper ideal, so at the second object every symmetric intension belongs to the domain. The evaluation point is the identity arrow on the first object.

meets.moving-proposition-stabilizers: At the first object choose distinct pinning points $a,b,c$ outside a given finite $N$ and take $g=(a\ c)$. The proposition $p_{ab}(w)\leftrightarrow w(a)=w(b)$ on every outgoing arrow is symmetric and pinned by $\{a,b\}$. It is false on the arrows back to the first object, which are permutations. An arrow to the second object is any function and may identify $a,b$ while keeping $c$ distinct, distinguishing $p_{ab}$ from $g\cdot p_{ab}=p_{cb}$. Only the evaluation object's supports must be finite; the second object's improper ideal causes no difficulty. The points here are pinning-carrier points, also when the individual domain is a singleton. Source: OpenAI Codex, prompted by Daniel Kodsi, 22 October 2026, singleton applications §2; recorded 30 October 2026.
meets.infinitely-many-orbits-everywhere: With the base as individuals, at both objects the properties of being one of a finite set of individuals lie in infinitely many orbits, symmetries preserving the size of the set. With one individual: at both objects the propositions that an arrow into the second object is injective on a given set of $n$ points lie in distinct orbits for distinct $n$, the arrows into the second object being all the functions.
meets.finitely-pinned-domains: The first object, the evaluation point, carries the ideal of finite sets, so its domains hold every symmetric intension pinned down by a finite set, and every entity in them is one.
meets.collapse-onto-point: Take $F:=\lambda x\, .\,x\ne a$, so $p\notin F_h$. $h$ is a function from the first object to the second that is constant on $N\cup\{a\}$; the symmetry group of the second object is all permutations.
meets.transposable: $M=\emptyset$, and for $N$ the property of not belonging to $N$, at the first object, where the domain is symmetric and finitely pinned: the transposition of $y$ with another individual of the first object outside $N$ lies in its symmetry group.
meets.separable-collapses: The pairs $\{n,m\}$ of individuals of the first object: a function into the second object that collapses $n$ with $m$ and nothing else is an arrow, all functions being arrows there.
meets.actual-world-isolated: The actual-world proposition is the set of arrows from the first object to itself, all permutations, in the domain by the source argument for Actuality; no arrow from the second object returns to the first.
meets.actuality-contingent: The actual-world proposition, the arrows from the first object to itself, is in the domain; at every world an arrow into the second object leads outside it, and such an arrow carries it to the empty set.
meets.irreversible-arrow: An arrow into the second object: no arrow returns from there to the first.
meets.hull-conditions: With $M_0=\emptyset$ (the draft's argument for this model, Proposition 40): an arrow to the first object is a permutation and so separated by any set, while for arrows to the second, splicing is unconstrained, every function being an arrow; points are moved off a finite set by a permutation of the first object.

models.notes: The point of the model is that boxed Boolean Completeness and boxed Actuality, and so Weak Rigid Comprehension, do not yield Rigid Comprehension. The gap is exactly the leading box of the inextensibility conjunct. The status of the unboxed BF schema at the base world is left unknown here: the draft's working comments report that higher-type instances fail there, which would make the schema fail, but its text does not. The source is a work in progress. Everything that implies these fails with them.

models.definition:
The arrows are all $27$ maps from $X$ to itself, so that the permutations are arrows and the symmetry condition is Dorr's; the collapses are the three constant maps. The arrows act on a three-element set $X$, and $G$ is the group of all its permutations, which are arrows in every member. An intension $D$ of a relational type is admitted exactly when it is symmetric: $\langle\bar x,h\rangle\in D$ implies $\langle g\cdot\bar x,g\circ h\rangle\in D$ for every $g\in G$, where $g$ acts on individuals as itself and on entities of higher types by relabelling (Dorr's Definition 17). At a collapse $c_i$, the constant map with value $i$, it says that $D(c_{g(i)})=g\cdot D(c_i)$. Every such domain is finite and closed under the operations of C: each $g$ is an automorphism of the whole structure, and every parameter transported along a collapse is fixed by $G$, so the extension at a collapse of any definable intension is invariant. The member has one object, $X$. Evaluation point: the sole object, at the identity arrow.

Individuals, fixed for this record: the individuals are the three elements of $X$, acted on by the arrows themselves.

Interpretation of Σ, fixed for this record: every constant of Σ is relational, and each denotes the top element of its type.

met.finitely-many-arrows-everywhere: The arrows are maps among the three-element set $X$ and, in the two-object member, the one-point $W_0$: finitely many out of every object.
met.finitely-many-individuals-everywhere: The individuals are the three elements of $X$ or one, and in the two-object member the single point of $W_0$.
met.rigid-haecceity-disjunctions: For any set $E$ the intension $k\mapsto k\cdot E$ is symmetric (as in the argument for Rigid Comprehension), so in the domain, and it is the smallest symmetric intension containing the transports of the members of $E$; so a weakly inextensible relation lies below it over its extension, and a rigid one equals it (as in the argument for Tame Rigidity).
met.symmetric-domains: The domains hold exactly the symmetric intensions; every intension is pinned down by the finite set $X$ of all individuals.
met.extensionally-full: Any set $S$ of tuples at the identity is the extension there of a symmetric intension: put $S$ at the identity, $g\cdot S$ at each permutation $g$, and the empty set at every other arrow.
met.finitely-many-propositions: The propositions are the symmetric sets of arrows, finitely many since there are finitely many arrows.
met.actuality-contingent: The actual-world proposition $a$ is the orbit of the identity under the symmetry group, the set of permutations; it is in the domain, true, and entails every truth, since a symmetric true proposition contains the identity and so its orbit. It is necessary at no world, since every world sees a collapse, which lies outside $a$; and a collapse $c$ does not fix it, since $l\circ c$ is a collapse for every $l$, so $c\cdot a$ is empty.
met.one-object-action-model: An action model with a single object.
met.irreversible-arrow: A collapse $c$: $l\circ c$ is a collapse for every arrow $l$, so from $c$ no world in $a$ is seen.
met.actual-world-isolated: $a$, the orbit of the identity, is in the domain and entails every truth; from a world outside $a$, a non-permutation $h$, every $l\circ h$ is again a non-permutation, outside $a$.
met.construction-individuals: The individuals are the three elements the arrows act on.
met.homogeneous-individuals: Relabelling by a permutation of $X$ is an automorphism of the model, carrying each individual to its image.
met.collapse-onto-point: Take an individual $a$ and $F:=\lambda x\, .\,x\ne a$, whose extension at every arrow $h$ is $X\setminus\{h(a)\}$, nonempty. For any $N$, the collapse $c_p$ onto any $p$ sends $N\cup\{a\}$ to $p$, and the transposition $\sigma$ of the two individuals other than $p$ fixes $p$, moves every $y\ne p$, and has $\sigma\circ c_p=c_p$ an arrow.
met.sigma-apart: The construction does not mention Σ.

models.definition:

Every such domain is finite and closed under the operations of C: each $g$ is an automorphism of the whole structure, and every parameter transported along a collapse is fixed by $G$, so the extension at a collapse of any definable intension is invariant. The member has one object, $X$. Evaluation point: the sole object, at the identity arrow.

Individuals, fixed for this record: the individuals are the three elements of $X$, acted on by the arrows themselves.

met.finitely-many-individuals-everywhere: The individuals are the three elements of $X$ or one, and in the two-object member the single point of $W_0$.
met.rigid-haecceity-disjunctions: For any set $E$ the intension $k\mapsto k\cdot E$ is symmetric (as in the argument for Rigid Comprehension), so in the domain, and it is the smallest symmetric intension containing the transports of the members of $E$; so a weakly inextensible relation lies below it over its extension, and a rigid one equals it (as in the argument for Tame Rigidity).
met.symmetric-domains: The domains hold exactly the symmetric intensions; every intension is pinned down by the finite set $X$ of all individuals.
met.extensionally-full: Any set $S$ of tuples at the identity is the extension there of a symmetric intension: put $S$ at the identity, $g\cdot S$ at each permutation $g$, and the empty set at every other arrow.

met.irreversible-arrow: A collapse $c$: $l\circ c$ is a collapse for every arrow $l$, so from $c$ no world in $a$ is seen.
met.actual-world-isolated: $a$, the orbit of the identity, is in the domain and entails every truth; from a world outside $a$, a non-permutation $h$, every $l\circ h$ is again a non-permutation, outside $a$.

met.homogeneous-individuals: Relabelling by a permutation of $X$ is an automorphism of the model, carrying each individual to its image.

references.note: The symmetry condition, here imposed on a full model over three individuals.

models.notes: The propositions are $\bot$, the set $P$ of the six permutations, the set of the three collapses, and $\top$: the symmetry condition makes a proposition contain all the permutations or none, and all the collapses or none. $P$ is the strongest true proposition, the true atom. So the propositional structure is that of the full model on the two-arrow idempotent monoid, the quotient of this one by the symmetries, and the relabellings act trivially on it; Intensional Choice fails only at type $e$, by the shared argument, and holds at type $t$, where every proposition is fixed by the relabellings. BF also fails at type $e$ when there are three individuals: the image intension $h\mapsto h(X)$, $X$ at a permutation and $\{i\}$ at $c_i$, is symmetric, holds necessarily of every individual, yet is not necessarily universal. That failure, and the failure of ND at type $e$ from two individuals that a collapse identifies, are derived from the group's arguments at type $t$ and are not recorded separately.

arguments.text: At type $e\to t$. The property $F:=\lambda y\, .\,y\ne x$ has extension $\varnothing$ at $1_{W_0}$ and $X\setminus\{n\}$ at $h_n$. Its pairs form one orbit, the transposition fixing $n$ swapping the two individuals other than $n$, so $F$ is an atom. At $h_n$ it is instantiated and its transport has value $X\setminus\{n\}$ at $1_X$, two individuals, so it is not an atom there: the property of being one of them lies strictly below it. So $F$ is an atom and not a self-atom; and since $F$ is possible and is the only possible property below it, Self-Atomicity fails at type $e\to t$ too. In the object language, $F$ entails that there are two things each of whose haecceities entails $F$.

references.note: Verifies the failure of Rigid Comprehension under the hypotheses; the boxed forms of Boolean Completeness and BF are not formalized there.
Definitions of intensional action models and the rigidity criterion used in the verification.
The proposition this model refutes.

models.definition: An intensional action model with one individual. The objects are the root $o$, $s$, $u$, and $n$ for each $n\ge1$; besides identities the arrows are $h_s\colon o\to s$, $j\colon s\to u$, $h_u:=j\circ h_s$ and $h_n\colon o\to n$, so the root reaches each object by exactly one arrow and worlds may be identified with objects. The domains at $s$, $u$ and each $n$ are full. Identify the domains at the terminal objects $u$ and $n$ with one finite full type structure $M$ over one individual. Fix a non-principal ultrafilter $\mathcal U$ on the positive integers. At the root, an element of a relational type is any element of the full intension space whose extension at $u$ is the $\mathcal U$-limit of its extensions at the worlds $n$; its extensions at $o$, at $s$ and at each $n$ are unconstrained. So a root proposition is any choice of truth values at $o$, $s$ and the $n$s, with its value at $u$ fixed as the limit. Evaluation point: the root. Interpretation of Σ, fixed for this record: every constant of Σ is relational, and each denotes the top element of its type.

meets.finite-reachable-object: The objects $u$ and $n$ carry one finite full type structure over one individual, and the root, extensionally full with continuum many propositions, has a real number structure of propositions.
meets.sigma-top: This is the interpretation the definition fixes.
meets.one-individual: The definition fixes one individual, at every world.
meets.extensionally-full: At the root an element's extension at $o$ is unconstrained, so every set of tuples is the extension there of an element of the domain; the domains at $s$, $u$ and each $n$ are full.
meets.infinitely-many-propositions: A root proposition is any choice of truth values at $o$, $s$ and the $n$s, so there are infinitely many.
meets.fewer-propositions-after: The root has at least three distinct propositions, while each world $n$, which sees only itself, has two.
meets.actual-world-isolated: The proposition true at $o$ alone (false at $s$, at every $n$, and so in the limit at $u$) is in the root domain and entails every truth, every true proposition being true at $o$; no world other than $o$ sees $o$.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, 25 October 2026
arguments.text: At the root, a proposition is a choice of truth values at $o$, $s$ and the $n$s, its value at $u$ the limit. Let $P$ be true at two worlds $n_1,n_2$ and false elsewhere, so false at $u$. It is possible. It is a self-atom: at $n_1$ and $n_2$, which see only themselves, it becomes the top proposition of the two-element domain, an atom. It is not an atom, since the proposition true at $n_1$ alone lies strictly below it. So Self-atoms are atoms (type t) fails at the root.

At the root, the map sending an element to its extensions at $o$, $s$ and the $n$s is an order isomorphism onto a product of powerset algebras, the extension at $u$ being recomputed as the limit. So every family has a meet and a join, computed coordinatewise except at $u$, and every nonzero element lies above an atom with one tuple in one free coordinate. The other worlds carry finite full powerset algebras. Hence Boolean Completeness and Atomicity hold at every world and every relational type.
Every arrow acts surjectively at every type, so BF holds at every world (write-up, Proposition 4).

At type $t\to t$ (write-up, Theorem 6). Let $A_0$ be the root propositions false at $s$ and at $u$, and $X$ the property with extension $A_0$ at the root and empty extensions elsewhere. A persistent property coextensive with $X$ contains both truth values at every world $n$, since members of $A_0$ take both values there; the limit condition then puts the true proposition in its extension at $u$. Rigidity at the root forces its extension at $s$ to be the proposition false at $s$ and $u$, and rigidity at $s$, tested against that proposition's haecceity, forbids the true proposition at $u$. The least upper bound of the haecceities of the $X$s, the candidate rigid coextension in the proof of Proposition 2.11, is weakly rigid but fails the rigidity condition at $s$. The model therefore refutes Proposition 2.11 (necessary-atomicity-completeness-bf-imply-rigid-comprehension); the gap is the normalization step of n. 42, part (iv), which the write-up runs inside the model (§5).

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, at Cian Dorr's suggestion
arguments.text: At the root: given $F$ with $\Box\exists x\, .\,Fx$, let $G$ pick the least element of $F$ at $o$, $s$ and each $n$, under fixed well-orderings, the same ordering of $M^\sigma$ at every $n$. The sets $\{n : G(n)=\{a\}\}$ for $a\in M^\sigma$ partition the positive integers into finitely many pieces, so exactly one is in $\mathcal U$, say for $a_0$; then $\lim_{\mathcal U}G(n)=\{a_0\}$, and $a_0\in F(u)=\lim_{\mathcal U}F(n)$. Setting $G(u):=\{a_0\}$ puts $G$ in the root domain, with $G\le F$ and every extension a singleton. At $s$, $u$ and the $n$ the domains are full, and the well-ordering argument (arguments/intensional-choice-well-ordering) applies there, so the boxed form holds too.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
arguments.text:
At every relational type and every world. Write $k\cdot E$ for the transport of a set $E$ of tuples along an arrow $k$, and $X_0(E)$ for the relation $k\mapsto k\cdot E$, the disjunction of the haecceities of the members of $E$. At $s$, $u$ and each $n$ the model is full, and Rigid Power holds there as in every full model (arguments/rigid-power-tight). At the root, call a set $E$ of root tuples admissible when $X_0(E)$ is in the domain, that is, when $h_u\cdot E$ is the $\mathcal U$-limit of the sets $h_n\cdot E$ (subsets of a finite set, so the limit is the set taken at $\mathcal U$-many $n$). Since each member of $E$ has its value at $u$ as the limit of its values at the $n$, $h_u\cdot E$ is always included in that limit; and every finite $E$ is admissible, the finitely many limits being attained together at $\mathcal U$-many $n$.

(1) The rigid relations at the root are exactly the $X_0(E)$ with $E$ admissible. Such an $X_0(E)$, being in the domain, is rigid: it is persistent, and at every world $w$ it is $X_0(w\cdot E)$ there, included in every $X$ that necessarily holds of the members of $w\cdot E$. Conversely let $Y$ be rigid with extension $E$. Persistence gives $Y_k\supseteq k\cdot E$ at every arrow $k$. The root element $X$ with extensions $E$ at $o$, $h_s\cdot E$ at $s$, $h_n\cdot E$ at each $n$, and the limit at $u$, necessarily holds of every member of $E$ (its extension at $u$ includes $h_u\cdot E$, by the above), so inextensibility at the root gives $Y\le X$: $Y$ has extension $h_s\cdot E$ at $s$ and $h_n\cdot E$ at each $n$. Rigidity at $s$, in the full model on $s$ and $u$, makes the extension of $Y$ at $u$ the transport $j\cdot(h_s\cdot E)=h_u\cdot E$, and since $Y$ is in the domain that is also the limit of the $h_n\cdot E$. So $E$ is admissible and $Y=X_0(E)$.

(2) Let $F=X_0(S)$ be rigid at the root, and $P:=\lambda X\, .\,\operatorname{Rigid}(X)\land X\le F$, in the domain since it is definable from $F$. By (1) its extension at the root is $E_P:=\{X_0(T) : T\subseteq S\text{ admissible}\}$, and at a world $k$ among $s$, $u$ and the $n$ it is the set of rigid relations there below $k\cdot F$, which in those full models are the $X_0(T')$ with $T'\subseteq k\cdot S$. Each such $T'$ is finite, the domains there being finite, so it is $k\cdot T$ for a finite, hence admissible, $T\subseteq S$ (one preimage for each member), and $X_0(T')=k\cdot X_0(T)$. So the extension of $P$ at every $k$ is $k\cdot E_P$: $P=X_0(E_P)$, a rigid relation. Hence Rigid Power holds at the root, and so at every world.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
arguments.text: At the root by the general argument transversal-choice-extensionally-full, the model being extensionally full there; at $s$, $u$ and each $n$ by the same argument, those worlds' domains being full and so extensionally full.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
arguments.text: The category is a poset: no non-identity arrow has a retraction. The actual-world proposition is in the domain at every object (at the root the proposition true at $o$ alone; the other objects are full), so $\Box_{\ne}p$ holds at an identity iff $p$ contains $\Diamond\{1\}=\{1\}$, i.e. iff $p$ is true: $\Box_{\ne}$ is the identity operator at every object, hence so are $\hat{\hat\Box}$ and $\Box_5$, and every truth is 5-necessary everywhere.

withdrawn.reason: The step from the equality of transports to membership in the carrier by inextensibility does not follow: inextensibility bounds a rigid carrier from above, by the transports of its actual instances, and puts nothing new into its actual extension.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Zachary Goodsell
arguments.text: At the root, at type $t$. A root proposition is any choice of truth values at $o$, $s$ and the $n$s, so the root propositions are continuum many, and the root being extensionally full there is a real number structure of propositions at it: its carrier, order, sum, product and natural numbers are the extensions at $o$ of root entities, and every subset of the carrier is the extension of a subproperty, so it is complete. A rigid one, necessarily a real number structure, is impossible: transport along $h_1$ reads only a proposition's value at $1$, and the root proposition differing from $p$ at $o$ alone is in the domain, so no proposition is determined by its transport along $h_1$; but an instance $x$ of a rigid carrier $X$ is, since for $y$ with $h_1\cdot y=h_1\cdot x$ persistence gives $h_1\cdot y\in X_{h_1}$, inextensibility $Xy$, and necessary distinctness $y=x$.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, auditing the withdrawn arguments for the failure of Analytic Necessitism
arguments.text: Let $V$ be the object of the condition, with finitely many entities of every type, and let a real number structure exist at the evaluation point. It is possible, so the antecedent of Analytic Necessitism holds. Any structure that is necessarily a real number structure would be one at the worlds into $V$, where every type is finite, but an ordered field has infinitely many distinct elements. So the consequent fails.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Zachary Goodsell
arguments.text: The numbers at a type $\sigma$ are the instances of $\mathbb N_\sigma$, the least property containing $\mathbf 0_\sigma$ and closed under $\operatorname{Suc}_\sigma$ (Background); the numerals $\mathbf 0_\sigma$, $\operatorname{Suc}_\sigma\mathbf 0_\sigma,\ldots$ are closed terms, so each denotes at every object, and transport along an arrow carries its denotation at the source to its denotation at the target. At any object $v$ reachable from the evaluation point, extensional fullness gives a property whose extension at $v$ is exactly the numerals there; it contains $\mathbf 0_\sigma$ and is closed under successor, so the numbers at $v$ are exactly the numerals, every numeral being an instance of every inductive property. Persistence of $\mathbb N_\sigma$ and, given $\Box I^*_\sigma$, the necessary distinctness of the numbers are theorems of C (the proof of necessary-rigid-comprehension-implies-arithmetic-necessitism). Inextensibility, $\Box\forall X\,.\,(\forall n\,.\,\mathbb N_\sigma n\to\Box Xn)\to\mathbb N_\sigma\le X$: at a reachable $v$ and for an arrow $j$ from $v$ to $u$, the numbers at $u$ are the numerals there, which are the transports along $j$ of the numbers at $v$, so any $X$ that necessarily holds of the numbers at $v$ holds at $u$ of the numbers there. So $\mathbb N_\sigma$ is rigid, and Arithmetic Necessitism holds at every type. No choice is used.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Zachary Goodsell
arguments.text: Let $v$ be any object reachable from the evaluation point and $\mathfrak R$ a real number structure at $v$ (Background, Analysis). Its completeness is tested against the subproperties of its carrier present at $v$, and by extensional fullness every subset of the carrier's extension there is the extension at the identity of one of them; so the carrier, with the extensions of $\le$, $+$ and $\times$, is a complete ordered field in the sense of the metatheory and, by Huntington's theorem, a theorem of ZF, is isomorphic to the real numbers. For the same reason the extension of $N$, the least subproperty containing $0$ and closed under adding $1$, is its set of natural numbers, that set being the extension of a subproperty. A second-order analytical sentence $A(\mathfrak R)$ quantifies over the relations among entities of the structure's type at $v$, applied to the structure's elements, and their extensions at the identity are all the relations on the carrier, again by extensional fullness. So $A(\mathfrak R)$ holds at $v$ exactly when $A$ holds in the real numbers under full second-order semantics, which depends neither on $v$ nor on $\mathfrak R$. Hence $\Box\forall\mathfrak R\,.\,\operatorname{Real}_\sigma(\mathfrak R)\to A(\mathfrak R)$ holds when $A$ is true of the reals and $\Box\forall\mathfrak R\,.\,\operatorname{Real}_\sigma(\mathfrak R)\to\neg A(\mathfrak R)$ when it is false: every instance of the Necessity of Second-Order Analysis holds, and with it the Necessity of Analysis and the Non-contingency of the Continuum Hypothesis, as recorded. No choice is used.

arguments.text: The natural numbers are the finite cardinalities at type $e$ (Background, after Goodsell), and with a single individual there are three: $\mathbf{0}_e$, true of the empty property; $\operatorname{Suc}_e\mathbf{0}_e$, true of the universal one; and the empty cardinality, which is $\operatorname{Suc}_e$ of the second and of itself. By extensional fullness the property of being one of these three is in the domain, so it bounds natural numberhood. A countable property therefore has at most three members in its extension, and their join is its least upper bound.

models.name: Henkin ultraproduct: countable full S5 models with n individuals

certificate.produced_by: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), prompted by Daniel Kodsi, 23 October 2026
certificate.recorded_by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, 25 October 2026

sources: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), prompted by Daniel Kodsi, Forcing Possibilism, Choice and Infinity, research note of 23 October 2026, §§2, 5 (unpaginated), in Daniel Kodsi's submission of 24 October 2026 (branch classicism-results-2026-10-24 of github.com/dkodsi/Logical-Maps, proofs/forcing-possibilism.md).

references.note: Full action models; the factors are full S5 models with countably many worlds.

arguments.text: In each factor there are infinitely many propositions, and the finite cardinalities, the domains being full, are the standard ones, so the Axiom of Infinity (type $t$) is true in each factor, hence in $M$.

In each factor the propositions are the $2^{\aleph_0}$ subsets of $\mathbb N$, and every relation on each domain is present. An infinite complete Boolean algebra has a countably infinite antichain, so at least $2^{\aleph_0}$ elements; so a complete Boolean algebra represented in a factor that is Dedekind-finite or strictly smaller than the propositions is finite, with $k$ atoms say, and is isomorphic to the propositions below any proposition true at exactly $k$ worlds, which is not $\top$. So each instance holds in every factor, hence in $M$.

models.notes: The Axiom of Infinity at $t$ with the Infinity Schema at $e$ does not imply the Axiom of Infinity at $e$, nor its possibility, even with Forcing Possibilism, □Functional Choice, C5 and BF.
models.definition:
For $n\ge1$ let $M_n$ be the full S5 model with the worlds $\mathbb N$ and $n$ individuals: the full action model on a category in which there is exactly one arrow between any two objects, with the same $n$ individuals at every object, fixed by every arrow, evaluated at one object. Regard each $M_n$ as a many-sorted first-order structure, with a sort for each type, application, the logical constants, the constants of Σ, and a predicate $T$ on the sort of $t$ for truth at the evaluation object. Let $U$ be a nonprincipal ultrafilter on the positive integers, and $M:=\prod_nM_n/U$, the evaluation point being the class of the factors' evaluation objects. By Łoś's theorem a first-order sentence holds in $M$ iff it holds in $M_n$ for $U$-many $n$. $M$ is a Henkin model of C, and a sentence of the object language is true in $M$ iff it is true in $U$-many $M_n$ (see the write-up). It is not full.

Interpretation of Σ, fixed for these records: every constant of Σ is relational, and each denotes the top element of its type in every factor, hence in $M$.

met.sigma-top: This is the interpretation the definition fixes.

models.name: Wreath-supported cofinite entrance over old and new individuals
models.definition: Use the base-individual symmetric old/new tail: E has individuals N, O has N disjoint union N', E-to-E arrows are all injections, E-to-O arrows have old range, O-to-E arrows are all injections, and O-to-O arrows are sort-preserving permutations G_O or old-range injections. Keep its symmetric finitely pinned domains. Add root R with individuals N, arrows y_u and x_u corresponding to old arrows out of E, and distinct replicas z_(n,g):R-to-O for n in N and g in G_O. A good O symmetry postcomposes z_(n,g) to z_(n,kg); the first exiting arrow h sends it to y_(hgi) or x_(hgi), where i:E-to-O is old inclusion. At each relational type, a root entity has a supported current table, an admitted E-entity a, and finitely supported O tables C_n eventually equal to a_i. Its replica transports have G_O rows g[C_n] and exiting rows a_(hi). Root support uses global old permutations, permutations of the replica indices, and independent new-individual permutations at each replica. The writeup gives the exact recursive domain, support, action and transport rules. Evaluate at R.

arguments.by: GPT-6 Astra, prompted by Daniel Kodsi
arguments.text: The global old and local new wreath actions preserve the category and recursive domains. The union tables of an admitted family are constant outside its finite replica support; independent local new permutations make the common table invariant under every new permutation, and global old permutations give a common finite old pin. The resulting coordinate union is admitted and is its least upper bound. Every nonzero entity contains a singleton free-coordinate atom, whose nonzero old transports are a strong proposition conjoined with a tuple haecceity. They decide every relation in the full target domain. See §§1–5 of the writeup.

arguments.by: GPT-6 Astra, prompted by Daniel Kodsi
arguments.text: Root Strong Atomicity gives root Atomicity. At both unchanged old objects the finite-pin stable-class proof supplies all-type Atomicity. Their proposition algebras have four and eight elements, so are complete; root Boolean Completeness includes type t. These are all possible target objects, yielding precisely the two necessary verdicts. See §§5–6.

arguments.by: GPT-6 Astra, prompted by Daniel Kodsi
arguments.text: Each y-arrow and each good z-arrow is onto the full target proposition domain. For one fixed admitted root property F of propositions, the hypothesis that every root proposition necessarily has F therefore makes all its replica rows universal. Outside F's finite exceptional set such a row is its eventual old O table, so that table and every bad x-row are universal as well. This proves the native current BF_t instance, with full target quantification and no uniform bound on the exceptions of all bound propositions. See §6.

arguments.by: GPT-6 Astra, prompted by Daniel Kodsi
arguments.text: At accessible E the universal individual property has no inextensible coextension: its finite pin makes all E-target rows universal, while inextensibility excludes new individuals at O and fails after their subsequent injection back into E. At accessible O the admitted family of old-individual haecceities has no least upper bound, by two injections agreeing on a proposed finite pin and identifying the images of a fresh old and fresh new individual. The failures occur at et. Old domains and outgoing arrows are unchanged. See §7.

arguments.by: GPT-6 Astra, prompted by Daniel Kodsi
arguments.text: No root et-entity transports to the whole haecceity of a new O-individual. At x-arrows its current row is new-invariant; at z-arrows two exits agreeing on all old individuals but exchanging two new ones give equal rows for a transported entity and unequal rows for that haecceity. The admitted constant-replica property excluding exactly these new haecceities therefore holds necessarily of every current et-entity but misses a full target entity. This refutes BF_et and hence the relational schema. See §8.

arguments.by: GPT-6 Astra, prompted by Daniel Kodsi
arguments.text: Every rigid root carrier is an exact-image profile. Its whole cofinite compatibility, together with injective E-originating tuple transport, gives one finite replica exception set outside which good transport agrees pointwise with the old inclusion on the entire carrier. Every finitely supported subcarrier therefore has an admitted rigid exact-image profile. The inverse image of any admitted target rigid subrelation is supported: at cone arrows use the common pointwise E pin, and at good replicas use the target relation's own finite setwise pin. Thus every target rigid subrelation lifts, and the admitted power property has exact-image rows and is rigid. The unchanged E/O tail satisfies Rigid Power independently, giving its necessary all-type form. See §9 of the writeup.

models.notes: ZFC construction. Boolean Completeness is internal to admitted families; all-type completeness is asserted currently, and necessary completeness only at t. Necessary propositional Barcan fails at the unchanged E tail; the writeup gives its direct witness and the map derives this failure from the retained verdicts. The old/new tail and the wreath action distinguish this model from the nominal sections/projection entrance.

groups.name: Coalesced sums at a new root

references.locator: Appendix E, Definition E.2, pp. 80–83; Theorem 3.26, §3.6, pp. 62–64

root-arrows.text: How the root's arrows reach the components.

distinguished.text: The root has one distinguished arrow to the root of each component, and every arrow from the root into a component factors through it.
distinguished.label: distinguished arrows

meets.actual-world-isolated: The singleton root proposition, true at the root's identity arrow and nowhere in a component, is in the domain and entails every truth; the components have no arrows back to the root (Classicism, Appendix E, p. 83, on the distinctness-preserving collapse).

interpretations.text: The root has an arrow to every object of every component, one for each interpretation there of a fixed signature, and the root's individuals are that signature's individual constants.
interpretations.label: interpretation arrows

meets.actual-world-isolated: The singleton root proposition, true at the root's identity arrow and nowhere in a component, is in the domain and entails every truth; the components have no arrows back to the root (Classicism, Appendix E, p. 83, on the distinctness-preserving collapse).

interpretations-and-substitutions.text: As for interpretation arrows, and the root has besides an arrow to itself for every type-preserving map of the signature's constants to themselves, acting on the root's individuals and composing with the interpretation arrows by precomposition.
interpretations-and-substitutions.label: interpretation and substitution arrows

construction.text: The components, how their individuals and constants meet at the root, and the evaluation point, as the member's source gives them.

values.fullest: Root domains are as full as compatibility allows: a root proposition is a choice, for each component, of a proposition of that component’s root domain, together with a truth value at the root’s identity arrow, and a root entity of a relational type is likewise a family of component entities with a root component that is an arbitrary function of the root arguments.

conditions.text: The components are a family of action models complete for C: every sentence consistent with C is true at the root of some component.
Every arrow from the root into a component factors through a single distinguished arrow to that component's root.
A root entity of a relational type has a root component that is an arbitrary function of the root arguments.

arguments.by: GPT-6 Astra, prompted by Daniel Kodsi
arguments.text: Every canonical necessary-Peano guard fails at the root. For each source type $\sigma$, the pure sentence $\neg I^*_\sigma$ is consistent with C: in a full one-world model with finite individuals every type is finite, and sufficiently large Frege cardinalities coincide. Completeness of the component family makes this sentence possible at the root, so $\Box I^*_\sigma$ is false. Every guarded FTN instance is therefore true. No fixed power carrier is asserted. This is the same guard argument as arithmetic-necessitism-complete-components, now applied to the exact FTN definition. Direct source: the mathematical-necessitism handoff, 29 October 2026, coalesced group supplement and reference-analytic- necessitism §6, unpaginated (misc).

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), answering Cian Dorr's conjecture
arguments.text: Tame Rigidity fails at a relational argument type in models of C (ultralimit-fork, symmetric-qualitative-links), so some component $M$ refutes it at its root $M_0$: some $F_M$ of type $\sigma\to t$, $\sigma$ relational, is weakly rigid there but not rigid. A root entity $F$ of that type is a root extension $F_o$ together with a component $F_N$ in each component $N$, and a formula about $F$ at a world of $N$ is the same formula about $F_N$ in $N$. Since the components of root entities are arbitrary, $F$ is weakly inextensible at the root exactly when, for every $N$, every $X_N$ that necessarily holds of the $N$-components of the members of $F_o$ has $F_N\le X_N$. For each other component $N$ fix $z_N$, and for each $y$ in the extension of $F_M$ at $M_0$ let $x_y$ be the root entity with $M$-component $y$ and $N$-components $z_N$, free at the root by the condition. Put $F_o:=\{x_y\}$, $F_N:=\lambda y\, .\,y=z_N$, a haecceity, rigid in every model of C, and keep $F_M$. Then $F$ is persistent and weakly inextensible at the root, each component's condition being the weak inextensibility of its own component, but not inextensible, since $F_M$ is not inextensible in $M$ and every arrow from the root into $M$ factors through the distinguished one. So Tame Rigidity fails at the root.

revisions.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
revisions.note: One direction of Fable's transfer theorem: at a coalesced root, Tame Rigidity at a relational type holds iff it holds at the root of every component. The other direction is not recorded, the engine deriving the positive verdict in the one model where it applies.

arguments.by: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), at Cian Dorr's request; checked and recorded by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic)
arguments.text:
The transfer of tame-rigidity-component, applied to a rigid relation whose power property is not rigid. The pure sentence $\exists A^{tt}\, .\,\operatorname{Rigid}(A)\land\neg\operatorname{Rigid} (\lambda X\, .\,\operatorname{Rigid}(X)\land X\le A)$ is consistent with C (it holds in the one-individual variants of finite-support-pair-injections-or-collapses and symmetric-collapse-pair, with $A:=\top$), so some component $m$ satisfies it at its root, with witness $A$. Its extension $D$ there is nonempty: otherwise weak inextensibility tested on $\bot$ makes $A=\bot$, whose power property is the haecceity of $\bot$, which is rigid.
For $p\in D$ let $\widehat p$ be the root proposition false at the root, with $m$-component $p$ and $\bot$ in every other component; let $F$ have root extension $\{\widehat p:p\in D\}$, $m$-component $A$, and in each other component $i$ the haecceity of $\bot$. Both are in the domain, the root domains being fullest. $F$ is weakly persistent at the root, $A$ and the haecceities being persistent. It is weakly inextensible there: if $H$ necessarily holds of every $\widehat p$, its root extension contains them, $A\le H_m$ by the weak inextensibility of $A$, and the haecceity of $\bot$ entails $H_i$; entailment in the sum is componentwise. Every other accessible world lies in a component, where $F$'s components are rigid; so $F$ is rigid. The $m$-component of its power property is that of $A$, transport respecting abstraction, rigidity and entailment, and every arrow into $m$ factors through the distinguished one; so it is not rigid. Rigid Power fails at the root, at type $t\to t$.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, at Cian Dorr's suggestion
arguments.text: The type-$e$ instance of Intensional Choice fails in a model of C (symmetric-all-surjections), so its negation is consistent with C and some component $M$ refutes it at its root $M_0$: some $F$ in $M_0$'s domain is necessarily instantiated and no $G\le F$ there is necessarily uniquely instantiated. As in barcan-t-component, the thread $F^{\prime}$ that is universal at the root and in every other component and is carried onto $F$ by the distinguished arrow to $M_0$ is in the root domain, and it is necessarily instantiated. A root $G\le F^{\prime}$ that is necessarily uniquely instantiated would be carried onto such a $G$ for $F$ at $M_0$, every arrow from the root into $M$ factoring through the distinguished one. So the unboxed principle fails at the root.

arguments.by: Cian Dorr, recorded by Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic)
arguments.text: The functionality of a subrelation is evaluated at the root’s identity arrow only, while the subrelation condition is boxed; so for a serial root relation take the subrelation whose root component is a functional choice from the root component, by choice in the metatheory, and whose component parts are empty. Where some component refutes Relational Choice at its root, as when the components are complete for C, its necessitation fails.

revisions.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
revisions.note: The three complete members' copies stated once; "Its necessitation fails, since some component refutes Relational Choice at its root" became conditional on that, since in the all-finite-domains member every component satisfies Relational Choice.

arguments.by: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr
arguments.text: The singleton root proposition witnesses Actuality.

revisions.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
revisions.note: The three members' versions stated once.

arguments.by: Cian Dorr, recorded by Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic)
arguments.text:
C is complete for the component set, so some component $M$ refutes BF at its root $M_0$, at type $t$ say: some $F$ in $M_0$’s domain has $ orall y\, .\,\Box Fy$ true and $\Diamond\exists y\, .\,
eg Fy$ true at $M_0$. Because the root’s domains are as full as possible, the thread $F^{\prime}$ that is universal at the root and in every other component and is carried onto $F$ by the distinguished arrow to $M_0$ is in the root domain. Every arrow from the root into $M$ factors through that distinguished arrow, so $ orall y\, .\,\Box F^{\prime}y$ at the root reduces to $ orall y\, .\,\Box Fy$ at $M_0$ together with trivial checks elsewhere, and $\Diamond\exists y\, .\,
eg F^{\prime}y$ at the root follows from $\Diamond\exists y\, .\,
eg Fy$ at $M_0$ through the same factorization.

revisions.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
revisions.note: The three members' verbatim copies stated once.

arguments.by: Cian Dorr, recorded by Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic)
arguments.text: C is complete for the components, so some component $M$ refutes Atomicity at its root, by a proposition $p_M$ with no atom below it in $M$’s domain; the root proposition that is $p_M$ on $M$, empty on every other component and false at the root has as its root lower bounds exactly the root propositions that are lower bounds of $p_M$ on $M$ and empty elsewhere, so it has no atom below it either.

revisions.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
revisions.note: The three members' verbatim copies stated once.

arguments.by: Cian Dorr, recorded by Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic)
arguments.text: The truncation model of Appendix D, part 6, refutes it at type $t$, as its record now shows, and the components are complete for C, so one of them does; the root propositions false at every arrow except those into that component form a copy of its propositional domain under the root’s entailment order, and a root property of propositions holding exactly of the copies of the members of that component’s counterexample family has no least upper bound at the root.

revisions.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
revisions.note: The three members' verbatim copies stated once.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's request
arguments.text: The components are complete for C and a closed pure sentence at the distinguished arrow into a component has its truth value at that component root, so every pure sentence consistent with C is possible at the root; the negation of Vicinity is consistent (the truncation model) and so is the negation of a closed instance of Weakly Inextensible Comprehension at type $t\to t$ (the permutation model). Since □Actuality fails here while Vicinity and Weakly Inextensible Comprehension hold, the boxed results show that at least one of the boxed principles had to fail.

revisions.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
revisions.note: The three members' verbatim copies stated once.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: Every pure sentence consistent with C is possible at the root (pure-sentences-possible): the negation of the type-$e$ instance of Transversal is a pure sentence consistent with C, since it holds in symmetric-infinite-classes, so it is possible at the root.

revisions.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
revisions.note: The three members' verbatim copies stated once; "By the same argument" became a reference to pure-sentences-possible.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Zachary Goodsell
arguments.text: Vacuously, at every type $\sigma$. The negation of $I^*_\sigma$, that zero is a successor or successor is not injective on the numbers at $\sigma$, is a pure sentence consistent with C: it holds in the full model with one world, one individual and two propositions, where every type is finite and the finite cardinalities beyond the size of the type coincide. So it is possible at the root (pure-sentences-possible), the antecedent $\Box I^*_\sigma$ fails there, and the instance of Arithmetic Necessitism at $\sigma$ is true.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Zachary Goodsell
arguments.text: The negation of an instance of the Necessity of Analysis is a closed pure sentence consistent with C: at the root of coalesced-two-extensional-arithmetics-root, with $\sigma$ and $A$ as in that model's argument, both $\Diamond\exists\mathfrak R\,.\,(\operatorname{Real}_\sigma(\mathfrak R)\land A(\mathfrak R))$ and $\Diamond\exists\mathfrak R\,.\,(\operatorname{Real}_\sigma(\mathfrak R)\land\neg A(\mathfrak R))$ hold. So it is possible at the root (pure-sentences-possible), and since arrows compose, what is possibly possible is possible: both conjuncts hold at the root, and the instance fails.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, 25 October 2026
arguments.text: Let $N$ and $M$ be two components whose roots satisfy Actuality, with true atoms $a_N$ and $a_M$, and let $P$ be the root proposition false at the root, with component $a_N$ at $N$, $a_M$ at $M$ and bottom elsewhere. $P$ is possible, and it is a self-atom: under the distinguished arrow into $N$ it becomes $a_N$, and a true atom is a self-atom, as it entails every truth, including the truth that it entails every truth; likewise at $M$; and at the root it is false. It is not an atom, since the root proposition with component $a_N$ alone lies strictly below it. So Self-atoms are atoms (type t) fails at the root, and with it Self-atoms are strong atoms (type t).

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, 25 October 2026
arguments.text: Atoms are self-atoms (type t) fails in a model of C, the full idempotent monoid, where the atom $\{k\}$ becomes $\{1,k\}$ under $k$; so some component $N$ refutes it at its root with an atom $q$. The root proposition with component $q$ at $N$ and bottom elsewhere, false at the root, is an atom at the root, is possible, and under the distinguished arrow into $N$ becomes $q$, which is true at a world of $N$ without being an atom there. So it is an atom that is not a self-atom, and as nothing possible lies below it but itself, Self-Atomicity (type t) fails at the root too.

groups.name: Finite-support action models on one object

references.locator: Appendix D, Definitions D.1–D.3 and Proposition D.5, pp. 73–79

groups.definition:
{{monoid}} In every part, $W_0^\ddagger$ is the set of finite subsets of $\mathbb N$ and the model is ideally full: a proposition is a set of arrows whose membership depends only on the arrows’ values on some finite set of numbers (it is pinned down by that set), and an entity of a higher type is an applicative behaviour profile pinned down by a finite set in the same sense. {{individuals}} Propositions and properties are thus about finitely many numbers and indifferent to how the arrows treat the rest. Evaluation point: the sole object, at the identity arrow.

{{sigma}}

monoid.text: The monoid of arrows, as the member's part of Proposition D.5 gives it.

individuals.text: What the individuals are. Each member is a model with the natural numbers; its variant with a single individual is generated.

naturals.text: The individuals are the natural numbers, acted on by the arrows themselves.
naturals.label: individuals ℕ
naturals.brief: the individuals are the natural numbers, moved by the arrows

meets.infinitely-many-individuals: The individuals are the natural numbers.

singleton.text: There is a single individual, which every arrow fixes; the arrows still act on $\mathbb N$, which supplies the pinning sets.
singleton.label: one individual
singleton.brief: a single individual, fixed by every arrow; the arrows still act on ℕ

meets.one-individual: The only individual is fixed by every arrow, at the sole object.

sigma.text: The interpretation of Σ. Each member fixes one; its variants with the others are generated.

top.text: Interpretation of Σ, fixed for this record: every constant of Σ is relational, and each denotes the top element of its type.
top.label: Σ top
top.brief: every constant of Σ denotes the top element of its type

meets.sigma-top: This is the interpretation.

true-atom.text: Interpretation of Σ, fixed for this record: one designated relational constant $c$ of type $\tau=\bar\sigma t$ denotes $\lambda\bar x\, .\,a$, where $a$ is the unique true atom of the model, the actual-world proposition, whose only member is the identity arrow; every other constant of Σ, of which there is at least one, is relational and denotes the top element of its type.
true-atom.label: Σ true atom
true-atom.brief: one constant denotes the true atom (as a constant relation), the others top

lean.binder: (M : Type) [Monoid M] [MulAction M ℕ] [FaithfulSMul M ℕ]

meets.extensionally-full: Classicism.Meta.Intensional.Premodel.ideal_extFull _ _ _ _

meets.finitely-pinned-domains: The model is ideally full: every entity is pinned down by a finite set of numbers, and every intension pinned down by one is in the domain (Definitions D.1–D.3).
meets.infinitely-many-propositions: The propositions that a given number is fixed by the arrow, one for each number, are pairwise distinct, each pinned down by that number (the shared argument axiom-of-infinity-t).
meets.codomain-intensions: With one object such an intension is constant, so it is pinned down by $\emptyset$, and the domain holds every finitely pinned intension.
meets.one-object-action-model: Each part of Proposition D.5 is a one-object category acting on $\mathbb N$ (Appendix D, Definitions D.1–D.3).
meets.extensionally-full: The model is ideally full, hence extensionally full at every object (Appendix D, the remark after Definition D.3): for any set $R$ of tuples from the domains at an object $V$, the intension that assigns to every arrow out of $V$ into an object $U$ a fixed set $R_U$ of tuples from $U$’s domains, with $R_V=R$, is pinned down by $\emptyset$, so it is the intension of an element of $V^{\bar\sigma\to t}$ with extension $R$ at $1_V$.

actual-world-isolated.text: The actual-world proposition, whose only member is the identity, is pinned down by a finite set, so it is in the domain and entails every truth; every other arrow is non-injective, so no composite with it is the identity.

actuality-contingent.text: The actual-world proposition is in the domain, being pinned down by a finite set; at every arrow some composite is not the identity, since every other arrow is non-injective, so it is necessary at no arrow, and a non-identity arrow carries it to the empty set.

irreversible-arrow.text: A non-identity arrow is non-injective, so no arrow composes it back to the identity.

conditions.text: For every finite $N_0\subseteq\mathbb N$ there are an arrow $i$ fixing $N_0$ pointwise, an even $b$, and a finite $N^{\prime}$ such that no arrow agreeing with $i$ on $N^{\prime}$ sends an even number to $b$.
The singleton of the identity arrow is pinned down by a finite set.
Every arrow other than the identity is non-injective.
Every nonempty proposition contains an arrow whose singleton is pinned down by a finite set.
The arrows other than the identity form a nonempty proposition pinned down by a finite set, and none of them has a singleton pinned down by a finite set.
Every arrow is monotone, and some arrow sends $0$ to a positive number.
For some set $A$ of individuals, the strongest persistent property whose extension contains $A$ and which is pinned down by $\{0,\ldots,n\}$ becomes strictly stronger as $n$ grows.

Every weakly rigid relation is the intension $k\mapsto k\cdot E$, the disjunction of the haecceities of the members of its extension $E$ at the identity, and $E$ is pinned down uniformly: some finite set pins down every member of $E$.
Some family $F$ of propositions has no least finitely pinned superset of its union $\bigcup F$.
Every arrow other than the identity is finitely determined: its singleton is a proposition pinned down by a finite set.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
arguments.text: Write $X_0(E)$ for the intension $k\mapsto k\cdot E$. For $E$ pinned down uniformly by a finite $S_0$, $X_0(E)$ is in the domain, pinned down by $S_0$, and so is $X_0(T)$ for every $T\subseteq E$ and $X_0(k\cdot E)$ for every arrow $k$. The extension at $k$ of the power property $\lambda X\, .\,\operatorname{Rigid}(X)\land X\le F$ is the set of rigid $X$ with $X\le k\cdot F$, the bound variable untransported and the parameter transported; by the condition, for rigid $F=X_0(S)$ it is $\{X_0(T'):T'\subseteq k\cdot S\}$, and transporting the extension at the identity along $k$ gives $\{X_0(k\cdot T):T\subseteq S\}$, the same set, since $T'\subseteq k\cdot S$ is $k\cdot T$ for $T:=\{s\in S:k\cdot s\in T'\}$. So the power property is $X_0$ of its own extension, which is pinned down uniformly, hence in the domain and rigid. In these models the rigid relations are thus (a) the haecceities, (b) the properties "being pinned down by $S$", which are $X_0(\operatorname{Pin}(S))$, and (c) the disjunctions, finite or infinite, of haecceities of entities pinned down by one finite set; the boxed form follows from No Pure Contingency.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), on Cian Dorr's request to settle Tame Rigidity where it was open
arguments.text: By the condition a weakly rigid relation is $k\mapsto k\cdot E$, and it is in the domain; such an intension is rigid in any one-object model, by part (1) of the argument tame-rigidity. So every weakly rigid relation is rigid, and with No Pure Contingency the map's results give $\Box$Tame Rigidity.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: Write a relation $Y$ as its intension $k\mapsto Y_k$. Then $Y\bar a$ holds at $k$ iff $k\cdot\bar a\in Y_k$, $(h\cdot Y)_k=Y_{k\circ h}$, and $\le$ is inclusion of intensions. Put $X_0(S)_k:=k\cdot S$. (1) In any one-object model, if $Y_k=k\cdot Y_1$ for every $k$ then $Y$ is rigid: persistence is immediate, and for the boxed weak inextensibility, $(h\cdot Y)_k=k\cdot(h\cdot Y_1)=X_0(Y_h)_k$, which lies inside every $X$ that contains $X_0(Y_h)$. (2) Let $Y$ be weakly rigid with extension $S$. For each finite $N^{\prime}$ the intension $B_{N^{\prime}}(S)_k:=\bigcup_{k^{\prime}\equiv_{N^{\prime}}k}k^{\prime}\cdot S$ is pinned down by $N^{\prime}$, so it is in the domain. It contains $X_0(S)$, so weak inextensibility gives $Y\subseteq B_{N^{\prime}}(S)$, and persistence gives $Y\supseteq X_0(S)$; hence $k\cdot S\subseteq Y_k\subseteq\bigcap_{N^{\prime}}\bigcup_{k^{\prime}\equiv_{N^{\prime}}k}k^{\prime}\cdot S$. By the condition, for $k$ other than the identity some finite $N^{\prime}$ has $k$ as the only arrow agreeing with it there, and the bounds meet: $Y_k=k\cdot S$. So every weakly rigid relation at every type is rigid by (1), and Tame Rigidity holds. With No Pure Contingency, which holds in a one-object model, the map's results give $\Box$Tame Rigidity.

arguments.text: The source (n. 92) conjectures this but does not show it. Any set $F$ of propositions is the extension at the identity of an element of the domain at type $t\to t$, namely the profile $\langle h,p\rangle\mapsto\{i : i\cdot p\in F\}$: it is natural, independent of $h$ and so pinned down by the empty set, and each of its values is pinned down by the pinning set of $p$, since $i\cdot p$ depends only on the values of $i$ there. A least upper bound of $F$ under entailment is a least finitely pinned superset of $\bigcup F$, and it exists only if the least $S$-pinned superset of $\bigcup F$ stops shrinking as the finite set $S$ grows. So the family $F$ of the condition has no least upper bound, and, taking pointwise negations, the family of complements has no greatest lower bound.

arguments.text: At $\sigma=\tau=t$: the family $F$ of the condition no-least-pinned-cover, which has no least upper bound by the shared argument boolean-completeness-t, is in every member a sequence of propositions $A_m$, and it is countable relative to $t$. The numerals at type $t$ are the finite cardinalities and are pairwise distinct (the shared argument axiom-of-infinity-t), and extensional fullness puts in the domain the relation pairing each $A_m$ with the $m$-th numeral, which injects $F$ into them. This needs no infinity of individuals, so it covers the members with a single individual.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), answering Cian Dorr’s question whether the failure of Actuality can be sharpened to a failure of Inextensible Comprehension
arguments.text: At type $e\to t$, for the property of being even, which is in the domain as the constant intension $\{\langle b,h\rangle : b\text{ even}\}$, pinned down by $\emptyset$. Unpacking $\operatorname{Inextensible}$ as in the left-to-right half of Dorr’s rigidity criterion (draft, Lemma 14, p. 7, with Lemma 13): even the unboxed matrix, evaluated at the identity, says that $Y$ is contained in every persistent (transport-closed) $B$ in the domain whose extension includes $Y$’s. For a finite $N^{\prime}$, the smallest such $B$ pinned down by $N^{\prime}$ is $B_{N^{\prime}}:=\{\langle b^{\prime\prime},i^{\prime}\rangle : i^{\prime\prime}(b)=b^{\prime\prime}\text{ for some even }b\text{ and some arrow }i^{\prime\prime}\text{ agreeing with }i^{\prime}\text{ on }N^{\prime}\}$, which is transport-closed and pinned down by $N^{\prime}$. Now let $Y$ be coextensive with evenness and pinned down by a finite $N_0$; then $\langle b,i\rangle\in Y$ for every even $b$ and every arrow $i$ fixing $N_0$ pointwise. Take the arrow $i$, the even $b$ and the finite $N^{\prime}$ that the condition provides for $N_0$: no arrow agreeing with $i$ on $N^{\prime}$ sends an even number to $b$. So $\langle b,i\rangle\in Y\setminus B_{N^{\prime}}$, and $Y$ is not even weakly inextensible.

groups.name: Finitely pinned action models on two objects

references.locator: Appendix D, Definitions D.1–D.3 and Proposition D.4, pp. 73–74
references.note: Ideally full action models over any category of sets and functions, with the ideal of finite sets; models of C by Proposition D.4.

groups.definition: An ideally full action model in the sense of Classicism, Appendix D, over a category with two objects, each carrying the ideal of finite sets: a model of C by Proposition D.4. The member's construction and evaluation point follow.

conditions.text: Every arrow $u$ out of the evaluation object $W_0$ has a left inverse $r_u$ ($r_u\circ u=1_{W_0}$) such that, for every finite set $P$ of points at the codomain of $u$, there is a finite set $N$ of points at $W_0$ with $r_{u'}$ agreeing with $r_u$ on $P$ whenever $u'$ has the same codomain as $u$ and agrees with $u$ on $N$.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, in a trawl for cheaply settled verdicts; checked by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: At $W_0$, at every type. Write a relation $Y$ as its intension $k\mapsto Y_k$, put $X_0(E)_k:=k\cdot E$, and let $B_N(E)_k$ be the union of the $k^{\prime}\cdot E$ for $k^{\prime}$ agreeing with $k$ on $N$ and having its codomain; $B_N(E)$ is pinned down by $N$, so in the domain at either object. (1) An $X_0(E)$ in the domain is rigid: its transports are $X_0$ of the transported extensions, persistent and below whatever holds necessarily of their members. (2) A weakly rigid $Y$ with extension $E$ has $X_0(E)\le Y\le B_N(E)$ for every finite $N$, by weak persistence and weak inextensibility. (3) If $x$ is in $B_N(E)_u$ for every $N$, then $x=u\cdot a$ for some $a\in E$: for $N$ large, $x=u^{\prime}\cdot a_N$ with $u^{\prime}$ agreeing with $u$ on $N$ and $r_{u^{\prime}}$ agreeing with $r_u$ on a pin of $x$, so $a_N=r_{u^{\prime}}\cdot x=r_u\cdot x=:a$, and taking $N$ to contain a pin of $a$ also, $x=u^{\prime}\cdot a=u\cdot a$. So a weakly rigid relation at $W_0$ is $X_0$ of its extension, and rigid: Tame Rigidity. (4) Let $F=X_0(E)$, $h$ an arrow out of $W_0$, and $X$ weakly rigid at its target with $X\le h\cdot F$ and extension $D$. Applying (2) at the target and (3) to the arrows $k\circ h$, $X=X_0(D)$, and $D=h\cdot A$ for $A:=\{a\in E:h\cdot a\in D\}$; $X_0(A)$, the transport of $X$ along $r_h$, is in the domain, weakly rigid and below $F$, with $h\cdot X_0(A)=X$. So the property of being weakly rigid and below $F$ has at each world the transports of its extension at the identity: it is $X_0$ of that extension, which is rigid by (1). Weakly Rigid Power holds at $W_0$.

constructible.text: Universe, fixed for this record: the construction is carried out inside Gödel's constructible universe $L$, which ZFC proves to be a model of ZFC + $V=L$. Read in the ambient universe, the result is still a Boolean-valued model of the same kind, with the same values: every element of the algebra lies in $L$, and every clause of the semantics takes the meet or join of a family that lies in $L$ (by induction on formulas), whose meet or join in $L$ is its meet or join outright, since every candidate bound is itself an element of the algebra, hence in $L$. Its domains are full in the sense of $L$, and every argument for the member, being a proof in ZFC about the model's values, holds of it. In particular $L\models\mathrm{CH}$, so an algebra chosen by cases on CH is the one for CH.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: At type $t$, for the analytical sentence $\Phi$ saying that every real is constructible: membership of a real in $L$ is $\Sigma^1_2$ (Shoenfield), so $\Phi$ is $\Pi^1_3$, a first-order analytical sentence in any real number structure, whose natural numbers code sets of naturals by its reals. Write $\pi,\rho$ for the projections of $B=\mathbf 2\times A$ onto the atom's coordinate and $A$. As in the argument for the contingency of CH, the $\pi$-coordinate of a box-free sentence of the kind used there, whose relation variables are only applied to carrier elements, with identity only between those, is its truth in the full model over $L$ and the $\rho$-coordinate its value in $L^A$, and both have real number structures on subsets of $D_t=B$. $L\models\Phi$, while forcing with $A$ adds a Cohen real over $L$, not constructible, and Shoenfield absoluteness makes the $\Sigma^1_2$ definition of constructibility mean the same in $L^A$; so $\Phi$ has value $0_A$ there. Real number structures being isomorphic within each coordinate, $\forall\mathfrak R\, .\,\operatorname{Real}_t(\mathfrak R)\to\Phi(\mathfrak R)$ has value $(1,0_A)$ and $\forall\mathfrak R\, .\,\operatorname{Real}_t(\mathfrak R)\to\neg\Phi(\mathfrak R)$ has value $(0,1_A)$. As $\Box p$ is $p=\top$, both disjuncts of the instance are $\bot$.

With one world, the boxed principles reduce to their unboxed forms, and the comprehension, completeness and atomicity principles hold as in every two-valued full model: each relational type is the complete atomic Boolean algebra of the subsets of a domain.

arguments.by: OpenAI Codex (GPT-6), prompted by Daniel Kodsi, 22 October 2026, for one predicate of type $et$; Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, for every such Σ
arguments.text: Permutations of the individuals act on every type, by conjugation, preserving application, identity, the Boolean operations and the quantifiers, so every closed pure term $A$ is equivariant: $\pi(A\,\bar d)=A\,(\pi\bar d)$. For distinct constants $c,d_1,\dots,d_n$ with $c$ relational, the transposition of $a_c$ and $b_c$ fixes the individuals of the $d_i$, hence each $d_i$, and so $A\,\bar d$; but it moves $c$, by induction on its type. So $c\ne A\,\bar d$. For an individual constant $c$ the instance is vacuous, no term $A\,\bar d$ being of type $e$. The restriction on Σ cannot be dropped: Extensionality and Independence (Σ) are inconsistent when Σ has a constant whose type does not contain $e$, since such a constant is provably one of finitely many closed pure terms (write-up).
