groups.definition: Work in ZFC. {{family}} Take the disjoint union of the nonzero parts of these complete Boolean algebras, with refinement given by their Boolean orders, and adjoin a refinement-isolated root r. The root sees every point and each cloud point sees its refinements. Use the full modalized-domain model of Definitions 2.1–2.10 and 4.1, with constant individual domain ω and literal individual identity. At t use all regular-open propositions; at function types use the full underlying function sets with the partial equivalence relations of Definition 2.2. Quantification uses existing entities at all refinements, as in §2.3. Evaluate at r. Interpret any relational signature constants as top; no signature verdict is recorded.

family.text: A nonempty family of nontrivial complete Boolean algebras, containing an atomless factor.

arguments.by: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), prompted by Daniel Kodsi, 25 October 2026; checked and recorded by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr

source.locator: Lemma 6.7, p. 31 (numbered so in the draft of 23 October 2026)

arguments.text: At the root $r$, quantifiers range over the entities existing at $r$ and identity is $\sim_r$ (Lemma 2.13), and every set of tuples of such entities closed under $\sim_r$ is the extension at $r$ of a relation existing at $r$ (Lemma 6.7: the relation with value $\{r\}$ on the tuples in the set and $\emptyset$ elsewhere, which respects identity at every cloud point because it is empty there). Given a relation $U$ serial at $r$, choose in the metatheory, for each $\sim_r$-class of inputs, one $\sim_r$-class of outputs to which its members bear $U$ at $r$. The set of pairs from chosen classes is closed under $\sim_r$, so it is the extension at $r$ of some $S$ existing at $r$; $S$ is functional at $r$ and its pairs bear $U$. This holds whatever the output type, $e$ included.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, 25 October 2026
arguments.text: At a cloud point $t$ every proposition is identical to $\top$ or to $\bot$ (Remark 4.6(iv)), and Atom $q$ holds at $t$ exactly when $q$ holds at $t$: if $t\in q$, then at every refinement $t^{\prime}$ a $z\le q$ is distinct from $q$ there iff $z$ is bottom there; if $t\notin q$, some refinement has $q=\bot$, where Atom $q$ fails, and holding persists. So a proposition not containing the root is a self-atom at the root whenever it is nonzero, and $\{r\}$ is an atom; every possible proposition has one of these below it, and Self-Atomicity (type t) holds at the root. At relational types, a possible $X$ at any point has, by no new entities (Lemma 4.3), an actual tuple $\bar x$ with $X\bar x$ possible; $Y:=\lambda\bar y\, .\,\bar y=\bar x\land X\bar x$ lies below $X$, is possible, and has at most one instance at every point, which at a cloud point where it is instantiated makes it an atom there (its parts are $\{\bar x\}$ cut down by propositions, and such a part differs from $Y$ at a refinement exactly when it is bottom there); so $Y$ is a self-atom. At cloud points every possible $X$ likewise has such a $Y$ below it, so Self-Atomicity holds at every point and every type. Self-atoms are atoms (type t) fails at the root: the set of points of an atomless component is a self-atom, and by Theorem 4.4(d) no atom lies below it.

The frame is a world–cloud frame. At transparent cloud points every relation is rigid. At the isolated root, the check-closure of an actual extension is a coextensive rigid relation (Definition 3.11 and Theorem 3.12). Thus RC holds at every point, and each boxed instance is valid.
arguments.by: Andrew Bacon and Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic)

arguments.text: Theorem 3.14 selects witnesses on a maximal antichain of decided cloud pieces and mixes their identity profiles. At a world, choose one actual witness; the world part and the cloud mixture together form a necessarily uniquely instantiated subrelation of the given necessarily instantiated relation. Hence IC and its necessitation are valid. The proof uses ZFC.
arguments.by: Andrew Bacon and Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic)

arguments.text: Lemma 4.3 proves no new entities at any type: at a cloud point x a relation can be cut down to the regular-open closure of the principal downset of x, yielding an entity existing at the root and identical to the original at x. Proposition 3.16 therefore gives BF and □BF at every type. This uses the paper’s variable-domain quantifiers, not a fixed-domain meet calculation.
arguments.by: Andrew Bacon and Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic)

arguments.text: The component proposition for an atomless factor is nonzero. At the root, propositional identity is literal and entailment is inclusion, so its lower interval is the atomless factor algebra. It therefore has no propositional atom below it.
arguments.by: Andrew Bacon and Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic)

arguments.text: The top proposition S and the cloud S minus {r} are distinct at the root, but identical at every cloud point. They witness failure of ND at type t.
arguments.by: Andrew Bacon and Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic)
Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, in a trawl for cheaply settled verdicts; checked by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: At the root identity of individuals is literal and every $\sim_r$-closed set of tuples is the root extension of a relation existing there (Lemma 6.7). So the property of cardinalities false at the root of every property with an infinite root extension exists at the root; it holds of $\mathbf 0_e$ and is closed under successor, so contains every finite cardinality, none of which holds of $\lambda u\,.\,\top$, whose root extension is $\omega$.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, in a trawl for cheaply settled verdicts; checked by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: At the root, $\{r\}$ is a true proposition (Proposition 1.12) possible only at $r$, which no cloud point sees, so every truth $p$ has $\Box(\Diamond\{r\}\to p)$. At a cloud point the box is idle (Lemma 3.9(c)), so with $q:=\top$ the condition is $p$ itself.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, in a trawl for cheaply settled verdicts; checked by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: Each member has the Cohen algebra as a component (the lottery's family includes it, of cardinality $2^{\aleph_0}<\mu$). At type $e\to t$ let $c$ send $n$ to the Cohen bit $\{p:p(n)=1\}$ on that component and to $\varnothing$ elsewhere; it is rigid at every Cohen point (Lemma 3.10). A relation rigid at the root with root extension $D$ agrees on the Cohen component with the check-closure $\check D$ (persistence, and inextensibility against $\check D$), which decides every $n$; so its identity with $c$ holds at no Cohen point. If $\lambda X\,.\,\operatorname{Rigid}(X)$ were rigid at the root, inextensibility against the check-closure of its root extension would make it entail, at every Cohen point, a join of such identities, none containing a Cohen point; but it holds of $c$ on the whole Cohen component. The same refutes Rigid Power at $\lambda x\,.\,\top$.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, in a trawl for cheaply settled verdicts; checked by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: Extensionality at $t$ fails at the root (Theorem 4.4(c)) and holds at every cloud point (Remark 4.6(iv)), which sees only cloud points; so its negation is true at the root and not possible at any cloud point.

groups.name: Restricted entrances to full one-object actions

references.note: Full action models, here the target, with a restricted domain at the entrance.

groups.definition: Two objects, the target $s$ and the entrance $r$. {{construction}} There is a single individual at both objects, and no arrow returns to $r$. Evaluation point: $1_r$. Interpretation of Σ: every constant of Σ is relational, and each denotes the top element of its type.

construction.text: The target's monoid, the arrows from $r$, and the restriction on the entities at $r$, as the member gives them.

meets.extensionally-full: At $r$ the current extension of an entity is arbitrary, and $s$ is a full action model.
meets.sigma-top: Every constant of Σ is relational and denotes the top element of its type, which every arrow fixes.
meets.one-individual: There is a single individual at both objects.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, in a trawl for cheaply settled verdicts; checked by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: At type $t$. The values of a proposition at $r$ along the $h_n$ are eventually constant, by the restriction. Let $p_n$ be true at $h_{2n}$ alone. An upper bound is true at every $h_{2n}$, so at all but finitely many $h_n$; making it false at one more odd index gives a smaller upper bound. So the $p_n$ have no least upper bound. They are countable relative to $t$: by extensional fullness and the infinitely many propositions the numbers at $t$ are the distinct numerals, and the relation pairing $p_n$ with the $n$th numeral is in the domain.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, in a trawl for cheaply settled verdicts; checked by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: At $e$ there is one individual. At a relational type, choose well-orders $A$ of the domain at $r$ and $W$ of the domain at $s$, and let $R$ have current extension $A$ and, along every arrow out of $r$, the transport with extension $W$ at every world of $s$, which every arrow of $s$ fixes. Every transport of $R$ is that one, so $\Box\operatorname{WO}(R)$, well-ordering being the external notion at both objects, as $s$ is full and current extensions at $r$ are arbitrary.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, in a trawl for cheaply settled verdicts; checked by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: At $r$, $\{1_r\}$ is true and possible only at $1_r$, no arrow returning to $r$; at $s$, $\{1\}$ is true and possible only at $1$, since in the target's monoid $jk=1$ only if $j=k=1$. So at each object some truth $q$ has $\Box(\Diamond q\to p)$ for every truth $p$.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, in a trawl for cheaply settled verdicts; checked by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: At $r$ every set of tuples is a current extension, so completeness, injections and isomorphisms there are the external ones. There are countably many propositions at $r$, their values along the $h_n$ being eventually constant, and an infinite complete Boolean algebra has at least continuum many elements, so a complete Boolean algebra at $r$ that is Dedekind finite or has fewer elements than the propositions is finite, with $2^k$ elements; it is isomorphic to the propositions below the one true at $h_0,\ldots,h_{k-1}$ alone, which is not $\top$.

groups.name: Ultraproducts of full S5 models

references.note: Full action models; the factors are full S5 models.

groups.definition:
For $n\ge1$ let $M_n$ be {{factors}}: the full action model on a category in which there is exactly one arrow between any two objects, with the same $n$ individuals at every object, fixed by every arrow, evaluated at one object. Regard each $M_n$ as a many-sorted first-order structure, with a sort for each type, application, the logical constants, the constants of Σ, and a predicate $T$ on the sort of $t$ for truth at the evaluation object. Let $U$ be a nonprincipal ultrafilter on the positive integers, and $M:=\prod_nM_n/U$, the evaluation point being the class of the factors' evaluation objects. By Łoś's theorem a first-order sentence holds in $M$ iff it holds in $M_n$ for $U$-many $n$. $M$ is a Henkin model of C, and a sentence of the object language is true in $M$ iff it is true in $U$-many $M_n$ (see the write-up). It is not full.

Interpretation of Σ, fixed for these records: every constant of Σ is relational, and each denotes the top element of its type in every factor, hence in $M$.

factors.text: The factors' worlds, as the member gives them.

finite-worlds.text: the full S5 model with $n$ worlds and $n$ individuals
finite-worlds.label: n worlds

countable-worlds.text: the full S5 model with the worlds $\mathbb N$ and $n$ individuals
countable-worlds.label: countably many worlds

meets.sigma-top: This is the interpretation the definition fixes.

arguments.by: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), prompted by Daniel Kodsi; checked and recorded by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: Each instance of each of these schemata is a sentence true in every factor, so true in $M$. The full domains contain every function, which gives the choice principles, Rigid Comprehension and Well-Ordering; constant domains give BF; identity is crisp, which gives ND; the algebras are atomic, the worlds being the atoms and every true proposition entailed by the actual one; and any two worlds are related by an automorphism, so a true pure sentence is necessary. All of this holds at every world.

arguments.by: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), prompted by Daniel Kodsi; checked and recorded by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: The instance of the Infinity Schema (type $e$) asking for $k$ distinct individuals holds in $M_n$ for $n\ge k$, a cofinite set of $n$, hence in $U$.

arguments.by: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), prompted by Daniel Kodsi; checked and recorded by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: In $M_n$, at every world, the domains being full, the finite cardinalities are the standard ones, and the $n$-th counts the universal property of individuals. So $\Box\exists Z\, .\,\operatorname{FiniteCardinality}_e(Z)\land Z(\lambda u\, .\,\top)$ is true in every factor, hence in $M$, where the witnessing cardinality is nonstandard.

groups.name: Stitched forcing models

references.note: Action models, of which the stitched models are; see §7.2 of the draft.

forcing.text: The forcing $P$, as the member gives it.

universe.text: The ground model. Each member is recorded over an arbitrary ground model of ZFC; its variant over $L$ is generated.

zfc.text: Ground model, fixed for this record: $V$ is an arbitrary model of ZFC.
zfc.label: over any ground model
zfc.brief: forcing over an arbitrary ground model of ZFC

constructible.text: Ground model, fixed for this record: $V$ is Gödel's constructible universe, so that $V[G]=L[G]$; that is, the construction is carried out over $L$, which ZFC proves to be a model of ZFC + $V=L$, so this adds nothing to what the construction presupposes. In particular $V\models\mathrm{CH}$.
constructible.label: over L
constructible.brief: forcing over L, where CH holds

conditions.text: The forcing $P$ adds a real: some subset of $\mathbb N$ in $V[G]$ is not in $V$.
The continuum hypothesis has the same truth value in $V[G]$ as in $V$.
The continuum hypothesis has different truth values in $V[G]$ and in $V$.

meets.sigma-top: This is the interpretation the definition fixes.
meets.finitely-many-propositions-everywhere: The root has four propositions and $C_0$ two.
meets.fewer-propositions-after: The root has four propositions; $C_0$, after which there is only itself, has two.

arguments.by: GPT-6 Astra, prompted by Daniel Kodsi
arguments.text: The canonical e-counting numbers at the root and terminal object are identified with the ground's natural-number carrier, with bijective transport and $\Box I^*_e$. The current members of its first canonical rigid power are precisely the paired predicates of ground subsets; terminally the full hierarchy includes a predicate for every extension subset. A new real is therefore a new terminal power member. The root predicate with all current power members in its current extension and exactly their transported images in its terminal extension is admitted: its terminal definition uses the ground parameter $\mathcal P(\omega)^V$ and the numeral coding. It necessarily contains each current member but misses the new one, refuting inextensibility of this power carrier and hence FTN. This uses the stated stitching construction, not an arbitrary Boolean-valued model. Direct source: Finite-type necessitism: canonical models and finite-level separations, §§2.3 and 3.1–3.3, 29 October 2026, unpaginated (misc); the source's Cohen instance uses only adds-a-real.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, 25 October 2026
arguments.text: The root sees itself and $C_0$ through one arrow each, and $C_0$ sees only itself. An entity at the root of a relational type is a pair $(E,D)$ of a root extension $E$ and a definable element $D$ of $C_0$, with transport $D$ along the arrow to $C_0$. It is an atom iff $E$ is a singleton and $D=\bot$, or $E=\varnothing$ and $D$ is a definable singleton of $C_0$; a self-atom likewise, since its transport along the identity is itself and along the arrow to $C_0$ is $D$, each of which must be an atom where the entity is instantiated. Each such entity is a strong atom, its two transports being an atom or bottom. At $C_0$, a one-world model with full extensional domains, the atoms are the singletons, which are self-atoms and strong atoms. So all four bridge principles hold at both worlds, at every type.

arguments.by: Neil Barton and Zachary Goodsell; in the map's terms by Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Zachary Goodsell
arguments.text: Lemma 16 of the source, in the map's terms. Write a root relation as the pair of its root extension $E$, a set in $V$ of root tuples, and its $C_0$-extension $g$, a definable relation of $C_0$; transport along $h$ sends it to $g$, and $h[E]$, the set of $C_0$-components of the members of $E$, is definable from the set in $V$ of their names. The relation is persistent iff $h[E]\subseteq g$. It is weakly inextensible iff $g\subseteq h[E]$: the root relation with root extension $E$ and $C_0$-extension $h[E]$ necessarily holds of every member of $E$, so weak inextensibility gives $g\subseteq h[E]$; conversely, a root relation that necessarily holds of each member of $E$ has root extension including $E$ and $C_0$-extension including $h[E]$. So a root relation is weakly rigid iff $g=h[E]$, and then rigid, since at $C_0$, which sees only itself, every relation is rigid. Hence $(E,g)$ is coextensive with the rigid $(E,h[E])$, and Rigid Comprehension holds at the root; at $C_0$ it holds trivially.

arguments.by: Neil Barton and Zachary Goodsell; in the map's terms by Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Zachary Goodsell
arguments.text: Lemma 17 of the source. A serial root relation $U$ has, by choice in $V$, a functional subrelation $E_S$ of its root extension; the root relation with root extension $E_S$ and the $C_0$-extension of $U$ is in the domain, lies within $U$ at the root and is functional there, which is all the unboxed principle asks. At $C_0$, $V[G]$ supplies a functional subrelation of any serial relation, and the full domain contains it.

arguments.by: Neil Barton and Zachary Goodsell; in the map's terms by Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Zachary Goodsell
arguments.text: The individuals are the natural numbers at both objects (Lemma 15 of the source). At the root the finite cardinalities of type $(et)t$ are the numerals $\operatorname{Suc}^k\mathbf 0$: the root property of cardinalities whose root extension is the set of numerals, with the corresponding definable property at $C_0$, holds of $\mathbf 0$ and is closed under successor, so every finite cardinality is a numeral; and the $k$-th numeral holds of a root property of individuals iff its root extension has exactly $k$ members, which the universal property has not.

arguments.by: Neil Barton and Zachary Goodsell; in the map's terms by Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Zachary Goodsell
arguments.text: Theorem 21 of the source, with the trivial group. The root has four propositions, the pairs of a truth value at the root and one at $C_0$, ordered coordinatewise, and $C_0$ has two; both algebras are finite, hence atomic.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Zachary Goodsell
arguments.text: Both propositions of $C_0$ are transports of root propositions, so a property of propositions at the root that necessarily holds of every root proposition holds at $C_0$ of both propositions there; at $C_0$, which sees only itself, BF is trivial.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Zachary Goodsell
arguments.text: At the root let $q$ be the proposition true at the root alone. $\Diamond q$ is true at the root and false at $C_0$, so for any truth $p$, $\Box(\Diamond q\to p)$ holds, and $q$ witnesses $\Box_{\ne}p$. At $C_0$, where necessity is truth, $\top$ witnesses $\Box_{\ne}p$ for every truth $p$.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Zachary Goodsell
arguments.text: The root has four propositions, so the instance of the schema asking for five pairwise distinct ones fails.

arguments.by: Neil Barton and Zachary Goodsell; in the map's terms by Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Zachary Goodsell
arguments.text: Lemma 19 of the source, with the universal property of individuals in place of the natural numbers. Let $F:=\lambda x^e\, .\,\top$; it is rigid, its root extension being $\mathbb N$ and its $C_0$-extension $h[\mathbb N]=\mathbb N$. Its power property $P:=\lambda X^{et}\, .\,\operatorname{Rigid}(X)\land X\le F$ is $\lambda X\, .\,\operatorname{Rigid}(X)$, as $X\le F$ is a theorem. By the criterion in the argument for Rigid Comprehension, the rigid root properties of individuals are the pairs $(E,E)$ with $E\subseteq\mathbb N$ in $V$, whose $C_0$-components are the reals of $V$, while at $C_0$ every property is rigid, so the $C_0$-extension of $P$ is the whole power set of $\mathbb N$ in $V[G]$. The root property of properties with the root extension of $P$ and $C_0$-extension $\mathcal P(\mathbb N)^V$, definable from that parameter, necessarily holds of every root instance of $P$, but not, at $C_0$, of a real of $V[G]$ not in $V$, which is rigid there. So $P$ is not weakly inextensible: Rigid Power fails at type $(et)t$ and, $P$ being rigidity itself, Rigid Rigidity fails at type $et$.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Zachary Goodsell
arguments.text: By the $V$-decisiveness of $P$, a real of $V[G]$ definable there from parameters in $V$ lies in $V$; so the $C_0$-components of the root properties of individuals are exactly the reals of $V$, and a real $c$ of $V[G]$ not in $V$ is the component of none. The root property of properties of individuals whose root extension is everything and whose $C_0$-extension is $\mathcal P(\mathbb N)^V$ necessarily holds of every root property of individuals, but $c$ does not fall under it at $C_0$: BF fails at type $et$.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Zachary Goodsell
arguments.text: At type $(et)t$. Let $F$ be the root property of properties of individuals whose root extension is a single root property and whose $C_0$-extension is the reals of $V[G]$ not in $V$. It is necessarily instantiated. A property $G\le F$ that is necessarily uniquely instantiated would have a one-element $C_0$-extension $\{c\}$, definable from parameters in $V$, with $c$ a new real, which the $V$-decisiveness of $P$ forbids.

revisions.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
revisions.note: Moved from stitched-cohen-extension into the group, for every member whose forcing adds a real; the Cohen real of the original text is now any real of $V[G]$ not in $V$, and the appeal to the weak homogeneity of Cohen forcing is to the $V$-decisiveness of $P$.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Zachary Goodsell
arguments.text: At type $et$, at the root. A real number structure exists there: the rigid properties of individuals are the pairs $(E,E)$ with $E\subseteq\mathbb N$ in $V$, the reals of $V$ as sets of naturals, and the field relations on them, defined from membership by arithmetical formulas, are root relations (a function in $V$ with the corresponding definable $C_0$-relation); completeness at the root holds because every root property of these is a set in $V$. Now let $\mathfrak R$ be any rigid real number structure at $et$ with necessarily distinct elements. At the root it is a complete ordered field, so by categoricity its domain $X$ is in bijection with the reals of $V$ and its rationals are a countable dense subfield. Its root extension is a set $E$ in $V$ and, $X$ being rigid, its $C_0$-extension is $h[E]=E$, the same reals. At $C_0$ every property is available, in particular the cut in the rationals of $X$ of a real of $V[G]$ not in $V$, a bounded subproperty of $X$ with no least upper bound in $E$, a least upper bound being a real of $V$ equal to that new real. So $X$ is not complete at $C_0$, $\Box\operatorname{Real}_{et}(\mathfrak R)$ fails, and the instance fails: a real number structure is possible, indeed actual, and no rigid one is necessarily a real number structure.

revisions.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
revisions.note: Moved from stitched-cohen-extension into the group, for every member whose forcing adds a real; the Cohen real of the original text is now any real of $V[G]$ not in $V$, and the appeal to the weak homogeneity of Cohen forcing is to the $V$-decisiveness of $P$.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: At each object, every real number structure satisfies the continuum hypothesis iff the universe that object is built in does: at the root $V$, at $C_0$ $V[G]$. At $C_0$ this is because $C_0$ is the full extensional model of $V[G]$ over the natural numbers: a real number structure there is a complete ordered field of $V[G]$, with every subproperty and every relation of $V[G]$ available, so it has $V[G]$'s continuum, and its satisfying CH is CH in $V[G]$. At the root it is because every set in $V$ of root tuples is the root extension of a root relation, whatever its $C_0$-extension: so the root, read at the root, is the full hierarchy of $V$ over its domains, and the same reasoning applies in $V$. Real number structures exist at both objects, at type $et$ (see the argument for the failure of Analytic Necessitism, or take any complete ordered field on $\mathcal P(\mathbb N)$ at $C_0$). When $P$ leaves CH unchanged, every real number structure, of any type, satisfies CH at both objects, or every one falsifies it at both; since the root sees exactly the two objects, one of the two disjuncts holds there.

arguments.by: Neil Barton and Zachary Goodsell; in the map's terms by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: Theorem 20 of the source. At each object, every real number structure satisfies the continuum hypothesis iff the universe that object is built in does: at the root $V$, at $C_0$ $V[G]$. At $C_0$ this is because $C_0$ is the full extensional model of $V[G]$ over the natural numbers: a real number structure there is a complete ordered field of $V[G]$, with every subproperty and every relation of $V[G]$ available, so it has $V[G]$'s continuum, and its satisfying CH is CH in $V[G]$. At the root it is because every set in $V$ of root tuples is the root extension of a root relation, whatever its $C_0$-extension: so the root, read at the root, is the full hierarchy of $V$ over its domains, and the same reasoning applies in $V$. Real number structures exist at both objects, at type $et$ (see the argument for the failure of Analytic Necessitism, or take any complete ordered field on $\mathcal P(\mathbb N)$ at $C_0$). When $P$ changes CH, at type $et$ some real number structure satisfies CH at one object and some falsifies it at the other, and the root sees both, so neither disjunct holds at the root.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: At type $et$, for the analytical sentence $\Phi$ saying that every real is constructible: membership of a real in $L$ is $\Sigma^1_2$ (Shoenfield), so $\Phi$ is $\Pi^1_3$, a first-order analytical sentence in any real number structure, whose natural numbers code sets of naturals by its reals. Real number structures exist at type $et$ at both objects (see the argument for the failure of Analytic Necessitism). At $C_0$, the full extensional model of $L[G]$, every real number structure has the reals of $L[G]$, among them a real not in $L$, and Shoenfield absoluteness makes the $\Sigma^1_2$ definition of constructibility mean the same in $L[G]$; so $\Phi$ fails in every real number structure there. At the root every set in $L$ of root tuples is the root extension of a root relation, whatever its $C_0$-extension, so the root read at the root is the full hierarchy of $L$ over its domains, and $\Phi$ holds in every real number structure there, as it does in $L$. The root sees both objects, so neither disjunct of the instance holds there.

groups.name: Supported-product action models, with glued constants

groups.definition: Fix an infinite cardinal $\kappa$, a set $I$ of size $\kappa^+$, and the free monoid $L$ of finite words on an alphabet of size $\kappa$. {{individuals}} There is one object, and the evaluation point is the identity. Write $m$ for the $L^I$-coordinate of an arrow. At a relational type the domain consists of the profiles $F$ on the arrows with a support: a set $S\subseteq I$ of size at most $\kappa$ such that $F$ takes the same value at arrows whose $L^I$-coordinates agree on $S$ (and whose other coordinates, if any, agree). Transport is $(h\cdot F)_k:=F_{kh}$, with the usual action-model semantics. Each relational constant of Σ denotes the gluing, at a coordinate outside every support involved, of chosen interpretations $J_\alpha(c)$, one for each $\mathcal L(\Sigma)$-sentence satisfiable over the pure model (the members' write-ups).

individuals.text: The individuals and the arrows, as the member gives them.

one.text: Here $\kappa\ge|\Sigma|$, and the arrows are $L^I$ with coordinatewise concatenation. There is one individual, which the individual constants denote.
one.label: one individual

meets.one-individual: There is one individual.

surjections.text: Here $\kappa\ge\max(|\Sigma|,2^{\aleph_0})$, and $U$ is a set of size $\kappa^+$. The arrows are the pairs $(m,s)$ with $m\in L^I$ and $s$ a surjection $U\to U$, composed by $(m,s)(m^{\prime},s^{\prime}):=(mm^{\prime},s\circ s^{\prime})$, with identity $(\varepsilon,\mathrm{id})$. The individuals are the members of $U$, with $(m,s)\cdot a:=s(a)$, and a profile may depend arbitrarily on $s$. The individual constants denote distinct individuals $a_c$.
surjections.label: moving individuals

meets.no-actuality-anywhere: One object, so Actuality, a closed pure sentence, holds at every world iff at the identity, where it fails (recorded in the members' verdicts).

arguments.text: The finite cardinalities at each type are exactly the standard numerals, so a countable property has countably many actual instances; their pointwise union is supported by the union of their supports and is their least upper bound. The schema is closed and pure, so it holds necessarily.

arguments.text: $\Diamond q_j=q_j$, the free monoid having no inverses. For a truth $p$ with support $S$ and $j\notin S$, the arrow with one letter at $j$ (and identity in any other coordinate) satisfies $p$ and not $\Diamond q_j$, though $q_j$ is true.

arguments.text: At $tt$, for the constant property $\{q_i:i\in I\}$: a coextensive $Y$ with support $S$, $j\notin S$, keeps $q_j$ at the arrow $h$ with one letter at $j$, while $Z$, all propositions where $m_j=\varepsilon$ and all but $q_j$ elsewhere, necessarily holds of each actual instance and omits $q_j$ at $h$. The $q_i$ ignore any other coordinate.

arguments.by: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), prompted by Daniel Kodsi; checked and recorded by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: At type $(tt)t$. Weakly rigid relations are exactly the exact images $h\mapsto h\cdot E$ of their actual extensions (the exact-image lemma, adapted to moving individuals in that variant's write-up); a family $e_{z,j}$ of properties of propositions, shifted in $z$ by the $j$th coordinate and marked by the squares, has a supported exact image $F$, but the rigid relation $X\le a\cdot F$ formed from the $y_j$ lifts to no rigid $Y\le F$, so the power property of $F$ is not weakly rigid.

arguments.by: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), prompted by Daniel Kodsi; checked and recorded by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: By the exact-image lemma (with the auxiliary profiles taken with the surjection fixed, for moving individuals), a weakly rigid relation is the profile $h\mapsto h\cdot E$ of its actual extension $E$, and such a relation, with all its transports, is rigid. The schema is closed and pure.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: The constant profile of any set of tuples has empty support and is fixed by every arrow. So a transversal of an actual equivalence relation, chosen in the metatheory, is the extension of an entity; and the constant profile of a well-order of a type's domain, chosen in the metatheory, well-orders the type at every arrow, every property's extension at an arrow being a subset of that domain. Transversal Choice is closed and pure, so it holds necessarily.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: If $\Box\exists x\, .\,Fx$ and $F$ has support $S$, choose for each arrow $h$ an element $g(h)\in F_h$ depending only on the restriction of its $L^I$-coordinate to $S$ (and on its other coordinates); then $G_h:=\{g(h)\}$ has support $S$, $G\le F$, and $G$ has exactly one instance at every arrow. Likewise, for $R$ necessarily serial with support $S$, a functional graph chosen inside each $R_h$. Both principles are closed and pure, so they hold necessarily.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: $\mathbb N_\sigma$ and the numerals are closed pure terms, so their profiles are constant and fixed by every arrow: $\mathbb N_\sigma$ is rigid with necessarily distinct instances.

arguments.text:
Fix $C\subseteq I$ of size $\kappa$, a set $P$ of $\kappa^+$ maps $x:C	o L$, and distinct coordinates $j_x
otin C$, and let $p_x$ be the arrows whose $L^I$-coordinate $n$ has $n|_C
e x$ or $n_{j_x}=\varepsilon$, with support $C\cup\{j_x\}$. A greatest lower bound of the constant property $\{p_x:x\in P\}$ would be the union of the supported subsets of $ igcap_xp_x$, the arrows with $m|_C

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: Every rigid $Y$ is, for every arrow $k$, the transport along $k$ of a rigid relation: with $Y$ the exact image of $D$ with support $S$, the members of $D$ lifted along $k$, by stripping $k$'s suffixes on $S$ (and, with moving individuals, peeling $k$'s surjection off and replacing each individual by a preimage chosen by a fixed section of it), have a supported exact image. So the constant property of being rigid, which is persistent, is weakly inextensible: a test necessarily holding of every rigid $X$ holds at $k$ of every $k\cdot X$, that is, of every rigid relation. The principle is closed and pure.

groups.name: Supported models over an S5 component

references.locator: §3.5, pp. 58–61; Appendix D, pp. 73–74; Appendix E, Definition E.2, pp. 80–83

groups.definition: Fix a set $W$ of worlds, a set $D$ of individuals, a group $G$ acting on $W$ and on $D$, and a set $X$ of support points on which $G$ acts. {{component}} The component is the action model on the category with object set $W$ and exactly one arrow between any two objects, every arrow acting on $D$ as the identity. Transport between its objects is then trivial, so an entity of relational type $\bar\sigma t$ there is a relation $F\subseteq D_{\bar\sigma}\times W$, giving its extension at each world, and the same entities are available at every world. $G$ acts on these relations by $g\cdot F:=\{(g\bar x,gw):(\bar x,w)\in F\}$, its action on the argument entities being defined in the same way by recursion on their types. $F$ is supported by a finite $P\subseteq X$ if $g\cdot F=F$ for every $g$ fixing $P$ pointwise. The component's domains hold the supported relations satisfying the member's further restriction, if any. Identity is genuine identity, transports being bijective. {{root}} Every constant of Σ is relational and denotes the top element of its type.

component.text: The worlds, individuals, group, support points and any further restriction on the component's domains, as the member gives them.

root.text: Whether an unrestricted root is attached in front of the component.

none.text: The evaluation point is a world of the component.
none.label: no root
none.brief: evaluation at a world of the component

free.text: A root object $r$ is added, with one arrow to each world of the component and none back. A root entity of relational type is a pair $(R,a)$ of an arbitrary set $R$ of tuples of root entities, its extension at $r$, and a component entity $a$, its transport along every arrow out of $r$; the root's individuals are those of $D$, each arrow acting on them as the identity. So the propositions at $r$ are the pairs of a truth value at $r$ and a component proposition. The evaluation point is $r$.
free.label: free root
free.brief: an unrestricted root sees every world of the component

meets.infinitely-many-individuals: The base is infinite.
meets.construction-individuals: The individuals are the base, acted on as the construction says.

meets.sigma-top: This is the interpretation.

true-atom.text: Interpretation of Σ, fixed for this record: one designated relational constant $c$ of type $\tau=\bar\sigma t$ denotes $\lambda\bar x\, .\,a$, where $a$ is the unique true atom of the model, the actual-world proposition, the symmetry group; every other constant of Σ, of which there is at least one, is relational and denotes the top element of its type.
true-atom.label: Σ true atom
true-atom.brief: one constant denotes the true atom (as a constant relation), the others top

meets.symmetric-domains: The relational domains hold exactly the symmetric intensions pinned down by a finite set (Dorr, draft, Definitions 15–18).

full-continuum-everywhere.text: At a reachable object $v$, let $\tau$ be a type with infinitely many orbits there, and for a set $A$ of them let $Y_A$ be the intension of type $\tau t$ whose value at an arrow into $v$ is the union of the orbits in $A$ and at other arrows is empty: symmetric, the values being invariant, and pinned down by $\emptyset$, so in the domain; its transport along any arrow depends only on the arrow's codomain. The $Y_A$ are continuum many and pairwise distinct at $v$. For a set $T$ of $k$-tuples of them, the intension whose value at an arrow $h$ is the set of transports along $h$ of the tuples in $T$ depends only on $h$'s codomain, is symmetric, each such transport being fixed by the target's symmetries, and is pinned down by $\emptyset$; its extension at $v$ is $T$.

infinitely-many-orbits-everywhere.text: For a finite set $N$ of individuals, the property of being one of them, $h\mapsto h(N)$, is symmetric and pinned down by $N$; symmetries preserve the size of $N$, so these properties lie in infinitely many orbits at the one object.

conditions.text: At the evaluation object V, for every finite subset N of the pinning carrier, some designated symmetry fixing N pointwise moves a proposition in D_t(V) as a whole intension. The pinning carrier need not be the individual domain.
At every object reachable from the evaluation point, the entities of some relational type there fall into infinitely many orbits under that object's symmetry group.
The pinning base at the evaluation object is infinite.

For each finite set $N$ of individuals at the evaluation object, some property $A$ in the domain has a nonempty extension there, and each individual $y$ in that extension is moved by a member of the symmetry group that fixes $N$ pointwise and fixes $A$.
There are infinitely many pairs of individuals such that, for any two of these pairs, some arrow collapses the one and not the other.
Every arrow is surjective.
At every object, the domains hold the symmetric intensions pinned down by a finite set: every object carries the ideal of finite sets.
The symmetry group, the smallest symmetric set of arrows containing the identity, is pinned down by a finite set.

There is a finite set $M_0$ of individuals at the evaluation object such that: (B1) for every finite $M\supseteq M_0$ and every arrow $h$ from the evaluation object to itself that $M$ does not separate (some arrow $k\notin G$ agrees with $h$ on $M$, or $h\in G$), every arrow $h'$ agreeing with $h$ on $M$, and finite $P,Q$ with $P\cap Q\subseteq M$, some arrow agrees with $h'$ on $P$ and with $h$ on $Q$; and (B2) for finite $N\supseteq M_0$ and finite $P,Q$, some member of the symmetry group fixes $N$ pointwise and moves every member of $P$ outside $N$ off $Q$. The arrows in (B1) go from the evaluation object to any one object, and $M$ separates $h$ when every arrow agreeing with $h$ on $M$ is a member of the symmetry group of the evaluation object. These are the hypotheses of Dorr's main theorem (draft, Definitions 28–30, Theorem 36).
There is a distinguished individual that every arrow either fixes or omits from its range, and some arrow moves it.

arguments.by: OpenAI Codex, prompted by Daniel Kodsi
arguments.text: At input type $tt$ and output type $t$. The full symmetric profile construction admits the property $A$ whose profile at $w:V\to W$ is the propositions moved by some symmetry of W fixing $w[N]$ pointwise. It is N-pinned, and conjugation of stabilizers proves symmetry. If a selector S for the serial membership relation were pinned by finite N, every symmetry fixing N would fix both S and A as whole intensions. The condition makes A nonempty at V. A selected member would therefore be fixed by every such symmetry, contradicting its membership in A. This uses finite supports only at the evaluation object, full admission of symmetric pinned profiles, and no external choice. The construction-specific condition witnesses and complete proof are in the writeup. Original arguments: 22 October 2026, §§1–2 of the stabilizer note and §§1–2 of its singleton applications; direct source misc.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, after Cian Dorr’s observation that a choice over the individuals cannot be finitely pinned down
arguments.text: At the types $(e\to t)$ and $e$. Let $U:=\lambda Xy\, .\,Xy\lor\neg\exists z\, .\,Xz$, a closed term, hence in the domain, and serial. A functional subrelation $S$ of $U$ would lie in the domain at the evaluation object, so it is symmetric and pinned down by a finite set $N$. Two facts about such an $S$ (Dorr, draft, Lemma 19(iv)): every $g\in G$ fixing $N$ pointwise satisfies $g^{[\sigma]}S=S$, and symmetry gives $\langle gA,gy,g\rangle\in S$ whenever $\langle A,y,1\rangle\in S$; together, $\langle gA,gy,1\rangle\in S$. Now let $A$ be the property the condition gives for $N$. Its extension is nonempty, so $S$ relates $A$ at the identity to some $y$ in its extension. The condition gives a member $g$ of the symmetry group that fixes $N$ pointwise, fixes $A$ and moves $y$ to some $gy\ne y$, so $S$ relates $A$ to $gy$ as well, and $S$ is not functional at the identity arrow. The well-ordering of the individuals that Cian Dorr had in mind is refuted by the same two facts, but the direct route needs no derivation of a well-ordering from Relational Choice in C.

revisions.note: The condition transposable no longer mentions the finite set $M$ or the pinning of $A$ by $N\cup M$: the argument uses only that $g$ fixes $N$, the set pinning down $S$, and that $A$ is in the domain. So $g$ is now said to fix $N$ pointwise. Proved in Lean.

arguments.text: There are infinitely many individuals, and identity at the identity arrow is literal, so no numeral counts them. The set of numerals at type $e$ is fixed by every arrow, hence symmetric and pinned down by the empty set, so finite cardinality is standard and no finite cardinality holds of the universal property.

revisions.note: The type-$e$ half of the members' argument, stated once; "the individuals are the natural numbers" became "there are infinitely many individuals", which also covers the qualitative links model. The type-$t$ half is axiom-of-infinity-t.

arguments.text: The propositions $C_{n,m}:=\{h : hn=hm\}$, that an arrow collapses $n$ and $m$, are symmetric, since relabelling the individuals of a world by a member of the symmetry group keeps identities among them, and each is pinned down by $\{n,m\}$; by the condition infinitely many of them are pairwise distinct, so there are infinitely many propositions. The set of numerals at type $t$ is fixed by every arrow, hence symmetric and pinned down by the empty set, so finite cardinality is standard and no finite cardinality holds of the universal property.

revisions.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
revisions.note: Replaces the members' argument of 20 September (Claude Fable 5.1), which used the propositions $\{h : hn=n\}$ that an arrow fixes a given individual. Those are not symmetric when the symmetry group moves $n$: symmetry asks that $h\in p$ imply $g\circ h\in p$, and $(g\circ h)n=gn$.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's request
arguments.text: At every type. Let $B$ be an entity at the target of an arrow $i$, pinned down by the finite set $M$, and choose a finite set $P$ with a map $s:M\to P$ such that $i\circ s$ is the identity on $M$, possible because $i$ is surjective. Put $A:=\{\langle\bar x,j\rangle : \langle\bar x,k\rangle\in B$ for some arrow $k$ with $k|_M=j\circ s\}$. This is well defined because $B$ is pinned down by $M$. It is pinned down by $P$ and symmetric, since $B$ is. And $i\cdot A=B$: $\langle\bar x,k\rangle\in i\cdot A$ iff $\langle\bar x,k\circ i\rangle\in A$ iff $\langle\bar x,k'\rangle\in B$ for some $k'$ with $k'|_M=k|_M$, iff $\langle\bar x,k\rangle\in B$. So every entity at every world is the transport of an entity at the evaluation point, and a relation that is necessarily true of every entity is necessarily true of all of them.

revisions.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
revisions.note: The qualitative links model's argument, which proves the draft's claim for the all-surjections model ("at every type because every arrow is surjective and a finitely pinned symmetric intension can be pulled back along an arrow"), stated once for every member whose arrows are surjective.

revisions.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
revisions.note: Requires finite-pinning as well, which the argument uses (a finite preimage of the pinning set): stated when the group's Lean parameter admitted a per-object ideal, for the two-object model whose second object is unpinned. Every member meeting surjective-arrows meets it.

arguments.text: The symmetry group is the smallest symmetric set of arrows containing the identity, and by the condition it is pinned down by a finite set, so it is a proposition in the domain, and an atom entailing every truth.

revisions.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
revisions.note: The three members' versions stated once; what pins the group down is each member's reason for meeting symmetry-group-pinned.

arguments.by: Cian Dorr
arguments.text: At type e. Take the property of being positive unless things are as they actually are, which is pinned down by the distinguished individual and is symmetric. Every individual necessarily has it, since an arrow either fixes the distinguished individual or omits it from its range and so sends everything to something positive; but it is not necessary that everything has it, since any arrow moving the distinguished individual leaves it out.

revisions.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
revisions.note: The range-gap model's argument, which its variant without Actuality invoked ("by the argument of the previous variant, which goes through verbatim"), stated once.

arguments.by: Cian Dorr
arguments.text: At every relational type: a property $F$ of type-$\tau$ entities has a least upper bound, the union of the hulls of its instances. Let $F$ be pinned down by $N\supseteq M_0$. For each instance $u$ of $F$ at the identity, its hull is the closure of $u$ under the arrows that $N$ does not separate from the identity, transported along the arrows agreeing with the identity on $N$; it is symmetric, pinned down by $N$ (by (B1), which splices an arrow agreeing with $h'$ on the instance's pinning set with $h$ on $N$), and an upper bound of $u$. Every upper bound $z$ of all the instances, pinned down by $N'$, contains every hull: given a member of a hull, (B2) supplies a symmetry fixing $N$ and moving the instance's pinning set off $N'$, whose image is again an instance (by the orbit lemma, Lemma 35), lying under $z$; and $z$, pinned down by $N'$, cannot tell the moved instance's tuple from the original. The union of the hulls is pinned down by $N$ and symmetric, so it is in the domain, and it is the least upper bound.

groups.name: Symmetric surjection products with free-word gluing

references.note: The symmetric ideally-full models, of which these are κ-pinned products with a monoid factor; the hull argument for Boolean Completeness is the κ-pinned form of Dorr's.
Gluing the interpretations of Σ at fresh arrows.
One-object action models and their semantics.

groups.definition: Fix an infinite cardinal $\kappa\ge|\Sigma|$, a set $U$ of size $\kappa^+$, the monoid $S$ of surjections $U\to U$, and a monoid $K$: {{monoid}} The arrows of the one object are the pairs $(k,s)$ with $k\in K$ and $s\in S$, composed by $(k,s)(k',s'):=(kk',s\circ s')$; the evaluation point is $1:=(1_K,\mathrm{id})$, and the symmetry group is $\{1_K\}\times\operatorname{Sym}(U)$. {{individuals}} A relational domain consists of the profiles $F$, assigning to each arrow a set of argument tuples, that are pinned down by a set $N\subseteq U$ of size at most $\kappa$ ($F_{(k,s)}$ depends only on $k$ and $s|_N$) and symmetric ($F_{(k,\pi s)}=\pi\cdot F_{(k,s)}$ for every permutation $\pi$ of $U$). Transport is $(h\cdot F)_j:=F_{jh}$. Σ is interpreted by gluing: individual constants denote distinct individuals (or the only one), and each relational constant glues, along fresh final letters of the word coordinate, chosen interpretations witnessing every satisfiable $\mathcal L(\Sigma)$-sentence (see the write-up).

monoid.text: The monoid factor $K$ of the arrows.

words-idempotent.brief: K is the free monoid times an idempotent, so not right cancellative

singleton.label: one individual
singleton.brief: a single individual; U supplies only the pinning sets and symmetries

meets.one-individual: There is a single individual at every world.

meets.infinitely-many-individuals: The individuals are the $\kappa^+$ members of $U$.
meets.moving-individuals: The individuals are the members of $U$, moved by the surjections.

meets.one-object-action-model: One object, with the semantics of Dorr's intensional action models: a formula holds at an arrow iff it holds at $1$ with its parameters transported.
meets.no-actuality-anywhere: One object, so Actuality, a closed pure sentence, holds at every world iff at the identity, where it fails (recorded in this group's verdicts).
meets.infinitely-many-propositions: The propositions $q_{a,b}$ of the argument atomlessness are pairwise distinct for distinct pairs.

conditions.text: The monoid factor of the arrows is right cancellative: $av=bv$ implies $a=b$.
The monoid factor of the arrows has an idempotent other than its identity.
The individuals are the members of the set $U$ on which the surjections act, and every arrow acts on them by its surjection.

arguments.by: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), prompted by Daniel Kodsi, 22 October 2026; checked and recorded by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: For each of the at most $\kappa$ $\mathcal L(\Sigma)$-sentences true at $1$ under some interpretation, choose one, $J_\alpha$, and a letter $f_\alpha$. Let $s_\alpha$ be a surjection sending each individual constant's denotation $a_c$ to $J_\alpha(c)$ (the identity with one individual), and $B_{\alpha,c}$ a preimage of $J_\alpha(c)$ under $(1_K,s_\alpha)$. Interpret a relational $c$ by $G_c$, equal at $(uf_\alpha,j,s)$ to $B_{\alpha,c}$ at $(u,j,s)$ and empty where the word is empty: pinned down by the union of at most $\kappa$ pinning sets, and symmetric. At $h_\alpha:=(f_\alpha,1,s_\alpha)$ every constant transports to its $J_\alpha$-value at once, so a Σ-sentence is possible iff it is true under some interpretation, which gives Logical Necessity.

arguments.text: Every arrow acts onto every domain. At $e$ the surjections are onto. At a relational type, given $F$ pinned down by $N$ and an arrow $(v,s)$: choose a permutation $\pi$ with $s\pi$ the identity on $N$, so that $(1_K,s)\cdot(\pi\cdot F)=F$; and lift along $(v,1)$ by the profile equal at $(uv,s)$ to $F$ at $(u,s)$ and empty elsewhere, well defined by right cancellation. So BF holds at every type, and, being closed and pure in a one-object model, necessarily.

arguments.by: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), prompted by Daniel Kodsi, 22 October 2026; checked and recorded by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: Let $p$ be the proposition that the monoid coordinate is $1_K$, and $R$ of type $tt$ hold of $p$ alone at the arrows with monoid coordinate $d_0$ and of nothing elsewhere; both are pinned down by $\varnothing$ and symmetric. Then $\Diamond\exists q\, .\,Rq$. But a transport $h\cdot q$ along an arrow with monoid coordinate $d_0$ takes the same value at $(1_K,s)$ and $(d_0,s)$, as $1_Kd_0=d_0d_0$, while $p$ does not; so no $q$ has $\Diamond Rq$, and BF fails at $t$.

arguments.text:
For distinct $a,b\in U$ let $q_{a,b}$ be the proposition that the arrow's surjection keeps $a$ and $b$ apart: symmetric, pinned down by $\{a,b\}$. Given $p
e ot$ pinned down by $N$, a member $(k,s)$ of $p$ and $a,b
otin N$, the restriction $s|_N$ extends to surjections that separate and that identify $a$ and $b$; so $p\land q_{a,b}$ and $p\land

arguments.by: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), prompted by Daniel Kodsi, 22 October 2026; checked and recorded by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: Let $p$ be true, pinned down by $N$, and $a,b\notin N$. A surjection $s$ fixing $N$ and identifying $a$ and $b$ gives an arrow $(1_K,s)$ at which $p$ holds, while the true $q_{a,b}$ is impossible there, as composition on the left keeps the collapse. So no truth entails the possibility of every truth.

arguments.by: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), prompted by Daniel Kodsi, 22 October 2026; checked and recorded by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: At input type $tt$ and output type $t$. Let $U$ relate a property of propositions with exactly two actual instances to each of them, and any other to every proposition: a closed term, serial. A functional subrelation $R$, pinned down by $N$, has an actual extension invariant under every permutation fixing $N$. For distinct $a,b,c\notin N$, the property $A$ whose instances are the transports of $q_{c,a}$ and $q_{c,b}$ is in the domain, and the transposition of $a$ and $b$ fixes $N$ and $A$ and exchanges $q_{c,a}$ and $q_{c,b}$; so $R$ relates $A$ to both.

arguments.by: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), prompted by Daniel Kodsi, 22 October 2026; checked and recorded by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: At every relational type, by the hull argument of Dorr's Theorem 36 with pinning sets of size at most $\kappa$. For $A$ pinned down by $N$ with actual instances $E$, let $J$ hold at $(k,s)$ of everything some $a\in E$ holds of at some $(k,t)$ with $t|_N=s|_N$: pinned down by $N$, symmetric, an upper bound. If $Z$, pinned down by $T$, bounds $E$ and $\bar b\in a_{(k,t)}$, take a permutation $\pi$ fixing $N$ and moving $a$'s pinning set off $T$ outside $N$, so that $\pi\cdot a\in E$, and a surjection $r$ agreeing with $s$ on $T$ with $r\pi=t$ on $a$'s pinning set; then $\bar b\in(\pi\cdot a)_{(k,r)}\subseteq Z_{(k,r)}=Z_{(k,s)}$. So $J$ is the least upper bound. The schema is closed and pure.

arguments.by: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), prompted by Daniel Kodsi, 22 October 2026; checked and recorded by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: A weakly rigid $Y$ pinned down by $N$, with actual extension $E$, is the profile $h\mapsto h\cdot E$, by the argument of tame-rigidity-factorizable with pinning sets of size at most $\kappa$: given $\bar b=(k,t)\cdot\bar a$ with $\bar a\in E$ and $t|_N=s|_N$, a surjection $u$ fixing $N$ with $su=t$ on the pinning set of $\bar a$ gives $u\cdot\bar a\in E$ and $\bar b=(k,s)\cdot(u\cdot\bar a)$. Such profiles, and their transports, are rigid.

arguments.by: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), prompted by Daniel Kodsi, 22 October 2026; checked and recorded by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: As rigid-power-surjections, with pinning sets of size at most $\kappa$ and the monoid coordinate held fixed. If $X\le h\cdot F$ is rigid at $h=(k,s)$, let $j_0$ agree with $s$ on a set $N$ pinning down $F$ and the test $Z$, and map the rest of $U$ bijectively onto the rest; then $j:=(k,j_0)$ has $j\cdot F=h\cdot F$, and the instances of $F$ that $j$ sends into $X$ form a set closed under the surjections fixing a set of size at most $\kappa$, whose exact image $Y$ is rigid, below $F$, with $j\cdot Y=X$. So the power property of $F$ is weakly inextensible, and rigid by Tame Rigidity.

arguments.by: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), prompted by Daniel Kodsi, 22 October 2026; checked and recorded by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: The numerals are closed pure terms, fixed by every arrow, so the constant profile with the numerals as instances is symmetric and pinned down by $\varnothing$; hence the finite cardinalities are the standard ones, each holding of exactly the properties with that many actual instances. The universal property of individuals has $\kappa^+$ instances.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: Let $p$ be true, pinned down by $N$, and $q$ the set of arrows $(1_K,s)$ with $s$ injective on $N$: true, pinned down by $N$, symmetric. In both monoid factors $jk=1_K$ only if $k=1_K$, so $\Diamond q=q$. A member $(1_K,s)$ of $q$ agrees on $N$ with a permutation $\pi$, and $(1_K,\pi)\in p$ by symmetry, so $(1_K,s)\in p$. Hence $\Box(\Diamond q\to p)$, and $p$ is ND-necessary. The principle is closed and pure.

arguments.text:
At type $t$, as intensional-choice-collapse. Fix $c\in U$, write $q_{x,y}$ for the set of arrows whose surjection keeps $x$ and $y$ apart, and let $F$ hold at $(k,s)$ of the $q_{s(c),y}$ with $y
e s(c)$: pinned down by $\{c\}$, symmetric, and necessarily instantiated. Let $G\le F$ be necessarily uniquely instantiated, pinned down by $N
i c$, and $h=(1_K,s)$ with $s$ sending $N$ to a single point $p$. Then $G_h=\{q_{p,y}\}$ with $y
e p$. A permutation $\pi$ fixing $p$ has $\pi h$ agreeing with $h$ on $N$, so $G_{\pi h}=G_h$ by pinning, while symmetry gives $G_{\pi h}=\{q_{p,\pi y}\}$; but some such $\pi$ moves $y$.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: As arithmetic-necessitism-finitely-pinned: the profile whose value at every arrow is the set of numerals at $\sigma$ is pinned down by $\varnothing$ and symmetric, numerals being closed terms fixed by every arrow; so the numbers are the numerals, rigid and, given the Infinity axiom, necessarily distinct.
