withdrawn.reason: The step from the equality of transports to membership in the carrier by inextensibility does not follow: inextensibility bounds a rigid carrier from above, by the transports of its actual instances, and puts nothing new into its actual extension.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: As analytic-necessitism-exact-collapses-symmetric, at type $tt$, with the arrows $(1_K,s)$. For finite $N\subseteq U$ the arrows whose surjection is constant on $N$ form a symmetric proposition pinned down by $N$, and the orbits of these under the permutations, one for each size of $N$, give continuum many invariant sets of propositions, the values of constant intensions fixed by every arrow, which carry a real number structure. None is rigid: for $(1_K,s)$ with $s(a)=s(b)$, toggling $\top$ in an entity $x$ of type $tt$ at the arrows that keep $a$ and $b$ apart gives a distinct entity $y$ with the same transport along $(1_K,s)$, so persistence, inextensibility and necessary distinctness of a carrier conflict.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: At type $tt$. For finite $N\subseteq U$ the arrows whose surjection is constant on $N$ form a symmetric proposition, and its orbit under the permutations depends only on $|N|$; for $A\subseteq\mathbb N$ the union $S_A$ of the orbits for sizes in $A$ is invariant under the permutations, so the constant intension $Y_A$ with value $S_A$ is symmetric, pinned down by $\varnothing$, in the domain, and fixed by every arrow, and distinct sets $A$ give distinct $Y_A$. Every set of tuples of the $Y_A$, and every set of such constant relations, is likewise invariant, so the value of a constant intension in the domain. With one object and all parameters fixed, a real number structure on the $Y_A$ by constant relations is one at every world, rigid with necessarily distinct instances, and the constant intensions of the sets of its constant relations are represented powers. So Analytic Necessitism and its second-order form hold.

arguments.by: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), prompted by Cian Dorr, 29 October 2026; checked and recorded by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
arguments.text: Given $X$ pinned down by $N$, let $Y_{(k,s)}:=X_{(k,s)}$ if $k=1_K$ and $s$ is injective on $N$, and $Y_{(k,s)}:=\varnothing$ otherwise: symmetric, pinned down by $N$, and coextensive with $X$ at $1$. In both monoid factors $jk=1_K$ only if $k=1_K$, and $ts$ is injective on $N$ only if $s$ is, so along an arrow without both properties $Y$ transports to $\bot$, and along one with them it transports to the same construction for the transport of $X$, pinned down by $s[N]$. It remains that $Y$ is weakly inextensible at $1$. Every surjection $g$ fixing $N$ maps $E:=X_1$ onto itself: for $\bar a\in E$ pinned down by $T$, a permutation $\tau$ fixing $N$ and sending each point of $T\setminus N$ to a $g$-preimage of it has $g\tau$ the identity on $T$, so $\tau\cdot\bar a\in E$ and $g\cdot(\tau\cdot\bar a)=\bar a$. If $(1_K,s)$ is injective on $N$, extend $s|_N$ to a permutation $\pi$ and put $g:=\pi^{-1}s$, fixing $N$; then $Y_{(1_K,s)}=\pi\cdot E$, and a member $\pi\cdot\bar a$ is the transport along $(1_K,s)$ of a $g$-preimage $\bar a'\in E$ of $\bar a$. So anything that necessarily holds of every member of $E$ contains $Y$ at every arrow. Inextensible Comprehension holds at $1$, and as a closed pure sentence in a one-object model, necessarily. Choice picks the preimages and the extending permutations.

groups.name: Symmetry-constrained full models

references.note: The symmetry condition on intensions, here imposed on a full action model over finitely many individuals instead of on a finitely pinned one over the natural numbers.
Full action models.

construction.text: The arrows on the three individuals, as the member gives them.

objects.text: The objects and the evaluation point.

one.text: The member has one object, $X$. Evaluation point: the sole object, at the identity arrow.
one.label: one object

meets.one-object-action-model: An action model with a single object.
meets.irreversible-arrow: A collapse $c$: $l\circ c$ is a collapse for every arrow $l$, so from $c$ no world in $a$ is seen.
meets.actual-world-isolated: $a$, the orbit of the identity, is in the domain and entails every truth; from a world outside $a$, a non-permutation $h$, every $l\circ h$ is again a non-permutation, outside $a$.

two.text: The member has two objects, $W_0$ with a single point $x$, and $X$; the symmetry group at $W_0$ is trivial, so the condition bites at the arrows into $X$. Evaluation point: $W_0$, at its identity arrow.
two.label: two objects

individuals.text: What the individuals are. Each member is recorded with the three individuals the arrows act on; its variant with a single individual, the arrows still acting on the three-element set that supplies the symmetry, is generated.

three.text: Individuals, fixed for this record: the individuals are the three elements of $X$, acted on by the arrows themselves.
three.label: three individuals
three.brief: the individuals are the three elements of X, moved by the arrows

meets.construction-individuals: The individuals are the three elements the arrows act on.
meets.homogeneous-individuals: Relabelling by a permutation of $X$ is an automorphism of the model, carrying each individual to its image.
meets.collapse-onto-point: Take an individual $a$ and $F:=\lambda x\, .\,x\ne a$, whose extension at every arrow $h$ is $X\setminus\{h(a)\}$, nonempty. For any $N$, the collapse $c_p$ onto any $p$ sends $N\cup\{a\}$ to $p$, and the transposition $\sigma$ of the two individuals other than $p$ fixes $p$, moves every $y\ne p$, and has $\sigma\circ c_p=c_p$ an arrow.

singleton.text: Individuals, fixed for this record: there is a single individual, which every arrow fixes; the arrows still act on the three-element set $X$, which supplies the symmetry.
singleton.label: one individual
singleton.brief: a single individual; X still supplies the symmetry

meets.one-individual: The only individual is fixed by every arrow, at the sole object.

sigma.text: The interpretation of Σ. Each member is recorded with Σ top; its variant with the other is generated.

top.text: Interpretation of Σ, fixed for this record: every constant of Σ is relational, and each denotes the top element of its type.
top.label: Σ top
top.brief: every constant of Σ denotes the top element of its type

meets.sigma-top: This is the interpretation.

true-atom.text: Interpretation of Σ, fixed for this record: one designated relational constant $c$ of type $\tau=\bar\sigma t$ denotes $\lambda\bar x\, .\,a$, where $a$ is the unique true atom of the model, the actual-world proposition, which is the orbit of the identity arrow under the symmetry group; every other constant of Σ, of which there is at least one, is relational and denotes the top element of its type.
true-atom.label: Σ true atom
true-atom.brief: one constant denotes the true atom (as a constant relation), the others top

meets.finitely-many-arrows-everywhere: The arrows are maps among the three-element set $X$ and, in the two-object member, the one-point $W_0$: finitely many out of every object.
meets.finitely-many-individuals-everywhere: The individuals are the three elements of $X$ or one, and in the two-object member the single point of $W_0$.
meets.rigid-haecceity-disjunctions: For any set $E$ the intension $k\mapsto k\cdot E$ is symmetric (as in the argument for Rigid Comprehension), so in the domain, and it is the smallest symmetric intension containing the transports of the members of $E$; so a weakly inextensible relation lies below it over its extension, and a rigid one equals it (as in the argument for Tame Rigidity).
meets.symmetric-domains: The domains hold exactly the symmetric intensions; every intension is pinned down by the finite set $X$ of all individuals.
meets.extensionally-full: Any set $S$ of tuples at the identity is the extension there of a symmetric intension: put $S$ at the identity, $g\cdot S$ at each permutation $g$, and the empty set at every other arrow.
meets.finitely-many-propositions: The propositions are the symmetric sets of arrows, finitely many since there are finitely many arrows.
meets.actuality-contingent: The actual-world proposition $a$ is the orbit of the identity under the symmetry group, the set of permutations; it is in the domain, true, and entails every truth, since a symmetric true proposition contains the identity and so its orbit. It is necessary at no world, since every world sees a collapse, which lies outside $a$; and a collapse $c$ does not fix it, since $l\circ c$ is a collapse for every $l$, so $c\cdot a$ is empty.

conditions.text: The construction does not itself interpret Σ, so either of the group's interpretations can be added to it.
Some arrow $c$ out of the evaluation object is absorbed by an arrow $m$ out of its codomain that is not a symmetry: $m\circ c$ lies in the orbit of $c$ under the symmetry group.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
arguments.text: At every type the domain is finite and closed under the pointwise lattice operations, since the union and intersection of symmetric intensions are symmetric; in a finite lattice every nonzero element has an atom below it.

arguments.by: Cian Dorr, recorded by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic)
arguments.text: At every object $V$ reachable from the evaluation point, not only there. Every domain at $V$ is finite and closed under the pointwise lattice operations, so it is atomic, as in the argument for Atomicity. For Actuality, the orbit of $1_V$ under the symmetry group at $V$, the set of arrows $g\circ1_V$, is a symmetric proposition, so in the domain, and true; and a true symmetric proposition contains $1_V$, hence the whole orbit, so the orbit entails every truth. A closed sentence holds at an arrow into $V$ iff it holds at $1_V$, so Atomicity and Actuality are necessary.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
arguments.text: The entailment order is the pointwise order on intensions, and the pointwise intersection of any set of symmetric intensions is symmetric and in the domain, so every set has a greatest lower bound at every type.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
arguments.text: For a set $S$ of tuples at the identity, the intension $Y$ with $Y(h):=h\cdot S$, the transports of the members of $S$ along $h$, is symmetric: relabelling by $g$ the transport of a tuple along $h$ gives its transport along $g\circ h$ (when the permutations are arrows because transport composes; otherwise because $g\cdot(c\cdot z)=c_{g(i)}\cdot z$ for a collapse $c=c_i$ and every admissible $z$, the collapses being absorbed, $l\circ c=l$ for $l\ne1$, and $z$ symmetric). $Y$ is coextensive with $S$, persistent, and inextensible at every world $h$, since any persistent $B$ with $B(h)\supseteq Y(h)$ has $B(k\circ h)\supseteq k\cdot Y(h)= Y(k\circ h)$. So every extension has a rigid coextension, at every type.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
arguments.text: Let $Y$ be weakly rigid with extension $E$ at the identity. The intension $h\mapsto h\cdot E$ is symmetric, as in the argument for Rigid Comprehension, and satisfies the hypothesis of weak inextensibility, so $Y(h)\subseteq h\cdot E$ for every $h$; persistence gives the converse. So $Y$ is that intension, which is rigid.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
arguments.text: Transport along a collapse $c$ sends every proposition to $\bot$ or $\top$: $l\circ c$ is the constant map with value $l(i)$ for $c=c_i$, and the constant maps form one orbit of the symmetry group, so a symmetric proposition contains all of them or none. The intension $X$ of type $t\to t$ with $X(c):=\{\bot,\top\}$ at every collapse and $X(h):=$ every proposition elsewhere is symmetric, since both values are fixed by every relabelling. So $\forall p\, .\,\Box Xp$ holds at the identity while $\Box\forall p\, .\,Xp$ fails.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
arguments.text: The actual-world proposition $a$ and $\bot$ are distinct, and a collapse $c$ transports both to $\bot$, since $l\circ c$ is a collapse for every $l$ and so never in $a$.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
arguments.text: There are finitely many propositions, $n$ say, with literal identity. The numerals are closed terms, so in the domain, and the numeral $n$ holds of the universal property of propositions, so the Axiom of Infinity at type $t$ fails, as does the instance of the schema asking for $n+1$ pairwise distinct propositions.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
arguments.text: There are exactly three individuals at every world, with literal identity, so the numeral $3$ holds of the universal property at type $e$ necessarily, and no four individuals are pairwise distinct.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, from Cian Dorr's observation
arguments.text: The constant maps form one orbit of the symmetry group, so the proposition $C$ that the arrow is constant (for individuals $a,b,c$, the proposition that $a=b=c$) is an atom: it is possible, and a symmetric proposition contains all the constant maps or none. It is not a strong atom. At a constant map $c_i$, every composite $l\circ c_i$ is constant, so $C$ transported there is $\top$; and $\top$ there lies neither below the proposition $P$ that the arrow is a permutation nor below its negation, both being possible. As an atom, $C$ has no possible proposition below it but itself, so no strong atom lies below it, and the type-$t$ Strong Atomicity fails.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, 25 October 2026
arguments.text: At every object the atoms are the orbits of single pairs under the symmetry group. The orbit $C$ of a collapse $c$ (in the two-object member, of the arrows $c_i:W_0\to X$) is an atom; its transport along $c$ is the set of arrows $m$ with $m\circ c$ in $C$, which includes every arrow $X\to X$, since $m\circ c$ is again a collapse, and so is not an atom there, the orbit of the permutations being a proper symmetric part. So $C$ is an atom and not a self-atom, and the only possible proposition below $C$ is $C$ itself: Atoms are self-atoms (type t) and Self-Atomicity (type t) fail. Conversely a self-atom $I$ at a relational type has, at each of its pairs $\langle k,\bar a\rangle$, a transport along $k$ that is an atom containing $\langle1,\cdot\rangle$, hence the orbit of the identity; so $m\circ k$ carries a pair of $I$ only for symmetries $m$, which excludes collapses ($c\circ c=c$) and leaves pairs at permutations, where symmetry makes $I$ the orbit of one pair, an atom, whose transport along a collapse is empty and along a permutation is an atom again: a strong atom. The same holds at every reachable object, the domains being the symmetric intensions everywhere.

conditions.text: The model is an action model (Classicism, Appendix D), or an intensional action model in the sense of Dorr's draft (Boolean Completeness does not imply Rigid Comprehension), with a single object.

The model is extensionally full at every object: every set of tuples from the domains at an object is the extension, at the identity arrow, of an element of the domain of the matching relational type there.
The model is an ideally full action model in which every arrow out of the evaluation object acts surjectively both on the individuals and on the pinning sets (Proposition D.6's hypothesis).
Every constant of Σ is relational, and each denotes the top element of its type.
There is exactly one individual, at every world.
The model is full: at each object, the domain of each relational type contains every intension of that type.
The model is a full action model: an action model (Classicism, Appendix D) that is full at every object.
At every object reachable from the evaluation point, the domain contains every intension whose value at an arrow depends only on the arrow's codomain.
At every object the individuals are the same infinite set, and every arrow acts on them as the identity.
The model's automorphisms carry every individual to every other.
There are finitely many propositions at the evaluation world.

Σ has a designated relational constant $c$ of type $\tau=\bar\sigma t$ denoting $\lambda\bar x\, .\,a$, where $a$ is the actual-world proposition, the unique true atom; every other constant, of which there is at least one, is relational and denotes the top element of its type.
The actual-world proposition $a$, the strongest truth, is in the domain; it is necessary at no world, and some arrow does not fix it.
Some world sees no world at which the actual-world proposition is true.
The actual-world proposition $a$ is in the domain and entails every truth, and no world outside $a$ sees a world in $a$.

The model is a one-object action model whose entities are finitely pinned, and there are a finite set $N$, an arrow $i$ and a proposition $q$ in the domain such that $q$ separates two arrows that agree on the range of every arrow agreeing with $i$ on $N$, and the intension $\{\langle r,j\rangle : r\ne q\text{ or }j\text{ disagrees with }i\text{ on }N\}$ is in the domain.

A group $G$ acts on the individuals at the evaluation object, and every element of a relational domain there is symmetric, meaning that $\langle\bar x,h\rangle\in D$ implies $\langle g\cdot\bar x,g\circ h\rangle\in D$ whenever $g\in G$ and $g\circ h$ is an arrow, and is pinned down by a finite set of individuals, its extension at an arrow depending only on the arrow's values there.
The individuals at the evaluation object are those the construction acts on, and the arrows act on them as the construction says.

There are an individual $a$ and a necessarily instantiated property $F$ in the domain such that, for every finite set $N$ of individuals at the evaluation object, some arrow $h$ sends $N\cup\{a\}$ to a single individual $p$, and every individual $y\ne p$ in $F$'s extension at $h$ is moved by a member $\sigma$ of the symmetry group that fixes $p$, with $\sigma\circ h$ again an arrow.

There is a necessarily instantiated entity $F$ of some type $\sigma t$ in the domain at the evaluation object such that, for every finite set $N$ of points of the pinning base there, some arrow $h$ out of the evaluation object has every member of $F$'s extension at $h$ moved by a member $g$ of the symmetry group of $h$'s codomain that fixes $h(N)$ pointwise, with $g\circ h$ again an arrow.

At every object reachable from the evaluation point, the rigid relations of each relational type are exactly the intensions $k\mapsto k\cdot E$, the disjunctions of the haecceities of the members of $E$, for $E$ any set of tuples from the domains there; in particular every such intension is in the domain.
Every arrow out of every object reachable from the evaluation point is an epimorphism (arrows after it that agree after it are equal) and acts surjectively on the individuals.
There are infinitely many individuals at the evaluation world.
The continuum injects into the arrows out of the evaluation object: there is an injection from the sets of natural numbers into them, given outright, without choice.
There are infinitely many propositions at the evaluation world.
There are finitely many propositions at every object reachable from the evaluation point.
There are infinitely many propositions at every object reachable from the evaluation point.
Some object reachable from the evaluation point has finitely many entities of every type, and there is a real number structure at the evaluation point.
Every arrow out of every object reachable from the evaluation point is invertible.
Every arrow out of the evaluation object has a retraction: an arrow back after which it composes to the identity.
Some arrow out of the evaluation object has no retraction.
Some arrow out of the evaluation object is not its identity.
Some arrow out of the evaluation object is not an epimorphism: two distinct arrows after it agree after it.
Some arrow out of the evaluation object other than its identity has a retraction: an arrow back after which it composes to the identity.
Every arrow $g$ out of the evaluation object has a retraction $r_g$, chosen so that $r_{x\circ g}\circ x=r_g$ for every arrow $x$ after $g$.
For some $n$, the evaluation object has $n$ distinct propositions, while some world after it, and every world after that one, has fewer.
At the evaluation object, and at the target of every arrow out of it, the singleton of the identity arrow is in the domain.
At the evaluation object, and at the target of every arrow out of it, every arrow out of that object has at most one retraction.

general_arguments.text: Every type is finite at every object $v$ reachable from the evaluation point, by induction on types: the individuals at $v$ are finitely many by hypothesis, the propositions at $v$ are sets of the finitely many arrows out of it, and an entity of a relational type $\bar\sigma t$ at $v$ is an intension assigning to each of those arrows a set of tuples of entities of types $\bar\sigma$ at its target, which is reachable too, so that finitely many values are available at each arrow. An ordered field has infinitely many elements, its $0$, $1$, $1+1,\ldots$ being pairwise distinct, so no real number structure exists at any reachable object, at any type. The antecedents $\Diamond\exists\mathfrak R\,.\,\operatorname{Real}_\sigma(\mathfrak R)$ of Analytic Necessitism and of Second-Order Analytic Necessitism are therefore false at every type, and both hold; and $\Box\forall\mathfrak R\,.\,\operatorname{Real}_\sigma(\mathfrak R)\to A(\mathfrak R)$ holds for every sentence $A$, so the Necessity of Second-Order Analysis holds, with the Necessity of Analysis and the Non-contingency of the Continuum Hypothesis. general_arguments.text: At type $\tau:=tt$. Along every arrow the structure is carried to the like structure at the target, an isomorphic copy, which is a real number structure there: bounded sets of its elements have least upper bounds among them and every inductive subproperty contains its natural numbers. Such a structure is rigid, its instances are necessarily distinct, and it is necessarily a real number structure; and the codomain-only intension of type $((\tau)^kt)t$ whose value at each object is the set of codomain-only $k$-ary relations among the carrier there is a represented power of arity $k$, since at every world each $k$-ary relation agrees on the carrier with one of them. So the consequents of Analytic Necessitism and of its second-order form hold, and both principles hold. (The argument of the withdrawn analytic-necessitism-unretracted-arrow would refute this structure; its step from inextensibility is the gap.)

general_arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Zachary Goodsell
general_arguments.text: Let $k$ be an arrow out of the evaluation object $w$ with $ka=kb$ for two distinct points $a$ and $b$ of the set the arrows act on, and let $q$ be the set of arrows $j$ out of $w$ with $ja\ne jb$. It contains the identity, is pinned down by $\{a,b\}$, is symmetric (an arrow separates $a$ from $b$ iff its composite with a permutation of the points does), and contains no arrow $j\circ k$. Let $\tau$ be $tt$, or $tttt$ in the case noted below. No entity $x$ of type $\tau$ at $w$ is determined by its transport along $k$: let $y$ agree with $x$ except at the arrows in $q$, where the top entity of the argument type of $\tau$ is added to its value or removed from it. Then $y$ is pinned down by a finite set along with $x$, is symmetric if $x$ is, so is in the domain; it differs from $x$ and has $k\cdot y=k\cdot x$, transport along $k$ reading only the values at the arrows after $k$. If $\mathfrak R$ were a rigid real number structure at $w$ of type $\tau$, necessarily a real number structure, with carrier $X$ (Background, Analysis), an instance $x$ of $X$ and $y$ as above would give $k\cdot y=k\cdot x\in X_k$ by persistence, $Xy$ by inextensibility, and $k\cdot y\ne k\cdot x$ by the necessary distinctness of the instances: so $X$ has no instance. The antecedent of Analytic Necessitism holds, however, at type $\tau$. The propositions are infinitely many and, in the recorded instances, include a copy of the natural numbers, so by extensional fullness the entities of type $tt$, which include one with any set of propositions as extension at the identity, include a copy of the sets of natural numbers and so of the reals, whose order, sum, product and natural numbers are the extensions at the identity of relations in the domain; the structure is complete, every subset of its carrier being the extension of a subproperty, so $\exists\mathfrak R\,.\,\operatorname{Real}_{tt}(\mathfrak R)$ holds at $w$. (Should the propositions be infinite without including a copy of the natural numbers, the same holds at type $tttt$, the sets of sets of propositions being Dedekind-infinite in ZF.) So Analytic Necessitism fails. No choice is used.

The conclusion is false in many of the models the argument was applied to: entities fixed by every arrow, or transported injectively, can carry a rigid real number structure that is necessarily one (see analytic-necessitism-codomain-fixed and analytic-necessitism-full-continuum).

general_arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Zachary Goodsell
general_arguments.text: Write $G$ for the symmetry group, which acts on the propositions by transport, $g\cdot p=\{j:j\circ g\in p\}$. For a finite set $N$ of points let $E_N$ be the set of arrows constant on $N$: a proposition in the domain, symmetric and pinned down by $N$, with $g\cdot E_N=E_{g(N)}$. Take for each $n\ge2$ a set $N_n$ of $n$ points and an arrow $j_n$ constant on $N_n$, injective off $N_n$ and taking other values there (the condition), so that the fibres of $j_n$ are $N_n$ and singletons. The orbits $O_n$ of the $E_{N_n}$ under $G$ are pairwise distinct: $E_{N_n}=E_N$ with $N=g(N_m)$ puts $j_n$ in $E_N$, so $N\subseteq N_n$, and puts $j_m\circ g^{-1}$, an arrow whose fibres are $N$ and singletons, in $E_{N_n}$, so $N_n\subseteq N$. For $A\subseteq\mathbb N$ the union $S_A$ of the $O_n$ with $n\in A$ is a $G$-invariant set of propositions, and $A\mapsto S_A$ is injective: there are continuum many $G$-invariant sets of propositions, in explicit bijection with the reals. Each $S_A$ is the value of a constant intension $Y_A$ of type $tt$, symmetric because $S_A$ is $G$-invariant, pinned down by the empty set, so in the domain, and fixed by transport along every arrow. The constant intensions whose values are the set of the $Y_A$, the order, sum and product of the reals carried over to it, and its natural numbers, with the $Y_A$ standing for $0$ and $1$, are symmetric, their values being made of fixed entities, and in the domain; they form a real number structure of type $tt$ at the evaluation point, complete since every bounded set of its elements has a least upper bound among them. So the antecedent of Analytic Necessitism holds at type $tt$. Its consequent fails there. Let $k$ be an arrow with $ka=kb$ for distinct points $a$ and $b$ (the condition at $n=2$) and $q$ the set of arrows $j$ with $ja\ne jb$: symmetric, pinned down by $\{a,b\}$, containing the identity and no arrow $j\circ k$. For $x$ of type $tt$ in the domain let $y$ agree with $x$ except at the arrows in $q$, where the top proposition is added to its value or removed from it: $y$ is symmetric and pinned down by a finite set, so in the domain, differs from $x$, and has $k\cdot y=k\cdot x$. If $\mathfrak R$ were a rigid real number structure of type $tt$, necessarily a real number structure, with carrier $X$ (Background, Analysis), an instance $x$ and this $y$ would give $k\cdot y=k\cdot x\in X_k$ by persistence, $Xy$ by inextensibility and $k\cdot y\ne k\cdot x$ by necessary distinctness: $X$ has no instance. So Analytic Necessitism fails. No choice is used.

The conclusion is false in many of the models the argument was applied to: entities fixed by every arrow, or transported injectively, can carry a rigid real number structure that is necessarily one (see analytic-necessitism-codomain-fixed and analytic-necessitism-full-continuum).

general_arguments.text: Let $h\colon w\to v$ be an arrow out of the evaluation object $w$ with a retraction $j$ but no inverse. Then $e:=h\circ j$ is an idempotent arrow out of $v$ other than its identity, since $e=1_v$ would make $h$ invertible, and $e$ has no retraction: $i\circ e=1_v$ would give $e=i\circ e\circ e=1_v$. Suppose $\mathfrak R$ were a rigid real number structure at $w$ at a relational type, necessarily a real number structure (Background, Analysis). Its boxed clauses hold at $h$ and along the arrows after $h$, which are arrows out of $w$; so at $v$ the instances $X_h$ of its carrier form a complete ordered field, and for $x\in X_h$ and any $y$ at $v$ with $e\cdot y=e\cdot x$, persistence gives $e\cdot y\in X_{e\circ h}$, inextensibility $y\in X_h$, and necessary distinctness $y=x$. But, the model being full at $v$ and $e$ having no retraction, no entity of a relational type at $v$ is determined by its transport along $e$, as in the argument analytic-necessitism-unretracted-arrow: its value at the identity of $v$ is free. So $X_h$ is empty, a contradiction. The antecedent of Analytic Necessitism holds at the relational type $ttt$, as in that argument, the propositions at $w$ being infinitely many. So Analytic Necessitism fails. No choice is used.

withdrawn.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, after a trawl subagent's report
withdrawn.reason: The step from $k\cdot y=k\cdot x\in X_k$ to $Xy$ (or $y\in X_h$) by inextensibility does not follow: inextensibility bounds a rigid carrier from above, by the transports of its actual instances, and puts nothing new into its actual extension. The conclusion is false in many of the models the argument was applied to: entities fixed by every arrow, or transported injectively, can carry a rigid real number structure that is necessarily one (see analytic-necessitism-codomain-fixed and analytic-necessitism-full-continuum).

general_arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Zachary Goodsell
general_arguments.text: As in the argument analytic-necessitism-unretracted-arrow, with the individuals supplying the real numbers in place of the propositions. Let $k$ be an arrow out of the evaluation object $w$ with no retraction; as there, the model being full, no entity of a relational type at $w$ is determined by its transport along $k$, so no rigid real number structure of a relational type at $w$ is necessarily a real number structure. But there is a real number structure at $w$ of the relational type $((et)t)t$: the individuals at $w$ are infinitely many, the sets of sets of individuals are Dedekind-infinite (a theorem of ZF for any infinite set), so the entities of type $(et)t$, which include one with any given set of properties of individuals as extension at the identity, include a copy of the natural numbers, and the entities of type $((et)t)t$ a copy of the sets of natural numbers, hence of the reals; the full domains equip that copy, at the identity, with the order, sum, product and natural numbers of the reals, and the structure is complete, every subset of its carrier being the extension of a subproperty. So the antecedent of Analytic Necessitism holds at that type and its consequent fails: Analytic Necessitism fails. No choice is used.

The conclusion is false in many of the models the argument was applied to: entities fixed by every arrow, or transported injectively, can carry a rigid real number structure that is necessarily one (see analytic-necessitism-codomain-fixed and analytic-necessitism-full-continuum).

general_arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Zachary Goodsell
general_arguments.text: Write $w$ for the evaluation object and $k$ for an arrow out of it with no retraction. No entity $x$ of a relational type at $w$ is determined by its transport along $k$: the identity of $w$ is not of the form $j\circ k$, such a $j$ being a retraction, and the model being full, the intension $y$ agreeing with $x$ at every arrow but the identity, where it takes another value, is in the domain, while $k\cdot y=k\cdot x$, transport along $k$ reading only the values at the arrows after $k$. Suppose then that $\mathfrak R$ were a rigid real number structure at $w$ at a relational type, necessarily a real number structure (Background, Analysis), with carrier $X$. For an instance $x$ of $X$ and $y$ as above, persistence gives $k\cdot x\in X_k$, so $k\cdot y\in X_k$; inextensibility then gives $Xy$; and the necessary distinctness of the instances gives $k\cdot y\ne k\cdot x$, a contradiction. So $X$ has no instance and is no complete ordered field. The antecedent of Analytic Necessitism holds nevertheless, at some relational type. The propositions at $w$ are the sets of the infinitely many arrows out of it, the sets of sets of propositions are Dedekind-infinite (a theorem of ZF for any infinite set), and the entities of type $ttt$ at $w$, which include one with any given extension at the identity, include a copy of the sets of natural numbers and so of the real numbers; the model being full, the order, sum and product of the reals are the extensions at the identity of relations in the domain, every subset of that carrier is the extension of a subproperty, so the structure is complete, and its least inductive subproperty is its natural numbers. So $\exists\mathfrak R\,.\,\operatorname{Real}_{ttt}(\mathfrak R)$ holds at $w$ while the consequent of Analytic Necessitism fails there: Analytic Necessitism fails. (When the arrows out of $w$ include a copy of the natural numbers, as in the recorded instances, the same argument runs at type $t$.) No choice is used.

The conclusion is false in many of the models the argument was applied to: entities fixed by every arrow, or transported injectively, can carry a rigid real number structure that is necessarily one (see analytic-necessitism-codomain-fixed and analytic-necessitism-full-continuum).

general_arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Zachary Goodsell
general_arguments.text: The numbers at a type $\sigma$ are the instances of $\mathbb N_\sigma$, the least property containing $\mathbf 0_\sigma$ and closed under $\operatorname{Suc}_\sigma$ (Background); the numerals $\mathbf 0_\sigma$, $\operatorname{Suc}_\sigma\mathbf 0_\sigma,\ldots$ are closed terms, so each denotes at every object, and transport along an arrow carries its denotation at the source to its denotation at the target. At any object $v$ reachable from the evaluation point, extensional fullness gives a property whose extension at $v$ is exactly the numerals there; it contains $\mathbf 0_\sigma$ and is closed under successor, so the numbers at $v$ are exactly the numerals, every numeral being an instance of every inductive property. Persistence of $\mathbb N_\sigma$ and, given $\Box I^*_\sigma$, the necessary distinctness of the numbers are theorems of C (the proof of necessary-rigid-comprehension-implies-arithmetic-necessitism). Inextensibility, $\Box\forall X\,.\,(\forall n\,.\,\mathbb N_\sigma n\to\Box Xn)\to\mathbb N_\sigma\le X$: at a reachable $v$ and for an arrow $j$ from $v$ to $u$, the numbers at $u$ are the numerals there, which are the transports along $j$ of the numbers at $v$, so any $X$ that necessarily holds of the numbers at $v$ holds at $u$ of the numbers there. So $\mathbb N_\sigma$ is rigid, and Arithmetic Necessitism holds at every type. No choice is used.

general_arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Zachary Goodsell
general_arguments.text: As the argument arithmetic-necessitism-extensionally-full, with the property of being a numeral supplied by pinning. The intension $Z$ whose value at each arrow $k$ out of the evaluation object is the set of numerals $\mathbf 0_\sigma,\operatorname{Suc}_\sigma\mathbf 0_\sigma,\ldots$ at the target of $k$ is pinned down by the empty set, its value depending on the arrow only through its target, and is symmetric, transport along a permutation of the points carrying numerals to numerals, as transport along any arrow does, numerals being closed terms; so it is in the domain, and so is its transport $k\cdot Z$ to any reachable object, whose extension there is exactly the numerals. Hence at every reachable object the numbers at $\sigma$, the instances of the least inductive property, are exactly the numerals, which transport to numerals; persistence and, given $\Box I^*_\sigma$, necessary distinctness are theorems of C, and inextensibility follows as in that argument. So Arithmetic Necessitism holds at every type. No choice is used.

general_arguments.by: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr
general_arguments.text: By Proposition D.6.

general_arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), answering Cian Dorr’s question whether the failure of BF sharpens to type $t$
general_arguments.text: In a one-object finitely pinned model, BF (type t) fails as soon as there are a finite $N$, an arrow $i$ and a proposition $q$ in the domain that is the transport $i^{\prime}\cdot p=\{k : k\circ i^{\prime}\in p\}$ of no proposition $p$ along any arrow $i^{\prime}$ agreeing with $i$ on $N$: the intension $X:=\{\langle r,j\rangle : r\ne q\text{ or }j\text{ disagrees with }i\text{ on }N\}$, which the condition puts in the domain, contains $\langle i^{\prime}\cdot p,i^{\prime}\rangle$ for every $p$ and $i^{\prime}$, so $\forall p\, .\,\Box Xp$ holds at the identity, and omits $\langle q,i\rangle$, so $\Box\forall p\, .\,Xp$ fails there. Since membership of $k$ in $i^{\prime}\cdot p$ depends only on $k$ restricted to the range of $i^{\prime}$, it suffices that $q$ separate two arrows agreeing on every such range, as the condition provides.

revisions.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
revisions.note: The finite-support group's argument and the symmetric range-gap models' copies stated once for the topic; that $X$ is in the domain (pinned down by $N$, and in a symmetric model symmetric) is now part of each record's reason for meeting transport-gap.

general_arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
general_arguments.text: Given $X$ with extension $E$ at the evaluation object, let $Y$ hold at an arrow $g$ of a tuple $\bar b$ at $g$'s target iff $r_g\cdot\bar b\in E$; it is in the domain since the model is full. It is coextensive with $X$, since $r_1=1$. And whether it holds is unchanged along every arrow: at $x\circ g$, of $x\cdot\bar b$, it holds iff $r_{x\circ g}\cdot x\cdot\bar b=r_g\cdot\bar b\in E$. So $Y$ and its negation are persistent. (The retract's own argument of 25 September, generalized.)

general_arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
general_arguments.text: Let $(A_n)$ be the family with no choice function. For a set $C$ of natural numbers let $p_C:=\{h_m : m\in C\}$, a proposition at the evaluation object since the model is full; along $h_n$ it becomes $h_n\cdot p_C$, from which $C$ is recovered as $\{m : h_m\circ r_n\in h_n\cdot p_C\}$, since $h_m\circ r_n\circ h_n=h_m$. Intensional Choice at type $t$: let $F$ hold at $h_n$ of the propositions $h_n\cdot p_C$ with $C\in A_n$, and at every other arrow of every proposition. It is in the domain, the model being full, and necessarily instantiated. A $G\le F$ necessarily uniquely instantiated holds at $h_n$ of a single $h_n\cdot p_{C_n}$ with $C_n\in A_n$, and $n\mapsto C_n$ would be a choice function. Relational Choice at types $t$ and $t$: let $U$ relate $p_{\{n\}}$ to each $p_C$ with $C\in A_n$, and every other proposition to every proposition. It is serial, and a functional subrelation would relate each $p_{\{n\}}$ to a single $p_{C_n}$ with $C_n\in A_n$, again a choice function. Both principles therefore fail. (The analysis of 3 October 2026: Intensional Choice is choice over worlds, Relational Choice over the elements of a domain.)

general_arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
general_arguments.text: For a true $p$, $a\le p$, since $a$ entails every truth. Take $q:=a$ in the definition of $\Box_{\ne}p$: at a world in $a$, $p$ holds; at a world outside $a$, $\Diamond a$ fails. So every truth is $\Box_{\ne}$-necessary.

revisions.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
revisions.note: The finite-support, symmetric and full action models' copies (eight records) stated once for the topic; what varied, why no world outside the actual world sees back into it, is each record's reason for meeting actual-world-isolated.

general_arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
general_arguments.text: Let $p$ be true, pinned by $N$ (and symmetric, when there is a symmetry group), and let $N^\prime$ be as in the condition. Let $q$ be the set of arrows that some arrow composes to agree with the identity on $N^\prime$; it is true, pinned by $N^\prime$, symmetric, and $\Diamond q=q$. By the condition every member of $q$ agrees on $N$ with a symmetry (or the identity), so lies in $p$ together with the identity. Hence $\Box(\Diamond q\to p)$ with $q$ true, i.e. $\Box_{\ne}p$.

general_arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
general_arguments.text: Let $p:=\{1\}$, in the domain since the model is full, and true. Any witness $q$ for $\Box_{\ne}p$ is true, so contains the identity; under an arrow $i\ne 1$ with a retraction $r$, the arrow $r\circ i=1$ makes $\Diamond q$ true, while $p$ is false. So no true $q$ has $\Box(\Diamond q\to p)$. (The surjection monoid's own argument of 23 September, stated once.)

general_arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
general_arguments.text: The pure sentence $\exists p_1\ldots p_n\bigwedge_{i<j}p_i\ne p_j$ is true at the evaluation object and false at the world $V$ after it and at every world after $V$; so $\Diamond$ of it is false at $V$, and $\Box\Diamond$ of it false at the evaluation object. (The chain's own argument of 25 September, stated once.)

general_arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
general_arguments.text: At a world with $n$ propositions, the numeral $\operatorname{Suc}^n_t\mathbf{0}_t$, a finite cardinality, holds of the universal property of propositions, so the Axiom of Infinity at type $t$ fails there. It fails at every world, so Possible Infinity at type $t$ fails.

general_arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
general_arguments.text: The propositions at the evaluation world are finitely many, and every intension of a full model is present, so the numerals are the finite cardinalities and one of them holds of the universal property of propositions: the Axiom of Infinity at type t fails, as does an instance of the schema.

revisions.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
revisions.note: The Axiom of Infinity's failure, which the text states, recorded as a verdict of its own, so that it is certified without the result that the Axiom implies the schema.

general_arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
general_arguments.text: In a full model the actual-world proposition $\{1\}$ is in the domain, and with it as witness $\hat{\hat\Box}p$ holds at the identity iff $p$ contains every invertible arrow out of the evaluation object (an arrow lies in $\hat\Diamond\{1\}$ iff some retraction of it has a retraction, i.e. iff it is invertible); full models satisfy necessary Actuality, so $\Box_5=\hat{\hat\Box}$ by Proposition D21 of The Bounds of Possibility. A non-identity invertible arrow lies outside the true proposition $\{1\}$, which is therefore not 5-necessary.

general_arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
general_arguments.text: In a full action model the actual-world proposition $\{1\}$ is in the domain at every object. Taking it as the witness, $\Box_{\ne}p$ holds at an identity iff $p$ contains every arrow out of that object with a retraction (these are the arrows at which $\Diamond\{1\}$ holds), and $\hat{\hat\Box}p$ iff $p$ contains every invertible arrow out of it (an arrow lies in $\hat\Diamond\{1\}$ iff some retraction of it has a retraction, i.e. iff it is invertible). Full models satisfy necessary Actuality, so $\Box_5=\hat{\hat\Box}$ by Proposition D21 of The Bounds of Possibility. With only identities invertible, $\Box_5$ is the identity operator at every reachable object, so every truth is 5-necessary everywhere.

general_arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Zachary Goodsell
general_arguments.text: In a full action model the propositions at the evaluation object are all the sets of arrows out of it, so the algebra of propositions is atomic, the singletons being its atoms, and it has $2^{|A|}$ elements for $A$ the set of those arrows. Since the sets of natural numbers inject into $A$, the sets of sets of natural numbers inject into the propositions. Take the regular-open algebra $B$ of Cantor space: a complete atomless Boolean algebra in ZF, of the size of the continuum, which therefore injects into the propositions while the propositions do not inject into it (Cantor), so that, realised as a property of propositions with its order as a relation among them, both present since the model is full, it is an internal complete Boolean algebra that is small. Forcing Possibilism would give a proposition $p\ne\top$ whose entailment algebra is isomorphic to $B$. But the entailment algebra below a nonzero proposition is atomic, every nonempty set of arrows including a singleton, and the one below $\bot$ has one element; neither is isomorphic to an infinite atomless algebra. So Forcing Possibilism fails. No choice is used: the injection into the arrows is given by the condition, and Cantor's theorem and the completeness of the regular-open algebra hold in ZF.

general_arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Zachary Goodsell
general_arguments.text: The propositions at the evaluation object are the sets of its countably many arrows, so they have the cardinality of the continuum, and a complete Boolean algebra that is finite or has strictly fewer elements than the propositions is finite, an infinite complete Boolean algebra having an infinite antichain and so at least continuum many elements (with choice). A finite Boolean algebra with $n$ atoms is isomorphic to the algebra of subsets of any $n$ arrows, the entailment algebra below the proposition consisting of those arrows, which is not top, the arrows being infinitely many; the one-element algebra is the entailment algebra below $\bot$. The isomorphism is a relation present in the full domains. The internal notions agree with the external ones: a property of entities carrying the order of a complete Boolean algebra, every subproperty having a least upper bound, is one in the metatheory, since every subset is the extension of a subproperty, and Dedekind finiteness and the existence of injective relations are read in a full model as in the metatheory. So Forcing Possibilism holds.

general_arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
general_arguments.text: Entailment is inclusion of intensions. Below a relation $Y\ne\bot_\tau$ lies the relation whose intension is the singleton of one of $Y$'s tuples, which is in the domain since the model is full, and is an atom: its only proper part is $\bot_\tau$. Every object being full, the same holds at every arrow, so Atomicity is necessary. The source notes that full models are atomic (p. 61); stated once for the topic, in place of the full models' own arguments.

general_arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, 25 October 2026
general_arguments.text: The argument of full-comparable-free-arrows-self-atoms at every reachable object: a self-atom there is a singleton intension, so an atom.

general_arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, 25 October 2026
general_arguments.text: Let $I$ be a self-atom of a relational type at the evaluation object. For $\langle k,\bar a\rangle\in I$, the transport of $I$ along $k$ is $\{\langle m,\bar b\rangle : \langle m\circ k,\bar b\rangle\in I\}$, an atom containing $\langle1,\bar a\rangle$, hence the singleton of it: so $k$ is fixed only by the identity, $I$ has no other pair at $k$, and no pair of $I$ sits at a proper left multiple of $k$. If $I$ had pairs at two arrows $k\ne k^{\prime}$, both fixed only by identities, comparability would make one a proper left multiple of the other. So $I$ is a singleton, an atom.

general_arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
general_arguments.text: The relational half of full-epic-barcan. In an action model BF at a type $\sigma$ holds at a world iff transport along every arrow out of it is onto the entities of type $\sigma$ at its target: if some $z$ there is no transport, the property of being one is necessary of everything at the world and fails of $z$ after the arrow; and if transport is onto, a property necessary of everything holds of every transport. In a full model the transport of intensions along an epimorphism $k$ is onto at every relational type: an intension $Y$ at its target is the transport of $\{\langle\bar a,k\circ m\rangle:\langle\bar a,m\rangle\in Y\}$, since $k\circ m=k\circ m'$ only if $m=m'$. Nothing here concerns the individuals. So BF holds at every relational type at every object reachable from the evaluation point.

general_arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
general_arguments.text: BF holds at an object whose arrows out all act surjectively at every type (Proposition 3.24(ii)). In a full model the transport of intensions along an epimorphism $k$ is onto: an intension $Y$ at its target is the transport of $\{\langle\bar a,k\circ m\rangle : \langle\bar a,m\rangle\in Y\}$, since $k\circ m=k\circ m'$ only if $m=m'$; and on the individuals the arrows are onto by the condition. So BF holds at every object reachable from the evaluation point, and BF is necessary.

general_arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, 25 October 2026
general_arguments.text: Let $m\ne1$ fix $k$: $m\circ k=k$. The singleton $\{k\}$, in the domain since the model is full, is an atom. Its transport along $k$ is $\{x : x\circ k=k\}$, which contains $1$ and $m$, and the proposition $\{1\}$ at $k$’s target, in the domain there, separates them; so $\{k\}$ is true at $k$ without being an atom there, and it is not a self-atom. As $\{k\}$ is the only possible proposition below itself, Self-Atomicity (type t) fails too.

general_arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, 25 October 2026
general_arguments.text: Let $j\circ h=j^{\prime}\circ h$ with $j\ne j^{\prime}$, the composite fixed only by the identity. The singleton of the composite is a self-atom: it is true only at the composite, where its transport is $\{m : m\circ j\circ h=j\circ h\}=\{1\}$, an atom. It is not a strong atom: under $h$ it becomes $\{m : m\circ h=j\circ h\}$, which contains $j$ and $j^{\prime}$, and the proposition $\{j\}$ at $h$’s target neither contains nor excludes it.

general_arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, 25 October 2026
general_arguments.text: The proposition $\{k,k^{\prime}\}$ is a self-atom: its transport along $k$ is $\{m : m\circ k\in\{k,k^{\prime}\}\}$, which is $\{1\}$ since only the identity fixes $k$ and $k^{\prime}$ is not a left multiple of $k$, and likewise along $k^{\prime}$; at every other arrow it is false. It is not an atom, since $\{k\}$ lies strictly below it.

general_arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
general_arguments.text: Given $X$ of type $\tau$ at an object $W$, let $Y$ be the relation whose extension at an arrow $i$ out of $W$ is $X$'s extension at $W$ transported along $i$, which is in the domain since the model is full. It is coextensive with $X$. It is persistent, since its extension at $i\circ j$ is its extension at $i$ transported along $j$. And it is inextensible: if $\Box X'$ holds at $i$ of everything $Y$ holds of there, then at $i\circ j$ everything $Y$ holds of is the transport along $j$ of something $Y$ holds of at $i$, of which $X'$ then holds. Every object being full, the same holds at every arrow, so Rigid Comprehension is necessary. The source notes that full models satisfy it (p. 61); stated once for the topic, in place of the full models' own arguments.

general_arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, 25 October 2026
general_arguments.text: In a full model the atoms of a relational type at an object are the singleton intensions $\{\langle k,\bar a\rangle\}$, with $k$ an arrow out of it. Such a singleton is instantiated only at $k$, and its transport along $k$ is $\{\langle m,\bar a\rangle : m\circ k=k\}$, which is the atom $\{\langle 1,\bar a\rangle\}$ at $k$’s target when only the identity fixes $k$. So every atom is a self-atom, and the atom below a non-bottom entity, which the full model supplies, is a self-atom below it. The same holds at every reachable object, so both principles are necessary.

general_arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, 25 October 2026
general_arguments.text: The argument of full-uniquely-factored-self-atoms-strong at every reachable object.

general_arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, 25 October 2026
general_arguments.text: By full-comparable-free-arrows-self-atoms a self-atom at the evaluation object is a singleton $\{\langle k,\bar a\rangle\}$ with $k$ fixed only by the identity. Its transport along any arrow $h$ out of the evaluation object is $\{\langle m,\bar a\rangle : m\circ h=k\}$, which has at most one pair since $k$ factors through $h$ in at most one way; a set of at most one pair lies below every entity at $h$’s target or its negation. So the self-atom is a strong atom.

general_arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
general_arguments.text: The Infinity schema holds, there being $n$ distinct individuals for every $n$. For the Axiom: by extensional fullness the domain has a property of cardinalities true of $Z$ exactly when every property $Z$ holds of has a finite extension. It holds of $\mathbf{0}_e$, which holds only of empty properties, and passes from $Y$ to $\operatorname{Suc}_e Y$, which holds of $F$ only if $Y$ holds of $F$ less one of its instances. So every finite cardinality has it, and none holds of the universal property, whose extension is infinite.

general_arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
general_arguments.text: As for individuals (the argument infinitely-many-individuals), at type $t$: the Infinity schema holds, and by extensional fullness the property of cardinalities that hold only of properties with finite extensions is in the domain, has every finite cardinality, and excludes those holding of the universal property of propositions, whose extension is infinite.

general_arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
general_arguments.text: At type $e$. Let $F$ and $a$ be as the condition gives them, and suppose $G\le F$ is necessarily uniquely instantiated. $G$ is in the domain, so it is symmetric and pinned down by a finite set, which we may take to contain $a$; call it $N$. Let $h$ be the arrow the condition gives for $N$. Then $G_h=\{y\}$ for some $y$ in $F_h$. If $\sigma$ in the symmetry group fixes $p$, then $\sigma\circ h$ agrees with $h$ on $N$, so $G_{\sigma\circ h}=G_h$ by pinning, while symmetry gives $G_{\sigma\circ h}=\{\sigma y\}$. So no symmetry fixing $p$ moves $y$, and by the condition $y=p$. Each model's witness takes $F$ with $p$ outside its extension at $h$, a contradiction. $\Box$Intensional Choice fails with it, by T.

It needs the individuals the construction gives. Not covered: the qualitative-links model, whose arrows preserve a ternary relation and so cannot send everything to one point, and the qualitative-contrast model, whose arrows are bijections and where Intensional Choice holds.

revisions.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction

general_arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
general_arguments.text: At an object reachable from the evaluation point the propositions are all the sets of arrows out of it, so there are finitely many arrows out. A necessarily instantiated $F$ there assigns to each of them a nonempty set, and a finite family of nonempty sets has a choice function without the axiom of choice; the intension holding at each arrow of the chosen member alone is in the domain, the model being full, lies below $F$ and is necessarily uniquely instantiated. So Intensional Choice holds at every reachable object, at every type. (The finite-germ argument of the 3 October 2026 analysis, for full models; with choice the well-ordering argument gives the same.)

general_arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, in a trawl for cheaply settled verdicts; checked by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
general_arguments.text: At the type of the condition's $F$. Suppose $G\le F$ is necessarily uniquely instantiated. $G$ is in the domain, so it is symmetric and pinned down by a finite set $N$. Let $h$ be the arrow the condition gives for $N$ and $\{y\}$ the extension of $G$ at $h$; $y$ is in $F$'s extension at $h$, since $G\le F$. Let $g$ be the symmetry the condition gives, fixing $h(N)$ pointwise and moving $y$. Then $g\circ h$ agrees with $h$ on $N$, so by pinning $G$'s extension at $g\circ h$ is $\{y\}$, while by symmetry it contains $g\cdot y$. So $g\cdot y=y$, a contradiction. $\Box$Intensional Choice fails with it, by T. The condition collapse-onto-point is the case in which $h(N)$ is a single point outside $F$'s extension at $h$; with invertible arrows there are no collapses, but an arrow may still carry $N$ to a position where every instance of $F$ is moved by the symmetries fixing the image of $N$.

general_arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, at Cian Dorr's suggestion
general_arguments.text: For each object $U$ and type $\sigma$ fix a well-ordering $<_U$ of the domain $D^\sigma_U$, and let $W$ be the intension of type $\sigma\to\sigma\to t$ with $W(h):={<_{\operatorname{cod}h}}$. Its value depends only on the arrow's codomain, so by the condition it is in the domain, and at every world its extension well-orders that world's type-$\sigma$ domain. Given $F$ with $\Box\exists x\, .\,Fx$, put $G:=\lambda x\, .\,Fx\land\forall y\, .\,(Fy\to\neg Wyx)$, the $W$-least $F$. It is definable from $F$ and $W$, so in the domain; $G\le F$, and its extension at every arrow is the singleton of the least element of $F$'s. So Intensional Choice holds, and the same at every reachable object gives $\Box$Intensional Choice. Cian Dorr's observation that such models are qualitatively full, made precise.

general_arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
general_arguments.text: Every arrow's action is a bijection at every type, so ND and BF hold at every object reachable from the evaluation point (Proposition 3.24(i) and (ii)), and are necessary.

general_arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
general_arguments.text: At any reachable object $W$, let $U$ be a serial relation in the domain there. Using the axiom of choice, pick for each $x$ a $y$ with $(x,y)$ in the extension of $U$ at the identity, and let $S$ be the intension whose value at every arrow $W\to W$ is the graph of this choice and whose value at arrows with any other codomain is empty; it depends only on the codomain, so the condition puts it in the domain, and at the identity it is a functional subrelation of $U$. Likewise a set of representatives of an equivalence relation at $W$, made into such an intension, is a transversal. Since $W$ was any reachable object, both principles hold at every world.

general_arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, 25 October 2026
general_arguments.text: A self-atom of any relational type at an object $W$ is instantiated at some arrow $k$ out of $W$, and its transport along $k$ is an atom at $k$’s target instantiated at the identity there. The existential projection of an atom $I$ of a relational type, the proposition $\exists\bar x\, .\,I\bar x$, is an atom of type $t$: it is in the domain, it is not bottom, and for any proposition $p$ the entity $I\land\lambda\bar x\, .\,p$ lies below the atom $I$, so is $I$ or bottom, which puts $p$ above the projection or disjoint from it. So the projection is a true atom at $k$’s target, which the condition excludes. Hence no reachable object has a self-atom, and Self-atoms are atoms and Self-atoms are strong atoms hold vacuously at every type and every reachable object, while Self-Atomicity (type t) fails at the evaluation point, the top proposition having no self-atom below it.

general_arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, 25 October 2026
general_arguments.text: An atom of a relational type at a reachable object would give, by existential projection, an atom of type $t$ there (as in the argument no-actuality-no-self-atoms), which the condition excludes; so no reachable object has an atom of any relational type, nor a self-atom, since a self-atom is an atom where it is instantiated. All four bridge principles therefore hold vacuously at every type and every reachable object, and Self-Atomicity (type t) fails at the evaluation point.

general_arguments.by: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr
general_arguments.text: Closed pure terms denote entities fixed by every arrow (§3.5, p. 58). With a single object, a proposition fixed by every arrow contains every arrow if it contains the identity and no arrow otherwise, so a true closed pure sentence is necessary: the source's one-object No Pure Contingency observation (p. 79), applied to each closed instance.

general_arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
general_arguments.text: Let $k$ out of the evaluation object have distinct $j\ne j^{\prime}$ after it with $j\circ k= j^{\prime}\circ k$. The proposition $\{j\circ k\}$, in the domain since the model is full, is possible, and the only possible proposition below it is itself. It is not a strong atom: under $k$ it becomes $\{m : m\circ k=j\circ k\}$, which contains $j$ and $j^{\prime}$, and the proposition $\{j\}$ at $k$'s target, in the domain there, neither contains nor excludes it. So the type-$t$ Strong Atomicity fails. (The idempotent monoid's and the retract's own arguments of 22–23 September, stated once.)

general_arguments.by: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), at Cian Dorr's request; checked and recorded by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic)
general_arguments.text:
Write $F_h$ for the extension of $F$ at the arrow $h$, so $(h\cdot F)_k=F_{kh}$, and $B_N(E)$ as in tame-rigidity-factorizable, whose part (1) is the criterion used throughout: a relation pinned down by $S$ with extension $E$ is weakly rigid iff it equals $B_N(E)$ for every finite $N\supseteq S$; Tame Rigidity holds at every type by that argument. Fix a type tuple.
(a) Stable sets. If a set $A$ of argument tuples is closed under the surjections fixing a finite $P$ pointwise, then $B_P(A)$ has extension $A$ and is weakly rigid, hence rigid. Given $Q\supseteq P$ and $l^{\prime}a$ with $l^{\prime}$ agreeing with $l$ on $P$ and $a\in A$ pinned down by $M$, take a surjection $u$ fixing $P$ that sends $M\setminus P$ to distinct fresh points outside $Q$, and a surjection $r$ agreeing with $l$ on $Q$ with $ru=l^{\prime}$ on $M$ (compatible finite prescriptions); then $ua\in A$ and $l^{\prime}a=r(ua)\in B_Q(A)_l$, so $B_P(A)=B_Q(A)$.
(b) Exact images. Let $F$ be weakly rigid, pinned down by $S$, with extension $E$. By weak persistence $uE\subseteq E$ for every surjection $u$ fixing $S$. For any surjection $j$, $F_j=jE$: a member $la$ of $B_S(E)_j$, with $l$ agreeing with $j$ on $S$ and $a\in E$ pinned down by $M$, is $j(ua)$ for a surjection $u$ fixing $S$ with $ju=l$ on $M$, preimages being supplied by the surjectivity of $j$.
(c) Lifting. Let $F$ be rigid, pinned down by $S$, $k$ an arrow, $N\supseteq S$ finite, and $X\le k\cdot F$ rigid, pinned down by $T$, with extension $D$. Extend $k|_N$ to a surjection $j$ whose non-singleton fibres are finitely many and finite (send the points outside $N$ bijectively onto the values not yet taken); then $j\cdot F=k\cdot F$ and $D\subseteq F_j=jE$. Let $P$ be finite, containing $N$, every non-singleton fibre of $j$, and a preimage of each point of $T$, and put $A:=\{a\in E:ja\in D\}$. For a surjection $u$ fixing $P$, $ju$ is constant on the fibres of $j$, so $ju=vj$ for a surjection $v$, which fixes $T$; so $vD\subseteq D$ by the weak persistence and pinning of $X$, and $uE\subseteq E$ by (b); hence $uA\subseteq A$. By (a), $Y:=B_P(A)$ is rigid, $Y\le F$ since $A\subseteq E$ and $P\supseteq S$, and by (b) $(j\cdot Y)_1=jA=D$. Weakly rigid relations with the same extension are identical, so $X=j\cdot Y$ with $j$ agreeing with $k$ on $N$.
(d) The power property of $F$ is persistent, and by (c) its extension at $k$ is contained in $B_N$ of its extension at the identity for every $N\supseteq S$; so it is weakly rigid by the criterion, and rigid by Tame Rigidity. So Rigid Power holds at every type. Nothing about the symmetry group is used beyond its being a group of permutations, and the individuals play no role, so the argument covers every member and variant meeting the conditions.

general_arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, 3 October 2026 (full action models); extended by Claude Fable 5.1, prompted by Cian Dorr (Anthropic), 4 October 2026, at Cian Dorr's direction
general_arguments.text: Write $X_0(E)$ for the intension $k\mapsto k\cdot E$. The extension at an arrow $h$ of the power property $\lambda X\, .\,\operatorname{Rigid}(X)\land X\le F$ is the set of rigid $X$ with $X\le h\cdot F$, the bound variable ranging over the domain untransported and the parameter transported. By the condition the rigid relations are the $X_0(E)$, and $X_0(T)\le X_0(S)$ iff $T\subseteq S$; so for rigid $F=X_0(S)$ the power property has extension $\{X_0(T'):T'\subseteq k\cdot S\}$ at $k$, while transporting its extension at the identity along $k$ gives $\{X_0(k\cdot T):T\subseteq S\}$. These coincide, since every $T'\subseteq k\cdot S$ is $k\cdot T$ for $T:=\{s\in S:k\cdot s\in T'\}$. So the power property is itself $X_0$ of its extension, hence rigid, and the same at every reachable object gives the boxed form.

general_arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), on Cian Dorr's request to settle Rigid Rigidity where it was open
general_arguments.text: Fix the type tuple $\bar\sigma$, let $\mathcal R$ be the set of rigid relations of type $\bar\sigma t$, and let $R:=\lambda X\, .\,\operatorname{Rigid}(X)$, the value of a closed pure term, so fixed by every arrow; in a one-object model its extension at every arrow is $\mathcal R$, and it is pinned down by $\emptyset$. Write $B_N(E)$ as in tame-rigidity-factorizable. By part (1) of that argument at type $(\bar\sigma t)t$, $R$ is weakly rigid iff $\mathcal R=B_N(\mathcal R)_k$ for every arrow $k$ and finite $N$; and since $h\cdot R=R$ for every arrow $h$, part (2) then makes $R$ rigid. The inclusion $B_N(\mathcal R)_k\subseteq\mathcal R$ holds because a transport of a rigid relation is rigid, rigidity being a necessitated condition. For the converse let $Z\in\mathcal R$ be pinned down by $T$, and let $k$ and $N$ be given. The condition gives $k^{\prime}$ agreeing with $k$ on $N$ and $\sigma$ with $k^{\prime}\circ\sigma$ the identity on $T$. Then $Z^{\prime}:=\sigma\cdot Z$ is rigid, and $k^{\prime}\cdot Z^{\prime}=(k^{\prime}\circ\sigma) \cdot Z=Z$, since $k^{\prime}\circ\sigma$ agrees with the identity on $T$. So $Z\in B_N(\mathcal R)_k$. Hence Rigid Rigidity holds at every type. This is the lifting of Rigid Power at $F:=\top$ by a section of $k$, noted for the symmetric all-surjections model on 9 October; without the condition the lift can still hold through rigid relations that are not transports of $Z$ (for instance the haecceity of any $x$ with $k^{\prime}x=1$ lifts that of $1$), so the condition is sufficient, not necessary.

general_arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Zachary Goodsell
general_arguments.text: Let $v$ be any object reachable from the evaluation point and $\mathfrak R$ a real number structure at $v$ (Background, Analysis). Its completeness is tested against the subproperties of its carrier present at $v$, and by extensional fullness every subset of the carrier's extension there is the extension at the identity of one of them; so the carrier, with the extensions of $\le$, $+$ and $\times$, is a complete ordered field in the sense of the metatheory and, by Huntington's theorem, a theorem of ZF, is isomorphic to the real numbers. For the same reason the extension of $N$, the least subproperty containing $0$ and closed under adding $1$, is its set of natural numbers, that set being the extension of a subproperty. A second-order analytical sentence $A(\mathfrak R)$ quantifies over the relations among entities of the structure's type at $v$, applied to the structure's elements, and their extensions at the identity are all the relations on the carrier, again by extensional fullness. So $A(\mathfrak R)$ holds at $v$ exactly when $A$ holds in the real numbers under full second-order semantics, which depends neither on $v$ nor on $\mathfrak R$. Hence $\Box\forall\mathfrak R\,.\,\operatorname{Real}_\sigma(\mathfrak R)\to A(\mathfrak R)$ holds when $A$ is true of the reals and $\Box\forall\mathfrak R\,.\,\operatorname{Real}_\sigma(\mathfrak R)\to\neg A(\mathfrak R)$ when it is false: every instance of the Necessity of Second-Order Analysis holds, and with it the Necessity of Analysis and the Non-contingency of the Continuum Hypothesis, as recorded. No choice is used.

general_arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr
general_arguments.text: Let $v$ be reachable from the evaluation point. If every type is finite at $v$ there is no real number structure there, an ordered field having the infinitely many distinct elements $0$, $1$, $1+1$, and so on. Otherwise let $D$ be as in the condition. Carry the real numbers onto $D$ by a bijection: the carrier, order, sum, product, $0$, $1$ and natural numbers are sets of tuples from $D$, so extensions at $v$ of entities there, which form a real number structure $\mathfrak R^*$ at $v$, its completeness and the leastness of its natural numbers being tested against subproperties whose extensions are all the subsets of $D$. Its second-order quantifiers, applied to tuples from $D$, range over all relations on $D$, so for each second-order analytical sentence $A$, $A(\mathfrak R^*)$ holds at $v$ iff $A$ is true of the real numbers under full second-order semantics. Any real number structure $\mathfrak R$ at $v$, of any type, is isomorphic to $\mathfrak R^*$ by a relation in the domain there (Huntington's theorem, a theorem of C: Background, Analysis), and $A(\mathfrak R)\leftrightarrow A(\mathfrak R^*)$ is a theorem of C given such an isomorphism, relations on one carrier being carried to the other by comprehension. So at every reachable object every real number structure satisfies exactly the second-order analytical sentences true of the reals, and each instance $\Box\forall\mathfrak R\,.\,\operatorname{Real}_\sigma(\mathfrak R) \to A(\mathfrak R)$ or $\Box\forall\mathfrak R\,.\,\operatorname{Real}_\sigma(\mathfrak R)\to\neg A(\mathfrak R)$ of the Necessity of Second-Order Analysis holds, with the Necessity of Analysis and the Non-contingency of the Continuum Hypothesis. The choice of the bijection with the reals needs no choice principle, $D$ having the cardinality of the continuum.

general_arguments.text: Let $h$ out of the evaluation object have retractions $j\ne j^{\prime}$, and let $q$ at $h$'s target contain $j$ but not $j^{\prime}$. A true proposition $p$ contains the identity, so under $h$ it becomes a proposition containing $j$ and $j^{\prime}$, since $j\circ h=j^{\prime}\circ h=1$. That proposition lies neither below $q$ nor below $\neg q$, so $p$ is not a strong atom. No true proposition is.

general_arguments.text: Each constant of Σ denotes what the closed pure term $\top_\tau$ of its type denotes, so a closed sentence of the language of Σ denotes what the pure sentence with $\top_\tau$ in place of each constant denotes; if true it is necessary by No Pure Contingency, which holds here. So No Contingency (signature Σ) holds, and B for sentences of Σ with it: a true Σ-sentence is necessary, hence necessarily possible.

general_arguments.text: At type $e$. The individuals, which every arrow fixes, are an unspecified infinite set, so here the union $D=\bigcup_n P_n$. Let $F$ hold at $h_n$ of the members of $P_n$, and at every other arrow of every individual. It is in the domain, the model being full, and necessarily instantiated. A $G\le F$ necessarily uniquely instantiated holds at $h_n$ of a single member of $P_n$, and $n\mapsto$ that member would be a choice function for the socks. (The witness of the 3 October 2026 analysis, with the numbered arrows in place of the transpositions of the pairs.)

general_arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
general_arguments.text: At type $e$. The individuals, which every arrow fixes, are an unspecified infinite set, so here the union $D=\bigcup_n P_n$. Let $U$ relate each member of $P_n$ to the members of $P_{n+1}$; it is in the domain, the model being full, and serial. A functional subrelation would send each sock to a sock of the next pair, and iterated from one member of $P_0$ it would choose a sock from every pair.

general_arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
general_arguments.text: Let $V$ be the evaluation object or the target of an arrow out of it, and $w:=\{1_V\}$, in the domain at $V$. It is true at $1_V$. Under an arrow $f$ out of $V$ it becomes $\{k : k\circ f=1_V\}$, the set of retractions of $f$, which has at most one member and so lies below $q$ or below $\neg q$ for every proposition $q$ at $f$'s target. So Strong Actuality holds at $1_V$. A closed sentence holds at an arrow iff it holds at the identity of the arrow's target, so Strong Actuality holds at every world after the evaluation point, and □Strong Actuality holds there.

general_arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), on Cian Dorr's request to settle Tame Rigidity where it was open
general_arguments.text: Write $B_N(E)$ for the intension $k\mapsto\bigcup\{k^{\prime}\cdot E:k^{\prime}\text{ agrees with }k \text{ on }N\}$; it is pinned down by $N$, and symmetric when the model is, since the symmetry group consists of arrows and $(gk)\cdot E=g\cdot(k\cdot E)$, so it is in the domain. (1) A relation $Y$ pinned down by $S$, with extension $E$ at the identity, is weakly rigid iff $Y=B_S(E)=B_N(E)$ for every finite $N\supseteq S$: weak persistence gives $k\cdot E\subseteq Y_k$, and with pinning $B_S(E)\subseteq Y$; a domain element $X$ with $\Box X$ true of each member of $E$, pinned down by $N$, contains $B_N(E)$, so weak inextensibility says exactly that $Y\subseteq B_N(E)$ for every finite $N$, and $B_N(E)\subseteq B_S(E)$ for $N\supseteq S$. (2) Rigidity is (1) at every world: for each arrow $h$, $h\cdot Y$, with $(h\cdot Y)_k=Y_{kh}$, must satisfy $k\cdot Y_h\subseteq Y_{kh}\subseteq B_N(Y_h)_k$ for all $k$ and finite $N$. (3) Let $Y$ be weakly rigid. Persistence at $h$: $k\cdot Y_h=\bigcup\{(kk^{\prime\prime})\cdot E:k^{\prime\prime}\text{ agrees with }h\text{ on }S\}\subseteq B_S(E)_{kh}=Y_{kh}$. Inextensibility at $h$: given $N$, take $N^{\prime\prime}$ from the condition. By (1), $Y_{kh}=B_{N^{\prime\prime}}(E)_{kh}$, so a member of it is $k^{\prime}\cdot e$ with $e\in E$, pinned down by some finite $M$, and $k^{\prime}$ agreeing with $kh$ on $N^{\prime\prime}$. The condition gives $k^{\prime\prime}$ agreeing with $h$ on $N^{\prime\prime}$ and $j$ agreeing with $k$ on $N$ with $jk^{\prime\prime}$ agreeing with $k^{\prime}$ on $M$, so $k^{\prime}\cdot e=j\cdot(k^{\prime\prime}\cdot e)$, where $k^{\prime\prime}\cdot e\in B_{N^{\prime\prime}}(E)_h=Y_h$; hence $k^{\prime}\cdot e\in B_N(Y_h)_k$. So every weakly rigid relation, at every type, is rigid. With No Pure Contingency, which holds in one-object models, the map's results give $\Box$Tame Rigidity.

general_arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), on Cian Dorr's question whether the failure of Boolean Completeness at type $t$ refutes its countable form here
general_arguments.text: The natural numbers are the finite cardinalities at type $e$ (Background, after Goodsell), and with a single individual there are three: $\mathbf{0}_e$, true of the empty property; $\operatorname{Suc}_e\mathbf{0}_e$, true of the universal one; and the empty cardinality, which is $\operatorname{Suc}_e$ of the second and of itself. By extensional fullness the property of being one of these three is in the domain, so it bounds natural numberhood. A countable property therefore has at most three members in its extension, and their join is its least upper bound.
