general_arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
general_arguments.text: In a full action model the actual-world proposition $\{1\}$ is in the domain at every object. Taking it as the witness, $\Box_{\ne}p$ holds at an identity iff $p$ contains every arrow out of that object with a retraction (these are the arrows at which $\Diamond\{1\}$ holds), and $\hat{\hat\Box}p$ iff $p$ contains every invertible arrow out of it (an arrow lies in $\hat\Diamond\{1\}$ iff some retraction of it has a retraction, i.e. iff it is invertible). Full models satisfy necessary Actuality, so $\Box_5=\hat{\hat\Box}$ by Proposition D21 of The Bounds of Possibility. Let $u$ have a retraction but no inverse. The true proposition $\{1\}$ excludes $u$, so it is not ND-necessary, while every invertible arrow is the identity or excluded from no such test: $\{1\}$ is two-hat necessary iff no non-identity arrow is invertible, and in any case the proposition $\{1\}\cup\{\text{invertible arrows}\}$ is in the domain, true, two-hat necessary and not ND-necessary.

general_arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
general_arguments.text: In a full action model the actual-world proposition $\{1\}$ is in the domain at every object. Taking it as the witness, $\Box_{\ne}p$ holds at an identity iff $p$ contains every arrow out of that object with a retraction (these are the arrows at which $\Diamond\{1\}$ holds), and $\hat{\hat\Box}p$ iff $p$ contains every invertible arrow out of it (an arrow lies in $\hat\Diamond\{1\}$ iff some retraction of it has a retraction, i.e. iff it is invertible). Full models satisfy necessary Actuality, so $\Box_5=\hat{\hat\Box}$ by Proposition D21 of The Bounds of Possibility. When every retracted arrow is invertible, the two boxes coincide at every reachable object, so $\Box_{\ne}=\hat{\hat\Box}$.

general_arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
general_arguments.text: Let $k$ out of the evaluation object have no retraction. The propositions $\bot$ and $\{1\}$ are in the domain, the model being full, and $k$ transports both to $\bot$: no arrow $m$ after $k$ has $m\circ k=1$. So $k$'s action at type $t$ is not injective, and ND fails there (Proposition 3.24(i)).

data.notes:
Does Relational Choice alone give a transversal for every equivalence relation? Christopher Sun observed that the literature claims this without proof. The converse is recorded. The quotient argument chooses from each cell $\lambda z\, .\,(Rx)z$ and needs the cells of two members of one class to be the same property; in C that is necessary coextension, and the hypothesis gives actual coextension only. No definable substitute for the cell helps, since an operation definable from $R$ identifies $x$ with $x'$ only when they are necessarily indiscernible with respect to $R$. A Zermelo-style well-ordering argument breaks at the same point: coextensive but distinct stages receive different chosen elements. The expectation is that the implication fails. What would settle it: a proof that uses the chosen relation to break the symmetry between coextensive cells, or a model of C with Relational Choice that is not extensionally full at its evaluation point. Every recorded model of Relational Choice is extensionally full there, in that every set of tuples from the domains is the extension of a rigid element, and that fullness verifies Transversal Choice by the same metatheoretic choice, so none separates the two. Symmetric Henkin models in the Fraenkel–Mostowski style cannot separate them either; see the write-up.
Update of 28 September 2026: Christopher Sun showed on 26 September that Transversal Choice is equivalent to Relational Choice together with Transversal (transversal-and-relational-choice-imply-transversal-choice), so this question is equivalent to whether Relational Choice implies Transversal. Anything that implies Transversal, such as Actuality, closes the gap.
Update of 28 October 2026: Vicinity also closes the gap ([[vicinity-and-relational-choice-imply-transversal-choice]], from GPT-6 Astra, prompted by Daniel Kodsi). So a model separating Relational Choice from Transversal Choice must falsify Vicinity, and hence ND at type $t$ and Actuality.

Stated by Bacon as a theorem, with the proof deferred to another venue; his handout of 19 October 2026 on the lottery-algebra model and the draft Modalized Domains on Possibility Frames do not reproduce it (the lottery record notes a transfer argument not given there). The expected proof: Forcing Possibilism supplies a proposition whose entailment algebra is a complete Boolean algebra forcing CH, and one forcing its negation; under □Rigid Comprehension and Intensional Choice the real number structures at the worlds below each are those of the corresponding generic extensions. Recorded as conjectured until a proof is supplied; a written proof, or a model of the three premises deciding CH one way necessarily, would settle it.

As encoded, with the map's strict reading of smallness (finite, or with strictly fewer elements than there are propositions), the conjecture is refuted: [[full-free-monoid-glued-constants]], [[full-free-monoid-glued-constants-singleton]], [[full-free-product-glued-constants]], [[full-double-retraction-glued-constants]] and [[ultraproduct-countable-full-s5-finite-individuals]] satisfy □Rigid Comprehension, Intensional Choice, Forcing Possibilism and Non-contingency of CH. Each has exactly $2^{\aleph_0}$ propositions, and an infinite complete Boolean algebra has at least $2^{\aleph_0}$ elements, so only finite algebras are small there, and Forcing Possibilism never asks for an algebra that changes CH. (For the ultraproduct, this holds in every factor.) The expected proof needs a CH-changing algebra to be small: an algebra forcing $\neg$CH has at least $\aleph_2$ elements, and one forcing CH over a model of $\neg$CH may have $2^{2^{\aleph_0}}$, so a premise saying that there are more than $2^{2^{\aleph_0}}$ propositions would suffice for that step, while one saying only that there are more than $2^{\aleph_0}$ might not. In the lottery cloud of Modalized Domains (Bacon and Claude Opus 5.5, Remark 6.12), which the source cites, every complete Boolean algebra of size below a strong limit $\mu$ is small and realized; Bacon's Theorem 6.1 is cited there as showing that CH is contingent in it.

Suggested repair (Cian Dorr, 25 October 2026): add the premise that there are more than $2^{2^{\aleph_0}}$ propositions, i.e. that no injective relation runs from the properties of the reals of some real number structure into the propositions. All five models above falsify it. It is not recorded as a principle until the repaired implication is proved, since by itself it would only call for large variants of many models.

Does adding Boolean Completeness to Relational Choice suffice for Transversal Choice in C? The question without Boolean Completeness is recorded separately. No proof was supplied. A proof of this implication, or a model of C satisfying both premises and failing Transversal Choice, would settle this conjecture.

Downgraded from proved to conjectured on 11 October 2026, at Cian Dorr's request. The proof of Theorem 8.2 in the book has a gap, found while formalizing it in Lean and confirmed by Cian Dorr; the write-up sets out the book's argument with the gap marked. The argument proves $\forall p\,.\,Wp\to p=r$ at the evaluation point and then boxes it as following "from necessary assumptions". But step (i), that a $W$-proposition $p$ falls under some member of $H$ at every world, uses the claim that the world property $U=\lambda q\,.\,v\land q=p$ is $H$ because it is a world property accessible to $W$; that holds at the evaluation point, where $H$ is coextensive with the accessible world properties, but at another world $H$ is known only to be rigid, and need not contain the world properties built there from that world's $v$ and $p$. The step is needed exactly at such worlds, since $W$ may have no actual instance. Boxing Rigid Comprehension does not obviously help, since $r$ must be defined from a single actual $H$. What would settle the conjecture: a repair of step (i), or a model of C with □Strong Atomicity and Rigid Comprehension in which BF fails at some relational type. No recorded model refutes it, and without this record the map does not derive it. With □Rigid Comprehension and Rigid Power in place of Rigid Comprehension the conclusion holds (strong-atomicity-necessary-rigid-comprehension-and-rigid-power-imply-bf-relational, Cian Dorr), so a countermodel must fail one of those. The converse half of Theorem 8.2, atomicity-and-bf-relational-imply-strong-atomicity and its boxed form, is unaffected.

Downgraded from proved to conjectured on 28 September 2026, at Cian Dorr's request. The source's proof (Proposition 2.11, note 42) has two gaps, found that day by an agent working in the Lean-Classicism formalization project; the write-up sets out the paper's argument with the gaps marked. (a) Part (iv) of note 42 boxes a claim that holds pointwise in the object variables by BF, where □BF would be needed. Cian Dorr agreed. (b) The same part's "without loss of generality" step replaces the atom $w'$ by $w''$, the greatest lower bound of the propositions $p$ with $w\le(p=w')$. The proof then needs $w\le(w''=w')$, so that $w''$ is still possible and below $X^*z\land\neg Yz$ where $w$ holds; nothing in the premises gives this, and □BF does not help. A propositional structure in which that step fails is sketched in the project's VERIFICATION.md; it has not been extended to a model of C with all the premises, so it shows that the step needs an argument, not that the proposition is false. What is proved there: Actuality, Boolean Completeness and BF (at the relevant types), together with a restriction principle, give Rigid Comprehension with the paper's witness $X^*$. The restriction principle says that for all $p,q$ there is an $r$ with $p\le(r=q)$ such that $r\le s$ whenever $p\le(q\le s)$. It holds in C5, with $r:=q\land\Diamond p$. Restructured this way, gap (a) disappears, and gap (b) becomes the question whether the premises here give the restriction principle. What would settle the conjecture: a derivation of the restriction principle, or another argument, from boxed Atomicity, Boolean Completeness and BF; or a model of C with those three principles that fails Rigid Comprehension. The source's first cross-reference to Proposition 2.6 was replaced in the earlier transcription by Proposition 2.7; the statement and premises are unchanged.

Refuted, 1 October 2026: the model ultralimit-fork, from Branden Fitelson (with Claude and GPT-6 Astra), satisfies Classicism, □Atomicity, □Boolean Completeness, □BF and □Actuality, and fails Rigid Comprehension at type $t\to t$. It extends the propositional structure mentioned above to a model of C with all the premises, so gap (b) is a genuine gap. The record stays conjectured, as the map's convention requires; the model is the refuting evidence. Gap-free in the end is part (ii), which gets Actuality: Atomicity (type $t$) and Weak Inextensible Comprehension imply Actuality (atomicity-t-and-weakly-inextensible-comprehension-imply-actuality), and Boolean Completeness implies Weak Inextensible Comprehension.

Cian Dorr proposed it on 10 October 2026, with an argument that assumed rigidity is closed under conjunction. It is not, in C: if $x\ne y$ but possibly $x=y$, the conjunction of their haecceities is persistent but not weakly inextensible, since weak inextensibility would require $\Box\,x\ne y$. Under □ND conjunctions of rigid relations are rigid and the argument goes through, but C5 already gives □Rigid Power. A countermodel must therefore have contingent identity at some accessible world: a rigid $Y$ not below a rigid $X$ that comes below it at an accessible world by identifications, without becoming identical there to any rigid subrelation of $X$ at the evaluation point. With the recorded results, the conjecture would make Rigid Rigidity equivalent to □BF + Rigid Power, and Weakly Rigid Weak Rigidity equivalent to BF + Weakly Rigid Power. Since Rigid Rigidity implies its necessitation, the conjecture is equivalent to Rigid Rigidity ⇒ □Rigid Power. It is refuted: coalesced-two-extensional-arithmetics-root (20 October 2026) satisfies Rigid Rigidity but not Rigid Power, as do the two supported-product models.

Equivalent to the claim that a finite count of individuals is necessary whenever it is true. It holds with No Pure Contingency and with BF, by the recorded results. A countermodel would need a world with finitely many individuals that can see one with more, and must violate both BF at type $e$ and No Pure Contingency; the coalesced sums on the map do not supply one, since their roots have infinitely many individuals.

Equivalent to the claim that a finite count of propositions is necessary whenever it is true. It holds with No Pure Contingency and with BF (type $t$), by the recorded results. If some finite $Z$ holds of $\lambda p\, .\,\top$ then every proposition is one of finitely many, and NI carries each identity across, but collecting them under a box is an instance of BF at type $t$, which C does not prove. A proof would need to bypass that; a countermodel would need a world with finitely many propositions that can see one with more, and must violate both BF (type $t$) and No Pure Contingency.

The converse of weakly-rigid-power-implies-tame-rigidity and weakly-rigid-power-implies-rigid-power. With □Tame Rigidity in place of Tame Rigidity it is proved (necessary-tame-rigidity-and-rigid-power-imply-weakly-rigid-power). The unboxed argument fails at weak inextensibility: for weakly rigid $F$, $P_F:=\lambda X\, .\,\operatorname{WeaklyRigid}(X)\land X\le F$ is weakly persistent, but $Z:=\lambda X\, .\,\operatorname{Rigid}(X)\land X\le F$ satisfies $\forall X\, .\,P_FX\to\Box ZX$, so the weak inextensibility of $P_F$ requires $P_F\le Z$, which is Tame Rigidity below $F$ at every accessible world. Weakly Rigid Power implies □Tame Rigidity at type $t$ (and, with BF, at every type: barcan-and-weakly-rigid-power-imply-necessary-tame-rigidity), so the conjecture would follow from Tame Rigidity + Rigid Power ⇒ □Tame Rigidity, and a countermodel must satisfy Tame Rigidity and Rigid Power while failing □Tame Rigidity at type $t$. No recorded model yet separates Tame Rigidity from □Tame Rigidity.

Refuted (25 October 2026): [[symmetric-finite-compression-entrance]], GPT-6 Astra's construction (prompted by Daniel Kodsi, 23 October 2026), satisfies Tame Rigidity and Rigid Power at every type and fails Weakly Rigid Power at type $et$, through a weakly rigid but not rigid relation below the transport of a rigid bound, at a world where □Tame Rigidity fails at type $et$. Since then [[symmetric-entrance-qualitative-links]] and this model both separate Tame Rigidity from □Tame Rigidity.

Suggested repair (Cian Dorr, 25 October 2026): add the premise that there are more than $2^{2^{\aleph_0}}$ propositions, i.e. that no injective relation runs from the properties of the reals of some real number structure into the propositions. All five models above falsify it. It is not recorded as a principle until the repaired implication is proved, since by itself it would only call for large variants of many models.

Equivalent to the claim that a finite count of propositions is necessary whenever it is true. It holds with No Pure Contingency and with BF (type $t$), by the recorded results. If some finite $Z$ holds of $\lambda p\, .\,\top$ then every proposition is one of finitely many, and NI carries each identity across, but collecting them under a box is an instance of BF at type $t$, which C does not prove. A proof would need to bypass that; a countermodel would need a world with finitely many propositions that can see one with more, and must violate both BF (type $t$) and No Pure Contingency.

data.notes:
Does Relational Choice alone give a transversal for every equivalence relation? Christopher Sun observed that the literature claims this without proof. The converse is recorded. The quotient argument chooses from each cell $\lambda z\, .\,(Rx)z$ and needs the cells of two members of one class to be the same property; in C that is necessary coextension, and the hypothesis gives actual coextension only. No definable substitute for the cell helps, since an operation definable from $R$ identifies $x$ with $x'$ only when they are necessarily indiscernible with respect to $R$. A Zermelo-style well-ordering argument breaks at the same point: coextensive but distinct stages receive different chosen elements. The expectation is that the implication fails. What would settle it: a proof that uses the chosen relation to break the symmetry between coextensive cells, or a model of C with Relational Choice that is not extensionally full at its evaluation point. Every recorded model of Relational Choice is extensionally full there, in that every set of tuples from the domains is the extension of a rigid element, and that fullness verifies Transversal Choice by the same metatheoretic choice, so none separates the two. Symmetric Henkin models in the Fraenkel–Mostowski style cannot separate them either; see the write-up.
Update of 28 September 2026: Christopher Sun showed on 26 September that Transversal Choice is equivalent to Relational Choice together with Transversal (transversal-and-relational-choice-imply-transversal-choice), so this question is equivalent to whether Relational Choice implies Transversal. Anything that implies Transversal, such as Actuality, closes the gap.
Update of 28 October 2026: Vicinity also closes the gap ([[vicinity-and-relational-choice-imply-transversal-choice]], from GPT-6 Astra, prompted by Daniel Kodsi). So a model separating Relational Choice from Transversal Choice must falsify Vicinity, and hence ND at type $t$ and Actuality.

The converse of weakly-rigid-power-implies-tame-rigidity and weakly-rigid-power-implies-rigid-power. With □Tame Rigidity in place of Tame Rigidity it is proved (necessary-tame-rigidity-and-rigid-power-imply-weakly-rigid-power). The unboxed argument fails at weak inextensibility: for weakly rigid $F$, $P_F:=\lambda X\, .\,\operatorname{WeaklyRigid}(X)\land X\le F$ is weakly persistent, but $Z:=\lambda X\, .\,\operatorname{Rigid}(X)\land X\le F$ satisfies $\forall X\, .\,P_FX\to\Box ZX$, so the weak inextensibility of $P_F$ requires $P_F\le Z$, which is Tame Rigidity below $F$ at every accessible world. Weakly Rigid Power implies □Tame Rigidity at type $t$ (and, with BF, at every type: barcan-and-weakly-rigid-power-imply-necessary-tame-rigidity), so the conjecture would follow from Tame Rigidity + Rigid Power ⇒ □Tame Rigidity, and a countermodel must satisfy Tame Rigidity and Rigid Power while failing □Tame Rigidity at type $t$. No recorded model yet separates Tame Rigidity from □Tame Rigidity.

Refuted (25 October 2026): [[symmetric-finite-compression-entrance]], GPT-6 Astra's construction (prompted by Daniel Kodsi, 23 October 2026), satisfies Tame Rigidity and Rigid Power at every type and fails Weakly Rigid Power at type $et$, through a weakly rigid but not rigid relation below the transport of a rigid bound, at a world where □Tame Rigidity fails at type $et$. Since then [[symmetric-entrance-qualitative-links]] and this model both separate Tame Rigidity from □Tame Rigidity.

Stated by Bacon as a theorem, with the proof deferred to another venue; his handout of 19 October 2026 on the lottery-algebra model and the draft Modalized Domains on Possibility Frames do not reproduce it (the lottery record notes a transfer argument not given there). Downgraded from proved to conjectured on 11 October 2026, at Cian Dorr's request. background_pages.title: Framework and conventions
background_pages.html:
Classicism

The fixed background is Classicism (C) of Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, using the paper’s relational type system. Its base types are e and t. Form \sigma\tau from admitted types only when \tau\ne e: every function type ends in t. Thus et, tt and (et)t are admitted, while ee and (ee)t are not. Individuals of type e remain available as arguments and quantified objects.

Use the definition in Classicism, §1.3: C is the smallest H-theory containing Logical Equivalence. This schema identifies \lambda-abstractions of formulas equivalent in H. Its theoremhood side condition must be preserved when reasoning from additional assumptions.

This is the type system called R in Classicism, §1.1. It is fixed throughout the map, so principle names omit a type-system suffix.

Notation

Types associate to the right: \sigma\tau\rho means \sigma\to(\tau\to\rho). Application also associates to the right: fgx=f(gx). Write (fx)y for curried application. A dot separates a binder from its scope. The abbreviation X[\bar x] means explicitly left-nested application to the displayed tuple; it is X for an empty tuple. For a finite, possibly empty, tuple of types \bar\sigma=\sigma_1\ldots\sigma_n, \bar\sigma\rho is the type \sigma_1\cdots\sigma_n\rho (so \bar\sigma t is \sigma_1\cdots\sigma_n t), and \bar x^{\bar\sigma} gives x_i the type \sigma_i. A tuple quantifier \forall\bar x or \exists\bar x binds x_1,\ldots,x_n one at a time; \bar x=\bar y is the conjunction of the identities x_i=y_i (true for the empty tuple), and \bar x\ne\bar y is its negation. With tuples in place of single arguments, the definitions below are read in the evident way; for instance \operatorname{Serial}(U):=\forall\bar x^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,\exists y^\tau\, .\,(U[\bar x])y for U^{\bar\sigma\tau t}, and \operatorname{Equiv}(R) for R^{\bar\sigma\bar\sigma t} uses (R[\bar x])[\bar y].

Definition (common shorthands)

For relations X,Y of a type \bar\sigma t, and the evaluation point unless a box is written:

  • X\subseteq Y (X is included in Y, a subrelation of Y) abbreviates \forall\bar z\, .\,X[\bar z]\to Y[\bar z]; this is actual inclusion, and X\le Y is \Box(X\subseteq Y) ().
  • X\equiv Y (X and Y are coextensive) abbreviates \forall\bar z\, .\,X[\bar z]\leftrightarrow Y[\bar z]. In C coextensive relations are identical only when necessarily coextensive (Intensionality).
  • For the empty tuple, at type t, p\subseteq q is p\to q and p\equiv q is p\leftrightarrow q. In Lean these are the notations X ⊆ Y and X ≡ Y, defined pointwise at every relational type.
  • \top_\tau and \bot_\tau, at a relational type \tau=\bar\sigma t, are \lambda\bar x\, .\,\top and \lambda\bar x\, .\,\bot, the top and bottom of \le_\tau.
  • H_{\bar x}:=\lambda\bar y\, .\,\bar y=\bar x is the haecceity of \bar x, the property of being \bar x.
  • X-y:=\lambda u\, .\,Xu\land u\ne y is X without y.
  • \exists!x\, .\,\varphi abbreviates \exists x\, .\,\varphi\land\forall x'\, .\,\varphi[x'/x]\to x'=x.
  • For a relation R^{\sigma\sigma t} given as an order, x\preccurlyeq y is (Rx)y, and x\prec y is x\preccurlyeq y\land x\ne y.
  • \bigwedge_{i<j\le n}x_i\ne x_j is the finite conjunction of the displayed distinctness claims, saying that x_1,\ldots,x_n are pairwise distinct.

Polyadic forms. A principle with a type variable that may take the value e has a polyadic form, listed among its equivalent forms. The polyadic form replaces that variable \sigma by a tuple \bar\sigma, and its variables of type \sigma by tuples. (Relational Choice has two such variables; only the input one is made a tuple.) The original form is the case of a one-element tuple. The converse is proved in one of two ways. - One argument at a time: by induction on the length of the tuple, currying the first argument. - Coding a tuple by its haecceity: H_{\bar x}:=\lambda\bar y^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,\bar y=\bar x, of type \bar\sigma t. C proves H_{\bar x}=H_{\bar y}\leftrightarrow \bar x=\bar y, so the original form at the single type \bar\sigma t, applied to a relation on codes, yields the polyadic form at \bar\sigma. For the empty tuple the code type is t and the only code is \top.

The equivalence of the boxed forms follows by necessitating these derivations. Several of the equivalences have been checked in a Lean formalization of C.

Two theorems of H

Lemma (Existence)

Every type is inhabited: \exists x^\sigma\, .\,x=x.

Proof. Reflexivity gives y=y, and existential introduction yields \exists x\, .\,x=x at each admitted type; equivalently, use the β and EG derivation on p. 7.

Polyadic form. \exists\bar x^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,\bar x=\bar x, the conjunction of the original at each \sigma_i; for the empty tuple it is \top.

Credit: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr · Sources: Classicism, §1.1, p. 7

Lemma (Ordinary Comprehension)

Every well-typed formula P with distinguished variables \bar y defines a coextensive relation: \exists X\, .\,\forall\bar y\, .\,X[\bar y]\leftrightarrow P, for X not free in P, any other free object variables being universally closed.

Proof. The λ-term \lambda\bar y\, .\,P is a witness: β-conversion makes its application equivalent to P at each tuple, and existential introduction supplies the instance.

The schema is in a formula, which no Lean statement with type parameters can quantify over. The Lean theorems state, for zero, one and two distinguished variables, that every relation P is coextensive with some X; each instance of the schema is the theorem at the λ-term \lambda\bar y\, .\,P, which is how the object language proves it.

Credit: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr · Sources: Classicism

Conventions

Type scope. A formula containing type variables (\sigma, \tau, \bar\sigma) is a schema. The principle is the set of its instances, one for each admissible assignment of types to the variables. Type variables range over the fixed type system above; \bar\sigma ranges over finite tuples, including the empty one. A relational type is any admitted type other than e, including t. A restriction is written as a parenthesized proviso after the formula, as in \ldots\qquad(\tau\ne e); a formula without a proviso admits every assignment. The type variables are metalinguistic: there is no quantification over types in C, and a type variable never falls within the scope of an object-language operator except as a fixed parameter. Finite tuples and formula schemata retain their stated metalinguistic side conditions.

Modal scope. A boxed schema means that each admitted, fully closed object-language instance is necessary. Close its object variables before boxing it. Type ranges and formula side conditions remain outside the box. C5 abbreviates C plus boxed ND at all types. It is an optional preset, not part of the fixed background. A proof under an optional premise cannot be necessitated unless that premise is discharged or supplied necessarily.

Negation. Failure of a type schema means failure of at least one of its admitted instances, not failure at every type: the negation of a principle A_\sigma says that \neg A_\sigma for some \sigma. A necessarily false instance, \Box\neg A_\sigma for some \sigma, is stronger and different from failure of the boxed schema. Negated principle nodes are not added by this positive import. Incompatibilities conclude False; model violates entries record schema failure.

Infinite sets in model descriptions. A model described with “an infinite set” works for any infinite set; where a construction needs a particular one, its description says so. “Infinite” means not finite, that is, in bijection with no natural number. This is the notion the Axioms of Infinity express, the finite cardinalities being defined inductively. Without the axiom of choice it is weaker than Dedekind-infinity, but it is all that the arguments for the Infinity principles use, so they hold in the choiceless variants of a model too. Those variants say which hypothesis replaces choice.

Evidence

Evidence. Classicism is Bacon and Dorr (2024), in Fritz and Jones (eds), Higher-Order Metaphysics, Oxford University Press, pp. 109–190. References use the numbering of the 87-page draft dated 16 May 2023, from which the map was built and which does not differ materially from the published version, and, for the symmetric ideally-full models and the weak rigidity principles, the 27-page draft of Dorr, Boolean Completeness does not imply Rigid Comprehension, dated 30 July 2026. That second source is a work in progress and is not distributed with the map; its records say so. Models cite the construction and evaluation point directly. The source models now use exactly the map’s type system. Their listed properties provide countermodel evidence at the stated evaluation point. The singleton-root coalesced model still awaits an expansion to the fixed nonlogical signature; its record explains this separate obligation. Two results reported without proofs in the draft retain pending verification status. No record claims an independent human check or Lean verification.

background_pages.title: Necessity
background_pages.html:
Definition (necessity and possibility)

Put \Box p:=(p=\top) and \Diamond p:=(p\ne\bot).

The facts below are theorems of C, schemata in their type variables. Each was formerly recorded as a result with no premises.

The propositional modal logic of \Box

Lemma (K)

Necessity distributes over implication: \forall p q\, .\,\Box(p\to q)\to(\Box p\to\Box q).

Proof. In the Boolean algebra of propositions, \Box(p\to q) says that the implication is \top. Together with p=\top, substitution and the Boolean identities identify q with \top.

Dual form. \forall p q\, .\,\Box(p\to q)\to(\Diamond p\to\Diamond q). Instantiate either form at \neg q,\neg p and contrapose the inner conditional, using \Box(\neg q\to\neg p)\leftrightarrow\Box(p\to q) and \Diamond=\neg\Box\neg.

Credit: Andrew Bacon (Classicism credits the S4 result to Bacon 2018) · Sources: Classicism, §1.5, p. 16

Lemma (T)

Necessary propositions are true: \forall p\, .\,\Box p\to p.

Proof. If p=\top, identity elimination and the truth of \top give p.

Dual form. Every truth is possible: \forall p\, .\,p\to\Diamond p, by contraposition and \Diamond=\neg\Box\neg.

Credit: Andrew Bacon (Classicism credits the S4 result to Bacon 2018) · Sources: Classicism, §1.5, p. 16

Lemma (4)

Necessary propositions are necessarily necessary: \forall p\, .\,\Box p\to\Box\Box p.

Proof. Apply NI to the identity p=\top. Its conclusion is \Box(p=\top), which is \Box\Box p.

Dual form. Whatever is possibly possible is possible: \forall p\, .\,\Diamond\Diamond p\to\Diamond p, by contraposition and \Diamond=\neg\Box\neg.

Credit: Andrew Bacon (Classicism credits the S4 result to Bacon 2018) · Sources: Classicism, §1.5, p. 17

Further laws. \Box and \Diamond are duals: \Diamond p=\neg\Box\neg p and \Box\neg p=\neg\Diamond p, and \Box\neg p is p=\bot . \Box distributes over conjunction, \Box(p\land q)=(\Box p\land\Box q) ; \Diamond(p\lor q)\to\Diamond p\lor\Diamond q ; and \Diamond p\land\Box q\to\Diamond(p\land q) .

By a result of Andrew Bacon (The Broadest Necessity, 2018), the propositional modal logic of \Box in C is exactly S4, the smallest normal modal logic containing T and 4. The 5 and B axioms are not theorems of C, though they can consistently be added.

Quantifiers and identity

Lemma (Necessity of Identity (NI))

Identity is necessary at every type: \forall x y^\sigma\, .\,x=y\to\Box(x=y).

Proof. Reflexivity is a theorem, so its necessitation gives \Box(x=x). Leibniz’s Law substitutes y for the second x under the premise x=y, giving \Box(x=y).

Polyadic form. \forall\bar x\,\bar y^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,\bar x=\bar y\to\Box(\bar x=\bar y): \bar x=\bar y is a conjunction of identities, each necessary, and a conjunction of necessities is necessary.

Credit: W. V. Quine (historical attribution in Classicism, p. 22) · Sources: Classicism, §2.1, p. 22

Lemma (Converse Barcan Formula (CBF))

\forall X^{\sigma t}\, .\,\Box(\forall x^\sigma\, .\,Xx)\to(\forall x^\sigma\, .\,\Box Xx).

Proof. Necessitate universal instantiation and use K to obtain \Box(\forall x\, .\,Xx)\to\Box Xx. Generalize x, preserving the side condition.

Other forms. The polyadic form, \forall X^{\bar\sigma t}\, .\,\Box(\forall\bar x\, .\,X[\bar x])\to(\forall\bar x\, .\,\Box X[\bar x]), follows by instantiating one variable at a time. The dual form says that if something possibly has a property, then possibly something has it: \forall X^{\sigma t}\, .\,(\exists x\, .\,\Diamond Xx)\to\Diamond(\exists x\, .\,Xx), and likewise for tuples; each comes from the corresponding form by contraposition and \Diamond=\neg\Box\neg.

Credit: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr · Sources: Classicism, §1.5, p. 19

Lemma (Broad Necessitism)

Every entity of a type is necessarily identical to something: \forall x^\sigma\, .\,\Box(\exists y^\sigma\, .\,y=x).

Proof. The theorem \forall x\, .\,\exists y\, .\,y=x can be necessitated, and CBF gives \forall x\, .\,\Box\exists y\, .\,y=x.

Polyadic form. \forall\bar x^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,\Box(\exists\bar y^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,\bar y=\bar x), taking \bar y:=\bar x coordinatewise.

Credit: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr · Sources: Classicism, §1.5

The Barcan Formula and the Necessity of Distinctness are not theorems of C, though they can consistently be added.

Intensionality

Lemma (Intensionality)

Necessarily coextensive relations are identical: \forall X Y^{\bar\sigma t}\, .\,\Box(X\equiv Y)\to X=Y.

Proof. Logical Equivalence identifies the λ-abstractions of X[\bar z]\land(X\equiv Y) and of the analogous expression with Y in the first conjunct. If the biconditional is necessary, substitute its identity with \top into the abstraction identity. Boolean identities and β-η conversion leave X=Y, as on p. 17.

Credit: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr · Sources: Classicism, §1.5, pp. 17–18

Lemma (Modalized Fregean Axiom)

Necessarily equivalent propositions are identical: \forall p q\, .\,\Box(p\leftrightarrow q)\to p=q.

Proof. The nullary instance of Intensionality: necessary equivalence identifies p\leftrightarrow q with \top, and the Boolean identities then identify p and q.

Credit: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr · Sources: Classicism, §1.5, p. 18

Lemma (Modalized Functionality)

Necessarily co-functional operations are identical: \forall X Y^{\sigma\tau}\, .\,\Box(\forall z^\sigma\, .\,Xz=Yz)\to X=Y\qquad(\tau\ne e).

Proof. From boxed pointwise identity, identity elimination gives boxed agreement after applying every remaining argument of the relational output type; quantification over those arguments is inside the necessary implication. Intensionality and η-conversion identify the operations. This relies on the output type’s ending in t.

Polyadic form. \forall X Y^{\bar\sigma\tau}\, .\,\Box(\forall\bar z\, .\,X[\bar z]=Y[\bar z])\to X=Y (\tau\ne e), one argument at a time, with the box carried through.

Credit: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr · Sources: Classicism, §1.5, n. 22

background_pages.title: Boolean structure and the algebraic order
background_pages.html:
At a relational type \tau, Boolean operations are defined pointwise. The order is algebraic entailment, X\le_\tau Y iff Y=X\lor_\tau Y, rather than material implication. At t this is equivalent to \Box(X\to Y); at a relation type it is equivalent to the necessary universal closure of the pointwise implication . So \le_\tau is a partial order: reflexive and transitive because necessary pointwise implication is, and antisymmetric by Intensionality . At t, \bot\le p\le\top, and p\land q and p\lor q are the greatest lower and least upper bounds of p and q ; at every relational type \bot_\tau\le X, and X\le\neg_\tau X only when X=\bot_\tau . An entailment, if true, is necessary: X\le Y\to\Box(X\le Y), since \le is boxed inclusion, by 4 .

Definition (lattice predicates)

The lattice predicates used in the principles are:

\begin{aligned} \operatorname{LB}_\tau(y,X)&:=\forall z^\tau\, .\,Xz\to y\le_\tau z,\\ \operatorname{GLB}_\tau(y,X)&:=\forall z^\tau\, .\, \operatorname{LB}_\tau(z,X)\leftrightarrow z\le_\tau y,\\ \operatorname{UB}_\tau(y,X)&:=\forall z^\tau\, .\,Xz\to z\le_\tau y,\\ \operatorname{LUB}_\tau(y,X)&:=\forall z^\tau\, .\, \operatorname{UB}_\tau(z,X)\leftrightarrow y\le_\tau z,\\ \operatorname{Atom}_\tau(y)&:=\forall z^\tau\, .\, (z\le_\tau y\land z\ne y)\leftrightarrow z\le_\tau\neg_\tau z. \end{aligned}

Thus an atom is non-bottom and has no non-bottom strict lower bound. \operatorname{LB}, \operatorname{GLB} and \operatorname{Atom} are the definitions of Classicism, §2.2, pp. 23–24; \operatorname{UB} and \operatorname{LUB} are their duals.

So y is a lower (upper) bound of X when it entails (is entailed by) every member of X, and a greatest lower (least upper) bound when the lower (upper) bounds of X are exactly what entails it (what it entails).

Lemma (greatest lower bounds and least upper bounds)

At a relational type \tau, the negation of a least upper bound of X is a greatest lower bound of the negations of the members of X, and conversely: \operatorname{GLB}_\tau(\neg_\tau y,\lambda w\, .\,X(\neg_\tau w))\leftrightarrow \operatorname{LUB}_\tau(y,X).

Proof. Negation reverses \le_\tau, since necessary pointwise implication contraposes, and \neg_\tau\neg_\tau z=z by Intensionality . Hence z\le_\tau\neg_\tau y iff y\le_\tau\neg_\tau z, and z is a lower bound of the negations of the members of X iff \neg_\tau z is an upper bound of X. So the lower bounds of \lambda w\, .\,X(\neg_\tau w) are exactly the entities below \neg_\tau y iff the upper bounds of X are exactly the entities above y. \square

The greatest lower bound of a property’s upper bounds is also its least upper bound, and dually .

Classicism does not entail that any relational type \tau forms a complete or an atomic Boolean algebra, though these claims can consistently be added: see Boolean Completeness and Atomicity.

background_pages.title: Atoms
background_pages.html:
Atoms are defined with the other lattice predicates. An entity of a relational type is an atom just when it is non-bottom and entails every entity of its type or that entity’s negation .

Definition (strong atoms)

At a relational type \sigma, with \Diamond_\sigma X:=X\ne\bot_\sigma, a strong atom is a possible entity that necessarily entails every entity of its type or its negation:

\operatorname{SAtom}_\sigma(W):=\Diamond_\sigma W\land\Box\forall Y^\sigma\, .\, W\le_\sigma Y\lor W\le_\sigma\neg_\sigma Y.

Bacon, A Philosophical Introduction to Higher-Order Logics, §8.2, pp. 165–166, calls these strong worlds; dropping the box gives his weak worlds, which are just the atoms. The map avoids the word “world” for them, since at types other than t they are not world-like.

By T, a strong atom is an atom. Unlike an atom, it necessarily settles every entity of its type, including entities that do not actually exist. Atomicity says that every possible entity is entailed by an atom; Strong Atomicity requires a strong atom. Each is one direction of a biconditional that Bacon calls the Weak and the Strong Leibniz Biconditionals; the other direction is a theorem of C. The type-t instance of each is recorded separately.

Self-atoms

Definition (self-atoms)

A self-atom is a possible entity that is necessarily an atom whenever it is instantiated:

\operatorname{SelfAtom}_\sigma(X):=\Diamond_\sigma X\land \Box\bigl(\exists\bar x\, .\,X\bar x\to\operatorname{Atom}_\sigma(X)\bigr), \qquad \operatorname{SelfAtom}_t(p):=\Diamond p\land\Box\bigl(p\to\operatorname{Atom}_t(p)\bigr).

Credit: Cian Dorr, 25 October 2026

At type t, since p\land\operatorname{Atom}_t(p) is equivalent in C to p\land\forall q\, .\,q\to p\le q, a self-atom is a possible proposition that entails that it is the actual world. A strong atom is an atom at every world, a self-atom an atom at every world where it holds, an atom an atom at the evaluation point; a strong atom is a self-atom and a true atom is a self-atom, but a self-atom need not be an atom. Self-Atomicity replaces \operatorname{SAtom} in Strong Atomicity by \operatorname{SelfAtom}, and the four bridge principles say that atoms are self-atoms, that self-atoms are atoms, that self-atoms are strong atoms, and that atoms are strong atoms; the last is what Strong Atomicity adds to Atomicity.

background_pages.title: Rigidity
background_pages.html:
Definition (persistence, inextensibility and rigidity)

For a relation Y with a finite argument tuple, including the empty tuple, the comprehension predicates are:

\begin{aligned} \operatorname{Persistent}(Y)&:=Y\le\lambda\bar x\, .\,\Box Y[\bar x],\\ \operatorname{Inextensible}(Y)&:=\Box\forall X\, .\, (\forall\bar x\, .\,Y[\bar x]\to\Box X[\bar x])\to Y\le X,\\ \operatorname{Rigid}(Y)&:=\operatorname{Persistent}(Y)\land \operatorname{Inextensible}(Y). \end{aligned}

This is the rigidity convention of §2.3, p. 28. Gallin’s alternative convention has its own principle.

Definition (the weak variants)

Since Y\le Z is itself the necessary universal closure of the pointwise implication, \operatorname{Persistent}(Y) unpacks as \Box\forall\bar x\, .\,Y[\bar x]\to\Box Y[\bar x], and both conjuncts of \operatorname{Rigid} carry a leading \Box. Dropping it gives the weak variants:

\begin{aligned} \operatorname{WeaklyPersistent}(Y)&:=\forall\bar x\, .\, Y[\bar x]\to\Box Y[\bar x],\\ \operatorname{WeaklyInextensible}(Y)&:=\forall X\, .\, (\forall\bar x\, .\,Y[\bar x]\to\Box X[\bar x])\to Y\le X,\\ \operatorname{WeaklyRigid}(Y)&:=\operatorname{WeaklyPersistent}(Y)\land \operatorname{WeaklyInextensible}(Y). \end{aligned}

\operatorname{Rigid} is thus necessary weak rigidity . These are the conventions of Dorr, Boolean Completeness does not imply Rigid Comprehension, pp. 2 and 12. By T, rigidity implies weak rigidity, persistence weak persistence, and inextensibility weak inextensibility .

Lemma (rigidity, if true, is necessary)

If X is rigid, then \Box\operatorname{Rigid}(X).

Proof. \operatorname{Rigid}(X) is \Box\operatorname{WeaklyRigid}(X), and 4 gives \Box\Box\operatorname{WeaklyRigid}(X), which is \Box\operatorname{Rigid}(X). \square

Lemma (weakly rigid relations are persistent)

A weakly rigid relation is persistent: weak inextensibility applied to \lambda\bar x\, .\,\Box Y[\bar x], whose hypothesis Y[\bar x]\to\Box\Box Y[\bar x] holds by weak persistence and 4, gives Y\le\lambda\bar x\, .\,\Box Y[\bar x]. So weak rigidity is equivalently persistence together with weak inextensibility, the combination used in the draft’s Proposition 1.

Sources: Dorr, Boolean Completeness does not imply Rigid Comprehension, draft of 30 July 2026

Lemma (coextensive weakly rigid relations are identical)

If F and G are weakly rigid and coextensive, then F=G.

Proof. Each is below the other: F\le G by weak inextensibility of F, since each instance of F is an instance of G and so, by weak persistence of G, necessarily one; and G\le F likewise. Since \le is antisymmetric, F=G. \square

Closure properties

The lemmas below use no BF, choice, ND or comprehension. That BF at \sigma makes \lambda z^\sigma\, .\,\top weakly rigid, and □BF makes it rigid, are forms of BF and □BF.

Lemma (haecceities are rigid)

For every x^\sigma, the haecceity H_x=\lambda y\, .\,y=x is rigid.

Proof. It is persistent by NI. For inextensibility, suppose, at any world, that \forall y\, .\,y=x\to\Box Zy. Then \Box Zx, and so \Box\forall y\, .\,y=x\to Zy, which is H_x\le Z. \square

Credit: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), prompted by Daniel Kodsi, 22 October 2026

Lemma (rigid unions of rigid families)

If R^{\sigma t} is rigid and F^{\sigma\tau t} is such that Fx is rigid for every x with Rx, then the union U:=\lambda y\, .\,\exists x\, .\,Rx\land(Fx)y is rigid.

Proof. First, necessarily every instance of R has a rigid fiber. For each x with Rx, Fx is rigid and so, by , necessarily rigid; so by the inextensibility of R, R\le\lambda x\, .\,\operatorname{Rigid}(Fx). Now argue at an arbitrary world, where R is weakly rigid and each instance of R has a rigid fiber. Weak persistence: if Uy, take x with Rx and (Fx)y; then \Box Rx and \Box(Fx)y, so \Box Uy. Weak inextensibility: suppose \forall y\, .\,Uy\to\Box Zy. For each x with Rx, \forall y\, .\,(Fx)y\to\Box Zy, so Fx\le Z by the inextensibility of Fx; that is, \Box(\forall y\, .\,(Fx)y\to Zy). By the weak inextensibility of R, R\le\lambda x\, .\,\forall y\, .\,(Fx)y\to Zy, which gives U\le Z. Both hold at every world, so U is rigid. \square

Credit: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), prompted by Daniel Kodsi, 22 October 2026

Lemma (rigidity is preserved by direct images)

If R^{\sigma t} is rigid and f^{\sigma\tau} is an operation (\tau\ne e), then \lambda y\, .\,\exists x\, .\,Rx\land y=fx is rigid.

Proof. It is the union of the haecceities H_{fx} over the instances of R, rigid by and . \square

Credit: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), prompted by Daniel Kodsi, 22 October 2026

Lemma (rigidity is preserved by inverse images under necessarily injective operations)

If P^{\tau t} is rigid, every instance of P is a value of f^{\sigma\tau} (\tau\ne e), and f is necessarily injective, then \lambda x\, .\,P(fx) is rigid.

Proof. Persistence is inherited from P. Being a value of f is necessary if true, by NI, so the inextensibility of P makes every instance of P necessarily a value of f. For inextensibility, suppose, at a world, that \forall x\, .\,P(fx)\to\Box Zx, and put Z':=\lambda y\, .\,\forall x\, .\,y=fx\to Zx. If Py, then y=fx_0 for some x_0, so \Box Zx_0; since f is necessarily injective, necessarily every x with fx=fx_0 is x_0, so \Box Z'y. By the inextensibility of P, P\le Z', and so \Box\forall x\, .\,P(fx)\to Zx. Both the range condition and injectivity keep their modal scopes. \square

Credit: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), prompted by Daniel Kodsi, 22 October 2026

background_pages.title: Varieties of necessity
background_pages.html:
Strong Possibility uses the distinctness-preserving modality of §2.6, p. 42:

\Box_{\ne}p:=\exists q\, .\,q\land\Box(\Diamond q\to p), \qquad \Diamond_{\ne}p:=\neg\Box_{\ne}\neg p.

Hats, two-hat necessity and 5-necessity. For an operator X^{tt} put

\hat X:=\lambda p\, .\,\exists q\, .\,q\land\Box(\neg X\neg q\to p).

In C, \hat\Box=\Box_{\ne} (The Bounds of Possibility, Appendix D, Proposition D17). Two-hat necessity is the hat of \Box_{\ne}, written \hat{\hat\Box}, with dual \hat{\hat\Diamond}p:=\neg\hat{\hat\Box}\neg p. Call X^{tt} an S5 operator when, necessarily, it is N, K and B:

\operatorname{S5}(X):=\Box\bigl(\forall p\, .\,\Box p\to Xp\bigr)\land \Box\bigl(\forall p\,q\, .\,X(p\to q)\to Xp\to Xq\bigr)\land \Box\bigl(\forall p\, .\,p\to X\neg X\neg p\bigr).

5-necessity is necessity under every S5 operator, \Box_5:=\lambda p\, .\,\forall X^{tt}\, .\,\operatorname{S5}(X)\to Xp, with dual \Diamond_5. Appendix D defines \Box_5 with the condition NKJF_{\langle\rangle} in place of NKB; its facts (A5) and (C5) make the two definitions necessarily equivalent. Theorems of C: \Box\le\Box_{\ne}\le\hat{\hat\Box}\le\Box_5\le\lambda p\, .\,p (the order is necessary pointwise implication) ; each of these operators is necessarily N, K, T and 4, and \Box_5 is an S5 operator; and if \Box_{\ne} or \hat{\hat\Box} is identical to its own hat, it is identical to \Box_5.

Appendix D of The Bounds of Possibility

Dorr, Hawthorne and Yli-Vakkuri, The Bounds of Possibility (2021), Appendix D, Narrower Modalities in Higher-Order S4, pp. 400–409, reads into C: the appendix’s primitive \Box is C’s \lambda p\, .\,p=\top, under which every theorem of its \mathrm H_{S4} is a theorem of C. Only the propositions the map uses are given here, and F and I are stated at type t only. Operators are of type tt.

Definition (properties of operators)

For X^{tt}:

\begin{aligned} \mathrm N\,X&:=\forall p\, .\,\Box p\to Xp, & \mathrm K\,X&:=\forall p\,q\, .\,X(p\to q)\to Xp\to Xq,\\ \mathrm J\,X&:=\forall p\, .\,p\to X\Diamond p, & \mathrm F_{\langle\rangle}X&:=\forall Y^{tt}\, .\,(\forall z\, .\,X(Yz))\to X\forall z\, .\,Yz, \end{aligned}

and NK, NKJ and NKJF_{\langle\rangle} are the conjunctions; F_{\langle\rangle} is BF for X at type t. The appendix’s 5-necessity is \Box_5^{\mathrm A}:=\lambda p\, .\,\forall X\, .\,\Box\,\mathrm{NKJF}_{\langle\rangle}X\to Xp, and W_@a:=a\land\forall q\, .\,q\to\Box(a\to q) says that a is the actual world.

Sources: The Bounds of Possibility, Appendix D, p. 400 and p. 407

Proposition (D1, at type t)

If X is NKJ, then y\ne z\to X(y\ne z) for y,z of type t, and dually \neg X\neg(y=z)\to y=z.

Proof. J gives X\Diamond(y\ne z), and necessarily \Diamond(y\ne z)\to y\ne z , so N and K give X(y\ne z). \square

Credit: Cian Dorr, John Hawthorne and Juhani Yli-Vakkuri · Sources: The Bounds of Possibility, Appendix D

Proposition (D11)

For every operator X: p\to\hat X\neg X\neg p, and \neg\hat X\neg Xp\to p. In C the second needs no hypothesis on X, since \neg\neg p=p.

Credit: Cian Dorr, John Hawthorne and Juhani Yli-Vakkuri · Sources: The Bounds of Possibility, Appendix D

Proposition (D12)

If X is NKJF_{\langle\rangle}, then p\to X\neg\hat X\neg p and \neg X\neg\hat Xp\to p.

Credit: Cian Dorr, John Hawthorne and Juhani Yli-Vakkuri · Sources: The Bounds of Possibility, Appendix D

Proposition (D14 and D15, the second at type t)

If \Box\,\mathrm{NK}\,X then \Box\,\mathrm{NKJ}\,\hat X (D14); and if \Box\,\mathrm{NKJF}_{\langle\rangle}X then \Box\,\mathrm{NKJF}_{\langle\rangle}\hat X (D14 with D15).

Proof of F_{\langle\rangle} for \hat X. Given \forall z\, .\,\hat X(Yz), the witness is q:=\forall z\, .\,\hat X(Yz): necessarily, \neg X\neg q gives \neg X\neg\hat X(Yz) for each z, by N and K, and hence Yz, by D12. \square

Credit: Cian Dorr, John Hawthorne and Juhani Yli-Vakkuri · Sources: The Bounds of Possibility, Appendix D

Theorem (D16, the parts the map needs)

\Box_5^{\mathrm A} is N, K and B, necessarily, so it is an S5 operator; hence \Box_5\le\Box_5^{\mathrm A}.

Proof of B. For X with \Box\,\mathrm{NKJF}_{\langle\rangle}X, D12 gives X\neg\hat X\neg p from p; and \hat X is necessarily NKJF_{\langle\rangle} (), so necessarily \Box_5^{\mathrm A}\neg p\to\hat X\neg p. \square

Credit: Cian Dorr, John Hawthorne and Juhani Yli-Vakkuri · Sources: The Bounds of Possibility, Appendix D

Proposition (relativization, as in Proposition D8)

For any X, \lambda r\, .\,\mathrm{NKJF}_{\langle\rangle}X\to Xr is NKJF_{\langle\rangle} outright, and so necessarily. So whatever is \Box_5^{\mathrm A} is X wherever X is NKJF_{\langle\rangle}.

Credit: Cian Dorr, John Hawthorne and Juhani Yli-Vakkuri · Sources: The Bounds of Possibility, Appendix D

Proposition (D18 and D19, at the actual world)

Suppose W_@a at the world of evaluation. If \Box\,\mathrm{NK}\,X, then \hat Xp\to\Box(\neg X\neg a\to p) (D18, left to right); and if \Box\,\mathrm{NKJ}\,X, then F_{\langle\rangle}\hat X (D19). The appendix assumes \mathrm H_{S5R}, used only for \BoxActuality; here the witness W_@a is needed at the world of evaluation only, as the map’s records need.

Credit: Cian Dorr, John Hawthorne and Juhani Yli-Vakkuri · Sources: The Bounds of Possibility, Appendix D, p. 407

The link \hat{\hat\Box}\le\Box_5 of the chain above is Proposition D21, right to left, and \hat\Box=\Box_{\ne} is Proposition D17.

Proposition (the Barcan formula for 5-necessity)

At every type \sigma, C proves \forall x^\sigma\, .\,\Box_5Rx\to\Box_5\forall x\, .\,Rx, and dually \Diamond_5\exists x\, .\,Rx\to\exists x\, .\,\Diamond_5Rx; iterating, the same holds for tuples of variables.

Proof. This is Prior’s derivation of the Barcan formula from B. It uses only that \Box_5 is an S5 operator, a theorem of C, so every step below is a theorem and may be necessitated. Put U:=\forall x\, .\,\Box_5Rx. For each x, U\to\Box_5Rx is a theorem, so by necessitation, N and K for \Box_5, \Diamond_5U\to\Diamond_5\Box_5Rx. The dual of B gives \Diamond_5\Box_5Rx\to Rx. So \Diamond_5U\to\forall x\, .\,Rx is a theorem, and necessitation, N and K give \Box_5\Diamond_5U\to\Box_5\forall x\, .\,Rx. B gives U\to\Box_5\Diamond_5U. \square

Credit: Cian Dorr, with help from GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), 29 October 2026

background_pages.title: Relations, orders and fixed points
background_pages.html:
For U^{\sigma\tau t}, set

\begin{aligned} \operatorname{Serial}(U)&:=\forall x^\sigma\, .\,\exists y^\tau\, .\,(Ux)y,\\ \operatorname{Functional}(U)&:=\forall x^\sigma\, .\,\exists y^\tau\, .\, (Ux)y\land\forall z^\tau\, .\,(Ux)z\to y=z. \end{aligned}

Functional includes totality. Relational Choice selects a functional subrelation; Functional Choice selects an operation. An operation’s output type must differ from e. Relational Choice also covers relations with individual outputs, since such a relation still ends in t.

Lemma (Modalized Plenitude)

If necessarily each argument has a value that is necessarily the relation’s unique value for it, then some operation necessarily represents the relation: \forall U^{\sigma\tau t}\, .\,\Box\bigl(\forall x^\sigma\, .\,\exists y^\tau\, .\,\Box((Ux)y\land\forall z^\tau\, .\,(Ux)z\to y=z)\bigr)\to\exists X^{\sigma\tau}\, .\,\Box\forall x^\sigma\, .\,\forall y^\tau\, .\,(Ux)y\leftrightarrow y=Xx\qquad(\tau\ne e). Plenitude, which asks only for actual functionality and an actual representation, is not a theorem of C.

Proof. Let \tau=\bar\rho\to t, which covers \tau=t with the empty tuple, and fix U^{\sigma\tau t}. Write \varphi(x,y):=(Ux)y\land\forall z\, .\,(Ux)z\to y=z and define the operation F:=\lambda x^\sigma\, .\,\lambda\bar u\, .\,\forall y^\tau\, .\,(Ux)y\to y[\bar u]; for \tau=t this is \lambda x\, .\,\forall p\, .\,(Ux)p\to p. (1) A theorem of C: \varphi(x,y_0)\to\forall\bar u\, .\,y_0[\bar u]\leftrightarrow(Fx)[\bar u]. Assume \varphi(x,y_0). If y_0[\bar u] and (Ux)y, then y=y_0 by uniqueness, so y[\bar u]; hence (Fx)[\bar u]. Conversely, if (Fx)[\bar u], instantiate y:=y_0 and use (Ux)y_0. (2) Necessitate (1) and apply K: \Box\varphi(x,y_0) gives \Box\forall\bar u\, .\,y_0[\bar u]\leftrightarrow(Fx)[\bar u], and Intensionality gives y_0=Fx. (3) Let H:=\forall x\, .\,\exists y\, .\,\Box\varphi(x,y) and G:=\forall x\, .\,\forall y\, .\,(Ux)y\leftrightarrow y=Fx. Then H\to G is a theorem of C. Given x and y, take y_0 with \Box\varphi(x,y_0); by (2) y_0=Fx, and by T \varphi(x,y_0). If (Ux)y then y=y_0=Fx by uniqueness. If y=Fx then y=y_0, and (Ux)y_0 gives (Ux)y. (4) Necessitate H\to G and apply K: \Box H\to\Box G. Existential generalization on the closed term F (with parameter U) gives \Box H\to\exists X\, .\,\Box\forall x\, .\,\forall y\, .\,(Ux)y\leftrightarrow y=Xx. Only necessitation of theorems of C is used, so the theoremhood side condition is respected.

The operation is definable from U, so no choice is involved. The outer box of the hypothesis is used only to get the boxed conclusion: the same proof shows, as a theorem of C, the unboxed variant H\to\exists X\, .\,\forall x\, .\,\forall y\, .\,(Ux)y\leftrightarrow y=Xx. The inner box is essential; it is what licenses the identity y_0=Fx in step (2).

Polyadic form. The same for U^{\bar\sigma\tau t}, one argument at a time, using each step’s instance under the box.

In Lean the proof is given at output type t and at output type \sigma'\to t for each type \sigma', the cases of none and of one remaining argument. Lean’s shallow layer has no induction on the shape of a type, so each further number of remaining arguments is a separate theorem of the same form.

Credit: Cian Dorr, 28 September 2026 (the statement, and the witness \lambda x\, .\,\forall p\, .\,(Ux)p\to p for output type t); Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), 28 September 2026 (the generalization to all relational output types and the written proof) · Sources: Classicism, §1.5, pp. 16–18 (necessitation, T and Intensionality)

For R^{\sigma\sigma t}, at any type \sigma including e,

\operatorname{Equiv}(R):=\forall x^\sigma\, .\,(Rx)x\;\land\; \forall x^\sigma y^\sigma\, .\,(Rx)y\to(Ry)x\;\land\; \forall x^\sigma y^\sigma z^\sigma\, .\,(Rx)y\land(Ry)z\to(Rx)z.

The cell of x is the property \lambda z\, .\,(Rx)z. Transversal Choice asks for a property with exactly one instance in each cell. The equivalence conditions and the transversal condition are unboxed, so they concern the evaluation point only. Two members of one cell have coextensive cells, but in C properties are identical only when necessarily coextensive.

For R^{\sigma\sigma t} and X^{\sigma t}, at any type \sigma including e, the order predicates relativized to X are

\begin{aligned} \operatorname{Trans}(R,X)&:=\forall x^\sigma y^\sigma z^\sigma\, .\, Xx\land Xy\land Xz\land(Rx)y\land(Ry)z\to(Rx)z,\\ \operatorname{Antisymm}(R,X)&:=\forall x^\sigma y^\sigma\, .\, Xx\land Xy\land(Rx)y\land(Ry)x\to x=y,\\ \operatorname{Total}(R,X)&:=\forall x^\sigma y^\sigma\, .\, Xx\land Xy\to(Rx)y\lor(Ry)x,\\ \operatorname{WellFounded}(R,X)&:=\forall Y^{\sigma t}\, .\, (\forall y^\sigma\, .\,Yy\to Xy)\land(\exists y^\sigma\, .\,Yy)\to \exists x^\sigma\, .\,Yx\land\forall y^\sigma\, .\,Yy\land(Ry)x\to y=x,\\ \operatorname{TotalOrder}(R,X)&:=\operatorname{Trans}(R,X)\land \operatorname{Antisymm}(R,X)\land\operatorname{Total}(R,X),\\ \operatorname{WO}(R,X)&:=\operatorname{TotalOrder}(R,X)\land \operatorname{WellFounded}(R,X). \end{aligned}

\operatorname{TotalOrder}(R,X) says that R totally orders X, or that X is an R-chain; \operatorname{WO}(R,X) says that R well-orders X. Omitting X means X:=\lambda x\, .\,\top, so that \operatorname{WO}(R) says that R well-orders the whole type. Further,

\begin{aligned} \operatorname{Refl}(R)&:=\forall x^\sigma\, .\,(Rx)x,\\ \operatorname{Preorder}(R)&:=\operatorname{Refl}(R)\land\operatorname{Trans}(R). \end{aligned}

These orders are non-strict: Total includes reflexivity on X, and when R totally orders X, an R-minimal instance of a property included in X is its R-least instance , and an instantiated property has a unique least instance . Like Equiv, all of these are unboxed, so they concern the evaluation point, and each depends only on the extensions of R and X there: coextensive arguments satisfy them together. A relation can be a well-order without necessarily being one, because instances that are distinct here may be identical elsewhere, where antisymmetry then fails. Orders on properties and relations defined by inclusion are typically only preorders: coextensive but distinct relations each include the other.

Lemma (the Bourbaki–Witt fixed-point lemma)

Work at any type \sigma, including e. Let X^{\sigma t} be a property, and R^{\sigma\sigma t} and F^{\sigma\sigma t} relations; write x\preccurlyeq y for (Rx)y. Since R need only be a preorder, put

x\approx y:=x\preccurlyeq y\land y\preccurlyeq x,\qquad x\prec y:=x\preccurlyeq y\land\neg\,y\preccurlyeq x .

When R is antisymmetric on X, this \prec agrees on X with the shorthand x\preccurlyeq y\land x\ne y. For Z\subseteq X put

\begin{aligned} \operatorname{UB}(s,Z)&:=Xs\land\forall z\, .\,Zz\to z\preccurlyeq s,\\ \operatorname{Sup}(s,Z)&:=\operatorname{UB}(s,Z)\land\forall u\, .\,\operatorname{UB}(u,Z)\to s\preccurlyeq u. \end{aligned}

In this lemma a chain is a property Z\subseteq X with \operatorname{Total}(R,Z). Because R is only a preorder, a chain need not be antisymmetric. That is weaker than being an R-chain in the sense above.

Assume, at the evaluation point:

  1. R preorders X: it is reflexive on X, and \operatorname{Trans}(R,X);
  2. every chain has a supremum in X: \forall Z\, .\,Z\subseteq X\land\operatorname{Total}(R,Z)\to\exists s\, .\,\operatorname{Sup}(s,Z);
  3. F is progressive and invariant on X: for every x with Xx, there is some y with (Fx)y, every such y has Xy and x\preccurlyeq y (progressive), and if moreover x\approx x', (Fx)y and (Fx')y', then y\approx y' (invariant).

Taking x':=x in the invariance clause, any two F-values of one x are \approx-equivalent; F is functional up to \approx.

Call Y^{\sigma t} closed if Y\subseteq X, \forall x\,y\, .\,Yx\land(Fx)y\to Yy, and \forall Z\,s\, .\,Z\subseteq Y\land\operatorname{Total}(R,Z)\land\operatorname{Sup}(s,Z)\to Ys. Let

M:=\lambda x\, .\,\forall Y\, .\,\operatorname{Closed}(Y)\to Yx

be the least closed property (the tower). Then:

    1. M is closed, and M\subseteq Y for every closed Y;
  • (b) for all b,c,d with Mb, Mc and (Fb)d: c\preccurlyeq b or d\preccurlyeq c. In particular M is a chain, and if b\prec c then d\preccurlyeq c;
  • (c) M has a supremum, and every supremum m of M satisfies Mm, and n\approx m whenever (Fm)n.

Two special cases:

  • Partial orders. Suppose R partially orders X (Antisymm as well) and F is functional on X. Then \approx is identity on X, a chain is an R-chain, invariance is automatic, and (c) gives an m in X with (Fm)m.
  • Inclusion. Suppose \sigma=\bar\tau t and \preccurlyeq is \subseteq. Then \approx is coextension \equiv. Invariance says that coextensive arguments have coextensive F-values.

No choice principle is used, and the lemma holds at the evaluation point only; it is a theorem schema of C, so it can be necessitated when its hypotheses hold necessarily.

Proof. Throughout, \preccurlyeq is transitive on X, and x\preccurlyeq y\prec z and x\prec y\preccurlyeq z each give x\prec z.

  1. By hypotheses 2 and 3, X is closed, so M\subseteq X. The remaining clauses are immediate from the definition of M.

Call c a pivot if Mc and \forall b\,d\, .\,Mb\land b\prec c\land(Fb)d\to d\preccurlyeq c.

Claim 1. Let c be a pivot and (Fc)e. Then for every b with Mb: b\preccurlyeq c or e\preccurlyeq b. Put M_{c,e}:=\lambda b\, .\,Mb\land(b\preccurlyeq c\lor e\preccurlyeq b). It is closed:

  • Let M_{c,e}b and (Fb)d. If b\prec c, then d\preccurlyeq c, as c is a pivot. If b\approx c, then d\approx e by invariance, so e\preccurlyeq d. If e\preccurlyeq b, then e\preccurlyeq b\preccurlyeq d.
  • Let Z\subseteq M_{c,e} be a chain with supremum s. Either z\preccurlyeq c for every z with Zz, and then s\preccurlyeq c; or e\preccurlyeq z\preccurlyeq s for some such z.

In each case the new member is in M, since M is closed. So M\subseteq M_{c,e} by (a).

Claim 2. Every c with Mc is a pivot. The pivots form a closed property:

  • Let c be a pivot and (Fc)e. Then Me, since M is closed. Let Mb, b\prec e and (Fb)d. By Claim 1, b\preccurlyeq c, since the alternative e\preccurlyeq b contradicts b\prec e. If b\prec c, then d\preccurlyeq c\preccurlyeq e. If b\approx c, then d\approx e by invariance. Either way d\preccurlyeq e, so e is a pivot.
  • Let Z be a chain of pivots with supremum s, and let Mb, b\prec s and (Fb)d. Then Ms, since M is closed. Some z with Zz has z\not\preccurlyeq b; otherwise b, which is in X, would bound Z, giving s\preccurlyeq b and contradicting b\prec s. Take e with (Fz)e. By Claim 1 for z and e, either b\preccurlyeq z or e\preccurlyeq b. The second would give z\preccurlyeq e\preccurlyeq b. So b\prec z, and d\preccurlyeq z\preccurlyeq s, as z is a pivot.

  1. Let Mb, Mc and (Fb)d. By Claim 2, b is a pivot. By Claim 1, applied to b, d and c, either c\preccurlyeq b or d\preccurlyeq c. In the second case b\preccurlyeq d\preccurlyeq c. So any two members of M are comparable. If b\prec c, then c\not\preccurlyeq b, and so d\preccurlyeq c.

  2. M is a chain included in X, so it has a supremum. Let m be one. Then Mm, since M is closed. If (Fm)n, then Mn, so n\preccurlyeq m; and m\preccurlyeq n, as F is progressive. So n\approx m. \square

The tower also supports induction: to show that every member of M has a property, show that the members of M having it form a closed property.

Lemma (the Bourbaki–Witt lemma for admissible chains)

The Bourbaki–Witt lemma has a variant for the case where only some chains are known to have suprema. These are the chains singled out by a property \mathcal A^{(\sigma t)t}, the admissible properties. Take X, R and F as there, and change it as follows.

  • Hypothesis 2 is required only for admissible chains: \forall Z\, .\,\mathcal AZ\land Z\subseteq X\land\operatorname{Total}(R,Z)\to\exists s\, .\,\operatorname{Sup}(s,Z).
  • In the definition of closed, the clause for suprema is likewise restricted to admissible Z. The tower quantifies only over admissible closed properties: M:=\lambda x\, .\,\forall Y\, .\,\mathcal AY\land\operatorname{Closed}(Y)\to Yx.
  • There is a new hypothesis. Each of the properties that the proof forms must be coextensive with an admissible property:
    • X;
    • M;
    • the property of being a pivot;
    • each M_{c,e} of Claim 1.

Conclusion (a) becomes: M is closed, and M\subseteq Y for every admissible closed Y. Conclusions (b) and (c) are unchanged.

The proof is the same. Two facts let it go through:

  • closedness depends only on a property’s actual extension;
  • the new hypothesis brings each property the proof forms within the scope of (a).

With \mathcal A:=\lambda Z\, .\,\top this is the original lemma.

Only the actual extensions of admissible properties matter, so two predicates with the same admissible extensions give the same lemma.

background_pages.title: Cardinality, arithmetic and analysis
background_pages.html:
The Axiom of Infinity is stated with Frege’s cardinality apparatus. At a type \sigma, a cardinality is an entity of type (\sigma t)t, and:

\begin{aligned} \mathbf{0}_\sigma&:=\lambda X^{\sigma t}\, .\,\forall u^\sigma\, .\,\neg Xu,\\ \operatorname{Suc}_\sigma(Z)&:=\lambda X^{\sigma t}\, .\,\exists y^\sigma\, .\, Xy\land Z(\lambda u^\sigma\, .\,Xu\land u\ne y),\\ \operatorname{FiniteCardinality}_\sigma(Z)&:=\forall W^{((\sigma t)t)t}\, .\, \bigl(W\mathbf{0}_\sigma\land\forall Y\, .\,WY\to W(\operatorname{Suc}_\sigma Y)\bigr)\to WZ. \end{aligned}

So \mathbf{0}_\sigma is the cardinality of the empty property, \operatorname{Suc}_\sigma adds one to a cardinality, and \operatorname{FiniteCardinality}_\sigma collects the cardinalities reached from \mathbf{0}_\sigma by finitely many successors, in the impredicative sense that they fall under every property of cardinalities that holds of \mathbf{0}_\sigma and of a successor whenever it holds of the cardinality succeeded. In C, \mathbf{0}_\sigma and the successor of a finite cardinality are finite cardinalities, and a finite cardinality that holds of a property holds of every property coextensive with it . Every type used here ends in t, so all of them are admitted, and no type \sigma\sigma is needed; that is why the axiom is not put in the Dedekind form, which would ask for an injective non-surjective operation from \sigma to \sigma.

Countable Boolean Completeness and the Necessity of Arithmetic follow Goodsell, Arithmetic is Necessary, which leaves the type \nu of numbers, zero and successor as parameters. The map takes them, at each type \sigma, to be \nu_\sigma:=(\sigma t)t, \mathbf{0}_\sigma and \operatorname{Suc}_\sigma, and states both principles as schemata in \sigma; the paper displays the instance \sigma=e in its eqs. (24)–(25) without assuming it. Natural numberhood \mathbb N_\sigma is then \operatorname{FiniteCardinality}_\sigma. Write \forall n\in\mathbb N_\sigma\, .\,A for \forall n^{\nu_\sigma}\, .\,\mathbb N_\sigma n\to A, and likewise for \exists. With these, for a type \sigma and a relational type \tau:

\begin{aligned} \operatorname{Ctbl}_{\sigma,\tau}(X)&:=\exists R^{\tau\nu_\sigma t}\, .\,\forall y^\tau z^\tau\, .\, Xy\land Xz\to\bigl((\exists n\in\mathbb N_\sigma\, .\,Ryn\land Rzn)\leftrightarrow y=z\bigr),\\ I^*_\sigma&:=\forall m\,n\in\mathbb N_\sigma\, .\,\mathbf{0}_\sigma\ne\operatorname{Suc}_\sigma m\land (\operatorname{Suc}_\sigma m=\operatorname{Suc}_\sigma n\to m=n),\qquad I_\sigma:=\Diamond I^*_\sigma,\\ \operatorname{Sum}_\sigma(m,n,o)&:=\forall R^{\nu_\sigma\nu_\sigma t}\, .\,R\mathbf{0}_\sigma m\to (\forall i\,j\in\mathbb N_\sigma\, .\,Rij\to R(\operatorname{Suc}_\sigma i)(\operatorname{Suc}_\sigma j))\to Rno,\\ \operatorname{Prod}_\sigma(m,n,o)&:=\forall R^{\nu_\sigma\nu_\sigma t}\, .\,R\mathbf{0}_\sigma\mathbf{0}_\sigma\to (\forall i\,j\,k\in\mathbb N_\sigma\, .\,Rij\to\operatorname{Sum}_\sigma(m,j,k)\to R(\operatorname{Suc}_\sigma i)k)\to Rno. \end{aligned}

So X is countable (relative to \sigma) when it injects into the natural numbers counted at \sigma, and I_\sigma says that possibly zero is not a successor and successor is injective on numbers. In C the first conjunct of I^*_\sigma is a theorem, since \mathbf{0}_\sigma and a successor differ at \lambda x^\sigma\, .\,\bot. An arithmetical sentence at \sigma is a closed formula built from atomic formulas \mathbb N_\sigma\mathbf n, \operatorname{Sum}_\sigma(\mathbf m,\mathbf n,\mathbf o), \operatorname{Prod}_\sigma(\mathbf m,\mathbf n,\mathbf o) and \mathbf m=\mathbf n, whose terms are variables of type \nu_\sigma, \mathbf{0}_\sigma and successors of terms, by \neg, \lor, \land and quantifiers \forall v\in\mathbb N_\sigma. These are Definitions 3–8 of Goodsell’s draft. Where the type is fixed by context the subscript \sigma is dropped.

Analysis. A real number structure at a type \sigma is a tuple \mathfrak R=(X^{\sigma t},\le^{\sigma\sigma t},+^{\sigma\sigma\sigma t}, \times^{\sigma\sigma\sigma t},0^\sigma,1^\sigma,N^{\sigma t}) such that \le, + and \times hold only of instances of X, X with them and with 0 and 1 is a complete ordered field, + and \times being functional on X and every nonempty subproperty of X with an upper bound in X having a least upper bound in X, and N is the least subproperty of X containing 0 and closed under adding 1; write \operatorname{Real}_\sigma(\mathfrak R). Any two real number structures, at one type or at two, are isomorphic (Huntington), a theorem of the non-modal fragment. A first-order analytical sentence is a closed formula in the variables of a real number structure built from the atomic formulas x\le y, +(x,y,z), \times(x,y,z), Nx and x=y, whose terms are variables of type \sigma, 0 and 1, by \neg, \lor, \land and quantifiers \forall v\in X; a second-order analytical sentence may also use variables R for relations of any finite arity among entities of type \sigma, in atomic formulas R\bar x and unrestricted quantifiers \forall R. For a sentence A, A(\mathfrak R) is its reading in \mathfrak R. These follow Barton and Goodsell, Continuum Contingency, §5.7, with the structure’s elements in place of their rigid properties of numbers, and Bacon’s second-order analysis (Could the truths of mathematics have been different?, Appendix C.2) without his restriction of the second-order quantifiers to rigid properties, which makes no difference under Rigid Comprehension (his Proposition C.3). The continuum hypothesis \operatorname{CH}(\mathfrak R) is the second-order analytical sentence \forall Y^{\sigma t}\, .\,(\forall x\, .\,Yx\to Xx)\to (Y\precsim N\lor Y\approx X), where Y\precsim Z says that some relation is an injection from the Ys into the Zs and Y\approx Z that some relation is a bijection between them. A real number structure is rigid, \operatorname{RigidStr}(\mathfrak R), when X, \le, +, \times and N are rigid and the instances of X are necessarily distinct, \forall x\,y\in X\, .\,x\ne y\to\Box\,x\ne y. A represented power of arity k for X, \operatorname{RepPower}_k(\mathcal P,X), is a rigid property \mathcal P of rigid k-ary relations holding only of tuples of instances of X, such that necessarily every k-ary relation agrees on such tuples with an instance of \mathcal P: \operatorname{Rigid}(\mathcal P)\land (\forall S\, .\,\mathcal PS\to\operatorname{Rigid}(S)\land\forall\bar y\, .\,S\bar y\to\textstyle\bigwedge_iXy_i)\land \Box\forall R\,\exists S\, .\,\mathcal PS\land\forall\bar x\in X\, .\,(S\bar x\leftrightarrow R\bar x).

The schematic \sigma is what lets the principles say what they intend whatever the size of a given type. Where \sigma necessarily has only finitely many members, \mathbb N_\sigma is finite, a property countable relative to \sigma is finite and so has a least upper bound in C, and I_\sigma is necessarily false; those instances are trivial.

background_pages.title: Signatures and sentence schemata
background_pages.html: Pure and signature schemata. In Maximalism, in its distinctness form and its possibility form alike, C denotes the fixed background logic. Its theoremhood and consistency side conditions are retained literally. “Pure” means free of nonlogical constants. The principles in the Signature schemata group give a special role to nonlogical constants: they concern an arbitrary fixed signature \Sigma of nonlogical constants of admitted types, with \mathcal L(\Sigma) and C(\Sigma) the language and background theory over \Sigma. When \Sigma is empty, some of these schemata have no instances or only trivial ones, and the others reduce to their pure versions; the results relating them need a constant of a type \tau\ne e, so \Sigma is assumed to contain one. Nothing further is assumed: no nonlogical axioms about the constants are standing assumptions, and “distinct constants” means distinct symbols, not an assumed inequality between their denotations. Where a schema mentions a tuple of distinct constants, its instances are those the signature supplies.

background_pages.title: The Lean formalisation
background_pages.html:
The map’s Lean project formalises C in base Lean 4 and checks many of the map’s claims. A Lean ✓ on a result, on a model’s verdict, or on a lemma on these pages means that a proof has passed an audit. This page says what each audit establishes. The project’s own README has the details.

Classicism as a theory in Lean

The shallow layer treats C as a theory in Lean itself. Individuals form a type e, Prop plays the role of t, and the classes Ty and Rel mark the Lean types that are types of the relational type system and the relational types among them. \Box p is p=\top, as on .

Lean’s rules for the connectives, the quantifiers and identity are the rules of H, short of two things that the library adds as axioms: excluded middle (em) and the existence of an individual (e_exists). Lean’s own three axioms are principles of the map, and none is a theorem of C:

Lean axiom Principle on the map
propext Fregean Axiom
funext Functionality
Classical.choice Functional Choice, and more

The rule of Logical Equivalence is rendered as a restriction on the first two, the gate: propext h and funext h may appear only when the proof h is closed, using no hypothesis. Applied to a closed proof they are exactly the rules C is closed under; applied to a hypothesis they would be the Fregean Axiom and Functionality. #classicism_check audits a shallow proof: it rests only on propext, funext, e, e_exists and em, and it passes the gate. It also reports whether the proof avoids e_exists, and so is a theorem of C⁻, the theory without Existence at e.

No formula quantifies over types. A principle is a family of formulas indexed by types, and a lemma is a theorem with type parameters, a schema in the sense of the conventions.

Lemmas on these pages

A lemma’s Lean ✓ badge opens a menu linking the shallow theorems that prove it. The ✓ means that each of them passes #classicism_check, and the menu says whether the lemma is a theorem of C or of C⁻. A badge in the running text, after a claim such as “\le_\tau is a partial order”, opens the same kind of menu for the theorems that prove that claim. Shallow proofs elsewhere in the library use these theorems directly. Whether a Lean statement says what the prose says is checked by reading the two together.

Results and their certificates

The metalogical layer makes the object language into Lean data: terms over a signature, derivability in C, and models. A result A_1,\ldots,A_n\Rightarrow B is stated, by a statement generated from the records, as an entailment between schemas: for every admitted signature \Sigma and every set of sentences over \Sigma, if it entails each A_i then it entails B. An incompatibility concludes instead that the set is inconsistent. Each principle’s schema comes from its record’s Lean definition.

A result’s certificate usually comes from a shallow proof, which a translator turns into a derivation in the object language. Stating results metalogically lets ordinary principles, schematic only in their types, be treated like the principles whose instances are sentences picked out by a condition on syntax, such as No Pure Contingency and Maximalism, which no shallow formula with type parameters can state. lean-check confirms that each certificate proves its generated statement in ordinary classical Lean, the metatheory, with no sorry.

Models

A model’s verdict is stated as the existence of a consistent, complete theory, deciding every sentence, that entails the principles the model satisfies and none of those it violates. The proof constructs the model, an action model or another of the map’s constructions, and applies the soundness theorem.

The strict layer

A third layer re-proves the shallow theorems from the eleven closed identities of Classicism, carrying out its Appendix A on Lean proof terms. It explores how the paper’s type system sits inside Lean’s and is not on the route to any certificate.

Where things are

What Where in the Lean project
The language, the gate, the axioms Classicism/Core.lean, Equivalence.lean
The lemmas of these pages, a module per page Classicism/Background/
The map’s principles Classicism/Principles/
The shallow proofs of results Classicism/Results/Records/
The object language and its models Classicism/Syntax/, Classicism/Semantics/, Classicism/Models/
The certificates Classicism/Map.lean, MapModels.lean, MapDerived.lean, MapArguments.lean
The statements they prove Classicism/Statements.lean, ModelStatements.lean, generated from the records
