background_items.title: common shorthands
background_items.body:
For relations $X,Y$ of a type $\bar\sigma t$, and the evaluation point unless a box is
written:

- $X\subseteq Y$ (*$X$ is included in $Y$*, a *subrelation* of $Y$) abbreviates
  $\forall\bar z\, .\,X[\bar z]\to Y[\bar z]$; this is actual inclusion, and
  $X\le Y$ is $\Box(X\subseteq Y)$ ([[order]]).
- $X\equiv Y$ (*$X$ and $Y$ are coextensive*) abbreviates
  $\forall\bar z\, .\,X[\bar z]\leftrightarrow Y[\bar z]$. In C coextensive relations are
  identical only when necessarily coextensive ([[intensionality-r|Intensionality]]).
- For the empty tuple, at type $t$, $p\subseteq q$ is $p\to q$ and $p\equiv q$ is
  $p\leftrightarrow q$. In Lean these are the notations `X ⊆ Y` and `X ≡ Y`, defined
  pointwise at every relational type.
- $\top_\tau$ and $\bot_\tau$, at a relational type $\tau=\bar\sigma t$, are
  $\lambda\bar x\, .\,\top$ and $\lambda\bar x\, .\,\bot$, the top and bottom of $\le_\tau$.
- $H_{\bar x}:=\lambda\bar y\, .\,\bar y=\bar x$ is the *haecceity* of $\bar x$, the
  property of being $\bar x$.
- $X-y:=\lambda u\, .\,Xu\land u\ne y$ is $X$ without $y$.
- $\exists!x\, .\,\varphi$ abbreviates
  $\exists x\, .\,\varphi\land\forall x'\, .\,\varphi[x'/x]\to x'=x$.
- For a relation $R^{\sigma\sigma t}$ given as an order, $x\preccurlyeq y$ is $(Rx)y$, and
  $x\prec y$ is $x\preccurlyeq y\land x\ne y$.
- $\bigwedge_{i<j\le n}x_i\ne x_j$ is the finite conjunction of the displayed
  distinctness claims, saying that $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ are pairwise distinct.

background_items.title: Existence
background_items.credit: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr
sources: Classicism, §1.1, p. 7
background_items.body:
Every type is inhabited: $\exists x^\sigma\, .\,x=x$.

*Proof.* Reflexivity gives $y=y$, and existential introduction yields
$\exists x\, .\,x=x$ at each admitted type; equivalently, use the β and EG derivation
on p. 7.

*Polyadic form.* $\exists\bar x^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,\bar x=\bar x$, the conjunction of the
original at each $\sigma_i$; for the empty tuple it is $\top$.

background_items.title: Ordinary Comprehension
background_items.credit: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr
sources: Classicism
background_items.body:
Every well-typed formula $P$ with distinguished variables $\bar y$ defines a coextensive
relation:
$\exists X\, .\,\forall\bar y\, .\,X[\bar y]\leftrightarrow P$, for $X$ not free in $P$, any
other free object variables being universally closed.

*Proof.* The λ-term $\lambda\bar y\, .\,P$ is a witness: β-conversion makes its
application equivalent to $P$ at each tuple, and existential introduction supplies the
instance.

The schema is in a formula, which no Lean statement with type parameters can quantify
over. The Lean theorems state, for zero, one and two distinguished variables, that every
relation $P$ is coextensive with some $X$; each instance of the schema is the theorem at
the λ-term $\lambda\bar y\, .\,P$, which is how the object language proves it.

background_items.title: necessity and possibility
background_items.body: Put $\Box p:=(p=\top)$ and $\Diamond p:=(p\ne\bot)$.

background_items.title: K
background_items.credit: Andrew Bacon (Classicism credits the S4 result to Bacon 2018)
sources: Classicism, §1.5, p. 16
background_items.body:
Necessity distributes over implication:
$\forall p q\, .\,\Box(p\to q)\to(\Box p\to\Box q)$.

*Proof.* In the Boolean algebra of propositions, $\Box(p\to q)$ says that the
implication is $\top$. Together with $p=\top$, substitution and the Boolean identities
identify $q$ with $\top$.

*Dual form.* $\forall p q\, .\,\Box(p\to q)\to(\Diamond p\to\Diamond q)$. Instantiate
either form at $\neg q,\neg p$ and contrapose the inner conditional, using
$\Box(\neg q\to\neg p)\leftrightarrow\Box(p\to q)$ and $\Diamond=\neg\Box\neg$.

background_items.title: T
background_items.credit: Andrew Bacon (Classicism credits the S4 result to Bacon 2018)
sources: Classicism, §1.5, p. 16
background_items.body:
Necessary propositions are true: $\forall p\, .\,\Box p\to p$.

*Proof.* If $p=\top$, identity elimination and the truth of $\top$ give $p$.

*Dual form.* Every truth is possible: $\forall p\, .\,p\to\Diamond p$, by contraposition
and $\Diamond=\neg\Box\neg$.

background_items.credit: Andrew Bacon (Classicism credits the S4 result to Bacon 2018)
sources: Classicism, §1.5, p. 17
background_items.body:
Necessary propositions are necessarily necessary: $\forall p\, .\,\Box p\to\Box\Box p$.

*Proof.* Apply [[identity-necessary-r|NI]] to the identity $p=\top$. Its conclusion is
$\Box(p=\top)$, which is $\Box\Box p$.

*Dual form.* Whatever is possibly possible is possible:
$\forall p\, .\,\Diamond\Diamond p\to\Diamond p$, by contraposition and
$\Diamond=\neg\Box\neg$.

background_items.title: Necessity of Identity (NI)
background_items.credit: W. V. Quine (historical attribution in Classicism, p. 22)
sources: Classicism, §2.1, p. 22
background_items.body:
Identity is necessary at every type: $\forall x y^\sigma\, .\,x=y\to\Box(x=y)$.

*Proof.* Reflexivity is a theorem, so its necessitation gives $\Box(x=x)$. Leibniz's
Law substitutes $y$ for the second $x$ under the premise $x=y$, giving $\Box(x=y)$.

*Polyadic form.* $\forall\bar x\,\bar y^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,\bar x=\bar y\to\Box(\bar x=\bar y)$:
$\bar x=\bar y$ is a conjunction of identities, each necessary, and a conjunction of
necessities is necessary.

background_items.title: Converse Barcan Formula (CBF)
background_items.credit: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr
sources: Classicism, §1.5, p. 19
background_items.body:
$\forall X^{\sigma t}\, .\,\Box(\forall x^\sigma\, .\,Xx)\to(\forall x^\sigma\, .\,\Box Xx)$.

*Proof.* Necessitate universal instantiation and use [[modal-k|K]] to obtain
$\Box(\forall x\, .\,Xx)\to\Box Xx$. Generalize $x$, preserving the side condition.

*Other forms.* The polyadic form,
$\forall X^{\bar\sigma t}\, .\,\Box(\forall\bar x\, .\,X[\bar x])\to(\forall\bar x\, .\,\Box X[\bar x])$,
follows by instantiating one variable at a time. The dual form says that if something
possibly has a property, then possibly something has it:
$\forall X^{\sigma t}\, .\,(\exists x\, .\,\Diamond Xx)\to\Diamond(\exists x\, .\,Xx)$,
and likewise for tuples; each comes from the corresponding form by contraposition and
$\Diamond=\neg\Box\neg$.

background_items.title: Broad Necessitism
background_items.credit: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr
sources: Classicism, §1.5
background_items.body:
Every entity of a type is necessarily identical to something:
$\forall x^\sigma\, .\,\Box(\exists y^\sigma\, .\,y=x)$.

*Proof.* The theorem $\forall x\, .\,\exists y\, .\,y=x$ can be necessitated, and
[[converse-barcan-r|CBF]] gives $\forall x\, .\,\Box\exists y\, .\,y=x$.

*Polyadic form.* $\forall\bar x^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,\Box(\exists\bar y^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,\bar y=\bar x)$,
taking $\bar y:=\bar x$ coordinatewise.

background_items.title: Intensionality
background_items.credit: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr
sources: Classicism, §1.5, pp. 17–18
background_items.body:
Necessarily coextensive relations are identical:
$\forall X Y^{\bar\sigma t}\, .\,\Box(X\equiv Y)\to X=Y$.

*Proof.* Logical Equivalence identifies the λ-abstractions of
$X[\bar z]\land(X\equiv Y)$ and of the analogous
expression with $Y$ in the first conjunct. If the biconditional is necessary,
substitute its identity with $\top$ into the abstraction identity. Boolean identities
and β-η conversion leave $X=Y$, as on p. 17.

background_items.title: Modalized Fregean Axiom
background_items.credit: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr
sources: Classicism, §1.5, p. 18
background_items.body:
Necessarily equivalent propositions are identical:
$\forall p q\, .\,\Box(p\leftrightarrow q)\to p=q$.

*Proof.* The nullary instance of [[intensionality-r|Intensionality]]: necessary
equivalence identifies $p\leftrightarrow q$ with $\top$, and the Boolean identities then
identify $p$ and $q$.

background_items.title: Modalized Functionality
background_items.credit: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr
sources: Classicism, §1.5, n. 22
background_items.body:
Necessarily co-functional operations are identical:
$\forall X Y^{\sigma\tau}\, .\,\Box(\forall z^\sigma\, .\,Xz=Yz)\to X=Y\qquad(\tau\ne e)$.

*Proof.* From boxed pointwise identity, identity elimination gives boxed agreement after
applying every remaining argument of the relational output type; quantification over
those arguments is inside the necessary implication. [[intensionality-r|Intensionality]]
and η-conversion identify the operations. This relies on the output type's ending in $t$.

*Polyadic form.* $\forall X Y^{\bar\sigma\tau}\, .\,\Box(\forall\bar z\, .\,X[\bar z]=Y[\bar z])\to X=Y$
$(\tau\ne e)$, one argument at a time, with the box carried through.

background_items.title: lattice predicates
background_items.body:
The lattice predicates used in the principles are:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{LB}_\tau(y,X)&:=\forall z^\tau\, .\,Xz\to y\le_\tau z,\\
\operatorname{GLB}_\tau(y,X)&:=\forall z^\tau\, .\,
  \operatorname{LB}_\tau(z,X)\leftrightarrow z\le_\tau y,\\
\operatorname{UB}_\tau(y,X)&:=\forall z^\tau\, .\,Xz\to z\le_\tau y,\\
\operatorname{LUB}_\tau(y,X)&:=\forall z^\tau\, .\,
  \operatorname{UB}_\tau(z,X)\leftrightarrow y\le_\tau z,\\
\operatorname{Atom}_\tau(y)&:=\forall z^\tau\, .\,
  (z\le_\tau y\land z\ne y)\leftrightarrow z\le_\tau\neg_\tau z.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus an atom is non-bottom {lean: Classicism.not_le_neg_of_atom, Classicism.atom_ne_false} and has no
non-bottom strict lower bound.
$\operatorname{LB}$, $\operatorname{GLB}$ and $\operatorname{Atom}$ are the definitions of
*Classicism*, §2.2, pp. 23–24; $\operatorname{UB}$ and $\operatorname{LUB}$ are their duals.

background_items.title: greatest lower bounds and least upper bounds
background_items.body:
At a relational type $\tau$, the negation of a least upper bound of $X$ is a greatest lower
bound of the negations of the members of $X$, and conversely:
$\operatorname{GLB}_\tau(\neg_\tau y,\lambda w\, .\,X(\neg_\tau w))\leftrightarrow
\operatorname{LUB}_\tau(y,X)$.

*Proof.* Negation reverses $\le_\tau$, since necessary pointwise implication contraposes, and
$\neg_\tau\neg_\tau z=z$ by [[intensionality-r|Intensionality]]
{lean: Classicism.neg_le_neg_rel, Classicism.neg_neg_rel}. Hence $z\le_\tau\neg_\tau y$ iff
$y\le_\tau\neg_\tau z$, and $z$ is a lower bound of the negations of the members of $X$ iff
$\neg_\tau z$ is an upper bound of $X$. So the lower bounds of $\lambda w\, .\,X(\neg_\tau w)$
are exactly the entities below $\neg_\tau y$ iff the upper bounds of $X$ are exactly the
entities above $y$. $\square$

background_items.title: strong atoms
background_items.body:
At a relational type $\sigma$, with $\Diamond_\sigma X:=X\ne\bot_\sigma$, a *strong atom* is a
possible entity that necessarily entails every entity of its type or its negation:

$$
\operatorname{SAtom}_\sigma(W):=\Diamond_\sigma W\land\Box\forall Y^\sigma\, .\,
  W\le_\sigma Y\lor W\le_\sigma\neg_\sigma Y.
$$

Bacon, *A Philosophical Introduction to Higher-Order Logics*, §8.2, pp. 165–166, calls these
*strong worlds*; dropping the box gives his *weak worlds*, which are just the atoms. The map
avoids the word "world" for them, since at types other than $t$ they are not world-like.

background_items.title: self-atoms
background_items.credit: Cian Dorr, 25 October 2026
background_items.body:
A *self-atom* is a possible entity that is necessarily an atom whenever it is instantiated:

$$
\operatorname{SelfAtom}_\sigma(X):=\Diamond_\sigma X\land
  \Box\bigl(\exists\bar x\, .\,X\bar x\to\operatorname{Atom}_\sigma(X)\bigr),
\qquad
\operatorname{SelfAtom}_t(p):=\Diamond p\land\Box\bigl(p\to\operatorname{Atom}_t(p)\bigr).
$$

background_items.title: persistence, inextensibility and rigidity
background_items.body:
For a relation $Y$ with a finite argument tuple, including the empty tuple,
the comprehension predicates are:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Persistent}(Y)&:=Y\le\lambda\bar x\, .\,\Box Y[\bar x],\\
\operatorname{Inextensible}(Y)&:=\Box\forall X\, .\,
  (\forall\bar x\, .\,Y[\bar x]\to\Box X[\bar x])\to Y\le X,\\
\operatorname{Rigid}(Y)&:=\operatorname{Persistent}(Y)\land
  \operatorname{Inextensible}(Y).
\end{aligned}
$$

background_items.title: the weak variants
background_items.body:
Since $Y\le Z$ is itself the necessary universal closure of the pointwise
implication, $\operatorname{Persistent}(Y)$ unpacks as
$\Box\forall\bar x\, .\,Y[\bar x]\to\Box Y[\bar x]$, and both
conjuncts of $\operatorname{Rigid}$ carry a leading $\Box$. Dropping it
gives the weak variants:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{WeaklyPersistent}(Y)&:=\forall\bar x\, .\,
  Y[\bar x]\to\Box Y[\bar x],\\
\operatorname{WeaklyInextensible}(Y)&:=\forall X\, .\,
  (\forall\bar x\, .\,Y[\bar x]\to\Box X[\bar x])\to Y\le X,\\
\operatorname{WeaklyRigid}(Y)&:=\operatorname{WeaklyPersistent}(Y)\land
  \operatorname{WeaklyInextensible}(Y).
\end{aligned}
$$

background_items.title: rigidity, if true, is necessary
background_items.body:
If $X$ is rigid, then $\Box\operatorname{Rigid}(X)$.

*Proof.* $\operatorname{Rigid}(X)$ is $\Box\operatorname{WeaklyRigid}(X)$, and
[[modal-four|4]] gives $\Box\Box\operatorname{WeaklyRigid}(X)$, which is
$\Box\operatorname{Rigid}(X)$. $\square$

background_items.title: weakly rigid relations are persistent
sources: Dorr, Boolean Completeness does not imply Rigid Comprehension, draft of 30 July 2026
background_items.body:
A weakly rigid relation is persistent: weak
inextensibility applied to $\lambda\bar x\, .\,\Box Y[\bar x]$, whose
hypothesis $Y[\bar x]\to\Box\Box Y[\bar x]$ holds by weak persistence and 4,
gives $Y\le\lambda\bar x\, .\,\Box Y[\bar x]$. So weak rigidity is equivalently
persistence together with weak inextensibility, the combination used in the
draft's Proposition 1.

background_items.title: coextensive weakly rigid relations are identical
background_items.body:
If $F$ and $G$ are weakly rigid and coextensive, then $F=G$.

*Proof.* Each is below the other: $F\le G$ by weak inextensibility of $F$, since each
instance of $F$ is an instance of $G$ and so, by weak persistence of $G$, necessarily one;
and $G\le F$ likewise. Since $\le$ is antisymmetric, $F=G$. $\square$

background_items.title: haecceities are rigid
background_items.credit: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), prompted by Daniel Kodsi, 22 October 2026
background_items.body:
For every $x^\sigma$, the haecceity $H_x=\lambda y\, .\,y=x$ is rigid.

*Proof.* It is persistent by [[identity-necessary-r|NI]]. For inextensibility, suppose,
at any world, that $\forall y\, .\,y=x\to\Box Zy$. Then $\Box Zx$, and so
$\Box\forall y\, .\,y=x\to Zy$, which is $H_x\le Z$. $\square$

background_items.title: rigid unions of rigid families
background_items.credit: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), prompted by Daniel Kodsi, 22 October 2026
background_items.body:
If $R^{\sigma t}$ is rigid and $F^{\sigma\tau t}$ is such that $Fx$ is rigid for every $x$
with $Rx$, then the union $U:=\lambda y\, .\,\exists x\, .\,Rx\land(Fx)y$ is rigid.

*Proof.* First, necessarily every instance of $R$ has a rigid fiber. For each $x$ with
$Rx$, $Fx$ is rigid and so, by [[rigid-necessary]], necessarily rigid; so by the
inextensibility of $R$, $R\le\lambda x\, .\,\operatorname{Rigid}(Fx)$. Now argue at an
arbitrary world, where $R$ is weakly rigid and each instance of $R$ has a rigid fiber.
*Weak persistence:* if $Uy$, take $x$ with $Rx$ and $(Fx)y$; then $\Box Rx$ and
$\Box(Fx)y$, so $\Box Uy$. *Weak inextensibility:* suppose $\forall y\, .\,Uy\to\Box Zy$.
For each $x$ with $Rx$, $\forall y\, .\,(Fx)y\to\Box Zy$, so $Fx\le Z$ by the
inextensibility of $Fx$; that is, $\Box(\forall y\, .\,(Fx)y\to Zy)$. By the weak
inextensibility of $R$, $R\le\lambda x\, .\,\forall y\, .\,(Fx)y\to Zy$, which gives
$U\le Z$. Both hold at every world, so $U$ is rigid. $\square$

background_items.title: rigidity is preserved by direct images
background_items.credit: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), prompted by Daniel Kodsi, 22 October 2026
background_items.body:
If $R^{\sigma t}$ is rigid and $f^{\sigma\tau}$ is an operation ($\tau\ne e$), then
$\lambda y\, .\,\exists x\, .\,Rx\land y=fx$ is rigid.

*Proof.* It is the union of the haecceities $H_{fx}$ over the instances of $R$, rigid by
[[haecceities-rigid]] and [[rigid-indexed-union]]. $\square$

background_items.title: rigidity is preserved by inverse images under necessarily injective operations
background_items.credit: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), prompted by Daniel Kodsi, 22 October 2026
background_items.body:
If $P^{\tau t}$ is rigid, every instance of $P$ is a value of $f^{\sigma\tau}$
($\tau\ne e$), and $f$ is necessarily injective, then $\lambda x\, .\,P(fx)$ is rigid.

*Proof.* Persistence is inherited from $P$. Being a value of $f$ is necessary if true, by
[[identity-necessary-r|NI]], so the inextensibility of $P$ makes every instance of $P$
necessarily a value of $f$. For inextensibility, suppose, at a world,
that $\forall x\, .\,P(fx)\to\Box Zx$, and put $Z':=\lambda y\, .\,\forall x\, .\,y=fx\to Zx$.
If $Py$, then $y=fx_0$ for some $x_0$, so $\Box Zx_0$; since $f$ is necessarily injective,
necessarily every $x$ with $fx=fx_0$ is $x_0$, so $\Box Z'y$. By the inextensibility of
$P$, $P\le Z'$, and so $\Box\forall x\, .\,P(fx)\to Zx$. Both the range condition and
injectivity keep their modal scopes. $\square$

background_items.title: properties of operators
sources: The Bounds of Possibility, Appendix D, p. 400 and p. 407
background_items.body:
For $X^{tt}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm N\,X&:=\forall p\, .\,\Box p\to Xp, &
\mathrm K\,X&:=\forall p\,q\, .\,X(p\to q)\to Xp\to Xq,\\
\mathrm J\,X&:=\forall p\, .\,p\to X\Diamond p, &
\mathrm F_{\langle\rangle}X&:=\forall Y^{tt}\, .\,(\forall z\, .\,X(Yz))\to X\forall z\, .\,Yz,
\end{aligned}
$$

and NK, NKJ and NKJF$_{\langle\rangle}$ are the conjunctions; F$_{\langle\rangle}$ is BF
for $X$ at type $t$. The appendix's 5-necessity is
$\Box_5^{\mathrm A}:=\lambda p\, .\,\forall X\, .\,\Box\,\mathrm{NKJF}_{\langle\rangle}X\to Xp$,
and $W_@a:=a\land\forall q\, .\,q\to\Box(a\to q)$ says that $a$ is the actual world.

background_items.title: D1, at type $t$
background_items.credit: Cian Dorr, John Hawthorne and Juhani Yli-Vakkuri
sources: The Bounds of Possibility, Appendix D
background_items.body:
If $X$ is NKJ, then $y
e z	o X(y
e z)$ for $y,z$ of type $t$, and dually
$
eg X
eg(y=z)	o y=z$.

*Proof.* J gives $X\Diamond(y
e z)$, and necessarily $\Diamond(y
e z)	o y
e z$
{lean: Classicism.ne_of_dia_ne}, so N and K give $X(y
e z)$. $\square$

background_items.title: D14 and D15, the second at type $t$
background_items.credit: Cian Dorr, John Hawthorne and Juhani Yli-Vakkuri
sources: The Bounds of Possibility, Appendix D
background_items.body:
If $\Box\,\mathrm{NK}\,X$ then $\Box\,\mathrm{NKJ}\,\hat X$ (D14); and if
$\Box\,\mathrm{NKJF}_{\langle\rangle}X$ then $\Box\,\mathrm{NKJF}_{\langle\rangle}\hat X$ (D14
with D15).

*Proof of F$_{\langle\rangle}$ for $\hat X$.* Given $\forall z\, .\,\hat X(Yz)$, the witness is
$q:=\forall z\, .\,\hat X(Yz)$: necessarily, $\neg X\neg q$ gives $\neg X\neg\hat X(Yz)$ for each
$z$, by N and K, and hence $Yz$, by [[appendix-d-d12|D12]]. $\square$

background_items.title: D16, the parts the map needs
background_items.credit: Cian Dorr, John Hawthorne and Juhani Yli-Vakkuri
sources: The Bounds of Possibility, Appendix D
background_items.body:
$\Box_5^{\mathrm A}$ is N, K and B, necessarily, so it is an S5 operator; hence
$\Box_5\le\Box_5^{\mathrm A}$.

*Proof of B.* For $X$ with $\Box\,\mathrm{NKJF}_{\langle\rangle}X$, [[appendix-d-d12|D12]] gives
$X\neg\hat X\neg p$ from $p$; and $\hat X$ is necessarily NKJF$_{\langle\rangle}$
([[appendix-d-d14-d15]]), so necessarily $\Box_5^{\mathrm A}\neg p\to\hat X\neg p$. $\square$

background_items.title: relativization, as in Proposition D8
background_items.credit: Cian Dorr, John Hawthorne and Juhani Yli-Vakkuri
sources: The Bounds of Possibility, Appendix D
background_items.body:
For any $X$, $\lambda r\, .\,\mathrm{NKJF}_{\langle\rangle}X\to Xr$ is NKJF$_{\langle\rangle}$
outright, and so necessarily. So whatever is $\Box_5^{\mathrm A}$ is $X$ wherever $X$ is
NKJF$_{\langle\rangle}$.

background_items.title: D18 and D19, at the actual world
background_items.credit: Cian Dorr, John Hawthorne and Juhani Yli-Vakkuri
sources: The Bounds of Possibility, Appendix D, p. 407
background_items.body:
Suppose $W_@a$ at the world of evaluation. If $\Box\,\mathrm{NK}\,X$, then
$\hat Xp\to\Box(\neg X\neg a\to p)$ (D18, left to right); and if $\Box\,\mathrm{NKJ}\,X$, then
F$_{\langle\rangle}\hat X$ (D19). The appendix assumes $\mathrm H_{S5R}$, used only for
$\Box$Actuality; here the witness $W_@a$ is needed at the world of evaluation only, as the
map's records need.

background_items.title: the Barcan formula for 5-necessity
background_items.credit: Cian Dorr, with help from GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), 29 October 2026
background_items.body:
At every type $\sigma$, C proves $\forall x^\sigma\, .\,\Box_5Rx\to\Box_5\forall x\, .\,Rx$, and
dually $\Diamond_5\exists x\, .\,Rx\to\exists x\, .\,\Diamond_5Rx$; iterating, the same holds for
tuples of variables.

*Proof.* This is Prior's derivation of the Barcan formula from B. It uses only that
$\Box_5$ is an S5 operator, a theorem of C, so every step below is a theorem and may
be necessitated. Put $U:=\forall x\, .\,\Box_5Rx$. For each $x$, $U\to\Box_5Rx$ is a
theorem, so by necessitation, N and K for $\Box_5$, $\Diamond_5U\to\Diamond_5\Box_5Rx$.
The dual of B gives $\Diamond_5\Box_5Rx\to Rx$. So $\Diamond_5U\to\forall x\, .\,Rx$ is a
theorem, and necessitation, N and K give $\Box_5\Diamond_5U\to\Box_5\forall x\, .\,Rx$.
B gives $U\to\Box_5\Diamond_5U$. $\square$

background_items.title: Modalized Plenitude
background_items.credit: Cian Dorr, 28 September 2026 (the statement, and the witness $\lambda x\, .\,\forall p\, .\,(Ux)p\to p$ for output type $t$); Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), 28 September 2026 (the generalization to all relational output types and the written proof)
sources: Classicism, §1.5, pp. 16–18 (necessitation, T and Intensionality)
background_items.body:
If necessarily each argument has a value that is necessarily the relation's unique value
for it, then some operation necessarily represents the relation:
$\forall U^{\sigma\tau t}\, .\,\Box\bigl(\forall x^\sigma\, .\,\exists y^\tau\, .\,\Box((Ux)y\land\forall z^\tau\, .\,(Ux)z\to y=z)\bigr)\to\exists X^{\sigma\tau}\, .\,\Box\forall x^\sigma\, .\,\forall y^\tau\, .\,(Ux)y\leftrightarrow y=Xx\qquad(\tau\ne e)$.
Plenitude, which asks only for actual functionality and an actual representation, is not
a theorem of C.

*Proof.* Let $\tau=\bar\rho\to t$, which covers $\tau=t$ with the empty tuple, and fix
$U^{\sigma\tau t}$. Write $\varphi(x,y):=(Ux)y\land\forall z\, .\,(Ux)z\to y=z$ and define
the operation $F:=\lambda x^\sigma\, .\,\lambda\bar u\, .\,\forall y^\tau\, .\,(Ux)y\to y[\bar u]$;
for $\tau=t$ this is $\lambda x\, .\,\forall p\, .\,(Ux)p\to p$. (1) A theorem of C:
$\varphi(x,y_0)\to\forall\bar u\, .\,y_0[\bar u]\leftrightarrow(Fx)[\bar u]$. Assume
$\varphi(x,y_0)$. If $y_0[\bar u]$ and $(Ux)y$, then $y=y_0$ by uniqueness, so $y[\bar u]$;
hence $(Fx)[\bar u]$. Conversely, if $(Fx)[\bar u]$, instantiate $y:=y_0$ and use
$(Ux)y_0$. (2) Necessitate (1) and apply [[modal-k|K]]: $\Box\varphi(x,y_0)$ gives
$\Box\forall\bar u\, .\,y_0[\bar u]\leftrightarrow(Fx)[\bar u]$, and
[[intensionality-r|Intensionality]] gives $y_0=Fx$. (3) Let
$H:=\forall x\, .\,\exists y\, .\,\Box\varphi(x,y)$ and
$G:=\forall x\, .\,\forall y\, .\,(Ux)y\leftrightarrow y=Fx$. Then $H\to G$ is a theorem
of C. Given $x$ and $y$, take $y_0$ with $\Box\varphi(x,y_0)$; by (2) $y_0=Fx$, and by
[[modal-t|T]] $\varphi(x,y_0)$. If $(Ux)y$ then $y=y_0=Fx$ by uniqueness. If $y=Fx$ then
$y=y_0$, and $(Ux)y_0$ gives $(Ux)y$. (4) Necessitate $H\to G$ and apply K:
$\Box H\to\Box G$. Existential generalization on the closed term $F$ (with parameter $U$)
gives $\Box H\to\exists X\, .\,\Box\forall x\, .\,\forall y\, .\,(Ux)y\leftrightarrow y=Xx$.
Only necessitation of theorems of C is used, so the theoremhood side condition is
respected.

The operation is definable from $U$, so no choice is involved. The outer box of the
hypothesis is used only to get the boxed conclusion: the same proof shows, as a theorem
of C, the unboxed variant $H\to\exists X\, .\,\forall x\, .\,\forall y\, .\,(Ux)y\leftrightarrow y=Xx$.
The inner box is essential; it is what licenses the identity $y_0=Fx$ in step (2).

*Polyadic form.* The same for $U^{\bar\sigma\tau t}$, one argument at a time, using each
step's instance under the box.

In Lean the proof is given at output type $t$ and at output type $\sigma'\to t$ for each
type $\sigma'$, the cases of none and of one remaining argument. Lean's shallow layer has
no induction on the shape of a type, so each further number of remaining arguments is a
separate theorem of the same form.

background_items.title: the Bourbaki–Witt fixed-point lemma
background_items.body:
Work at any type $\sigma$, including $e$. Let $X^{\sigma t}$ be a property, and
$R^{\sigma\sigma t}$ and $F^{\sigma\sigma t}$ relations; write $x\preccurlyeq y$ for
$(Rx)y$. Since $R$ need only be a preorder, put

$$
x\approx y:=x\preccurlyeq y\land y\preccurlyeq x,\qquad
x\prec y:=x\preccurlyeq y\land\neg\,y\preccurlyeq x .
$$

When $R$ is antisymmetric on $X$, this $\prec$ agrees on $X$ with the shorthand
$x\preccurlyeq y\land x\ne y$. For $Z\subseteq X$ put

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{UB}(s,Z)&:=Xs\land\forall z\, .\,Zz\to z\preccurlyeq s,\\
\operatorname{Sup}(s,Z)&:=\operatorname{UB}(s,Z)\land\forall u\, .\,\operatorname{UB}(u,Z)\to s\preccurlyeq u.
\end{aligned}
$$

In this lemma a *chain* is a property $Z\subseteq X$ with $\operatorname{Total}(R,Z)$.
Because $R$ is only a preorder, a chain need not be antisymmetric. That is weaker than
being an $R$-chain in the sense above.

Assume, at the evaluation point:

1. $R$ preorders $X$: it is reflexive on $X$, and $\operatorname{Trans}(R,X)$;
2. every chain has a supremum in $X$:
   $\forall Z\, .\,Z\subseteq X\land\operatorname{Total}(R,Z)\to\exists s\, .\,\operatorname{Sup}(s,Z)$;
3. $F$ is progressive and invariant on $X$: for every $x$ with $Xx$, there is some $y$
   with $(Fx)y$, every such $y$ has $Xy$ and $x\preccurlyeq y$ (*progressive*), and if
   moreover $x\approx x'$, $(Fx)y$ and $(Fx')y'$, then $y\approx y'$ (*invariant*).

Taking $x':=x$ in the invariance clause, any two $F$-values of one $x$ are
$\approx$-equivalent; $F$ is functional up to $\approx$.

Call $Y^{\sigma t}$ *closed* if $Y\subseteq X$,
$\forall x\,y\, .\,Yx\land(Fx)y\to Yy$, and
$\forall Z\,s\, .\,Z\subseteq Y\land\operatorname{Total}(R,Z)\land\operatorname{Sup}(s,Z)\to Ys$. Let

$$
M:=\lambda x\, .\,\forall Y\, .\,\operatorname{Closed}(Y)\to Yx
$$

be the least closed property (the *tower*). Then:

- (a) $M$ is closed, and $M\subseteq Y$ for every closed $Y$;
- (b) for all $b,c,d$ with $Mb$, $Mc$ and $(Fb)d$: $c\preccurlyeq b$ or $d\preccurlyeq c$.
  In particular $M$ is a chain, and if $b\prec c$ then $d\preccurlyeq c$;
- (c) $M$ has a supremum, and every supremum $m$ of $M$ satisfies $Mm$, and $n\approx m$
  whenever $(Fm)n$.

Two special cases:

- *Partial orders.* Suppose $R$ partially orders $X$ (Antisymm as well) and $F$ is
  functional on $X$. Then $\approx$ is identity on $X$, a chain is an $R$-chain, invariance
  is automatic, and (c) gives an $m$ in $X$ with $(Fm)m$.
- *Inclusion.* Suppose $\sigma=\bar\tau t$ and $\preccurlyeq$ is $\subseteq$. Then
  $\approx$ is coextension $\equiv$. Invariance says that coextensive arguments have
  coextensive $F$-values.

No choice principle is used, and the lemma holds at the evaluation point
only; it is a theorem schema of C, so it can be necessitated when its
hypotheses hold necessarily.

*Proof.* Throughout, $\preccurlyeq$ is transitive on $X$, and $x\preccurlyeq y\prec z$
and $x\prec y\preccurlyeq z$ each give $x\prec z$.

(a) By hypotheses 2 and 3, $X$ is closed, so $M\subseteq X$. The remaining clauses are
immediate from the definition of $M$.

Call $c$ a *pivot* if $Mc$ and
$\forall b\,d\, .\,Mb\land b\prec c\land(Fb)d\to d\preccurlyeq c$.

*Claim 1.* Let $c$ be a pivot and $(Fc)e$. Then for every $b$ with $Mb$:
$b\preccurlyeq c$ or $e\preccurlyeq b$. Put
$M_{c,e}:=\lambda b\, .\,Mb\land(b\preccurlyeq c\lor e\preccurlyeq b)$. It is closed:

- Let $M_{c,e}b$ and $(Fb)d$. If $b\prec c$, then $d\preccurlyeq c$, as $c$ is a pivot.
  If $b\approx c$, then $d\approx e$ by invariance, so $e\preccurlyeq d$. If
  $e\preccurlyeq b$, then $e\preccurlyeq b\preccurlyeq d$.
- Let $Z\subseteq M_{c,e}$ be a chain with supremum $s$. Either $z\preccurlyeq c$ for
  every $z$ with $Zz$, and then $s\preccurlyeq c$; or $e\preccurlyeq z\preccurlyeq s$ for
  some such $z$.

In each case the new member is in $M$, since $M$ is closed. So $M\subseteq M_{c,e}$ by
(a).

*Claim 2.* Every $c$ with $Mc$ is a pivot. The pivots form a closed property:

- Let $c$ be a pivot and $(Fc)e$. Then $Me$, since $M$ is closed. Let $Mb$, $b\prec e$
  and $(Fb)d$. By Claim 1, $b\preccurlyeq c$, since the alternative $e\preccurlyeq b$
  contradicts $b\prec e$. If $b\prec c$, then $d\preccurlyeq c\preccurlyeq e$. If
  $b\approx c$, then $d\approx e$ by invariance. Either way $d\preccurlyeq e$, so $e$ is
  a pivot.
- Let $Z$ be a chain of pivots with supremum $s$, and let $Mb$, $b\prec s$ and $(Fb)d$.
  Then $Ms$, since $M$ is closed. Some $z$ with $Zz$ has $z\not\preccurlyeq b$; otherwise
  $b$, which is in $X$, would bound $Z$, giving $s\preccurlyeq b$ and contradicting $b\prec s$. Take $e$ with $(Fz)e$.
  By Claim 1 for $z$ and $e$, either $b\preccurlyeq z$ or $e\preccurlyeq b$. The second
  would give $z\preccurlyeq e\preccurlyeq b$. So $b\prec z$, and
  $d\preccurlyeq z\preccurlyeq s$, as $z$ is a pivot.

(b) Let $Mb$, $Mc$ and $(Fb)d$. By Claim 2, $b$ is a pivot. By Claim 1, applied to $b$,
$d$ and $c$, either $c\preccurlyeq b$ or $d\preccurlyeq c$. In the second case
$b\preccurlyeq d\preccurlyeq c$. So any two members of $M$ are comparable. If $b\prec c$,
then $c\not\preccurlyeq b$, and so $d\preccurlyeq c$.

(c) $M$ is a chain included in $X$, so it has a supremum. Let $m$ be one. Then $Mm$,
since $M$ is closed. If $(Fm)n$, then $Mn$, so $n\preccurlyeq m$; and
$m\preccurlyeq n$, as $F$ is progressive. So $n\approx m$. $\square$

The tower also supports induction: to show that every member of $M$ has a
property, show that the members of $M$ having it form a closed property.

background_items.title: the Bourbaki–Witt lemma for admissible chains
background_items.body:
The [[bourbaki-witt|Bourbaki–Witt lemma]] has a variant for the case where only some
chains are known to have suprema. These are the chains singled out by a property
$\mathcal A^{(\sigma t)t}$, the *admissible* properties. Take $X$, $R$ and $F$ as there,
and change it as follows.

- Hypothesis 2 is required only for admissible chains:
  $\forall Z\, .\,\mathcal AZ\land Z\subseteq X\land\operatorname{Total}(R,Z)\to\exists s\, .\,\operatorname{Sup}(s,Z)$.
- In the definition of *closed*, the clause for suprema is likewise restricted to
  admissible $Z$. The tower quantifies only over admissible closed properties:
  $M:=\lambda x\, .\,\forall Y\, .\,\mathcal AY\land\operatorname{Closed}(Y)\to Yx$.
- There is a new hypothesis. Each of the properties that the proof forms must be
  coextensive with an admissible property:
  - $X$;
  - $M$;
  - the property of being a pivot;
  - each $M_{c,e}$ of Claim 1.

Conclusion (a) becomes: $M$ is closed, and $M\subseteq Y$ for every admissible closed
$Y$. Conclusions (b) and (c) are unchanged.

The proof is the same. Two facts let it go through:

- closedness depends only on a property's actual extension;
- the new hypothesis brings each property the proof forms within the scope of (a).

With $\mathcal A:=\lambda Z\, .\,\top$ this is the original lemma.

Only the actual extensions of admissible properties matter, so two predicates with the
same admissible extensions give the same lemma.

background_md: ## Framework and conventions ### Classicism The fixed background is **Classicism (C)** of Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, using the paper's **relational type system**. Its base types are $e$ and $t$. Form $\sigma\tau$ from admitted types only when $\tau\ne e$: every function type ends in $t$. Thus $et$, $tt$ and $(et)t$ are admitted, while $ee$ and $(ee)t$ are not. Individuals of type $e$ remain available as arguments and quantified objects. Use the definition in *Classicism*, §1.3: C is the smallest H-theory containing Logical Equivalence. This schema identifies $\lambda$-abstractions of formulas equivalent in H. Its theoremhood side condition must be preserved when reasoning from additional assumptions. This is the type system called R in *Classicism*, §1.1. It is fixed throughout the map, so principle names omit a type-system suffix. ### Notation Types associate to the right: $\sigma\tau\rho$ means $\sigma\to(\tau\to\rho)$. Application also associates to the right: $fgx=f(gx)$. Write $(fx)y$ for curried application. A dot separates a binder from its scope. The abbreviation $X[\bar x]$ means explicitly left-nested application to the displayed tuple; it is $X$ for an empty tuple. For a finite, possibly empty, tuple of types $\bar\sigma=\sigma_1\ldots\sigma_n$, $\bar\sigma\rho$ is the type $\sigma_1\cdots\sigma_n\rho$ (so $\bar\sigma t$ is $\sigma_1\cdots\sigma_n t$), and $\bar x^{\bar\sigma}$ gives $x_i$ the type $\sigma_i$. A tuple quantifier $\forall\bar x$ or $\exists\bar x$ binds $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ one at a time; $\bar x=\bar y$ is the conjunction of the identities $x_i=y_i$ (true for the empty tuple), and $\bar x\ne\bar y$ is its negation. With tuples in place of single arguments, the definitions below are read in the evident way; for instance $\operatorname{Serial}(U):=\forall\bar x^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,\exists y^\tau\, .\,(U[\bar x])y$ for $U^{\bar\sigma\tau t}$, and $\operatorname{Equiv}(R)$ for $R^{\bar\sigma\bar\sigma t}$ uses $(R[\bar x])[\bar y]$. **Definition (common shorthands).** `shorthands` For relations $X,Y$ of a type $\bar\sigma t$, and the evaluation point unless a box is written: - $X\subseteq Y$ (*$X$ is included in $Y$*, a *subrelation* of $Y$) abbreviates $\forall\bar z\, .\,X[\bar z]\to Y[\bar z]$; this is actual inclusion, and $X\le Y$ is $\Box(X\subseteq Y)$ ([[order]]). - $X\equiv Y$ (*$X$ and $Y$ are coextensive*) abbreviates $\forall\bar z\, .\,X[\bar z]\leftrightarrow Y[\bar z]$. In C coextensive relations are identical only when necessarily coextensive ([[intensionality-r|Intensionality]]). - For the empty tuple, at type $t$, $p\subseteq q$ is $p\to q$ and $p\equiv q$ is $p\leftrightarrow q$. In Lean these are the notations `X ⊆ Y` and `X ≡ Y`, defined pointwise at every relational type. - $\top_\tau$ and $\bot_\tau$, at a relational type $\tau=\bar\sigma t$, are $\lambda\bar x\, .\,\top$ and $\lambda\bar x\, .\,\bot$, the top and bottom of $\le_\tau$. - $H_{\bar x}:=\lambda\bar y\, .\,\bar y=\bar x$ is the *haecceity* of $\bar x$, the property of being $\bar x$. - $X-y:=\lambda u\, .\,Xu\land u\ne y$ is $X$ without $y$. - $\exists!x\, .\,\varphi$ abbreviates $\exists x\, .\,\varphi\land\forall x'\, .\,\varphi[x'/x]\to x'=x$. - For a relation $R^{\sigma\sigma t}$ given as an order, $x\preccurlyeq y$ is $(Rx)y$, and $x\prec y$ is $x\preccurlyeq y\land x\ne y$. - $\bigwedge_{i**Lemma (Existence).** `existence-r` Every type is inhabited: $\exists x^\sigma\, .\,x=x$. *Proof.* Reflexivity gives $y=y$, and existential introduction yields $\exists x\, .\,x=x$ at each admitted type; equivalently, use the β and EG derivation on p. 7. *Polyadic form.* $\exists\bar x^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,\bar x=\bar x$, the conjunction of the original at each $\sigma_i$; for the empty tuple it is $\top$. *Credit:* Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr *Sources:* Classicism, §1.1, p. 7 *Lean:* `Classicism.existence_rel`, `Classicism.existence_e` **Lemma (Ordinary Comprehension).** `ordinary-comprehension-r` Every well-typed formula $P$ with distinguished variables $\bar y$ defines a coextensive relation: $\exists X\, .\,\forall\bar y\, .\,X[\bar y]\leftrightarrow P$, for $X$ not free in $P$, any other free object variables being universally closed. *Proof.* The λ-term $\lambda\bar y\, .\,P$ is a witness: β-conversion makes its application equivalent to $P$ at each tuple, and existential introduction supplies the instance. The schema is in a formula, which no Lean statement with type parameters can quantify over. The Lean theorems state, for zero, one and two distinguished variables, that every relation $P$ is coextensive with some $X$; each instance of the schema is the theorem at the λ-term $\lambda\bar y\, .\,P$, which is how the object language proves it. *Credit:* Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr *Sources:* Classicism *Lean:* `Classicism.ordinary_comprehension_nullary`, `Classicism.ordinary_comprehension`, `Classicism.ordinary_comprehension₂` ### Conventions **Type scope.** A formula containing type variables ($\sigma$, $\tau$, $\bar\sigma$) is a schema. The principle is the set of its instances, one for each admissible assignment of types to the variables. Type variables range over the fixed type system above; $\bar\sigma$ ranges over finite tuples, including the empty one. A relational type is any admitted type other than $e$, including $t$. A restriction is written as a parenthesized proviso after the formula, as in $\ldots\qquad(\tau\ne e)$; a formula without a proviso admits every assignment. The type variables are metalinguistic: there is no quantification over types in C, and a type variable never falls within the scope of an object-language operator except as a fixed parameter. Finite tuples and formula schemata retain their stated metalinguistic side conditions. **Modal scope.** A boxed schema means that each admitted, fully closed object-language instance is necessary. Close its object variables before boxing it. Type ranges and formula side conditions remain outside the box. C5 abbreviates C plus boxed ND at all types. It is an optional preset, not part of the fixed background. A proof under an optional premise cannot be necessitated unless that premise is discharged or supplied necessarily. **Negation.** Failure of a type schema means failure of at least one of its admitted instances, not failure at every type: the negation of a principle $A_\sigma$ says that $\neg A_\sigma$ for some $\sigma$. A necessarily false instance, $\Box\neg A_\sigma$ for some $\sigma$, is stronger and different from failure of the boxed schema. Negated principle nodes are not added by this positive import. Incompatibilities conclude False; model `violates` entries record schema failure. **Infinite sets in model descriptions.** A model described with "an infinite set" works for any infinite set; where a construction needs a particular one, its description says so. "Infinite" means not finite, that is, in bijection with no natural number. This is the notion the Axioms of Infinity express, the finite cardinalities being defined inductively. Without the axiom of choice it is weaker than Dedekind-infinity, but it is all that the arguments for the Infinity principles use, so they hold in the choiceless variants of a model too. Those variants say which hypothesis replaces choice. ### Evidence **Evidence.** *Classicism* is Bacon and Dorr (2024), in Fritz and Jones (eds), *Higher-Order Metaphysics*, Oxford University Press, pp. 109–190. References use the numbering of the 87-page draft dated 16 May 2023, from which the map was built and which does not differ materially from the published version, and, for the symmetric ideally-full models and the weak rigidity principles, the 27-page draft of Dorr, *Boolean Completeness does not imply Rigid Comprehension*, dated 30 July 2026. That second source is a work in progress and is not distributed with the map; its records say so. Models cite the construction and evaluation point directly. The source models now use exactly the map's type system. Their listed properties provide countermodel evidence at the stated evaluation point. The singleton-root coalesced model still awaits an expansion to the fixed nonlogical signature; its record explains this separate obligation. Two results reported without proofs in the draft retain pending verification status. No record claims an independent human check or Lean verification. ## Necessity **Definition (necessity and possibility).** `box-and-diamond` Put $\Box p:=(p=\top)$ and $\Diamond p:=(p\ne\bot)$. The facts below are theorems of C, schemata in their type variables. Each was formerly recorded as a result with no premises. ### The propositional modal logic of $\Box$ **Lemma (K).** `modal-k` Necessity distributes over implication: $\forall p q\, .\,\Box(p\to q)\to(\Box p\to\Box q)$. *Proof.* In the Boolean algebra of propositions, $\Box(p\to q)$ says that the implication is $\top$. Together with $p=\top$, substitution and the Boolean identities identify $q$ with $\top$. *Dual form.* $\forall p q\, .\,\Box(p\to q)\to(\Diamond p\to\Diamond q)$. Instantiate either form at $\neg q,\neg p$ and contrapose the inner conditional, using $\Box(\neg q\to\neg p)\leftrightarrow\Box(p\to q)$ and $\Diamond=\neg\Box\neg$. *Credit:* Andrew Bacon (Classicism credits the S4 result to Bacon 2018) *Sources:* Classicism, §1.5, p. 16 *Lean:* `Classicism.modal_K` **Lemma (T).** `modal-t` Necessary propositions are true: $\forall p\, .\,\Box p\to p$. *Proof.* If $p=\top$, identity elimination and the truth of $\top$ give $p$. *Dual form.* Every truth is possible: $\forall p\, .\,p\to\Diamond p$, by contraposition and $\Diamond=\neg\Box\neg$. *Credit:* Andrew Bacon (Classicism credits the S4 result to Bacon 2018) *Sources:* Classicism, §1.5, p. 16 *Lean:* `Classicism.modal_T` **Lemma (4).** `modal-four` Necessary propositions are necessarily necessary: $\forall p\, .\,\Box p\to\Box\Box p$. *Proof.* Apply [[identity-necessary-r|NI]] to the identity $p=\top$. Its conclusion is $\Box(p=\top)$, which is $\Box\Box p$. *Dual form.* Whatever is possibly possible is possible: $\forall p\, .\,\Diamond\Diamond p\to\Diamond p$, by contraposition and $\Diamond=\neg\Box\neg$. *Credit:* Andrew Bacon (Classicism credits the S4 result to Bacon 2018) *Sources:* Classicism, §1.5, p. 17 *Lean:* `Classicism.modal_four` **Further laws.** $\Box$ and $\Diamond$ are duals: $\Diamond p=\neg\Box\neg p$ and $\Box\neg p=\neg\Diamond p$, and $\Box\neg p$ is $p=\bot$ (Lean: `Classicism.dia_eq_not_box_not`, `Classicism.box_not_eq_not_dia`, `Classicism.box_not_eq`). $\Box$ distributes over conjunction, $\Box(p\land q)=(\Box p\land\Box q)$ (Lean: `Classicism.box_and_eq`); $\Diamond(p\lor q)\to\Diamond p\lor\Diamond q$ (Lean: `Classicism.dia_or`); and $\Diamond p\land\Box q\to\Diamond(p\land q)$ (Lean: `Classicism.dia_and_of_dia_box`). By a result of Andrew Bacon (*The Broadest Necessity*, 2018), the propositional modal logic of $\Box$ in C is exactly S4, the smallest normal modal logic containing T and 4. The [[modal-five|5]] and [[modal-b|B]] axioms are not theorems of C, though they can consistently be added. ### Quantifiers and identity **Lemma (Necessity of Identity (NI)).** `identity-necessary-r` Identity is necessary at every type: $\forall x y^\sigma\, .\,x=y\to\Box(x=y)$. *Proof.* Reflexivity is a theorem, so its necessitation gives $\Box(x=x)$. Leibniz's Law substitutes $y$ for the second $x$ under the premise $x=y$, giving $\Box(x=y)$. *Polyadic form.* $\forall\bar x\,\bar y^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,\bar x=\bar y\to\Box(\bar x=\bar y)$: $\bar x=\bar y$ is a conjunction of identities, each necessary, and a conjunction of necessities is necessary. *Credit:* W. V. Quine (historical attribution in Classicism, p. 22) *Sources:* Classicism, §2.1, p. 22 *Lean:* `Classicism.necessity_of_identity` **Lemma (Converse Barcan Formula (CBF)).** `converse-barcan-r` $\forall X^{\sigma t}\, .\,\Box(\forall x^\sigma\, .\,Xx)\to(\forall x^\sigma\, .\,\Box Xx)$. *Proof.* Necessitate universal instantiation and use [[modal-k|K]] to obtain $\Box(\forall x\, .\,Xx)\to\Box Xx$. Generalize $x$, preserving the side condition. *Other forms.* The polyadic form, $\forall X^{\bar\sigma t}\, .\,\Box(\forall\bar x\, .\,X[\bar x])\to(\forall\bar x\, .\,\Box X[\bar x])$, follows by instantiating one variable at a time. The dual form says that if something possibly has a property, then possibly something has it: $\forall X^{\sigma t}\, .\,(\exists x\, .\,\Diamond Xx)\to\Diamond(\exists x\, .\,Xx)$, and likewise for tuples; each comes from the corresponding form by contraposition and $\Diamond=\neg\Box\neg$. *Credit:* Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr *Sources:* Classicism, §1.5, p. 19 *Lean:* `Classicism.converse_barcan` **Lemma (Broad Necessitism).** `broad-necessitism-r` Every entity of a type is necessarily identical to something: $\forall x^\sigma\, .\,\Box(\exists y^\sigma\, .\,y=x)$. *Proof.* The theorem $\forall x\, .\,\exists y\, .\,y=x$ can be necessitated, and [[converse-barcan-r|CBF]] gives $\forall x\, .\,\Box\exists y\, .\,y=x$. *Polyadic form.* $\forall\bar x^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,\Box(\exists\bar y^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,\bar y=\bar x)$, taking $\bar y:=\bar x$ coordinatewise. *Credit:* Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr *Sources:* Classicism, §1.5 *Lean:* `Classicism.Proofs.classicism_implies_broad_necessitism_r` The [[barcan-r|Barcan Formula]] and the [[distinctness-necessary-r|Necessity of Distinctness]] are not theorems of C, though they can consistently be added. ### Intensionality **Lemma (Intensionality).** `intensionality-r` Necessarily coextensive relations are identical: $\forall X Y^{\bar\sigma t}\, .\,\Box(X\equiv Y)\to X=Y$. *Proof.* Logical Equivalence identifies the λ-abstractions of $X[\bar z]\land(X\equiv Y)$ and of the analogous expression with $Y$ in the first conjunct. If the biconditional is necessary, substitute its identity with $\top$ into the abstraction identity. Boolean identities and β-η conversion leave $X=Y$, as on p. 17. *Credit:* Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr *Sources:* Classicism, §1.5, pp. 17–18 *Lean:* `Classicism.intensionality` **Lemma (Modalized Fregean Axiom).** `modalized-fregean` Necessarily equivalent propositions are identical: $\forall p q\, .\,\Box(p\leftrightarrow q)\to p=q$. *Proof.* The nullary instance of [[intensionality-r|Intensionality]]: necessary equivalence identifies $p\leftrightarrow q$ with $\top$, and the Boolean identities then identify $p$ and $q$. *Credit:* Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr *Sources:* Classicism, §1.5, p. 18 *Lean:* `Classicism.modalized_fregean` **Lemma (Modalized Functionality).** `modalized-functionality-r` Necessarily co-functional operations are identical: $\forall X Y^{\sigma\tau}\, .\,\Box(\forall z^\sigma\, .\,Xz=Yz)\to X=Y\qquad(\tau\ne e)$. *Proof.* From boxed pointwise identity, identity elimination gives boxed agreement after applying every remaining argument of the relational output type; quantification over those arguments is inside the necessary implication. [[intensionality-r|Intensionality]] and η-conversion identify the operations. This relies on the output type's ending in $t$. *Polyadic form.* $\forall X Y^{\bar\sigma\tau}\, .\,\Box(\forall\bar z\, .\,X[\bar z]=Y[\bar z])\to X=Y$ $(\tau\ne e)$, one argument at a time, with the box carried through. *Credit:* Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr *Sources:* Classicism, §1.5, n. 22 *Lean:* `Classicism.modalized_functionality` ## Boolean structure and the algebraic order At a relational type $\tau$, Boolean operations are defined pointwise. The order is algebraic entailment, $X\le_\tau Y$ iff $Y=X\lor_\tau Y$, rather than material implication. At $t$ this is equivalent to $\Box(X\to Y)$; at a relation type it is equivalent to the necessary universal closure of the pointwise implication (Lean: `Classicism.le_iff_prop`, `Classicism.le_iff_arrow`). So $\le_\tau$ is a partial order: reflexive and transitive because necessary pointwise implication is, and antisymmetric by [[intensionality-r|Intensionality]] (Lean: `Classicism.le_refl_rel`, `Classicism.le_trans_rel`, `Classicism.le_antisymm_rel`). At $t$, $\bot\le p\le\top$, and $p\land q$ and $p\lor q$ are the greatest lower and least upper bounds of $p$ and $q$ (Lean: `Classicism.bot_le_prop`, `Classicism.le_top_prop`, `Classicism.and_le_left_prop`, `Classicism.and_le_right_prop`, `Classicism.le_and_prop`, `Classicism.le_or_left_prop`, `Classicism.le_or_right_prop`); at every relational type $\bot_\tau\le X$, and $X\le\neg_\tau X$ only when $X=\bot_\tau$ (Lean: `Classicism.bot_le_rel`, `Classicism.eq_bot_of_le_neg_rel`). An entailment, if true, is necessary: $X\le Y\to\Box(X\le Y)$, since $\le$ is boxed inclusion, by [[modal-four|4]] (Lean: `Classicism.box_le_rel`). **Definition (lattice predicates).** `lattice-predicates` The lattice predicates used in the principles are: $$ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{LB}_\tau(y,X)&:=\forall z^\tau\, .\,Xz\to y\le_\tau z,\\ \operatorname{GLB}_\tau(y,X)&:=\forall z^\tau\, .\, \operatorname{LB}_\tau(z,X)\leftrightarrow z\le_\tau y,\\ \operatorname{UB}_\tau(y,X)&:=\forall z^\tau\, .\,Xz\to z\le_\tau y,\\ \operatorname{LUB}_\tau(y,X)&:=\forall z^\tau\, .\, \operatorname{UB}_\tau(z,X)\leftrightarrow y\le_\tau z,\\ \operatorname{Atom}_\tau(y)&:=\forall z^\tau\, .\, (z\le_\tau y\land z\ne y)\leftrightarrow z\le_\tau\neg_\tau z. \end{aligned} $$ Thus an atom is non-bottom (Lean: `Classicism.not_le_neg_of_atom`, `Classicism.atom_ne_false`) and has no non-bottom strict lower bound. $\operatorname{LB}$, $\operatorname{GLB}$ and $\operatorname{Atom}$ are the definitions of *Classicism*, §2.2, pp. 23–24; $\operatorname{UB}$ and $\operatorname{LUB}$ are their duals. So $y$ is a lower (upper) bound of $X$ when it entails (is entailed by) every member of $X$, and a greatest lower (least upper) bound when the lower (upper) bounds of $X$ are exactly what entails it (what it entails). **Lemma (greatest lower bounds and least upper bounds).** `glb-neg-lub` At a relational type $\tau$, the negation of a least upper bound of $X$ is a greatest lower bound of the negations of the members of $X$, and conversely: $\operatorname{GLB}_\tau(\neg_\tau y,\lambda w\, .\,X(\neg_\tau w))\leftrightarrow \operatorname{LUB}_\tau(y,X)$. *Proof.* Negation reverses $\le_\tau$, since necessary pointwise implication contraposes, and $\neg_\tau\neg_\tau z=z$ by [[intensionality-r|Intensionality]] (Lean: `Classicism.neg_le_neg_rel`, `Classicism.neg_neg_rel`). Hence $z\le_\tau\neg_\tau y$ iff $y\le_\tau\neg_\tau z$, and $z$ is a lower bound of the negations of the members of $X$ iff $\neg_\tau z$ is an upper bound of $X$. So the lower bounds of $\lambda w\, .\,X(\neg_\tau w)$ are exactly the entities below $\neg_\tau y$ iff the upper bounds of $X$ are exactly the entities above $y$. $\square$ *Lean:* `Classicism.glb_neg_iff_lub`, `Classicism.lb_neg_iff_ub_neg` The greatest lower bound of a property's upper bounds is also its least upper bound, and dually (Lean: `Classicism.lub_of_glb_ubs`, `Classicism.glb_of_lub_lbs`). Classicism does not entail that any relational type $\tau$ forms a *complete* or an *atomic* Boolean algebra, though these claims can consistently be added: see [[boolean-completeness-r|Boolean Completeness]] and [[atomicity-r|Atomicity]]. ## Atoms Atoms are defined with the other [[lattice-predicates|lattice predicates]]. An entity of a relational type is an atom just when it is non-bottom and entails every entity of its type or that entity's negation (Lean: `Classicism.atom_le_or_le_neg_rel`, `Classicism.atom_of_decides`, `Classicism.atom_of_decides_arrow`). **Definition (strong atoms).** `strong-atoms` At a relational type $\sigma$, with $\Diamond_\sigma X:=X\ne\bot_\sigma$, a *strong atom* is a possible entity that necessarily entails every entity of its type or its negation: $$ \operatorname{SAtom}_\sigma(W):=\Diamond_\sigma W\land\Box\forall Y^\sigma\, .\, W\le_\sigma Y\lor W\le_\sigma\neg_\sigma Y. $$ Bacon, *A Philosophical Introduction to Higher-Order Logics*, §8.2, pp. 165–166, calls these *strong worlds*; dropping the box gives his *weak worlds*, which are just the atoms. The map avoids the word "world" for them, since at types other than $t$ they are not world-like. By [[modal-t|T]], a strong atom is an atom. Unlike an atom, it necessarily settles every entity of its type, including entities that do not actually exist. [[atomicity-r|Atomicity]] says that every possible entity is entailed by an atom; [[strong-atomicity-r|Strong Atomicity]] requires a strong atom. Each is one direction of a biconditional that Bacon calls the Weak and the Strong Leibniz Biconditionals; the other direction is a theorem of C. The type-$t$ instance of each is recorded separately. ### Self-atoms **Definition (self-atoms).** `self-atoms` A *self-atom* is a possible entity that is necessarily an atom whenever it is instantiated: $$ \operatorname{SelfAtom}_\sigma(X):=\Diamond_\sigma X\land \Box\bigl(\exists\bar x\, .\,X\bar x\to\operatorname{Atom}_\sigma(X)\bigr), \qquad \operatorname{SelfAtom}_t(p):=\Diamond p\land\Box\bigl(p\to\operatorname{Atom}_t(p)\bigr). $$ *Credit:* Cian Dorr, 25 October 2026 *Lean:* `Classicism.P.SelfAtom` At type $t$, since $p\land\operatorname{Atom}_t(p)$ is equivalent in C to $p\land\forall q\, .\,q\to p\le q$, a self-atom is a possible proposition that entails that it is the actual world. A strong atom is an atom at every world, a self-atom an atom at every world where it holds, an atom an atom at the evaluation point; a strong atom is a self-atom and a true atom is a self-atom, but a self-atom need not be an atom. [[self-atomicity-r|Self-Atomicity]] replaces $\operatorname{SAtom}$ in Strong Atomicity by $\operatorname{SelfAtom}$, and the four *bridge principles* say that [[atoms-are-self-atoms-r|atoms are self-atoms]], that [[self-atoms-are-atoms-r|self-atoms are atoms]], that [[self-atoms-are-strong-atoms-r|self-atoms are strong atoms]], and that [[atoms-are-strong-atoms-r|atoms are strong atoms]]; the last is what Strong Atomicity adds to Atomicity. ## Rigidity **Definition (persistence, inextensibility and rigidity).** `rigidity-predicates` For a relation $Y$ with a finite argument tuple, including the empty tuple, the comprehension predicates are: $$ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{Persistent}(Y)&:=Y\le\lambda\bar x\, .\,\Box Y[\bar x],\\ \operatorname{Inextensible}(Y)&:=\Box\forall X\, .\, (\forall\bar x\, .\,Y[\bar x]\to\Box X[\bar x])\to Y\le X,\\ \operatorname{Rigid}(Y)&:=\operatorname{Persistent}(Y)\land \operatorname{Inextensible}(Y). \end{aligned} $$ This is the rigidity convention of §2.3, p. 28. Gallin's alternative convention has its own principle. **Definition (the weak variants).** `weak-rigidity-predicates` Since $Y\le Z$ is itself the necessary universal closure of the pointwise implication, $\operatorname{Persistent}(Y)$ unpacks as $\Box\forall\bar x\, .\,Y[\bar x]\to\Box Y[\bar x]$, and both conjuncts of $\operatorname{Rigid}$ carry a leading $\Box$. Dropping it gives the weak variants: $$ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{WeaklyPersistent}(Y)&:=\forall\bar x\, .\, Y[\bar x]\to\Box Y[\bar x],\\ \operatorname{WeaklyInextensible}(Y)&:=\forall X\, .\, (\forall\bar x\, .\,Y[\bar x]\to\Box X[\bar x])\to Y\le X,\\ \operatorname{WeaklyRigid}(Y)&:=\operatorname{WeaklyPersistent}(Y)\land \operatorname{WeaklyInextensible}(Y). \end{aligned} $$ $\operatorname{Rigid}$ is thus necessary weak rigidity (Lean: `Classicism.rigid_iff_box_weaklyRigid`). These are the conventions of Dorr, *Boolean Completeness does not imply Rigid Comprehension*, pp. 2 and 12. By T, rigidity implies weak rigidity, persistence weak persistence, and inextensibility weak inextensibility (Lean: `Classicism.weaklyRigid_of_rigid`, `Classicism.weaklyPersistent_of_persistent`, `Classicism.weaklyInextensible_of_inextensible`). **Lemma (rigidity, if true, is necessary).** `rigid-necessary` If $X$ is rigid, then $\Box\operatorname{Rigid}(X)$. *Proof.* $\operatorname{Rigid}(X)$ is $\Box\operatorname{WeaklyRigid}(X)$, and [[modal-four|4]] gives $\Box\Box\operatorname{WeaklyRigid}(X)$, which is $\Box\operatorname{Rigid}(X)$. $\square$ *Lean:* `Classicism.rigid_necessary` **Lemma (weakly rigid relations are persistent).** `weakly-rigid-persistent` A weakly rigid relation is persistent: weak inextensibility applied to $\lambda\bar x\, .\,\Box Y[\bar x]$, whose hypothesis $Y[\bar x]\to\Box\Box Y[\bar x]$ holds by weak persistence and 4, gives $Y\le\lambda\bar x\, .\,\Box Y[\bar x]$. So weak rigidity is equivalently persistence together with weak inextensibility, the combination used in the draft's Proposition 1. *Sources:* Dorr, Boolean Completeness does not imply Rigid Comprehension, draft of 30 July 2026 *Lean:* `Classicism.persistent_of_weaklyRigid` **Lemma (coextensive weakly rigid relations are identical).** `coextensive-weakly-rigid-identical` If $F$ and $G$ are weakly rigid and coextensive, then $F=G$. *Proof.* Each is below the other: $F\le G$ by weak inextensibility of $F$, since each instance of $F$ is an instance of $G$ and so, by weak persistence of $G$, necessarily one; and $G\le F$ likewise. Since $\le$ is antisymmetric, $F=G$. $\square$ *Lean:* `Classicism.eq_of_weaklyRigid_coext` ### Closure properties The lemmas below use no BF, choice, ND or comprehension. That BF at $\sigma$ makes $\lambda z^\sigma\, .\,\top$ weakly rigid, and □BF makes it rigid, are forms of [[barcan-r|BF]] and [[necessary-barcan-r|□BF]]. **Lemma (haecceities are rigid).** `haecceities-rigid` For every $x^\sigma$, the haecceity $H_x=\lambda y\, .\,y=x$ is rigid. *Proof.* It is persistent by [[identity-necessary-r|NI]]. For inextensibility, suppose, at any world, that $\forall y\, .\,y=x\to\Box Zy$. Then $\Box Zx$, and so $\Box\forall y\, .\,y=x\to Zy$, which is $H_x\le Z$. $\square$ *Credit:* GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), prompted by Daniel Kodsi, 22 October 2026 *Lean:* `Classicism.Rigidity.singleton_rigid` **Lemma (rigid unions of rigid families).** `rigid-indexed-union` If $R^{\sigma t}$ is rigid and $F^{\sigma\tau t}$ is such that $Fx$ is rigid for every $x$ with $Rx$, then the union $U:=\lambda y\, .\,\exists x\, .\,Rx\land(Fx)y$ is rigid. *Proof.* First, necessarily every instance of $R$ has a rigid fiber. For each $x$ with $Rx$, $Fx$ is rigid and so, by [[rigid-necessary]], necessarily rigid; so by the inextensibility of $R$, $R\le\lambda x\, .\,\operatorname{Rigid}(Fx)$. Now argue at an arbitrary world, where $R$ is weakly rigid and each instance of $R$ has a rigid fiber. *Weak persistence:* if $Uy$, take $x$ with $Rx$ and $(Fx)y$; then $\Box Rx$ and $\Box(Fx)y$, so $\Box Uy$. *Weak inextensibility:* suppose $\forall y\, .\,Uy\to\Box Zy$. For each $x$ with $Rx$, $\forall y\, .\,(Fx)y\to\Box Zy$, so $Fx\le Z$ by the inextensibility of $Fx$; that is, $\Box(\forall y\, .\,(Fx)y\to Zy)$. By the weak inextensibility of $R$, $R\le\lambda x\, .\,\forall y\, .\,(Fx)y\to Zy$, which gives $U\le Z$. Both hold at every world, so $U$ is rigid. $\square$ *Credit:* GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), prompted by Daniel Kodsi, 22 October 2026 *Lean:* `Classicism.Rigidity.indexed_union_rigid` **Lemma (rigidity is preserved by direct images).** `rigid-direct-image` If $R^{\sigma t}$ is rigid and $f^{\sigma\tau}$ is an operation ($\tau\ne e$), then $\lambda y\, .\,\exists x\, .\,Rx\land y=fx$ is rigid. *Proof.* It is the union of the haecceities $H_{fx}$ over the instances of $R$, rigid by [[haecceities-rigid]] and [[rigid-indexed-union]]. $\square$ *Credit:* GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), prompted by Daniel Kodsi, 22 October 2026 *Lean:* `Classicism.Rigidity.direct_image_rigid` **Lemma (rigidity is preserved by inverse images under necessarily injective operations).** `rigid-inverse-image` If $P^{\tau t}$ is rigid, every instance of $P$ is a value of $f^{\sigma\tau}$ ($\tau\ne e$), and $f$ is necessarily injective, then $\lambda x\, .\,P(fx)$ is rigid. *Proof.* Persistence is inherited from $P$. Being a value of $f$ is necessary if true, by [[identity-necessary-r|NI]], so the inextensibility of $P$ makes every instance of $P$ necessarily a value of $f$. For inextensibility, suppose, at a world, that $\forall x\, .\,P(fx)\to\Box Zx$, and put $Z':=\lambda y\, .\,\forall x\, .\,y=fx\to Zx$. If $Py$, then $y=fx_0$ for some $x_0$, so $\Box Zx_0$; since $f$ is necessarily injective, necessarily every $x$ with $fx=fx_0$ is $x_0$, so $\Box Z'y$. By the inextensibility of $P$, $P\le Z'$, and so $\Box\forall x\, .\,P(fx)\to Zx$. Both the range condition and injectivity keep their modal scopes. $\square$ *Credit:* GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), prompted by Daniel Kodsi, 22 October 2026 *Lean:* `Classicism.Rigidity.inverse_image_rigid` ## Varieties of necessity Strong Possibility uses the distinctness-preserving modality of §2.6, p. 42: $$ \Box_{\ne}p:=\exists q\, .\,q\land\Box(\Diamond q\to p), \qquad \Diamond_{\ne}p:=\neg\Box_{\ne}\neg p. $$ **Hats, two-hat necessity and 5-necessity.** For an operator $X^{tt}$ put $$ \hat X:=\lambda p\, .\,\exists q\, .\,q\land\Box(\neg X\neg q\to p). $$ In C, $\hat\Box=\Box_{\ne}$ (*The Bounds of Possibility*, Appendix D, Proposition D17). *Two-hat necessity* is the hat of $\Box_{\ne}$, written $\hat{\hat\Box}$, with dual $\hat{\hat\Diamond}p:=\neg\hat{\hat\Box}\neg p$. Call $X^{tt}$ an *S5 operator* when, necessarily, it is N, K and B: $$ \operatorname{S5}(X):=\Box\bigl(\forall p\, .\,\Box p\to Xp\bigr)\land \Box\bigl(\forall p\,q\, .\,X(p\to q)\to Xp\to Xq\bigr)\land \Box\bigl(\forall p\, .\,p\to X\neg X\neg p\bigr). $$ *5-necessity* is necessity under every S5 operator, $\Box_5:=\lambda p\, .\,\forall X^{tt}\, .\,\operatorname{S5}(X)\to Xp$, with dual $\Diamond_5$. Appendix D defines $\Box_5$ with the condition NKJF$_{\langle\rangle}$ in place of NKB; its facts (A5) and (C5) make the two definitions necessarily equivalent. Theorems of C: $\Box\le\Box_{\ne}\le\hat{\hat\Box}\le\Box_5\le\lambda p\, .\,p$ (the order is necessary pointwise implication) (Lean: `Classicism.box_le_boxNe`, `Classicism.boxNe_le_boxHH`, `Classicism.boxHH_le_box5`, `Classicism.box5_le`); each of these operators is necessarily N, K, T and 4, and $\Box_5$ is an S5 operator; and if $\Box_{\ne}$ or $\hat{\hat\Box}$ is identical to its own hat, it is identical to $\Box_5$. ### Appendix D of *The Bounds of Possibility* Dorr, Hawthorne and Yli-Vakkuri, *The Bounds of Possibility* (2021), Appendix D, *Narrower Modalities in Higher-Order S4*, pp. 400–409, reads into C: the appendix's primitive $\Box$ is C's $\lambda p\, .\,p=\top$, under which every theorem of its $\mathrm H_{S4}$ is a theorem of C. Only the propositions the map uses are given here, and F and I are stated at type $t$ only. Operators are of type $tt$. **Definition (properties of operators).** `appendix-d-operator-properties` For $X^{tt}$: $$ \begin{aligned} \mathrm N\,X&:=\forall p\, .\,\Box p\to Xp, & \mathrm K\,X&:=\forall p\,q\, .\,X(p\to q)\to Xp\to Xq,\\ \mathrm J\,X&:=\forall p\, .\,p\to X\Diamond p, & \mathrm F_{\langle\rangle}X&:=\forall Y^{tt}\, .\,(\forall z\, .\,X(Yz))\to X\forall z\, .\,Yz, \end{aligned} $$ and NK, NKJ and NKJF$_{\langle\rangle}$ are the conjunctions; F$_{\langle\rangle}$ is BF for $X$ at type $t$. The appendix's 5-necessity is $\Box_5^{\mathrm A}:=\lambda p\, .\,\forall X\, .\,\Box\,\mathrm{NKJF}_{\langle\rangle}X\to Xp$, and $W_@a:=a\land\forall q\, .\,q\to\Box(a\to q)$ says that $a$ is the actual world. *Sources:* The Bounds of Possibility, Appendix D, p. 400 and p. 407 **Proposition (D1, at type $t$).** `appendix-d-d1` If $X$ is NKJ, then $y\ne z\to X(y\ne z)$ for $y,z$ of type $t$, and dually $\neg X\neg(y=z)\to y=z$. *Proof.* J gives $X\Diamond(y\ne z)$, and necessarily $\Diamond(y\ne z)\to y\ne z$ (Lean: `Classicism.ne_of_dia_ne`), so N and K give $X(y\ne z)$. $\square$ *Credit:* Cian Dorr, John Hawthorne and Juhani Yli-Vakkuri *Sources:* The Bounds of Possibility, Appendix D *Lean:* `Classicism.AppD.prop_D1`, `Classicism.AppD.prop_D1_dual` **Proposition (D11).** `appendix-d-d11` For every operator $X$: $p\to\hat X\neg X\neg p$, and $\neg\hat X\neg Xp\to p$. Only the actual extensions of admissible properties matter, so two predicates with the same admissible extensions give the same lemma. ## Cardinality, arithmetic and analysis The Axiom of Infinity is stated with Frege's cardinality apparatus. At a type $\sigma$, a *cardinality* is an entity of type $(\sigma t)t$, and: $$ \begin{aligned} \mathbf{0}_\sigma&:=\lambda X^{\sigma t}\, .\,\forall u^\sigma\, .\,\neg Xu,\\ \operatorname{Suc}_\sigma(Z)&:=\lambda X^{\sigma t}\, .\,\exists y^\sigma\, .\, Xy\land Z(\lambda u^\sigma\, .\,Xu\land u\ne y),\\ \operatorname{FiniteCardinality}_\sigma(Z)&:=\forall W^{((\sigma t)t)t}\, .\, \bigl(W\mathbf{0}_\sigma\land\forall Y\, .\,WY\to W(\operatorname{Suc}_\sigma Y)\bigr)\to WZ. \end{aligned} $$ So $\mathbf{0}_\sigma$ is the cardinality of the empty property, $\operatorname{Suc}_\sigma$ adds one to a cardinality, and $\operatorname{FiniteCardinality}_\sigma$ collects the cardinalities reached from $\mathbf{0}_\sigma$ by finitely many successors, in the impredicative sense that they fall under every property of cardinalities that holds of $\mathbf{0}_\sigma$ and of a successor whenever it holds of the cardinality succeeded. In C, $\mathbf{0}_\sigma$ and the successor of a finite cardinality are finite cardinalities, and a finite cardinality that holds of a property holds of every property coextensive with it (Lean: `Classicism.finiteCardinality_zero`, `Classicism.finiteCardinality_suc`, `Classicism.finiteCardinality_coext`). Every type used here ends in $t$, so all of them are admitted, and no type $\sigma\sigma$ is needed; that is why the axiom is not put in the Dedekind form, which would ask for an injective non-surjective operation from $\sigma$ to $\sigma$. Countable Boolean Completeness and the Necessity of Arithmetic follow Goodsell, *Arithmetic is Necessary*, which leaves the type $\nu$ of numbers, zero and successor as parameters. The map takes them, at each type $\sigma$, to be $\nu_\sigma:=(\sigma t)t$, $\mathbf{0}_\sigma$ and $\operatorname{Suc}_\sigma$, and states both principles as schemata in $\sigma$; the paper displays the instance $\sigma=e$ in its eqs. (24)–(25) without assuming it. Natural numberhood $\mathbb N_\sigma$ is then $\operatorname{FiniteCardinality}_\sigma$. Write $\forall n\in\mathbb N_\sigma\, .\,A$ for $\forall n^{\nu_\sigma}\, .\,\mathbb N_\sigma n\to A$, and likewise for $\exists$. With these, for a type $\sigma$ and a relational type $\tau$: $$ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{Ctbl}_{\sigma,\tau}(X)&:=\exists R^{\tau\nu_\sigma t}\, .\,\forall y^\tau z^\tau\, .\, Xy\land Xz\to\bigl((\exists n\in\mathbb N_\sigma\, .\,Ryn\land Rzn)\leftrightarrow y=z\bigr),\\ I^*_\sigma&:=\forall m\,n\in\mathbb N_\sigma\, .\,\mathbf{0}_\sigma\ne\operatorname{Suc}_\sigma m\land (\operatorname{Suc}_\sigma m=\operatorname{Suc}_\sigma n\to m=n),\qquad I_\sigma:=\Diamond I^*_\sigma,\\ \operatorname{Sum}_\sigma(m,n,o)&:=\forall R^{\nu_\sigma\nu_\sigma t}\, .\,R\mathbf{0}_\sigma m\to (\forall i\,j\in\mathbb N_\sigma\, .\,Rij\to R(\operatorname{Suc}_\sigma i)(\operatorname{Suc}_\sigma j))\to Rno,\\ \operatorname{Prod}_\sigma(m,n,o)&:=\forall R^{\nu_\sigma\nu_\sigma t}\, .\,R\mathbf{0}_\sigma\mathbf{0}_\sigma\to (\forall i\,j\,k\in\mathbb N_\sigma\, .\,Rij\to\operatorname{Sum}_\sigma(m,j,k)\to R(\operatorname{Suc}_\sigma i)k)\to Rno. \end{aligned} $$ So $X$ is countable (relative to $\sigma$) when it injects into the natural numbers counted at $\sigma$, and $I_\sigma$ says that possibly zero is not a successor and successor is injective on numbers. In C the first conjunct of $I^*_\sigma$ is a theorem, since $\mathbf{0}_\sigma$ and a successor differ at $\lambda x^\sigma\, .\,\bot$. An *arithmetical sentence* at $\sigma$ is a closed formula built from atomic formulas $\mathbb N_\sigma\mathbf n$, $\operatorname{Sum}_\sigma(\mathbf m,\mathbf n,\mathbf o)$, $\operatorname{Prod}_\sigma(\mathbf m,\mathbf n,\mathbf o)$ and $\mathbf m=\mathbf n$, whose terms are variables of type $\nu_\sigma$, $\mathbf{0}_\sigma$ and successors of terms, by $\neg$, $\lor$, $\land$ and quantifiers $\forall v\in\mathbb N_\sigma$. These are Definitions 3–8 of Goodsell's draft. Where the type is fixed by context the subscript $\sigma$ is dropped. **Analysis.** A *real number structure* at a type $\sigma$ is a tuple $\mathfrak R=(X^{\sigma t},\le^{\sigma\sigma t},+^{\sigma\sigma\sigma t}, \times^{\sigma\sigma\sigma t},0^\sigma,1^\sigma,N^{\sigma t})$ such that $\le$, $+$ and $\times$ hold only of instances of $X$, $X$ with them and with $0$ and $1$ is a complete ordered field, $+$ and $\times$ being functional on $X$ and every nonempty subproperty of $X$ with an upper bound in $X$ having a least upper bound in $X$, and $N$ is the least subproperty of $X$ containing $0$ and closed under adding $1$; write $\operatorname{Real}_\sigma(\mathfrak R)$. Any two real number structures, at one type or at two, are isomorphic (Huntington), a theorem of the non-modal fragment. A *first-order analytical sentence* is a closed formula in the variables of a real number structure built from the atomic formulas $x\le y$, $+(x,y,z)$, $\times(x,y,z)$, $Nx$ and $x=y$, whose terms are variables of type $\sigma$, $0$ and $1$, by $\neg$, $\lor$, $\land$ and quantifiers $\forall v\in X$; a *second-order analytical sentence* may also use variables $R$ for relations of any finite arity among entities of type $\sigma$, in atomic formulas $R\bar x$ and unrestricted quantifiers $\forall R$. For a sentence $A$, $A(\mathfrak R)$ is its reading in $\mathfrak R$. These follow Barton and Goodsell, *Continuum Contingency*, §5.7, with the structure's elements in place of their rigid properties of numbers, and Bacon's second-order analysis (*Could the truths of mathematics have been different?*, Appendix C.2) without his restriction of the second-order quantifiers to rigid properties, which makes no difference under Rigid Comprehension (his Proposition C.3). The *continuum hypothesis* $\operatorname{CH}(\mathfrak R)$ is the second-order analytical sentence $\forall Y^{\sigma t}\, .\,(\forall x\, .\,Yx\to Xx)\to (Y\precsim N\lor Y\approx X)$, where $Y\precsim Z$ says that some relation is an injection from the $Y$s into the $Z$s and $Y\approx Z$ that some relation is a bijection between them. A real number structure is *rigid*, $\operatorname{RigidStr}(\mathfrak R)$, when $X$, $\le$, $+$, $\times$ and $N$ are rigid and the instances of $X$ are necessarily distinct, $\forall x\,y\in X\, .\,x\ne y\to\Box\,x\ne y$. A *represented power* of arity $k$ for $X$, $\operatorname{RepPower}_k(\mathcal P,X)$, is a rigid property $\mathcal P$ of rigid $k$-ary relations holding only of tuples of instances of $X$, such that necessarily every $k$-ary relation agrees on such tuples with an instance of $\mathcal P$: $\operatorname{Rigid}(\mathcal P)\land (\forall S\, .\,\mathcal PS\to\operatorname{Rigid}(S)\land\forall\bar y\, .\,S\bar y\to\textstyle\bigwedge_iXy_i)\land \Box\forall R\,\exists S\, .\,\mathcal PS\land\forall\bar x\in X\, .\,(S\bar x\leftrightarrow R\bar x)$. The schematic $\sigma$ is what lets the principles say what they intend whatever the size of a given type. Where $\sigma$ necessarily has only finitely many members, $\mathbb N_\sigma$ is finite, a property countable relative to $\sigma$ is finite and so has a least upper bound in C, and $I_\sigma$ is necessarily false; those instances are trivial. ## Signatures and sentence schemata **Pure and signature schemata.** In Maximalism, in its distinctness form and its possibility form alike, $C$ denotes the fixed background logic. Its theoremhood and consistency side conditions are retained literally. “Pure” means free of nonlogical constants. The principles in the Signature schemata group give a special role to nonlogical constants: they concern an arbitrary fixed signature $\Sigma$ of nonlogical constants of admitted types, with $\mathcal L(\Sigma)$ and $C(\Sigma)$ the language and background theory over $\Sigma$. When $\Sigma$ is empty, some of these schemata have no instances or only trivial ones, and the others reduce to their pure versions; the results relating them need a constant of a type $\tau\ne e$, so $\Sigma$ is assumed to contain one. Nothing further is assumed: no nonlogical axioms about the constants are standing assumptions, and “distinct constants” means distinct symbols, not an assumed inequality between their denotations. Where a schema mentions a tuple of distinct constants, its instances are those the signature supplies. ## The Lean formalisation The map's [Lean project](lean/) formalises C in base Lean 4 and checks many of the map's claims. A **Lean ✓** on a result, on a model's verdict, or on a lemma on these pages means that a proof has passed an audit. This page says what each audit establishes. The project's own README has the details. ### Classicism as a theory in Lean The *shallow layer* treats C as a theory in Lean itself. Individuals form a type `e`, `Prop` plays the role of $t$, and the classes `Ty` and `Rel` mark the Lean types that are types of the relational type system and the relational types among them. $\Box p$ is $p=\top$, as on [[necessity]]. Lean's rules for the connectives, the quantifiers and identity are the rules of H, short of two things that the library adds as axioms: excluded middle (`em`) and the existence of an individual (`e_exists`). Lean's own three axioms are principles of the map, and none is a theorem of C: | Lean axiom | Principle on the map | | --- | --- | | `propext` | Fregean Axiom | | `funext` | Functionality | | `Classical.choice` | Functional Choice, and more | The rule of Logical Equivalence is rendered as a restriction on the first two, the *gate*: `propext h` and `funext h` may appear only when the proof `h` is closed, using no hypothesis. Applied to a closed proof they are exactly the rules C is closed under; applied to a hypothesis they would be the Fregean Axiom and Functionality. `#classicism_check` audits a shallow proof: it rests only on `propext`, `funext`, `e`, `e_exists` and `em`, and it passes the gate. It also reports whether the proof avoids `e_exists`, and so is a theorem of C⁻, the theory without Existence at $e$. No formula quantifies over types. A principle is a family of formulas indexed by types, and a lemma is a theorem with type parameters, a schema in the sense of [[framework|the conventions]]. ### Lemmas on these pages A lemma's **Lean ✓** badge opens a menu linking the shallow theorems that prove it. The ✓ means that each of them passes `#classicism_check`, and the menu says whether the lemma is a theorem of C or of C⁻. A badge in the running text, after a claim such as "$\le_\tau$ is a partial order", opens the same kind of menu for the theorems that prove that claim. Shallow proofs elsewhere in the library use these theorems directly. Whether a Lean statement says what the prose says is checked by reading the two together. ### Results and their certificates The *metalogical layer* makes the object language into Lean data: terms over a signature, derivability in C, and models. A result $A_1,\ldots,A_n\Rightarrow B$ is stated, by a statement generated from the records, as an entailment between schemas: for every admitted signature $\Sigma$ and every set of sentences over $\Sigma$, if it entails each $A_i$ then it entails $B$. An incompatibility concludes instead that the set is inconsistent. Each principle's schema comes from its record's Lean definition. A result's certificate usually comes from a shallow proof, which a translator turns into a derivation in the object language. Stating results metalogically lets ordinary principles, schematic only in their types, be treated like the principles whose instances are sentences picked out by a condition on syntax, such as No Pure Contingency and Maximalism, which no shallow formula with type parameters can state. `lean-check` confirms that each certificate proves its generated statement in ordinary classical Lean, the metatheory, with no `sorry`. ### Models A model's verdict is stated as the existence of a consistent, complete theory, deciding every sentence, that entails the principles the model satisfies and none of those it violates. The proof constructs the model, an action model or another of the map's constructions, and applies the soundness theorem. ### The strict layer A third layer re-proves the shallow theorems from the eleven closed identities of *Classicism*, carrying out its Appendix A on Lean proof terms. It explores how the paper's type system sits inside Lean's and is not on the route to any certificate. ### Where things are | What | Where in the Lean project | | --- | --- | | The language, the gate, the axioms | `Classicism/Core.lean`, `Equivalence.lean` | | The lemmas of these pages, a module per page | `Classicism/Background/` | | The map's principles | `Classicism/Principles/` | | The shallow proofs of results | `Classicism/Results/Records/` | | The object language and its models | `Classicism/Syntax/`, `Classicism/Semantics/`, `Classicism/Models/` | | The certificates | `Classicism/Map.lean`, `MapModels.lean`, `MapDerived.lean`, `MapArguments.lean` | | The statements they prove | `Classicism/Statements.lean`, `ModelStatements.lean`, generated from the records | ## Literature ### Source literature - Bacon, Andrew, and Cian Dorr (2024). Classicism. In Peter Fritz and Nicholas K. Jones (eds), Higher-Order Metaphysics, Oxford University Press, pp. 109–190. (1946). A Functional Calculus of First Order Based on Strict Implication. Journal of Symbolic Logic 11, 1–16. Bibliography and attribution as given in Classicism. - Prior, A. N. (1963). Formal Logic. Oxford University Press. Pages 206–207, as credited in Classicism, Proposition 2.2. - Prior, A. N. (1956). Modality and Quantification in S5. Journal of Symbolic Logic 21(1), 60–62. See also Prior (1967), Past, Present, and Future, p. 146, crediting E. J. Lemmon’s simplified proof. Attribution as given in Classicism, Proposition 2.3. - Gallin, Daniel (1975). Intensional and Higher-Order Modal Logic: With Applications to Montague Semantics. North-Holland. Page 77, as cited in Classicism, n. 37. - Bacon, Andrew (2020). Logical Combinatorialism. # Contribute

Thanks to Cian Dorr for major contributions to Classicism + Logical Maps!

Email me (Zach) at [zacharyw.goodsell@gmail.com](mailto:zacharyw.goodsell@gmail.com?subject=%5BLogical%20Maps%5D%20Classicism) with further suggestions. To contribute to Classicism, please include **[Logical Maps] Classicism** in the subject line of your email. You can suggest a new principle, establish a new result, or define a new model, along with supporting documents if necessary (e.g. a PDF or Markdown file).
