shared_arguments.text: Write $w$ for the evaluation object and $k$ for an arrow out of it with no retraction. No entity $x$ of a relational type at $w$ is determined by its transport along $k$: the identity of $w$ is not of the form $j\circ k$, such a $j$ being a retraction, and the model being full, the intension $y$ agreeing with $x$ at every arrow but the identity, where it takes another value, is in the domain, while $k\cdot y=k\cdot x$, transport along $k$ reading only the values at the arrows after $k$. Suppose then that $\mathfrak R$ were a rigid real number structure at $w$ at a relational type, necessarily a real number structure (Background, Analysis), with carrier $X$. Take the regular-open algebra $B$ of Cantor space: a complete atomless Boolean algebra in ZF, of the size of the continuum, which therefore injects into the propositions while the propositions do not inject into it (Cantor), so that, realised as a property of propositions with its order as a relation among them, both present since the model is full, it is an internal complete Boolean algebra that is small. But the entailment algebra below a nonzero proposition is atomic, every nonempty set of arrows including a singleton, and the one below $\bot$ has one element; neither is isomorphic to an infinite atomless algebra. So Forcing Possibilism fails. No choice is used: the injection into the arrows is given by the condition, and Cantor's theorem and the completeness of the regular-open algebra hold in ZF.

shared_arguments.text: At type $\tau:=tt$. With one object, an intension whose value is the same at every arrow is in the domain by the condition, and it is fixed by transport along every arrow: $(h\cdot Y)_j=Y_{jh}=Y_j$. The propositions are infinitely many, so the constant intensions $Y_E$, for $E$ a set of propositions, are at least continuum many and pairwise distinct. Carry the real numbers onto continuum many of them, and take as carrier, order, sum, product, $0$, $1$ and natural numbers the constant intensions whose values are the corresponding sets of tuples of the $Y_E$. All parameters are fixed, so a formula about them has the same truth value at every world, and at the evaluation point they form a real number structure: any bounded set of carrier elements has a least upper bound among them, and every inductive subproperty contains the copy of the natural numbers. Such a structure is rigid, its instances are necessarily distinct, and it is necessarily a real number structure; and the codomain-only intension of type $((\tau)^kt)t$ whose value at each object is the set of codomain-only $k$-ary relations among the carrier there is a represented power of arity $k$, since at every world each $k$-ary relation agrees on the carrier with one of them. So the consequents of Analytic Necessitism and of its second-order form hold, and both principles hold. (The argument of the withdrawn analytic-necessitism-unretracted-arrow would refute this structure; its step from inextensibility is the gap.)

shared_arguments.text: Write $w$ for the evaluation object and $k$ for an arrow out of it with no retraction. No entity $x$ of a relational type at $w$ is determined by its transport along $k$: the identity of $w$ is not of the form $j\circ k$, such a $j$ being a retraction, and the model being full, the intension $y$ agreeing with $x$ at every arrow but the identity, where it takes another value, is in the domain, while $k\cdot y=k\cdot x$, transport along $k$ reading only the values at the arrows after $k$. Suppose then that $\mathfrak R$ were a rigid real number structure at $w$ at a relational type, necessarily a real number structure (Background, Analysis), with carrier $X$. For an instance $x$ of $X$ and $y$ as above, persistence gives $k\cdot x\in X_k$, so $k\cdot y\in X_k$; inextensibility then gives $Xy$; and the necessary distinctness of the instances gives $k\cdot y\ne k\cdot x$, a contradiction. So $X$ has no instance and is no complete ordered field. The antecedent of Analytic Necessitism holds nevertheless, at some relational type. The propositions at $w$ are the sets of the infinitely many arrows out of it, the sets of sets of propositions are Dedekind-infinite (a theorem of ZF for any infinite set), and the entities of type $ttt$ at $w$, which include one with any given extension at the identity, include a copy of the sets of natural numbers and so of the real numbers; the model being full, the order, sum and product of the reals are the extensions at the identity of relations in the domain, every subset of that carrier is the extension of a subproperty, so the structure is complete, and its least inductive subproperty is its natural numbers. So $\exists\mathfrak R\,.\,\operatorname{Real}_{ttt}(\mathfrak R)$ holds at $w$ while the consequent of Analytic Necessitism fails there: Analytic Necessitism fails. (When the arrows out of $w$ include a copy of the natural numbers, as in the recorded instances, the same argument runs at type $t$.) No choice is used.

shared_arguments.text: In a full action model the propositions at the evaluation object are all the sets of arrows out of it, so the algebra of propositions is atomic, the singletons being its atoms, and it has $2^{|A|}$ elements for $A$ the set of those arrows. Since the sets of natural numbers inject into $A$, the sets of sets of natural numbers inject into the propositions. Take the regular-open algebra $B$ of Cantor space: a complete atomless Boolean algebra in ZF, of the size of the continuum, which therefore injects into the propositions while the propositions do not inject into it (Cantor), so that, realised as a property of propositions with its order as a relation among them, both present since the model is full, it is an internal complete Boolean algebra that is small. Forcing Possibilism would give a proposition $p\ne\top$ whose entailment algebra is isomorphic to $B$. But the entailment algebra below a nonzero proposition is atomic, every nonempty set of arrows including a singleton, and the one below $\bot$ has one element; neither is isomorphic to an infinite atomless algebra. So Forcing Possibilism fails. No choice is used: the injection into the arrows is given by the condition, and Cantor's theorem and the completeness of the regular-open algebra hold in ZF.

shared_arguments.text: As in the argument analytic-necessitism-unretracted-arrow, with the individuals supplying the real numbers in place of the propositions. Let $k$ be an arrow out of the evaluation object $w$ with no retraction; as there, the model being full, no entity of a relational type at $w$ is determined by its transport along $k$, so no rigid real number structure of a relational type at $w$ is necessarily a real number structure. But there is a real number structure at $w$ of the relational type $((et)t)t$: the individuals at $w$ are infinitely many, the sets of sets of individuals are Dedekind-infinite (a theorem of ZF for any infinite set), so the entities of type $(et)t$, which include one with any given set of properties of individuals as extension at the identity, include a copy of the natural numbers, and the entities of type $((et)t)t$ a copy of the sets of natural numbers, hence of the reals; the full domains equip that copy, at the identity, with the order, sum, product and natural numbers of the reals, and the structure is complete, every subset of its carrier being the extension of a subproperty. The antecedents $\Diamond\exists\mathfrak R\,.\,\operatorname{Real}_\sigma(\mathfrak R)$ of Analytic Necessitism and of Second-Order Analytic Necessitism are therefore false at every type, and both hold; and $\Box\forall\mathfrak R\,.\,\operatorname{Real}_\sigma(\mathfrak R)\to A(\mathfrak R)$ holds for every sentence $A$, so the Necessity of Second-Order Analysis holds, with the Necessity of Analysis and the Non-contingency of the Continuum Hypothesis. No choice is used.

shared_arguments.text: At a cloud point $t$ every proposition is identical to $\top$ or to $\bot$ (Remark 4.6(iv)), and Atom $q$ holds at $t$ exactly when $q$ holds at $t$: if $t\in q$, then at every refinement $t^{\prime}$ a $z\le q$ is distinct from $q$ there iff $z$ is bottom there; if $t\notin q$, some refinement has $q=\bot$, where Atom $q$ fails, and holding persists. So a proposition not containing the root is a self-atom at the root whenever it is nonzero, and $\{r\}$ is an atom; every possible proposition has one of these below it, and Self-Atomicity (type t) holds at the root. At relational types, a possible $X$ at any point has, by no new entities (Lemma 4.3), an actual tuple $\bar x$ with $X\bar x$ possible; $Y:=\lambda\bar y\, .\,\bar y=\bar x\land X\bar x$ lies below $X$, is possible, and has at most one instance at every point, which at a cloud point where it is instantiated makes it an atom there (its parts are $\{\bar x\}$ cut down by propositions, and such a part differs from $Y$ at a refinement exactly when it is bottom there); so $Y$ is a self-atom. At cloud points every possible $X$ likewise has such a $Y$ below it, so Self-Atomicity holds at every point and every type. Self-atoms are atoms (type t) fails at the root: the set of points of an atomless component is a self-atom, and by Theorem 4.4(d) no atom lies below it.

shared_arguments.text: At type $\tau:=tt$. For each object $V$ reachable from the evaluation point fix an injection $A\mapsto E^A_V$ from the sets of natural numbers into the sets of propositions at $V$, possible as these are infinitely many, and let $Y_A$ be the intension whose value at an arrow into $V$ is $E^A_V$: it depends only on the codomain, so it is in the domain, and its transport along an arrow into $V$ is the $Y_A$ of $V$, distinct for distinct $A$. Carry the real numbers onto the $Y_A$ and take as relations the codomain-only intensions whose value at $V$ is the corresponding set of tuples of the $Y_A$ of $V$. Along every arrow the structure is carried to the like structure at the target, an isomorphic copy, which is a real number structure there: bounded sets of its elements have least upper bounds among them and every inductive subproperty contains its natural numbers. Such a structure is rigid, its instances are necessarily distinct, and it is necessarily a real number structure; and the codomain-only intension of type $((\tau)^kt)t$ whose value at each object is the set of codomain-only $k$-ary relations among the carrier there is a represented power of arity $k$, since at every world each $k$-ary relation agrees on the carrier with one of them. So the consequents of Analytic Necessitism and of its second-order form hold, and both principles hold. (The argument of the withdrawn analytic-necessitism-unretracted-arrow would refute this structure; its step from inextensibility is the gap.)

At any object $v$ reachable from the evaluation point, extensional fullness gives a property whose extension at $v$ is exactly the numerals there; it contains $\mathbf 0_\sigma$ and is closed under successor, so the numbers at $v$ are exactly the numerals, every numeral being an instance of every inductive property. Persistence of $\mathbb N_\sigma$ and, given $\Box I^*_\sigma$, the necessary distinctness of the numbers are theorems of C (the proof of necessary-rigid-comprehension-implies-arithmetic-necessitism). Inextensibility, $\Box\forall X\,.\,(\forall n\,.\,\mathbb N_\sigma n\to\Box Xn)\to\mathbb N_\sigma\le X$: at a reachable $v$ and for an arrow $j$ from $v$ to $u$, the numbers at $u$ are the numerals there, which are the transports along $j$ of the numbers at $v$, so any $X$ that necessarily holds of the numbers at $v$ holds at $u$ of the numbers there. So $\mathbb N_\sigma$ is rigid, and Arithmetic Necessitism holds at every type. No choice is used.

shared_arguments.text: For each object $U$ and type $\sigma$ fix a well-ordering $<_U$ of the domain $D^\sigma_U$, and let $W$ be the intension of type $\sigma\to\sigma\to t$ with $W(h):={<_{\operatorname{cod}h}}$. Its value depends only on the arrow's codomain, so by the condition it is in the domain, and at every world its extension well-orders that world's type-$\sigma$ domain. Given $F$ with $\Box\exists x\, .\,Fx$, put $G:=\lambda x\, .\,Fx\land\forall y\, .\,(Fy\to\neg Wyx)$, the $W$-least $F$. It is definable from $F$ and $W$, so in the domain; $G\le F$, and its extension at every arrow is the singleton of the least element of $F$'s. So Intensional Choice holds, and the same at every reachable object gives $\Box$Intensional Choice. Cian Dorr's observation that such models are qualitatively full, made precise.

Using the axiom of choice, pick for each $x$ a $y$ with $(x,y)$ in the extension of $U$ at the identity, and let $S$ be the intension whose value at every arrow $W\to W$ is the graph of this choice and whose value at arrows with any other codomain is empty; it depends only on the codomain, so the condition puts it in the domain, and at the identity it is a functional subrelation of $U$. Likewise a set of representatives of an equivalence relation at $W$, made into such an intension, is a transversal. Since $W$ was any reachable object, both principles hold at every world.

shared_arguments.text: Let $v$ be any object reachable from the evaluation point and $\mathfrak R$ a real number structure at $v$ (Background, Analysis). Its completeness is tested against the subproperties of its carrier present at $v$, and by extensional fullness every subset of the carrier's extension there is the extension at the identity of one of them; so the carrier, with the extensions of $\le$, $+$ and $\times$, is a complete ordered field in the sense of the metatheory and, by Huntington's theorem, a theorem of ZF, is isomorphic to the real numbers. For the same reason the extension of $N$, the least subproperty containing $0$ and closed under adding $1$, is its set of natural numbers, that set being the extension of a subproperty. A second-order analytical sentence $A(\mathfrak R)$ quantifies over the relations among entities of the structure's type at $v$, applied to the structure's elements, and their extensions at the identity are all the relations on the carrier, again by extensional fullness. So $A(\mathfrak R)$ holds at $v$ exactly when $A$ holds in the real numbers under full second-order semantics, which depends neither on $v$ nor on $\mathfrak R$. Hence $\Box\forall\mathfrak R\,.\,\operatorname{Real}_\sigma(\mathfrak R)\to A(\mathfrak R)$ holds when $A$ is true of the reals and $\Box\forall\mathfrak R\,.\,\operatorname{Real}_\sigma(\mathfrak R)\to\neg A(\mathfrak R)$ when it is false: every instance of the Necessity of Second-Order Analysis holds, and with it the Necessity of Analysis and the Non-contingency of the Continuum Hypothesis, as recorded. No choice is used.

Write $\mathrm{fix}^{WW}_N$ for the arrows $W\to W$ agreeing with the identity on the finite set $N$, the least true proposition at $W$ pinned by $N$. For a proposition $q$ at the evaluation object put $C_0(q):=\Diamond q$ and $C_{n+1}(q):=\{u : \text{for every } r \text{ true at } \mathrm{trg}(u) \text{ some } v \text{ has } vu\in q \text{ and } v\in C_n(r)\}$; then $\hat\Diamond q=C_1(q)$, $\hat{\hat\Diamond}q=C_2(q)$, and $\hat{(n+1)}\Box\,s$ holds at the identity iff $C_n(q)\subseteq s$ for some true $q$ (the game form of the hat tower, conversation of 14 October 2026). At $1_{W_0}$ both $C_0(\mathrm{fix}^{00}_N)$ and $C_1(\mathrm{fix}^{00}_N)$ are the arrows out of $W_0$ (to either object) that are injective and block-injective on $N$: such an arrow $u$ is undone on $N$ by a block-respecting $v$ into $W_0$, and $v$ can be chosen to be injective and block-injective on any finite set named at $\mathrm{trg}(u)$, sending $\star$ (if present) to a fresh block, so that a block-respecting $x$ with $xv$ fixing that set exists, collapsing that block onto $\star$ when needed. Hence $\Box_{\ne}$ and $\hat{\hat\Box}$ are coextensive at the evaluation point.

shared_arguments.text: The canonical e-counting numbers at the root and terminal object are identified with the ground's natural-number carrier, with bijective transport and $\Box I^*_e$. The current members of its first canonical rigid power are precisely the paired predicates of ground subsets; terminally the full hierarchy includes a predicate for every extension subset. A new real is therefore a new terminal power member. The root predicate with all current power members in its current extension and exactly their transported images in its terminal extension is admitted: its terminal definition uses the ground parameter $\mathcal P(\omega)^V$ and the numeral coding. It necessarily contains each current member but misses the new one, refuting inextensibility of this power carrier and hence FTN. This uses the stated stitching construction, not an arbitrary Boolean-valued model. shared_arguments.text: The root sees itself and $C_0$ through one arrow each, and $C_0$ sees only itself. An entity at the root of a relational type is a pair $(E,D)$ of a root extension $E$ and a definable element $D$ of $C_0$, with transport $D$ along the arrow to $C_0$. It is an atom iff $E$ is a singleton and $D=\bot$, or $E=\varnothing$ and $D$ is a definable singleton of $C_0$; a self-atom likewise, since its transport along the identity is itself and along the arrow to $C_0$ is $D$, each of which must be an atom where the entity is instantiated. Each such entity is a strong atom, its two transports being an atom or bottom. At $C_0$, a one-world model with full extensional domains, the atoms are the singletons, which are self-atoms and strong atoms. So all four bridge principles hold at both worlds, at every type.

shared_arguments.text: Lemma 16 of the source, in the map's terms. Write a root relation as the pair of its root extension $E$, a set in $V$ of root tuples, and its $C_0$-extension $g$, a definable relation of $C_0$; transport along $h$ sends it to $g$, and $h[E]$, the set of $C_0$-components of the members of $E$, is definable from the set in $V$ of their names. The relation is persistent iff $h[E]\subseteq g$. It is weakly inextensible iff $g\subseteq h[E]$: the root relation with root extension $E$ and $C_0$-extension $h[E]$ necessarily holds of every member of $E$, so weak inextensibility gives $g\subseteq h[E]$; conversely, a root relation that necessarily holds of each member of $E$ has root extension including $E$ and $C_0$-extension including $h[E]$. So a root relation is weakly rigid iff $g=h[E]$, and then rigid, since at $C_0$, which sees only itself, every relation is rigid. Hence $(E,g)$ is coextensive with the rigid $(E,h[E])$, and Rigid Comprehension holds at the root; at $C_0$ it holds trivially.

At $C_0$, $V[G]$ supplies a functional subrelation of any serial relation, and the full domain contains it.

shared_arguments.text: Lemma 19 of the source, with the universal property of individuals in place of the natural numbers. Let $F:=\lambda x^e\, .\,\top$; it is rigid, its root extension being $\mathbb N$ and its $C_0$-extension $h[\mathbb N]=\mathbb N$. Its power property $P:=\lambda X^{et}\, .\,\operatorname{Rigid}(X)\land X\le F$ is $\lambda X\, .\,\operatorname{Rigid}(X)$, as $X\le F$ is a theorem. By the criterion in the argument for Rigid Comprehension, the rigid root properties of individuals are the pairs $(E,E)$ with $E\subseteq\mathbb N$ in $V$, whose $C_0$-components are the reals of $V$, while at $C_0$ every property is rigid, so the $C_0$-extension of $P$ is the whole power set of $\mathbb N$ in $V[G]$. The root property of properties with the root extension of $P$ and $C_0$-extension $\mathcal P(\mathbb N)^V$, definable from that parameter, necessarily holds of every root instance of $P$, but not, at $C_0$, of a real of $V[G]$ not in $V$, which is rigid there. So $P$ is not weakly inextensible: Rigid Power fails at type $(et)t$ and, $P$ being rigidity itself, Rigid Rigidity fails at type $et$.

shared_arguments.text: At type $et$, at the root. A real number structure exists there: the rigid properties of individuals are the pairs $(E,E)$ with $E\subseteq\mathbb N$ in $V$, the reals of $V$ as sets of naturals, and the field relations on them, defined from membership by arithmetical formulas, are root relations (a function in $V$ with the corresponding definable $C_0$-relation); completeness at the root holds because every root property of these is a set in $V$. Now let $\mathfrak R$ be any rigid real number structure at $et$ with necessarily distinct elements. At the root it is a complete ordered field, so by categoricity its domain $X$ is in bijection with the reals of $V$ and its rationals are a countable dense subfield. Its root extension is a set $E$ in $V$ and, $X$ being rigid, its $C_0$-extension is $h[E]=E$, the same reals. At $C_0$ every property is available, in particular the cut in the rationals of $X$ of a real of $V[G]$ not in $V$, a bounded subproperty of $X$ with no least upper bound in $E$, a least upper bound being a real of $V$ equal to that new real. So $X$ is not complete at $C_0$, $\Box\operatorname{Real}_{et}(\mathfrak R)$ fails, and the instance fails: a real number structure is possible, indeed actual, and no rigid one is necessarily a real number structure.

shared_arguments.text: Theorem 20 of the source. At each object, every real number structure satisfies the continuum hypothesis iff the universe that object is built in does: at the root $V$, at $C_0$ $V[G]$. At $C_0$ this is because $C_0$ is the full extensional model of $V[G]$ over the natural numbers: a real number structure there is a complete ordered field of $V[G]$, with every subproperty and every relation of $V[G]$ available, so it has $V[G]$'s continuum, and its satisfying CH is CH in $V[G]$. At the root it is because every set in $V$ of root tuples is the root extension of a root relation, whatever its $C_0$-extension: so the root, read at the root, is the full hierarchy of $V$ over its domains, and the same reasoning applies in $V$. Real number structures exist at both objects, at type $et$ (see the argument for the failure of Analytic Necessitism, or take any complete ordered field on $\mathcal P(\mathbb N)$ at $C_0$). When $P$ changes CH, at type $et$ some real number structure satisfies CH at one object and some falsifies it at the other, and the root sees both, so neither disjunct holds at the root.

shared_arguments.text: At type $et$, at the root. A real number structure exists there: the rigid properties of individuals are the pairs $(E,E)$ with $E\subseteq\mathbb N$ in $V$, the reals of $V$ as sets of naturals, and the field relations on them, defined from membership by arithmetical formulas, are root relations (a function in $V$ with the corresponding definable $C_0$-relation); completeness at the root holds because every root property of these is a set in $V$. Now let $\mathfrak R$ be any rigid real number structure at $et$ with necessarily distinct elements. At the root it is a complete ordered field, so by categoricity its domain $X$ is in bijection with the reals of $V$ and its rationals are a countable dense subfield. Its root extension is a set $E$ in $V$ and, $X$ being rigid, its $C_0$-extension is $h[E]=E$, the same reals. At $C_0$ every property is available, in particular the cut in the rationals of $X$ of a real of $V[G]$ not in $V$, a bounded subproperty of $X$ with no least upper bound in $E$, a least upper bound being a real of $V$ equal to that new real. So $X$ is not complete at $C_0$, $\Box\operatorname{Real}_{et}(\mathfrak R)$ fails, and the instance fails: a real number structure is possible, indeed actual, and no rigid one is necessarily a real number structure.

shared_arguments.text: At each object, every real number structure satisfies the continuum hypothesis iff the universe that object is built in does: at the root $V$, at $C_0$ $V[G]$. At $C_0$ this is because $C_0$ is the full extensional model of $V[G]$ over the natural numbers: a real number structure there is a complete ordered field of $V[G]$, with every subproperty and every relation of $V[G]$ available, so it has $V[G]$'s continuum, and its satisfying CH is CH in $V[G]$. At the root it is because every set in $V$ of root tuples is the root extension of a root relation, whatever its $C_0$-extension: so the root, read at the root, is the full hierarchy of $V$ over its domains, and the same reasoning applies in $V$. Real number structures exist at both objects, at type $et$ (see the argument for the failure of Analytic Necessitism, or take any complete ordered field on $\mathcal P(\mathbb N)$ at $C_0$). When $P$ leaves CH unchanged, every real number structure, of any type, satisfies CH at both objects, or every one falsifies it at both; since the root sees exactly the two objects, one of the two disjuncts holds there.

shared_arguments.text: A self-atom of any relational type at an object $W$ is instantiated at some arrow $k$ out of $W$, and its transport along $k$ is an atom at $k$’s target instantiated at the identity there. The existential projection of an atom $I$ of a relational type, the proposition $\exists\bar x\, .\,I\bar x$, is an atom of type $t$: it is in the domain, it is not bottom, and for any proposition $p$ the entity $I\land\lambda\bar x\, .\,p$ lies below the atom $I$, so is $I$ or bottom, which puts $p$ above the projection or disjoint from it. So the projection is a true atom at $k$’s target, which the condition excludes. Hence no reachable object has a self-atom, and Self-atoms are atoms and Self-atoms are strong atoms hold vacuously at every type and every reachable object, while Self-Atomicity (type t) fails at the evaluation point, the top proposition having no self-atom below it.
Given a true proposition pinned down by a finite set, the proposition that a fresh individual is not collapsed with that set is a strictly stronger truth.
The same construction, applied to an arbitrary nonzero proposition rather than a true one, splits every possible proposition, which is Atomlessness and hence the failure of Atomicity at type t.

shared_arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, checked by Cian Dorr
shared_arguments.text:
At every relational type. It extends the earlier observations at types $t$ and $e\to t$ and the case $X=\lambda p\, .\,p$ at type $t\to t$, which are instances. Worlds are the arrows $h$, and $h$ sees $i\circ h$. Write $i\cdot r$ for the transport of an entity along $i$; for propositions $i\cdot p=\{k : k\circ i\in p\}$. Three facts about the model are used. (1) Transport: a formula with parameters $\bar r$ holds at $h$ iff it holds at $1$ with parameters $h\cdot\bar r$; in particular whether $Z$ holds of $\bar r$ at $i$ depends only on $i\cdot\bar r$. (2) Pinning: if $r$ is pinned down by $S$ and $g$ fixes $S$ pointwise, then $g\cdot r=r$. (3) Symmetry: the worlds $h$ and $\sigma\circ h$, for a permutation $\sigma$, agree on every root entity; with (2), the extension at $1$ of an $X$ pinned down by $S_X$ is closed under $\tau\cdot$ for every permutation $\tau$ fixing $S_X$ pointwise.
The witness. Given $X$ pinned down by the finite set $S_X$, let $\delta_{S_X}$ be the proposition that no two members of $S_X$ are collapsed, and put $Y:=\lambda\bar z\, .\,\delta_{S_X}\land X\bar z$. It is symmetric and pinned down by $S_X$, and since $\delta_{S_X}$ is true at $1$ it is coextensive with $X$.
Transversal lemma. If $g$ fixes $S_X$ pointwise and $r$ is pinned down by a finite $T$, then $r=g\cdot(\tau\cdot r)$ for a permutation $\tau$ fixing $S_X$ pointwise; so if $r$ is in the extension of $X$ at $1$, then $r=g\cdot r^{\prime}$ for some $r^{\prime}$ also in it. Proof: each $t\in T\setminus S_X$ has a preimage under $g$, as $g$ is surjective, and it lies outside $S_X$, as $g$ fixes $S_X$; choose distinct preimages $t^{\prime}$ and let $\tau$ be a permutation of $\mathbb N\setminus S_X$ with $\tau(t)=t^{\prime}$. Then $g\circ\tau$ fixes $T$ pointwise, so $g\cdot(\tau\cdot r)=(g\circ\tau)\cdot r=r$ by (2), and $\tau\cdot r$ is in the extension of $X$ by (3). The same holds for tuples.
Weak inextensibility at $1$. Let $Z$ hold necessarily of every instance of $Y$, and let $i$ be a world. If $i$ collapses two members of $S_X$, then $\delta_{S_X}$ is false at $i$, so $Y$ is empty there. Otherwise relabel by a permutation, which does not change the world by (3), so that $i$ fixes $S_X$ pointwise. By (1) and (2), $Y$ holds of $\bar r$ at $i$ iff $i\cdot\bar r$ is in the extension of $X$ at $1$; the lemma gives $\bar r^{\prime}$ in that extension with $i\cdot\bar r^{\prime}=i\cdot\bar r$; $Z$ holds of $\bar r^{\prime}$ at $i$, being necessary of it; so by (1) $Z$ holds of $\bar r$ at $i$. Hence $Y\le Z$.
The leading box. At a world $h$ injective on $S_X$, relabel so that $h$ fixes $S_X$; then $h\cdot Y=Y$, and by (1) weak inextensibility at $h$ is weak inextensibility of $Y$ at $1$. At a world collapsing $S_X$, $Y$ is empty there and at every world it sees, since a collapse persists, so it is trivially weakly inextensible. So $Y$ is inextensible. Nothing depends on the argument types. The argument explains the cheapness of inextensibility here: surjectivity and the full permutation group make the necessity of $Z$ cover everything that pinning forces into the extension of $Y$, and the conjunct $\delta_{S_X}$ removes the worlds that collapse the pinning set. The Appendix D models refuting Inextensible Comprehension lack one of these features: an arrow fixing the pinning set may leave points without a preimage outside it, or the relabelling permutations may be missing.

shared_arguments.text: At every type. Write $A_h$ for the extension of a property $A$ at the arrow $h$; transport gives $(k\cdot A)_h=A_{h\circ k}$, symmetry gives $A_{g\circ h}=g\cdot A_h$ for permutations $g$, and pinning by $S$ makes $A_h$ depend only on $h{\restriction}S$. If $A$ is pinned by $S$, every permutation fixing $S$ pointwise fixes $E:=A_{\mathbf 1}$; finite supports for the full permutation group are closed under intersection, so $E$ has a least support $S_E$, and $S_{g\cdot E}=g[S_E]$. Let $\hat E$ have extension $g\cdot E$ at $h$ when $h$ is injective on $S_E$, for any permutation $g$ agreeing with $h$ on $S_E$ (well defined, since two such $g$ differ by a permutation fixing $S_E$), and $\varnothing$ when it is not. Then $\hat E$ is pinned by $S_E$, symmetric, and coextensive with $A$ at $\mathbf 1$, and $g\cdot\hat E=\widehat{g\cdot E}$. So the property $F$ whose extension at every arrow is the set of all such $\hat E$ is pinned by $\varnothing$ and symmetric, hence in the domain; at $\mathbf 1$ it holds of exactly one property coextensive with any given property, since $\hat E$ is determined by $E$. Qualitatively, $F$ holds of $X$ iff the least pinning set of $X$ is the least support of its actual extension and, necessarily, if $X$ is instantiated then the members of that set are pairwise distinct; the minimality clause is needed, since a property pinned by $S_E$ together with one further point, and empty wherever that point collides with $S_E$, is coextensive with $\hat E$ but distinct from it. Since a one-object model has No Pure Contingency and $F$ is pinned by $\varnothing$, every instance of Transversal holds at every world.

shared_arguments.text: At every type. Let $B$ be an entity at the target of an arrow $i$, pinned down by the finite set $M$, and choose a finite set $P$ with a map $s:M\to P$ such that $i\circ s$ is the identity on $M$, possible because $i$ is surjective. Put $A:=\{\langle\bar x,j\rangle : \langle\bar x,k\rangle\in B$ for some arrow $k$ with $k|_M=j\circ s\}$. This is well defined because $B$ is pinned down by $M$. It is pinned down by $P$ and symmetric, since $B$ is. And $i\cdot A=B$: $\langle\bar x,k\rangle\in i\cdot A$ iff $\langle\bar x,k\circ i\rangle\in A$ iff $\langle\bar x,k'\rangle\in B$ for some $k'$ with $k'|_M=k|_M$, iff $\langle\bar x,k\rangle\in B$. So every entity at every world is the transport of an entity at the evaluation point, and a relation that is necessarily true of every entity is necessarily true of all of them.

The arrows in (B1) go from the evaluation object to any one object, and $M$ separates $h$ when every arrow agreeing with $h$ on $M$ is a member of the symmetry group of the evaluation object. These are the hypotheses of Dorr's main theorem (draft, Definitions 28–30, Theorem 36).

shared_arguments.text: At every relational type: a property $F$ of type-$\tau$ entities has a least upper bound, the union of the hulls of its instances. Let $F$ be pinned down by $N\supseteq M_0$. For each instance $u$ of $F$ at the identity, its hull is the closure of $u$ under the arrows that $N$ does not separate from the identity, transported along the arrows agreeing with the identity on $N$; it is symmetric, pinned down by $N$ (by (B1), which splices an arrow agreeing with $h'$ on the instance's pinning set with $h$ on $N$), and an upper bound of $u$. Every upper bound $z$ of all the instances, pinned down by $N'$, contains every hull: given a member of a hull, (B2) supplies a symmetry fixing $N$ and moving the instance's pinning set off $N'$, whose image is again an instance (by the orbit lemma, Lemma 35), lying under $z$; and $z$, pinned down by $N'$, cannot tell the moved instance's tuple from the original. The union of the hulls is pinned down by $N$ and symmetric, so it is in the domain, and it is the least upper bound.

shared_arguments.text: At type $tt$. As in the withdrawn analytic-necessitism-exact-collapses-symmetric: for each $n\ge2$ the propositions $E_N$, the arrows constant on a set $N$ of $n$ points, form an orbit $O_n$ under the symmetry group $G$, pairwise distinct for distinct $n$; for $A\subseteq\mathbb N$ the union $S_A$ of the $O_n$, $n\in A$, is $G$-invariant, so the constant intension $Y_A$ with value $S_A$ is symmetric, pinned down by $\varnothing$, in the domain, and fixed by transport along every arrow; and $A\mapsto Y_A$ is injective. Every set of tuples of the $Y_A$ is $G$-invariant, so it is the value of a constant intension in the domain, and so is the set of all those constant relations of a given arity. With one object and all parameters fixed, a real number structure on the $Y_A$ by constant relations is one at every world, rigid with necessarily distinct instances, and the constant intensions of the sets of its constant relations are represented powers. So Analytic Necessitism and its second-order form hold.

shared_arguments.text: Write $G$ for the symmetry group, which acts on the propositions by transport, $g\cdot p=\{j:j\circ g\in p\}$. For a finite set $N$ of points let $E_N$ be the set of arrows constant on $N$: a proposition in the domain, symmetric and pinned down by $N$, with $g\cdot E_N=E_{g(N)}$. Take for each $n\ge2$ a set $N_n$ of $n$ points and an arrow $j_n$ constant on $N_n$, injective off $N_n$ and taking other values there (the condition), so that the fibres of $j_n$ are $N_n$ and singletons. The orbits $O_n$ of the $E_{N_n}$ under $G$ are pairwise distinct: $E_{N_n}=E_N$ with $N=g(N_m)$ puts $j_n$ in $E_N$, so $N\subseteq N_n$, and puts $j_m\circ g^{-1}$, an arrow whose fibres are $N$ and singletons, in $E_{N_n}$, so $N_n\subseteq N$. For $A\subseteq\mathbb N$ the union $S_A$ of the $O_n$ with $n\in A$ is a $G$-invariant set of propositions, and $A\mapsto S_A$ is injective: there are continuum many $G$-invariant sets of propositions, in explicit bijection with the reals. Each $S_A$ is the value of a constant intension $Y_A$ of type $tt$, symmetric because $S_A$ is $G$-invariant, pinned down by the empty set, so in the domain, and fixed by transport along every arrow. The constant intensions whose values are the set of the $Y_A$, the order, sum and product of the reals carried over to it, and its natural numbers, with the $Y_A$ standing for $0$ and $1$, are symmetric, their values being made of fixed entities, and in the domain; they form a real number structure of type $tt$ at the evaluation point, complete since every bounded set of its elements has a least upper bound among them. So the antecedent of Analytic Necessitism holds at type $tt$. Its consequent fails there. Let $k$ be an arrow with $ka=kb$ for distinct points $a$ and $b$ (the condition at $n=2$) and $q$ the set of arrows $j$ with $ja\ne jb$: symmetric, pinned down by $\{a,b\}$, containing the identity and no arrow $j\circ k$. For $x$ of type $tt$ in the domain let $y$ agree with $x$ except at the arrows in $q$, where the top proposition is added to its value or removed from it: $y$ is symmetric and pinned down by a finite set, so in the domain, differs from $x$, and has $k\cdot y=k\cdot x$. If $\mathfrak R$ were a rigid real number structure of type $tt$, necessarily a real number structure, with carrier $X$ (Background, Analysis), an instance $x$ and this $y$ would give $k\cdot y=k\cdot x\in X_k$ by persistence, $Xy$ by inextensibility and $k\cdot y\ne k\cdot x$ by necessary distinctness: $X$ has no instance. So Analytic Necessitism fails. No choice is used.

Carry the real numbers onto the $Y_A$ at $v$ and take as relations the codomain-only intensions with the corresponding values at each object. Along every arrow the structure goes to an isomorphic one at the target, which is a real number structure there, every bounded set of its elements having a least upper bound among them. So the structure is rigid, with necessarily distinct instances, and necessarily a real number structure: the consequent of Analytic Necessitism holds, and so does the principle. shared_arguments.text:
Write $F_h$ for the extension of $F$ at the arrow $h$, so $(h\cdot F)_k=F_{kh}$, and $B_N(E)$ as in tame-rigidity-factorizable, whose part (1) is the criterion used throughout: a relation pinned down by $S$ with extension $E$ is weakly rigid iff it equals $B_N(E)$ for every finite $N\supseteq S$; Tame Rigidity holds at every type by that argument. Fix a type tuple.
(a) Stable sets. If a set $A$ of argument tuples is closed under the surjections fixing a finite $P$ pointwise, then $B_P(A)$ has extension $A$ and is weakly rigid, hence rigid. Given $Q\supseteq P$ and $l^{\prime}a$ with $l^{\prime}$ agreeing with $l$ on $P$ and $a\in A$ pinned down by $M$, take a surjection $u$ fixing $P$ that sends $M\setminus P$ to distinct fresh points outside $Q$, and a surjection $r$ agreeing with $l$ on $Q$ with $ru=l^{\prime}$ on $M$ (compatible finite prescriptions); then $ua\in A$ and $l^{\prime}a=r(ua)\in B_Q(A)_l$, so $B_P(A)=B_Q(A)$.
(b) Exact images. Let $F$ be weakly rigid, pinned down by $S$, with extension $E$. By weak persistence $uE\subseteq E$ for every surjection $u$ fixing $S$. For any surjection $j$, $F_j=jE$: a member $la$ of $B_S(E)_j$, with $l$ agreeing with $j$ on $S$ and $a\in E$ pinned down by $M$, is $j(ua)$ for a surjection $u$ fixing $S$ with $ju=l$ on $M$, preimages being supplied by the surjectivity of $j$.
(c) Lifting. Let $F$ be rigid, pinned down by $S$, $k$ an arrow, $N\supseteq S$ finite, and $X\le k\cdot F$ rigid, pinned down by $T$, with extension $D$. Extend $k|_N$ to a surjection $j$ whose non-singleton fibres are finitely many and finite (send the points outside $N$ bijectively onto the values not yet taken); then $j\cdot F=k\cdot F$ and $D\subseteq F_j=jE$. Let $P$ be finite, containing $N$, every non-singleton fibre of $j$, and a preimage of each point of $T$, and put $A:=\{a\in E:ja\in D\}$. For a surjection $u$ fixing $P$, $ju$ is constant on the fibres of $j$, so $ju=vj$ for a surjection $v$, which fixes $T$; so $vD\subseteq D$ by the weak persistence and pinning of $X$, and $uE\subseteq E$ by (b); hence $uA\subseteq A$. By (a), $Y:=B_P(A)$ is rigid, $Y\le F$ since $A\subseteq E$ and $P\supseteq S$, and by (b) $(j\cdot Y)_1=jA=D$. Weakly rigid relations with the same extension are identical, so $X=j\cdot Y$ with $j$ agreeing with $k$ on $N$.
(d) The power property of $F$ is persistent, and by (c) its extension at $k$ is contained in $B_N$ of its extension at the identity for every $N\supseteq S$; so it is weakly rigid by the criterion, and rigid by Tame Rigidity. So Rigid Power holds at every type. Nothing about the symmetry group is used beyond its being a group of permutations, and the individuals play no role, so the argument covers every member and variant meeting the conditions.

shared_arguments.text: Fix the type tuple $\bar\sigma$, let $\mathcal R$ be the set of rigid relations of type $\bar\sigma t$, and let $R:=\lambda X\, .\,\operatorname{Rigid}(X)$, the value of a closed pure term, so fixed by every arrow; in a one-object model its extension at every arrow is $\mathcal R$, and it is pinned down by $\emptyset$. Write $B_N(E)$ as in tame-rigidity-factorizable. By part (1) of that argument at type $(\bar\sigma t)t$, $R$ is weakly rigid iff $\mathcal R=B_N(\mathcal R)_k$ for every arrow $k$ and finite $N$; and since $h\cdot R=R$ for every arrow $h$, part (2) then makes $R$ rigid. The inclusion $B_N(\mathcal R)_k\subseteq\mathcal R$ holds because a transport of a rigid relation is rigid, rigidity being a necessitated condition. For the converse let $Z\in\mathcal R$ be pinned down by $T$, and let $k$ and $N$ be given. The condition gives $k^{\prime}$ agreeing with $k$ on $N$ and $\sigma$ with $k^{\prime}\circ\sigma$ the identity on $T$. Then $Z^{\prime}:=\sigma\cdot Z$ is rigid, and $k^{\prime}\cdot Z^{\prime}=(k^{\prime}\circ\sigma) \cdot Z=Z$, since $k^{\prime}\circ\sigma$ agrees with the identity on $T$. So $Z\in B_N(\mathcal R)_k$. Hence Rigid Rigidity holds at every type. This is the lifting of Rigid Power at $F:=\top$ by a section of $k$, noted for the symmetric all-surjections model on 9 October; without the condition the lift can still hold through rigid relations that are not transports of $Z$ (for instance the haecceity of any $x$ with $k^{\prime}x=1$ lifts that of $1$), so the condition is sufficient, not necessary.

shared_arguments.text: Let $v$ be reachable from the evaluation point. If every type is finite at $v$ there is no real number structure there, an ordered field having the infinitely many distinct elements $0$, $1$, $1+1$, and so on. Otherwise let $D$ be as in the condition. Carry the real numbers onto $D$ by a bijection: the carrier, order, sum, product, $0$, $1$ and natural numbers are sets of tuples from $D$, so extensions at $v$ of entities there, which form a real number structure $\mathfrak R^*$ at $v$, its completeness and the leastness of its natural numbers being tested against subproperties whose extensions are all the subsets of $D$. Its second-order quantifiers, applied to tuples from $D$, range over all relations on $D$, so for each second-order analytical sentence $A$, $A(\mathfrak R^*)$ holds at $v$ iff $A$ is true of the real numbers under full second-order semantics. Any real number structure $\mathfrak R$ at $v$, of any type, is isomorphic to $\mathfrak R^*$ by a relation in the domain there (Huntington's theorem, a theorem of C: Background, Analysis), and $A(\mathfrak R)\leftrightarrow A(\mathfrak R^*)$ is a theorem of C given such an isomorphism, relations on one carrier being carried to the other by comprehension. So at every reachable object every real number structure satisfies exactly the second-order analytical sentences true of the reals, and each instance $\Box\forall\mathfrak R\,.\,\operatorname{Real}_\sigma(\mathfrak R) \to A(\mathfrak R)$ or $\Box\forall\mathfrak R\,.\,\operatorname{Real}_\sigma(\mathfrak R)\to\neg A(\mathfrak R)$ of the Necessity of Second-Order Analysis holds, with the Necessity of Analysis and the Non-contingency of the Continuum Hypothesis. The choice of the bijection with the reals needs no choice principle, $D$ having the cardinality of the continuum.

shared_arguments.text:
No tail object $V$ has an atom of type $t$. Let $p$ be a nonzero proposition there, pinned down by a finite subalgebra $S$, and $h:V\to W$ in $p$. Choose a $d$-generator $y$ outside the finitely many generators $S$ depends on, and let $j_0,j_1$ agree with $h$ on the other generators except an infinite set of further $d$-generators, which they send onto the base of $W$, with $j_0(y)=0$ and $j_1(y)=1$. Both are tail arrows agreeing with $h$ on $S$, so both lie in $p$, and the proposition $\{j : j(y)=0\}$, symmetric and pinned down by $\{y\}$, splits $p$. By existential projection (as in the argument no-actuality-no-self-atoms) no tail object has an atom of any relational type either. Nothing returns from the tail to $A$, so every world seen from a tail world is a tail world.

So Actuality, a closed pure sentence true at $1_A$, is impossible at an entrance $A\to V_0$, and B for pure sentences fails. Vicinity fails at each tail object $V$: given a truth $p$ pinned down by $T$, the endomorphism fixing every generator except $d_n,d_{n+1},\dots$ for a $d_n$ outside $T$'s generators, sending $d_n$ to $0$ and $d_{k+1}$ to $d_k$, is an arrow in $p$ at which the truth that $d_n\ne0$ is impossible. So □Vicinity fails.

Self-atoms. At a tail object a self-atom would be possible, so instantiated at some arrow, and an atom at its target; so there are none, and the bridge principles hold there vacuously. At $A$, a self-atom $X$ of any relational type is instantiated at no entrance, since it would be an atom at a tail object; being nonzero it is instantiated at an automorphism, hence by symmetry at $1_A$ and at every automorphism, so it is an atom there. Its transport along an entrance $h$ is $\bot$, every arrow after $h$ being an entrance. So $X$ is necessarily an atom or $\bot$, a strong atom. At type $t$ the only self-atom is the actual-world proposition. Hence self-atoms are necessarily atoms and strong atoms, at every type.

shared_arguments.text: Write $G$ for the symmetry group, which acts on the propositions by transport, $g\cdot p=\{j:j\circ g\in p\}$. For a finite set $N$ of points let $E_N$ be the set of arrows constant on $N$: a proposition in the domain, symmetric and pinned down by $N$, with $g\cdot E_N=E_{g(N)}$. Take for each $n\ge2$ a set $N_n$ of $n$ points and an arrow $j_n$ constant on $N_n$, injective off $N_n$ and taking other values there (the condition), so that the fibres of $j_n$ are $N_n$ and singletons. The orbits $O_n$ of the $E_{N_n}$ under $G$ are pairwise distinct: $E_{N_n}=E_N$ with $N=g(N_m)$ puts $j_n$ in $E_N$, so $N\subseteq N_n$, and puts $j_m\circ g^{-1}$, an arrow whose fibres are $N$ and singletons, in $E_{N_n}$, so $N_n\subseteq N$. For $A\subseteq\mathbb N$ the union $S_A$ of the $O_n$ with $n\in A$ is a $G$-invariant set of propositions, and $A\mapsto S_A$ is injective: there are continuum many $G$-invariant sets of propositions, in explicit bijection with the reals. Each $S_A$ is the value of a constant intension $Y_A$ of type $tt$, symmetric because $S_A$ is $G$-invariant, pinned down by the empty set, so in the domain, and fixed by transport along every arrow. The constant intensions whose values are the set of the $Y_A$, the order, sum and product of the reals carried over to it, and its natural numbers, with the $Y_A$ standing for $0$ and $1$, are symmetric, their values being made of fixed entities, and in the domain; they form a real number structure of type $tt$ at the evaluation point, complete since every bounded set of its elements has a least upper bound among them. So the antecedent of Analytic Necessitism holds at type $tt$. Its consequent fails there. Let $k$ be an arrow with $ka=kb$ for distinct points $a$ and $b$ (the condition at $n=2$) and $q$ the set of arrows $j$ with $ja\ne jb$: symmetric, pinned down by $\{a,b\}$, containing the identity and no arrow $j\circ k$. For $x$ of type $tt$ in the domain let $y$ agree with $x$ except at the arrows in $q$, where the top proposition is added to its value or removed from it: $y$ is symmetric and pinned down by a finite set, so in the domain, differs from $x$, and has $k\cdot y=k\cdot x$. If $\mathfrak R$ were a rigid real number structure of type $tt$, necessarily a real number structure, with carrier $X$ (Background, Analysis), an instance $x$ and this $y$ would give $k\cdot y=k\cdot x\in X_k$ by persistence, $Xy$ by inextensibility and $k\cdot y\ne k\cdot x$ by necessary distinctness: $X$ has no instance. So Analytic Necessitism fails. No choice is used.

withdrawn.reason: The step from $k\cdot y=k\cdot x\in X_k$ to $Xy$ (or $y\in X_h$) by inextensibility does not follow: inextensibility bounds a rigid carrier from above, by the transports of its actual instances, and puts nothing new into its actual extension. shared_arguments.text: At $W_1$ a proposition is a set $A$ of points closed under the symmetries of $W_0$ (a union of the orbits $\{0,1\}$ and $\mathbb N\setminus\{0,1\}$), given as the $c_n$ with $n\in A$, together with a bit for $1_{W_1}$: eight propositions $q$. Their transports along $c_n$ are $c_n\cdot q=\{h:W_0\to W_0 : hn\in A\}$, with $!$ added if the bit is set. The intension $F$ of type $t\to t$ with all eight at $1_{W_1}$ and the eight $c_n\cdot q$ at each $c_n$ is pinned down by $\{0\}$ and symmetric, since $g\cdot(c_n\cdot q)=c_{gn}\cdot q$; so every proposition at $W_1$ necessarily has it. But at $c_2$ the proposition $\{h:h2=h3\}$, symmetric and pinned down by $\{2,3\}$, does not: it contains every constant map, so it could only be a $c_2\cdot q$ with $A=\mathbb N$, which contains the identity. So BF at type $t$ fails at $W_1$, which $!$ reaches.

Every world is an arrow into $W_0$ or $W_1$, so Strong Actuality and, with the group's argument boolean-completeness at $W_0$, Boolean Completeness at type $t$ are necessary.

shared_arguments.text: At the types $(e\to t)$ and $e$. Let $U:=\lambda Xy\, .\,Xy\lor\neg\exists z\, .\,Xz$, a closed term, hence in the domain, and serial. A functional subrelation $S$ of $U$ would lie in the domain at the evaluation object, so it is symmetric and pinned down by a finite set $N$. Two facts about such an $S$ (Dorr, draft, Lemma 19(iv)): every $g\in G$ fixing $N$ pointwise satisfies $g^{[\sigma]}S=S$, and symmetry gives $\langle gA,gy,g\rangle\in S$ whenever $\langle A,y,1\rangle\in S$; together, $\langle gA,gy,1\rangle\in S$. Now let $A$ be the property the condition gives for $N$. Its extension is nonempty, so $S$ relates $A$ at the identity to some $y$ in its extension. The condition gives a member $g$ of the symmetry group that fixes $N$ pointwise, fixes $A$ and moves $y$ to some $gy\ne y$, so $S$ relates $A$ to $gy$ as well, and $S$ is not functional at the identity arrow. The well-ordering of the individuals that Cian Dorr had in mind is refuted by the same two facts, but the direct route needs no derivation of a well-ordering from Relational Choice in C.

shared_arguments.text: At every relational type: a property $F$ of type-$\tau$ entities has a least upper bound, the union of the hulls of its instances. Let $F$ be pinned down by $N\supseteq M_0$. For each instance $u$ of $F$ at the identity, its hull is the closure of $u$ under the arrows that $N$ does not separate from the identity, transported along the arrows agreeing with the identity on $N$; it is symmetric, pinned down by $N$ (by (B1), which splices an arrow agreeing with $h'$ on the instance's pinning set with $h$ on $N$), and an upper bound of $u$. Every upper bound $z$ of all the instances, pinned down by $N'$, contains every hull: given a member of a hull, (B2) supplies a symmetry fixing $N$ and moving the instance's pinning set off $N'$, whose image is again an instance (by the orbit lemma, Lemma 35), lying under $z$; and $z$, pinned down by $N'$, cannot tell the moved instance's tuple from the original. The union of the hulls is pinned down by $N$ and symmetric, so it is in the domain, and it is the least upper bound.

Let $F$ and $a$ be as the condition gives them, and suppose $G\le F$ is necessarily uniquely instantiated. $G$ is in the domain, so it is symmetric and pinned down by a finite set, which we may take to contain $a$; call it $N$. shared_arguments.text: Self-Atomicity at every relational type, necessarily, there being one object. Let $I\ne\bot$ be an entity of type $\bar\sigma t$, pinned down by $N$, and take a pair $\langle k,\bar x\rangle$ in it, $k$ an arrow and $\bar x$ a tuple of individuals and of symmetric entities at $k$’s world. A symmetry $g$ acts on such a pair by relabelling, fixing every symmetric entity and permuting the individuals. Choose a finite $N^{\prime}\supseteq N$ with $k(N^{\prime})$ containing the collapsed pair and every individual in $\bar x$, which surjectivity allows (if $k$ is a symmetry, $N^{\prime}\supseteq k^{-1}$ of those individuals suffices), and let $J$ be the set of pairs $\langle g\circ k_1,g\cdot\bar x\rangle$ with $g$ a symmetry and $k_1$ agreeing with $k$ on $N^{\prime}$. $J$ lies below $I$, since $I$ is pinned down by $N$ and symmetric; it is symmetric and pinned down by $N^{\prime}$. Its transport along a member $\langle g\circ k_1,g\cdot\bar x\rangle$ consists of the pairs $\langle m,\bar y\rangle$ with $m\circ g\circ k_1=g^{\prime}\circ k_2$ and $\bar y=g^{\prime}\cdot\bar x$; then $h:=g^{\prime-1}\circ m\circ g$ fixes $k(N^{\prime})$ pointwise, so is a symmetry fixing the individuals of $\bar x$, and $\bar y=m\cdot g\cdot\bar x$. So the transport is the orbit of the single pair $\langle1,g\cdot\bar x\rangle$, an atom, and $J$ is a self-atom below $I$.

shared_arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, 25 October 2026
shared_arguments.text: Write $\{a,b\}$ for the collapsed pair and $G$ for the symmetry group, the orbit of the identity and the only atom containing it, pinned down by the pair. Let $k$ be a collapser and $N$ a finite set such that $k(N)\supseteq\{a,b\}$; one exists for any collapser, every arrow being surjective. Let $q$ be the set of arrows agreeing on $N$, up to symmetry, with $k$: it is symmetric and pinned down by $N$. For $k^{\prime}\in q$, an arrow $m$ has $m\circ k^{\prime}\in q$ only if some $g\circ m$ fixes $k^{\prime}(N)\supseteq\{a,b\}$ pointwise, which no collapser does; so $m\in G$, and conversely $G\circ k^{\prime}\subseteq q$. So the transport of $q$ along each of its members is $G$, and $q$ is a self-atom. It is not an atom: the arrows agreeing with $k$ on a larger finite set, up to symmetry, form a proper nonempty symmetric pinned part. So Self-atoms are atoms (type t) fails, and with it Self-atoms are strong atoms (type t). Self-Atomicity (type t) holds, and necessarily, there being one object: a possible proposition $p$, pinned down by $N$, contains some arrow; if a permutation, $p\supseteq G$, a self-atom; if a collapser $k$, $p$ contains the self-atom built from $k$ and a finite $N^{\prime}\supseteq N$ with $k(N^{\prime})\supseteq\{a,b\}$. The relational form is the argument that follows.

At every relational type. Given a relation with extension S pinned down by a finite set, take the least upper bound of the union of the haecceities of the members of S, computed with the fixed pair adjoined to the pinning set. Persistence is immediate, and the extension is exactly S because an arrow agreeing with the identity on a set containing the fixed pair is invertible. The rigidity criterion is then checked separately at invertible worlds, where leastness delivers it, and at collapsing worlds, where surjectivity supplies the preimages that persistence demands.
With the proposition that the two members of the fixed pair are identical as a nonzero proposition having no atom below it.

shared_arguments.text:
At type $e\to t$, with $F:=\top$: the argument of finite-support-pair-injections-or-collapses, whose witnesses are all symmetric, with the collapses kept surjective. Write $Z_k$ for the extension of a property $Z$ at the arrow $k$, so that $(h\cdot Z)_k=Z_{k\circ h}$. The step that needs care changes an arrow $j$ to hit a value $y$ at a point $x$ outside a finite $N\supseteq\{0,1\}$: for a collapse, put $j':=j\circ\tau$, where $\tau$ fixes $N$ pointwise, sends $x$ to a $j$-preimage $p$ of $y$, and maps the rest of $\mathbb N\setminus N$ onto $\mathbb N\setminus N$ (possible even if $p\in N$, $\tau$ not being required to be injective); then $j'$ is a surjective collapse agreeing with $j$ on $N$, with $j'x=y$. For a permutation and $y\notin j[N]$, put $j':=(y\ jx)\circ j$, a permutation preserving $\{0,1\}$ since $y,jx\notin\{0,1\}$.

(1) $\top$ is rigid: its inextensibility is $\Box$BF at type $e$, which holds.

(2) $Y$, with $Y_k:=\mathbb N\setminus\{k2\}$ at a permutation and $\mathbb N$ at a collapse, is in the domain (pinned down by $\{0,1,2\}$; symmetric, since $y\ne k2$ gives $gy\ne(g\circ k)2$) and rigid. It is persistent, every composite with a collapse being a collapse. It is inextensible at every world $w$: let $X$, pinned down by $N\supseteq\{0,1\}$, contain $\langle jx,j\rangle$ for every $x\in Y_w$ and arrow $j$, and let $y\in Y_{j\circ w}$. If $y=jn$ with $n\in N\cap Y_w$, then $\langle y,j\rangle\in X$. If $y=jn$ with $n\in N\setminus Y_w$, then $w$ is a permutation, $n=w2$, and $j\circ w$ is a collapse, so $j$ identifies $w0$ with $w1$ and is a collapse; if $y\notin j[N]$, $j$ is either. In both cases change $j$ as above at a fresh $x\notin N\cup\{w2\}$, so that $x\in Y_w$, $\langle y,j'\rangle\in X$, and by pinning $\langle y,j\rangle\in X$.

(3) Along a collapse a weakly rigid property $Z$, with extension $S$ and pinned down by $N\supseteq\{0,1\}$, has extension $\mathbb N$ or a finite one. If $S$ is infinite, then for any $b$ change the collapse $m$ as above at some $x\in S\setminus N$ to $m'x=b$; persistence gives $b\in Z_{m'}=Z_m$. If $S$ is finite, the symmetric property $k\mapsto k[S]$, pinned down by $S$, necessarily holds of each member of $S$, so $Z_m\subseteq m[S]$.

Let $R:=\lambda X\, .\,\operatorname{Rigid}(X)\land X\le\top$, the value of a closed pure term, so that its extension at every arrow is the set of rigid properties. Let $\mathbf X$ hold of $W$ at $k$ iff $W=k'\cdot Z$ for some rigid $Z$ and some arrow $k'$ agreeing with $k$ on $\{0,1\}$: pinned down by $\{0,1\}$, and symmetric, since $g\cdot(k'\cdot Z)=(g\circ k')\cdot Z$ and the rigid properties are closed under transport along symmetries. It necessarily holds of every instance of $R$. At a collapse $c$, every $k'$ agreeing with $c$ on $\{0,1\}$ is a collapse, so by (3) every member of $\mathbf X$'s extension has extension $\mathbb N$ or a finite one, while $Y$, in $R$'s extension there by (2), has extension $\mathbb N\setminus\{2\}$. So $R\not\le\mathbf X$: $R$ is not even weakly inextensible, though $\top$ is rigid. With Rigid Comprehension holding, Rigid Comprehension (boxed, and with Actuality, BF and Boolean Completeness) does not imply Rigid Power.

Put $A:=\{\langle\bar x,j\rangle : \langle\bar x,k\rangle\in B$ for some arrow $k$ with $k|_M=j\circ s\}$. This is well defined because $B$ is pinned down by $M$. It is pinned down by $P$ and symmetric, since $B$ is. And $i\cdot A=B$: $\langle\bar x,k\rangle\in i\cdot A$ iff $\langle\bar x,k\circ i\rangle\in A$ iff $\langle\bar x,k'\rangle\in B$ for some $k'$ with $k'|_M=k|_M$, iff $\langle\bar x,k\rangle\in B$. For each instance $u$ of $F$ at the identity, its hull is the closure of $u$ under the arrows that $N$ does not separate from the identity, transported along the arrows agreeing with the identity on $N$; it is symmetric, pinned down by $N$ (by (B1), which splices an arrow agreeing with $h'$ on the instance's pinning set with $h$ on $N$), and an upper bound of $u$. Every upper bound $z$ of all the instances, pinned down by $N'$, contains every hull: given a member of a hull, (B2) supplies a symmetry fixing $N$ and moving the instance's pinning set off $N'$, whose image is again an instance (by the orbit lemma, Lemma 35), lying under $z$; and $z$, pinned down by $N'$, cannot tell the moved instance's tuple from the original. shared_arguments.text: Write $G$ for the symmetry group, which acts on the propositions by transport, $g\cdot p=\{j:j\circ g\in p\}$. For a finite set $N$ of points let $E_N$ be the set of arrows constant on $N$: a proposition in the domain, symmetric and pinned down by $N$, with $g\cdot E_N=E_{g(N)}$. Take for each $n\ge2$ a set $N_n$ of $n$ points and an arrow $j_n$ constant on $N_n$, injective off $N_n$ and taking other values there (the condition), so that the fibres of $j_n$ are $N_n$ and singletons. The orbits $O_n$ of the $E_{N_n}$ under $G$ are pairwise distinct: $E_{N_n}=E_N$ with $N=g(N_m)$ puts $j_n$ in $E_N$, so $N\subseteq N_n$, and puts $j_m\circ g^{-1}$, an arrow whose fibres are $N$ and singletons, in $E_{N_n}$, so $N_n\subseteq N$. For $A\subseteq\mathbb N$ the union $S_A$ of the $O_n$ with $n\in A$ is a $G$-invariant set of propositions, and $A\mapsto S_A$ is injective: there are continuum many $G$-invariant sets of propositions, in explicit bijection with the reals. Each $S_A$ is the value of a constant intension $Y_A$ of type $tt$, symmetric because $S_A$ is $G$-invariant, pinned down by the empty set, so in the domain, and fixed by transport along every arrow. The constant intensions whose values are the set of the $Y_A$, the order, sum and product of the reals carried over to it, and its natural numbers, with the $Y_A$ standing for $0$ and $1$, are symmetric, their values being made of fixed entities, and in the domain; they form a real number structure of type $tt$ at the evaluation point, complete since every bounded set of its elements has a least upper bound among them. So the antecedent of Analytic Necessitism holds at type $tt$. Its consequent fails there. Let $k$ be an arrow with $ka=kb$ for distinct points $a$ and $b$ (the condition at $n=2$) and $q$ the set of arrows $j$ with $ja\ne jb$: symmetric, pinned down by $\{a,b\}$, containing the identity and no arrow $j\circ k$. For $x$ of type $tt$ in the domain let $y$ agree with $x$ except at the arrows in $q$, where the top proposition is added to its value or removed from it: $y$ is symmetric and pinned down by a finite set, so in the domain, differs from $x$, and has $k\cdot y=k\cdot x$. If $\mathfrak R$ were a rigid real number structure of type $tt$, necessarily a real number structure, with carrier $X$ (Background, Analysis), an instance $x$ and this $y$ would give $k\cdot y=k\cdot x\in X_k$ by persistence, $Xy$ by inextensibility and $k\cdot y\ne k\cdot x$ by necessary distinctness: $X$ has no instance. So Analytic Necessitism fails. No choice is used.

shared_arguments.text: At $A$ the propositions are the four subsets of $\{1_A,i\}$. The atom $\{i\}$ is not a self-atom: its transport along $i$ is the set of all arrows out of $B$, since $m\circ i=i$ for every $m$, which is not an atom at $B$. So Atoms are self-atoms (type t) fails, and Self-Atomicity (type t) fails, $\{i\}$ being possible with no self-atom below it. No self-atom at $A$ has a pair at $i$, for the same reason: its transport along $i$ would be the constant intension of a set of tuples at $B$ over all arrows out of $B$, which has a proper nonzero part over any nonzero proper proposition of $B$. So the self-atoms at $A$ sit over $1_A$ with one tuple, are atoms, and are strong atoms, their transport along $i$ being empty: Self-atoms are atoms and Self-atoms are strong atoms hold at $A$, at every type. At $B$, the tail of symmetric-qualitative-links with the fixed point $d$, the self-atom of that model built from a collapsing arrow $k$ and a finite $N$ with $k(N)\supseteq\{0,1\}$ is again a self-atom that is not an atom, $d$ being fixed by every arrow and every symmetry; so Self-atoms are atoms (type t) and Self-atoms are strong atoms (type t) fail at $B$, which $i$ reaches, and their boxed forms fail at $A$.

The entities at $A$ are the pairs $(E,S)$ of an extension $E$ at $1_A$ and a $G$-invariant extension $S$ at $i$, and transport along $i$ gives the constant intension $S$, fixed by every arrow. So $(E,i\cdot E)$ is persistent and weakly inextensible at $A$ and at $B$: a rigid coextension of any relation with extension $E$.
The entities at $A$ of each relational type form the complete atomic algebra of pairs of a set of tuples at $A$ and a union of $G$-orbits of tuples at $B$.
A graph chosen in the metatheory, paired with the empty set, is an entity at $A$.

For weakly rigid $F=(E,i\cdot E)$, a weakly rigid relation below its transport at $B$ is the constant intension of a set $D$ of transported tuples, which is the transport of $(E_D,i\cdot E_D)$ for $E_D:=\{\bar x\in E:i\cdot\bar x\in D\}$. So the weak power property of $F$ is the pair of its extension and that extension's transport, and is rigid.
The proposition true at $A$ only is a strong true atom there, its transport being $\bot$; at $B$ the tail's strong true atom serves.

With one individual, $d$ is a pinning point only, so the domains at $B$ are those of symmetric-qualitative-links-individuals-singleton, which fails Tame Rigidity at $(t\to t)\to t$ (the argument tame-rigidity of symmetric-qualitative-links), and $B$ is reachable from $A$.

With $r$ the proposition true at $A$ only: every proposition $p$ at $A$ necessarily satisfies $r\lor p=\top\lor p=\bot$, its transport being $\top$ or $\bot$, but a contingent proposition of the tail does not, so BF at $t$ fails; $r\ne\bot$ while their transports agree; and $\neg r$ is an atom whose transport $\top$ is split at $B$, so no strong atom lies below it.

shared_arguments.text: At both objects. A nonzero proposition $p$ there, pinned down by a finite $S$, contains an arrow $h$. Choose distinct $a,b\in N$ outside $S$, in a block whose label is not in $S$, and in no fibre $R(q_D)$ with $q_D\in S$. Change $h$ only off $S$: keep its values on $S$, on the blocks whose labels are in $S$ and on the fibres $R(q_D)$ with $q_D\in S$; send every label outside $S$ to $q_\top$; send $a$ and $b$ to one point, or to two distinct points; and make the map onto $N$ by way of a further block whose label is not in $S$. Into $A$, or out of $A$ into $B$, any surjection of $N$ is an arrow; out of $B$, condition (1) holds for the labels in $S$, whose fibres keep their values, and for the others, whose image is $q_\top$. Both arrows agree with $h$ on $S$ and so lie in $p$. The proposition $C_{a,b}=\{k : ka=kb\}$ is symmetric, the symmetries being injective on $N$, and pinned down by $\{a,b\}$, so it splits $p$. No proposition is an atom at either object.

shared_arguments.text: Let $Z$ be the property of propositions whose extension at an arrow into $A$ is every proposition there, and at an arrow into $B$ the set of transports $j\cdot p$ of propositions $p$ at $A$ along arrows $j:A\to B$. Its value depends on an arrow only through its target, and the symmetries there preserve it, since $s\cdot(j\cdot p)=(s\circ j)\cdot p$; so $Z$ is symmetric, pinned down by $\varnothing$, and in the domain. Every proposition $p$ at $A$ necessarily satisfies $Z$, since $h\cdot p\in Z_h$ for every arrow $h$. But at the entrance $i$ the proposition $r:=\{(f,g) : g(q_1)\text{ is a block label}\}$, symmetric and pinned down by $\{q_1\}$, is not a transport. If $j=i\circ f_j$, then $(f,g)\in j\cdot p$ iff $i\circ f\circ f_j\in p$, which depends only on $f$; but $(\mathrm{id}_N,\mathrm{id}_Q)\in r$ while $(\mathrm{id}_N,g^{\prime})\notin r$, where $g^{\prime}$ sends $q_1$ to $q_\top$ and fixes every other label, an arrow since $R(q_\top)=N$. So BF fails at type $t$.

shared_arguments.text: Let $p$ be true, pinned down by a finite $S\subseteq N$, and let $q$ be the proposition that the arrow goes into $A$ and is injective on $S$: symmetric, pinned down by $S$, and true. If $\Diamond q$ holds at an arrow $h$, then $k\circ h\in q$ for some $k$; there are no arrows from $B$ to $A$, so $h$ goes into $A$ and is injective on $S$, and it agrees on $S$ with a permutation $\sigma$ of $N$. As $p$ is symmetric and true, $\sigma\in p$, and as $p$ is pinned down by $S$, $h\in p$. So $\Box(\Diamond q\to p)$ with $q$ true: every truth is ND-necessary.

Then $r\circ c$ agrees with $1_B$ on $P$, so $r\circ c\in q$ and $\Diamond q$ holds at $c$; but $c$ sends $q_1$ to the finite label $q_{D_1}$, so $c\notin p$. So $p$ is a truth at $1_B$ that is not ND-necessary there.

shared_arguments.text: Write $\mathrm{fix}_N$ for the arrows agreeing with the identity on the finite set $N$, the least true proposition pinned by $N$, and $\delta_N$ for the arrows injective on $N$. A true symmetric proposition pinned by $N$ contains the surjections that agree on $N$ with an automorphism of the equivalence relation. The set $\delta_N$ is symmetric, pinned by $N$ and true, with $\Diamond\delta_N=\delta_N$, and every true $q$ pinned by $N$ has $\Diamond q\supseteq\delta_N$, since a surjection injective on $N$ is undone on $N$ by some surjection. So $\Box_{\ne}p$ iff $p\supseteq\delta_N$ for some $N$. Likewise $\hat\Diamond\delta_N=\delta_N$ (undo by a bijection, which returns to every truth), so $\hat{\hat\Box}$ and $\Box_{\ne}$ coincide, and BF at type $t$ holds for them by the bijection argument (a symmetric $Y$ pinned by $X_Y$ has $Y_k=Y_b$ for a bijection $b$ agreeing with $k$ on $X_Y$); by Proposition D8 of The Bounds of Possibility, $\Box_5$ implies ND-necessity. The truth that $0$ and $1$ are collapsed into one class... more precisely, with $0\sim1$, the true symmetric proposition $\{h:h(0)\sim h(1)\}$, pinned by $\{0,1\}$, is not ND-necessary, since a surjection injective on $\{0,1\}$ may separate the classes of $h(0)$ and $h(1)$; so not every truth is 5-necessary.

shared_arguments.text: At every type. Let $B$ be an entity at the target of an arrow $i$, pinned down by the finite set $M$, and choose a finite set $P$ with a map $s:M\to P$ such that $i\circ s$ is the identity on $M$, possible because $i$ is surjective. Put $A:=\{\langle\bar x,j\rangle : \langle\bar x,k\rangle\in B$ for some arrow $k$ with $k|_M=j\circ s\}$. This is well defined because $B$ is pinned down by $M$. It is pinned down by $P$ and symmetric, since $B$ is. And $i\cdot A=B$: $\langle\bar x,k\rangle\in i\cdot A$ iff $\langle\bar x,k\circ i\rangle\in A$ iff $\langle\bar x,k'\rangle\in B$ for some $k'$ with $k'|_M=k|_M$, iff $\langle\bar x,k\rangle\in B$. So every entity at every world is the transport of an entity at the evaluation point, and a relation that is necessarily true of every entity is necessarily true of all of them.

shared_arguments.text: Write $G$ for the symmetry group, which acts on the propositions by transport, $g\cdot p=\{j:j\circ g\in p\}$. For a finite set $N$ of points let $E_N$ be the set of arrows constant on $N$: a proposition in the domain, symmetric and pinned down by $N$, with $g\cdot E_N=E_{g(N)}$. Take for each $n\ge2$ a set $N_n$ of $n$ points and an arrow $j_n$ constant on $N_n$, injective off $N_n$ and taking other values there (the condition), so that the fibres of $j_n$ are $N_n$ and singletons. The orbits $O_n$ of the $E_{N_n}$ under $G$ are pairwise distinct: $E_{N_n}=E_N$ with $N=g(N_m)$ puts $j_n$ in $E_N$, so $N\subseteq N_n$, and puts $j_m\circ g^{-1}$, an arrow whose fibres are $N$ and singletons, in $E_{N_n}$, so $N_n\subseteq N$. For $A\subseteq\mathbb N$ the union $S_A$ of the $O_n$ with $n\in A$ is a $G$-invariant set of propositions, and $A\mapsto S_A$ is injective: there are continuum many $G$-invariant sets of propositions, in explicit bijection with the reals. Each $S_A$ is the value of a constant intension $Y_A$ of type $tt$, symmetric because $S_A$ is $G$-invariant, pinned down by the empty set, so in the domain, and fixed by transport along every arrow. The constant intensions whose values are the set of the $Y_A$, the order, sum and product of the reals carried over to it, and its natural numbers, with the $Y_A$ standing for $0$ and $1$, are symmetric, their values being made of fixed entities, and in the domain; they form a real number structure of type $tt$ at the evaluation point, complete since every bounded set of its elements has a least upper bound among them. So the antecedent of Analytic Necessitism holds at type $tt$. Its consequent fails there. Let $k$ be an arrow with $ka=kb$ for distinct points $a$ and $b$ (the condition at $n=2$) and $q$ the set of arrows $j$ with $ja\ne jb$: symmetric, pinned down by $\{a,b\}$, containing the identity and no arrow $j\circ k$. For $x$ of type $tt$ in the domain let $y$ agree with $x$ except at the arrows in $q$, where the top proposition is added to its value or removed from it: $y$ is symmetric and pinned down by a finite set, so in the domain, differs from $x$, and has $k\cdot y=k\cdot x$. If $\mathfrak R$ were a rigid real number structure of type $tt$, necessarily a real number structure, with carrier $X$ (Background, Analysis), an instance $x$ and this $y$ would give $k\cdot y=k\cdot x\in X_k$ by persistence, $Xy$ by inextensibility and $k\cdot y\ne k\cdot x$ by necessary distinctness: $X$ has no instance. So Analytic Necessitism fails. No choice is used.

shared_arguments.text:
Write $F_h$ for the extension of $F$ at the arrow $h$, so $(h\cdot F)_k=F_{kh}$, and $B_N(E)$ as in tame-rigidity-factorizable, whose part (1) is the criterion used throughout: a relation pinned down by $S$ with extension $E$ is weakly rigid iff it equals $B_N(E)$ for every finite $N\supseteq S$; Tame Rigidity holds at every type by that argument. Fix a type tuple.
(a) Stable sets. If a set $A$ of argument tuples is closed under the surjections fixing a finite $P$ pointwise, then $B_P(A)$ has extension $A$ and is weakly rigid, hence rigid. Given $Q\supseteq P$ and $l^{\prime}a$ with $l^{\prime}$ agreeing with $l$ on $P$ and $a\in A$ pinned down by $M$, take a surjection $u$ fixing $P$ that sends $M\setminus P$ to distinct fresh points outside $Q$, and a surjection $r$ agreeing with $l$ on $Q$ with $ru=l^{\prime}$ on $M$ (compatible finite prescriptions); then $ua\in A$ and $l^{\prime}a=r(ua)\in B_Q(A)_l$, so $B_P(A)=B_Q(A)$.
(b) Exact images. Let $F$ be weakly rigid, pinned down by $S$, with extension $E$. By weak persistence $uE\subseteq E$ for every surjection $u$ fixing $S$. For any surjection $j$, $F_j=jE$: a member $la$ of $B_S(E)_j$, with $l$ agreeing with $j$ on $S$ and $a\in E$ pinned down by $M$, is $j(ua)$ for a surjection $u$ fixing $S$ with $ju=l$ on $M$, preimages being supplied by the surjectivity of $j$.
(c) Lifting. Let $F$ be rigid, pinned down by $S$, $k$ an arrow, $N\supseteq S$ finite, and $X\le k\cdot F$ rigid, pinned down by $T$, with extension $D$. Extend $k|_N$ to a surjection $j$ whose non-singleton fibres are finitely many and finite (send the points outside $N$ bijectively onto the values not yet taken); then $j\cdot F=k\cdot F$ and $D\subseteq F_j=jE$. Let $P$ be finite, containing $N$, every non-singleton fibre of $j$, and a preimage of each point of $T$, and put $A:=\{a\in E:ja\in D\}$. For a surjection $u$ fixing $P$, $ju$ is constant on the fibres of $j$, so $ju=vj$ for a surjection $v$, which fixes $T$; so $vD\subseteq D$ by the weak persistence and pinning of $X$, and $uE\subseteq E$ by (b); hence $uA\subseteq A$. By (a), $Y:=B_P(A)$ is rigid, $Y\le F$ since $A\subseteq E$ and $P\supseteq S$, and by (b) $(j\cdot Y)_1=jA=D$. Weakly rigid relations with the same extension are identical, so $X=j\cdot Y$ with $j$ agreeing with $k$ on $N$.
(d) The power property of $F$ is persistent, and by (c) its extension at $k$ is contained in $B_N$ of its extension at the identity for every $N\supseteq S$; so it is weakly rigid by the criterion, and rigid by Tame Rigidity. So Rigid Power holds at every type. Nothing about the symmetry group is used beyond its being a group of permutations, and the individuals play no role, so the argument covers every member and variant meeting the conditions.

Write $B_N(E)$ as in tame-rigidity-factorizable. By part (1) of that argument at type $(\bar\sigma t)t$, $R$ is weakly rigid iff $\mathcal R=B_N(\mathcal R)_k$ for every arrow $k$ and finite $N$; and since $h\cdot R=R$ for every arrow $h$, part (2) then makes $R$ rigid. The inclusion $B_N(\mathcal R)_k\subseteq\mathcal R$ holds because a transport of a rigid relation is rigid, rigidity being a necessitated condition. For the converse let $Z\in\mathcal R$ be pinned down by $T$, and let $k$ and $N$ be given. The condition gives $k^{\prime}$ agreeing with $k$ on $N$ and $\sigma$ with $k^{\prime}\circ\sigma$ the identity on $T$. Then $Z^{\prime}:=\sigma\cdot Z$ is rigid, and $k^{\prime}\cdot Z^{\prime}=(k^{\prime}\circ\sigma) \cdot Z=Z$, since $k^{\prime}\circ\sigma$ agrees with the identity on $T$. So $Z\in B_N(\mathcal R)_k$. Hence Rigid Rigidity holds at every type. shared_arguments.text: At $E$ the only symmetric propositions over the arrows $E\to E$ are empty or everything, any two injections of $\mathbb N$ agreeing on a finite set up to a permutation; so the set of all arrows $E\to E$ is the atom containing $1_E$. At $O$ the symmetry group $G_O$ is pinned down by any new individual, since an injection into the old individuals cannot agree with a permutation preserving old and new at it, and is the atom containing $1_O$. No self-atom at $E$ contains an arrow $f$ into $O$: its transport along $f$ would be $G_O$, but an injection $m$ into the old individuals fixing $f(N)$ pointwise, for $N$ pinning the self-atom, is not in $G_O$ and carries $f$ to an arrow agreeing with it on $N$. So the self-atoms at $E$ sit over the atom of all arrows $E\to E$, and are atoms; at $O$, likewise, no self-atom contains an injection into the old individuals, and the symmetric pinned propositions over the arrows $O\to E$ are empty or everything, so the self-atoms there are $G_O$ and the set of all arrows $O\to E$, both atoms. Each is a strong atom: the atom at $E$ is the recorded true strong atom; $G_O$ becomes empty under an injection into the old individuals and under an arrow to $E$; the set of all arrows $O\to E$ becomes itself under an arrow $O\to O$ and the set of all arrows $E\to E$ under an arrow to $E$, atoms. At relational types a self-atom sits over one of these as the orbit of a single pair, an atom and a strong atom. So both principles hold at both objects, at every type.
