Boxed Rigid Power, for either choice of individuals. Arrows are injective; at $E$ the symmetry group is all permutations, at $O$ those preserving old and new; the arrows out of $O$ other than symmetries (exiting arrows) go to $E$ or have old range.
(a) At $E$, a rigid $F$ pinned down by $S$ has every tuple of its extension pinned down by $S$. Each tuple has a least finite support under the permutations. Suppose $z\in F_1$ has a point $n\notin S$ in it. Let $i:E\to O$ be the inclusion into the old individuals, $b$ a new point, and $r:O\to E$ an injection with $rb=n$ and $ri$ fixing $S$; so $z\in F_{ri}$. Every tuple of $F_i$ is pinned down by old points (it is $lz^{\prime}$ for an arrow $l:E\to O$, of old range). By the weak inextensibility of $i\cdot F$ at $O$, tested on $B_Q(F_i)$ with $Q\ni b$ containing $iS$ (part (1) of tame-rigidity-factorizable, which holds with several objects), $z=r^{\prime}z^{\prime\prime}$ for an $r^{\prime}$ agreeing with $r$ on $Q$ and $z^{\prime\prime}\in F_i$ pinned down by old points $M$; then $z$ is pinned down by $r^{\prime}M$, which omits $n=r^{\prime}b$ by injectivity, contradicting the least support. Support by $S$ then gives pinning by $S$, through injections agreeing on $S$ factored through permutations fixing $S$.
(b) So $X_0(A)$ ($k\mapsto kA$) is in the domain and rigid for every $A\subseteq F_1$, and $F=X_0(F_1)$. For an arrow $h$ and rigid $X\le h\cdot F$ with extension $D$, the tuples of $D\subseteq hF_1$ are pinned down by $hS$, so $X=X_0(D)$, and $X=h\cdot X_0(A)$ for $A:=\{z\in F_1:hz\in D\}$. So the power property is $X_0$ of its extension, and rigid.
(c) At $O$: let $F$ be rigid, pinned down by $S$ containing a new point. Composing with a bijection $O\to E$ and (a), each exiting arrow $h$ acts on the tuples of $F_1$ through $h|_S$, and $F_1$ is invariant under the symmetries fixing $S$; a symmetry and an exiting arrow cannot agree on $S$. At $O$, with strong atom $G_O$, $\hat\Diamond G_O=G_O$ (a member of $K$ or an arrow to $E$ cannot be brought back into $G_O$), so every truth at $O$, each containing $G_O$, is two-hat necessary. shared_arguments.text: Let $p$ be a possible proposition, pinned down by a finite $N$ and containing the arrow $h$. Take distinct points $m,m^{\prime}\notin N$ and put $q:=\{k\in p : km\sim km^{\prime}\}$, symmetric and pinned down by $N\cup\{m,m^{\prime}\}$, so in the domain, with $q\le p$. A permutation agreeing with $h$ on $N$ and sending $m$ and $m^{\prime}$ to two fresh points of one class lies in $q$, and one sending them to fresh points of different classes lies in $p$ but not in $q$, both lying in $p$ by pinning. shared_arguments.text: Write $E_k:=\{(x,y) : kx\sim ky\}$ for an arrow $k$. If $E_k$ and $E_{k^{\prime}}$ agree on a finite $M$, the map $k(m)\mapsto k^{\prime}(m)$ preserves and reflects $\sim$, so it extends to an automorphism $g$ of the equivalence relation, the classes being infinitely many and infinite, and $g\circ k$ agrees with $k^{\prime}$ on $M$; so a proposition pinned down by $M$ contains $k$ iff it contains $k^{\prime}$. And for finite sets $A$ and $B$ and arrows $k_A$, $k_B$ with $E_{k_A}$ and $E_{k_B}$ agreeing on $A\cap B$, some permutation $k$ has $E_k$ equal to $E_{k_A}$ on $A$ and to $E_{k_B}$ on $B$: amalgamate the two equivalence relations over $A\cap B$ and send each class of the result into its own class. Now let $X$ be a property of propositions, pinned down by a finite $N$, and let $\ell$ hold at $h$ iff every arrow $k$ with $E_k=E_h$ on $N$ belongs to every member of $X$'s extension at the identity. $\ell$ is symmetric and pinned down by $N$, and it entails every member. Let $q$, pinned down by $M\supseteq N$, entail every member, and let $h\in q$; suppose some $k$ with $E_k=E_h$ on $N$ lies outside some member $p$, pinned down by $P$. Take a symmetry $g$ fixing $N$ pointwise that moves each point of $P\setminus N$ inside its class to a point outside $M$. Then $g\cdot p=\{k^{\prime} : k^{\prime}\circ g\in p\}$ is a member, $X$ being fixed by $g$, it is pinned down by $g(P)$, whose intersection with $M$ lies in $N$, and $k\circ g^{-1}$, which agrees with $k$ on $N$, lies outside it. An arrow $h^{\prime}$ with $E_{h^{\prime}}$ equal to $E_h$ on $M$ and to $E_{k\circ g^{-1}}$ on $g(P)$ lies in $q$ but not in $g\cdot p$, a contradiction. So $q\le\ell$, and $\ell$ is the greatest lower bound.

shared_arguments.text: At every relational type. First, an entity $Y$ pinned down by a finite $T$ and fixed by every symmetry fixing a finite $N$ pointwise is pinned down by $N$. For $Y$'s extension at $k\circ w$ equals its extension at $k$ both when $w$ is a symmetry fixing $N$ pointwise and, by pinning, when $w$ is any permutation fixing $T$ pointwise. These $w$ generate every permutation fixing $N$ pointwise: a transposition $(a\,b)$ of points outside $N$, with $a\in T$ say, is $(a\,c)(c\,b)(a\,c)$ for $c\notin T\cup N$ in the class of $a$, where $(a\,c)$ is a symmetry fixing $N$ and $(c\,b)$ fixes $T$ if $b\notin T$ (if $b\in T$, do the same for $b$); so every finitary permutation of the points outside $N$ is generated, and every permutation fixing $N$ pointwise agrees on $T$ with one of those. Now let $X$ be countable, and let a finite $N$ pin down both $X$ and an injection $I$ of $X$ into the finite cardinalities. These are standard and fixed by every arrow, as in the group's arguments for the Axiom of Infinity, so for a symmetry $g$ fixing $N$ pointwise and a member $Y$ of $X$'s extension, $g\cdot Y$ is a member too and $I$ assigns it the cardinality it assigns $Y$; so $g\cdot Y=Y$, and every member is pinned down by $N$. Their union, taken arrow by arrow, is then symmetric and pinned down by $N$, so in the domain, and it is the least upper bound, the order being inclusion of intensions.

shared_arguments.text: No Contingency (signature Σ) fails, since the Σ-sentence $\forall\bar x\, .\,c\bar x$ denotes $a$, true and contingent; Witnessed Possibility fails for the pure formula $x=\top_\tau$, witnessed by $\top_\tau$, since $\Diamond(c=\top_\tau)$ is $\Diamond\Box a$ and $a$ is necessary at no world; Separated Structure fails with it, being equivalent to Possibly Witnessed Possibility; Independence (signature Σ) and Distinctness Maximalism (signature Σ) fail through the other relational constants: such a constant $c'$ of type $\tau'$ denotes what the closed pure term $\top_{\tau'}$ denotes, and $c'=\top_{\tau'}$ is a true identity that C(Σ) does not prove. The designated constant refutes neither: closed pure terms denote entities fixed by every arrow (Classicism, §3.5, p. 58), whereas some arrow does not fix $a$, so no closed pure term denotes $\lambda\bar x\, .\,a$.

shared_arguments.text: The symmetry group $G$ is the atom containing the identity, pinned down by the distinguished pair $0,1$. Let $k$ be a collapsing arrow and $N$ a finite set with $k(N)\supseteq\{0,1\}$, which exists since $k$ is surjective, and let $q$ be the set of arrows agreeing with $k$ on $N$ up to symmetry: symmetric, pinned down by $N$, and below the proposition $C$ of the collapsing arrows. For $h\in q$, an arrow $m$ has $m\circ h\in q$ only if some $g\circ m$ fixes $h(N)\supseteq\{0,1\}$ pointwise, which no collapsing arrow does, so $g\circ m$ and $m$ are symmetries; conversely $G\circ h\subseteq q$. So the transport of $q$ along each of its members is $G$, and $q$ is a self-atom. By the recorded argument that Atomicity (type t) fails, every nonzero pinned part of $C$ splits, so $q$ is not an atom: Self-atoms are atoms (type t) fails, and with it Self-atoms are strong atoms (type t). Self-Atomicity (type t) holds, and necessarily, there being one object: a possible proposition pinned down by $N$ contains a symmetry, and then $G$, or a collapsing arrow $k$, and then the self-atom built from $k$ and a finite $N^{\prime}\supseteq N$ with $k(N^{\prime})\supseteq\{0,1\}$. The relational form is the argument that follows.

By the draft's main theorem in its closure-operation form: the constant closure operations do not work here, and the operation used instead adds to a finite set the point coordinates of its members and then both companions of each of its points.

At type e. The property of being related to the distinguished pair is persistent and finitely pinned, and it is shown to be the only candidate coextensive with itself. But at a world collapsing the pair, its extension shrinks to a two-element fibre, and the union of the two haecceities of that fibre is persistent with the same extension there while being strictly stronger, because some arrow merges the two companions. So the rigidity criterion fails at that world.

shared_arguments.text: Confirming the draft's unwritten claim, by the splitting argument it indicates. The proposition $C:=\{h : h0=h1\}$ of the collapsing arrows is nonzero, symmetric and pinned down by $\{0,1\}$. Suppose $q\le C$ is nonzero and pinned down by a finite $N$, and take $h\in q$. Enlarge $N$ to its closure in the draft's sense, which includes $0$ and $1$, and choose a point $m$ outside it. The draft's extension step (proof of its Proposition 50) extends any $R$-coherent prescription on a closed finite set that merges $0$ with $1$ to a collapsing arrow. So there are arrows $k_1,k_2$ agreeing with $h$ on $N$ with $k_1m=k_1 0$ and $k_2m\ne k_2 0$: prescribe $h$ on the closure of $N$, send $m$ to $h0$ or to a fresh point, and send its companions to companions of its image. Both lie in $q$. The proposition $\{k : km=k0\}$ is symmetric and pinned down by $\{0,m\}$, and it contains $k_1$ but not $k_2$, so $q$ is not an atom. So nothing below $C$ is an atom. With No Pure Contingency, □Atomicity fails too, as the recorded implication from □Atomicity, Boolean Completeness and BF to Rigid Comprehension requires, BF being now established.

shared_arguments.text: At type $e$. Let $F$ be the constant property whose extension at every world is the distinguished pair $\{0,1\}$: symmetric, since the symmetry group preserves the pair setwise, pinned down by $\varnothing$, and necessarily instantiated. Suppose $G\le F$ is pinned down by a finite $N$ with every extension a singleton, so $G(h)\in\{\{0\},\{1\}\}$. Choose a surjective relation-preserving arrow $h$ that sends $0$ and $1$ to a point $p\notin\{0,1\}$ and whose preimages of $0$, $1$, their companions and the links at $0$ or $1$ avoid $N$ (take as preimages of $0$ and $1$ two points outside $N$ that are endpoints of no link in $N$; the pair's links go to companions of $p$, and surjectivity is arranged on the infinite fibres). Let $\sigma$ be the relation automorphism swapping $0$ and $1$ with their companions and links and fixing every other point. It is in the symmetry group, fixes $h(N)$ pointwise, and $\sigma\circ h$ is again an arrow. Pinning gives $G(\sigma\circ h)=G(h)$, while symmetry gives $G(\sigma\circ h)=\sigma(G(h))\ne G(h)$. The collapse argument of the group cannot reach this model, its arrows preserving sorts; the pair property sidesteps that.

shared_arguments.by: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), at Cian Dorr's request; checked and recorded by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic)
shared_arguments.text:
At type $t\to t$, with propositions as arguments, so for either choice of individuals; the argument for symmetric-range-gap with the link structure. Let $L$ be the points, $a,b$ the distinguished pair, $c\in L\setminus\{a,b\}$, and $q_{uv}:=\{h:hu=hv\}$, $Q(A):=\{q_{uv}:u,v\in A\}$. Every arrow fixes $\{a,b\}$ setwise or collapses it, so $q_{ax}=q_{bx}$; codes of pairs of points outside $\{a,b\}$ determine their pairs, by the draft's extension step (proof of its Proposition 50), which extends an $R$-coherent prescription on a closed finite set to a collapsing arrow.
Let $F_k:=Q(L)$ at every arrow: every arrow is surjective on points, so $F=X_0(Q(L))$, which is rigid. Let $Y_k:=Q(L\setminus\{kc\})$ at a symmetry $k$ and $Q(L)$ at a collapse. It is symmetric, pinned down by $\{a,b,c\}$, and equal to its $B_N$ for every finite $N$ (at a collapse, two point coordinates outside the closure of $N$ under point coordinates and companions can be sent to any two points, by the extension step), so weakly rigid. It is rigid without appeal to Tame Rigidity (which fails here): its transport along a symmetry has the same form, and along a collapse it is $F$, every later composite being a collapse.
No rigid $Z\le F$ has $Z_h=Y_1$ at a collapse $h$. Close a finite pinning set $T$ of $Z$ under point coordinates and companions, with $a,b,c\in T$, and take distinct points $x,y$ outside $hT\cup\{a,b,c\}$. Part (1) of tame-rigidity-factorizable gives $q_{uv}\in Z_1$ and a collapse $g$ agreeing with $h$ on $T$ with $g\cdot q_{uv}=q_{xy}$; so $\{gu,gv\}=\{x,y\}$ and $u,v\notin T$. No member of $T$ is a link at $u$ or $v$, $T$ being closed, so the prescription agreeing with $h$ on $T$ and sending $u$ to $c$ and $v$ to $y$, with their companions, extends to a collapse $g^{\prime}$; then $q_{cy}=g^{\prime}\cdot q_{uv}\in Z_{g^{\prime}}=Z_h$, which is not in $Q(L\setminus\{c\})$.
So the test $B_{\{a,b\}}$ of the extension of $F$'s power property (constant, since $h\cdot F=F$) necessarily holds of its instances but omits $Y$ at a collapse, every arrow agreeing with a collapse on $\{a,b\}$ being one. The power property is not weakly inextensible: Rigid Power fails.

shared_arguments.text: At the types $(e\to t)$ and $e$. Let $U:=\lambda Xy\, .\,Xy\lor\neg\exists z\, .\,Xz$, a closed term, hence in the domain, and serial. A functional subrelation $S$ of $U$ would lie in the domain at the evaluation object, so it is symmetric and pinned down by a finite set $N$. Two facts about such an $S$ (Dorr, draft, Lemma 19(iv)): every $g\in G$ fixing $N$ pointwise satisfies $g^{[\sigma]}S=S$, and symmetry gives $\langle gA,gy,g\rangle\in S$ whenever $\langle A,y,1\rangle\in S$; together, $\langle gA,gy,1\rangle\in S$. Now let $A$ be the property the condition gives for $N$. Its extension is nonempty, so $S$ relates $A$ at the identity to some $y$ in its extension. The condition gives a member $g$ of the symmetry group that fixes $N$ pointwise, fixes $A$ and moves $y$ to some $gy\ne y$, so $S$ relates $A$ to $gy$ as well, and $S$ is not functional at the identity arrow. The well-ordering of the individuals that Cian Dorr had in mind is refuted by the same two facts, but the direct route needs no derivation of a well-ordering from Relational Choice in C.

shared_arguments.text: At every type. Let $B$ be an entity at the target of an arrow $i$, pinned down by the finite set $M$, and choose a finite set $P$ with a map $s:M\to P$ such that $i\circ s$ is the identity on $M$, possible because $i$ is surjective. Put $A:=\{\langle\bar x,j\rangle : \langle\bar x,k\rangle\in B$ for some arrow $k$ with $k|_M=j\circ s\}$. This is well defined because $B$ is pinned down by $M$. It is pinned down by $P$ and symmetric, since $B$ is. And $i\cdot A=B$: $\langle\bar x,k\rangle\in i\cdot A$ iff $\langle\bar x,k\circ i\rangle\in A$ iff $\langle\bar x,k'\rangle\in B$ for some $k'$ with $k'|_M=k|_M$, iff $\langle\bar x,k\rangle\in B$. So every entity at every world is the transport of an entity at the evaluation point, and a relation that is necessarily true of every entity is necessarily true of all of them.

shared_arguments.text: At type $(t\to t)\to t$, with propositions indexed by nonpoints, so with one individual. Let $V$ be the companions and links, which every arrow maps onto $V$, and $q_{uv}:=\{h:hu=hv\}$. Codes of distinct unordered pairs of nonpoints differ: by the draft's extension step (proof of its Proposition 50), any binary assignment on finitely many nonpoints is realized by a collapse sending them to the two companions of one point. Let $C_z:=T(\{q_{zw}:w\in V\})$; it is symmetric, pinned down by $\{z\}$, rigid, and $h\cdot C_z=C_{hz}$, and $z\mapsto C_z$ is injective. Let $U_h:=\{C_z:z\in R(ha,hb)\}$, where $a,b$ is the distinguished pair and $R(p,q)$ is the link fibre over $p\ne q$ or the two companions of $p=q$. $U$ is symmetric, pinned down by $\{a,b\}$, and weakly rigid by part (1) of tame-rigidity-factorizable: at a symmetry each $B_N$ is $U_h$, and at a collapse a fresh link can be sent to either companion. At a collapse $h$ with $p:=ha=hb$, $U_h=\{C_{d_0},C_{d_1}\}$ for $p$'s companions; the rigid $T(\{C_{d_0},C_{d_1}\})$ necessarily holds of both, but after a collapse $k$ merging $d_0$ and $d_1$ it holds of $C_{kd_0}$ alone, while $U_{kh}$ has both companions' codes. So $h\cdot U$ is not weakly inextensible: $U$ is weakly rigid and not rigid.

shared_arguments.text:
At every relational type, by an adaptation of the argument recorded for the all-surjections model (symmetric-all-surjections), whose facts (1)–(3) and transversal lemma are used here. Write $0$ for the distinguished individual, $A$ for the first class of arrows (surjections with $0$ as its own only preimage) and $B$ for the second (arrows omitting $0$ from their range). $B$ is absorbing: if $h\in B$ then $i\circ h$ omits $0$, since $i0=0$ only when $i\in A$ and then $i$ sends nothing else to $0$. So the proposition $\alpha:=\{k : k0=0\}$, the class $A$, is true at $1$, pinned down by $\{0\}$, symmetric, and once false stays false.
Given $X$ pinned down by $S_X$, put $S:=S_X\cup\{0\}$ and $Y:=\lambda\bar z\, .\,\alpha\land\delta_S\land X\bar z$, with $\delta_S$ the proposition that no two members of $S$ are collapsed. $Y$ is symmetric, pinned down by $S$ and coextensive with $X$. At a world in $B$, or one collapsing $S$, $Y$ is empty there and at every world it sees. A world $i\in A$ injective on $S$ can be relabelled by a permutation fixing $0$, hence in the symmetry group, so that it fixes $S$ pointwise. For such $i$ the transversal lemma holds: $i$ is surjective, preimages of points outside $S$ lie outside $S$, the permutation $\tau$ of $\mathbb N\setminus S$ fixes $0$ and so lies in the symmetry group, which keeps the extension of $X$ at $1$ closed under $\tau\cdot$, and $i\circ\tau\in A$ fixes the pinning set of $r$. The rest of the argument, including the leading box, goes through verbatim. BF fails here, so the surjectivity used in the lemma is available only at the worlds in $A$; the conjunct $\alpha$ removes the others.

shared_arguments.text:
The argument rigid-power-surjections, adapted. Let $d$ be the distinguished individual and $B$ the others; the kind-$A$ arrows are the surjections with $d$ its own only preimage, the kind-$K$ arrows the maps into $B$; an arrow's kind is its value at $d$. Put $d$ in every pinning set below; Tame Rigidity holds at every type (tame-rigidity-factorizable).
Stable sets: if a set of tuples is closed under the kind-$A$ arrows fixing $P$, its $B_P$ is weakly rigid. In the proof take $u$ of kind $A$ fixing $P$, sending $M\setminus P$ to fresh points of $B$ outside $Q$, and $r$ of the kind of $l$; every prescribed value other than at $d$ lies in $B$, so $r$ extends to an arrow of that kind.
Exact images: call $j$ regular when it maps $B$ onto $B$; every kind-$A$ arrow is regular. For weakly rigid $F$ with extension $E$, $F_j=jE$ for every regular $j$, taking the $u$ of the exact-image step of kind $A$ fixing $S$; the values prescribed off $S$ lie in $B$ and regularity supplies preimages in $B$.
Lifting: extend $k|_N$ to a regular $j$ of $k$'s kind with finitely many non-singleton fibres, all finite, put them inside $P$, and take $T\setminus\{d\}\subseteq jP$. shared_arguments.text: Write $G$ for the symmetry group, which acts on the propositions by transport, $g\cdot p=\{j:j\circ g\in p\}$. For a finite set $N$ of points let $E_N$ be the set of arrows constant on $N$: a proposition in the domain, symmetric and pinned down by $N$, with $g\cdot E_N=E_{g(N)}$. Take for each $n\ge2$ a set $N_n$ of $n$ points and an arrow $j_n$ constant on $N_n$, injective off $N_n$ and taking other values there (the condition), so that the fibres of $j_n$ are $N_n$ and singletons. The orbits $O_n$ of the $E_{N_n}$ under $G$ are pairwise distinct: $E_{N_n}=E_N$ with $N=g(N_m)$ puts $j_n$ in $E_N$, so $N\subseteq N_n$, and puts $j_m\circ g^{-1}$, an arrow whose fibres are $N$ and singletons, in $E_{N_n}$, so $N_n\subseteq N$. For $A\subseteq\mathbb N$ the union $S_A$ of the $O_n$ with $n\in A$ is a $G$-invariant set of propositions, and $A\mapsto S_A$ is injective: there are continuum many $G$-invariant sets of propositions, in explicit bijection with the reals. Each $S_A$ is the value of a constant intension $Y_A$ of type $tt$, symmetric because $S_A$ is $G$-invariant, pinned down by the empty set, so in the domain, and fixed by transport along every arrow. The constant intensions whose values are the set of the $Y_A$, the order, sum and product of the reals carried over to it, and its natural numbers, with the $Y_A$ standing for $0$ and $1$, are symmetric, their values being made of fixed entities, and in the domain; they form a real number structure of type $tt$ at the evaluation point, complete since every bounded set of its elements has a least upper bound among them. So the antecedent of Analytic Necessitism holds at type $tt$. Its consequent fails there. Let $k$ be an arrow with $ka=kb$ for distinct points $a$ and $b$ (the condition at $n=2$) and $q$ the set of arrows $j$ with $ja\ne jb$: symmetric, pinned down by $\{a,b\}$, containing the identity and no arrow $j\circ k$. For $x$ of type $tt$ in the domain let $y$ agree with $x$ except at the arrows in $q$, where the top proposition is added to its value or removed from it: $y$ is symmetric and pinned down by a finite set, so in the domain, differs from $x$, and has $k\cdot y=k\cdot x$. If $\mathfrak R$ were a rigid real number structure of type $tt$, necessarily a real number structure, with carrier $X$ (Background, Analysis), an instance $x$ and this $y$ would give $k\cdot y=k\cdot x\in X_k$ by persistence, $Xy$ by inextensibility and $k\cdot y\ne k\cdot x$ by necessary distinctness: $X$ has no instance. So Analytic Necessitism fails. No choice is used.

At type $t\to t$, with propositions as arguments, so for either choice of individuals. For points $u,v$ let $q_{uv}:=\{h:hu=hv\}$, a symmetric proposition pinned down by $\{u,v\}$, with $h\cdot q_{uv}=q_{hu,hv}$; let $Q(A):=\{q_{uv}:u,v\in A\}$. The arrows into $B$ (the points other than the distinguished $d$) are arbitrary, so $q_{uv}=q_{xy}$ for distinct $u,v$ only if $\{u,v\}=\{x,y\}$ (an arrow merging just $u$ and $v$).
Let $F$ have extension $Q(B)$ at every arrow, and, for a fixed $c\in B$, let $Y_k:=Q(B\setminus \{kc\})$ at a symmetry $k$ (a permutation fixing $d$) and $Y_k:=Q(B)$ at an arrow omitting $d$. Both are symmetric, pinned down by $\emptyset$ and $\{d,c\}$, and equal to their $B_N$ for every finite $N$ (at an arrow omitting $d$, two fresh points can be sent anywhere in $B$), so they are weakly rigid (tame-rigidity-factorizable, part (1)) and rigid by Tame Rigidity; $Y\le F$, and $h\cdot F=F$ for every arrow $h$.
No rigid $Z\le F$ has $Z_h=Y_1=Q(B\setminus\{c\})$ at an arrow $h$ omitting $d$. Let $T\supseteq\{d,c\}$ pin $Z$ down and take distinct $x,y\in B$ outside $hT\cup\{c\}$. Then $q_{xy}\in Z_h$, so by part (1) $q_{xy}=g\cdot q_{uv}$ with $q_{uv}\in Z_1$ and $g$ agreeing with $h$ on $T$; so $gu=x$, $gv=y$ (after swapping), and $u,v\notin T$. Changing $g$ at $u$ to $c$ gives an arrow $g^{\prime}$ omitting $d$ and agreeing with $h$ on $T$, and weak persistence and pinning put $q_{cy}=g^{\prime}\cdot q_{uv}$ in $Z_{g^{\prime}}=Z_h$, which is not in $Q(B\setminus\{c\})$.
The power property $R$ of $F$ has the set of rigid $Z\le F$ as its extension at every arrow. The test $B_{\{d\}}$ of that extension necessarily holds of each of its instances, but at an arrow omitting $d$ it would contain $Y$ only as $h^{\prime}\cdot Z$ with $Z_{h^{\prime}}=Y_1$ and $h^{\prime}$ omitting $d$, which was just excluded. So $R$ is not weakly inextensible, though $F$ is rigid: Rigid Power fails.

shared_arguments.text: At every relational type: a property $F$ of type-$\tau$ entities has a least upper bound, the union of the hulls of its instances. Let $F$ be pinned down by $N\supseteq M_0$. For each instance $u$ of $F$ at the identity, its hull is the closure of $u$ under the arrows that $N$ does not separate from the identity, transported along the arrows agreeing with the identity on $N$; it is symmetric, pinned down by $N$ (by (B1), which splices an arrow agreeing with $h'$ on the instance's pinning set with $h$ on $N$), and an upper bound of $u$. Every upper bound $z$ of all the instances, pinned down by $N'$, contains every hull: given a member of a hull, (B2) supplies a symmetry fixing $N$ and moving the instance's pinning set off $N'$, whose image is again an instance (by the orbit lemma, Lemma 35), lying under $z$; and $z$, pinned down by $N'$, cannot tell the moved instance's tuple from the original. The union of the hulls is pinned down by $N$ and symmetric, so it is in the domain, and it is the least upper bound.

shared_arguments.text: Write $G$ for the symmetry group, which acts on the propositions by transport, $g\cdot p=\{j:j\circ g\in p\}$. For a finite set $N$ of points let $E_N$ be the set of arrows constant on $N$: a proposition in the domain, symmetric and pinned down by $N$, with $g\cdot E_N=E_{g(N)}$. Take for each $n\ge2$ a set $N_n$ of $n$ points and an arrow $j_n$ constant on $N_n$, injective off $N_n$ and taking other values there (the condition), so that the fibres of $j_n$ are $N_n$ and singletons. The orbits $O_n$ of the $E_{N_n}$ under $G$ are pairwise distinct: $E_{N_n}=E_N$ with $N=g(N_m)$ puts $j_n$ in $E_N$, so $N\subseteq N_n$, and puts $j_m\circ g^{-1}$, an arrow whose fibres are $N$ and singletons, in $E_{N_n}$, so $N_n\subseteq N$. For $A\subseteq\mathbb N$ the union $S_A$ of the $O_n$ with $n\in A$ is a $G$-invariant set of propositions, and $A\mapsto S_A$ is injective: there are continuum many $G$-invariant sets of propositions, in explicit bijection with the reals. Each $S_A$ is the value of a constant intension $Y_A$ of type $tt$, symmetric because $S_A$ is $G$-invariant, pinned down by the empty set, so in the domain, and fixed by transport along every arrow. The constant intensions whose values are the set of the $Y_A$, the order, sum and product of the reals carried over to it, and its natural numbers, with the $Y_A$ standing for $0$ and $1$, are symmetric, their values being made of fixed entities, and in the domain; they form a real number structure of type $tt$ at the evaluation point, complete since every bounded set of its elements has a least upper bound among them. So the antecedent of Analytic Necessitism holds at type $tt$. Its consequent fails there. Let $k$ be an arrow with $ka=kb$ for distinct points $a$ and $b$ (the condition at $n=2$) and $q$ the set of arrows $j$ with $ja\ne jb$: symmetric, pinned down by $\{a,b\}$, containing the identity and no arrow $j\circ k$. For $x$ of type $tt$ in the domain let $y$ agree with $x$ except at the arrows in $q$, where the top proposition is added to its value or removed from it: $y$ is symmetric and pinned down by a finite set, so in the domain, differs from $x$, and has $k\cdot y=k\cdot x$. If $\mathfrak R$ were a rigid real number structure of type $tt$, necessarily a real number structure, with carrier $X$ (Background, Analysis), an instance $x$ and this $y$ would give $k\cdot y=k\cdot x\in X_k$ by persistence, $Xy$ by inextensibility and $k\cdot y\ne k\cdot x$ by necessary distinctness: $X$ has no instance. So Analytic Necessitism fails. No choice is used.

Then $\Diamond\exists q\, .\,Rq$. But a transport $h\cdot q$ along an arrow with monoid coordinate $d_0$ takes the same value at $(1_K,s)$ and $(d_0,s)$, as $1_Kd_0=d_0d_0$, while $p$ does not; so no $q$ has $\Diamond Rq$, and BF fails at $t$.

At every type, at $W_0$. If $\forall x\,\Box Fx$ with $F$ pinned down by $S$, and $y$ is an entity at the target of an arrow $h$, choose an arrow $h^{\prime}$ agreeing with $h$ on $S$ that is surjective, a map being changeable off a finite set; by the section construction of the group's argument barcan-surjective, $y=h^{\prime}\cdot x$ for some entity $x$ at $W_0$, so $y$ is in $F_{h^{\prime}}$, which is $F_h$.

At $W_1$ symmetry forces a proposition to contain all the $c_n$ or none, so there are four propositions, and their transports along any $c_n$ are $\varnothing$, $\{!\}$, the arrows $W_0\to W_0$, and these with $!$. The property with all four at $1_{W_1}$ and those four transports at each $c_n$ is symmetric and pinned down by $\varnothing$, so every proposition at $W_1$ necessarily has it; but at $c_0$ the proposition $\{f:f(0)=f(1)\}$ does not. So BF at type $t$ fails at $W_1$, which $!$ reaches.

A proposition at $W_0$ pinned down by $S$ is, by symmetry, a set of patterns of identification on $S$ together with a bit for $!$: the part over $W_0$ is atomless, a pattern on $S$ splitting into its extensions to $S\cup\{a\}$, and the atom $\{!\}$ is false; so Atomicity (type $t$) and Actuality fail. Boolean Completeness holds at $W_0$ (the group's argument, with the hull conditions), and at $W_1$, which has four propositions, at type $t$; so it holds at type $t$ at every world.

shared_arguments.text: At every relational type: a property $F$ of type-$\tau$ entities has a least upper bound, the union of the hulls of its instances. Let $F$ be pinned down by $N\supseteq M_0$. For each instance $u$ of $F$ at the identity, its hull is the closure of $u$ under the arrows that $N$ does not separate from the identity, transported along the arrows agreeing with the identity on $N$; it is symmetric, pinned down by $N$ (by (B1), which splices an arrow agreeing with $h'$ on the instance's pinning set with $h$ on $N$), and an upper bound of $u$. Every upper bound $z$ of all the instances, pinned down by $N'$, contains every hull: given a member of a hull, (B2) supplies a symmetry fixing $N$ and moving the instance's pinning set off $N'$, whose image is again an instance (by the orbit lemma, Lemma 35), lying under $z$; and $z$, pinned down by $N'$, cannot tell the moved instance's tuple from the original. shared_arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), prompted by Cian Dorr, 25 October 2026
shared_arguments.text: At $W_0$ the orbit $G$ of the identity, all permutations, is pinned down by $\varnothing$ and is the only atom, the symmetric propositions over the arrows into $W_1$ refining by kernels; it is a self-atom and a strong atom, its transport along an arrow into $W_1$ being empty. So Atoms are self-atoms and Atoms are strong atoms hold at $W_0$, at every type, atoms of relational types sitting over $G$ as orbits of one pair. At $W_1$, where every symmetric intension is in the domain, the atoms are the orbits of single arrows, and the orbit of a non-injective or non-surjective $k$ is not a self-atom: some non-permutation $m$ has $m\circ k=k$ or $m\circ k$ in the orbit, as $m$ may act freely off the range of $k$. So the boxed forms of both fail at $W_0$. No self-atom at $W_0$ contains an arrow $f$ into $W_1$: the transport along $f$ would be the orbit of $1_{W_1}$, but a non-permutation fixing $f(N)$ pointwise, for $N$ pinning the self-atom, carries $f$ to an arrow agreeing with it on $N$. So the self-atoms at $W_0$ are $G$ and its relational counterparts, atoms and strong atoms; at $W_1$ the only self-atoms are the orbits of permutations, by the same reasoning, which are atoms; so Self-atoms are atoms holds at both objects. But the orbit of $1_{W_1}$ is not a strong atom there (the recorded failure of Strong Actuality at $W_1$), so Self-atoms are strong atoms (type t) fails at $W_1$ and its boxed form fails at $W_0$. Self-Atomicity (type t) fails at $W_0$: the proposition of the arrows into $W_1$ is pinned down by $\varnothing$, possible, and has no self-atom below it.

At both objects, and hence necessarily: at each, the orbit of the identity under the symmetry group is the smallest symmetric set of arrows containing it, and it is in the domain, at the first object because it is pinned down by the empty set and at the second because nothing is required there.

No rigid property of individuals is coextensive with the universal one. Weak persistence together with finite pinning forces any candidate to contain every pair whose arrow targets the second object, so its transport there is the top property. But the property of being in the range of one's arrow is symmetric and persistent, its extension at that world is everything, and the top property does not entail it, because the arrows out of the second object include non-surjections. So the rigidity criterion fails at that world.

The draft records that the type-e instance of BF is true at the base world and false at the second object, so BF is true while boxed BF is false; that is what the violation of boxed BF records, and it also refutes No Pure Contingency, since that instance is a closed pure sentence true at the base and false at an accessible world.

shared_arguments.text: Strong Actuality fails at the second object, which an arrow from the first reaches. There a true proposition contains the identity and, being symmetric, every permutation. Let $s$ be the successor map, an arrow from the second object to itself, and $k_0,k_1$ its retractions sending $n+1$ to $n$ and $0$ to $0$ and to $1$ respectively. Under $s$ the true proposition becomes one containing $k_0$ and $k_1$. The proposition that the arrow sends $0$ and $1$ to the same individual is closed under composition with permutations, so in the domain at the second object, where every symmetric intension is; it contains $k_0$ and not $k_1$. shared_arguments.text: Boxed Rigid Power, for either choice of individuals. At $W_1$ every symmetric intension is in the domain, so every $X_0(A)$ ($k\mapsto kA$) is, and a weakly rigid relation is $X_0$ of its extension; a rigid $X\le h\cdot F$ is $h\cdot X_0(A)$ for the inverse image $A$ of its extension, so Rigid Power holds there. At $W_0$ let $F$ be rigid, pinned down by a nonempty finite $S$, with extension $E_0$. For $h:W_0\to W_1$, $h\cdot F=X_0(F_h)$ is pinned down by $hS$; for an idempotent retraction $r$ onto $hS$, $F_h=F_{rh}=rF_h$, so $r$ fixes every tuple of $F_h$, and for $k,k^{\prime}$ agreeing on $hS$, $kz=krz=k^{\prime}rz=k^{\prime}z$. Through a bijection $W_0\to W_1$, every $h:W_0\to W_1$ acts on the tuples of $E_0$ through $h|_S$; with the invariance of $E_0$ under the permutations fixing $S$, $X_0(E_0)$ is in the domain, so $F=X_0(E_0)$. For a rigid $X\le h\cdot F$, $X=X_0(D)$ and $X=h\cdot X_0(A)$ with $A:=\{z\in E_0:hz\in D\}$, in the domain for the same reason; permutations are lifted by their inverses. So the power property is $X_0$ of its extension and rigid, at both objects.

shared_arguments.text: At the base world. Every transport of a proposition $p$ of the first object along an arrow $h$ into the second is pinned down by $h(N)$, for $N$ a finite set pinning $p$ down, since $k\circ h$ and $k^{\prime}\circ h$ agree on $N$ when $k,k^{\prime}$ agree on $h(N)$. Let $X$ hold, at an arrow into the first object, of every proposition, and at an arrow into the second, of the finitely pinned ones; it depends only on the codomain, so is pinned down by $\emptyset$, and it is symmetric, a permutation carrying finitely pinned propositions to finitely pinned ones. Then $\forall p\, .\,\Box Xp$ holds at the base world. But the second object's domain is unrestricted and contains $q:=\{k:k\text{ injective}\}$, symmetric and pinned down by no finite set, so after any arrow into the second object $X$ fails of $q$ and $\Box\forall p\, .\,Xp$ fails. This does not involve the individuals.

shared_arguments.text: At the second object the domains are the symmetric intensions, so a proposition is a set of functions determined by their kernels, and the least true proposition is the set $B$ of bijections. $\Diamond B$ is the set of injections (an injection is completed to a bijection by a further map), so $\Box_{\ne}p$ holds there iff $p$ contains every injection; but $\hat\Diamond B=B$, since $v\circ u$ bijective with $v$ injective forces $u$ to be bijective, so $\hat{\hat\Box}$ is the identity operator at the second object. Hence $B$ is two-hat necessary but not ND-necessary there, and the identity $\Box_{\ne}=\hat{\hat\Box}$ fails; while every truth at either object is 5-necessary: at the second because $\hat{\hat\Box}$ is the identity, at the first because every truth there is ND-necessary (recorded).

shared_arguments.text: At the types $(e\to t)$ and $e$. Let $U:=\lambda Xy\, .\,Xy\lor\neg\exists z\, .\,Xz$, a closed term, hence in the domain, and serial. A functional subrelation $S$ of $U$ would lie in the domain at the evaluation object, so it is symmetric and pinned down by a finite set $N$. Two facts about such an $S$ (Dorr, draft, Lemma 19(iv)): every $g\in G$ fixing $N$ pointwise satisfies $g^{[\sigma]}S=S$, and symmetry gives $\langle gA,gy,g\rangle\in S$ whenever $\langle A,y,1\rangle\in S$; together, $\langle gA,gy,1\rangle\in S$. Now let $A$ be the property the condition gives for $N$. Its extension is nonempty, so $S$ relates $A$ at the identity to some $y$ in its extension. The condition gives a member $g$ of the symmetry group that fixes $N$ pointwise, fixes $A$ and moves $y$ to some $gy\ne y$, so $S$ relates $A$ to $gy$ as well, and $S$ is not functional at the identity arrow. The well-ordering of the individuals that Cian Dorr had in mind is refuted by the same two facts, but the direct route needs no derivation of a well-ordering from Relational Choice in C.

shared_arguments.text: As the argument arithmetic-necessitism-extensionally-full, with the property of being a numeral supplied by pinning. The intension $Z$ whose value at each arrow $k$ out of the evaluation object is the set of numerals $\mathbf 0_\sigma,\operatorname{Suc}_\sigma\mathbf 0_\sigma,\ldots$ at the target of $k$ is pinned down by the empty set, its value depending on the arrow only through its target, and is symmetric, transport along a permutation of the points carrying numerals to numerals, as transport along any arrow does, numerals being closed terms; so it is in the domain, and so is its transport $k\cdot Z$ to any reachable object, whose extension there is exactly the numerals. Hence at every reachable object the numbers at $\sigma$, the instances of the least inductive property, are exactly the numerals, which transport to numerals; persistence and, given $\Box I^*_\sigma$, necessary distinctness are theorems of C, and inextensibility follows as in that argument. So Arithmetic Necessitism holds at every type. No choice is used.

Let $F$ and $a$ be as the condition gives them, and suppose $G\le F$ is necessarily uniquely instantiated. $G$ is in the domain, so it is symmetric and pinned down by a finite set, which we may take to contain $a$; call it $N$. If $\sigma$ in the symmetry group fixes $p$, then $\sigma\circ h$ agrees with $h$ on $N$, so $G_{\sigma\circ h}=G_h$ by pinning, while symmetry gives $G_{\sigma\circ h}=\{\sigma y\}$. So no symmetry fixing $p$ moves $y$, and by the condition $y=p$. Each model's witness takes $F$ with $p$ outside its extension at $h$, a contradiction. $\Box$Intensional Choice fails with it, by T.

shared_arguments.text: No Contingency (signature Σ) fails, since the Σ-sentence $\forall\bar x\, .\,c\bar x$ denotes $a$, true and contingent; Witnessed Possibility fails for the pure formula $x=\top_\tau$, witnessed by $\top_\tau$, since $\Diamond(c=\top_\tau)$ is $\Diamond\Box a$ and $a$ is necessary at no world; Separated Structure fails with it, being equivalent to Possibly Witnessed Possibility; Independence (signature Σ) and Distinctness Maximalism (signature Σ) fail through the other relational constants: such a constant $c'$ of type $\tau'$ denotes what the closed pure term $\top_{\tau'}$ denotes, and $c'=\top_{\tau'}$ is a true identity that C(Σ) does not prove. The designated constant refutes neither: closed pure terms denote entities fixed by every arrow (Classicism, §3.5, p. 58), whereas some arrow does not fix $a$, so no closed pure term denotes $\lambda\bar x\, .\,a$.

shared_arguments.text: At input type $tt$ and output type $t$. The full symmetric profile construction admits the property $A$ whose profile at $w:V\to W$ is the propositions moved by some symmetry of W fixing $w[N]$ pointwise. It is N-pinned, and conjugation of stabilizers proves symmetry. If a selector S for the serial membership relation were pinned by finite N, every symmetry fixing N would fix both S and A as whole intensions. The condition makes A nonempty at V. A selected member would therefore be fixed by every such symmetry, contradicting its membership in A. This uses finite supports only at the evaluation object, full admission of symmetric pinned profiles, and no external choice. The construction-specific condition witnesses and complete proof are in the writeup. So every extension has a rigid coextension, at every type.

So $\forall p\, .\,\Box Xp$ holds at the identity while $\Box\forall p\, .\,Xp$ fails.

shared_arguments.text: The constant maps form one orbit of the symmetry group, so the proposition $C$ that the arrow is constant (for individuals $a,b,c$, the proposition that $a=b=c$) is an atom: it is possible, and a symmetric proposition contains all the constant maps or none. It is not a strong atom. At a constant map $c_i$, every composite $l\circ c_i$ is constant, so $C$ transported there is $\top$; and $\top$ there lies neither below the proposition $P$ that the arrow is a permutation nor below its negation, both being possible. As an atom, $C$ has no possible proposition below it but itself, so no strong atom lies below it, and the type-$t$ Strong Atomicity fails.

shared_arguments.text: At every object the atoms are the orbits of single pairs under the symmetry group. The orbit $C$ of a collapse $c$ (in the two-object member, of the arrows $c_i:W_0\to X$) is an atom; its transport along $c$ is the set of arrows $m$ with $m\circ c$ in $C$, which includes every arrow $X\to X$, since $m\circ c$ is again a collapse, and so is not an atom there, the orbit of the permutations being a proper symmetric part. So $C$ is an atom and not a self-atom, and the only possible proposition below $C$ is $C$ itself: Atoms are self-atoms (type t) and Self-Atomicity (type t) fail. Conversely a self-atom $I$ at a relational type has, at each of its pairs $\langle k,\bar a\rangle$, a transport along $k$ that is an atom containing $\langle1,\cdot\rangle$, hence the orbit of the identity; so $m\circ k$ carries a pair of $I$ only for symmetries $m$, which excludes collapses ($c\circ c=c$) and leaves pairs at permutations, where symmetry makes $I$ the orbit of one pair, an atom, whose transport along a collapse is empty and along a permutation is an atom again: a strong atom. The same holds at every reachable object, the domains being the symmetric intensions everywhere.

shared_arguments.text: Every type is finite at every object $v$ reachable from the evaluation point, by induction on types: the individuals at $v$ are finitely many by hypothesis, the propositions at $v$ are sets of the finitely many arrows out of it, and an entity of a relational type $\bar\sigma t$ at $v$ is an intension assigning to each of those arrows a set of tuples of entities of types $\bar\sigma$ at its target, which is reachable too, so that finitely many values are available at each arrow. An ordered field has infinitely many elements, its $0$, $1$, $1+1,\ldots$ being pairwise distinct, so no real number structure exists at any reachable object, at any type. The antecedents $\Diamond\exists\mathfrak R\,.\,\operatorname{Real}_\sigma(\mathfrak R)$ of Analytic Necessitism and of Second-Order Analytic Necessitism are therefore false at every type, and both hold; and $\Box\forall\mathfrak R\,.\,\operatorname{Real}_\sigma(\mathfrak R)\to A(\mathfrak R)$ holds for every sentence $A$, so the Necessity of Second-Order Analysis holds, with the Necessity of Analysis and the Non-contingency of the Continuum Hypothesis. No choice is used.

shared_arguments.text: The numbers at a type $\sigma$ are the instances of $\mathbb N_\sigma$, the least property containing $\mathbf 0_\sigma$ and closed under $\operatorname{Suc}_\sigma$ (Background); the numerals $\mathbf 0_\sigma$, $\operatorname{Suc}_\sigma\mathbf 0_\sigma,\ldots$ are closed terms, so each denotes at every object, and transport along an arrow carries its denotation at the source to its denotation at the target. At any object $v$ reachable from the evaluation point, extensional fullness gives a property whose extension at $v$ is exactly the numerals there; it contains $\mathbf 0_\sigma$ and is closed under successor, so the numbers at $v$ are exactly the numerals, every numeral being an instance of every inductive property. Persistence of $\mathbb N_\sigma$ and, given $\Box I^*_\sigma$, the necessary distinctness of the numbers are theorems of C (the proof of necessary-rigid-comprehension-implies-arithmetic-necessitism). Inextensibility, $\Box\forall X\,.\,(\forall n\,.\,\mathbb N_\sigma n\to\Box Xn)\to\mathbb N_\sigma\le X$: at a reachable $v$ and for an arrow $j$ from $v$ to $u$, the numbers at $u$ are the numerals there, which are the transports along $j$ of the numbers at $v$, so any $X$ that necessarily holds of the numbers at $v$ holds at $u$ of the numbers there. So $\mathbb N_\sigma$ is rigid, and Arithmetic Necessitism holds at every type. No choice is used.

The extension at an arrow $h$ of the power property $\lambda X\, .\,\operatorname{Rigid}(X)\land X\le F$ is the set of rigid $X$ with $X\le h\cdot F$, the bound variable ranging over the domain untransported and the parameter transported. By the condition the rigid relations are the $X_0(E)$, and $X_0(T)\le X_0(S)$ iff $T\subseteq S$; so for rigid $F=X_0(S)$ the power property has extension $\{X_0(T'):T'\subseteq k\cdot S\}$ at $k$, while transporting its extension at the identity along $k$ gives $\{X_0(k\cdot T):T\subseteq S\}$. These coincide, since every $T'\subseteq k\cdot S$ is $k\cdot T$ for $T:=\{s\in S:k\cdot s\in T'\}$. So the power property is itself $X_0$ of its extension, hence rigid, and the same at every reachable object gives the boxed form.

shared_arguments.text: Let $v$ be any object reachable from the evaluation point and $\mathfrak R$ a real number structure at $v$ (Background, Analysis). Its completeness is tested against the subproperties of its carrier present at $v$, and by extensional fullness every subset of the carrier's extension there is the extension at the identity of one of them; so the carrier, with the extensions of $\le$, $+$ and $\times$, is a complete ordered field in the sense of the metatheory and, by Huntington's theorem, a theorem of ZF, is isomorphic to the real numbers. For the same reason the extension of $N$, the least subproperty containing $0$ and closed under adding $1$, is its set of natural numbers, that set being the extension of a subproperty. A second-order analytical sentence $A(\mathfrak R)$ quantifies over the relations among entities of the structure's type at $v$, applied to the structure's elements, and their extensions at the identity are all the relations on the carrier, again by extensional fullness. So $A(\mathfrak R)$ holds at $v$ exactly when $A$ holds in the real numbers under full second-order semantics, which depends neither on $v$ nor on $\mathfrak R$. So $X$ has two propositions, every atom there is a strong atom, and its atoms of a relational type are the intensions whose value at $1_X$ is a singleton. The arrows $h_n$ form one orbit, $g\circ h_n=h_{g(n)}$, so the propositions at $W_0$ are $\varnothing$, $a=\{1_{W_0}\}$, $H=\{h_0,h_1,h_2\}$ and $\top$. With $X$, this gives □Strong Atomicity (type $t$). At a relational type the atoms at $W_0$ are the orbits of single pairs: $\{\langle\bar y,1_{W_0}\rangle\}$, whose transport along $h_n$ is empty, a strong atom; and the orbit of $\langle\bar y,h_n\rangle$, whose transport along $h_n$ has as its value at $1_X$ the orbit of $\bar y$ under the transposition fixing $n$, an atom at $X$ just when $\bar y$ is fixed by it, and then the orbit is a strong atom. revisions.note: The argument sigma-single-top, for Σ a single constant of type $t$ denoting $\top$, stated for every interpretation of Σ by top elements, now that such interpretations have no individual constants. It replaces that argument and nc-sigma-homogeneous, which reached the same verdicts through an individual constant when the model's automorphisms carry every individual to every other. With an individual constant and no such automorphisms the verdicts were unknown in 19 models, and nowhere did the individual constants settle a verdict differently.

shared_arguments.text: Each constant of Σ denotes what the closed pure term $\top_\tau$ of its type denotes, so a closed sentence of the language of Σ denotes what the pure sentence with $\top_\tau$ in place of each constant denotes; if true it is necessary by No Pure Contingency, which holds here. So No Contingency (signature Σ) holds, and B for sentences of Σ with it: a true Σ-sentence is necessary, hence necessarily possible.
